_childDocuments_.review: I changed my mind... it's good, but it could be better. I really like the Oda Clan and the badass Nobunaga Oda, but I'd like to see other characters too. They drastically rebooted the appearance of some characters, like Hideyoshi, Tokugawa, and Honda, who now look like teens, the whole game. When Nobunaga and Mitsuhide became adults, they could have aged other characters as well.We don't see too many good innovations in this SW. Now we have generic weapons. If you want, you can grab a great spear and give it to a small character like No or a ninja. In the other hand, you can equip a ninja's weapon to big guys like Honda or Shigen, making them ridiculously fast and overpowered. You don't get that sense of your character having unique move sets, weapons, etc.The gameplay is fun, though. Even with generic weapons, you can have a lot of fun jumping into the middle of a crowd of enemies. It's satisfying to pull off combos on them.In past SW games, even if your character was fully upgraded and had a super overpowered weapon, you would probably struggle on Nightmare difficulty.In this one? Nah. If you max out your level and get a rare weapon, you can beat Nightmare easily.We don't have Survival Mode anymore. Now we have Citadel Mode instead. You just need to survive against swarms of enemies and complete some silly side quests. It's not the best mode, but it's not the worst either. I still think Survival Mode was better.The music is perfect, and I loved the story. I mean, the story is the same: the rise of Nobunaga's power, being a badass dude with an evil appearance, Mitsuhide betraying Nobunaga, and Hideyoshi seeking revenge. The only difference is that now we see why Nobunaga became so bad (in this SW, at least), and we have new stages that weren't in previous SW games.If you like the Oda Clan, you'll probably enjoy this. If not, save your money and buy Samurai Warriors 4 DX instead.I know we're facing a silly cultural war against 'woke' stuff. Now we have Teen Warriors and the 'inclusion' of Yasuke stealing the place from an old-school character. I really hope SW doesn't go  woke.Anyway, I loved and enjoyed the game, but just because it revolves around my favorite character and clan doesn't mean I should sugarcoat it. It could be better.

_childDocuments_.review: KOEI TECMO’s Warriors games have always seemed to end up offering an experience far superior to what you would expect of them on paper. You spend most of your time rushing around, killing hordes of fodder dudes at once, and focusing on hunting down single dudes who are much, much stronger than those that you’re killing thirty at a time. While, of course, slaughtering your enemies en masse on such a scale sounds like a good time, it doesn’t seem like it would necessarily hook you for very long before you find yourself moving on to greener pastures. Some years ago, Dynasty Warriors proved that it had what it took to hold serious staying power especially if you were playing with a friend and so I was more than open to jumping into Samurai Warriors 5 which seemed to better understand what drew players into Warriors than a certain catastrophic recent release that we don’t speak of in good company.Nobunaga Oda and His Amorphous Band of FriendsIt could be argued that Samurai Warriors 5 has two protagonists, though it’s clear that the majority of the work went into Nobunaga’s story. While Mitsuhide Akechi’s path is equally as well-designed, there are significantly fewer scenarios and they mostly play into adding to the overarching plot of Nobunaga’s ambitions. That said, the story that’s told between these two and the occasional other heroes that get some time in the limelight is exciting and I often found myself looking forward to the next chapter’s drama. If you’re looking for a historical tale on the era, I might recommend you take a look for that elsewhere, but if you’re hoping to find a good, fun historical-ish story, this title provides.For those going in without in-depth knowledge of the era, I’ll avoid any kind of spoilers for the story overall. What’s easy enough to detail is the general theme of the story as a whole. Nobunaga Oda, the leader of the Oda clan, has set out to unify the land and to bring all other leaders to heel, either through their oaths of loyalty or through their annihilation. As the years pass, you’ll see his inner circle go through drastic changes where old enemies become trusted allies and vice versa. At times you may even see a character swap sides more than once and every once in awhile it’ll be one that surprises you. Nobunaga’s increasing ambitions aren’t for everyone and the further he expands, the more enemies he finds, both inside and outside of his own territories.Samurai Warriors 5 didn’t disappoint my Warriors expectations with its fast-paced, over-the-top combat. Hero characters are overpowered to an extreme level making it so that the massive armies that populate the battlefield are little more than speed bumps along the way. With a roster of nearly thirty characters, there are plenty of playstyles to bounce between and each weapon feels noticeably different from those of another type. The odachi, for example, does somewhat slow but serious damage to large groupings of enemies at a single time, while the twin blades tear through a smaller selection of enemies with rapid attacks that give them little chance to retaliate. Multiple combos for each weapon type further diversify them and bring new strengths and weaknesses even as you continue to gain experience and train your roster. You’ll find out which weapons you like the feel of pretty quickly; I liked most of them with a slight preference for Nobunaga and his masterful odachi work, but I never had anywhere near as much fun using the cannon.Skill trees are something that many don’t expect in a Warriors game, though this title implements them with enough depth to please any action-RPG fan. Each character has a web that has a relatively unique lineup of skills and patterns that they’re placed into that you’re able to purchase with points. Your points are shared across your roster so you’ll have to use them sparingly unless you’re dead set on only playing a character or two, but you’ll often be able to get a feel for what strengths the character will develop by looking over their web once you gain access to them. While some characters may have plenty of passive speed bonuses, another may have several damage resistance bonuses against enemy officers, or exceptional bonuses while mounted. This system adds another layer of depth to a game that at first glance might seem quite simple and I found myself pleasantly surprised with it. I don’t imagine there will be many slamming the forums with their favorite builds as you can eventually fill out the entire web, but it’s a nice touch.Scenarios are not a simple hack-and-slack and push forward affair in Samurai Warriors 5. Every battle has multiple goals, often causing you to have to rush to another front to ensure some disaster doesn’t take place or an opportunity can be seized. I found myself more synched up with such events here than in any other entry in the genre and I can’t think of a single battle that I didn’t enjoy. Objectives tended to be straightforward and clear with little room for them to be misinterpreted. Even those that were particularly inconvenient always had a purpose with the telling of the story and I never found myself irked by them, only surprised as I nodded my head with approval. Playing in coop with objectives that are pulling you all over the map is a thrill as you can focus on different fronts if need be, though even if you’re playing alone you’re granted a supporting character of your choice in each battle that acts on their own and can be swapped to with a simple press of a key.Battlefields are populated with a variety of units that are both fighting for and against you. Spearmen, swordsman, riflemen, warrior monks, and so on all show their faces during the course of the war with varying levels of proficiency. Though none of them are on par with any of the name hero characters, they are exceptionally capable of turning the tide of battle against other generic enemies of lesser tiers and can even provide a more serious obstacle for a hero in a headlong bullrush. If I was trying to push the frontline, I’d often find myself gummed up on shield infantry or a heavy spear line when I would’ve barely had to slow down for the more standard fodder infantry. This made battle far more dynamic and made it so that the unnamed soldiers on the battlefield existed as something more than just a lawn to be mowed.

_childDocuments_.review: If you are a fan of this series and at least somewhat interested in playing this new one, I probably do not really need to sell you on it. It’s literally just the same classic Musou formula, but with a bunch of upgrades. Regardless, I'm going to give a quick rundown.This is probably the best-looking Musou game to date that isn’t a spin-off. It’s a bit more stylized, but the studio decided to go for a “Japanese painting” aesthetic and I was a bit surprised with just how fitting that is for this series. Fluid animations, great character models, detailed 2D art – it is a Musou game so it isn’t gonna blow your mind or anything, but it’s pretty good for the series.It plays just like any other Musou game before it. You have a large cast of characters to choose from and a mountain of literal thousands of enemies to mow through in EACH level. You have a bunch of different skills, combo strings, and other mechanics to aid in this destruction and new to 5 is this really cool ultimate skill system. At its core though, the combat is still immensely satisfying, even before you add all the bells and whistles. It’s not for everyone, but if you’re a fan of just racking up combos and kills in the thousands, then you’re probably going to have a good time here. Responsive movement, hits with actual impact, plenty of customization – it’s one of the more refined Musou games to date.SW5 carries over the same cons from previous Musou games: absurd damage sponging on higher difficulties, the general lack of mission variety, and the braindead AI. Fans of the series will already be familiar with all of these negatives, but it’s worth noting for newcomers.The new Citadel Mode basically takes the tried-and-true gameplay of the base game and spins it into this new castle-building grindfest where you’re dumped into different scenarios in order to farm for material. The main game already can drag a bit, so this mode was completely wasted on me given that its sole purpose is to inflate the game time through grinding. Some might enjoy it, but it’s a definite pass for me (it is optional).There’s more dialogue, more context, more character building – they actually tried to make it interesting this time around even if they can’t completely escape some past series' faults. They also upped the presentation across the board. Gone are the mostly 2D sprites talking back and forth – now we have actual 3D dialogue parts and even full-blown action cutscenes. Granted, it’s still the same old Sengoku-era history lesson, but it is a flashy one at least.Fortunately, the PC port is actually not terrible this time around (surprising for Koei Tecmo). FPS is still capped to 60, but it is a constant 60. I never had any dips, no crashes, no freezing, no technical issues like that even with hundreds of enemies on-screen flying around. There’s also a decent selection of graphical settings – including shadows, grass, bloom, and fog options to name a few. It’s much better than what we just got with the Ninja Gaiden Master Collection and I had no issues running the game at 1440p max settings on my 1070 Ti.Controls are a mixed bag. It plays great on controller and can even be rebound, but keyboard and mouse is a bit more iffy. It technically works, but the mouse movement is kinda jerky and I wasn’t a fan. There’s at least the option to rebind these controls, but this is still definitely a game I’d recommend a controller for.Samurai Warriors 5 is deserving of a light recommendation. It takes the same classic Musou formula, adds a few cool additions, and wraps it up in a nice package – the best-looking from the series thus far and a very good starting point for newcomers. Not all of its new additions might land and it still carries over the negatives from past games in the series, but it’s a worthwhile play if you’re into hack and slash games.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

_childDocuments_.review: Will preface this by saying I am a longtime fan of the Warrior series, with the Samurai Warriors game arguably being my favourite.This was always described as a reboot to the series and thats exactly what it is. I went into this not comparing it with Samurai Warriors 4 as the Samurai Warriors 5 isn't intended as a sequel. My thoughts, after playing it for 10 hours? This is a *great* reboot of the series. Visually it is stunning, the art style suits the world and the way it is portrayed. While every character can equip any weapon (allowing you to simply use your favourite moveset if you prefer) each character does have a preferred weapon, which allows for unique additions/alterations to its standard moveset. Musou Mode focuses on Nobunaga and Mitsuhide (with a story path for each) but large portions of the rest of the cast are available in most fights. Free Mode is available for any cleared Musou Mode stage during which you can use any character. Citadel Mode is where you gather various resources needed to power up the facilities of the game, such as the Dojo, Blacksmith or Shop. The higher level these facilities are the higher they can boost your characters and their gear. The characters you use during this mode will aquire relationship/trust "points" with each other, with each character having at least one of character they have a special relationship with (family, friends, rule-officer ect) which unlock events as you increase there relationship with each other. The gameplay is, at its core, good ol' Hack'n'slash, but each weapon has a unique playstyle, with weapons such as the Nagatina having long aerial combos and Spears having the best horseback moveset. Ultimate skills come in general increases to attack, speed and defense, to skills related to the weapon type (which unlock as you increase your mastery in each weapon on an individual character level) and skills unique to the character, earned via unlocking Skills on each characters skill tree. These skills can combo into movesets for some unique combo finishers if you time it right.At the end of each battle you receive various points: Stock EXP, Stock Weapons Mastery and Skill. These can be used by any character to increase there level, weapon mastery and unlock skills, meaning you can use your favourite/most powerful character to grind out these points and use them to bring your other characters up to their level, rather than painstakingly levelling each one up individually. Tl:dr, if you already like the warriors series, you will love this. If you are on the fence on the Warriors series... there is a Trial version of the game. If you like it and choose to buy the main game your progress is carried over!

This addition offers exactly what you expect from a "warriors" game but just looks more like a modern game.And is that a bad thing? Well, that depends on how picky of a critic you are. This game absolutely delivers exactly what you expect, and for me, that's all I wanted. I haven't played a "warriors" game in years, and it did not disappoint. The story was entertaining and funny, there a few well done cut scenes, and the the fighting is just pure ASMR as you improve your ability to send waves of bodies flying. There are around 40 characters, and I found 5 or so very interesting, which is plenty for me. Pros:0 - Combat0 - Character variety and customization0 - Fun story and cut scenesCons:X - 60 FPS capX - Hyper and Mounted attacks are overpowered.X - Missing story/mission beats during battle because you can't stop fighting to read the textOverall, I had a great time with this game and recommend it if you're either new or experienced with the game, especially if you can grab it on sale for $40 or less like I did.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a new engine.  It doesn't have the plethora of models that the old workhorse of WO2 and 3 had.  So it's a smaller roster.  That being said, it still feels like SW game.  I enjoy it more as I play more of it.Each weapon does have a basic moveset.  But each character brings a couple special moves to their weapons.  For instance Saito's spear has very basic moveset up to C5.  Toshiie's spear has an unique C1 and unique C5 barrage and a max of C6.  Tadakatsu's spear has an unique C1 and an unique C6 move also.  On top of this, they have Ultimate skills which are Rb+ face buttons.  Each character has a at least 1 Ultimate skill on their weapon that is unique to them.  There are more offensive Ultimate skills that are sometimes shared between characters.  For instance, Toshiie has  Autumn Snow, Avalanche, Steel Splicer, and Relentless Storm.  Tadakatsu has Autumn Snow, Avalanche, and Flames of Wrath..  And I have not fully leveled these characters yet, they may be more skills still available later.So while we do have cloned weapons, there are mechanics to alleviate the sameness that can result from it.  It's not as bad as DW6 was, where we had Ma Chao with Guan Ping's greatsword.  The art is akin to the character sketches from the SW1 and SW2 Artbooks they released back then.  It fits in nicely with the storytelling.  I am attached to the previous models and wish there were some kind of option to include the older character designs.  Ieyasu is jarring.  But I think this would only affect long term fans of the series.  And if this wasn't a numbered entry, I don't think you'd see as many people care about the redesigns.  It has some Spirit of Sanada flavor about it too, which is probably what this feels most like.  Not a numbered entry, but Spirit of Oda.There's a lot of stuff that could be better or done differently.  I really, really just wanted more 4-II stuff.  Same everything with just more stuff to do .  Instead, we got this.  And it's fun in its own right.  It's just hard to adjust to this when compared with 4-II and WO4.  If you're into this stuff, still give it a go if you can.  And drop a line to KoeiTecmo NA and tell them you'd be interested in other SW games on PC.  Maybe we could see a SW3 or SW2 Empires on Steam someday.  But the fans need to let them know, or we'll never see our old favs on pc.  Good luck.

_childDocuments_.review: I have mixed feelings on this rendition of this game, since my only prior experience to the franchise was Samurai Warriors 3. TL;DR recommend this game if you're a fan of the series, but I'd highly advise waiting for a sale if any at all because I don't find the $60 price tag worth it compared the $40 SW3.Regarding the story, I enjoyed being able to go more into the Nobunaga Arc, since that always stood out to me as a major storyline during the Sengoku period. SW3 doesn't really glance over Nobunaga outside of his decimation over the Sanada cavalry and the infamous Honnoji event. While we're introduced to new characters like Mitsuki and Toshimitsu Saitou, we also lose very important characters, specifically Ujiyasu Hojou, Nene, and Yukimura Sanada. I would argue the story is slightly worse off without the inclusion of these characters, but I didn't really feel like I was missing out on anything extremely relevant to this part of history without them.Visually, I like a lot of the newer appearances of pre-existing fighters, such as Mitsuhide Akechi, Shingen Takeda, and Yoshimoto Imagawa. Other character designs like Oichi, Tadakastu Honda, & Nagamasa Azai stand out to me because of the change from their more mature appearances to relatively "young and hip" attitudes they've donned this time around, which I wasn't a huge fan of. (in tandem to this, I think making Ieyasu Tokugawa younger was a better choice because "realistically" Ieyasu was a much younger lord than Nobunaga who always looked up to him as a role model).Voice acting was phenomenal. There weren't many characters where I'd hear them and think it wouldn't belong. Almost every voice fit with what their design was intended for and how I'd imagine them sounding with that in mind.In terms of gameplay, the mechanics were shifted slightly to make the game feel. . . easier?  Not too crazy about this.There is no spirit gauge, so you can't dash cancel attacks outside of gauntlets, but this is replaced with being able to have a Rush attack that charges a mid-to-long range distance that can cancel into your normal attacks. You are also unable to cast a Ultimate Musou attack without your warriors gauge active (which instantly depletes by using that move) but your stats feel significantly increased during warrior mode.Some of the maps feel smaller than what I remember in SW3, but I can't tell if it's because movement is overall faster/better or if SW3 maps were just enormous to begin with. I also felt there was a lack of extreme (ones that'd end the game if you didn't succeed in time) or multiple objectives that needed to be completed at once, making the map progression feel very linear. There are hidden objectives that need to be triggered, so there are times that reward exploration around the map if you do it properly.Weapon Upgrades were based off gems instead of random stat drops that you'd have to keep rolling for. Now you just have to wait to get a higher tier weapon with 6 slots and you're set : ^)I think THE worst offender of this has to be character movesets. In SW3, every character had one of three attack types (I believe it was normal, power, and special?) but every single one of their attacks were unique to their character. In this game, everyone is formatted into one of 10+ swappable weapon types (in a FE:3H style) and has to use that particular moveset outside of a few unique attacks for their preferred weapon type. To me, this absolutely ruins any sort of 'power' a character has in-game to have players feel like "Yeah, this HAS to be my main (warrior)" and has to be carried by their personality/voice lines. Also bows are ass never use them they feel clunky they don't do damage odachis do a better job of zoning than bows holy.DLC is a complete non-factor. Outside of extra stages, costumes, weapons, there is almost no need to buy them to enjoy the game. If anything, it's insulting to have you pay $35+ for a season pass when the content there isn't worth $35.

_childDocuments_.review: Its better than DW9.EDIT: Time for a proper Review.-MovesetsI've seen some negative reviews regarding movesets. Its true theres a smaller amount of weapons in the game than the usual mosou games. But every playable character has one OR multiple unique attacks with each of his preferred weapon. Meaning: They have unique movesets with each preferred weapon. In my opinion, its worth it to grind a character to unlock more preferred weapon for this character just to see its unique move with that weapon.-Base building.The game has minor basebuilding. You can grind materials which you can upgrade buildings with. Its nothing special. I wish they could expand this option more though.-Story mode.The story is good with unlockable scenrios depending on the bonus objectives you do per scenrio. It also has more stories for different characters. So its not just "The Story of Nobunaga Oda" like some people suggest. They just didnt play more than a few hours in the game.-Citadel Mode.This mode is where its at. You know the feeling when you have a favorite character, but you sometimes don't even play the character in the main story in mosou games. You can play them in this game mode and play unique base defending scenario's and grind materials / gold / horses for your story mode. Great way to level up your underleveled characters while grinding materials / gold.-ArtI'm going to divide this to 2 pieces. Cutscenes and Ingame art.~Cutscenes:There are 2 kinds of cutscenes in this game. 1 is while the narrator is talking with Animations. The other is when characters are talking to each other. The cutscenes where the narrator is talking is a letdown for me. The game is locked on 60fps but these cutscenes look like its 24 fps. But that is just the art. The ingame cutscenes, i have no problems with.~Ingame: The ingame art looks fantastic and seeing every characters Rage Mosou attack animation is very satisfying.-OveralGame runs smooth on 60fps with almost no drops. finally a game that came out in 2021 that doesnt destroy your video card. I wish it was running 144 FPS but its locked on 60 unfortunately and theres no .ini file (so far) or something to adjust that.Good job Koei. Thanks for bringing out this gem. 8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a little confused what all these negative reviews are for.I have played every samurai, dynasty and one piece warriors game so far and love how this one plays.The roster may be a little smaller than the previous titles, but the characters feel fun to play and their interactions are even engaging to watch.The combat is smooth and very impactful. Every character has a charge/clear attack, so anyone you pick can also have tons of fun clearing waves, racking up the epic kill and combo counts. The trigger abilities are flashy and break officers out of their equally strong telegraphed abilities, 1v4 officer fights can actually feel dangerous on the right difficulty setting.Being able to freely switch between two characters (when available, some story mission only allow a single character) makes things feel fantastic. You can vary combat, clear and control the entire map and never lose your combo for an entire mission. The castle defence mode makes this especially fun as you have to command both characters to keep multiple points defended from waves of officers and their ninja hoard while still trying to complete objectives around the map.I am one of the people that actually got the digital deluxe edition and do not regret it at all. I will definitely get enough hours of fun to justify the cost and will support Koei games until I die. These games continue to give me endless hours of ninja hoard killing enjoyment!

Overall unlike what they did with dw6 by tossing out the charge movesets for renbu, I feel like samurai warriors 5 just built up what was in sw4 and added in more features.Another feature newly added into sw5 for those familiar with it are skills like in pirate warriors 4 where the skills are on another menu mapped to the face buttons. Unlike pirate warriors 4 we still get our musou attack with the B/O face buttons, but we also have the options for other skills with this menu.With that said, I don't think this really deserves to be a mainline numbered title because it feels more like a "spirit of sanada" spin off, in that it mostly just focuses on nobunaga, but I guess they needed the sales so they just called it 5. _childDocuments_.review: >>I changed my review from Not Recommended to Recommended because, in hindsight, I think this game is ok and I was too harsh on it. Everything said below still applies though. The game was enjoyable enough for me to want to 100% it and I won't overlook that. Original review below:If you are new to Warriors games, you might enjoy this game, but as a longtime fan, after 100%-ing this game and playing it for over 190 hours, I have to say that I cannot recommend it. This series used to be great and now it just... exists. I tried really hard to like this game and at one point I felt really pleased with what was offered, but after the hype wore off, I realized that this game is yet another half-baked Koei Tecmo Warriors release.With this game, the developers set out to reimagine Samurai Warriors with an interesting new art style, but that's about as good as it gets. Every time Koei Tecmo decides to "reboot" something, they always cut corners, and this game is no different. Characters that used to be unique before are now just bland copies of each other with 3 unique moves each. The exciting new updated movesets that we were promised are just boring generic attacks because creativity is not something they're familiar with anymore. Of course the movesets have to be really bland and boring, otherwise they wouldn't be able to copy-paste them on other characters. The worst part about this is that the unique moves that are there show that the team was capable of making something great, but were weighed down by greedy corporate decisions. Those unique moves are all quite flashy and have a lot of personality, but the rest of the moves are really forgettable. There comes a point in the game where you just stop being excited about unlocking new characters because you quickly realize that they play exactly like characters that you already have, so it just makes you wonder why you're even playing anymore.As is the case with every Koei Tecmo "reboot", the historical figures depicted in the series have also been drasticaly redesigned to the point that they're not recognizable anymore. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, but a lot of the changes were made for the worst. Characters like Nobunaga and Mitsuhide have great new designs, but the vast majority of the cast have rather uninspired looks. Most of it is subjective, but an example of an objectively bad redesign is that of Shibata Katsuie, who is meant to be a brutal war-hardened general that you wouldn't want to mess with. While he retains that aspect of his character in the way he's portrayed, his design makes him appear to be a rather suave man, akin to Saika Magoichi from the previous games.One controversial aspect of these redesigns is that all of the figures look a lot younger than they did in previous games. This is understandable because this game covers the early Sengoku era, but as the game progresses and years pass, they retain their youthful look. The only ones that do receive updated older looks are again Nobunaga and Mitsuhide. Why they couldn't do this for all of the characters that remained alive after the time skip, I don't know. They didn't even have to give them new movesets because they're all clones of each other anyway. It ends up looking rather ridiculous when older Nobunaga interacts with young Ieyasu, or when Mitsuhide reunites with Shikanosuke after said time skip.I mentioned earlier that the way these characters are portrayed is drastically different, and so is the story. For the first time, we get to witness the rise of the Great Fool of Owari and his inevitable transformation into the Demon King. The story of this game is probably its second strongest aspect, but it's not without flaws. Because the story is much more fleshed out than usual, the presentation takes a bit of a hit as cutscenes become scarcer with every chapter you play. The majority of the story content is viewed through RPG-like idling models that talk to each other in an environment. This is nothing new to the series, but it ends up feeling a bit worse in this game because there are a lot more of them this time around, despite them being objectively a lot better than they were in the past. Key moments in the story that should've had fully-fledged cutscenes are instead presented in the generic dialogue events. Some characters don't even appear in cutscenes at all and some of them even die in these events. It's incredibly difficult to care about the death of a character when they don't even bother to create a cutscene for it. Overall, I really enjoyed the story of this game, but I'm left a bit dissatisfied.The music is arguably the best part about the game. I wouldn't say it's better than what came before it, but it's pretty good and serves its purpose. Some of the soundtracks in the past have been a bit of a mixed bag, in the sense that there were tons of great tracks, but there were also quite a lot of uninteresting ones. This game's soundtrack I'd say strikes more of a balance. While the highs are not incredibly high, the lows are not as low as they were in other games. It's a great soundtrack that I frequently jam to. I do have some small complaints, which could also be classified as nitpicks really. I felt that the mixing was a bit poor this time. The various flutes and violins often seem to have too much priority and it can feel a bit cheap at times, but it's not a big bother.Audio design, on the other hand, is quite bad this time around. The sound effects in these games are really important because they play a huge part in how the game feels. Unfortunately, a lot of the sound in this game is too "tame" and it ends up feeling like your attacks don't really land.  Even Musou attacks, which are supposed to be the flashiest move in your arsenal, feel really weak and underpowered. The sounds of the footsoldiers flying into the air, knocking over each other and hitting the ground are all too underwhelming and overall provides a much inferior gameplay experience compared to games from the past. It really pains me to have to write such a harsh review for a series I love so much, but if this is the direction the series is heading into, then I'm going to lose interest in it. There are a lot of improvements needed for this new formula to work and I really hope they manage to get it right in the next installment 7 years from now. Yes, 7 years. I waited 7 years for this game, just to be disappointed by yet another budget title. Doesn't seem like the budget stopped them from making an overpriced season pass, which by the way was announced before we even saw what the game played like. Goes to show what Koei Tecmo's priorities are.TL;DR: If you are new to these games, it's decent. If you are not, it's very mediocre and you might want to skip this one, unless you want to experience it for the story alone.For people who are into numbered scores, I would give this game a 5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Samurai Warriors 5 has all the makings of a great game, but can't manage to stop shooting itself in the shoot, getting stunlocked and shooting itself in the foot again. The devs are lucky musou players go in expecting the comforting jank, boneheaded decisions, and mindless button mashing.The core game here really is fantastic. Beat up thousands of enemy soldiers, hunt down enemy generals, capture enemy bases to stop spawns, and deal with the ever changing situations of totally realistic historical combats. New to me, was Samurai Warriors unique troop types like "Drum Captains", "Supply Captains", and "Spy Captains" that have particular buffs or abilities that make even weak mobs matter. It's a nice new layer for me and despite minor complaints I enjoyed the core game loop as much as any other Musou game.But everything around this core is a stew of conflicting ideas that each undercut one another. For example, imagine a scoring system that rewards long combos. - Imagine 45 second long cutscenes that break your combo unless you juggle a dead body on your spear. - Imagine certain moves having animation delays that automatically miss that combo time.- Imagine getting an objective "Defeat 200 enemy" immediately AFTER you cleared out all the enemy in a zone so that you can only watch for two minutes while it fails.This constant conflicting design carries into the games two major game modes Musou (story) and Citadel (Grind-For-Upgrades). The idea is fine and it's worked in other games before... But the progression is so unbalanced that neither mode actually feels good. I've had to run 15-20 story missions to unlock the next battle in Citadel so that I can unlock a higher level weapon to make story missions feel better. But by the time I get my new citadel level... I have more than enough money to immediately max out my weapon and I'm stuck waiting for the next unlock.There is a fantastic running online cooperative mode, but it can only be run if you've already completed the missions in single player, in certain missions only, that you need to leave in order to upgrade weapons.My coop partner and I kept logging in only to find out that there was more offline stuff we needed to do to continue. It was amazing for the 5 minutes it took to run a mission... and then it all it crashed again as we needed to decode the next unlock.Ultimately, this game hit the buttons you'd want from a musou game and when I was having fun... it was absolutely amazing. But that fun is uneven due to constant baffling design decisions.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: This game is great, they really upped the graphics, motion capture and slowed the game down a little bit so that the fights have a bit more weight and difficulty to them. The new art style is gorgeous in action and they applied a lot of learned lessons from previous Warriors games, specially the ones that were exclusive to Nintendo. 8,5/10 if you aren't a fan. 9.0/10 if you already like Musou games.I've been a longtime Musou/Warriors fan, starting way back with DW2 for the PS2. They had some amazing outings from the PS era (DW3, SW2, DW4), and more recently, I really enjoyed established classics like DW8, SW4 and some of the Nintendo exclusives like Warriors of Hyrule and Fire Emblem Warriors.However, since SW2 and DW3-4, I feel like they sped up and powered up the game in some very, shall I say, superficial ways. Tons of characters with increasingly ridiculous weapons, movesets that were completely busted and over powered to the point where it stopped feeling like a 'anime style chinese/japanese battlefield' and just started feeling like a 'crazy anime that makes no sense and doesn't even try to tell anything remotely comparable to the source of inspiration'. There were exceptions to this, Legend of Sanada really picked up the 'historical' part of the series and was quite a nice breath of fresh air, but I remember feeling very bored with it's other SW counterparts, specially SW4-II.Enter SW5, a soft reboot of sorts. Instead of even more characters, what we have is a smaller but more polished roster that focuses on the story of Oda Nobunaga. Nobunaga now has a far more distinct Samurai feel, wielding a Nodachi and with a very cool new move-set. Characters have amazing redesigns, more fleshed out personalities and great voice acting. Hell, even characters that I previously disliked (Hideyoshi, Nagamasa Azai) are now some of my favorites thanks to this reboot. The emphasis on Nobunaga's story is a very cool change of pace (even with some made up stuff, but that's fine), and I appreciated the better animations and cutscenes.Speaking of which, the new art style is super nice. It looks almost cell-shaded, with very flashy moves during combat and some gorgeous artwork when you pull off the super/hyper musou moves.Gameplay wise, I feel that the combat took a very solid step in the right direction. Weapons feel quite distinct, which each character having a specific favorite one with exclusive 'Ultimate Moves'. These remind me of the Hyrule Warriors/One Piece warriors series, where you can hold down the right trigger and press one of the face button to pull off either a support move or a very cool offensive move. This brings a lot of variety and personality to each character, as well as some customization since you can't bring all of your Ultimate Moves to every battle, you only have access to 4 of them.The game, as I mentioned before, is a little bit slower compared to SW4, and I see this as a huge improvement. By just slowing down your hyper attacks a little bit, Koei made sure that you feel and see what is going on a little bit better. When you pull off a 10k or 20k hut combo, you really feel like you earned it, instead of just hammering away at triangle/Y until you get there since your character is so overpowered. In SW5, you can actually feel the build up of your character's momentum, you feel the flow again, which is exactly what I felt playing DW3/SW2 back in the day. Playing as Mitsuhide with a nice build and wrecking enemies during the later stages felt incredibly satisfying.All in all, I am quite impressed with the quality they managed put into this outing. I am having a blast. I don't care about having 90 characters if most of them aren't fun to play and are there just to take up space in the roster. I like a smaller roster with more fleshed out characters and that's exactly what I got. I am really hoping they continue this formula and explore the

_childDocuments_.review: Samurai Warriors 5 has a great story with some fun reworked movesets, but as usual KOEI have cut corners and taken shortcuts that make the game fail to a wider audience. It seems this company is happy appealing to their hardcore fans unless it's another company providing the budget for the game. Pros - - Cut characters means more time for the characters that made it in the roster. A lot of KOEIs recent games are failing to grab my attention with its characters due to how many there are! I like that they had the guts to rework the entire roster, even removing staples like Yukimura and Keiji. - The combat feels really smooth and has a few advancements compared to other Warrior games. At its core it's the same mindless hack and slash, but they ramped up the moveset potential for a lot of characters, - I adore the artstyle in this game, they did a beautiful job! Graphics like this one allow the title to remain playable for years to come, as they never feel as dated as a game that's trying to look "realistic".- Music is good, but when is KOEIs music ever that bad?- I really enjoyed the story, it had some great emotional moments. I was way more invested in the characters in this game than any previous Samurai Warriors game, the stories all felt more personal thanks to the smaller roster. Cons-- Clones...Why the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ clones? Clones butcher the end game grind replayability completely. Who on earth wants to grind mindlessly with CLONES! I really don't understand how KOEI cut a tonne of characters but still made CLONES! Was the budget that tight KOEI? This was a bad move. Any game featuring this many clones is a one time play for me.- The DLC as usual with mainline KOEI games is disgusting. Nothing worthy of the price, all copy paste BS missions and mounts from previous games, gross! Age of calamity got a season pass for LESS than this one that added new movesets, characters, stages, cutscenes, challenges, skill trees and more. WHY KOEI? Why are your mainline games still missing the love and attention your crossovers are getting? If you're not going to keep them up to par why bother carrying on with them? - The side mode outside of story is this tower defence like mode that is tedious, repetitive and shallow. If the missions aren't enough to turn you away then the fact you're having to do them all with the same small amount of movesets over and over again surely will. This game had the potential to be on Dynasty Warriors 8 and Warriors Orochi 3s level in terms of quality, everything was looking great at the start of promotion, but sadly the reality is very different. The game shines with its story and a few other pros make sure it shines above games like Dynasty Warriors 9 and Warriors all stars. But the tragic amount of clones, terrible DLC and Pathetic attempt at endgame content keep this entry from being great, I would recommend this game to KOEI fans, but it's not one I'll be suggesting a newcomer plays. 6.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: SAMURAI WARRIORS 5

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay is incredibly fun and addictive. As a Musou-style game, you’ll be slashing through hordes of enemies, executing flashy combos, and unleashing powerful special attacks. The combat is fluid and satisfying, allowing you to feel like a true warrior as you conquer your foes. Each character has unique abilities, which encourages experimentation and lets you find your favorite playstyle. Plus, the addition of the new “Musou Frenzy” system adds an exciting layer of strategy to battles, enabling you to unleash devastating attacks when the moment is right.One of the game’s standout features is its engaging story mode, which dives into the lives of iconic figures from the Sengoku period. The narrative is rich and immersive, filled with historical events that add depth to the gameplay. It’s not just about fighting; you’ll also experience the personal stories and relationships that shape the characters, making the journey feel meaningful.The sound design and music also deserve a mention, as they enhance the overall experience. _childDocuments_.review: Just an absolute blast (with some notable imperfections). Let's break it down with the pros first: 1. This is easily one of the best PC ports of a Musou title. KoeiTecmo finally did us right. I've encountered virtually no stutter, have not had to fiddle blindly with gamepad settings. Yeah - this is how all KoeiTecmo PC ports *should* be. 2. Stylish graphics for a Musou title. Some of the "setting the table" cut scenes draw on a painting aesthetic, others look a bit more familiar. The character models shine, the semi cel shaded look is really evocative. I'm on a 1070ti and this game purrs. 3. Storywise this kind of feels like the Kessen 3 of Musou games, leaning heavily on legends and implied relationships far more than cut-and-dry history. Of course no Musou game is cut-and-dry history, but this feels like it takes some of the strong narrative features of Spirit of Sanada and puts them to use in a much broader way. It's sometimes a bit ridiculous, but it's also a lot of fun. 4. I still think Spirit of Sanada has a better OST, but SW 5 is definitely up there as far as Mousou titles.5. It's got enough extra stuff beyond Musou mode to keep you busy, some of it isn't that interesting but it's mostly decent or better.Cons:6. Reduced character roster. Personally this doesn't bother me, as the game is still decently filled out. 7. Weapon clonesets rather than individual weapons per character. This is probably the weakest part of the game. If, like me, you're just down for the ridiculous take on Sengoku stories and hacking and slashing your way across a map this won't be too much of an issue. But it is notable. Verdict: It's not a perfect Musou game, but it's damn good and it's a near perfect Musou PC port (which really is a big deal). I've been playing these games since DW 2 waaaaay back in the day, and this one is rock solid and a lot of fun. There really is nothing game breaking, though there are some choices (reduced roster, weapon clonesets) that can be mildly annoying. But I'm having a blast regardless. And I'm glad to have a Samurai Warriors title that is near the level of Spirit of Sanada that's broader than that game's rock solid, but singularly focused narrative.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Bland all around and lazy design and implementation. This is the most generic hack n slash of the SW franchise with zero soul to it. Skip this and do not support the direction this game is being taken in.Longer version: Samurai Warriors 5 is the latest installment of the hack n slash warriors franchise. This iteration focuses on the story of Nobunaga Oda and Mitsuhide Akechi. If you've played previous entries, you will be familiar with the story. What I don't understand is why this is the sole focus of Samurai Warriors 5 after previous versions have had much more robust story lines across multiple characters. Because of this focus on Nobunaga Oda, every other character feels like a side addition to the game and there is zero development on their story and why they are there. The whole draw to the series is to play through each character and getting a taste of what their role was throughout various battles and that has all been scrapped in SW5 in favor of focusing on Nobunaga. There are 30 something characters to choose from, which is a reduction from previous games. You would think with the roster reduction, there would be more focus on each individual character, but nope, there's zero logic behind the roster reduction. The biggest flaw in the entire game is there is no English dub/translation. This not only makes for long cutscenes as you read along, but the in-game dialogue is just constantly garbled. Gameplay-wise there is a lot of questionable decisions here. The weapons system is a long-time draw to the series and SW5 offers somewhere around 18 weapons in total. These weapons are shared across all officers, so there is nothing unique about them. Long-standing weapon and officer combinations are just gone and it creates this bland cookie-cutter feeling. For example, Nagamasa Azai has always had a giant jousting spear through all iterations of SW. Now he has a sword. A bland sword that every other character can use. The identities of the characters are tied to the weapons they previously used and to eliminate that, eliminates a huge portion of their identity.SW5 also suffers from the worst gameplay-is-ahead-of-design mechanics of all of the warriors games. In-game missions generate waaaay after you have already defeated the target and so you are left standing still sometimes waiting for the game to catch up to where you currently are. Because of this, you just simply fail some missions because you receive a specific criteria to complete it, i.e. defeat this officer with a musou attack, and the officer is already dead because the game can't keep up with you as the player. This all wouldn't be a problem, but the missions are tied to a grading system and failing these missions lowers your stage grade, which later on, you need to achieve the highest stage grade to unlock further stages. It's really horrible design. There is an additional mode called citadel mode and it is hot garbage and really magnifies this mission/stage timing issues and only serves as a grinding tool to advance the game. In addition, the season pass allows you to skip the grind by providing max level weapons and character leveling resources, it is psuedo-pay-to-win. The DLC stages are meant to be fun and light-hearted but end up being weird and annoying. One has you playing as the female characters and you have to defeat the male characters to show how good you are at cleaning! (This is no joke) Another is a test where you are asked 15 questions about the lore of the game and you need to go defeat the correct officer as your answer. This would be fine if it was general SW knowledge questions but it's questions like "Which officers appears the most in SW5???" and it's a bunch of bland no-name officers as answers. The dlc/missions are just dumb and add nothing to the game.In the end, I cannot recommend SW5. They took away everything that made the game unique. From characters, to stories, to weapons and beyond. The absence of an English dub/voiceover is a transparent cost-cut, and the overall design of not only the story but gameplay and systems is the most bland product of the Warriors franchise to date. I am a long time fan of the Warriors franchise (besides DW9, we don't talk about that one) and this was an extreme let-down. It pains me to leave this negative review. Nothing hit the mark and it was a boring grind from start to finish with zero replayabilitty. Do not support this watered-down, generic and boring game.

_childDocuments_.review: Disappointingly Dull: Samurai Warriors 5 Falls Short of ExpectationsAs a long-time fan of the Samurai Warriors series, I had high hopes for Samurai Warriors 5. Unfortunately, this latest installment left me sorely disappointed and questioning whether the franchise has lost its edge.One of the most glaring issues with Samurai Warriors 5 is its lackluster gameplay. What used to be fast-paced and exhilarating battles now feel sluggish and repetitive. The combat mechanics, which should be the heart of any Warriors game, feel outdated and uninspired. It's a shame to see a series that once innovated in the genre now feeling like it's stuck in the past.Graphically, Samurai Warriors 5 is a mixed bag. While the character designs are well-executed and visually appealing, the environments are bland and uninspired. It's as if the developers put all their effort into the character models and forgot about the world they inhabit. The result is a game that looks dated and fails to immerse players in its setting.Another major letdown is the lack of meaningful progression and customization options. In previous titles, players had the opportunity to customize their characters with different weapons, skills, and upgrades. In Samurai Warriors 5, these elements feel watered down and insignificant, robbing the game of depth and replay value.The story mode, which should be the driving force behind the game's narrative, falls flat. The storytelling feels disjointed and fails to engage players in any meaningful way. Characters lack depth, and their motivations are poorly developed, making it difficult to care about their struggles or triumphs.Overall, Samurai Warriors 5 feels like a step backward for the franchise. Its lackluster gameplay, uninspired visuals, and shallow progression systems make it hard to recommend to both longtime fans and newcomers alike. Unless significant improvements are made in future installments, it's hard to see how the series can regain its former glory. Save your money and invest your time in more fulfilling gaming experiences.

_childDocuments_.review: I have a lot of thoughts on this game, some good and some bad so I'll just throw them into this review and re-write it in a more structured way sometime in the future.The tl;dr - Game is fun, combat is solid as usual, not many characters, get for half price, very short in comparison to Samurai Warriors 4. Nō now plays like Ina and there's no Nene despite monkey man being in the game. Should've been a spin-off like Spirit of SanadaOkay, now for some rambling;It's a good game with interesting combat mechanics, however some feel gimmicky and I'm not certain many of them will stay for future releases. It doesn't feel like a mainline Warriors game and should've been released as a spin-off game like Spirit of Sanada. I don't consider it worth paying the full price as you simply won't have as much content to go through like Samurai Warriors 4 or 4-II.The voice acting is superb and the chosen voices for each character feel very fitting and appropriate.Considering the story is only focused on Oda Nobunaga's and Akechi Mitsuhide's journey, there are a decent amount of characters to choose from however compared to the previous Samurai Warriors game, the roster smaller with only 39 in SW5 and 55 in SW5, but it does make sense as many of the old roster weren't even born or old enough to pick up a weapon during Nobunaga's campaign. Unfortunately that means no Ina, Sanada bros, Kai, or Kunoichi but we do get 7 new characters that have neat designs and fit into the story naturallyMusic is very good, Japanese rock instrumentals got me bobbing my head and humming alongCombat is typical hack n slash but also includes a skill system similar to the one in DW9 that allows for easy high combos, which is needed as all officers now have a much higher health pool and bosses have multiple health bars. There's also an actually in-game effect to ally/enemy morale which can boost your attack or increase the defence and aggression of ally/enemy units. Pretty interesting and engages me a bit more during battle.Troop mechanics; spearmen block dash attacks, shield troops can block paths (break through or jump over them), cavalry can charge and knock down units, barack captains allow for reinforcements and capturing a reinforcement point actually allow for ally reinforcements to show up, riflemen will slow you down, drum corps captains will buff nearby allies or enemiesI'll add more eventuallyExtra notes;SHIBATA HAS HAIR, and nice hair tooThey made Imagawa less like a silly fat clown and more like a buff intimidating warlord

_childDocuments_.review: At the time I'm writing this, I have 39 hours of gameplay, have finished the Nobunaga story.So I'll go fast over the minor details to get to the important stuff.The new cell shading art on the effects is really nice. Give the game a new fresh looks, and doesn't make the fights cluttered or confusing. Music is nice but mostly forgettable. The stages are nice, with the importants stages being very scenic.Now for what is really interesting, I have two things to really discuss :- The gameplay :There is the usual mix of simple (X) and powerful (Y) attacks, but now mixed in are the ultimate skills, which are basically 4 specials attacks or buffs (RB + ABXY). This makes the combat quite fluid, you can jump around easily, get away from big packs of ennemies when they stunlock you.The best gameplay decision for me is how every type of weapons has it's own uniqueness. There are 15 weapons overall. All of them have specific mechanics that changes the way you are meant to play. Naginata are weapon who have air-combos, and you can press jump anytime to throw ennemies in the air and start comboing them. Cannons you can change the ammunition you use, and they have different effects. Lances are meant to be used while riding a horse. Every single one of the 15 weapons have something unique about them that changes the gameplay.But, there are only 15 weapons for 44 playables characters. And for every weapons there are only 2 categories : bronze and silver. Gold weapons are either unlocked through specific conditions, or bought on the Steam store. That is not enough weapons, there are too many clones.- The Story :Love the way the story of Nobunaga and Mitsuhide is told in a lot of details. However that is also for me the biggest downfall of this game : THERE IS ONLY A NOBUNAGA AND MITSUHIDE STORY MODE. Even if your game is supposed to focus on those two, this is not possible. This game has 44 characters and 42 of them are secondary characters who have to do with the secondary missions of Nobunaga's and Mitsuhode's stories. If you like Hideyoshi or Ieyasu it's nice because they have a lot of missions (of course, they're important). But you like Shingen Takeda, or Kenshin Uesugi, or Magoichi Saika ? Well you can go suck it, because they barely appear in the actual story. This means for example that Shingen Takeda only has a single mission where he is playable on story mode, and the rest of his leveling you will have to do on free mode.The devs promised that we would be able to "see Tadakatsu Honda become the undomitable warrior that we know him to be". This isn't true, because Tadakatsu is just a secondary characters and he barely gets any attention.Here's what I think could have been done to help solve the clones and the lack of stories : Reduce the cast. This game has already gone from 61 characters in SW:SOS to 44 in SW5. Do that even more. I've made a list and to me 20 characters have so little impact on the story that they could be shaved off and instead become "Unique unplayables NPCs".With 20 something characters to work with, you could actually take the time to give them all a story mode and the 15 weapons for 20 characters doesn't seem that horrible.If you're a fan of Musou games, I recommend SW5 because it's a beautiful story, told in a beautiful way, and the gameplay is really satisfying. If you're just looking to make yourself an opinion there are a lot of them that you could like more : Samurai Warriors 2 (a bit old, still the best SW), Dynasty Wariors 8 XL and DW6, hell even Hyrule Warriors and One Piece : Pirate Warriors 4 are masterpieces of musou gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: OverviewKOEI TECMO’s Warriors games have always seemed to end up offering an experience far superior to what you would expect of them on paper. You spend most of your time rushing around, killing hordes of fodder dudes at once, and focusing on hunting down single dudes who are much, much stronger than those that you’re killing thirty at a time. While, of course, slaughtering your enemies en masse on such a scale sounds like a good time, it doesn’t seem like it would necessarily hook you for very long before you find yourself moving on to greener pastures. Some years ago, Dynasty Warriors proved that it had what it took to hold serious staying power especially if you were playing with a friend and so I was more than open to jumping into Samurai Warriors 5 which seemed to better understand what drew players into Warriors than a certain catastrophic recent release that we don’t speak of in good company.Nobunaga Oda and His Amorphous Band of FriendsIt could be argued that Samurai Warriors 5 has two protagonists, though it’s clear that the majority of the work went into Nobunaga’s story. While Mitsuhide Akechi’s path is equally as well-designed, there are significantly fewer scenarios and they mostly play into adding to the overarching plot of Nobunaga’s ambitions. That said, the story that’s told between these two and the occasional other heroes that get some time in the limelight is exciting and I often found myself looking forward to the next chapter’s drama. If you’re looking for a historical tale on the era, I might recommend you take a look for that elsewhere, but if you’re hoping to find a good, fun historical-ish story, this title provides.For those going in without in-depth knowledge of the era, I’ll avoid any kind of spoilers for the story overall. What’s easy enough to detail is the general theme of the story as a whole. Nobunaga Oda, the leader of the Oda clan, has set out to unify the land and to bring all other leaders to heel, either through their oaths of loyalty or through their annihilation. As the years pass, you’ll see his inner circle go through drastic changes where old enemies become trusted allies and vice versa. At times you may even see a character swap sides more than once and every once in awhile it’ll be one that surprises you. Nobunaga’s increasing ambitions aren’t for everyone and the further he expands, the more enemies he finds, both inside and outside of his own territories.Surprise! This Is an RPGSamurai Warriors 5 didn’t disappoint my Warriors expectations with its fast-paced, over-the-top combat. Hero characters are overpowered to an extreme level making it so that the massive armies that populate the battlefield are little more than speed bumps along the way. With a roster of nearly thirty characters, there are plenty of playstyles to bounce between and each weapon feels noticeably different from those of another type. The odachi, for example, does somewhat slow but serious damage to large groupings of enemies at a single time, while the twin blades tear through a smaller selection of enemies with rapid attacks that give them little chance to retaliate. Multiple combos for each weapon type further diversify them and bring new strengths and weaknesses even as you continue to gain experience and train your roster. You’ll find out which weapons you like the feel of pretty quickly; I liked most of them with a slight preference for Nobunaga and his masterful odachi work, but I never had anywhere near as much fun using the cannon.Skill trees are something that many don’t expect in a Warriors game, though this title implements them with enough depth to please any action-RPG fan. Each character has a web that has a relatively unique lineup of skills and patterns that they’re placed into that you’re able to purchase with points. Your points are shared across your roster so you’ll have to use them sparingly unless you’re dead set on only playing a character or two, but you’ll often be able to get a feel for what strengths the character will develop by looking over their web once you gain access to them. While some characters may have plenty of passive speed bonuses, another may have several damage resistance bonuses against enemy officers, or exceptional bonuses while mounted. This system adds another layer of depth to a game that at first glance might seem quite simple and I found myself pleasantly surprised with it. I don’t imagine there will be many slamming the forums with their favorite builds as you can eventually fill out the entire web, but it’s a nice touch.Unforgiving BattlefieldsScenarios are not a simple hack-and-slack and push forward affair in Samurai Warriors 5. Every battle has multiple goals, often causing you to have to rush to another front to ensure some disaster doesn’t take place or an opportunity can be seized. I found myself more synched up with such events here than in any other entry in the genre and I can’t think of a single battle that I didn’t enjoy. Objectives tended to be straightforward and clear with little room for them to be misinterpreted. Even those that were particularly inconvenient always had a purpose with the telling of the story and I never found myself irked by them, only surprised as I nodded my head with approval. Playing in coop with objectives that are pulling you all over the map is a thrill as you can focus on different fronts if need be, though even if you’re playing alone you’re granted a supporting character of your choice in each battle that acts on their own and can be swapped to with a simple press of a key.Battlefields are populated with a variety of units that are both fighting for and against you. Spearmen, swordsman, riflemen, warrior monks, and so on all show their faces during the course of the war with varying levels of proficiency. Though none of them are on par with any of the name hero characters, they are exceptionally capable of turning the tide of battle against other generic enemies of lesser tiers and can even provide a more serious obstacle for a hero in a headlong bullrush. If I was trying to push the frontline, I’d often find myself gummed up on shield infantry or a heavy spear line when I would’ve barely had to slow down for the more standard fodder infantry. This made battle far more dynamic and made it so that the unnamed soldiers on the battlefield existed as something more than just a lawn to be mowed.Steam character limit restriction: check out the rest of the review in the comments or at the link below!

_childDocuments_.review: While this game improves on some things from the older games and adds some nice new mechanics, the negative far outweights the positive.Pros: - A new and refreshing artstyle. It looks especially amazing at the end of a character's frenzy musou attack.- A closer focus on the Oda's story. The earliest we've usually begun their story in any of the former games has been at the battle of Okehazama, but in this game, we don't get to that point before the seventh battle. This adds a lot more depth and nicely builds up to the Oda's gamechanging victory over the Imagawa.- Nobunaga Oda and Mitsuhide Akechi ages and changes appearances as you reach Chapter 5. These outfits look great and they even change up the gameplay a bit by giving them new musou attacks to accomodate their new preferred weapons.- Skills similar to those from Warriors Orochi 4 make an appearance, but this time they are fully interchangable. You can have four different special attacks, or four different buffs, or a mix of both. Each character (excluding UNPCs) also has their own unique special attack that no one else can use.- Hyper attacks have been changed for the better. Instead of having characters specialize in them like in Samurai Warriors 4, each character can now do up to eight hyper attacks before stopping. Hyper charge attacks have been removed, and will immediately transition into normal attacks instead. This is great for combo potential and feels smooth.- Some characters get new weapons from their SW1-4 counterparts with the best examples being Hanbei Takenaka (goes from a bladed yoyo to a wardrum that shoots out shockwaves) and Hanzō Hattori (goes from a chain sickle to a blade and shurikens. It may not be a big upgrade visually, but the new moveset is what makes it great).Cons:- Cloned movesets make an appearance, which we haven't had in ANY Samurai Warriors game thus far (the only exception is Nene and Kunoichi being half-clones of each other).- Lackluster story presentation and decisions. When a character decides to rebel or do something questionable, it usually happens less than one battle before they do it, and often without good reason (Hisahide Matsunaga as an example). This makes more sense after you've completed Nobunaga's story mode, but having to clear an entire story mode just to learn that is just baffling and stupid.- Repeated stages in both main characters' story modes. Only two characters in the game, namely Nobunaga Oda and Mitsuhide Akechi, get their own story modes. Despite this, there are still stages in the game you have to play through in BOTH story modes, which have NO distinction from each other beside maybe one or two voice lines. Playing through the same stage twice multiple times is annoying and repetitive, especially when there is nothing different on your second playthrough,- Uninteresting endgame content. Once you've cleared both story modes, as well as the Reverie chapters, the only thing you have left to do besides replay Musou Mode is Citadel Mode. This mode sucks. Every stage is the same: you defend a gate or two from approaching enemies for five minutes and complete up to three side objectives to try to get a high score. The only difference between the stages is the map layout and opposing officers, otherwise every battle is the same. You get Matsukaze (the best horse in the game) for completing all the stages, but other than that there is really no reason to play this gamemode other than to grind resources.- Grindy. The game expects you to grind your ass off in that poor excuse of a second gamemode to upgrade the different buildings to a higher level. Upgrading buildings is necessary to upgrade your characters' weapons, as well as level them up so you can unlock their full movesets and boost their stats. But doing so is time-consuming, repetitive, and uninteresting.- While Nobunaga and Mitsuhide ages at the start of Chapter 5, no one else does. The two characters Hideyoshi Hashiba and Ieyasu Tokugawa are glaring examples of this as they both look like kids when they should be looking a lot older. If not giving them entirely new costumes like the two main characters, at least change up their face and hair to make them look A LITTLE older.- A LOT of characters from SW1-4 have been cut, reducing the playable roster from 56 characters (SW4-II) to 37 (28 if you exclude all the UNPCs). This, on top of the cloned movesets, greatly harms the game's replayability.It's a fun game if played in short amounts, but the repetitive gameplay and lack of endgame content really hurts the game's quality. Enjoyment can be had, but your money is better spent elsewhere.

At most this should have been a spin-off game like Spirit of Sanada.    It is ENTIRELY focused on Oda Nobunaga...  It doesn't feature half the usual Samurai Warriors cast.  It doesn't even have Ranmaru Mori, who is explicitly Nobunaga's little butt-buddy, IN Nobunaga's personal story.  So I'll get to the main point. The point I want to rub everyone's faces in:That is a terrible thing. You might think I'm joking, if you happen to be a degenerate with sh!t taste...  but I'm not even remotely joking.  Dynasty Warriors 9 was a wonderful game which, for reasons mostly relating to people being pathetic little sh!ts with no tolerance for change, got a very bad rep it didn't deserve.  This was the opportunity to make a proper, open world Samurai Warriors game.  But since so many losers screamed and cried over DW9, instead we got served up this utter mess.  ~ It has less weapon variety than DW9 (which itself got complaints about cloned weapons, but nowhere near this bad).  ~ It has the old style of isolated stages, only even fewer than usual and recycled a bunch of times (so clone stages too). ~ As already noted it is missing half the usual cast and replaced them with a bunch of throwaway characters from psycho man's past.  ~ It even has two "routes" that are almost entirely the same, since Mitsuhide was with Nobunaga for most of the game narrative. ~ The art style is a failed attempt at replicating a Japanese painting style that has excessively thick outlines on things, but looks horribly jarring in 3D.   Oh, and the frenzy musou ending frames might seem cool until you realise those are ALSO cloned between characters of the same element. ~ The characters that have returned are nigh unrecognisable.  I had to look up a few of them because I had no idea whether I'd seen them before or not.~ The camera is janky and needs constant manual correction. ~ The minimap has no manual control mode, so it is impossible to keep it zoomed in if anything whatsoever is happening. Oh... and here comes another bonus. .More grind than I've ever encountered in any other musou game. Ranking grind in musou mode.  Objective grind in musou mode. Material grind in citadel mode. Event grinding in both modes.  Level grind. Skill point grind. Weapon mastery grind.   It is insanity.  Complete derangement. See... this is what we're stuck with. _childDocuments_.review: 12 hours in over a few sessions, and this game is a pretty satisfying Warriors entry. The art style pops, the music hits well, and every hit feels meaty. There's enough variety in the characters and movesets to keep me happy, and the combo counter and rewards encourage a constant flow of action, which is surprisingly achievable with charge attacks and good route planning on the battlefield. It's a little grindy but that feels ok for a Warriors game, and my tastes have changed over the years so that the fact that there is no English dub for the game is not a problem for me - though it does mean I have to pause battles and check the log every so often to avoid missing out on interesting dialogue. The objective popups which halt the battle are actually very useful in that regard.I played a lot of Dynasty Warriors growing up, and the Orochi crossover games, and this is my first SW game. The story is immediately more well presented than most of the DW games, and I find myself invested in Oda's path. Not sure I would recommmend highly to the average gamer, but anyone with a passing interest in the Warriors franchise, or even just generally hack and slash genres + feudal Japan, will probably find this enjoyable.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a musou game, not much to say on that front, you can expect the usual gameplay from these. Kill tons of guys at once and try to kill more of them faster.The artstyle is very nice, some songs are cool too. The animations are also very fun to sit through, even if some of the effects can feel somewhat overblown. ==== STORY MODE AND SCENARIOS ====The story mode has one cool element: Nobunaga's character and voiceactor. I really enjoyed it and if you're a fanboy of hero becomes villain stories, you'll enjoy what the story mode offers. Sadly Mitsuhide and his stages and development are not as great, always in Nobunaga's shadow, he doesn't get time to shine on his own which is to be expected considering where the story goes but still disappointing considering he was chosen to have one of the two scenario paths in this game.I do miss a character story mode for other cool daimyos like Mori, Uesugi and Takeda. All three have great stories to tell but they're not here in this game, they're relegated as enemies of Nobunaga. I would also enjoy a set of what-if scenarios, but again, nothing here.==== STAGES ====The stages are generally boring. DW4 through 8 (the ones I played) bring in moving elements to the stages, or try to be at least a little bit innovative with the gameplay and/or provide cool cutscenes for the story given. Since Samurai Warriors is based on historical events, they don't have as many cool romanticized events as ROTK does, but I'm very sure that if given the time, the dev teams can come up with some cool scenarios that isn't just two armies clashing against one another. What they do come up with often falls flat. The battle of Nagashino surprised me the most, it was a limp cavalry charge by two officers on horses towards the guns. If you can't provide cool visuals in gameplay, at least provide a decent cutscene, it's what the other musou games do. There are some stages, like the Burning of Hiei, that I found to be more evocative and fun to play through, but they were few and far inbetween.Considering the low amount of missions, it's sad that each playable character doesn't really get their own thing to do during the missions. Plus, since you control two characters per mission, you'll usually do most if not all the optional objectives in your first playthrough. When you replay through the mission with another character, you'll do the same thing with another character.==== CASTLE UPGRADING ====Unless you want to replay through the same mission multiple times, you'll be forced to upgrade your castle to use characters that aren't Nobunaga and Mitsuhide later in the game. For this you have to sit through 'defend the castle' missions that are extremely repetitive in order to farm resources for castle upgrades. You get money from story missions, but not resources, so you have to play these missions.As I said, they're boring, and it's a very archaic way of making you upgrade your stuff. The gameplay just doesn't provide enough variation to make itself fun on its own without some story beats and cool moments to accompany it. ==== CONCLUSION ====Not worth its full price, wait for a big Koei discount that reduces the price to 35€. If you like musou games and want more that isn't DW9, this is a good place to go.If you are new to musou games. Try out Dynasty Warriors 4 to 8, depending on how well you can stomach old graphics. If you want a good story, play DW7, though if you really like Nobunaga, you will enjoy Samurai Warriors 5, it's hyperfocused on his life.
