_childDocuments_.review: Terra Nil was one of those few games that I closely followed for ages, even though it's not some big budget hype machine. The clever puzzle-like gameplay which enforces some counter-intuitive strategies , plus a very wholesome and refreshing theme of restoration in the era of perpetual negativity, and Meydan's lovely soundtrack all caught my attention from when the Steam demo was released (almost 2 years ago!) I stuck around and watched the weekly dev streams for ages, seeing the demo turn into what we have today. I don't really do that much, but Terra Nil is definitely something special.As much as we all know we have the power to destroy, Terra Nil offers a reminder that we also have the power to create, even when destruction is at its worst. The only time when it is too late to create is when we give up. Maybe the exact technologies in the Terra Nil toolbox don't have real-life counterparts, but with the right willpower this is almost certainly something that could be done on Earth too-and in the meantime steps can be taken to prevent turning our planet into the Terra Nil wasteland in the first place. Even in digital form, this creation is still a rewarding experience that feels worthwhile without any sort of monetary gain or scoreboard-.With such a refreshing experience, I was hoping for a sizable supply of levels to complete. But, even before release (remember those dev streams), I had concerns for the potentially limited amount of gameplay we'd get. There are 4 different climates, each of which plays quite differently from the others, and each has one normal level and one alternate level. These 8 levels are procedurally generated, but with a fairly   which . Even if multiple generations of the same level aren't technically identical, they play with identical strategies.I do  than the 6 hours it took to 100% (including achievements), but I want to take the 4 climates we already have, then play with more varied maps which have more varied challenges. I would suggest the idea of a custom level generator, where we could manually adjust the parameters of map generation to create our own challenges. Now that could be properly infinitely replayable. None of that is to say I don't recommend the game, it is a wonderful experience despite being short, but I can understand if some folks aren't as passionate about Terra Nil and don't want to spend $25 for something that will most likely grow repetitive within 10 hours of play.For a lower price option, I also recommend the pay-what-you-want ($0 and up) 2D pixel art , which plays nearly identically to the final game's temperate climate but has 5 unique level generators for the region, instead of 2.

_childDocuments_.review: Terra Nil is an eco-conscious city-building game developed by Free Lives and published by Devolver Digital. The game sets itself apart from other games in the genre by focusing on the restoration of the environment rather than traditional city-building goals like population growth and wealth accumulation. Players take on the role of a nature spirit tasked with rejuvenating a barren wasteland and transforming it into a thriving ecosystem. From a gameplay perspective, Terra Nil succeeds in offering a refreshing take on city-building games. Rather than focusing on expansion and conquest, the game prioritises environmental restoration and preservation. The gameplay is straightforward yet satisfying, as players must balance the use of different resources to restore the land and cultivate a diverse ecosystem. The game rewards players for creating a balanced and sustainable environment, adding an educational element to the game. The game's emphasis on planning and foresight, as well as the importance of every action, encourages critical thinking and problem-solving skills.The game's art style is another highlight. The game features a beautiful, minimalist design that emphasises the beauty of nature. The use of soft colours and simple shapes contributes to the game's overall calming and peaceful atmosphere. The game's art style complements the gameplay and reinforces the message of environmental restoration. It emphasises the importance of preserving the beauty of nature and the impact of our actions on the world around us. The game's developers have clearly put a lot of effort into making the game's environment feel alive and vibrant. The attention to detail is evident in the way that the game's landscapes evolve as the player progresses, with plants and animals gradually returning to the world as the ecosystem becomes more stable.The music in Terra Nil is a perfect complement to the game's art style. The game's soundtrack is a calming, atmospheric collection of tracks that help to create a serene, peaceful atmosphere. The music is mostly instrumental, with a focus on acoustic guitars and other natural-sounding instruments that add to the game's overall aesthetic. The music complements the visuals and contributes to the overall immersion of the game. It adds an extra layer of emotional depth to the game and helps to create a more impactful experience.However, one of the main criticisms is the lack of content. While the game is enjoyable to play, it can be completed relatively quickly, with players able to finish the main objectives within a few hours. There are only a handful of maps to play on, and while the game does have some replayability in the form of alternate scenarios, it still feels somewhat limited. Some players have also criticised the game for being too easy, with the challenge level not ramping up significantly as the player progresses.The unique concept and gameplay of Terra Nil are undeniably a major highlight of the game. It offers players an interesting and different take on the city-building genre, where the main objective is to restore a wasteland into a thriving ecosystem. The game's puzzles and mechanics are well-designed, and the sense of satisfaction one gets from seeing a once-barren land teeming with life is rewarding.However, as mentioned earlier, the lack of content is a significant downside to the game. With only four maps and eight scenarios, players can finish the game relatively quickly, and the lack of replayability may not appeal to everyone. For some, this may not justify the game's price point.Ultimately, whether or not to purchase Terra Nil is a matter of personal preference.  Overall, while the game has its flaws, it is still a unique and enjoyable experience that could be worth the investment for some players.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great comfort game; everything about it is amazing. The difficulty curve of the main campaign is quite good, and the challenges within each individual stage also flow together nicely as you progress through different phases required to complete each map.The sound and graphics are beautiful. UI is nice and clean, though a bit laggy on the main menu. My experience with Terra Nil was positive overall.The game feels incomplete though. For $25, the game only has 8 stages. There are 4 main campaign challenges that are about 30-60 minutes each, and 1 remix version of each map after completing the story mode. 100% all game play and achievements in about 10 hours.What's baffling about this is the seeming ease with which additional challenges could have been created using only the features and assets already in the game; the remix stages were created simply by changing initial map parameters and the order/availability of structures the player can access.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is gripping. Its increasingly-complex puzzles set up by its very simple premise are supported by some incredibly appealing art, visual effects, and animation. The buildings are easilyA lot of options are missing. There's no way to better-highlight buildings hidden behind trees or other buildings. One of the maps, Polluted Fjord, gives you exactly 4 spots to place a starting tidal generator, one of which never reaches the mainland and includes no associated ocean-building tiles to facilitate its use. There are a lot of good options for gameplay, but no colorblind modes that I could find.The game is a little buggy. More than once I placed down a species call, decided it was the wrong move, pressed the undo button, and found the species stuck around to poke at grass. On other occasions, I reached the precipitation benchmark for a map and then precipitation did not start (which was especially frustrating when I very much needed the burst of resources rain would have provided).The game is fairly poorly tutorialized, making the figuring out of the gameplay portion of the game a puzzle all its own. Some of the text ill-explains itself unless you read each tooltip -thoroughly. The monorail in particular took a few minutes of trial and error.Despite these issues, I want more of this game. I want DLC, paid or otherwise, which I will devour. I want mapmaking tools to enable players to challenge one another to renew particularly challenging stretches of wasteland. New levels would be nice but aren't necessary-- I just want to be able to tackle the same levels with new tools. Or make my own levels, or make my own ecosystems. Whatever the next major content update for this game is, I will be watching closely and with interest.

_childDocuments_.review: Terra Nil has an idea about itself and it makes the game stand out in its genre. It's not your everyday job to save a planet and restore biomes in a way that allows different animals to thrive. It's a resource management game in its early stages, then it turns into a puzzle game with very satisfying aesthetics during biome planting, and at the very end becomes a logistic planner to clean up all left-out technology.I found Terra Nil easy to learn, with just enough challenge on the recommended difficulty to still be relaxing and enjoyable after a whole day at work. At the same time, I feel like this game is a bit short and does not provide enough replayability, but I count on devs to release some more content or maybe Workshop support. _childDocuments_.review: I'm disappointed by what I feel is ultimately more shallow and a lot less beautiful than I hoped. It plays as a strict puzzle game with definable objectives, made interesting each level only by the introduction of new mechanics. It's not that the puzzle solving loop isn't enjoyable, it is to a degree - but it's also a little tedious and ultimately unrewarding. One of the promises of those rewards is to be left with a gorgeous, sprawling, multi-biome, fauna and flora enriched space... and it just never happens. It never looks as good as it perhaps good and part of that reason is the late stage if the game loop where you need to pick up everything you put down. Doing so (dependent on the tech in the level) re-scars the land in some way. The puzzle itself is quite open ended, so there are many ways to win. It feels easy. Although you may not get all the fauna challenges because again, these are introduced late game and you may not have been building up to the specifics required to scan a zone that includes that combination of biomes. The game would benefit from showing you what you need from the start so that the player had more agency at the start of the level. By late level... you've done what you need to to surpass the first two gates... and unlikely to undo those successes for the third. Plus, as I said... picking up after yourself (a noble message) carries with it its own destructive cost to the game's visuals.It's not as pretty as Dorfromantik. It's not as puzzly as I expected. I expected an emergent game play loop to occur... but that doesn't happen. Ultimately disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: it's way too short and way too easy, but otherwise it's fantasticThings I like:The game is beautiful! The visuals are simple but pleasant to look at. The music is great too, and the way that it expands as you bring life to the wasteland until it swells as you approach completion of a map is one of my favorite audio phenomena in any game I've played.The gameplay is simple but fun. I've never played a game that was this relaxing while remaining engaging. The central conceit is one of hope. No matter how ruined the world is, not all hope is lost. Sometimes that's a message I need to be reminded of, and if you feel the same way, you might benefit from sitting down with this one for a few hours.Things I don't like:It's too short. As other reviews have mentioned, if you blitz through the game just clearing each map, you can beat the whole game in a couple hours. 100%ing it took me six hours.It's too easy. On the easiest difficulty, Gardener, you can essentially completely ignore the game's primary resource. You simply cannot fail a map without intentionally trying. On the normal difficulty, Ecologist, it is still extremely difficult to fail a map. If you've never played a strategy game of any kind in your life, then maaaybe you'll fail a map one time. There isn't much replay value. Once you've completed each of the maps (contrary to the most popular review, there are 8 maps, not 4) once, there isn't much of a reason to replay them for anything other than completionism (100% and achievement hunting) because while the maps are procedurally generated, they're still pretty much identical every time you play them.All told, get it if you want a brief little jaunt into a beautiful world of hopeful restoration, but if you're looking for a game you can play for hours and hours and hours, look elsewhere.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit 26/07/2024:There was an update with new content and redone animal system. I very much recommend this game right now. There is enough to keep you entertained for a while. It is still short and I'd like to see some random levels, but I understand that is a difficult technical challenge. ---------This is a very sincere review. I'd like to clarify from this moment that the game is good. I enjoyed it very much, but there are certain aspects that need to be addressed before I can fully recommend this game.Overall, I'd say I'm on the fence between recommend and not recommend, and here are the reasons.I DO recommend the game if: you are seeking a new experience different from pretty much all games out there, you have the money to spare, you like zen games, you like puzzle games, you don't get frustrated restarting the game from zero, and you don't mind the game being short.I DON'T recommend it if: you are looking for a 20+ hour experience, you want variety and replayability, you are on the fence about whether you like the idea or not, and you don't have the money to spend on this game without regretting the purchase.All in all, the game is very fun. There are only four regions/themes/ecosystems, and each one of them presents its own challenges and mechanics. The game has three difficulty levels. I played on medium, and it felt very easy. Don't be fooled; this isn't a completely zen game. It is much more of a puzzle experience with rewarding visuals and sound effects for solving every piece of it. The game does a very good job of explaining the mechanics and guiding you through the objectives. I only felt lost once on the last level, but it was a brain fart on my part.GAMEPLAY: At the start of a level, you recover toxic land and rivers by scrubbing toxins and irrigating the soil to create grass as groundwork for the next phase. In phase 2, you start shaping the land by using machines to create different varieties of biomes, and you're also controlling humidity and temperature while expanding the green land to the edges of the map. In phase 3, you are spotting animals by scanning regions of the map. Every animal requires a different combination of biomes, requirements, and sometimes temperature. There are six animals, and you need to spot at least three. The game is very generous on this end because until you get to this phase, you don't know the requirements, which encourages replayability but in a bad manner. In phase 3, you are also scraping all your buildings so when you leave the area there are no buildings left. After all that, you leave the area and move to the next level while the game gives you a zen view of all you've accomplished.Here's why I won't recommend the game for now: it's very short. I finished it in under 4 hours, and the game is relatively expensive for this length. What I would like to see is more levels. The game doesn't need more mechanics; it needs more variety, more combinations of those mechanics and themes. I would like to see a daily or weekly challenge map with hand-crafted challenges, support for mods, DLCs, and updates. The game has huge potential to be such a big hit if it gets a bit more work. I hope this review gets to the developers because I really want to see this game reach its full potential. If you can, please mark this review as helpful.EDIT 1: It took me less than 7 hours to complete 100% on medium, including the variants of each level. All that is left now is only 4 achievementsEDIT 2: All achievements in about 8hrsThank you!

_childDocuments_.review: If you love strategy games, have a love of animals and nature, and want to do your part in saving the planet (albeit in a fictional planet setting), then Terra Nil will be the ideal game for you. _childDocuments_.review: Terra Nil is a strange game. On the surface, it appears to be a city-builder of sorts about terraforming. Then you realize it's a puzzle game about trying to discover how you can terraform in such a way that you can meet different restoration criteria. THEN, after you've reset once or twice, you realize it's actually a strategy game about planning out those puzzle elements in as efficient way as possible. This made Terra Nil a very captivating discovery process as I went from screwing around wasting resources to really understanding how to use my tools to make a very ugly area look very pretty. The more satisfying and relaxing element of watching your dirt ball grow into an ecosystem feels earned and all the better for it.The game is split into several biomes and each of the areas function almost entirely differently, so you get this whole discovery loop about 4-5 times before the credits roll. It's a great gameplay loop and it's also why it's  that Terra Nil has very little in the way of replay value. I still very much recommend the game for the first playthrough, but I'm begging the devs to add in a mode with randomized goals, layouts, and wildlife.(Note: After this review was posted, the game has been updated with a new biome and more post-game content added, which does help with the replayability of content.)

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful, soothing puzzle game. Ever play Slipways? It's a bit like that. You get a randomly generated map and you need to logistics your way to success, which in this game means restoring a polluted wasteland to its beautiful and majestic natural state.It is definitely satisfying to work your way through a map, then look at the overall sum of the happy accidents that resulted from your efforts. You may have been focused on the logistics during the run, but once it's over (within an hour usually), you can step back and see the unique landscape you've more-or-less accidentally crafted, replete with different sub-biomes, flora, and of course, little animals tacked on at the end.Each level comes with cool optional unlocks for meeting certain conditions, like an aurora borealis or salmon spawning or something.The one thing that seems gamey and unsatisfying to me is the idea that once you hit a condition once, that thing sticks around for good. For example, snowfall requires a certain coldness of temperature and moisture level. But once you unlock snowfall, it doesn't seem to matter if you crank up the heat afterwards. It will keep snowing.NOTE: You will get the end credits after about 6 hours as there are only 4 basic regions with unique mechanics. After that, you can replay the map types on randomized maps and increase the difficulty, but they didn't seem to make an effort to randomize elements of the mechanics or bonus rewards that could theoretically lead to an endless gameplay loop. Shame.Also, the in-game resources are incorrect and unreliable at times. Imagine an in-game encyclopedia on game mechanics that tells you something that is wrong, which obscures the solution to an advanced stage. This is bad but patchable.

_childDocuments_.review: Full video review here: Terra Nil is an extremely relaxing and enjoyable "reverse city builder"/"environment restoration" strategy/puzzle game. There are three difficulty modes to accommodate all play styles, from those who want to casually figure things out to those who want a challenge that will keep you on your toes.The game mechanics are easy to understand but hard to master. The easy difficulty "Gardener" provides a good tutorial that will teach you the basics, but even on the easy mode I do think there is a bit of trial and error to figure things out (in a good way). The maps are procedurally generated, so every time you start/restart you get to play on a new terrain with new challenges. The art style is really beautiful and well done, and the soundtrack is mellow, blends well with the ambient game sounds, and isn't repetitive.I touch on this part a bit more in my video review, but I appreciate the developers' philosophy regarding the game, and I love that they are donating a portion of the profits to the Endangered Wildlife Trust.This game is 100% worth purchasing for both casual/cozy gamers and those that seek out tough strategy games!Disclaimer: I received a game code free from thee publishers for review purposes, but I played the demo a year ago and sought out this game myself!
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Not worth the price unless on a big sale and under $10. Achievements are easy to get. If you're looking for an extremely peaceful, slow paced puzzle game with great graphics, interesting mechanics, and a bit of repetitive gameplay, buy this. But if not, don't waste your money on it. You won't get much playtime honestly unless you really love min-maxing stuff.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: A really cool, but regretfully pretty short and shallow reverse city builder. It nails the vibes and general feel it was going for, but I found myself wanting more. I really think they have something powerful here, and I would love to see it fleshed out with a whole narrative, more game play mechanics, more complicated maps, and more than four levels. I would love to see what the Devs do for a Terra Nil 2, or if another Dev takes the concept and runs with it. I really think there's something here that tugs at a really deep core desire in the same way something like powerwash simulator does, but also has this environmentalist spin that makes it fresh and interesting, I would just like to see it explored more! Lets go further with it!
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely LOVE this game. Probably in my top 5 list of favourite games (and I've played alot of games). I really really REEEEEALLY hope that one day they will make an expansion because I can't get enough of the graphics, the music, the mission and the peace of putting a world back together. This is a breath of fresh air.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Very peaceful, somewhat confusing at first, but VERY rewarding when you finally reclaim each of the areas.Several different types of place to reclaim (tropical, temperate, polar, etc.) Each level is a kind of puzzle and has its own level of complexity, which I love!Finally a game about creating something, doing something useful.I only wish we could reclaim our own planet similar to these. A man can dream!
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I'm always on the lookout for environmental restoration games. Terra Nil is a refreshing entry in the emerging ecology genre. Fun and moderately challenging but a little clunky at times. The different biomes, animals, and plants are cute and it feels good to restore the landscape. Like many others I think the game is currently (3/29/23) lacking content. I found myself wishing there was more to the game such as more diversity, maps, and challenges. Also, the instantaneousness of restoration felt odd to me. It seemed like it should take a while, a progression, or as they say in ecological restoration circles: a succession. Forests and grasslands just popping up instantly felt weird.Anyway, I'm glad the game is out there. Everyone should play it!
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: 100% Enjoyed this game. It's short, which is ok, but it's peaceful and right up my alley. You take a barren wasteland and make it habitable for life again. The graphics are cute, not overly realistic so my computer had zero issues running the game. If you're wanting something that'll pass the time without stressing you out, check this game out. I loved the demo, I love the official release, I plan on playing more than just the four hours and redoing everything time and time again to see what different map layouts I can get.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I tried the Terra Nil demo a while ago & loved it, it went straight onto my wish list. I picked it up in the wholesome games sale recently and I am SO glad that I did!!I've been playing on Gardener difficulty, enjoying the relaxing & interesting game play - and it really does fit the "wholesome" category! Rebuilding an environment from scratch, seeing the plants re-inhabit the world, followed by different animal species is really wonderful. I'm so glad I didn't forget about this game after playing the demo so long ago.I can't recommend Terra Nil more!!
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Great for casual gamers. Really enjoying this one. Once you finish the four maps, it gives different, more challenging starting conditions which basically gives you another four maps that require much more planning and understanding of the mechanics. But there's something about this that isn't frustrating when you get stuck. You eventually get is by restarting/re-randomizing the map of one of the four regions until you figure it out.Also nice to have an eco game that doesn't throw in politics, agendas, global warming blame, and all that nonsense. It's simply a nice nature game set on an enjoyable puzzle mechanic.Highly recommend this one if you're looking for a small download and a few hours to kill.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Love this little game. I'm not the best at puzzle games (as evidenced by my performance in the challenge levels) but it's well worth your time if a quiet puzzle game is something you like, or would like to try. Some people are complaining about the price, I think it's worth the cost. I've gotten a good 15+ hours out of it now, and with more content hopefully coming later, there's even more to look forward to.Great job, Free Lives!
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: There doesn't seem to be much to this game. You just position the various pieces of equipment properly and the barren wasteland transforms into a beautiful landscape. But, unfortunately, I didn't get very far in it. There didn't seem to be any goal to work toward other than "make everything green." It didn't keep my interest but was fun while it did.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly relaxing and oddly fulfilling. If you love nature, plants, trees and animals this game lets you enjoy bringing them back to a barren landscape. It is one of those games which is oddly zen like trimming a bonsai. Each level has specific features and challenges but is procedurally generated within those limits so you can replay again and again. In my opinion the only thing it's missing is the ability to make custom maps to challenge yourself or perhaps share with other players.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Was my favourite after-work decompress game, when I really needed something quick and comforting.After the Vita Nova update, I don't like it anymore. It used to be a reverse city builder, now it's an animal manager. Each animal has a name (unnecessary), only it's not the name of the animal, it's the name of the whole herd? I can no longer click the animals to make them do cute animations. The animal managing is so complex and time-consuming, I was excited for the new maps, but now I can't even finish the first levels. I'll be downgrading to the previous version for the more casual minigame vibe.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: The company advertised Terra Nil as "reverse city builder." I came into the game with expectations of endless hours of relaxing biome building game-play. This isn't that, and It's turned into a short and sweet puzzle game. It's not bad, but I can't recommend this game, because it's not what was originally advertised. Do you like puzzles? Buy this game. Do you like relaxing music? Buy this game. Do you like pixel style artwork? Buy this game. Do you like city builders? Don't buy this game. At the end of the day, I'm glad I purchased the game to support the developer's intentions, I just think the video game community has strict standards about how much content a gamer should get for $25. The price is worth the money if you go into the game knowing you're getting a pretty chill puzzle experience, but it isn't worth the price if you want to endlessly build pretty landscapes.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: It's OK, but, not engrossing, and not so much an ecology game as a puzzle game.  I am pretty much finished with it already.  Far too expensive, even at sale price, for the amount of use I have had from it.  I expect I will try again, but, not yet.  I guess I was hoping for something like the ecology game, where we had to manage a National Park, which I used to play with my grandchildren, on disk, 30 years ago.  This is not as realistic, or anywhere near as beautiful.  Over all I am disappointed and bored rather than relaxed which is why I cannot recommend this.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Devs responded to initial launch experience of having a very limited amount of gameplay. The newer missions have unique mechanics and the maps are challenging. This game has a fun gameplay loop, and while the puzzles aren't impossible- its a very satisfying game to play. I'm pretty sure this is a small team, and they have so far done a lot to optimize their game and bring in new content-- innovative gameplay/concepts should be rewarded and I believe this game is worth the price.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: 5/10Maybe I was expecting something more, but this got old fast. Not exactly a strategy game - more a platform version of a strategy game. Each level is a one-off, meaning you start repeating a lot of the same moves & steps. Different environments give different technology, but the small level sizes mean there is no real sense of creation.Fun for short bursts, but not something you would spend hours on
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: This is such an interesting concept for a game! It's just so darn hard for me. It feels like probably there is something fundamental that I'm missing here, some essential game mechanic I'm missing. I just can't beat even the lower levels.I can't recommend this game in its current state, but I think if it had an extended tutorial mode I would be willing to give it another try.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I have been waiting for this game for a while. (2021) I loved the demo (2102) and was very excited to see the launch. I will recommend this game before I get into any criticisms. Its beautiful relaxing puzzle game and I cant wait to play more. But that is my first and main complaint. There are only 4 regions with 2 areas. That's 8 puzzles for a $20 game. I have 4 slow hours and im already into the last 3 puzzles. I really hope there is more hiding in the post game but I don't think there is. So I just wonder what took 2 years from the demo? The demo was just the fist level and aside from the new stage to find the animals the game seems about the same. There are also a few bugs, the dredgers don't properly connect to existing monorail towers. Some of the building don't properly show the cost to place. These are minor and didnt affect my ability to play. I am hoping DLC and more levels follow soon, keep up the work Free Lives!
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know what I thought Terra Nil *was*, I just know I didn't like it.  All I can say is that looking at screenshots and reading the descriptions I'm not even sure I actually played it.  It may just be the introduction to the game fails at being compelling but I was not engaged enough to keep going.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a very chill and satisfying puzzle game. A few continental levels will require you to think differently, but they are not that much harder than the others. Watching biomes getting restored bit by bit with animals coming back, and cleaning your stuff is without a doubt what makes this game stand out. You can aim for the Platinum in 10-18h depending on the difficulty you are playing. Definitely would recommend. 9/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. While not perfect, the concept of restoring an ecosystem and then leaving no trace is refreshing when many sim games are building/destroying. I have a biology background and I think this game has potential as an educational tool. My main complaint is that more guidance about the mechanics during the tutorial  is needed. I thought I saw pop up hints once or twice, but they popped up and disappeared so quickly that I am not sure if they exist or not. Overall though, this is a fun game I can see myself spending hours playing.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: The game is fun and relaxing. For me, it does have replayability-value. I keep coming back to playing whenever I want a relaxing time. If you're only into problem-solving though, there may be too little content for you as of now. It took me about 36 hours to play through all the difficulties and get all the achievements ( I played slowly, though). If you're looking for a lovely, pretty-looking game to relax  and satisfy you, this is the right game for you. If you're looking for a challenging city-builder, you may be disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Makes me sad to leave this review, I so wish there was a "Yes but no" option. I have to agree that at $24.99 for 8 hours of game play that isn't particularly complex is rough.The game itself was good, love the concept, but it could use a little more depth. I feel like if this were ultimately expanded to include an "open world" or huge type map that you really had to work for, and with a bit more complexity in the mechanics,  then the price would be justified and it would feel more complete. If enjoy simulation puzzle types, it is great, and if it's in your budget to blow the money, then do it. But if you watch your dollars to game ratio, wait for it to be on sale
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Some might say the game is a bit overpriced for the amount of content, but nevertheless - it's a great game, that brought me a decent amount of joy, so I consider this money well spent.Interesting puzzle, which probably also has some resemblance with city builders, but doing the opposite.The theme, visuals, sounds, gameplay - all great and captivated me when I've first played the demo. The actual game feels just as good as the demo.Who likes games with chill atmosphere yet quite complicated tasks - it is for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful and chill game. Graphics and music are top notch. Will put you in a great mood.Gameplay is innovative. It's a base-building game where you end up with no base at the end.Having played more than my share of Factorio and Satisfactory, it's nice to restore nature for a change :DTakes about 8 hours to finish in easy mode, a lot more in hard mode if you like a challenge. (You'll have to restart maps a few times before you succeed).
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very relaxing game. as is with Townscaper, Dorfromantik and co. it aims at being visually pleasing while doing some tasks of balancing environments and eco-systems. The play time of the main 4 levels is about 4-8hours depending on difficulty and wether one rushes it or goes for a complete finish. In my opinion it could be a little cheaper as others have also said before, however it still has good potential for further maps and development so I for my part hope there will be new regions to discover in the future.As far as I can see there aren't really any bugs though I had a problem at several points where one loses the game by doing something too early (don't wanna spoiler) and you don't get told, resulting in having to restart the region since you can't reverse some processes (SPOILER: the problem has to do with Lava getting turned into stone). Maybe it's actually wanted to be that way but I found it to be kind of fustrating the first time. But hey it kind of also poses a challenge and maybe I was just too incautious.Other than that it really is fun to play and I can defenitely recommend the game as long as it is on sale or something. Hope this helps, have fun!
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I'm really conflicted about recommending the game, but I on the whole I don't think I can recommend. I keep having game crashes while playing it, which was the tipping point for me. Beyond that though a lot of the design of the game keeps interrupting the gameplay loop so you never get the feeling that you're understanding and mastering game systems. Notably the game is constantly adding new mechanics or tweaks so your prior understanding isn't helpful, and as the level progresses in phases you have no way of knowing what is needed to set yourself up for success in the next phase. There are levels where the undo button is just how you have to play it. Overall the game is kinda fun, but it keeps getting in the way of itself over and over again. It feels like the core satisfying loop isn't enough and instead of expanding on that loop they just keep adding fiddly little things that detract rather than add.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Terra Nil is a wonderful game. Not overly complex, but complex enough to be interesting. The concept of revitalizing an area and then leaving it, leaving no trace behind, is really fun and rewarding when you get to appreciate this pristine wilderness you have created. I wish it was longer, so I was happy to see there is a big update coming. The music is great too! Reminded me of Breath of the Wild, it has that similar slightly melancholy feel. Really lovely game, highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: This game is my stoned play of choice. If I've been hammering away at work all day, and I've smoked a bowl but I'm not ready to go straight into reading myself to sleep, Terra Nil with garlic popcorn and a cup of decaf mocha is clutch, especially with a nature documentary going on my other screen. Nominating this one for the 2023 Sit Back & Relax Award. Hoping to nominate it for the Labor of Love Award in the future. Please hit us with some more content. I'd love a feature where we could save our favorite coordinates for ease of access, just some nice quality of life improvements.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: The first 4 maps have different buildings to discover with different mechanics. It's a little odd that they roll the credits at the half-way point (4 maps out of 8), but I'm finding the later maps interesting and sufficiently challenging. The buildings and terrain are a mix of those found in previous levels. One thing I hope they fix is that you can "restart phase" by choice, but if you run out  of "money", it only lets you restart from the very beginning of the map. Give the demo a try to see if you like it. Terra Nil and chill.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I was looking forward to this game and it didn't let me down. It's a really fun interpretation of the city building/strategy sim. I love the idea of restoring nature and ecosystems. The game has a simple loop and easy to learn mechanics. But it's still challenging to find new/better ways to do things and it feels a little different each time.I'm also a big fan of the art style, graphics, and music! If this game catches your eye then give it a shot! If you're on the fence, then check out some reviews or gameplay footage. I'm very satisfied and still enjoying my time with it :3
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: First thing to state: It's hard to vote positive or negative in this case, it's more like neutral with a slight negative touch.Pro:* Original idea* Nice and relaxing atmosphere* I enjoyed delving into the different biomesCon:* The game is quite short, I have finished all scenarios (four coming in two variations, eight in total) in ~ 10 h* This is fine for a small puzzle game but then it should be more like ~ 15 € instead of 25 €
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Very pleasant and relaxing. The puzzle elements are casual and the challenge is minimal, but it's more about the serenity of the natural aesthetic than anything else. Starting with an empty husk and ending with a vibrant pixel ecosystem is satisfying, especially after a stressful day. Don't go into this expecting something complex, emergent, or dynamic, because its none of those things. It's more of a simple canvas that you can draw on using the given tools while working towards the level's objectives.As of this writing, there's 4 main levels with unique themes, and 4 bonus levels that iterate on each original level. Each restoration takes under an hour unless your pace is very relaxed or you're self-imposing additional challenges on yourself.Personally, I don't think it's worth $25 at this stage. The quality is there but there content isn't. $20 is a fair price (and what I paid) if you want to support the devs, but I think $15 is really where this game should land.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: The reviews generally aren't wrong - the game is short. That doesn't deserve a negative rating though. For $37AUD, I got 12 hours of relaxing entertainment (100%'d all achievements). If I was to watch 12 straight hours of movies, it would cost me more than $37.The game is different, interesting, and has a different type of problem solving. You never feel rushed, and the game encourages you to slow down and enjoy the view.I do wish you could save a reclamation mid-progress. I had trouble setting aside a full hour on occasion so many locations I have now played multiple times due to how it saves. Not a big issue since it was so relaxing to do them again.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game soo bad, but the procedural generation killed it.I played the tutorial map x2 and on both tries I couldn't achieve an optional objective because the map didn't spawn with the features to do so. Then I tried the next map and I couldn't even finish it because there weren't enough "hills". I ended up asking for a refund. Hopefully the devs will address this in the future, but for now stay away.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Lovely Visuals, Concept and Soundtrack. Personally I feel like a larger map with a more intricate, long stretching progression would help this game to become an outstanding one. Right now I think the game is, relative to its price, lacking content but with more development I am sure that it could become a great option for people looking to build and manage.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Terra Nil is, easily, one of the most touching and beautiful games of all time.There's not a single aspect of this game I could complain about; it's barren of nits to pick. The art is absolutely stunning, the music is sublime, and the gameplay feels satisfying and incredibly well-refined. It's a refreshing new take on the city-builder genre, with its aspect of having to tear down all you've built to leave a pristine environment in your wake. No, it's not the longest game... but you'll spend every moment of it wanting for more.Terra Nil is just one of those games -- the kind that only comes around once in a while, that stands above the rest as something truly unique.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Here's a list of what's in the full game that's not in the demo:The game in general and the UI are more polished now. There is a weather system where weather buildings must be placed to reach specific humidity and temperature thresholds that must be met for certain buildings to be placed and for events to happen in the world. Most of these are cosmetic and just grant points, but a few aren't such as rain which fills in grass in all the stray tiles you missed. There is an animal system during the recycling phase where you have to find places in the map that are suitable to each species. Some of these are pretty specific and may require you to manipulate the map a bit to create the right conditions. In terms of content, the demo is level 1 of the final game and is mostly the same outside of adding the above features. There are three more levels each with their own unique biomes, buildings, and mechanics that are generally more complex as you progress. There is also a second version of each level where the goals are the same but the terrain generation is different and some of your buildings are replaced with ones from different levels, significantly changing the experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Terra Nil is a game that attempts to subvert common city builder tropes. With an environmentalist mindset, the aim of the game is to essentially work backwards and turn destroyed, barren wastelands into thriving ecosystems, wiping any trace of your influence, and leaving. It's a great premise for a game. But it lacks the foundational complexity of city builders to really be much more than a painfully linear experience who's entire purpose is nothing other than subversion. As a result, the game plays almost the exact same way every time, and what's being played can more or less rather simply be dumbed down to 'try to maximise the amount of tiles'. It becomes less about planning as a result, and more like a loose jigsaw puzzle that can only really be completed in a few number of ways.  Games are more than the sum of their parts. I can't honestly judge a game by picking it apart and estimating its value through its individual components because that defeats the purpose of examining how I actually *felt* playing it. That being said, I genuinely don't see what the fuss is about with this game. I don't think I would have lost much by just looking it up and watching someone else play it on Youtube.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: This is a good game but not yet great!This review is based on completion of the basic (easy-mode) game.Terra Nil is an interesting and compelling take on a city builder turned on its head. It looks great and plays well. In the first 8 hours it took me to complete the basic game, I had one issue with the game freezing and then shutting down but it saves my progress so I was able to jump right back in and continue. And yes, it's short on content for 20 quid (this is not tagged as early access as far as I can see!) but seems to have replay-ability - once you complete the basic play-through you 'unlock' different, more challenging, versions (only just started playing at time of this review). Once I had finished the basic game I wanted to immediately play again to improve as each map I achieved around 70% (I think to do with habitat, diversity, animals - I definitely missed a few as I didn't have the ideal conditions etc.) on each area. I had to restart a couple of times on one map but you do not have to restart from the beginning - each 'map' has 3 phases and you can restart your current phase, otherwise the game saves ever action automatically with only a redo for the last thing you did! And I quickly learned from my mistakes and got better!I really hope the devs continue to add new content and improve the UI (a few tweaks needed but it plays well imho) and do not charge too much for future DLC (I was pleased to see that if you buy the game you now get the soundtrack - which is excellent, and and artwork book for free!). Please reward those who invested in Terra Nil with new game content!Overall, Terra Nil is a chill game with some challenging moments and you can increase the difficulty playing on different modes - and this is when the puzzle aspect comes in as you have to really think about the choices you make. The options you have make you think about the environments you are trying to create, especially when it comes to introducing animals to your new worlds.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: After the demo and then the first level, I was really loving this game. And I really wanted to love the rest too, but once I moved on it dawned on me that the "campaign" really isn't one. There is no progression here, other than the artificial percentage of terraforming, and the amount of landmass available to terraform on the planet is apparently about 2 square miles or so.The tech is locked to each map specifically, so there is no unlocking of tech which you can bring along, the maps have a static and separate (but partially overlapping) tech tree. You get a new procedurally generated map everytime you play a biome type, but forget about learning how to solve a problem on map 1 to get creative on map 3. You get to solve the same problem in exactly the same way, by placing the same buildings in slightly different places, but really, if you've done one level, there is no replayability there.There are map variations, which means that the static set pieces move from being 4 biomes to 4*2 biome/approach combinations. And, no overlap. No grassland with a bit more of a djungle in a corner. No tundra/grassland combinations that requires skills or tech unlocked from the other maps. No interactions between the different animals, they basically just show up and walk around the map making it prettier.It really is a pretty title, and it conveys a lush feeling once you green up the map. But there is no gameplay here of significance. A walking simulator in the shape of a strategy game, but with none of the strategy, progression or satisfaction of solving new problems after the first playthrough of each map. If you are looking for super-casual and good-looking, this might be for you. If you want more than that, unfortunately, nothing to see here.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I truly cannot explain how much this game means to me. It's a brilliant puzzle game, the theme of ecological restoration is fantastic, the visuals are gorgeous, and the whole thing is very thoughtfully designed.I guess the best way to express my feelings on this game is that it is worth so much more to me than the $25 being charged, I've been buying copies for friends. I really want more games like this (and more DLC like Surviving the Aftermath's Rebirth) allowing you to restore devastated environments.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: The positive first. The game is a fun concept and I like the art style. I generally find terraforming games very satisfying and I do enjoy watching the different ecosystems emerge as you play. It's fun trying to discover what conditions different animals needed to then populate those ecosystems. This game is cute, but it plays like a demo. The tutorial takes up basically the whole game and it never gets into enough complexity to be interesting--any difficulty is just from confusion with the mechanics. It's often hard to understand why you can't place a building somewhere, for example. In terms of satisfying-ness, it's very difficult to completely detoxify an area, which leaves me with an unfinished feeling.It only took me four hours to complete, which is not nearly enough for a $20 game. There are alternate versions of the levels which might boost that to closer to 7-8 hours, but it just wasn't interesting enough for me to want to.I think if the game were cheaper or longer I'd give it a thumbs up, but as it is now I think you'd be better off waiting a bit and hope that they add more content in future updates.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I've been waiting for this for so long, was so hyped up, pre-purchased...Not a cent wasted 🚀🚀🚀 This was hands down one of the best gaming experiences I've had in recent years. To me it's a masterpiece from the art design, through to the game play, the musical score and an opportunity to let thoughts dwell on ecological restoration really hit home and made for many an hour of immersive fun! Planning on chasing 100% Completion and many more achievements. Well done! Can't believe the idea flourished so well from a game jam many moons ago! Bravo 👏👏👏
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Terra Nil is a solid and rather unique indie title with a lot of polish. It is in a way a city builder but it's also not. You spend your time going from zone to zone (Of which there are 4/8, we'll get to that later) using a variety of tools to effectively clean the land. You only have one resource which allows you to build more buildings and you gain resources by placing buildings to either add greenery or convert it as well as completing objectives such as making it warmer or more humid which adds plant life to the map (this is also visually indicated) The game from an aesthetic standpoint is beautiful, this games polish is its strongest suit by far. Visually everything looks lovely, all of the sounds function well, all of the little music cues that occur as you engage with the game are great and all of the biomes and their respective flora and fauna are really nice to look at.A major point of contention for the game as seen in the reviews is the length of play time available to complete the game. Terra Nil takes on average around 4 hours to reach the credits given there are only four unique levels. The levels themselves definitely offer more unique and interesting elements as you progress that helps to change up the game. Terra Nil also offers remixed levels which take elements and tools from other levels to make a more challenging areas that I found to be a little more fun. Overall this in total brings the amount of levels to eight which gives you a bit more to do and will likely take around 7 - 8 hours to get through. There are also some additional achievements to hunt if that is your thing. Overall I do wish the game released with a little more content, maybe some additional levels/biiomes such as Savannahs, Deserts or a purely oceanic level. Hopefully this is something we see in the future but overall the game is a little on the pricey side for what you get. The quality of the game does however shine and by no means do I think that the content in the game deserves a negative review. It's just something to be aware of when purchasing.Overall I thoroughly enjoyed my time with the game, it's unique, thoughtful and delightfully charming. I just really hope that the future holds some extra content for the game either in the form of levels or custom workshop content/ a level creator.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good game but there's not that much content.  There's 4 map styles that present unique puzzles to solve, then 4 more alternative versions of those maps but doesn't seem to be anything beyond that.  I finished all 8 maps to 100% in 2 sittings, about 6-7 hours.  They put so much work into each map type, but only have 2 maps per map type.What I think would help this game immensely is a longer "campaign" .  Have 3-5 maps that ramp up in difficulty per map style, this would extend the gameplay and also slowly introduce players to each map's mechanics and give more of a sense of progression.  For instance the river valley map could start out with a dead easy map with rocks and rivers perfectly set up to be a cakewalk, but then the next map has a generator that is less perfect, then finally a much more challenging one that forces the player to use what they learned.  Have each climate zone function this way.

_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Highly recommended as a beautiful, chill game with a unique inversion of the accelerating resource extraction of most games. Excellent stylised visuals, soothing sound design, intuitive mechanics, and a bit of puzzling. I don't normally replay games, but I find myself coming back to Terra Nil.Players focusing on doing the bare minimum in restoration goals to pass a level will probably be unsatisfied and blast through pretty quickly. But, very much in the spirit of the game and its themes, where Terra Nil really shines is when you take the time to meet all the optional targets to maximise biodiversity, make a balanced mix of biomes, and ensure there are habitats for animals (all of which are very satisfyingly visually represented). The fun is in taking a barren wasteland and making it into something beautiful and varied.On hard mode this requires husbanding of resources and thinking about efficiently placing buildings earlier in each stage, with things accelerating nicely (again, thematically fitting) as the ecosystem is restores and begins to work on its own. It is possible to screw yourself over with careless placement of biomes (especially when it comes to animal habitats), but even with that, this is never a particularly challenging game. People looking for a high intensity, high stakes city-building should look elsewhere (Frostpunk this is not - though I do love Frostpunk).As for replayability, each map type has a different combination of biome and tools, and while these are the same each time, the layout is procedurally generated, meaning that the challenge is slightly different every time.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Not enough variety to challenges; hate that you have no foresight to later requirements in a level, such that you can get into such a bind that you have to restart a level from scratch in order to resolve (if I'm wrong on this, then it's not clear to me how to avoid problems on levels like Archipelago on your first play through).May be a recommend at sales pricing, but not at full.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: It's a very enjoyable game and is unique in that everything built is temporary and recycling should be kept in mind from the start of each level (i.e., making sure the building are accessible).  This isn't particularly difficult but it does add an interesting dimension.  There is some mild number crunching on the hardest difficulty but it's not the sort of thing where you'd have to keep a notebook nearby; being mindful of costs and incomes is enough.  The vibe is quite relaxing even on the more intense levels and it is gratifying to see animals appear and making sure their needs are met (food animals, certain biomes being adjacent, etc.).  The update definitely made that work a lot better and it ads another mild puzzle to solve here and there.  This was a surprise hit for me and I highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: After managing to 100% the original game in just under 20 hours, I left Terra Nil very pleased with the experience. Charmingly aesthetic and inherently calming, it was my choice of relaxing evening game, and I was very excited to learn the developers had updates planned for Earth Day. Sadly, I have not been able to enjoy the full breadth of experience they delivered, as I have found myself too frustrated simply replaying older missions to learn the new mechanics to even attempt the new maps.The developer has commented earnestly on similar reviews so I shall try to keep it succinct. While the first two phases play essentially the same as before, the third animal phase was changed to be more dynamic. Aesthetically its rather nice, giving the impression of wildlife returning to nature. In terms of gameplay, however, it introduces a metric curveball at the end of the run that can completely ruin even the most carefully crafted map. The animals choose where they want to appear seemingly at random as long as some of the area meets some of the requirements, and while tools exist to bride gaps in their habitation zones or corral them in a directions, theres no way to actually remove them once they move in or choose where they should next appear. This has the potential to cheese the player out of earning achievements or even being able to completely soft lock the run with relative ease.Concrete examples include; -Failing a run on Polluted Fjord as the various Tundra, Forest, and Lichen biomes never managed to patch together viable sized zones for animal habitation, though all of them were 'adequate' enough that no animals would leave. Ditto for Abandoned Quarry-Failing to unlock 'Whales' on Archipelago as they choose small spots far away from the many open ocean tiles left available to them, with inadequate points left to drop multiple sonic becons-Soft locking the following attempt at 'Whales' on Achipelago as a desperate attempt to dump dirt into a spot whales have spawned and will not leave results in a pylon too far from water to be recycled. (This admittedly is a bug, as it was oddly recycler-proof)-Quiting the following attempt as ten beacons later, whales forced into the unpolluted ocean around the edges of the landmasses leave as this does not appear to qualify the 'ocean' requirement, despite inability to find indication as to why. This was the point at which I stopped, as half or more of the sessions had ended in frustration and/or failure, and I was not enjoying my time with the game anymore. Restoring pastoral landscapes loses its charm when it feels like fine tuning a park for twelve incredibly picky guests who may still ignore your enormous forested accommodations in favor of the few spares you had to throw up to meet the previous steps requirement. I really did love relaxing to this game and hope to be able to again.

_childDocuments_.review: Terra Nil is a gentle, sweet little game that is a delight from start to finish. As others have pointed out, yes, it is short; there are only four regions which you take a tour of twice with the maps and your tools being remixed on the second go-around. However, I really don't see that as a negative. The core mechanics are solid, the puzzles are both engaging and forgiving, the atmosphere is relaxing with a couple neat little surprises peppered in, and it never overstays its welcome. Because the maps are (to a small extent) procedurally generated it's easy to replay missions repeatedly without it feeling stale or samey and the map specific goals/trophy challenges are fun to collect. Likewise, while the first run through the regions is largely about learning and mastering the mechanics, the second run through changing your tools and goals creates some really unexpected and interesting challenges that are fun to think around.$25 is a touch more than I'd have preferred to pay, agreed, but I still feel like I got my money's worth and I suspect most people will too (especially if they find it on sale) so long as they don't rush their way through. Terra Nil is a genuinely unique addition to the city builder/management sim/god sim genres, so take it slow, soak in the atmosphere, and really bask in how hopeful it feels to do something positive to your digital environment for a change.All in all, if you're looking for something that's going to twist your brain into knots over logistical puzzles or where you focus on building huge constructions as quickly and efficiently as possible, then go play Factorio and Satisfactory; The Factory Must Grow, I agree, but when you're feeling run down by FICSIT's ballooning quotas or like you might have done a bit too much biter nest eradication on Nauvis for one week, Terra Nil will be here for you. :)

_childDocuments_.review: Terra Nil is a joy. The music is beautiful, the mechanics are satisfying, and the animals are cute. The core game loop is a pleasant mix of finding adjacency optimizations and puzzling out how to do the most with the resources you can. On the medium difficulty setting, it can be occasionally challenging, but if you get stuck, you'll always have learned exactly the lesson you need to achieve victory on the second try. It's not a super long game- 10 hours to get through all 8 levels on medium difficulty- but it is excellent because it is a tight, core experience. It isn't bloated, there is no grind, it doesn't waste your time. It is a tight, creative game that deserves praise! Oh, and a share of the profits from the game are donated to wildlife conservancy, so it practices what it preaches. Play this game and be a force for good!All of that praise said, I can't not say- Please, Free Lives, figure out how sea otters swim. Watching them doggy paddle across the surface is just... terrifying.   - signed, a big fan of sea otters

_childDocuments_.review: I was playing this through my shared Family Library as my partner had bought it, and I love it so much that I bought my own copy just so I could leave a positive review. The idea of turning wastelands into beautifully realised, lush, living environments appealed to me from the outset far more than any city building or farming sort of simulator, and it's such a great game to spend a few minutes on here and there just to de-stress and chill out with making things grow and finding just the right way to restore things to make all the fauna happy.Having played it prior to buying my own copy, I already have all the achievements, but I'm going to start a new profile and rebuild everything over from scratch. I love everything from the visuals to the music to the sense of satisfaction from lining up the irrigators just right for maximum plant growth. _childDocuments_.review: 9/10. Baie lekker!Simple, relaxing, and beautiful game. It is great for a short, thirty-minute gaming session or for a three-hour terraforming romp! And did I mention it's beautiful? I was hooked since the demo and was following this game for months before the release. The finished product did not disappoint. More of the same, which if you put in as much time into the demo as I did, is a good thing. The recurring criticism I have seen is that it is short. There are eight scenarios. Two scenarios for every biome (four biomes - urban, tundra, tropical, and temperate. That said, there is a "hidden" randomly generated mode, of sorts. If you change the landing coordinates in the World Map menu, you can create a slightly different version of each of the eight scenarios. It is not very obvious, though. The other thing is it doesn't seem to have a genuine sandbox mode. I would love an option to be able to play a scenario with all the tools available, rather than being constrained by biome or scenario. And the ability to save individual terraforming projects would be nice, for those of us who are trying to make especially beautiful looking worlds. On a final note, and a more personal one. I spent my childhood in South Africa. I was genuinely delighted to learn that this game was produced there.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely beautiful game with a lot of potential to grow in interesting directions in the future. It is for me a one-of-its-kind game. Music is quite serene. Attention to details for Flora and Fauna strike the right amount of balance. Overall, playing this game was a peaceful and relaxing experience. _childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Have been following this game for a while now, and I feel great about this game. One thing that really puts the cherry on top is the music and the sound design. The music reacts to the environment, becoming increasingly more "hopeful" as you progress through the restoration process. The sound of the animals returning and the wind blowing through the lush forest you created is nothing less than extremely soothing to the ear.One of the reason I decided to purchase Terra Nil, is the limited time I often have to play video games I enjoy these days. My sessions tend to be frequent, yet unfortunately short. Terra Nil is really great in this sense, as it is a perfect game to just boot up and play when you feel like it. It doesn't require half an hour to get into, and is something which is easy to just play after work or school. Of course you can play for prolonged periods of time, too!The graphics are beyond stunning. There were a couple performance issues I found in regard to the demo, however these all seem to have been fixed, and the game runs smoother than ever now. The game allows you to zoom in on all your vegetation, which stays just as stunning no matter the zoom level you are on.Overall, if you're looking for a soothing and calm experience, yet challenging at times, I'd highly recommend this game to you :).
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: What a nice game,As an avid Strategy Game player, this is like a nice sunny walk in the park. It does have it's challenge though!It's just a very nice, comprehensive game about restoring nature, and even getting rid of your own constructions after you reintroduce flora and fauna back to the wild.Coming from ravaged places, battlefield of either ancient times or giant futuristic battles of 40k. This is none of that, no battles, no killing (the occasional floor burning doesn't count... right?) but you really feel great "when a plan comes together" and you see the little deer on the meadow or crab on the beach you just created.I *had* a feeling i was softlocked at the beginning of the game, what it doesn't tell you is that you have to clean the buildings up again, and i kinda had to work around that, but you live and learn, no stress about it!The only thing that annoys me or i would change, is the visibility, it's kinda hard to figure out where something is or "where is *this building* on the map", especially in the tropical area after i created a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of tropical flora, the outlining of where i could place a unit was very hard to see.Otherwise, this game is a very relaxing take on strategy games, don't be afraid to play it though if you dislike strategy! It can be more of a puzzle, the maps are quite small as well so you don't get lost that easily or have to min max or something you would do in a more traditional start game or competitive game.It even has three modes to be more or less engaging gameplay, you want to relax or engage in serious conservationism?I enjoy games like these, well made, good price, nice artwork, and they even donate some of their well earned money!

_childDocuments_.review: The game has a great idea and gorgeous graphics, but that's the only thing preventing it from being among the worst games I've ever played. anyway here's a list of problems I have with it1. something that I noticed really quickly is the difficulty, you'd think doing the first level on normal difficulty wouldn't be too challenging. _childDocuments_.review: Terra Nil is relaxing and fun. It has a chill soundtrack and an alright gameplay loop, and the focus on restoring nature is a nice contrast to most games' focus on either dominating nature or just killing things. Overall, I give it a 3/5 "solid if you're really into that kind of thing." Unfortunately I can't recommend it, because it has too many bugs. It's quite the mess. I've played 11 hours so far and finally got too sick of it. I'm going to wait to play more until a bugfix update comes out. Here's the ones I can remember off the top of my head:* Animal detector sometimes permanently fails to detect animals, instead giving a weird error message about the state of the map having changed. I haven't found any workaround; once the error appears, those animals are undetectable for the remainder of the mission.* Lowering and raising the temperature on the snow map will make it snow or melt, but only once; after that, it doesn't matter what you do to the temperature, you're stuck with the permanent snow.* Newly-built dredgers don't connect to existing monorail nodes, even if they're in range.* Clicking "undo" after creating the bamboo structure will remove the bamboo forest, but won't remove the structure, meaning the structure is useless for the rest of the mission.* The boat sometimes refuses to traverse pound locks* Snow can fall next to solar amplifier if the solar amplifier was built on snowy ground after it had already started snowing.There's also some QOL and game-design decisions that are annoying.* Rain and snow are far too powerful. The whole early game becomes a one-dimensional race to get to those weather conditions, because they give you SO MUCH money and eliminate the need for toxic scrubbers/irrigators.* Far too few hotkeys. 1234 for the different structure panels aren't enough; I want to be able to choose specific buildings  with the keyboard.* You can't save and quit halfway through a mission. When you relaunch the game, you have to start the mission over.* The third gameplay phase (recycling) isn't challenging, because it gives you far too much money. It's mostly just annoying. The recycling drone is really slow and has weird artificial limits on what they can recycle. I've had to make a Turbine, Excavator (which blew a hole in my landscaping), Calcifier, and lone monorail node just so my FLYING drone can be commanded to recycle the Silo that I had already built.* Insufficient explanation is sometimes given to why certain actions are disallowed. I had to Google why I couldn't burn grass with the Solar Amplifier, and Google again to find out that it can burn the scrub resulting from the Humidity Pylon. This kind of head-scratching "why can't I do this?" confusion happened to me a bunch of times. I'm sure it was covered in the tutorial at some point, but it's a lot of tutorial, and moment-to-moment tooltips and warnings should be given.Finally, It feels more like a $10 game than a $25 one. The campaign is only about 12-15 hours long (I've almost completed the entire thing in 11 hours without much effort nor a single loss), and the gameplay loop is too long, buggy, and irritating to want to repeat very many times.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Bask in the soothing fantasy of a planet without humans, where ecological destruction can be undone and nature can reclaim urban wastelands.  Lovely music and visuals, nicely challenging gameplay, good replay value.Notes for things I got stuck on: You have to place sandbars BEFORE turbines for them to count as "in range" for the power source; and you're supposed to let the earthquake happen.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: A refreshingly unique take on the city builder genre! Rather than focusing on infinite growth and expansion, Terra Nil chooses to focus on terraforming the environment. In this context, your buildings are simply a means to an end, not the end in and of themselves. My favorite part is how, once you are done terraforming each environment, you have to remove all of your buildings before moving on. It's easy to imagine a far less interesting alternative: a game which plays like Sim City, but where trees and flowers spring up around your buildings, simply wearing a thin veneer of environmentalism while reinforcing the same expansionist mindset which is destroying the environment. But, by flipping the genre on its head, Terra Nil is able to convey a radically different set of values from other city builders, not only through its theming, but most importantly through its gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: An absolutely wonderful strategy puzzle game which is as chill or unforgiving as you want it to be. The most recent update overhauled the animals which was a much needed change as they felt like an afterthought before, and now adds an extra level of complexity the third phase needed.Gameplay aside, the game is just.... *beautiful*. Not just in its artstyle (Especially compared to its original beta pixelated style), but also, almost moreso, in its gameplay. It's hard to explain, but Terra Nil gives me the same vibes as playing Flower. Absolutely would recommend if you like strategy or puzzle games, or if nature is your thing.
