_childDocuments_.review: Recommended, with the caveat to get it on sale, not at full price. I spent almost $20 on it, which seems a little steep, I'm glad I didn't spend more.Game is very pretty, the premise is neat, the biome puzzles are engaging.  It's also very, very short. Like, there are 4 regions, and your first play through of all 4 will be less than 10 hours: it took me not quite 7, including having to replay one due to the game allowing me to place something in a location it was impossible to recycle it from and having to start a level over, and leaving the game running while I made and ate dinner.  Granted, I did play at the most chill difficulty, so maybe it'd take a little longer if a harder difficulty required more restarts.  So far I've played one of the "second version" regional maps, and it looks like no new content, just the same regional biomes and animals with a slightly shuffled toolset and challenge based on what you get in other regions the first time around. There's probably some level of replayability but it seems like with so few options it will get stale pretty fast.Also, many of the conceits about how to terraform are just ... wrong. Leaving aside the obvious fantasy ones (), and things like for some reason eagles require ruined buildings and can't use trees or cliffs to roost, there were a number of times where the game required  me to do things and all I could think was "it doesn't really work like that...."   If you want to actually learn how ecology works, please read a book or something, don't rely on what you learn in this game.It's also kind of buggy. Besides the aforementioned letting me place something where it wasn't possible to recycle it (it wouldn't have been possible even with later game tools like the flying recycler since there was no rocks close enough to place any monorails and no way to get any close), it also leaves the outlines from animal scanning on the surface of the water, and the UI lags often, especially when trying to rotate buildings to place them (user input? we don't need it, just throw it away!)  Also lacks some quality of life features like remembering the rotation of an object, it doesn't do this even if you're holding shift to place multiple objects. And, of course, the nice long straight irrigation placement patterns are the  ones on the list....  I basically never used the corner ones except when I didn't care enough to spend a minute and a half waiting for the game to accept my rotate input so I could finally get to the straight ones.All that said it is pretty, and it was fun to rebuild places and see all the tiny little animal sprites move in. Worth getting on sale, don't bother paying full price.

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished the four main story-continent terraforming. Few solo games give me experiences I will remember for any length of time but Terra Nil is one of them. This is a fabulous eco-building simulator but in a closed, puzzle sort-of way. No, this isn't a Rimworld or SimCity open world infinite replayable simulator but with it's more focused, puzzle approach I found my time with it incredibly enjoyable.It also accomplished something simulations games don't generally do; I found myself relaxed while playing and very peaceful after each level as I admired my creation for a loooong time prior to continuing. I only wish there was a way to convert the ending animation screen in to an animated background for the computer desktop. If any or all the above appeals to you, I cannot recommend the Terra Nil enough !!!

_childDocuments_.review: [8/10] If you want to read why I gave this score:Terra Nil is a wonderful, relaxing ‘reverse city builder’, that offers an engaging, calming experience that will get you hooked. The message behind the game, as well as the care put in by its developers is felt throughout the experience!I do wish that there was more to explore in the game beyond what I experienced in the 8.5 hours it took me to 100%, but it still felt like a very worthwhile experience nonetheless. Support indies! [8/10] The game overs a unique spin on city-building/puzzle games where, instead of colonising a new space and building up civilisation, you seek to heal the damage done by humanity.The game’s core flow covers restoring the natural environment to its intended state, fixing the climate and reintroducing wildlife with clever placement of machinery, followed by a satisfying cleanup phase leaves you with an incredibly satisfying feeling of fixing the puzzle laid out conclusively.The game offers a healthy variety of maps and structures to leave it feeling engaging for a reasonable amount of time, but I really wish there was more to sink my teeth into- it ended too soon! [7/10]Simple, but effective. Terra Nil’s art clearly communicates its range of flora and fauna and brings some unique, pretty illustrations to the handbook that functions as your guide throughout. A pretty game, but nothing groundbreaking going on here. Solid nonetheless! [7/10] I’m writing this review a few days after 100% the game, and I actually had to open it up again to remind myself of the audio :P at the very least, it wasn’t too memorable.The game’s music is light, calming, and augments the curious/peaceful atmosphere that the game presents everywhere else. The addition of crunchy sound effects in both the structures and the ambient environment really fill the void very well between music tracks.  [9/10] No major crashes or bugs in my playthrough. My only complaint is that there are some really sticky tooltips that you have to wrestle against to declutter your screen. I’m sure this will get fixed in future.  [-/10] While this game has a somewhat implied story, it doesn’t feel appropriate to judge it on this!  [9/10] Terra Nil comes together to form a really engaging experience that just… hits right. It’s a relaxing, cathartic experience that is really hard to put down once you get started. A game I thoroughly enjoyed and, will most definitely pick up again as soon as more content drops.(There’s something really magical when the rain starts to fall on a new map <3)

_childDocuments_.review: A fun, relaxing game that thought I'd try "for a bit" and three hours later, found myself totally engrossed. I "rolled credits" after about 10.5 hours but didn't 100% any of the regions. Nevertheless, Terra Nil is wonderful. I like that it is pretty short, peaceful, and allows players to move on without maxing out every square on a map. Players can attempt alternate versions of the regions after finishing and always try to 100% each area, which will add replay value and hours. _childDocuments_.review: I heartily recommend this game. I was playing the demo years ago when that was released and I've always found it a game I come back to again and again when I want a relaxing puzzle builder game. It can be tricky but not in a stressful kind of way.The puzzles in this game are all related to how can you reclaim the current wasteland given the selected tools while not running out of your building resource. That resource is there more to increase the puzzle aspect rather than increase any sort of stress. There's no time limit for the map you're on and you can restart either the entire map or the current phase, which is very forgiving.Each map provides a different set of challenges to overcome and the challenge difficult increases at a very friendly pace. The first map introduces you to basic game concepts while providing enough of a challenge to pull you in, while the final maps take some thinking and knowledge of existing mechanics to overcome.And in the end, you get to enjoy the fact that you're restoring a planet. Sometimes it's nice to take a break from beating back waves of zombies or hordes of enemies and build something nice. And having just 100% the entire map, I'm super happy with it. And I"ll keep coming back to the game in the future for those relaxing moments when I need them.So if you want something fun, somewhat challenging, but not stressful, go ahead and pick this up and enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: ( full review with screenshots:  )Terra Nil is a puzzle strategy game in which you're dropped into a wasteland and need to build machines to restore the climate and habitat without running out of resources. Each level follows the same basic flow of starting out with a toxic patch of dirt that needs to be cleaned up and covered in grass, then that grass needing to be replaced with more developed biomes like forests or wetlands, and finally needing to both find homes for native animal species and clean up all of your machines. It sounds like a lot, but since your currency is greenery and most machines generate plenty of that when you place them, it's generally more meditative than strategically demanding. The game has four major climates: the river valley, the tropical archipelago, the volcanic glacier, and an urban continental map. Although the core gameplay loop is largely unchanged between these, each has its own features that keep the game from getting stale. The glacier and continents map have very different ways of generating power, for instance, and the archipelago's focus on water and jungle is quite different from the initial valley map. Each climate also has its own tier 2 biomes, like tundra for the glacier or coral reef for the archipelago, and its own set of six animals. Finally, there are different helpful events for reaching climate milestones like certain humidity levels or temperatures, and most maps have their own way of recycling all your machines when you're finishing up. Once you've completed the four main maps, you'll unlock an additional four that remix and combine the ideas of the original set. These largely don't introduce new ideas, but you do get more challenging layouts that use the power generation from one map and the climate from another. One of two of these might be too much to 100% if you're playing this as an entirely meditative game, but for the most part they add challenge without getting in the way of the game's relaxing core loop. Still, it does have a couple of noteworthy flaws. The main one is that it's not always very good at communicating what's going on. I frequently had issues with not being sure why I wasn't allowed to place a machine in certain places or with only realizing that a particular set up wasn't good enough once I was already past the point of being able to undo it. This isn't a huge deal since the maps don't take that long to play and it's easy enough to just start over, but it also could have been rectified with clearer tooltips and overlays. Second, the price tag will be an issue for some people. I feel like the $20 I paid was fair for the 9 hours it took me to do everything, but it's harder to justify if you're just going to do the base maps. A fifth biome or user created maps could have gone a long way here. --------For more reviews, see

_childDocuments_.review: I personally think that a lot of people, the negative reviews in fact do have some very good points in what they're saying about the game. I get the game is very short but the developers themselves have stated that they're planning on adding more content, patches,  and maybe DLC in the future. They haven't abandoned it and for some I can understand where they might be coming from with the whole "Lack of content" argument I see a lot on these reviews. _childDocuments_.review: Brought here by RCE, liked the look of the game and I like these sorts of methodical relaxing games.Then I found out they changed the Recycle stage; you can't 'chain' the recyclers to get them to the waterways and not have to carve rivers EVERYWHERE. I'm stuck at a 98% recycle because I have ONE windmill way off in a corner surrounded by forest I can't burn. As the you bring about life, there are additional challenges to bring about various wildlife to individual biomes.Often times, other puzzle games can cause frustration, but with the calm environment and lovely aesthetic, Terra Nil offers a calm and challenging opportunity to spend time after work.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most stunning and relaxing strategy games I've ever played. I got a chance to get a review code from Devolver and participate in their Free Lives Terra Nil tree warriors. Played about 2.5 hours on stream and just finished the last two biomes just now. One the downside, the price is way too expensive for a game you can complete in 10 hours, including challenge maps. Don't see it taking more than 20 to 100% including all achievements. Therefore i cannot get 2 out of the 3 required biomes and it'm in a lost state i can't seem to break out of even by regenerating the map. _childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I dislike how people call this a city builder. It is not. It is a puzzle game with parameters that are often hidden until you get to the final stage of animal finder and suddenly the place you have "saved" is no longer applicable so then you restart.I really enjoyed the first two levels, sort of; however, I really disliked that game play elements changed between them and things are hidden until you reach the final stage.I disagree with other reviews that this is a mobile game. _childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: The game has multiple difficulties, e.g. you can play on 'zen mode'; you don't have to worry about resources (so this solves the issue of people struggling with it being 'too hard', which it isn't anyway, or too short). Each area has 2 versions as well, so if you're completing this game in under 3-4 hours, you aren't even completing everything but just rushing it. This is not a game to rush.It is a short game, but infinitely re-playable. The price imo reflects the quality, its finished to a high standard. Took me about 10 hours to 100% the game (incl achievements), but now I like just replaying the maps and doing some landscaping in zen mode. If the price is too steep for you, definitely buy it on sale.Easily 10/10. Super relaxing, chill game that's fun to play to unwind after work. Can see this game being one I constantly go back to.

_childDocuments_.review: A bit short, but worth the price if on sale.  Took me roughly four hours to complete the four maps initially, and another two to complete the four variant levels, each at 100%.  Fun, relaxing structure placement game.  More of a puzzle game than a city builder.  Interesting twist on the game loop, where you must remove all your structures at the end of map, following varying game rules depending on the level.  I'd love to see an expansion that builds on more complex interactions.  I'd also love to buy a printed version of the book from the game, though killing a bunch of trees might be opposite the intent of the game's narrative.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Terra Nil offers a unique and enjoyable gaming experience, blending the challenges of construction and resource management with the spirit of exploration and adventure. The game features simple yet elegant graphics and colorful environments that captivate players from the get-go.The core concept of the game revolves around reshaping the environment and rebuilding the ecosystem in a desolate world. Players start with the task of transforming dry and decaying land into lush, beautiful sites teeming with life. Players must use available resources wisely to create water purification units, generate alternative energy, and cultivate plants.However, Terra Nil faces some issues, most notably its short duration. Players can complete all levels and rebuild the environment relatively quickly, reducing replay value and overall challenge. Additionally, some players may feel boredom after completing the basic challenges without additional challenges or rewards to enhance replayability.Overall, Terra Nil is a fantastic experience for those who enjoy construction games and resource management with a beautiful artistic touch. However, it needs expansion and diversification in content and increased challenges to maintain its appeal in the long run.If you're looking for a peaceful and enjoyable experience of rebuilding and transforming the environment, Terra Nil is an intriguing option.That was the review of Terra Nil. I hope you find it helpful!
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Eh. Pretty dull.  Nothing exciting happens in Terra Nil.  The video clips being used to advertise the game showing frolicking animals aren't in the game and look nicer than the game.  It's not a bad game, it's just not all that interesting.  I like the idea of taking a city/colony sim and turning it on it's head -- restore the environment and then remove all of your buildings to leave it pristine.  It reminds me a lot of games like "powerwash simulator" -- clean up and leave.  There's some small satisfaction in turning a dead simulated environment into a bucolic one... but nothing *happens*.  Having restored one such environment I really don't have any interest in restoring another.  I guess the game is not for me.  I suspect if you like games like powerwash simulator you will probably like this game.  I honestly do not think it will appeal to fans of city sims.  Anyway, I don't want to yuck anybody else's yum, if it's for you, knock yourself out.  I think it is boring. Sorry!

_childDocuments_.review: A short, calming, "clean up" game.The overall gameplay loop is to arrive, clean things up, make sure things will be OK with you gone, then pack up your machines and leave the environment to recover itself. I found myself wanting more at the end. More levels, larger, more machines unlocked, sandbox / free play mode... I got 100% completed within two three-hour-ish play sessions, and found myself dreaming of ecosystem grids with nowhere to put that energy. I guess that just means that the game is better than it is long.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Relaxing game with focus on ecosystem restoration. That's in short what is main goal. Turning hostile, often poisonous wasteland into thriving and blooming nature.Concept brings quite fresh wind into management genre games. Allowing player to control how will land change based on his actions. Every game is different thanks to random map generator. And even identical map can end up with differently based on steps player takes.Four basic "bioms" require versatility in restoration approach. Ever single of them provides different set of tools. By utilizing them nature can be restored into quite breath taking landscapes.After completing campaign , alternated maps are unlocked. These provide altered set of tools and therefore restoration takes different road. Maps are also slightly more challenging.In conclusion I recommend this game since it was not only entertainment but also quite calming experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Genuinely a very fun game, if lacking a bit in content at launch.Pros:- Really good atmosphere and soundtrack- Puzzle aspect of the gameplay is engaging without being stressful- Achievements and challenges provide a bit of longevity with reasons to go back and play levels againCons:- Lacking in content for the price point- Mechanics can feel a bit simple once you know what you're doing- Ending is (imo) a bit frustrating Overall, if it seems like the type of game you'd enjoy you'll probably really like it! Hopefully future content updates help flesh things out a bit more, but for now it's still a good little experience
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to preface this: I am very likely bad at this game. That said, I find this game more annoying than relaxing as actually staying within budget and also filling out the map properly is more an exercise in frustration and failure than it is a chill, environment restoring game. I get what the game's trying to do, but it's making it hard for me to do it my way and gets in my way too much while trying to do it. If you're into deep optimisation and figuring out the exact angles and perfect building placement, good news! This is the game for you! But I would've loved to be able to play this game sub-optimally and still come away at least having filled out the map, but I can't. Not without getting everything just right. So if you're like me and you too would like to mess around and still somewhat succeed, do not get this game. You will come away more frustrated than relaxed. And I don't think that's the game's intention. Which honestly I wish wasn't the case, as the aesthetic and the presentation are incredibly nice and the concept is really cool. The execution is just lacking.

_childDocuments_.review: You can read my other reviews What if there was a city builder that wasn't about expanding and industrializing land, but rather restoring nature over map tiles stripped of any properties? That is the question addressed in Terra Nil, built on a super relaxing environment that leaves anyone in a zen state, in a different approach to the city-building and puzzle genre.Terra Nil's goal will be to rehabilitate a planet that is effectively dead and devoid of any traces of fauna or flora. Divided into four areas with different environments, it all starts with an element that makes it possible to generate energy, the wind turbine. In this sense, this element becomes the main mean of building the sub-elements that make it possible to create an environment conducive to the growth of vegetation, with the help of a toxin purifier and subsequent irrigator. With the appearance of water and vegetation, the perfect conditions are created for the approximation of animal life. The puzzle component comes into play when placing all the mechanisms created to create life. For example, the wind turbine only works on top of stones, and the sprinkler only has X number of tiles per area, among others. The same applies when letting the area breathe freely without using machines. The final phase of each level is recycling all equipment.Each zone corresponds to certain areas of the planet, such as a forest area, a tropical area, or an icy area. It is indeed fascinating to see the world come to life in different areas with a simple click of the mouse button. One of the tasks presented to the player along his journey is the need to create the necessary conditions for the necessary flora to grow. Controlling temperature and humidity become very important aspects. Not being a super difficult particularity, it made me repeat the tropical biome since it was necessary to reach a certain percentage of humidity so that the corals could grow.After all the weather conditions have been met, the second phase of each zone's journey begins, the possibility of looking for the different animals. Even if the necessary climatic conditions are met, some animals have specific needs for areas in which to proliferate.Some aspects in Terra Nil are fully explained, but others are learned through experience using various tools. It's not a negative element, nor is the game itself difficult, but it can leave some players a little lost not knowing their next move. It is always possible to return to the starting point and if you spend all the resources needed to build each piece of equipment without reaching the next objective, that will really be the only possible choice.Terra Nil is a super relaxing but short experience. It does have some replayability, with the implementation of different difficulty levels, but just four different zones seem pretty short. However, it is a fully recommended title for fans of city-builder games.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Very satisfying and relaxing. I think I played through the 20 minute demo about 4 times, so buying this the moment it went on sale was not something I had to think much about. It took about 4 hours at a leisurely pace to see the credits and about 8 hours to reach 100% completion, so it's pretty short, but I also think there's plenty of replayability here thanks to the procedural maps and satisfying nature of watching the landscape transform. I'm currently playing through a second time on the hard difficulty setting and still having a good time (although it's not noticeably more challenging). Might even be a good game to play to circumvent climate anxiety and hopelessness. It's great to play with environmental restoration mechanics and think about their real world implications. The small team who made Terra Nil did an excellent job with what they set out to do. I would have liked to see more than two scenarios per climate (of which there are only 4), and maybe for later scenarios to include much larger maps to play with. I'm more than happy with the game as it is, but that makes me want more content than it has. If they ever release DLC for more scenarios and climates/regions, I'd buy it in a heartbeat.

_childDocuments_.review: First thank you to the dev team--It has been ages since I bought a game that made me want to instantly write a review saying "Hey! Play this!"ABOUT THE GAME:In reducing Terra Nil to a catchy phrase or some alternate title I suppose I would call it "Sim-Environment." As you would expect with a self-proclaimed "reverse city builder" You start with a budget of resources and a tier of "buildings and features" that eventually unlocks another tier and another. In this case the "Buildings and features" are climate reclamation tools, weather controls, and animals. You start with a desolate, destroyed, wasteland and (ideally) end with a vibrant map teeming with flora and fauna. GENERAL GAME-PLAY: The map has four zones, after you complete these four, a second map for each zone is unlocked. after you have completed all 8, you have "restored" the planet--how well restored it is depends on how well you played. completing these 8 maps on one planet (save) constitutes "one play-through" I guess you would say.There is a tutorial that will walk you through the first four maps, introducing you to all of the tools, concepts, and basic strategies to alter the wasteland and reclaim it.  As mentioned in the description the maps are procedurally generated landscapes--Which is great! it means you can play multiple times and never have the same map. it also means if you have made an absolute mess of your map or hate the map layout you are working on, no problem, get a new one.THOUGHTS:I love the art style and music. Do not, however, be fooled by the trailer--there is no 1st person point of view in the game, not that I was expecting one, but in the trailer they bounce back and forth. I found this game really relaxing, at one point relaxing with my feet on the desk, my cat under hand, and coffee in the other just listening to soundtrack and watching the animations.  I have a $1/hr rule on games and other entertainments (books DvDs etc). If I "play" one hour for every dollar spent, it was worth the expense. Maybe I like it, maybe I don't; as long as I "play" at least 1hr per $ I don't complain.. In this game's case will well exceed the cost of the game in hours played--and I am happy the devs support ecological efforts with part of the profit from the game. DEFENSE:Not that this game needs defending with Very Positive reviews status but I have seen other commentary I would like to offer comment about. Don't worry I'm not going to call out or argue with specific commentators, but I have seen a number of the negative reviews saying it is too short, or that there is not enough to the game. While I can not speak with authority as I  am not a dev, I respectfully submit this is not a game you buy to "beat." In some ways it is a much an art tool to create a slice of your own world as it is game or puzzle. For me, a large part of my positive experience was taking time to look at and admire the world I had created--because my decisions had consequence. I put those trees there, instead of a beach. I put that wetland there, instead of a river and lake. If you are looking for a game that is about checking boxes and getting a score, I respectfully submit this may not be the best game for you. If you like to spend time creating something from near nothing, then you will probably no-life this game like I am about to. That extends to the criticism of the tutorial some people had, saying if they knew in advance how some things worked they would have made other decisions. .... welcome to life kids! Sorry to be a jerk about it but it's not chess. you made a mistake, change that part of the map. burn it down, build something different. don't winge about not making perfect on your first try. It goes back to my comment about this game being an organic sim; not something with a leader's board.A word of warning as my final reflection: to once again poach from the sales text "Levels are not about infinite growth, but rather balancing and nurturing the environment before leaving it in peace." This is not minecraft or sim-city or some other game that rolls on indefinitely. Each map will have a time that it is completed, and you will leave. Some maps you won't really care, some you may even be glad about leaving. But there WILL be ones you will be sad to leave, that you would like to find in real life even. Make sure to screenshot them because once you have left, it is gone. But don't worry,  when you have restored the world, another will be waiting for you.COMPLAINTS, CRITICISM, AND A SUGGESTION:In spite of my obvious love letter to this game, there are suggestions I would like to see and things that I did not like mainly because at a coding level I am not sure they were working they way they were supposed to.First the suggestion. a "quick map" mode. When you don't feel like the challenge of an entire planet or just want to kill an hour two it would be nice to have the ability to select just one map/zone type,play it, and then go to bed or work or w/e.Complaints and criticism--Two of my three are documented on other threads on Steam relating to this game so I will try to be brief First on Map 8, I also had problems reclaiming my "stuff". I would click on the object to tell the monorail to go claim, but then could not actually click on any monorail poles--it would just select the square I clicked on.  In one case I had to resort to using the "collection bin" thingy, building a new monorail and collecting that way.Second. I could not find a away to turn tool tips off. Tried game settings and did not seem to work. Maybe I am just dumb but by map 8 having the tool tip pop up telling me what the tool was and how to use it made me want to REEEEEEPOTENTIAL MINI SPOILER-SKIP TO CONCLUSION:the last one was the eagle thing. Man... devs gotta do something, unless it was just me. clicked are that had boar, would NOT register skyscrapper (map 4 & 8) had to erase EVERYTHING around skyscraper including my tools/buildings. rebuild are, remove my stuff AGAIN, and THEN, FINALLY, clicking exact same spot i had before... it registered as skyscraper. don;t know what is up with that, but that was very much a buzz-kill and almost ruined the honeymoon I am currently having for this game.CONCLUSION:I love this game, love the art music and play. I am have played through once, will play through many more times I am sure. hope you get it and love it too.

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely fun, I've anticipated this release for maybe a year and it was well worth the wait. A wonderful reverse of management/builder games that ask you to take from the environment without a care in the pursuit of building magnificent structures, instead restoring the beautiful and varied ecosystems of the world ravaged by a civilization that participated in those selfsame pursuits to its planet's near end. _childDocuments_.review: It's a cute game, very satisfying and makes you think strategy and about the state of our world. Let me be clear though, if I could rate it a maybe I would except for just 1 fact. (Outside of the fact that maybe ratings dont exist.) A percentage of the profits are going to charities. This alone kept me from even thinking about a negative review, however from a gameplay standpoint there's some big problems.For starters the undo button only works for your previous move, and there are several buildings that once place also need to be activated, which counts as 2 moves. It makes it very hard to experiment and learn in the early game as even a few mistakes will require an entire reset of the level, and these take ~30 minutes on average. Secondly the recycling feature where you remove your buildings is awesome, except for when the only way to do it is by boat when there's several levels where you can do it by drone or monorail. What's the issue with the boat? Half the time you have to carve new rivers into the landscape, doing so also corrupts the grass so if you aren't planning for the recycle stage before laying grass in phase one you could end up in trouble. That and the straight lines the excavators make can look ugly against the more wild rivers. This both potentially seperates animals, ruins the landscape after you worked so hard to restore it, and just generally fights against the theme of the game.Then there's RNG portions. Some biomes can only be created within certain conditions, such as a small pond. A few of the levels provide you limited tools to create ponds, and depending on terrain generation, you may not be able to at all, at least not enough to satisfy the "x amount of biome required to progress" bar. I've had to reset 6 different levels to get new generation to pass them.But hey, when the game wasn't bending me over it was a calm and relaxing experience. If the devs would just fix these issues this game would be 10/10 on a bad day.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I was very excited for this game when I played the demo.  Little did I know, that was functionally a full quarter of the game. _childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: A fun, relaxing game featuring beautiful little landscapes that you revive. While good, I think the content to expense ratio is tipped ever so slightly in the wrong direction. With the addition of another biome or game mode it would completely change that calculation. _childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: It's a pretty cool game, interesting idea, and, quite a fun puzzle to achieve the set goal... I wish i could recommend it, but... I've played this game for 2 days with Steam Recording enabled, and have collected enough material to fill the entire thread with documented bugs. The game is completely broken, some systems not function at all or are bugged to all hell.And don't get me started on the performance. What you see on the screenshots above gets ~20fps on a machine that gets stable 60 in modern AAA games on mid-settings. The optimisation is atrocious, and game doesn't have graphics settings, except for LOD that goes from "♥♥♥♥ quality even when you zoom in all the way" to "max resolution textures and highest quality models for every single object, even when you zoom out all the way out", with no settings in-between.The state of this game is dreadful.On top of that, some design decisions in this game are completely arse-backwards. Like needing to have all species of animals present for level to be considered 100%-ed. A species of animals will only appear when it has *correct* conditions present for it. You're not told for which animals you need to create conditions for on each individual level, you just have to luck out into them, then luck out for RNG to spawn that specific animal in that specific place, then you can see. Oh, did i also mention that same animal species will have different conditions in different levels? Can't see which animals can be present on this map until you satisfy their conditions, and you can't see their conditions until they appear, from you satisfying their conditions. Fun!Or terraforming tools being revealed out in two stages. Not "unlocked" - revealed! So when you're doing the first stage of terraforming, which is supposed to serve as a base for the second stage - you are not told which tools you will have in the second stage. Why would you want to know that? That is, on top of not knowing which animals you will need to satisfy until they start spawning late into stage 2, some of which require conditions you could only really set up in stage 1. That is, on top of many terraforming changes being irreversible, and potentially softlocking you half an hour later. Naturally, game has no manual saves, "revert to start of the phase" that partially forgets the progress you made by the start of that phase, often in such way that you are unable to achieve the "forgotten" goals from this point on, and, naturally, "undo" button not working quite often.That is, if you can even finish a level, because, surprise! One of the VERY frequent bugs is game just refusing to let you leave once you've satisfied all of the animals and recycled all of the buildings. The button to do so simply doesn't appear, and you have to screw around to try to unsstuck the game, and pray.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely adore Terra Nil. In this reverse builder, you must work strategically to restore landscapes decimated by climate catastrophe. After you've cleaned the soil, planted forests, and observed the return of wildlife to your manufactured Edens, you pack everything up and leave. This short and singular game is a balm to the soul for those of us terrified by the threat of climate collapse. Play Terra Nil and ask yourself: what could we accomplish by leaving some spaces well enough alone? This little beam of hope is beautiful but brief - Terra Nil will present you with four distinct biomes to restore, and each of these biomes will present its own restoration challenges. After you have completed your first four restoration projects, four new variant scenarios are made available; for a total of eight playable scenarios. Randomization of precise terrain layout and a few levels of difficulty provide a little bit of replay value, but you may decide you've seen all that Terra Nil has to offer in a few days.The relatively small amount of content is not a criticism - I feel this game is well worth the price. I know I will return to this snackable ray of sunshine and be soothed by its beautiful ambient soundtrack and lovely pixel ecosystems again and again.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: For context, it took me about 9 hours to complete the full game on medium difficulty, but Im replaying it on the highest difficulty for a challenge. This is a very enjoyable game, and the progress from desolate wasteland to a paradise of your making is very satisfying; the music and graphics of the world help this immensely. My only gripe with this is much like a few other reviews I saw on here, about the lack of content. It has eight levels in it, each with their own challenges in trying to figure out how to complete your objectives. They were unique enough that it didn't feel old. I would recommend this game as a relaxing, turn your brain  off sorta game. Hopefully they expand on the game though, I'd love a level expansion with more biomes and challenges.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Delightful. The animal scanning tool is bit buggy and sometimes leaves the scanned outlines all over my map, which kind of ruins the otherwise great aesthetics. _childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: This game is Geo Engineering Propaganda and I am here for it. Price point to game play this is not worth it, there are city building games with more complex systems to master for less money. What you are paying for is the fantasy of turning a barren wasteland into a thriving ecosystem. The game drip feeds the player new mechanics that build off previous mechanics. Often I felt frustration over building placement because I did not know how the next mechanic would interact with my previous buildings and I had placed them sub optimally. Thankfully the low difficulty of the game mode I was playing meant sub optimal placement did not cause me to fail a level. There are only 4 biomes and 8 total levels, so the game is pretty short. However the levels are randomly generated, and there is joy in replaying a level whose mechanics you have mastered just to take in the scenery. Ultimately this game is for a niche audience of which I am a part. If the novelty of the concept is worth the price point I would suggest getting it. Otherwise don't.

_childDocuments_.review: A rewarding solarpunk game, more puzzle than simulation - this is not a "grand strategy" game. Difficulty setting is purely for personal satisfaction, which is wonderful to see.Accessibility notes: sound not required for gameplay. Some reading (tutorials and level goals).
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: For the better part of a decade Rimworld and Factorio players have caused untold devistation to countless environments.  No one is here to say whether their actions were morally right or wrong, but the fact remains that it's happened.  In your own little corner of the multiverse, it's your job to return one planet to a healthy state for countless generations to come.Terra Nill is a delightful little puzzle game were you return a barren wasteland to a functional home for wildlife.  Sometimes the game is annoying as a few bad move at the start of a stage can force you to redo the whole thing 30 minutes later (at least on harder difficulties).  Even so, it remains one of the most relaxing and fulfilling puzzle games out there.  It's free form and somewhat forgiving style makes it so there is minimal hand holding, several ways to solve problems, and just the right amount of challenge.There's not a huge amount of content for the price, but I'd still say it's worth it

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so satisfying at the end once you have fully restored each map. Its especially gratifying to see all the climate challenges completed and all the technology removed leaving the pristine landscape. This game introduced me to some unique and interesting game mechanics like the wildlife scanner, which makes you think about how to terraform strategically in the earlier phases. I also think the economy system was well constructed to maintain a challenge and force you to think about how to solve each of the different ecological problems. Its a very comfy game that is perfect for the switch so I hope it gets ported. It was a bit lacking in content so I would love to see some DLC added down the road.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: The game is less of a strategy game and more of a puzzle game with some simple, but time delayed puzzles. You would think there is little that could go wrong with that formula, alas it is not the case.The first phase of each puzzle, where you always purify the land/water is painfully boring but messing up placements of buildings can (and does) soft lock you in later phases. This is particularly true in any map where you are dealing with lava as it's far less forgiving to adjust where it flows. The second phase of each puzzle you build out the habitats. While this is more interesting there are several habitats that are spawned by single use objects (sky scrapers for example) and activating them at the wrong time can and will softlock you. For example if you get taken off guard by nuclear waste in a few of the puzzles, you might watch your bamboo get deleted and be unable to make more.The third phase of each puzzle is optimizing the environments and... clean up. As far as optimizing goes, the AI that determines how a creature's habitat spreads is not very smart. For example it's entirely possible for you to drop an animal that needs water tiles next to a river or lake and watch it's territory expand entirely away from the water and not satisfy it's water need even if there's plenty of unused tiles. Instead the game expects you to corral territories with sonic devices that disrupt all habitats around them for a short while. This can obviously mess up perfectly happy nearby animals and shouldn't need to be done.Cleanup is a tedious chore on most of the puzzles as it involves guiding a little boat or monorail car around the map recycle all your buildings. For the boat if you don't have nearby water it then becomes a silly game of blasting new channels to make rivers after everything is in place. For the monorails, it's a silly game of shuffling around rocks so that you can build a monorail network. Monorail cars can also get stuck in their animation and requires going back to the main menu and back into the game to free them.

_childDocuments_.review: Im an student at Eco & Wildlife and i like to see what you can do with peoples minds with just a beautiful game like this. It will inspire people to deep further in nature. _childDocuments_.review: It's a cute game. It's a little more structured and less open sandbox than I'd hoped, but it's still fun. There are 4 major biomes to repair. You have to complete all 4 of them to unlock secondary sites in each biome. The secondary sites are a little but more like a puzzle to solve. There aren't always the landscape features you want where you need them, so there's a little more creativity involved.That said, I've been playing for ~10 hours, and I've knocked out all 4 regular scenarios and 2 of the bonus sites (and that's with starting over a few times because I'm a perfectionist). I imagine it'll only take a few more hours to complete the last 2. After that, I'm not sure how much more I'll want to play because there doesn't seem to be too much other variety to the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Terra Nil is a fun, gorgeous game of simple puzzles and logic. There are an array of buildings and objects to place with their own impacts and ranges, and you are asked to efficiently place them to terraform the dead planet.I encountered too many bugs to properly have fun, though. Bugs in building placement (one map generates sources of nuclear radiation and I found after several resets that for some reason capping one made it illegal to place the precursor radiation scrubbers), bugs in UI (satellite recall button didn't appear in one mission, after confirming via watching youtube play videos I just gave up), etc. My frustration outstripped my fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Playing Terra Nil is like curling up with a comfy book, just a chill game to terraform and leave no trace to. _childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I played the game all the way through when it first came out and loved it, but I think the latest update smoothed out the few rough spots I initially encountered, and I'm enjoying playing it all the way through a second time. So I figured it's time for a review!Terra Nil is really easy to sink into for longer than intended because each puzzle flows smoothly from one phase into the next. Purging pollution, restoring nature and then cleaning up all traces of your involvement before calling the job finished all feels really satisfying. And finally, it's beautiful - the end of a level looks so dramatically different to the polluted land you started with, and you're rewarded with some time to take it all in while gentle music plays in the background. I may have even felt an emotion or two while doing so, but ymmv!

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game very much, it just fills in my short period of free time at night and soothes my mind. It is $25, perhaps a bit high for some people. But being a scientist, I feel sympathetic for working on a small project that you (and your small but loyal team) really cares about for months/years and putting a ton of love into it, and eventually hoping it gets accepted and appreciated by the audience. I can feel the love that the devs put into the game. And their love for mother earth. I always buy indie games like this and enjoy them a lot, and appreciate the love and effort that the developers injected into their game like it's their own child.Okay some real review -This game is a "reverse city builder", by that they mean you restore the world polluted by human. Cool idea. After you restore each region, the scenery and animals running around gives you a rewarding feeling that's different from winning an online multiplayer match. Each level does not take more than half an hour to finish, and most of them are not hard to complete all objectives (one of the extra levels is a bit challenging). It is just a soothing experience. Fine music, no obvious glitches, UI is fine. Although there are not a lot of levels, they said they plan to develop it further in the future; if you like the demo but feel the game is expensive for a ~5 hour indie game, wishlist and wait. But I think it is totally worth its price.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a zen puzzle game that really hits something in my core. Your first half of your first playthrough will likely be no problem, but once you slide up on the difficulty by engaging the second half, it might make you realize how careless you had been all along.Regardless, extremely fun and engaging to play. _childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Super fun puzzle game! At first I thought the game would be more adjacent to Factorio in a singleplayer survival world, but it's actually closer to a puzzle game where you learn to use your resources in the best way to complete the level. _childDocuments_.review: Great concept, but poor execution.TLDR:  The game plays like a Beta version, rather than a final release.  It needs A LOT of fine tuning.  I spent 9 hours playing it.  A third of that was so irritating, that I'll probably never touch this game again.The first region (temperate) plays fairly well.  Beginning with the second one (tropical), it all falls apart.  The tutorial fails to provide important information, causing you to fail maps after spending hours on them.  Contextual information elements block your needed view of the ground.  The game will sometimes tell you that you've failed (forcing a restart of the map) due to being out of resources when you aren't, and other times, when you ARE out of resources, it does NOT tell you you've failed.  Once you select an item to place (generating contextual pop-ups and info), you can't deselect it - there is no way to revert to a normal, blank cursor.  Many buildings require multiple steps to place them, but you can only undo a single step.  If you're placement of a building is off, you may not know till several steps have passed, and then it's too late to redo it.  Why are there tools/buildings available in the first stage, that aren't in the second?  That doesn't even make sense...I enjoyed the temperate maps, despite some minor annoyances, but after my second attempt at a tropical map, I was too frustrated to keep trying.  It's so unnecessarily complex, that it's just not enjoyable.  Given that the tropical map is only the second stage, I have to assume that it only gets worse from there on.

_childDocuments_.review: Relatively fun game with mechanics that turn it from cozy to tedious and annoying. The Vita Nova update has made getting critters more irritating than rewarding. _childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Terra Nil is a fairly lightweight game about restoring an ecosystem, then packing up and departing having returned it all to pristine nature.  IMO it's much more a puzzle game than a sandbox: you have a sequential series of tasks (green the area, restore biomes, introduce wildlife, pack up and leave) leading to completion: it isn't a sandbox. Something more complex/artistic than "smash through the level at the minimum possible speed" will require a degree of problem-solving and thinking, not helped by annoyinglu simplistic man pages.As a puzzle game, it's good fun. There is no time pressure, no requirement to hit any target with any specific time, simply managing your existing resources and the terrain to achieve whatever it is you want to achieve. That can be as pretty-and-internally-logical or as goal-orientated as you choose. That makes it one of the very few games I play that's actually relaxing, without feeling like a total waste of time.There are four regions each with radically different considerations, and the game walks you through how to play each one during the first play-through. This unlocks a second map in each region, though maps are procedurally generated so replayability is fairly good. There are some nice little feedback mechanisms and additional considerations (e.g. bonus points for planting in ideal conditions, so the sequencing of planting, controlled burns and cloud seeding to obtain the most resource). The later regions are more complex and require further thought.The graphics are 2D and based on an orthogonal square grid. They're pretty, but nothing spectacular. This does have the upside that the game requires very little disk space! Further, the transformation of blasted wasteland to green and pleasant land is done sufficiently well to be pleasing in itself.I'm four hours in with five of eight maps complete; I am confident that I'll get another two-to-four hours from the game before I've done everything once, and even then I can leave the game installed for something to chill out for an hour or so with. The game is sufficiently satisfying to give it good replayability value even once you've knocked off all the goals.Recommended at full value.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so fun. It's less of a city building sim, and more of a puzzle where you have to decide the perfect place to put each building on a small budget. At the end you have to figure out how to recycle everything which is also more puzzle-like. Less simulation, more strategy. Love this game just wish it was longer. _childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoy this game. It's relatively small and depending on what you like in a game it might not have much replay value, but for me particularly, it hits exactly the right sweet spot between relaxing, not-too-difficult puzzle game and city-(un)builder. I use this game for meditation (disclaimer: I know I'm probably not doing meditation right). Get this game if you're looking for a chill time with JUST enough challenge to keep it interesting.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Game-breaking bugs and glitches on launch. Only 4 levels "With randomization!" which adds minimal extra game mechanics.As a core concept, it's a great idea for a game! Restore a wasteland and then clean up and look at your handiwork. But there's too much that doesn't make sense for it to be engaging. Most buildings "fire" once and are done. Your irrigation center sprays water once, and it's ready to be recycled... unless you have a monorail system, in which case you move it 1 foot to the left and presto it can be used again! Everything is paid for with leaves which come from... grass? Is someone paying us? Are we doing this out of the kindness of our hearts? Come to think of it, where is everyone else on planet Earth and how did the humans die, but the pandas survive? There are too many questions and I can safely say the game does not answer them."Well, sometimes realism is sacrificed in the name of good gameplay" Fair point, fair point. But uh, what *is* the gameplay? The closest this can be mapped to is a puzzle game where you optimally overlap building ranges. It is about as challenging as building a sandwich, slicing the cheese and the tomato and the bread to the right sizes. Spatial optimization is nifty, but in most games I've seen it (like Anno) it's a background mechanic. The one change this game brings to the concept is threatening bankruptcy if you misclick and only giving 1 undo at a time. Which seems to run counter to the wholesome, relaxed atmosphere every other component is trying to build.Lastly, let's talk about pricing. This is a low-gear game for either children or adults who want to relax like a kid again. It is very pretty to look at when the visuals aren't glitching. It is well-paced to 1-hour game sessions. It makes me feel wholesome, despite everything in it going against my training as an environmental engineer. I would pay 5, maybe 10 dollars. 20 dollars on release, because I was still hyped from the demo almost a year ago. But $25 is too much. For that price, I could grab one of the older, greener, high-tech-ier Anno games and still be obsessing over building placement for eight hours this weekend... and I could undo my mistakes.Oh, right, last little stinger: the RNG is so broken I spent 4 of my 8 hours on levels that were impossible to win from the start. Thanks for wasting as much of my time as you improved. I hope sunflowers over nuclear waste becomes a meme.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Love the game, super relaxing and cute graphics. Perfect for the chill gamer, anyone could also play this, considering the different difficulity settings, and it is easy to understand. _childDocuments_.review: From the creators of Broforce and Gen*tal Jousing, they take a relatively unknown indie game and made a pretty polished game out of it. _childDocuments_.review: A delightful experience!I have long wished for a game in this genre which was not about expansion and industrialization - I greatly appreciate the philosophy behind the game, and it seemed fairly well researched at that. It isn't an educational game, but I don't think educational elements would be out of place if they wanted to add them; I was delighted by seeing elk and pandas appear on my map and would have been eager to read a few facts about them as part of the milestone. The UI is charming, with illustrations mimicking a field journal for fauna and a technical manual for the machines. The sound design is excellent, with new nature sounds unlocking as you restore different biomes. I was happy to see that despite having few levels, once you're finished it unlocks new versions of them (unplayed at time of review), so there's some replayability on top of the levels being procedurally generated.It's very relaxing. My minor grievances are:- The tutorial is short, but unskippable, and having already played the demo I was not super patient with that.- At times, the next step I needed to take was slightly unclear, although not a major obstacle, and I enjoyed playing with the systems to see how to move forward efficiently even when I didn't immediately understand what I was doing.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: My only gripe is how short the game is - the "second half" of the game was a pleasant extra twist to what i grew to understand. It's beautiful and a great premise. Truly love the art and whole aesthetic. I think the different biomes could be a little more nuanced to help space out different territories and stretch the game. There is a great opportunity to expand to sea biomes as a DLC - open ocean, deep sea, caves, better kelp forests, underwater volcanoes, better shallows and coastal regions. And Desert biomes, not everything is lush and full of water, doesn't mean it's not a thriving and diverse ecosystem. The city ruins offers opportunity to turn these biomes on their heads too with how they could add extra challenges or opportunities.If the developers are willing to keep growing this game, i would love to keep supporting it to see how it evolves.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, a fun little game.The premise behind it is cool (cleaning up polution and terraforming a planet), and the elements they've included (equipment for increasing or lowering humidity, initiating controlled burns, creating rock formations, etc.) each have their place in the various regions that you're tasked with repairing.Once your'e done terraforming and restoring life to what was a wasteland, you get to clean up after yourself by recycling all the equipment you deployed.  Afterwards, you can relax and enjoy the scenery, which is reward unto itself.From what I can tell, there are 4 different continents, each with 2 regions you'll need to terraform.  I was able to complete all 8 regions, and hit a planetary score of 100%, but it required re-doing a couple of regions.You do have to monitor the resources you have available to you, or you can find yourself stuck.  Each piece of equipment you deploy has a cost, and if you don't generate enough resources with your actions, you may get to a point where there's nothing you can do but start that region over.  Not all of the mechanics were extremely obvious, and while the instructions gave you an overall idea of the objectives you need to complete, it's up to you to figure out how to get there.If you enjoy puzzles, strategy, city builders, and helping the environment, you'll likely enjoy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a puzzle game with eco-restoration schemes... but rest assured, it's a puzzle game through and through. The first part of the game has you restoring 4 environments that are largely accessible and allow you to learn the game mechanics. Completionists will continue onto the 2nd part of the game, where you restore another 4 environments, but the map mechanics effectively push the game into a challenging tier.What makes this game very much a puzzle game, is that there's a very limited undo mechanic. Mistakes can compound and it's very likely that you'll need to restart the map... and restarting the map is actually a map regeneration, so you can't really take map-instance key learnings and necessarily apply them to a different map. Lessons learned from mechanics absolutely carry forward, but individual map-geography lessons do not.Lastly, people looking for a "realistic eco restoration" story just need to set those expectations aside. This is not an eco-restoration sim. It's a puzzle game... a largely relaxing puzzle game so long as you stay off the challenge maps.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a forest ecologist / forest health specialist and I enjoy Terra Nil. I'm also a longtime gamer, so I do see some design issues that could make this puzzle game significantly better, but they have done a great job here in general. Recognize that despite the ecosystem restoration theme of this game, it's basically a puzzle game. The ecology aspect is not terribly strong; nothing like SimLife or Gundan Frontier. But all aspects of the game do have some connection to ecology or ecosystem restoration. The biggest issues of the game, in my opinion are: 1. One of your final goals is to make all the animal populations happy by creating ideal mixes of adjacent environments. HOWEVER, you don't get info on how good these are until after multiple stages of the game, including AFTER you create the habitats. So you are forced to guess at good habitat placement during the stage where it matters most. 2. Fine tuning environments to give ideal conditions after the animals show up can be really frustrating. Many of your methods for manipulating environments AFTER they have been built are destructive and have significant tradeoffs that can ruin other habitats. Again, the time to make these habitat combinations properly is during the habitat building phase, NOT at the end when everything is already on the board. 3.  The encyclopedia gives only vague information on what animals want. Only in game ONCE THEY ARE ALREADY PRESENT do you see the finer details of what they need. The time to have this information available is during the habitat building stage. 4. Replayability isn't very strong, as you create most of the content yourself, so replaying a level doesn't add anything new to the experience. On top of that, there are no technology unlocks so there's no incentive to put additional time into the game. Finally, due to the frustrations above, I just want to call my previous successes good and not re-experience the frustrations. Ok, so that's alot of criticism, and there's more I could get into, but the overall game is good and it's clear the developers care about this game and the subject. A recent update came out that adds some quality of life improvements and some new dynamics that improve the game (plus new content that I haven't unlocked yet). Terra Nil is priced appropriately for the quality of its content, and there isn't much else like it. I highly recommend this game, just be prepared for some frustration as noted above.

_childDocuments_.review: 8,5/10In a not so distant future, humanity reached the level of being able to explore space, allowing it to reach other planets and transform them, to allow its colonization. Unfortunately despite all these advances, certain things unfortunately still seem not to have changed, such as the desire for natural resources, even if that means having to destroy all the fauna and flora of a planet, while at the same time polluting the soil and waters. But one planet in particular could be the beginning of a big change in humanity's relationship with nature. ^^It is here that a great project begins, on a planet that no longer harbors humanity, but where traces of it are found everywhere. Here, the mission will begin, through the use of a wide variety of technologies, to transform this barren soil, with dry riverbeds and polluted seas, into a green paradise again, from tropical islands to cold tundra, cleaning and restoring vegetation, and later the fauna back, thus allowing nature in this world to have a new chance, and who knows if everything works out, in the future the same will happen in other worlds. ^^+ A very relaxing and fun game, where we don't have to build cities, nations or empires, but use technology to restore nature back to its place.+ Four biomes, with their vegetation, animals, characteristics and specific constructions for their restoration.+ Procedurally generated map, so even if the region and biome are the same, the map will always have a unique terrain.+ Simple system that uses points, which are spent when building buildings, and earned as vegetation is restored, from grass to jungles and forests.+ All biomes have at least three different types of vegetation, and six species of animals to restore and appreciate the beauty.+ Beautiful arts, I really liked the artist part and thought it was very beautiful.+ Relaxing music and sound effects.- It's a fun game, but unfortunately it only has four biomes, with a smaller and a larger map for each.- Most of the time is relaxing, but the beginning of all maps can be a little stressful, as it is the part with the highest expenditure of points that are limited and the lowest return.And so begins the player's mission with the objective of restoring the regions of the planet, using a very simple system, with the currency of exchange being points, these points are spent when making constructions to clean the soil, produce energy, change the climate, and is gained by making the flora grow, promoting the growth of vegetation such as grass, forests, coral reefs, mosses among other biomes, thus allowing the player to seek the balance between spending preparing the environment, and the return by making the vegetation flourish. ^^Once I've learned how to balance the points, I need to learn how to balance the environment, as each biome has three or four different types of vegetation, which need to occupy a minimum area, as well as each one has its prerequisites, some can only be done in places of low or high terrain, others need to be built on land and then taken to the sea, some need the place to have grass first, while others even need the region to have suffered a fire beforehand, thus making it equally more challenging and interesting, the mission to restore while adapting to the requirements of each type of vegetation. ^^Produced by the South African studio Free Lives, I was really surprised by the quality of the art, I really liked it and found it to be very beautiful, both during the restoration process and in the final part, where we can see the art and beauty of the restored nature of the various biomes, and the plants and animals that live in them. As for the soundtrack, I was also very satisfied, finding the songs very calm and peaceful, and very pleasant to listen to while playing or even outside the game to relax. ^^Terra Nil was a game I'd had my eye on for some time, having played since the first demo that was made available, and bought it on pre-order. And now after having played and explored it, I can say that I liked what I saw, while restoring the four available biomes, some more challenging than others. For those looking for a large amount of content, maybe this game is not very pleasing, because as said before, it only has four biomes, but for those looking for a different, relaxing and fun experience, while looking to make the places gray and lifeless, again in landscapes full of green and life, this is a game that I recommend. ^^

_childDocuments_.review: One of the nicest chill games I've played in a long while. I've seen a lot of reviews trying to call this a puzzle game or an eco-restoration simulator. It has a little bit of both, but ultimately it's just a nice relaxing ecosystem creator, with a bit of layered gameplay to teach players how those ecosystems are formed.You start out with a barren wasteland, then use little machines and buildings to remove toxins from the land and the ocean, plant grass, raise or lower the temperature and humidity, etc. Good advice I can give to new players would be to not worry too much about getting all the grass planted perfectly or the ground detoxed in the most ideal way possible. Once you raise the humidity high enough, it will start to rain naturally, wash away all the poop and the puzzle will solve itself! It's a nice feeling to lay out your toxin scrubbers and grass planters for maximum efficiency, but not vital.Also seen a lot of people complaining about the price. I 100%ed this game over 20 hours and I would quite happily dip into it again, just for the fun of making a little custom landscape from scratch. If you're not that sort of person, either wait for it to go on sale or just play the demo. I wouldn't say the pricetag justifies giving the whole game a negative review.If I was going to suggest improvements for any future development, the animal stage could be a bit more in-depth. Currently, you just plonk a building down and look for animals that, (in the game's logic) are already there, you just need to confirm they exist. Might be fun if you needed to tailor the landscape in order to balance the population of certain predator/prey species. Example - too many deer will munch up all the grass in an area before it can grow back and go extinct. Too many wolves will over-hunt the deer and both species will vanish, etc.tldr; Friendly Nature Tetris. Good game. Worth the time.

_childDocuments_.review: While I did enjoy the experience, it was a mild enjoyment that I cannot recommend at full price due to the lack of content and depth. I would suggest you wait for a sale for many reasons. Games like this are why I wish the recommendation system wasn't so strict on forcing you to choose yes or no with no middle-ground options - because I did like it, I just don't think it's worth $25.The game concept is certainly interesting, but the problem is that it lacks depth and falls short. I was able to 100% the whole game, with bonus levels, achieving all optional goals, and 6/6 animals on all maps in just over 5 hours. This itself isn't a huge problem but it lacks replay-ability which I'll get to later. This play time is including time spent troubleshooting the numerous bugs I ran into that required me to reload multiple times.Bugs aren't a huge issue as those should be fixed soon, but as I said the game lacks depth. It was a very easy game start to finish, which might be what you're looking for, but if you want a challenge then skip this one. The animals are a good example, the "harder" levels really should have had different species, at least cosmetically. I was honestly expecting the last 4 levels to do something new but they are just the first 4 again, with a slightly different strategy that stops being different once you get into making biomes.It is a charming game, and it has great visuals. It has a good concept and a good gameplay loop in the levels. There just isn't enough there for me. I don't find it to be an enjoyable replayable experience either because of the fact that the entire game is sort of the same thing on repeat with slight variations, and no real change in strategy along the way aside from different buildings that do the same things as previous ones, only with different placement requirements.Tbh the most strategic depth this game had for me was being required to do things they don't flat-out tell you for some levels, such as:1. Building a  will  immediately.2. You can use a  to  to make them  when you lack .Overall I find myself walking away from this one feeling unimpressed. It was not a memorable experience because it felt so repetitive with not enough distinct content to break the repetition. I certainly think it needed to be longer with more variety of strategies. 4 main levels and 4 bonus levels that are just slightly harder versions of the main levels is not enough to justify a $25 release imo. Maybe $15 - $20,TL;DR: 8 Levels, giving 4-6 Hours of gameplay - for 25 Dollars? Idk about that one chief. I can't say this one is worth it at full price, especially considering the game is essentially the same 4 levels, twice in a row.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: An extremely enjoyable and addictive unique terraforming game that feels a little limited.I love this game. That's the short of it. I've followed it's development and played the demos whenever I could, and now that the end product is out, I love it. You're presented with a campaign of sorts where you work through four separate biomes and restore them from apocalyptic wastelands to vivid and beautifully realised habitats; contending with each biomes relatively unique challenges but fundamentally using the same mechanics in each to achieve the goals. A little buggy occasionally but nothing game breaking and certainly nothing that got in the way of my overall enjoyment. The animals are meant to be the cherry on the cake once the habitat is restored, and while they look great they are frustratingly mismatched and poorly researched; penguins are presented alongside a roster of Arctic animals even though they are from the Antarctic (just use seals...), tortoises don't live on beaches (they're predominant grazers), and hawksbill turtles are marine turtles and not lagoon/freshwater dwelling (there's plenty of actual freshwater turtles that they could be swapped with). At 11 hours playtime I have completed it, secured all bar one of the steam achievements and replayed some of the maps a number of times. It is a short game with limited replayability aside from achievement hunting, perhaps best treated as a kick back and relax puzzle game to fill time or chill.A wishlist:- Bigger maps for that 'great plains' feel and to make the tundra really feel like a tundra, the maps often end up feeling cluttered.- Creative mode? The art style is outstanding and an opportunity to fully utilise and appreciate it in a freeform creative mode would be incredible.

This is also problematic within the final area in which ZERO explanation is given that earth dredging makes it possible to place tidal generators where the dredge is.TL;DR Lacking content, Needs QoL improvements for UI descriptions and game play
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I really wish there was a mixed option, but the fact of the matter is the game wasn't worth the asking price.Don't get me wrong, the game is visually wonderful, and what's there gameplay-wise was really cool when it comes to its ideas of reclaiming a destroyed ecosystem. My problems are similar to many others reviewing it, I beat this game in two hours on the normal difficulty, and the game only has 4 maps with no real replayability. Visually pretty maps with its own mechanics, but in the end, each map plays out the same with no real puzzle solving that really uses all the tools at your disposal. Are there ways to make it interesting? Yeah, and I feel that might be possible through more environmental challenges that could pop up during the reclamation, but this game doesn't have that factor to it, leading to a no stress one track puzzles with no real deviations.The no stress nature of this is not really a problem, hell, it's pretty relaxing at its core, but I feel that compared to games like Dorf Romantik or Islanders, which fall in that relaxing puzzle solving gameplay loop this game tries to tap into, it falls very short. I think what ties into that is the fact the latter two have fun puzzles to solve that are guided by your own planning, and replay-ability despite the randomness of tiles, buildings, and maps. At the moment, Terra Nil doesn't have enough of that similar design philosophy to really make replaying it any more fun.That said, if they do add stuff and improve it, I'd gladly change my review, but as it stands $25 is pretty steep for something that could be completed in two lunchbreaks.
