_childDocuments_.review: A joy to play, and great take on city builders. The basic idea is that you start with a toxic wasteland and slowly build an ecosystem. The game is based on short cycles, each of which focuses on a small map.- Phase 1: start adding buildings to clean toxins, humidify the land, plant "pioneer species"- Phase 2: add more buildings to create the right conditions for specific ecosystems and grow them.- Phase 3: clean up everything y ou have build and leave the ecosystem to function on its own.It's a great idea, and it's just a neat concept that your own buildings are not the "thing" you are building, but rather a means to an end, something you eventually want to get rid of.The game works very nicely but is also quite simple, so there were some systems that I would have loved to have seen a more complex and intricate version of. This is fine: I like a game that gives you some neat ideas without taking up all of yoru time, but this one did make me think: oh, I wish these ideas make it into a bigger game some day.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Wow! This game has grown so much since I first played the demo nearly THREE years ago! I cannot believe it has been that long but I am so ready to be back and explore all the new content.Firstly, I love the new animal system. I think it finally gets them involved in the whole restoration of the area and they are the perfect difficulty; Not too finicky that you have to plan ages ahead but not so easy that its a given your region can fully satisfy the animals needs. I think it really gives you a direction for where to put certain biomes, especially when playing maps after the initial playthrough. Also, the new maps are incredible! I know that many of them have been in the game for a long time but they are all difficult enough that they do really bring a challenge for the player to make sure they plan and efficiently use the leaves to their full extent. I found myself doing regions again to just play through the map again and make more beautiful versions. I rarely found myself really stuck and at most had to restart a couple times after understanding the unique twist of each map.Overall, The game has just become so fun and varied to play now and its still got the replayability just like the demo which had only the temperate map. I remember sitting for hours redoing that one map over and over just because everytime the result for different. Now I have so many more options and I will continue playing this game, waiting for the next updates.

_childDocuments_.review: Update 27.06.: The new update "Vita Nova" improves an already awesome game in almost every aspect. This also eliminates the criticism I voiced during the release (see below). In it's current version the game is very fleshed out and deserves all the recognism it can get. First things First: Let us please take a moment to step back and appreciate, that it´s not the hundred Battle Royale clones out there, but innovative gems like this that push gaming as a whole forward. Terra Nil takes a risk, introduces something new and I am very thankful for that.The game itself is pretty awesome and delivers what the demo promised a year ago. It´s also pretty hard - at least at the medium difficulty I´m playing it at. But I won´t complain because Terra Nil might be too shallow if it where easier. But the gameplay loop of building a basic infrastructure, filling it with vegetation and finally cleaning everything up checks out and is massively satisfiying.My one complaint is that Terra Nil sometimes does not seem to be sure about what kind of game it wants to be. Presentation and scope make it feel like a mobile game, yet the complexity and price tag are the one of a desktop game.While advertised as "reverse city builder", Terra Nil has little to no similarities to city builders and is indeed much more of a puzzle game.And last but not least Terra Nil clearly aims at a "Zen Experience" yet it´s pretty hard and can even be frustrating at times.Perhaps those little inconsistencies are the price we have to pay for Terra Nils innovative approach but I cannot help thinking that it would be an even better game if those design choices would have been made clearer.

_childDocuments_.review: This is such a beautiful, calm puzzle game. You are on a planet that has fallen into ruin and it's your job to help nature recover and thrive again. You do this in 3 phases:1. Clean the toxic wasteland, create fertile soil, water it.2. Grow vegetation, create different biomes until animals return to the area.3. Make sure the animals are happy, recycle your man-made buildings until only nature remains, leave with your space ship.In these 3 phases you also manipulate the climate (temperature, humidity). There are main goals and optional tasks to make sure the area is restored as best as possible.Unlike others, I had little problem satisfying animal needs. The key to make sure that every animal group is happy is to diversify the landscape (for example, don't place one big forest in one corner of the map, but place three or four smaller forests across the map).To me, other mechanics were more frustrating, so I think the following mechanics need some improvement:1. You can undo only the very last step. I wish you could undo the last three or maybe five last steps because sometimes you need to place three or more buildings in order to see if everything works out the way you planned. Undoing only one step and then realizing that my plan wouldn't work out was frustrating because I wasted precious resources.2. I don't like the way the save game works. If you play a session, you have the 3 phases mentioned above. If you pass a phase but fail the next one, you can restart the failed phase. I wish I could save freely, but I guess the developers felt the need to restrict this in order to make the game feel more like a puzzle.3. If you pass a phase, you sometimes unlock new buildings. The problem is, you don't see which buildings you will unlock. This can potentially lead to you making mistakes in the phases before because you don't know how the session will unfold. I wish you could see the upcoming buildings in order to plan everything better.Still, I enjoyed this game a lot and if new maps will come out in a future update, I will definitely pick up the game again. I wish there was more content because I had a lot of fun with this game.

_childDocuments_.review: An absolutely stunning inversion of the city builder/planner game -- in practice, it feels almost like Cultist Simulator. Instead of dictating what and how and when, you have to understand how the systems interact with one another, feel them out, take advantage of the natural patterns of the earth, in order to bring life back.EDIT: As someone who has played the game for more than 5 hours, I can tell you there is plenty to do after 4 hours. It's like saying "there's not a lot to do in Dorfromantik after you make a train" or something. If you like this game, you will be playing it for a long time. Also, complaints about it "not being worth the price" -- I would invite you to look at the price of going to the movies for 2 hours and what a trash experience most movies are. This game is a GREAT value for the $25 you pay.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Play the demo, that is the game. If $25 is a lot for you wait for a sale.I don't review stuff often on steam but I played like 20+ hours of the original prototype of this game so I felt important to review the final version. Part of me wishes there was a mixed option, but I'd still recommend this over not.First off this game is getting a lot of flack for not having enough "content". Yes after 4 hours you will see every biome and every building, I feel like if this is the main criticism of the game maybe people have only been playing games from the last 8 years or something. It's a puzzle game that has procedural levels, that is what the content and replayability is, the gameplay, not what types of biomes there are.To me it's like complaining that you've seen all the content in a game like Tetris or Sim City after 5 minutes, because you technically have. There is no meta progression where you get new pieces in Tetris, there is no alternate biomes or mechanics in Sim City. You just get one thing done well.I do think the price of the game is a little high and it feels like it was because it was picked up by a "larger indie" publisher and they felt they needed to recoup their costs. Which is a little disappointing.It would also be nice if we did get just some basic updates with more achievements, optional larger maps, maybe a custom map maker, and some additional challenge modes or difficulty. In a lot of ways this game feels a bit easier than the hardest maps on the prototype, and as someone who has basically already played it a lot in an earlier for it would have been nice to see something to allow for that without having to add "new content".If $25 for a game is a lot for you then you should probably hold off. Play the demo, that is what the game is + a few more biomes. The replayability is just enjoying the puzzle mechanics of the game, not meta progression or unlocking things. If you NEED that kind of gameplay to be engaged by a game then this probably isn't for you. That doesn't make it a bad game though as there are TONS of games that do one thing simple, and straightforward, without a ton of content and they are fantastic.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't really care for these types of games, as I'm not into growing civilizations or anything of the sort. But since Terra Nil is about rejuvenating the environment instead of building onto it, I find it very compelling. The premise is simple – you have a wasteland and it's your job to restore it. You generate power, scrub a small area of toxins, and then add greenery. The first phase is always about adding enough of this greenery (or purifying enough of the nearby waters). The game is fairly complex but it does a pretty good job of guiding you forward. The second phase is trickier, as you need to restore four biomes. The last phase is about reintroducing animal life and then removing all of your machines so you can leave the land without a trace of your involvement. It's immensely satisfying.The game has four areas that you unlock sequentially, but each area has a second version that unlocks once you complete all of the initial ones. These mix things up by adding in machines and features from across the initial four levels. They can get pretty difficult, though. In the second version of the second area requires you to build forests by constructing shade pillars. But shade pillars can only be placed on cliffs and need to be in a triangle and you have to dredge up all of the level's land from the ocean. If you don't dredge up the ocean in preparation for this, you'll need to restart the whole level. But things aren't usually THIS demanding. You can zoom in extremely close and the graphics are lovely and detailed. The game isn't massively long but I feel like it's got enough content, especially since the levels are all generated, which makes attempts feel fresher than otherwise. At the end of the last area, you have to build a rocket, which is neat and it does a great job of making you feel like you accomplished something during the last four levels. You can restart any of a level's three phases once you get stuck and you can often undo your last move, which is helpful, but you can't quicksave or undo multiple moves in a row, so the game isn't extremely forgiving of mistakes, so you can sink yourself if you're not careful. But I think Terra Nil is highly enjoyable and recommend it to anyone who wants an anti-city builder that often feels like a puzzle game.

_childDocuments_.review: It's quick, but very zen.  It's deceptively simple, appearing at first to just be a "color the land green" simulator. _childDocuments_.review: instead of the 4X genre (Explore, Expand, Exploit, Exterminate) which normally formes the foundation for ressource management games where you start out exploring your surroundings to find ressources, then expanding with those ressources to build larger and larger industry, which you can then use to further exploit the ressources in your enviornment, before finally exterminating some kind of threat meant to test the efficiency of your industry this game is instead a new genre of its own the 4R (Reclaim, Restore, Rewild, Retreat) firstly to reclaim the irradiated wasteland, completely devoid of nature and exploited to the fullest extend, then you restore bringing back green planes and water ways, however this is still a wasteland so you'll need to rewild it restore ecosystems and inefficiency, and finally, your ultimate goal is to tear down all the infrastructure you have build, to clean up all the little buildings you have littered the region with, and to retreat.and this is very much something that is needed in our current day, because the colonialist conventions of the 4X genre are exatly the same processes which have placed us in the ecological collapse which we are facing in the real world, which is why its in some ways reassuring and nice to see a game that presents an alternative game structure, and grounds itself in real approaches to enviornmental restoration and highlights some enviornmental lessons about how even fire and volcanic erruptions are an important part of a healthy ecosystem, to how sunflowers can even play an important role in restoring enviornments we would otherwise consider dead and gone.

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked this game, I consider it worth it at full price, but I'm not sure after 15 hours I would come back to this, but I still do have some achievements left over that are fairly reasonable to get. Probably a few more hours just for that.Trying to get shade tents to work was the greatest challenge that this game could offer. It is not tedious, but each level you reach a point where you're an unstoppable restorative force. This usually happens when you figure out how to make the rain fall again. Once you're surveying for animals there isn't really much of a challenge at that point. The part after you plant enough grass to reach the next phase is by far the difficult part of making it work. Realizing you have to start over was never enough of a pain that made me stop playing. It was a struggle to figure out how to make forests (realizing burning grass was not going to make arable enough land, you have to cultivate the secondary biome features and burn them away).Looking for animals was fun, because you had to use what you made as a sort of final check that everything was done right. You will do additional biome crafting to accommodate some of the animals you haven't found yet. It is never the same process in each biome and it was always interesting to go back to the second area and see what new challenge there was.Game is super pretty, it felt very nice when thunder and rain finally came to the valley I was working in. Sound design is fantastic and immersive.Very lovely game, you all should be very proud.

_childDocuments_.review: Hopecore. Fun, casual puzzle/resource management game about cultivating an ecosystem that supports a set of animals. It's certainly not a city builder, and not turn based either. Every other tag is accurate though.  You purify soils, water them, seed clouds, control-burn vegetation so you can grow large forests. Animals start to move in and you satisfy their requirements. It keeps sending different subspecies based on the composition of your ecosystem, so if you want a certain set of animals then yes it becomes complicated. However, the game only requires a certain number, not specific kinds (at least for the first two levels). In my experience it's easy to end each level having pleased enough species. Then you place log bridges for animals to cross streams or climb cliffs, and once you're done it's one last puzzle to use your water-fairing recycle drone to clean up your tech. At the end you sit back and admire your work with a cutscene that showcases your ecosystem. I think it's pretty neatThere's no time limit on each level, but the ecosystem does slowly changed over time. There are time requirements before animal groups are unsatisfied and leave, but they get replaced by another group so no big deal. There's also an option called Zen Mode that gets rid of resource requirements for a super casual mode.For all the reviews there are on this game, only 6.8% of players have completed the second level according to the achievements.

There are certain aspects that remind me of Creeper World - which is a compliment as that is another favourite of mine.Altogether a beautifully designed and put-together game, with great mechanics, novel toy-box, lovely music, and a nice message 🤗🌼🌻🌲

_childDocuments_.review: Terra Nil is basically a resource management game at its core, with no story beyond "fix this planet". You have a set number of leaves to build stuff with, you get more leaves for improving the environment you're dropped into. Sometimes that means spending a while building windmills and toxin scrubbers so you can irrigate the land and bring back grass, sometimes that means setting off explosives to make literal rivers of lava to heat up everything enough that you can melt the snow on the poles. There are also just four separate maps, with an alternative version of each that unlocks once you've completed the final island once (the alternative version will have the same goals as the original, but with some added challenges and tricks to employ).It's not a super long game. It'll take a few afternoons, or a very focused day-long session, to complete all 8 maps and get all the various sub-goals within them. But Terra Nil's benefit is that the maps are randomly generated, so every map is literally unique. Sometimes good, and sometimes nearly unplayable because of terrain generation making large swaths of the land unreachable at all and thus making it impossible to fix the environment enough to complete. So, replayability in that aspect.One could wish that there were more overlapping elements from the different maps (windmills with power lines, anyone?), and also more maps to play. But it's still a new game at the time of writing, so perhaps we'll see more being implemented later on.For now, it's a very pretty, very zen game about restoring a barren wasteland into a vibrant eco system teeming with plants and animals.

Finding the animals (flamingo and beaver) could be a little annoying but otherwise I loved finding each species. I also appreciate how they are supporting Endangered Wildlife Trust. Part of me wishes it was a little longer but I'm also glad to feel like I've accomplished a game 100% I can see myself opening this on occasion in the future just to relax and restore the planet a bit since its different every time.

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR / Conclusion at the bottomSummary: This is a top-down desolation restoration game. If you enjoy taking destroyed environments and restoring them to life, then this game may be for you. This is a point-and-click sandbox type game. All stages have the same objective structure:1. Objective 1: Use limited leaves, they are your currency for building everything, to detoxify and restore land and water. Creating grassland earns you leaves to buy more terra-forming machines. Restore most, ~85%, of the land to reach objective 2.2. Objective 2: New machines are unlocked at this point. Restore a large enough percentage of total land into 3-4 specified biomes using your machines, efficient biome conversions generate more leaves than you spend in the process.3. Objective 3: New machines are unlocked. Use whatever the stages method of recycling to remove all buildings and ensure at least 12 animals have green level happiness. (Animals spawn when environmental conditions are met).Pros: 1. Stage objectives, terrain, and animals vary on every stage reducing redundancy. For example: every stage has a list of option objectives which results in bonus leaves and visual effects (ie moss spawning or migrating birds flying). Stages are challenging enough to make these optional achievements all but necessary to max complete some of the harder stages. One of the optional objective rewards on every stage is either rain or snow, which randomly detoxifies the land while occurring which is all but required to clean all land and get a much needed leaf bonus. Machines, animals, and biomes vary between stages so you will always be forced to adapt to available machines and cater to new biomes and animal needs which forces active thinking.2. The artwork is quite well done, both in the handbook, icons, and visual effects and ambiance are well polished.Cons: 1. I max completed the game in 13 hours with about 3 needed to redo already completed levels. So I'd recommend waiting for a sale and tempering your gameplay runtime expectations.2. The game is poorly optimized. Some visual effects, I'm looking at you hawk smoke cloud, can continuously loop which causes severe lag. Hopefully this is addressed in the future.3. The AI on the recycling water drone is horrendous and pauses continuously to recalculate routes, which is very irritating. Ironically turning up drone move speed to max makes it stop even more frequently so it actually goes even slower.4. Every stage has 3 main objectives and completing 1 unlocks machines of the next. However, many of the later objective machines, like recyclers, power pylons, railways, and solar amplifiers would be very useful in earlier parts of the stage. This makes objectives much harder to complete and forces additional leaf use which is annoying, feels unnecessary (since no machines are locked via resource or technology), and forcing extra machine placement (this covers additional land which you need to be free to terraform) which compounds, at least my, annoyance factor. 5. Some machines are finicky, tedious, or annoying to use, making parts of this game more work than enjoyable. and I like Power Washer Simulator! The excavator and pipe irrigation system stand out to me as particularly egregious. 6. Stages are lengthy and it's easy to permanently screw up objectives and make them impossible. For example: Water segments aren’t large enough to satisfy whale size preference but the stage doesn’t have seismic detonators (they can expand liquid pools), cold temperatures permanently freeze rivers and wolves cannot get water (so they will never reach green happiness), burning too much of a rainforest and not having enough cliff-face to replant the required forest percentage (so you can’t even beat the stage despite a surplus of leaves), raising a temp over the requirement on stages where you cannot lower (only raise) the temperature. This leads to having to redo, potentially, the entire stage again.7. Several machines are position dependent and the position resets after every place which forces continual re-orientating. Additionally, machines have weird hit, or click, boxes when arranged on or around buildings forcing you to click off their icon to select them.8. Machines are split into 3 tabs with tabs 2 and 3 becoming unlocked as objective 1 and 2 are completed respectively. However, in order to meet some objectives you may need many of objective 2 machines and objective 3 machines where others you will use rarely or not at all. The forced switching between tabs when placing many that aren’t on the same tab can be irritating since tab swap, machine placement, and lag time exaggerate how long it takes to do this.9. Rain and snow will overwrite certain tile types, this is normally a good thing since they detoxify land, however, there are times you need snowless land, dry land, or ashy land all of which get overridden by the weather. Which can botch land into a mix of types which reduces the efficiency of a single type or prevents blending of synergistic biomes (many animals want a particular 2 biomes). Additionally, you’re forced to wait until the weather effect ends if you’re looking to create/interact with one of the land types they effect. 10. The process is more fantastical and less scientific, animals spawning from nothing, dredging up an ocean of water from desolate wasteland, spraying water on barren soil to make grass and with only 1 type of currency, no research, and machines being completely locked to objective points. Being locked out of machines you’ve used before, that cost currency you already have, that would make the process much easier, exaggerates the feeling of lack of control and forced difficulty. Note this would be fine if there was a reason.11. (Potentially unpopular opinion) The lack of control, logic, reasoning, and poor logistic optimization especially in contrast to how polished aesthetics are makes the game feel like it’s unrealistically elevating the beauty of nature beyond what it actually is and takes away from my allegiance to the message.Conclusion: Don’t get me wrong its clear a lot of heart, soul, and effect were put into this game, and I think there’s a lot a lot of potential but there are some pretty glaring issues that I believe need to be addressed in order to make this experience what I believe the producers wanted to provide.As it stands, there are sparks of brilliance but ultimately, they are drowned by lack of control, poor optimization, and a few design flaws which resulted in a game with a mere runtime of 13 hours that felt more like work than an enjoyable experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Earth is destroyed, it’s full of toxins, and all life disappears. You are sent here to return everything back and make Earth green again. First things first, you need electricity to power up a Toxin Scrubber that clears soil and prepares it for an Irrigator that creates grass. The game offers four regions: Temperate, Tropical, Polar and Continental. Each of them has different starting conditions. For example, while in the Temperate region, you can easily build wind turbines on rocks, in the Polar you will have to blow up fissures to create magma, and then you will be able to build a power plant. The game has a nice guide which will teach you everything you need to know.So when you successfully finish the first phase you can move to the second – create biomes. Again, each region is specific and has its own biomes to make a perfect biodiversity. You will be creating forests, tundras, tropical rainforests, beaches, swamps, corals and more. To achieve perfect conditions in a biome, it is a good idea to complete optional tasks that tell you how high or low the air temperature should be, how much humidity you should have, or how many toxins you should remove. Completing them will give you more leaves, which can be used as currency to build more buildings, or you can summon rain or snow, which will clean every tile on a map and give you a huge amount of leaves. I recommend you complete the optional tasks as they will help you complete your restoration mission.Once you have created biomes, you can move on to the final stage - life and recycling. Each biome hides animals that you can discover using the Animal Observatory. Most animals require two or more types of biome to be discovered successfully. So, if you build biomes in the wrong places, you won't be able to find them all in one playthrough. It’s ok, you can replay the region, but keep in mind that it will be a little bit different because each map is randomly generated. It won’t be completely different, but some small changes can appear, like repositioned rocks or river bands. To complete your mission you have to find only three species of animals. After that, you can finally build an airship by recycling buildings. You can achieve it by boat, monorail train or later you will unlock a flying drone as well.After clearing your traces, you can enjoy a nice view of how beautiful the region you created. The game doesn’t have ultra-modern graphics with raytracing, but it has a nice colourful palette and an awesome drawn environment that fits the game perfectly. I call it eye candy visuals. Only one thing can ruin immersion. It's an outline created by Animal Observatory that won’t disappear after closing a popup of a scanned location. It happens only on water, but it’s a little bit distracting when you want to create a nice screenshot or just watch what you have created. I also run into two bugs. First was when I wasn’t able to recycle a building, but returning to main main fixed it and sometimes movement around the map was lagging.

_childDocuments_.review: Visually delightful tessellation based puzzle game with solar punk aesthetic. Really need more games to go for this genre, good soul food.Latest update has been a major overhaul, that has added more content but frustrated the game to the point of disappointment.One major complaint I have is that the game now chugs, on my high end spec gaming PC, this games chug, both the pathing of the little boat, the mono rails and all the animals, feels like a memory leak, it really chugs and needs fixing.  It has somehow both complicated the animals in a very frustrating manner. They spawn without control in inappropriate conditions then trap you in a game phase until you chase them across the map with a ping tool. The update has also revamped the games levels, whilst there are technically more maps, it now uses most of the mechanics less feeling more underutilised than ever. we have so many slight variations of the same puzzles, none of them have been balanced well enough to be satisfying.Some maps have the balance completely broken, buildings that are supposed to be bought and placed down once and then relocated are so cheap they can be spammed.fix the performance, and pick whether the game is about making beautiful landscapes (make it easier and double the map size greater land height variation, give us control of that too) OR a difficult puzzle game (make the buildings much more expensive and the level very failable, let us introduce animals manually as a 4th puzzle phase) as it is, it currently fails at both.

_childDocuments_.review: I have mixed feeling about this game. On one hand it looks very nice, has an interesting concept and pretty original theme. But unfortunately that's where the good stuff ends. The game is pretty expensive for the amount of levels and time it takes to get through them, but yeah, ok fine. That's the price, I could live with it if this was the sole problem. The game is relaxing to play, but can also be frustrating. The levels are a bit repetitive - the structures change a bit, yes, but not that much - it only changes name of the structures in the build progression. Place the structures in this one special order and you're good to go. The interface doesn't really help in planning, so there were some situations where I put something 1 tile off and later in the level there was no way around it apart from level restart. The research center is a bit no brainer - no real decision to make here, just build it. I do have a feeling that there is something missing with the gameplay. Maybe more interaction between structures, some better interface to plan things. The animal placement mechanic is a bit frustrating, since successful introduction doesn't give any bonus. It's just click in various places and hope you have those required 20 tiles in range.The recycling phase does not pose any challenge, because at this point you're usually swimming in resources and after first recycling you get so much of them, that it is just a formality afterwards. Also some buildings can hide behind foliage and you can miss them easily, which leads to more tedious clicking.After the demo I was hoping for something more, but the demo covers pretty much 80% of the availaable gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: A small scope RTS terrafromer with thought out mechanics that blend together nicely and allow for a lot of freedom. The best of its kind i have ever played. Economy is fairly simple but requires some planning to not run out of resources. Game mechanics and tools are diverse but have enough constraints to make accomplishing objectives engaging.cons:Not that much content - 4 destinations with 2 levels each, 8 levels in total. At 6.3 hours i have completed all 4 destinations for 100% but due to procedural maps the game is fairly replayable.Map generator is not always friendly, generally you have all the tools you need for a turnaround but this makes difficulty fluctuating. The game does not give you all the information (goals, conditions, requirements) beforehand so your strategic planning is limited to the current terraforming phase, and while phases transition seamlessly some past decisions might make some of the new conditions/requirements extremely hard to accomplish, sometimes impossible for the lack of tools or without sacrificing other goals. Thou generally you can clear a level anyway with some practically applied creativity, just not always for 100%.The game has some minor bugs, like resolution resets on profile load and animation glitches but so far only minor inconvenience.

_childDocuments_.review: Prior to the recent update, I used to LOVE this game, I have replayed it twice now (once on a friend's account and once on this one) and I was so excited about the new levels in the new update. Unfortunately, the animal system was also changed completely and now the game is so infuriating. I'm struggling to get through the first tutorial level on medium difficulty (and I've played this game twice already so I understand there is some level of early-game strategy to it). I'm gonna attempt to make this concise but I've never been good at that so here goes:- Adding the animals to the game earlier is distracting and unnecessary, I'm likely going to drastically change the terrain before I'm ready to consider what the animals want so there is no need to have their pop ups and needs jumping up on screen.- The amount of animal groups you need to have is wild, it's so many more than before and it has me scratching my head wondering how on earth the later, more completed levels are gonna go if I only got 9/12 on the first one before it started feeling too crowded to continue.- Once I DID get 9/12 animals happy, the icon that shows the list of animals on the side of the screen just disappeared and I couldn't actually finish the level (probably just a bug but still added to my frustration).- The timers until the animals leave are so short and barely give new (or seasoned!) players time to make significant or complex changes to the terrain to keep the animals- The needs of the animals aren't as clear as they once were and it's really unnecessarily confusing.- I don't understand what the names down the list of animals is for. Why do I have 4 different groups of deer all with randomised names? Is that the name of the herd? Is it meant to be a single deer that has shown up? - I have seen BoonMike mention that this new animal system has soft-locked them from continuing to play the game and I have to say that it's the same for me.Overall, I'm not really going to touch the game again if the animal system is like this. I honestly feel that this could've been the beta version of the animal system and the one before the update was the improved, simplified one. I know lots of work went into this update but unfortunately I just can't recommend it like this. The animal system wasn't broken and seemed to work perfectly fine before, it just seems odd that it's been overhauled like this for no reason.----Edit to respond to dev: Hi Sam, I played on medium difficulty (I've forgotten the terms for it now, apologies). I do understand that it was meant to feel more reactive and I suppose it does in a literal sense of the word but it feels clunky and not nearly as satisfying. Before, with the scanning method, it felt like a satisfying last piece of the puzzle, to get that last tick on the last animal.It takes away some of the control that you have throughout the rest of the game, just to have the animals randomly appear. I liked that I could control where I placed the animals rather than just winging it with the terrain and waiting for them to show up and hope it's enough for them to stay. When you're trying to do that and balance multiple different demanding species (I didn't get far but for example, the wolves in the first level), it can get hectic, especially when the only way to change the terrain for some animals is to destroy a whole area and start again (heck, sometimes you'd have to restart the whole map), thus getting rid of other connecting animal groups that share habitats close by, all of which may not come back if you change the habitat drastically enough to suit that first species that wasn't happy. Maybe a way to make this feel less random is to have the animal needs made easily accessible and clearly stated in the book (at least the needs of the species that arrived but left due to them being unsatisfied) so it's possible to mould the terrain around them as you go.When you don't know what habitats you need at the start, it makes is frustrating when you're doing your best to unlock all the tabs to get to the end of the level only to realise you don't have two particular biomes directly next to each other and you have to (literally) burn a significant part of the map down just to start again. I know a lot of effort and passion has been put into this so I'm sorry the game didn't feel as amazing to me as what I think it was meant to be, it's an awesome and unique concept and I haven't see anything like it but this change has really put me off of it now unfortunately. I don't see many negative reviews to perhaps it's just not working for me or I'm missing something but I hope my response might've also clarified something for you? Thanks for the response Sam!

_childDocuments_.review: Terra Nil: A unique reverse city-builder game set in a post-apocalyptic world. Restore the environment by reclaiming barren lands, rewilding nature, and creating a self-sustaining ecosystem. Use strategic planning and renewable resources to revitalize the world. A beautiful and relaxing experience promoting ecological restoration.The gameplay revolves around a simple yet deeply satisfying loop. Players start with a depleted environment and limited resources, requiring strategic planning and decision-making to bring life back to the land. By placing various environmental elements, such as soil tiles, trees, and water sources, players set in motion a delicate ecological balance.The gameplay's appeal lies in its intricacy. Players must carefully manage their resources, optimizing the placement of each element to maximize the ecosystem's revival while ensuring its stability. The game doesn't penalize experimentation, allowing players to learn from mistakes and adapt their strategies as they progress through the levels.Furthermore, it features procedurally generated levels, providing an element of surprise and variety in each playthrough. This design choice enhances replayability, as no two landscapes are ever the same, challenging players to rethink their approach and try out new strategies.A visual strike a perfect balance between simplicity and beauty. The use of vibrant colors brings life to the previously desolate landscapes, while the clean and uncluttered design allows players to focus on the core mechanics of restoration. Each element, from flora to water bodies, is distinct and easily recognizable, adding to the overall sense of accomplishment as the ecosystem flourishes under the player's nurturing.Accompanied by a soothing and atmospheric soundtrack, the audio design complements the gameplay remarkably well. The serene melodies blend seamlessly with the contemplative gameplay, creating an immersive and peaceful environment that encourages players to immerse themselves fully in their ecological endeavors.Beyond its gameplay and aesthetics, it also serves as an environmental allegory, urging players to reflect on real-world ecological challenges. As they witness the rejuvenation of the virtual landscapes, players are encouraged to contemplate the impact of human actions on the environment and the importance of conservation and sustainability.  Terra Nil is an exquisite gem in the city-building and simulation genre. With its visually arresting minimalism, calming soundtrack, and stimulating gameplay, the game crafts a serene and immersive experience that resonates long after the player has put down the controller. Moreover, its poignant environmental message elevates Terra Nil from being just another game to a powerful and relevant artistic statement.For gamers seeking a meditative and environmentally conscious journey, It's an absolute must-play. Embrace the role of an ecological steward and embark on a serene quest to restore nature's balance in this captivating and thought-provoking gem.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an absolutely gorgeous game, and it's almost everything I hoped it would be. It's relaxing but still challenging at times, albeit in all the right ways. It only falls short on a couple of things for me, but the Developers have been working actively to resolve issues, so I don't doubt that this will improve with time:Animal Happiness feels so finicky at the moment. Sometimes I feel like animals will be smack bang in the middle of their favourite biome, but will still complain about it and die out. I feel like the entire issue with the Animals is that their happiness is very position dependant. I'd prefer it if the map at least had the right balance of Biomes, the animals should be happy. I just unfortunately find that some of my runs get killed because of some obscure or confusing reason that the animals are unhappy, and it's the only time this game makes me feel confused and frustrated. There is a huge toolset to help you make animals happy, but it feels like none of them are very useful or good at accomplishing the goal.Other than that, the game is lovely. I'm hoping the Animal Happiness system is improved and reworked in the future, because In my mind it's the only thing holding the game back.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite its brevity, Terra Nil is definitely worth a play. I thoroughly enjoyed my time with it. I just wish there was more of it. The game is painfully short, and I was left wanting more. A sign of a good game, I suppose, but not the feeling I was anticipating being left with. I think I was expecting more in the replay department. Once you know how to puzzle your way through the four different map scenarios, the challenge the game presented kind of diminishes. In the end, I'm satisfied with the time I spent playing, and truly hope Free Lives gets the chance to build on what they have here. Here's to more Terra Nil.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is exactly my cup of tea - puzzle and resource management meet the satisfaction of cleaning up a mess. It took me about eight hours to beat the game, which is a little quick for the price point, however I thoroughly enjoyed the time I spent. I did hope for some extra challenge type maps at the end rather than just the four bonus environments. I'll definitely come back to this in the future to try it on a harder difficulty! I'd say if you really like what you see and have the money then it is worth the purchase at the current price, otherwise I'd probably grab it on a sale. No regrets from me!
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: My greatest take-away from this game is how much in need I am/we are of engaging with the destruction of our planet in a positive, constructive light. This game is just that - a fictional take at restoration engineering which makes actual restoration feel as a not-so-fictional prospective after all. Without undermining the pragmatic issues of actual restoration, I think that some playful space to reinforce hope in the human agent is a welcome and meaningful contribution to the problem.I will not go into details of the actual mechanics since the game is still evolving - my summary on the high level game design is that the game is fully playable, offers difficulty settings which transform the game from a chilled experience to a multifaceted puzzle (where failure can also be a valid outcome), thereby making it accessible for various playstyles, and I will positive comment on the concept of "Appreciate" at the end of the levels for its originality and value. Overall, solid game and solid good vibes. Thank you.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: The game is wonderfully relaxing, the music and nature ambience put me in a state of mind that meant I could take my time with each placement and consider its effects.There are still one or two UI bugs, minor really and they don't detract from the game.My only real qualm is it feels small. The individual maps are small, and I'd love for there to be more regions. I hope there'll be more updates and (free) expansions.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Soothing, peaceful, and therapeutic, Terra Nil is a game about helping heal a world left in disrepair, and then teaching yourself to stand aside and let it flourish. This is basically the game I play to calm myself when Im stressed, and its worked every time.Genuinely fun mechanics, and there is a strategy that has to be considered. I'd best describe it as the inverse of Sim City: You are building a better world for everything besides humans. No spoilers on the ending, but it's incredibly satisfying, and worth playing again and again!If you've been looking for a good solarpunk, gardening, or sim game, Terra Nil has got you.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I beat the first half of the game (main story) and one of the levels after you finish the main game. I would recommend this game to anyone that likes nature, puzzles, or relaxing games. Its very fun and sometimes very challenging especially in the optional levels. I found myself having to restart several times because i kept spending all my resources on accident. The music is beautiful and compelling, the art style in simply gorgeous and worthy of being framed and hung on my walls. Watching barren landscapes turn into thriving ecosystems is a wonderful feeling and makes me appreciate nature so much more.However ive stumbled into far too many GAME BREAKING bugs to be able to give this game a positive review. In the last level of the main game after spending 30-45 minutes on the map i couldnt finish the game because the mechanics wouldnt progress themselves.  and when these bugs occurred i had to completely restart my game and restart the level to fix it. I also find some of the mechanics lacking self explanations for instance  The price tag is a little high for but i dont mind spending it because ive enjoy just about every second of this game.My final thought is that this game is a work of art but beware the bugs that can cause serious issues. I think the people that say this game needs more to do are greedy. Plain and simple.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: A very relaxing and fun little game with a beautiful style. The player has to think strategically and sometimes plan his moves to complete a map or get an achievement. The strategic planning can get a bit more complex and complicated on later maps and higher difficulties, creating a challenging experience. There are some minor bugs or shortcomings, such as resetting the resoultion every time you exit the game.It took me about 10 hours to complete the game with all achievements on the lowest difficulty.  Would recommend
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: So far, I've finished three maps, and it's very satisfying. I have played the demo, and I was worried about the repeating process, but with different maps there are different requirements, so I had to keep thinking which was fun. I really had to think about all the requirements of finding animals to find them. It doesn't require much attention, just some patience. I really enjoyed it. _childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I've been waiting eagerly for this game since I played the demo last year. I would have been happy with simply more of what the demo offered, but the full game has much more interest and depth. It's a beautiful combination of strategy and soothing. The main map art and audio is quite splendid. I really enjoy the theme of environmental restoration, which I think adds to the relaxing nature of the game for me. It's a great way to relax while keeping your mind just busy enough to not focus on other things.There's a few items that could be polished in the UI like multiple pop-up boxes/dialogs at one time, or the large tool tips for the buildings that pop up when hovered over, getting in the way of the map. There's maybe a few tricky things to parse when using the map and the buildings, but overall it's a very smooth experience. I'm looking forward to playing more.It's a similar feeling as Dorfromantik, but with more gameplay elements.For fun, I read the reviews of what other people are thinking about the game. There are more than a few that "don't recommend" based on the price alone. As a game dev, this makes me a bit sad. I know how much work goes into making a game even this "small", so for me $25 seems like a very fair price. It's about the same cost as a good burger and fries in Seattle... There are certainly games out there with massive replay value that are less $/hour than something like this, but I think that metric discounts the kinds of unique and interesting experiences that can be had in smaller games.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

It does suffer from not combining some of core elements learnt in the first couple levels later on, mostly power generation and recycling mechanics, but this is forgiven with the sheer joy of seeing the wasteland being reclaimed.Would highly recommend

_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Is this a chill nature theme puzzle game? Absolutely.Is it a anti-city builder? No. I enjoyed my time with it, and if it at all sounds interesting, I'd recommend it.My biggest gripe is that Terra Nil does not believe humans and nature can co-exist. You either have wasteland (product of man), or wildness. Human's job is not to work in harmony with the natural world, but to undo damage and go away. I don't think is the intended message, merely a product of what the game is trying to focus on, but you will never a single human in the entire game. Everything is automated drones, and it must all go in the end (save for the rocket silo cause we can't take that with us).I dislike the notion that humanity is simply doomed to never live amongst nature, that we must, for its own good, disappear and remain distant. I find that a frankly disgusting attitude. But, again, I don't think that's intentional. Play the game, enjoy it. I just found it really hard to shake this feeling of anti-humanism.

_childDocuments_.review: I am an environmental scientist (bachelor's and master's), and I do love a terraforming game. Most city/terrain builders are based on exploitation, the flawed idea that nature, of which we are, is there to serve only as a resource to expand your civilisation, the relationship becomes parasitic, and as another wise individual has mentioned, IS WHY WE ARE IN THE SITUATION WE'RE IN TODAY. The solution? Restoration and rewilding.I tried this out and within the first two levels (temperate and tropical, respectively) I immediately loved this game. The gameplay is very addictive and it is rewarding when the climate starts to adapt. Where this could improve is a meter that measures the biogeochemical cycles of the regions, how much nitrogen, carbon and phosphorus is stored in each ecosystem type, and this changes relative to the amount of habitat type that is available (more nitrogen is stored in grasslands and more carbon stored in forests for example), this could provide an excellent education opportunity within the game.Perhaps for further expansion, making larger maps upon which you can build sustainable permacultures and economies, using renewable energy technologies, regenerative farming techniques and wild foraging, sustainable and small-scale infrastructures etc. This could enable a more sandbox feel that combines some elements of Tropico perhaps, while still maintaining the very relaxing atmosphere that this game has. And more of an impact on the planet when the game is 100% completed, with some more end-game scenarios and maybe different game-modes.The music and overall ambience suits the game perfectly, and this game could definitely become a massive hit. We need more games like this.I highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I love Terra Nil. I love Terra Nil so much. I spent many hours replaying the demo and I'm going to spend so many more hours playing the full version. This game is a "city builder" in genre only; there are buildings you must place to develop the land around them, and you have to think strategically about where to place those buildings (because it will have consequences later when you recycle them), but that's it. Instead of building a city, the land has already been ruined, and we're bringing nature back to these barren wastes.You start off in the temperate region (which was featured in the demo), which is sort of a middle ground to get you situated with the controls and objectives, but once you've restored the wildlife there you're off to the tropical, polar, and continental regions. Each region has unique mechanics, wildlife, and resources to keep track of. Maps are procedurally generated, so no two sessions in a particular region will be the same unless you specify exact "coordinates" (basically a map seed) to travel to.The goals in each region are to restore the basic terrain from the wasteland, then develop more complex areas such as forests and wetlands, then survey the landscape for fauna, and finally recycle your buildings and depart the map. Where this gets tricky are with the fauna and recycling. Fauna only appear if certain conditions are met; in the temperate zone, for example, you have to induce a wildfire to create forests, which is simple enough, but bears will only appear in a forest that is on a hill and has a beehive in it. Not all animals are so complex as this, but it's something you may need to plan for in advance. You have to recycle all of your buildings in order to depart the map, but to do so, you must use recycling drones that travel on water with a limited radius to dismantle buildings. This means you have to either be careful about your placements from the start, or devise a strategy to get out of the corner; one such method is by re-destroying a piece of the landscape to create a new riverbed. It all gets really interesting and makes you consider a few different strategies to accomplish the mission.I can understand the feeling that there isn't enough content for the $25 price point. What I described above is basically the gameplay loop that you'll go through each and every time, and after a couple of hours you've pretty much seen all there is to see. That being said, the charm in this game's animations, the message it sends, the unique strategy gameplay elements, the fact that I can sit back after completing the map and just watch nature continue on... this is probably the most relaxing strategy game I've ever played, and those aren't words that are supposed to go together. Not to mention, a part of every Steam sale of this game goes directly to the Endangered Wildlife Trust in South Africa. It's awesome to see a game like this being used to support charities doing this incredibly important work in real life.Before writing this review, I was watching a map that I had finished, and while I was watching, the "Goldilocks" achievement had suddenly popped. It requires that you have three bears in forests at least 10 tiles apart. I was confused, because I had only successfully surveyed for two bears, but while I was watching, another forest I had developed was healing further and allowed a natural bear spawn. Even if that is a bug, I choose not to believe that. The notion that I had created a small forest that was then able to further develop and naturally attract wildlife into it is, admittedly, a really small moment in the grand scheme of my life, but it certainly made me smile. Even after "completing" Terra Nil, I'm absolutely going to come back to it just to play more when I need a moment of calm. If Euro/American Truck Simulators are the zen games of driving, then this is the zen game of strategy.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Terra Nil is a puzzle game about transforming barren wastelands into thriving ecosystems. The gameplay is easy to get to grips with and the puzzles are fairly simple, so it doesn't take long to get your head around it. There are four regions (temperate, tropical, tundra, urban), with two maps per region. The maps are semi-randomly generated, so there is some replayability there, but probably not a massive amount. You could reasonably expect to put six to eight hours into the game before you fully restore all four regions on the planet, completing each map once.The gameplay loop is simple: You start with a toxic wasteland, which you clean up to allow for the growth of grass. Once the grass is well established, you can build on that to establish more complex biomes like boreal forests. Once those are established, you reintroduce native wildlife. Finally, you clean up after yourself, dismantling everything you've built to leave a pristine wilderness, and then move on to the next region. There's only one resource to track, which is a currency spent on buildings and certain actions and earned by restoring the environment and finishing optional objectives. You do need to keep the currency in mind or you could run out and have to restart the current map, but that's the only point of failure.For me, the game was satisfying and relaxing to play. The peaceful soundtrack, charming art style and straightforward gameplay lent itself well to just sitting back and enjoying myself, and it's short length meant I was finished before it started to grow repetitive. All in all, I'd happily recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I've enjoyed Terra Nil since its game jam release. With its polished release as a game for sale, they added a number of novel environments and new experiments. But wow, the Vita Nova update really knocks the whole game out of the park. Having animals organically enter your map really ties the bow on making your map feel like a natural environment. It's hard to convey the sense of beauty and hope you feel upon seeing the rain return or the animals arrive, and it's a feeling I can't say I've experienced in any other game. If there was ever a game that was a piece of art, it's this one. I'd whole-heartedly recommend Terra Nil so you can feel that for yourself.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Terra Nil is a fairly relaxing game where you reconstitute an ecosystem and then leave without a trace. While the full length of the game is on the shorter side (at the time of writing, I've completed the main campaign and am starting on the alternate maps), the experience is a quaint and pleasant introduction to ecosystem balance. It does throw its own logic aside at points—you can raise the temperature well above freezing and still get snow after you "unlock" it in the mission—but overall the core concept is interesting and relevant to our own bleeding world. All in all, if you're interested in short-form, randomly-generated terraforming sessions with steadily progressing mechanics, this one's a good one to try, though I'd likely wait for a sale given the short nature of the game. Congrats to the devs on the launch! Hope this game gets more content down the line.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Very nice and relaxing game, although sometimes it can be frustrating that you can mess up a map without a way to fix it. I think there should be a way to recycle buildings from the very beginning on, so that you can get rid of a building that is in the way or some such. The game is designed for the player to replay a phase/map if they mess up. There is not that much content, however. Although the replayability is great because there are essentially 8 different maps that are generated at random and three degrees of difficulty, which you can try to master, it will always be the same type of map. That said, the higher degrees of difficulty are quite difficult and require an optimal playstyle and long-term planning. That is, if you feel motivated to try. My recommendation is to get Terra Nil on sale because 25 € is a little much for the amount of content that you get. I hear they are working on a major content update, so this info may be outdated soon. I'm predicting that Terra Nil will become one of those timeless classics that people will still recommend in a few years time.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Very nice and cozy. Relaxing soundtrack, wonderful sounds of nature, a cute artstyle and a good experience overall. It has an annoying UI bug where the description of something hangs until you flash over it again and it only has 8 "missions" with mildly random layouts. The post-game missions were good brainteasers, having to use combinations that had not been relevant before. Price is the biggest problem that I can see, and that comes down to personal preference. I'm glad I bought it, but I can understand why others didn't feel like it was worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Genuinely really enjoyed this game and I feel like it's good for those who like strategy and want a more relaxing version. Pretty easy to "beat" all the levels the first time around, but the procedural map generation and different strategies made it worthwhile to play everything through a few more times. I can tell I have a few more playthrough's in me now at 6.5 hours and will probably come back to this periodically when I want a palette cleanser and a game that makes me feel like I'm using my brain in a calm way. Def glad to see more games of this type getting recognition! Go team!
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: If you go into Terra Nil expecting a deep Paradox-tier strategy game, you're gonna have a bad time.If you go into Terra Nil expecting a huge city-builder, you're gonna have a bad time.Terra Nil is a beautiful, chill puzzle game with some fun strategic elements. That's it. The game's description is completely accurate. It has lovely art and graphics as well as pleasant music that never felt too repetitive or got boring.If you're not sure that's going to be your thing, play the demo or wait for a sale. If it doesn't hold your attention, you're not going to want to pay $25 for it.I don't usually spend much time in sandbox modes because I prefer some sort of direction or challenge but it's really satisfying and relaxing to just build beautiful landscapes without restrictions.I do hope it is expanded upon a little more in the future -- I would really like to be able to adjust height and depth to fine tune rivers and lakes -- but I don't feel ripped off in the slightest. I've absolutely gotten my $25 worth.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I've finished it in 8 hours, and I'm quite the completionist.After you've finished the main 4 worlds there's nothing left to do, you can repeat the same scenarios with different maps but at the end of the day is quite boring.Really a shame, the concept and the art are amazing, definitely not worth 25 euros.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to recommend Terra Nil because I think it's an important game and the developers clearly worked hard and had good intentions.But...I loved the demo. I played it a lot. After I discovered Terra Nil existed, I played the demo pretty much every single day. It was so immensely gratifying to see your (digital) work restoring a dead planet. It made me happy to see so much positive change in that virtual world when the real world feels so immutable and headed for destruction. For 15-20 minutes a day, Terra Nil kept the imminent doom at bay and made me think maybe, just maybe, it was possible to change the world. It was like interactive ASMR that gave me hope.The full release was... Not gratifying. It was frustrating and annoying and even more obtuse than the demo. I don't need games to hold my hand, but I do need them to maintain consistent objectives -- AND TO NOT COMPLETELY BRICK THE GAME STATE IF/WHEN THOSE OBJECTIVES CHANGE! Now, that was 18 months ago and the game has been updated several times since then, so it's likely those broken game states have been addressed. But I cannot bring myself to try it again. Maybe you can.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I recently had the pleasure of playing Tera Nil, and I must say, I was thoroughly impressed! This game has come a long way since I played the demo a few years back. The developers have clearly put a lot of time and effort into refining the gameplay mechanics and creating a truly immersive experience.One of the things I loved most about Tera Nil is how it serves as the perfect chill, stress-relieving game. The soothing soundtrack and gorgeous visuals make for a calming environment that really allows you to get lost in the gameplay. And speaking of gameplay, it's a lot of fun! The mix of puzzle-solving, resource management, and strategic decision-making keeps you engaged without ever feeling overwhelming.Another thing that really stood out to me was the game's environmental message. It's clear that the developers put a lot of thought into the message they wanted to convey, and they did so in a way that doesn't feel preachy or heavy-handed. It's a great reminder of the importance of taking care of our planet, and it's done in a way that's both entertaining and thought-provoking.Overall, I would highly recommend Tera Nil to anyone looking for a relaxing, engaging game with a positive message. The game has clearly come a long way since its demo days, and I can't wait to see what the developers come up with next!
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Short but incredibly beautiful, this is an experience that will stay with me forever. This game, in a matter of just 4 hours, changed my life. This game is an ode to what makes humanity beautiful and a vision of hope for the future. If you are someone who cares about the planet and has any interest in rewilding and/or conservation, please play this.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: A wasteland greets one with barren view,In Terra Nil you repair the world anew, With gentle touch the earth you heal, Until a paradise you reveal.Lush landscapes bloom from barren ground, A stunning world where life is foundRivers flow and meadows rise, Beauty found beneath the skies.Gameplay puzzles are a mindful quest, Reclaim the earth and restore to its best, Strategise with careful thought, Each step forward, a lesson taught.Vita Nova is fresh and bright,Brings lots more content to delight,This update adds to nature’s tale,More to love and new paths to sail.For those who cherish nature's call, And love to game, this has it all,Purchase this and take the stand, Restore the earth with your own hand.A very enjoyable puzzler, not reliant on actions per minute.
