_childDocuments_.review: First off, I hate the new camera. You have to use a third party software to increase the FOV because they don't give any options for FOV within the game itself, and its just too close to Kratos' shoulder. Enemies are constantly flanking me while other enemies attack from the front, and then when I try to swing around to face the direction the arrows say attacks are coming from, I often end up taking the attack to the side of my face.It is so damn hard to keep track of all the enemies or keep them all on the screen, and its because of how close the camera is to Kratos. I don't have this issue on other third person action games like The Witcher 3 or FF7R.The other thing is all the hidden loading screens. Squeeze through this corridor, duck under this pillar, crawl under this pathway, climb this wall. Wait for the fast travel door to assemble, trek around the world tree. Oh you wanna switch realms? Wait for this 5 minute star gate sequence.It makes backtracking an absolute chore, and its so painfully obvious the dialogue during these sequences is there just to try to fill the tedium it makes me feel more annoyed.Also the resource management and upgrading your equipment. There's so few resources during the first half of the game, I didn't ever know if I should invest in my equipment or hold onto the resources for when I get better equipment later. I found myself constantly pulling up my web browser to look up the stats of the different armor pieces and how many resources they'll take to fully upgrade so I could decide whether or not to invest in them.I was also constantly looking up solutions to the different chests because I would look around for 5 minutes to find the last rune to break, and then when I finally found it and broke it, half the time my reward was a special ability I didn't even want to use because it didn't do enough damage. I just really would rather have had most of the rewards and upgrades and abilities come as rewards after bosses or mini-bosses so the game could focus more on combat instead of adding tedious mini-puzzles on top of the already tedious hidden loading screens and travel time. Which, speaking of travel time, don't even get me started on how much time I spent boating around the damn lake. Or the fact that two way fast travel is locked until the later half of the game.(STORY SPOILERS INCOMING)The story has its emotional moments, but its rather average and predictable overall. They dig in a bit into how Atreus is upset with Kratos' detachment and how he feels Kratos doesn't care, even at one point saying he wishes it had been Kratos who died instead of his mother. But they immediately gloss over it with Atreus saying "But I don't really mean that." So instead of Kratos having to muster up the emotional intelligence to understand how his son feels or forget his pride so he can admit to his son that he's been wrongfully distant, Atreus does most of the work in trying to forge a connection.Later, after finding out he's part god, Atreus starts getting violent and full of himself. But instead of Atreus facing any consequences by, say, getting himself severely hurt trying to fight Baldur or going off on his own or even fighting his own father -- this also gets glossed over when Kratos screams at him in Helheim. And just a minute later Atreus looks at a vision of himself killing Thor's cousin and says "Wait, that's not me. It can't be." Really, the only time Kratos ever has to face consequences for his poor parenting is when his son is sick. (END OF STORY SPOILERS)I also don't like how the sidequest with the valkyries gets locked behind mandatory time sinks. The last two valkyries are in helheim and niflheim -- so you have to beat 5 trials before you can get to the valkyrie in helheim. And in niflheim you can go straight to the valkyrie, but she's in the maze of mist and the mist timer is still active during the fight. So if you haven't gotten any of the equipment that increases the mist timer, you're not gonna have much time to try to complete that fight. So the devs expect you to go through the maze a bunch of times and get all the mist echoes for that equipment first before you attempt the fight with the valkyrie. And at that point in the game, I just wasn't willing to spend that much more time with tedium.After beating the game and deciding I'd had enough, I had 38 hours playtime. 10 of those hours was the main story, another 10 was sidequests, and the other 18 was just travel time - walking, boating, progressing through hidden loading screens, backtracking.It just honestly felt like I spent more time walking/boating around than I did actually engaging with meaningful gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: As a big fan of the original PS2 game, this... did not flip my cookie. Instead of a clean, frantic hack and slash game, now it's a behind the shoulder view, where you move like a tank. I hated the fighting in this game. And I hated that the world was too big, with lots of collectibles, but no good way to get from place to place. I'd rather watch a movie of this game than play it.

_childDocuments_.review: Was my favorite game on PS4 Pro, and is my favorite game of all time on PC. JUST DON'T TOUCH the Give Me God Of War + diff. SERIOUSLY.... For what was originally on easier diffs a maybe 3 day excursion with mild to fun game-play turned into absolute hell on the hardest diff even with the best NG+ gear and enhancement gems. And I know what your wondering then why suggest the game and recommend it. Well the games fantastic on the other 3 diffs even their NG+ diffs. But Give Me God Of War + gave me by the end of my main story playthrough ACTUAL HAND, FOREARM and wrist cramps. What is a fun exciting end on easier difficulties with Baldur at the end becomes a sluggfest. And honestly a nightmare of a 5 hrs of continual try agains from the checkpoints to try and figure out the final bosses tactics. Which I might add as a little spoiler on the hardest diff Baldur's fire floor aoe moves will after a while start tracking the player so they actively punish you for being too passive and far away.As someone who's never played a previous GoW game before this was apsolute fluffing blast of a game. Just do it more casually and enjoy the game don't be a masochist like me and end up regretting it. I'll definitely do another NG+ run on a lower diff XD. Gameplay: 4/5 - Fun but its a little jaring to be pure bare hand with rage mode (IK: ragnarok fixes this...)Difficulty 4/5 - Hard but fair Art: 4/5 they left in a bug... from the PS4 release *sweats* Graphics: 5/5- Stunning and beautiful. Enemy Diversity: 3/5 - But this isn't really a knock against the game its more so just an objective note.Weapons: 4/5 - HUGE departure I've learned from previous games only 2 really main weapons not that big of a dealGear 4/5 - Artistically unique and beautifulNG+ Content 5/5 - A genuine true would want to play it again experience a rare treatCharacters 4/5 - very authentic feeling however some characters have weak dialogues that feel like they were cut. The Thor kids felt really awkward with their only purpose to chase you down and hunt/kill Atreus and Kratos. Would have been more interesting to like hear their perspective of the war with the Giants. May have been a more interesting button push for Atreus than your momma jokes. Story 4/5 - A lot of the story feels great and is well voice acted but some of the plot gets watered down by the ironic extreme immersiveness from just Kratos and Atreus's POV. I get that Kratos and Atreus wouldn't know what the Asgardians are up to. But there could have been like some cutscenes to kinda fill in the connection between Baldur and Odin. And imo objectively it wouldn't have ruined the sequel Ragnarok. As its like Odin would know what Kratos is known for so it doesn't really make sense to throw his best searcher gods like lambs to the slaughter. And I get the idea that Baldur was suppose to be kinda driven mad by his anger at Freya but Thors kids why did they get dragged into this mess. 41/50 or a respectful 82/100 as my final score and I am proud that this title on the PS4 in 2018 won its GOTY  don't get me wrong about being a bit critical of this game. I love this game and its flaws cause its a true "experience" within gaming. As thats what gaming is suppose to be. A perfect imo clean slate to start if you want to enter the God of War IP without feeling ashamed of not playing the previous titles. A great 3rd person adventure single player game. And to those who are like 82 is too low for a game like this... Trust me you don't wanna know what my scores are for a game I don't like or is objectively bad/unfun. I'm very much the type to go negative scores if a feature that was promised isn't there in a game. I give high regards to games that over deliver and God of War is definitely one of the few for its time that over delivered. A 100% garentee that I will replay this game in the near future.

_childDocuments_.review: I think the story and characters are done well as is the artwork. That would make me want to recommend the game. Some of the laggy control responses on puzzles like nornir bells, and boss fights with valkries, and the grind for armor make me feel like not recommending it so much.+ Story telling and characters+ Wold art and atmosphere+ Outside some boss battles and challenges, the combat is generally decent+ Platforming was a key press rather than the jump and hope nightmare I see in other recent games, which was a refreshing change.- Timed puzzles with (like Normir Bells) that make the game frustrating with laggy input response (developers could fix if they added an option to just give you more time in accessibility options)- Some boss fights that rely on fast dodging like some valkrie attacks with the laggy response to input not allowing the dodge (There should be some nerfing to those big hit attacks available in accessibility for those that have trouble either due to needing accessibility, or because the game doesn't respond to thier input device fast enough- just changing QTES from multi-tap to hold isn't enough for that with this game)- 2nd Fight with Baulder on dragon, specifically when Kratos is pinned down getting beaten. This needs a fail-safe advance condition like they put when Kratos is in the dragon's mouth earlier, so if the timing the game wants isn't registered after a minute (yeah if you do nothing when in the dragon's mouth Kratos will take over and strike for you). Similar scene in third fight wasn't as bad.- A lot of grinding to get armor sets you may need for later battles. It does seem some of them were intended for after the story was finished though.

Especially when going against a big boss or a lot of elemental effects on screen, I get hitched to around 40fps and occasionally looks as though the game is going to crash.Overall though, I am very pleased with my purchase and supporting these devs as this game is super fun, looks great (at my settings), enjoyable combat that is a good repetitiveness and for only £40 which is £15 less than most AAA games. _childDocuments_.review: I wish I would of seen a review outside the scope of "It's a Masterpiece" before buying this game. So, I will write something very contrary to popular opinion. I've played games that are Masterpieces before, this is not one. At best, it's below average. Here's why:Combat: It's not bad, but it certainly doesn't bring anything new to the table. Kratos feels pretty sluggish and even with the "other weapon," it doesn't feel effective or good in use. Runic attacks are pretty cool, but they have a 30-60 second cooldown and end-game enemies are really good at avoiding them. Parry system was probably my favorite thing about combat. Kratos/Atreus Upgrade System: The first few skills feel very helpful (Executioner Cleave for sure); late game, super difficult to use on more difficult enemies. Middle skills aren't bad, but the enemies move so fast, you'll typically stick to basic weapon combos and rhunic attacks to take them down. The switch stance makes absolutely no sense (end of the skill trees) because it takes almost two seconds to trigger and enemies are on you by that time. I barely noticed a difference with upgrading skills when stats were high enough to enhance them too.Crafting: Probably the main reason to explore. After a awhile, it's just tiring to go around looking for one (or a few) ultra rare components--especially in the Muspelheim and Niflheim realms. Don't even get me started on Niflheim. With the end result of grinding out components with gear that isn't really much better than what you'd find organically in the story. The side quests (even the Valkyrie story), felt shallow and unfufilling.Main Story: Truly, truly could not believe the ending. This was one of the main things that lead me to even writing a review. After "interacting" with the gods in the game, I knew they were teeing this up for a sequel. Hey, that's fine. Make a great game and want to make another one? By all means, please do. But, the first game needs to be waaaaaay better than this. What they did was reshape Norse mythology to create tension and drama with gods who wouldn't do that according to the sagas; that way, they didn't burn through familiar ones securing that you would buy the subsequent games. It felt like they were more concerned with the second and third games, than what's going on right now with this one. Overall: Its fine if you're looking for a hack n slash with a decent upgrade/crafting system and don't mind slow travel mechanisms to reach all the realms and areas of midgard. But, I would not expect a a compelling story or a genuine Masterpiece going into this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is based off the PS4 version, though I did play it on PC. God of War is one of those games that embodies the AAA aesthetic and feel of a game. It's overloaded with things to do, a world map that gives you the impression of freedom but not ACTUAL freedom, and a combat system that trips over itself trying to be multiple different genres.To add onto the gameplay problems, while the characters aren't GENERALLY terrible, no option to simply silence Atreus or Mimir in combat is a huge flaw. Combat can get overwhelming enough without 2 voices telling you 3 different instructions ("Behind you!" "To the left!" "Find healing!") while trying to navigate enemies that feel like they belong in completely different games.Which brings me to the combat...the combat doesn't know what it wants to be. Sometimes it wants a Dark Souls style "be ready to dodge, move in, and attack before the next swing", where you want to be ready to dodge and maneuver around attacks and obstacles. Othertimes it wants Devil may Cry style "keep attacking so they never get the opportunity to retaliate". This would be fine if it were simply spread out among battles or enemies, but it does not take long at all before the game demands both of you at the same time.But luckily, there is a helpful indicator telling you where an attack is coming from! It's a small 3D arrow that is hard to parse because it does not stand out on some terrains so anywhere but the stark white snowfields, you are going to be squinting to see if that's from the left, behind, or right.The puzzles are pretty simple and exploration is interesting, but the best the game will give you is "we'll wait a little longer to tell you how to solve the puzzle, you big dumb oaf".God of War isn't a BAD game, but it's a game that doesn't know what it wants to be and refuses to compromise about what it wants you to think it is. I cannot recommend this unless you are absolutely feral for some triple A slop being spooned onto your plate while everyone tells you how much Kratos scowls like it's a funny joke the 9 millionth time.It's like a comic book movie for video games. But less The Dark Knight and more Batman v Superman; it feels more like there was an expectation to make it the way they did rather than any attempt to make it enjoyable or fun.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a masterpiece and people have known it for years. I'm not here to tell you that.This PC port is yet another breath of fresh air from the guys and gals over on the playstation port teams. Days Gone and Horizon:ZD were both stunningly well pulled off (IMO), but in comparison they've got nothing on this latest entry. Both of the previous games had some issues here and there that were fixed fairly quickly, but it seems like they mostly got everything sorted out BEFORE the release day this time around (shocking in the modern climate, I know). Control support and binding were a breeze and the game played very naturally on M+KB.The smooth "no-cut" "filming" style (even the cutscenes are rendered in realtime with 0 transitions) is something I love and hate at the same time. The game is incredibly cinematic from start to finish, but the drawback of that is that it can be VERY hard to put down... there aren't many great "this is a good place to stop" moments in this game because it flows from cutscene to gameplay to QTE all without you noticing (well, noticing for longer than a maybe slightly too long elevator ride here and there... we all know about elevator loading screen tricks but this one actually pulled them off well). _childDocuments_.review: I elected to play at difficulty level "God of War" - big mistake.  Not because it is difficult, but because of the way the difficulty is created.  If you are a glutton for punishment and rely on luck to win then perhaps it is worth playing at this difficulty level however I regret trying this.  The opponents are the same but the seemingly have MUCH shorter cooldown times on special moves than a god, their health bars decrease less easily than those of a god and they seem to move faster than a god.  Their self-healing is MUCH better than Kratos', and him a god, even if in reduced circumstances.  The opening fight promised epic, the game fights - not so much. When I consider that in his first fight he barefist punches a rock pillar to smithereens in a fight with a god eventually beating the god but he has difficulty punching a dent into an enemies health bar of ?mortal? grunts in a mortal world during gameplay,  Kratos swings a tree trunk to bash an opponent into orbit but his axe strokes are stopped by mortal shields? No way.  The promise of godly powers and the reality of equipment reliance disappointed me.You cannot change the difficulty level if you elected "God of War" so I 'm stuck.  Example:   I'm in the Northri Stronghold looking for a whetstone, I land on a beach and face an Ogre and a Viken/Hel-Viken.  The Ogre throws stones hat curve towards you if you dodge close to the outer paved circle around the fire brazier/bowl.  Why he does not punch the rock to smithereens as he had done before I don't know.  Another example is a fight you have as you enter Helheim and try to go past the locked gate.  You have to climb down a tall spire which has a treasure chest caught in frozen vines halfway down.  After climbing down you  enter a bowl-like arena.  An "Ice-Viken?" appears right next to an huge gap into an abyss, you can stun him fairly easily but then Kratos throws him into the middle of the arena where he recovers instead of the abyss right next to him.  Eventually you wait for a lucky break and Kratos does throw him into the abyss.  The rest of the enemies have many ranged attacks so the combination of Ice-Viken and them is painful to overcome without luck.  I also did not experience the "reduced damage" the tips mentioned that battered enemies would have.  That could be simply a mathematically small percentage of total damage that is actually reduced and is difficult to see in the heat of combat.  It is also frustrating that even weak enemies have ranged attacks that are devastating to Kratos' health whereas his ranged attacks are weak - even against weak enemies.  This reduces Kratos from "God of War" to a simple grunt with godly aspirations trying desperately to upgrade equipment from too ineffectual to barely adequate which, to me, is a great pity.Other than the tedium of repeating fights until you luck out.  Levelling Kratos was fun and made sense if you ignore my previous point that he's a god, not a grunt.  I enjoyed the story and the graphics is GREAT.  The keyboard/mouse combinations were easy to learn and made sense during play and combat.  Character movements and actions are brilliantly done and you can almost forget you are not watching a movie.  The difficulty setting I was unhappy with for the reasons I stated but the combination of enemies at the level I chose was obviously perfectly chosen to give the player the most difficult combination of enemies possible, I can understand that.  One surprise was that the enemies were upgraded during the same fight from level 5 in one instance to level 7, now that was unexpected.In all I love the game even with the issues stated.  It is an old game and my comments are aimed at giving occasional players like myself a heads-up on difficulty level choices.This part comes months later:I finished "God of war" difficulty, hating the fights.  I replayed at "Give me a challenge" and loved the fights, you can actually use all these special moves effectively, as well as strategise some other than "run and dodge and die till you luck out".  The last fight with Baldur was "run and dodge again" but overall - play the game at "give me a challenge" level - great fun.

_childDocuments_.review: God of War : By Triple FThe 2018 installment of "God of War" serves as a masterclass in game design, narrative structure, and character evolution. Developed by Santa Monica Studio, this soft reboot of the franchise reimagines the saga of Kratos, the once vengeful Greek demigod, and thrusts him into the complex, mythological world of Norse gods. It is a profound journey of redemption, fatherhood, and survival that shifts the tone from its hyper-violent roots to a more introspective, emotionally nuanced experience. Yet, the game never loses sight of the raw, visceral combat that defined the series.The heart of "God of War" is its story, which is deeply personal and emotionally resonant. Kratos is now living in Midgard, attempting to lead a quiet life with his son, Atreus, following the death of his second wife, Faye. The game begins with the pair preparing for her funeral, which serves as a narrative catalyst for their journey to scatter her ashes from the highest peak in all the realms. What stands out here is the dynamic between Kratos and Atreus. Kratos, once a symbol of unbridled rage, is now a conflicted father struggling to connect with a son who is innocent yet carries the burden of divinity. This parent-child relationship is explored in nuanced ways throughout the game, with their emotional arcs interwoven with the overarching narrative of Norse mythology.The combat system in "God of War" is a revelation, offering a more methodical and strategic approach than the previous games. Kratos has traded his iconic Blades of Chaos for the Leviathan Axe, a weapon that adds depth to the gameplay through its weight and versatility. The axe can be thrown and recalled, and its integration into combat and puzzle-solving creates a seamless blend of action and exploration. Combat is closer and more personal, and the camera remains tight on Kratos, enhancing the sense of immediacy. Enemy encounters are challenging, requiring both precision and tactical thinking, as different foes have unique weaknesses and attack patterns. The inclusion of Atreus as a combat companion, who aids in both ranged attacks and puzzle-solving, adds another layer of strategy.Visually, "God of War" is a breathtaking achievement. The game’s artistic design marries the harsh, unforgiving beauty of Norse environments with an intricate attention to detail. From the dense forests and snow-capped mountains of Midgard to the fire-scorched landscapes of Muspelheim and the eerie glow of Alfheim, each realm feels distinct, rich with history, and alive with secrets. The single-shot camera technique, which never cuts away from Kratos and Atreus during gameplay, is a bold technical achievement that enhances immersion and heightens emotional investment. This continuous shot ensures that players feel deeply connected to the characters and the world they inhabit.The game’s sound design and score are equally remarkable. The music, composed by Bear McCreary, perfectly complements the tone of the game, balancing moments of intense action with quieter, more introspective beats. The chanting, deep percussion, and use of traditional Norse instruments create a soundtrack that feels simultaneously ancient and epic. Voice acting, especially Christopher Judge’s portrayal of Kratos, is stellar, capturing the character’s gruff exterior and internal turmoil. The dialogue between Kratos and Atreus is natural and often poignant, making their relationship feel authentic.Narratively, the game expertly weaves mythological themes with personal stakes. God of War delves into the complexities of the Norse pantheon, introducing figures like Baldur, Freya, and Mimir, each with their own rich backstory and motivations. These characters are not merely obstacles for Kratos but integral to the story’s exploration of fate, loss, and the consequences of divine power. The pacing of the story is carefully crafted, with moments of high-stakes action balanced by quieter, reflective sequences that allow for character development and world-building.One of the game’s most commendable achievements is its treatment of Kratos. He has evolved from a one-dimensional avatar of rage into a more nuanced and tragic figure. His past actions haunt him, and his attempts to be a better father to Atreus are often undercut by his inability to express emotion or vulnerability. This is a game about a man who is trying, despite his nature, to change. Kratos’ stoicism contrasts with Atreus’ youthful curiosity and occasional petulance, creating tension and, at times, tenderness between them.Exploration is another strong suit of the game. "God of War" moves away from the linear design of its predecessors, offering a semi-open world filled with hidden areas, puzzles, and side quests that enrich the story. These optional quests, often involving interactions with minor gods or legendary creatures, add depth to the world and reward players with unique gear, experience, or lore. The Lake of Nine acts as a hub area, and as the story progresses, more areas become accessible, encouraging players to revisit locations with newfound abilities.In conclusion, "God of War (2018)" is a bold reinvention of a beloved franchise, expertly blending action, storytelling, and emotional depth. It marks a profound shift in tone and structure, offering players an experience that is not only thrilling but also thought-provoking. With its stellar performances, deep combat system, breathtaking visuals, and richly woven narrative, "God of War" stands as one of the finest examples of what modern gaming can achieve. It's a game that transcends the medium, telling a story that resonates on a deeply human level, while still delivering the epic scale fans have come to expect from the series.

_childDocuments_.review: God of War (2018) is the fourth – or perhaps like the eighth, depending on what you count – game in the God of War series. Set in the lands of the Norse Gods after Kratos pretty much wrecked the Greek world, Kratos has been living a quiet life with his wife and son. Naturally, by the time the game has started, his wife has died – apparently of natural causes – and she requests that Kratos and their son, Atreus, take her ashes to the top of the highest mountain in all the land to scatter them.Needless to say, things get a bit complicated, the Norse gods get involved, and before you know it you are off on an adventure through… well, the majority of the nine realms of Norse mythology, though in truth most of your adventure is in one realm (Midgard, i.e. the world of mortals) with your excursions to the other worlds little more than brief dungeons or series of challenges at most.The game is not enormously long, but it has a huge amount of side content which greatly stretches out its length. There’s a lot of places to explore and treasures to find, but the game is actually a bit short on actual monsters to fight.The problem is, the game actually runs out of new things to show you surprisingly early in its length. While there’s ostensibly a number of types of enemies, in reality there’s only a few actually different types – basically a very fast one that jumps on you, a standard melee trash mob, an enemy with a shield, an enemy with a big hammer, an enemy that throws ranged attacks at you, a teleporting witch, a big hulking ogre, a werewolf, trolls with big clubs, some flying enemies who shoot blinding things at you and then engage in melee, some other flying enemies who shoot things at you and sometimes buff enemies, and trolls.The game shows you all these types of enemies pretty early, though, and as a result, it feels like the game runs out of things to throw at you long before the game’s length ends. It doesn’t help that there’s really only five bosses apart from the trolls (which are very similar to each other) resulting in the game feeling like it is lacking for actually interesting combat content – which it kind of is. You fight some bosses multiple times (for story related reasons, but still) and unfortunately, it kind of becomes old hat by the end. The nine Valkyrie bosses do try to mix things up a bit themselves, and are the most interesting boss fights in the game, but they, too, get repetitive after a while.For all the spectacle that the game has, the game’s combat is honestly pretty mediocre – and that’s very unfortunate, because there is a fair amount of it.This is broken up by exploration, which is okay, but nothing super amazing – it’s pretty standard “puzzles”, but they’re all very simple and mostly are pretty much the same, just “the puzzle pieces are hidden differently”.Really, the only thing the game has to make it stand out from the competition is presentation – but fortunately, it does have that in spades. The voice acting is really good, the characters are fun to interact with (even if Kratos himself is mum about things for much of the game), and if you are a fan of Norse mythology, you can see all sorts of fun references in here, along with the game’s various twists and attempts to make the gods the bad guys (because, this is, after all, God of War, the series infamous for deicide – and while gods do die, you will likely be disappointed by the number, though fans of Norse Mythology will also be able to predict who is going to die and more or less how).The game’s core relationship – between Atreus and Kratos – works well, even if it is frustrating at times with just how taciturn Kratos is, but you can see how scarred Kratos is from his past experiences. The game, then, is about Kratos coming out of his shell a little while his son has to figure out who he is and what is going on. Atreus helps out in combat, and also helps with some puzzles, and while none of it is particularly spectacular in execution it works well enough.All in all, I felt like the game stretched itself out too long relative to its interesting content – it added two grindy sidequests for no good reason, as the combat is not anywhere near good enough to justify them, and it just adds to the length of the game without adding to the main thing that the game delivers on – the story of the relationship between Kratos and Atreus and their role in the world, including Kratos’ own undesired role, as he clearly detests his own nature as a god and fears what his son will be like when he realizes that he, too, is a son – trying to keep things as low-key as possible while avoiding giving too much away.I would have liked to have seen more variety in bosses, even if it led to less side content – in fact, especially if it did so, because the side content was weak while the core story was the strongest part of the game. The game diluted itself too much, and didn’t deliver as strongly on its core promise as it could have.All in all, I liked it, but it reminded me of all of the largest issues that game design has long possessed, with a desire to add in more content, even when that extra content actually diminishes the product instead of adding to it. The actual game is only okay, and it is saved by the execution of everything around it.

God of War is a must-play for any fan of action-adventure games and should not be missed. It sets a new standard for the genre and is a true work of art.

_childDocuments_.review: I went into the game blind and I am extremely pleasantly surprised! I don't really like games that have a lot of long cutscenes and very little exciting gameplay. Here, the exact opposite is the case. Within the first few hours the action was priority number one, I felt so much adrenaline in my body and the game totally captivated me. The battles are extremely action-packed, challenging and simply well done. The voice acting is also absolutely top notch.I can only recommend the game so far, it plays great and I have nothing to complain about so far, it is just extremely fun and I am very impressed with the gameplay mechanics. There is so much detail in the game, there are always little puzzles to think about, there is always something optional to explore. The game runs buttery smooth, looks fantastic - there's nothing wrong with the port at all, it's really great. And it's release day, release hour.

_childDocuments_.review: A game that rightfully won game of the year. The graphics are still breathtaking nearly 6 years later, really making the story a fun experience. Two things of note, ensure you enable DLSS instead of FSR if you're getting grainy visuals upon boot-up. Also, if you plan on playing controller, I recommend disabling steam input as it created joystick and button sensitivity issues for me. The translation to PC is nearly perfect, just might need some small tweaking to get the game where you want it.

Cant wait to play Ragnarok!

_childDocuments_.review: I was hesitant to give this game a try after being a longtime fan of the franchise and being disappointed by the new direction this game took. Overall, my misgivings about the combat system mostly held true, but the game gets a recommendation purely for the incredible presentation and terrific writing. This game is worth it for the story alone, and I'd highly recommend playing on the standard or easy difficulty for the best experience. I played the game on the Give Me God of War difficulty for my first playthrough. This difficulty really highlights how terrible this game's combat system can be. There are other better summaries of the issues with the combat system though, and there are also great examples of awesome combos/cancels you can do that make the combat look fun. I won't deny that the system offers a solid amount of options and can have a lot of depth, but I will say that I was mostly just annoyed and frustrated for many encounters during my initial playthrough. I did complete the game, but situations that would be annoying in a normal playthrough were downright tedious on the hardest difficulty, so don't bother with it.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best ports if not THE BEST port for PC I have ever seen. No extra launchers, no need to create an account, no denuvo or other crap. I actually feel that I'm getting full worth of my money from GoW. Very good. Runs great on my 3060 non ti on all high + ultra textures in 1440p (DLSS on),  DLSS 2.0 support, FidelityFX also available for non RTX users. Gripping, fans of Norse mythology will like it. Voice acting is great. Good sound quality. Engaging, fun and there is a lot of variety. Enemy pool is diverse, a LOT of unique enemy types, from small to huge, that require a different approach. It never gets boring. VERY difficult on 3rd and 4th difficulty settings, you will die A LOT in the beginning, but when you start learning enemy patterns and combos, clearing enemies becomes fun and rewarding. there is A LOT to do, visit and collect, Ubisoft fans will approve. It is very rewarding though, because scenery is fantastic, locations are unique and pretty. Good. Yes, this game is better with a gamepad, but Keyboard + Mouse controls are decent, which is rare for console ports. I was pleased with controls and I consider myself a very picky guy. If you like story driven games, action and can stomach violence, you have to play this game. I literally can't stop playing it. One of the few games that I got 100%.

_childDocuments_.review: God of War is widely considered a masterpiece of modern gaming, blending compelling narrative with intense combat and immersive world-building. The game follows Kratos, the former Greek god, as he navigates his complex relationship with his son, Atreus, while embarking on a journey through the Norse realms. The emotional depth and character development are a highlight, particularly the father-son dynamic that drives the plot. Kratos, once a vengeful god, is now protective and reflective, showing significant growth from earlier entries in the series​The combat system is another standout feature. The Leviathan Axe, a primary weapon that can be thrown and summoned back like Thor's Mjölnir, feels both satisfying and versatile in battle. The combat emphasizes both strategic and fast-paced action, combining physical attacks with magical abilities. Kratos also uses a shield and fists in combat, and the addition of Atreus’ bow attacks adds depth to the fighting mechanics​The game also introduces a semi-open world, allowing Kratos and Atreus to explore several diverse Norse realms, each with distinct environments and challenges. While there's some backtracking as you unlock new abilities to access previously unreachable areas, the world is rich with side quests and hidden treasures. The visuals are stunning, with detailed environments, impressive lighting effects, and lifelike character models, particularly on the PlayStation 4 Pro​God of War offers a perfect blend of combat, story, and exploration, with its emotional narrative and innovative gameplay making it one of the best games in the action-adventure genre. Whether you're a fan of the series or new to the world of Kratos, this game is an unforgettable experience.

name: Clid The Snail
detailed_description: In a world where only the distant memory of human existence still lingers, you play as Clid, a troublemaking, eccentric snail who has just been exiled from his home citadel. Joined by a faithful and talkative firefly, Belu, you will meet a peculiar gang of outcasts and find a place to call home. Among this new group of friends, you will discover a newfound purpose: Exterminating the mysterious slug plague that is ravaging the land. Clid The Snail is a unique top-down shooter where character-driven narrative and mindful combat take the center stage. Through Clid, you’ll experience a story about exile, friendship, and betrayal, and live the adventures of a troublesome, unruly snail that doesn’t belong. Explore a treacherous world full of threats and challenges, where strategic positioning, precise gunplay, and enemy behavior are paramount to your survival. Discover the truth behind the slug plague corrupting the world and save the land from ultimate ruin. Get creative with your guns, grenades, and unique snail shells to outsmart your enemies. Use the environment to your advantage and learn to position yourself to emerge victorious. A shy hedgehog, a shaman turtle, a mute bat, a ninja frog, and a one-eyed chameleon: these are the members of Alastor. Return home after each quest to rest, stock up on resources, upgrade equipment, and develop friendships. Get to know these unique characters and unravel their past to find out the key to the story. Swamps, desserts, mountains, islands... Each quest will take you to a new location waiting to be discovered. Help the local residents fight off the slug threat and become their hero! And don’t forget to keep a keen eye: Explore every level in search for extra goodies. Powerful threats await you at the end of each mission. You will need to study their behavior, pay attention to detail, and choose your weapons wisely to survive these dangerous encounters. Shooting isn´t always the answer. Use your weapons and intellect to solve puzzles, find secrets, and progress through the story. Sometimes, the answers are hidden in plain sight…

_childDocuments_.review: I think I like the idea of Clid the Snail more than the actual game. The idea of playing a Gears of War style game based on an anthropomorphic snail is fascinating, but in execution the game feels more like a watered down version of an already watered down tactical shooter like Warhammer: Inquisitor Martyr. Clid could've used an inventory or something else to vary the game play. As it stands, it feels more like a mix between one of the aforementioned shooters and an adventure platformer. There are puzzles, but they don't take much effort to solve. The graphics look wonderful at first glance, but after a while the overall presentation feels muddled and watered down. That isn't to say effort didn't go into this game, but the game got old for me within about an hour of playing. You just use the same sniper weapon with unlimited ammo to kill wave after wave of brainless enemy. There's no strategy, and as long as you lead your targets by keeping a distance and using the aim assist it's basically impossible to die. Of course you get your grenades, and then your little collectibles in the form of pieces of life bar upgrades. The only reason to kill enemies not directly in your way is to get money which you barely need because the most useful weapon has unlimited ammo. This game needed a lot more work put into it to differentiate it from the countless other games that adopt this game play style. I admit I was lured in by the idea of playing as a snail with a gun, but the game play isn't as quirky or unique as that initial concept would lead you to believe. In fact, playing as a snail has no impact on any of the gameplay. You would think you could at least hide in your shell for defense or something, but the fact that you're playing as a snail has no bearing on anything in terms of the game design.Also, something I really don't like is that you get half of the remaining weapons just before the game ends. This needed an extra three or four levels to pad it out- honestly it feels unfinished. The final boss fight is solid though. I think the developers wanted to create something story-driven but forgot that gameplay must always come before story, particularly when advertisements for your game showcase the gameplay as an incentive to buy it.

_childDocuments_.review: After completing the game I must change my review from recommended to not recommended. I really hoped the game would become more difficult as it went on, but at no point is the game ever challenging, even when encountering new enemies, they never deviate enough to become challenging. The bosses also arent difficult.What I enjoyed about the game -THE WORLD. I think this was definitely the highlight of the game, exploring a world without humans and populated by highly developed creatures was pretty interesting. I think if the game had placed more focus on the world, and less on the combat (which was already beyond easy) it could have truly been special. What I didnt enjoy about the game -Targeted aim seemed to be broken, and would often cause me to aim in the complete wrong direction, or shots would go inches away from the crosshair.The plot was rushed, you only spend a limited amount of time in each zone or talking to each being, so you never get to have a lasting impression from anything.The combat was very easy and repetitive.currency was easy to come by, and nothing in the shops were expensive, so seems pointless.I think for the game to improve, fast travel should be added. In your room in alastor you have a map on the wall you can interact with, why cant we fast travel and revisit areas to look for things we may have missed?More optimized graphics with more eye candy in the different regions to make them more unique from one another.adjustable difficulty so the game can be at least somewhat challenging.More fleshed out lore of the world and creatures within it, collectables in the world with lore even.So much potential in this game, but just feels rushed and forced, could have been such a great game. I hope if any DLC or future titles in the world are released, they spend more time to fully develop and explore the unique world.

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to like this game. The world seems really interesting and the visual style is cool, but the sheer volume of particle effects, muddy bloom, lack of contrast, and zero options to tweak anything beyond the brightness and quality, and the general oversight for any reasonable UI/UX design makes for a game far lesser than the sum of its parts.Gameplay is fine. A bit clunky. Mostly due to the randomness of if set decoration will or will not have collision on it and the aforementioned muddy visuals. There were times I had no idea there were several enemies on screen due to the constant cacophony of visual noise. I'd like to be able to see the important parts of this VIDEO game :) The UI is awful. The huge blue and red color splashes make me feel like I'm looking through Vaseline coated frosted glass in a night club and the bright colors hide the important information from being readable in the player's peripheral vision. The "heads up display" is generally supposed to provide quickly readable information, not hide it... Maybe it stands for "Hazy, unreadable display" internally.Cutscenes are a drag. World conversations are great since you can click through at your reading speed, but scripted cutscenes are so damn slow. You hear 5 syllables of meaningless babble and then get to read "Welcome!" for 7 seconds before the next line auto progresses. Even if you had intelligible dialogue skipping forward on a per-line basis would be the best solution.Luckily I only paid $4 on humble for this, so I'm not too upset as that's what it feels worth as an experience. But it's so close to being good that I hope these eventually get addressed. I literally just want to be able to see the game

_childDocuments_.review: l is a twin-stick shooter set in a post-apocalyptic world where humanity has been brought to extinction after a catastrophic event, while anthropomorphic creatures have built their own citadels and need to defend themselves from the slug plague. You play as Clid, a mercenary snail followed by a cute firefly called Belu. After a troublesome rescue mission, they are exiled from their village and forced to look for a new home, which they find in Alastor, a group of outcasts with a mission to exterminate the slug menace. The premise itself is nothing original since other games such as  already feature anthropomorphic animals fighting in post-human environments, but the world building is solid and the gameplay cleverly alternates shooting stages with puzzles and narrative sections.Cid and Belu are a funny duo and both well-characterized, but it’s difficult to connect with all the other characters for how little they appear on screen and this unfortunately ruins a few good twists during the final part of the game. Characters don’t talk but only mumble and you can’t skip a single line of dialogue during a cutscene, you can only skip it entirely. I’m saying this cause it often took me a few seconds to read the dialogue lines, but I still had to wait for the characters to stop mumbling in order to move on with the narrative. Fortunately this doesn’t happen during standard NPCs conversations, which can be skipped at your own pace of reading.As mentioned earlier, the game is a twin-stick shooter with an isometric view. Clid has a good set of weapons and gadgets, which can be purchased from merchants or unlocked simply by progressing with the story. The game is generally easy, with only a few spikes towards the end. Most of the time we will be forced to back away, dodge and move constantly while shooting enemies, so there isn’t much strategy involved and only a few bosses require a change of tactics.Despite the main trailer showing some fast-paced combat, what I found was rather slow shooting, recharging and rolling, which became bothersome at times. The gunplay is pretty decent, but there is still some input lag. Fans of the genre will probably have a hard time dealing with this and the low difficulty, but overall the combat experience still feels enjoyable.The art direction is really great and environments feature different biomes, from desert landscapes to snowy mountains. It’s a pity that the level design is mostly linear and the exploration feels optional. You can only find seeds that can be used to increase your vitality or some chests containing in-game currency, but you will eventually be so rich that it will become pointless.Overall, Clid the Snail is a beautiful and enjoyable experience, but short. While the game is clearly a good debut for the team, it never meets its potential as a twin-stick shooter. The world building puts a solid base with Clid and Belu being a charismatic duo, but everything else is left rough and too vague.

_childDocuments_.review: The year is 2004. At Toys 'R Us you survey the shiny, shrink-wrapped denizens of the gaming department, perhaps accompanied by a parent, or maybe a chum who, like you, is raring to go for a new experience in our favorite of favorite hobbies: Video Games.There's a jingle of coin in your or your mother or father's pocket and you will not be leaving this store without seeing it spent. You glance at Snake Eater, unsure of what exactly goes in in that game; you pick up a display case promoting Prince of Persia: Warrior Within. "Nah dude," your sagacious friend cautions. He is wise beyond his years.Past the stack of empty GameCube boxes and the innumerable advertisements for Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, something rimmed in the Mountain Dew green of an Xbox case catches your eye. It's Clid the Snail. And it's Only on Xbox.You're immediately struck by the cover art. Sure you've seen the likes of anthropomorphic marsupials wield heavy weaponry before, but never before has it dawned on you to consider that a snail--let alone a snail with legs--might festoon his hearty hollow with the armaments of warfare. Your curiosity gets the better of you. You buy Clid the Snail for $49.99.At home, past the glowing architecture of your Xbox's interface, you're enraptured by a sailor-mouthed snail and his Navi-like companion as they slowly, deliberately atomize crazed slug tribesman and conspire with Banjo Kazooie-soundin' critters who, like our titular mollusk, find themselves exiled of their own kind and forced into a ragtag mercenary outfit of gunslingers-for-hire, carving a bloody swath through the scourge of slugs that would infest this strange, edgy, somehow strongly-considered fantasy world our crinkled pal Ulysses Grant purchased us admittance to.You beat Clid the Snail.It wasn't terribly lengthy. You grew frustrated with the game's shotgun simplicity. The trudging, languid pace of navigation (although I guess, for real, you are LITERALLY a snail, so to level any criticism at the actual pace of Clid the Snail's movement is almost providing the developers with the argumentative equivalent of a silver bullet with which they may respond "Well duh, you fool, it's in the title") and the not-always-quite-landing banter between our gritty gastropod and co. Here was a game with flaws. Deep flaws.Yet, for all that one might devastate Clid the Snail for, for its mediocrity or just-passability in most of its gameplay fundamentals, you stop yourself from feeling this self-righteous critic's scorn. You stop yourself because, you realize, Clid the Snail had heart. Clid the Snail HAS heart. Here was a game so warped in its premise yet diligently-realized, scripted by a precocious child yet still hammering at shards of painful truth in its characterizations, and simple in its twin-stick ambitions yet satisfying in its gibbing of slug assailants that, in hindsight, you had Fun. And while you're likely to swap discs for Halo 2 and not swap discs again for some long duration, you won't forget Clid. Sure, his was a remarkably simple journey, propelled by waves of mindless slugs for the slaughter and some uninspired level design that even you, a child, could see was a little iffy. A minor episode on a literally-miniature scale. History will likely not smile fondly at the memory of Clid the Snail the way she may recall the adventures of Ratchet and friend Clank, or the crude quips of Conker on his most baddest of fur days. Heck, Clid might not even stand a chance against Blinx. Or Voodoo Vince!But Clid was a snail with GUNS, for Pete's sake. And boy howdy did he know how to use them.

_childDocuments_.review: So I'm not even sure where I saw this game, I think it was a PS showcase somewhere - been on my wishlist ever since. Bought it the day it came out, raised my eyebrow on the discount from day one - but hey, don't look a gift horse in the mouth.Well, I'd buy this game all over again not knowing what it is, but...·Beautiful graphics. Coming from a studio that is essentially unheard of - their first game is pretty rock solid.·Great engine - no powerhogging, despite the advanced effects.·Fantastic music - the guitar in the menu brings back Tristram memories.· Sigh. The game does sell itself for something that it isn't. I expected more shooty shooty and less talky talky.· · Terrible bump-mapping. Occasional clipping through objects, enemies moving through solids, yadda yadda.· Key gameplay not explained. Like when you first encounter the · Story is... lacklustre. You can see it coming a mile away, at the speed of a snail. The game tries to be cute with multiple winks at geek and nerd culture (I have the highground!) but ultimately fails to bring an exceptional story to probably one of the most unique (!) game experiences I've had.Snails rock. _childDocuments_.review: Clid the Snail mixes up combat with exploration where you can find seeds to increase your max health along with plenty of chests full of currency that can be spent at the local trading posts to resupply.  There’s nothing terribly original about the core game design; we’ve all done this same stuff in dozens of other games, but Clid puts a unique spin on the design with its visionary creature design and the microcosmic world they inhabit.  There is a fun assortment of weapons that encourages close and long-range combat along with tactical use of the landscape.  There are also some fun puzzle-solving and traversal challenges that require you to navigate these deadly lasers.  And don’t forget about some insanely creative boss fights; that rat with the flamethrower and rocket launcher is only the beginning.The overall difficulty is pretty tame and doesn’t seem to increase as you progress the story.  Boss fights are pretty easy too once you figure out the “gimmick” for each.  I suppose this is a god design for younger gamers looking to simply pass the time.  There is also a lot of dialogue in the game, conversation and exposition, and it’s all spoken in gibberish, which means you get to read a lot of text.  You can skip it with a button press but there is often important info lurking in those text boxes.  Some text boxes will auto-advance while others make you click a button between sentences.  I wasn’t expecting voice acting, but this much reading can really mess with the momentum of the gameplay.  I did appreciate the French accent for Clid.Read the full review at Watch the first two hours of the game at More Steam reviews on our Curator page -

_childDocuments_.review: First off, Tinykin is not like Pikmin. Any review that says it's similar has no idea what makes either game unique. So, if you're thinking about playing Tinykin because of the comparison, stop right there. Let me explain the difference.Pikmin is an RTS about managing and nurturing a growing army of tiny soldiers. You must guide them through battle and away from hazards that will crush, burn, and drown their fragile little bodies. When they die, it will be due to your own incompetence, and you will feel bad because you have failed them as a commander.Tinykin is a 3D platformer with a sort of metroidvania exploration style. Your tinykin cannot die. They do not need to be controlled. They cannot fall off cliffs and get stuck. They do not get lost. You receive an exact and precise number of them and that number never rises or falls until you collect more from preset locations.There are, however, two similarities between this and Pikmin. The first is that you have a swarm of small critters that follow you around. And yet, the gameplay of Tinykin would barely change if that swarm were taken away and replaced with a resource counter. If you did that to Pikmin, the strategy of the entire game would change.The second thing is that it gives you a childlike feeling of being very small in a very large world. In fact, I think Tinykin does that far better than Pikmin. All of the terrain and obstacles are brilliantly constructed out of the things that a child might use to build a world for tiny people.All I can really say is, if you like 3D platformers, buy this game! This is a very fun game. The controls are extremely tight and responsive. The music is fantastic and enjoyable, especially some of the boom box tracks. The level design is very clever and highly polished.I bought this game because it looked like Pikmin and I love Pikmin. I loved this game because of its own strengths.
_childDocuments_.name: Tinykin

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot say enough kind things about Tinykin. I really feel like the trailer did not do this game justice, as this game is way more fun than how it looked in the trailer. If you're a completionist, someone who loves collecting every little thing in a game, and someone who loves cute games—Tinykin is for you. I had so much fun playing this and I definitely plan on going back to try and 100% it. The concept is incredibly cute and the ending was unlike anything that I expected. There were few to no bugs that I experienced in my playthrough, and it seemed to be very polished.The artstyle is gorgeous. I love the 2D character (Milodane) mixed with the 3D, real-life world. It just fit perfectly, and it was so addicting and painfully hard to put this game down. I highly recommend this game if you're on the fence about it or if you're skeptical about paying full price, wait for a sale. I would say that this game is worth the price with the number of hours that you can get in just your first playthrough alone. While there isn't much replay value (that I know of), this game is a great and beautiful experience.All in all, like I said before, I highly recommend this game. I really enjoyed it, and it's super fun and unique!Rating: 9.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: What a delight!Pure exploration and platforming fun! I really love the concept of being tiny in a huge world so this one caught my eye from the get go and more than delivered.The game is a a 3D collectathon platformer with a dose of Pikmin. This is a very dry way to describe it, I would say it's Pikmin but you are very mobile and fast in a extremely well designed world (maps like fromsoftware, everything is beautifully connected). To complete the package, the art, OST, sound effects and writing (if you want) is all great!Each room in the house is it's own little town with it's theme, culture and characters. Also, by the end, the story revels to be more than what it appears...On a side note, the guys from this studio are former Ubisoft Montpellier devs. When I see such a indie gem like this coming from former huge studio devs I can't help but wonder how many cool ideas are trapped behind corporate bottom line focus... or maybe I'm just salty because Ubi doesn't make a new 3D Rayman...

_childDocuments_.review: It's not pikmin at all, in the sense that there is no managing of your tinykin, you don't tend to them and they frankly don't need you at all, they're collectible that you need to find to do puzzles and that's it.Tinykin is a collectathon in interesting setpieces with light platforming elements. I found the story pretty bland and the music, while not being out of place, to be serviceable at best.I enjoyed the environment, the exploration of the levels (with little things hidden everywhere) and its character design (too bad I didn't actually enjoy interacting with said characters)Get it if you want a chill low difficulty platformer about exploring places and collecting things, that's what it's good at.

_childDocuments_.review: So far, probably the best 3D collect-a-thon platformer on Steam.It may look like a Pikmin clone on the surface, but beyond collecting a small army of little helper NPCs to throw at your problems, it's really nothing like that.  The movement around the levels, and general gameplay is much more acrobatic, so it feels more like a 3D Mario or Banjo game, and the Tinykin are really just the tools you collect in order to deal with the various obstacles in your way.The music is nice, the levels are big, and packed densely with stuff to do, and stuff to collect.  The graphics are very pleasant, the controls are responsive and rarely if ever frustrating. You get to skate around on a little piece of soap and that isn't even a feature that's locked off until later.. you'll get it 10 or 15 minutes into the game, and it makes movement a lot of fun.Speaking of the levels again, I've mostly seen the first one so far (the first big one, not the tutorial room), but they seem designed really well.  Big, complex, crammed with stuff, full of little secret nooks and crannies with collectibles in them.  As you move throughout, you'll find ropes and silk lines that you can deploy to create shortcuts and interconnectivity between different parts.The stages are all based on being a tiny-sized person in a normal-sized house, and bugs have been developing a society in the house, so you get to see how they've built and repurposed objects in the house to make their own little homes and businesses.All those various pieces of furniture, books, instruments, toys, and other household objects all make for a big, beautiful world that presents itself in a way that begs you to explore everywhere.  Not even just for the collectibles, but to see all the little areas up-close.  I found a place where an old VHS box was turned into a tall, narrow little house, with an upper balcony and everything.  Very cute.If you've been hankering for a good 3D platformer, and either you're done with stuff like Hat in Time and Yooka Laylee, or never liked them that much to begin with, give this one a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Tinykin

_childDocuments_.review: You can't tell a hero by his size, just a Tinykin little super guy.Ah yes, Bizarro Pikmin.Me: As a cultured, hardcore gamer I just cannot get into those Pikmin Nintendo games!Also Me: Guys, you’ve GOT to check out this cute little leadership game on Steam… Tinykin!This is one of those games I got for my kids, then proceeded to play until 3 in the morning. Very lighthearted, lots of fun, great animation, and puzzles that were challenging but not too challenging. Tinykin is one of the most delightful and charming gaming experiences I've had in a long time.I heard about it from a comments section on a Facebook gaming group a couple of months ago. They described it as Pikmin meets Paper Mario and I thought ‘that sounds like a bloody good time’.After downloading and playing for an hour I knew it was something special. I had to stop for the night because I had work the next morning but the next day all I could think about was getting to play it when I got home, which is a feeling I haven’t had since a certain other game this year (Sex with Hitler 3D).Well now this has easily become one of my favorite games of the past year, if not of all time. It's a 3D platformer that shares a lot of its DNA with collect-a-thons of old. You're an explorer trying to get the pieces to put a spaceship together so you can get back to your home planet, and you're thrown into these massive, intricately-crafted levels to get the various pieces.You're about the size of a beetle, and the whole game takes place in a house, with each of the levels being various rooms, like the kitchen or bathroom or greenhouse. Think the “Honey, I Shrunk The Kids!” environment as you are running around someone’s 1990s house as a 6 inch tall tiny person.So you get that cool perspective of being miniature in these settings that you're familiar with. The house and its different rooms are populated by various bug species, and there's so much charm in seeing how they've terraformed these various human rooms into insect societies. The kitchen is their agricultural sector, so they leave the kitchen faucet flowing and have an assortment of straws leading the water into a waterfall beneath the sink which then becomes a river that flows down the kitchen and provides irrigation for the farmland—which is really just overturned sponges. Each of the rooms have their own purpose and it's so charming exploring them and seeing how they're arranged. The levels are all pretty big, but not overwhelmingly so. It's fun to explore all of the different areas, and there's usually a central area in the level. As you explore around, you reveal these webs that allow you to quickly move between the hub and the outer areas. So you get that satisfaction of unlocking new shortcuts for yourself. As you explore around you find and can talk to various NPCs, who usually have something funny to say. Your goal for the level is to complete whatever task is asked of you in order to get the spaceship part, but there's also two or three sidequests that various NPCs will ask of you. Beyond that, you're also collecting pollen which is scattered about everywhere. That's the "coins" of this game, and it's super enjoyable to collect.Something else you'll be collecting is the game's namesake: the tinikyn. These are little guys you find throughout the levels that follow you around and can be used for different tasks or interactions as you play. You need to find tinykins who follow you around, each with their own abilities such as lifting objects, blowing up road blocks, conducting electricity, building towers or bridges in order to progress through the level. This might make you think of Pikmin, but it’s not like that at all.So the levels consist of exploring around, collecting tinykin and pollen and completing the task that'll get you the spaceship part—which'll be something like baking a giant cake, requiring you to collect the eggs, sugar, flour, etc. scattered around the level and putting them in the mixing bowl. I truly think this game is a masterclass in 3D platformer design. All of the exploration and the signposting feels so organic in that at every moment you have three or four options of where to go next, will choose one, end up looping around on yourself and then find that you’re at the start of another path of pollen to follow and explore.The frame rate and controls are silky smooth and, as a result, it’s always a pleasure to play. The puzzles are super simple but the reward is in going for 100% - which I know isn’t everyone’s bag but finding all of the pollen in a level is an experience that’s always fun and never tiring/arduous.Normally I don’t feel obligated to 100% these collect-a-thon games but I was having so much fun exploring and zipping around that I wanted to make sure I saw all the nooks and crannies of the house and obtained every last collectable in the game. I think maybe Paper Mario meets Pikmin isn’t quite right - I’d say something along the lines of Banjo-Kazooie meets Pikmin meets Chibi-Robo is a more accurate description (big vibes of all three throughout).The movement and gameplay is tight and just feels right. You can run and can do a single jump, but holding the jump button puts you in this bubble that you can use to float around temporarily. As you collect pollen you can increase the duration of this bubble float, which is cool. You also get this soapboard (it's a skateboard, but a bar of soap) that you can use to skate around the level for some extra speed. This thing carries its momentum into jumps and can be really fun to use while zooming around levels. The soapboard and upgraded bubble—along with the tinykin that gives you an instant ladder—allows for some really versatile movement, and you're able to cover a lot of ground with these tools. After you complete a level, you can go back and do one or two races that are available, and I found these to be a ton of fun. You're really able to zip around the map and the races are really well designed. Getting gold medals for them also unlocks new costumes for your characters. So that's basically the long and short of it. I've loved it. It really appeals to a childlike fantasy of being a tiny little guy in a big house and traversing things from that perspective. This game has been nothing but an unbridled joy to play, and it's been so fun to sit back and play what feels like such a classic video game. Just a man and his controller, jumping around a world. It’s one of the best feelings when you play a game you had no idea you needed in that moment in time. Tinykin, you beautiful bastard, you took me back to my childhood of playing Banjo Kazooie. If you enjoy 3D platformers and collect-a-thons this one is a must play. It’s a great “turn your brain off” and just have fun kind of game. I highly recommend it.10/10

_childDocuments_.review: is a rather incredible 3D platformer. I knew it was something special ever since I played the demo... the full game manages to exceed my expectations. It's a fun, relaxing, wholesome, and extremely polished experience.At first glance you may think the game is inspired by Pikmin, but in reality it's more like a mix of Overlord and Super Mario Odyssey gameplay-wise. Sure, you do collect Tinykins that have special abilities, but those only serve the platforming aspect. You don't need to manage your tiny companions or use them in combat like Pikmin. As a 3D platformer Tinykin gets the basics right: your movement throughout the levels is smooth and effortless and the actual platforming is top-notch. The game smartly gives you the majority of the platforming options as early as possible, making it quite enjoyable to explore each level. And the levels themselves are great: you really will feel like a tiny person inside a huge house. Something about that early 90s (specifically, 1991) setting is just so fascinating to me as it also reflects my childhood. You may feel overwhelmed when you're dropped inside such massive levels, but the game quickly allows you to overcome that feeling thanks to the memorable layouts and paths you can take through them. I cannot praise the level design enough, it's downright brilliant how you discover secrets and shortcuts. The way you are guided subtly towards your objectives without any obvious handholding is another nice touch. Collectibles add enough replay value to the levels as it's unlikely you'll get every single one the first time. Some collectibles like the bubble upgrades also enhance the actual gameplay potential as you can practically fly forever once you've fully collected them. Performance is another area where the game impresses. I did not notice any framedrops or stutters. No noticeable bugs either during my playthrough and zero crashes. Loading times are fast enough, it's easy to start the game and immediately jump into a level.I can't find much to criticize here, aside from the fact that the game is a bit on the shorter side (6-8 hours to complete the main story, around 10-12 hours if you want to do ). But I feel like it's the perfect length for the game as it emphasizes quality over quantity. The last two Tinykin types feel a bit underutilized and underwhelming compared to the first four which you'll use a lot. The lack of a dedicated photo mode is a bit of a downside to me as I love taking screenshots while playing. Still, all of these are minor complaints.If you love 3D platformers, you'll enjoy Tinykin.

_childDocuments_.review: is a love letter to collect-a-thon games, very reminiscent of the classic Nintendo 64 games back in the day. Its 3D puzzle platformer also takes inspiration from Pikmin, whereby you acquire  to help you solve puzzles throughout the game. It definitely stands its own ground with being a completely different game from aforementioned Pikmin, spliced together with satisfying, but not overly challenging, platforming. • Intricately designed levels• Addictive collect-a-thon that doesn’t outstay its welcome• Loads of secrets and hidden areas for thoroughly exploring• Huge, sprawling, open levels that make you excited to explore• Adorable and cute art style• Attention to detail in the music and environment• Be a small guy exploring a huge house• Lacks challenge in platforming that you might expectThroughout the game, you’ll be exploring a house as a shrunk person, with each room being a different level. Each is intricately crafted to complement the puzzle platforming you’ll be doing throughout the game. Unlocking shortcuts and destroying obstacles allow you to access previously hard to reach areas in case you need to come back later. The level design is very reminiscent of Nintendo 64 collect-a-thons, huge open sprawling maps that, at first, seem overwhelming, but offer more than just a linear path. You’ll find yourself stumbling across hidden paths, secret areas (oh boy do they love hiding stuff) and shiny collectibles that only side track you more and more away from your primary goal. Just like moths to a flame, as soon as you see something you haven’t collected, you’ll instantly be drawn to it, at least that’s what happens to me often. The puzzle elements come in forms of using your Tinykin to solve and work around problems. Each level starts you out with no Tinykin to command, but by the end of it, you will have amassed an army big enough to go to war with anyone who might look at you funny… *ahem*… Tinykin can come in different forms and variations, using them to move objects around the map, stack and climb up to access new areas, throw at objects to destroy them (they die in this process and seem to enjoy it… I kinda had to question that…) and so on. These are your puzzle pieces, your pawns to do your bidding, throwing them at obstacles you want to move, using them as your own personal bombs to clear a path or to access different areas. Never once was I stumped by a puzzle throughout my playthrough. If I came across something I didn’t know how to overcome yet, I’d simply put it on the back burner, and keep exploring the level.That being said, whilst each level was a joy in itself to explore, along with the constant supply of dopamine by collecting pollen (a collectible), solving puzzles to gain artifacts and accumulating an army of Tinykin to help you solve puzzles and explore previously inaccessible areas, the lack of challenge was apparent, especially in the later levels. Not to say that this took away from the enjoyment this game offers, but I did feel like more could’ve been done with the platforming elements.Your main objective throughout the game is to build a machine from a blueprint found to get back to your home planet, Aegis. Conveniently, all the pieces you need are held in different parts of the house, which are guarded or owned by different insect species. They, obviously, want a favour in exchange for the part you require, which is what’ll keep you busy most of the time. Actually no, what will keep you busy most of the time is your inability to say no to collecting shiny collectibles whilst doing the primary objective. These favours range from resolving conflict between two different species, to solving hunger by baking a cake.The idea of being small and puny whilst exploring a now huge house has always been a fun and interesting environment for me, putting so many things into a new perspective because of your size. The way each level is designed using common household objects as platforms or slopes for that particular room really does something for me, and I can’t explain why or how. The creativity used to build each level is second to none, the cartoonish art style that I couldn’t help but be in awe with for most of the game never ceased to impress me. Yes, the Tinykin were adorable to look at throughout this game, and I now wonder what it would be like to have them as pets… But I digress. Even though the cutscenes were far and few between, I was always pleasantly surprised when they did come up. Though short, they really captured the essence of this adorable game, both in and outside the cutscenes.Whilst I didn't really expect much from this game going into it, I can’t help but praise it for how fun, compelling and adorable it was from start to finish. I couldn’t get enough of collecting things and whilst I didn’t get 100% completion, I can see myself getting back into it to clean up what I missed. This is a must-have for anyone who adores collect-a-thons, it's short, sweet and to the point that doesn’t outstay its welcome, highly recommended.
