_childDocuments_.review: After the main story completed, let me share what my time with Tinykin was like.The art style is beautiful, the mix of 2D for characters and 3D for the environment is seamless, the devs really pulled it off. Very fitting for the tone of the game. As far as level design and controls go, Tinykin is a dream to play. It's a platformer through and through, and not once did it get frustrating in these eight hours. Because even if you do miss a jump, there are cleverly placed shortcuts everywhere to help you get back.The mechanics took Pikmin as a basis and ran with it in its own direction, which is cool. I especially enjoyed how mobile the green (climbing) Tinykins made me feel. When you get the hang of using them, traversing the house becomes an absolute joyride and easily my favorite part of the game. Just scaling the furniture around the rooms and zooming on a soapboard.The sound design is very nice, especially in relation to movement and interactions with the world. However, the soundtrack didn't really stand out.Story-wise, the main premise and goals are very clear, but I can't say I very much cared for all the side objectives and characters. THAT BEING SAID, I can appreciate the love and care given to each insect inhabitant of the house, and all the clever pop culture references inserted. It's obvious the devs had fun with the game, and their dedication shows.Also - I really liked the ending. It was unexpected, to be honest, the twist was really cool.All in all, Tinykins was a wonderful experience, 8 hours long for the main story and all the side quests (I still haven't done some of the post-game challenges and missed a bit of the achievements). I would recommend it if you're a fan of platformers, since Splashteam really delivers on that front. I would also recommend it if you liked the trailer and the visual style, because the game is PACKED with eye-candy. Just don't go in looking for a Pikmin carbon-copy, or something overly complex. The puzzles are easy, and there to just enhance the whole experience. You collect Tinykins, collect pollen nuggets, solve small quests, and platform around. That's it. But it's done JUST RIGHT //chefkissA lot of effort was put into the game, and for that it's well worth the price.

_childDocuments_.review: I’ve always enjoyed the concepts used in Pikmin and games similar to that like Overlord. Games where you’re managing minions and making use of them for some greater goal land somewhere between action games, puzzle games, and real-time strategies. Tinykin takes this seldom used, but often entertaining design and blends it with player-friendly “collect-a-thon” gameplay to create something unique but also so familiar and intuitive that it immediately feels like cozy warm nostalgia.Abbreviated Review: It’s easy to look at Tinykin and say “this is a Pikmin knockoff.” It’s even playing off the name a bit with the title – which is the name also used for the little creatures you make use of as tools within the game. However, despite some overlaps in the gameplay, the feel of the game is quite different from that classic franchise. The biggest change is that there isn’t any sort of failure state in Tinykin. You can die from falling too far or ending up in water or fire – which are both uncommon – but even then you respawn instantly where you were last alive. You also can’t lose any of your tinykin (aside from the ones you use to explode barriers) as there’s no combat and they aren’t affected by any environmental hazards. The gameplay challenge comes entirely from platforming and puzzle solving.Platforming is another big departure from Pikmin’s inspiration. Much of what is necessary to succeed comes from you using your tinykin and abilities to move through the levels. There is a massive amount of verticality within each level and most of the time your goal is to track down enough tinykin and enhance your floating bubble power so you can access it all. You won’t have to fight any of the bug creatures you encounter and usually, the most challenging aspect is figuring out where hidden secrets are and unlocking them. Here, it leans much more toward games like Banjo Kazooie and other games where opening pathways and picking up floating doodads are the focus.The premise of Tinykin does also overlap a bit with that of Pikmin. You venture from your planet of humans to investigate what you believe is the homeworld of humanity and, in the process, lose your ability to travel. You end up a small fish in what appears to be a big pond but is actually just a normal size house. Being about the size of a bug, you soon come face to face with a whole collection of them – though they have evolved into a complex human-like society with structures and jobs. One of them becomes your guide and directs you to the plans to build a transportation ship that would serve as your rescue vessel and thus creates the central theme of the game – finding parts.This splits the game into five(ish) levels that are represented within the unique rooms in a house. The bedroom has been turned into the central capital with a large temple dedicated to the insect world’s teacher and mystical figurehead Ardwin. An atrium-styled workshop is the plant-dominated greenhouse home of the mantises. The bathroom is split between the timid dung beetles and the flashy party squad of silverfish where toilets, vanities, and bathtubs all become catalysts for puzzles and adventure. These themes of turning everyday rooms and objects within them into massive set pieces for your character to climb over, under, and through are common throughout the game. Some of the most appealing aspects of the whole experience are discovering what you can unlock and how you’ll manipulate the world to achieve your goals. It makes the environment as much a part of the allure as anything else you do.When you’re introduced to a new area, you don’t have any tinykin available (they stay within each level), so after a brief introduction to the new map and the discovery of the tasks ahead of you, you’ll need to start exploring. This is made pretty easy with the inclusion of a bar of soap that serves as a speed-enhancing skateboard and your ability to press the jump button in the air to float on a soap bubble. Your bubble ends up being one of the primary non-tinykin tools you need to navigate levels and solve puzzles. However, you’re not going to make it very far without picking up some of those little fuzzy boys.Tinykin come in a select variety – each of which is collected from a color-specific egg on surfaces. The first ones you encounter have the strength to carry objects, weigh down pullies, and just generally knock ♥♥♥♥ around. They’re soon joined by the only expendable group, the bomb tinykin that are used to break open collections of pollen and passageways you need to navigate. Green tinykin can stack up to form a ladder giving you that all-too-important access to the vertically designed worlds and yellow tinykin perform a similar task but with a ramp that can only be used in designated areas. The final type, the blue tinykin, are used in niche situations of chaining together to connect power outlets to exposed cables. This assortment of characters is used seamlessly to help you transition around each level and often are given in an abundance that allows you to get where you need to go even without having all of them. However, the collect-a-thon nature of the game encourages you to find them all regardless.I believe if you avoided the side missions and the somewhat tedious task of finding every tinykin and last speck of popcorn-shaped pollen dotted in the recesses of every map, Tinykin would only be a few hours long at best. Even completing majority of that, I only clocked in less than seven hours. Of course, I put in probably three hours in the demo (over two playthroughs) which carried over to the full game, so it may be at least an hour or two longer. Still, it might not be as appealing of a prospect if you’re racing through it. However, it’s so rewarding to find these items and fully explore the worlds that I can’t imagine playing the game without attempting to get most of it. The little details, bug characters, and magnificent environment design are, on their own, worth every moment invested.If I could find any fault in the game, it's that the insect NPCs and much of the world are very static without your involvement. I think it would have done a great deal for the immersion and brought life to the environment if the bugs were moving around and performing basic tasks. I didn’t mind the 2D character design and it’s one of the most well-integrated examples of 2D sprites in a 3D environment. Yet, the only real problem I have is that I can’t have even more of this game. It was such an engrossing and enjoyable experience that I felt like I could easily play twice as much without any hesitation. I can only hope that the developers are willing to add to this exceptional experience soon.I somehow forgot to mention how great the soundtrack is for this game. Each of the five rooms/zones has its own theme - and all of those are great - but the best part is that they change depending on where you go within the map. For instance, in the first area, you can go into a guitar that serves as a nightclub and the theme takes on the twang of a guitar. The rooms have at least a few of these areas and it makes exploration even more rewarding. Ok now that's all - play this game!

_childDocuments_.review: Tinykin is a delightful 3D platformer that merges elements of classic collect-a-thon gameplay with unique puzzle-solving mechanics. Set in a miniature world within a human household, you’ll explore vibrant, intricately designed levels, all while leading an army of adorable creatures called Tinykin.Why You Should Play:- Charming Visuals: The blend of 2D characters in a 3D environment creates a captivating and nostalgic aesthetic reminiscent of Saturday morning cartoons.- Engaging Puzzles: Each type of Tinykin has distinct abilities, and mastering how to combine them to navigate obstacles and solve puzzles keeps the gameplay fresh and rewarding.- Exploration: The level design encourages exploration and rewards players with collectibles, hidden areas, and clever environmental storytelling.- Smooth Platforming: The controls are tight and responsive, making it a joy to leap, glide, and command your Tinykin army through the game's diverse environments.If you enjoy games like Pikmin, Katamari Damacy, or classic platformers, Tinykin will be a refreshing and charming addition to your library. _childDocuments_.review: Tinykin is a difficult game to evaluate.Is it fun? Sure, the movement feels good, tight, and responsive. Skating around levels on your soapboard is satisfying and quick. The levels are massive and intuitively designed, possibly some of the best 3D level design I've experienced for that matter; constantly offering multiple options to explore that always seem to loop back in on themselves and branch into other routes. After getting the hang of the game it flows extremely naturally and you wind up completing the entire level without ever losing the wind in your sails until, essentially, the very end when you're just doing cleanup of the last few ambrosia you missed (this game's sort of "coin" collectible, with over a thousand per level).The visuals are incredibly charming as well, transforming everyday objects into not just obstacles but things that are functional for the NPCs as much as they are engaging to interact with. One particular level has an entire sink with a running faucet that overflows into an irrigation system, using sponges for farmland (which happen to be as evergreen as grass). The character designs are similarly cute and visually interesting.And... Surprisingly, the game's writing is pretty good. There's actually somehow relatively interesting politics internally from stage to stage that showcases thoughtful worldbuilding. Similarly I didn't expect the very ending to be so... Strangely melancholic and tragic. Still, it wasn't an unwelcomed tonal shift to close out the ten hour runtime.So what's the hang-up? Why can't I rate it any higher when the game is so expertly and lovingly crafted?The game is just... Too easy. It feels like wasted potential. There isn't a single stretch of difficult platforming to be seen nor is there an engaging puzzle. The highest compliment I can give this game amounts to "the most fun you can have with your brain turned off", which is an unfortunate statement to have to make. There's no fail state, no way to be punished or to make a decision that can lead to any form of punishment. You can't even lose progress in longer stretches of vertical platforming because there are shortcuts to the bottom every layer up.I'm not asking for tedium, but even Mario Odyssey, a game that (at times) just hands you a decent amount of your moons for free in the name of accessibility, still offers entirely optional venues for sometimes extremely challenging platforming. I don't think this is a particularly difficult design choice to at least keep in mind, but what Tinykin offers in the ways of intriguing challenge is entirely zero. I understand that challenge isn't the point of every game, games are made to be fun, but it's the extreme lack of stimulation I felt while engaging with the content that bogged down an otherwise great experience.I still highly recommend the game in spite of this if you have a few hours to burn and find yourself even remotely interested. It's short and I do believe it deserves full support, but I just found it lacking. I hope they continue to make games as they clearly have an incredible vision for this type of thing.

_childDocuments_.review: 13h 3/10 1  made some very nice video's with all the collectibles with time stamps and also mentions the hidden pollen, which are most likely the ones you're missing.  No No, at any point you can go back to each level and find the collectibles No No No No No No difficulty option NoI had such high hopes for this game.... and I'm still BLOWN AWAY!!! I fell in love with tinykin in the first 20 minutes of the game and that feeling got stronger and stronger. What an amazing game, I loved the looks, the feeling, the stories! Each level felt overwhelming at first, but so so amazing and they aren't that big when you understand the layout and open up a lot of shortcuts. And that last level.... that was such an amazing theme... but wait, let me stop here and first tell you more about the game. UPDATE: They have added information of the tinykin you found in each level on the status screen, which is a very welcome addition and makes this game just easier for achievement hunters, now you know where to search for those last few pesky tinykin. I loved loved loved Tinykin...did I already told you that I love Tinykin? And that ending... it leaves the door open for a second installment and I'm all in! Please "Splashteam" make a second installment <3

_childDocuments_.review: I'm shocked at the small review count for this game, but not even remotely surprised at the 98% positive rating. This game is incredibly good.Tinykin is a 3D Collect-a-Thon with two gimmicks: 1) you're a tiny person in an ordinary household and 2) there's a bunch of little bugs scattered in every level that will do your bidding when you find them. These bugs have abilities depending on their color-- some can climb on top of one another to build a ladder for you, some will group up to carry around objects that are way to heavy for you, etc. This encourages you to explore the first sub-region of a level pretty thoroughly before you move on to the next one (e.g. you might need a 20-bug ladder in order to reach the next area). This keeps you from zooming through levels and rushing to the end. That might sound inconvenient, but it's an idea that perfectly suits this game because you'll find that slowing down is the best way to play. There's tons of insect npcs with really funny dialogue, and the world is really fun to look at and think about. Once you have completed the whole level and are just cleaning up some collectibles, you'll find it much easier to zoom around-- the movement is fluid, and there's even an optional time trial in every level to highlight this. I can comfortably say that Tinykin is one of my favorite 3D Collect-a-Thons of all time. It's also, surprisingly, somewhat obscure-- so please check it out and tell a friend about it.

_childDocuments_.review: Tinykin is one of those games that you start playing and have to force yourself to stop because you're having too much fun and don't want to end it all too quickly. I suggest you stop reading right now and go buy it, but if you're interested in knowing more about it, go on.This is a puzzle 3D platformer collectathon. The game wears its influences on its sleeve. It's clearly patterned after other games, but it doesn't pretend otherwise, and is its expert execution that makes it great. Both of its most obvious influences are Pikmin and Super Mario 64, both Nintendo games that have never seen a PC release, so it's great that we finally have something to compensate for their absence in this platform. That being said, this game isn't content with just aping those titles and comes up with its own formula.The main mechanic borrowed from Pikim is the title characters themselves: the tinykin. These are small creatures that you encounter as you progress through the game, color-coded according to their respective ability, who follow you around and help you achieve your goals. Some of them allow you to push or carry heavy objects, others allow you to create platforms to cross, others can destroy obstacles and so on. Puzzles are generally solved by finding an objective and figuring out how to reach that goal with the use of your available tinykin.From Super Mario 64 this game borrows its level design and sense of exploration. Levels are large and open without feeling overwhelming or labyrinthine. They are expertly designed to let you see just enough without making it obvious at first how you're going to reach all those interesting places and just what you might find in them. As you progress through each level you get to see areas you've visited from different angles and realize you might have missed something, which encourages to revisit those places. I'm a sucker for games that reward exploration, and this one is fantastic in that regard.Each level has a main objective (usually divided in parts) you need to complete to advance and a few sidequests you can discover and do if you choose. There's no combat and character progression is minimal (you only really upgrade one ability), but sidequests allow you to grab collectibles, which gradually help you make sense of the world and its story. They are also fun to do, so there's really no reason to avoid them. There are, of course, a bunch of achievements to do as well, tied to the story, collectibles and a few specific actions you need to do.The best way to describe this game is just pure, undiluted fun. Challenge isn't high, but movement is fast, dialogue is funny and the visuals are beautiful. While I did encounter a few frame dips a couple of times generally the game runs great and it'll take you between 8-9 hours to complete if you do all the sidequests and hunt for achievements, which is a lot of bang for your buck.I wholly recommend this game and I'm looking forward to a potential sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: With these cryptic sentence blocks, the puzzle platformer Tinykin welcomes you and gives the starting signal for an insanely sweet adventure.While narrative has never really been a focus in a platformer, Tinykin has a premise that is interesting enough to get players invested right away. When they take on the role of Milodane, an explorer who comes to earth in search of discoveries, things take a eerie turn when there are no humans left and time hasn't passed since 1991, but the feeling that someone or something is watching his every move remains.To get home, with the help of the funny creatures known as Tinykin and other colorful characters, you'll have to build a special machine in a sprawling ant-sized metropolis full of bugs and other insects to make things even more fun.As if this wasn't strange enough, the friendly Ridmi – a strange, white-bearded creature that appears out of nowhere – offers you his help and explains the simple of the game in a short tutorial. Thus, you'll jump over gigantic records, float through the air for a short time thanks to your bubble backpack, and get to know your first little helpers – the droll Tinykin.These lively henchmen all have special abilities that you can take advantage of during your adventure. For example, purple Tinykins are extremely strong and can combine forces to move heavy objects or transport them around to open up new paths, while green Tinykins can stack on top of each other and serve as useful ladders. Blue gnomes are excellent conductors of electricity, red bombers blow up obstacles, and yellow acrobats quickly build a staircase out of nothing to reach unimagined heights with ease.Of course, not all types of Tinykins are available to you at the beginning. However, in the course of your adventure, you'll gradually meet new ones, so your gaming experience will always be motivating, and each new level will bring a breath of fresh air into the game. The music also underlines the whole experience. The melodies in every part of the house never become an annoyance, and the various tunes fit the ambience of the area Milo is currently in.Nevertheless, the game takes you firmly by the hand at all times and literally "asks" you to use the required Tinykins in explicit places. In addition, all objects that can be interacted with flash in the respective color of the needed Tinykins, so you don't have to experiment wildly to finally make progress. However, even though the objects literally jump out at you, you still need the required number of Tinykins to solve the task or puzzle. For example, a door will only open when enough purple helpers join forces.If you are still lacking energetic support, you may have to take a different path first. This makes the levels a bit more complex and extensive, but with a bit of patience and perseverance you will inevitably reach your goal. This also forces you to remember the exact path you took because if you can't solve a puzzle, you should know later on where you left off. Furthermore, collected Tinykins are only available in the level in which you collected them – simply taking a whole motley crew with you to the next doesn't work.Your main task will be to restore your aircraft, which has been damaged, so that you can leave this strange place. For this, however, you'll need some objects that are hidden in the different rooms of the house. You'll travel through the fragrant kitchen, the untidy children's room or the foaming bathroom and complete various tasks and solve one or the other puzzle.The Chrysal workshop is your base, from which all future operations start. Here you return the found objects from the levels and start new missions to other rooms. Unfortunately, there is no quick travel function in Tinykin, so if you want to restart a level, to find all the pollen or to finish optional missions, you'll have to take the sometimes tedious path that often leads you back to the workshop – fortunately, a smooth soap board is already at your disposal at the beginning, with which you can slide through the levels quite quickly.In the varied levels, you'll find countless details and lovely cuteness that will undoubtedly enhance your entertaining adventure. The creative level design is really impressive and offers plenty of space for extensive explorations through the insects' cities inside the house. Everywhere you can uncover exciting secrets, discover hidden passages and solve puzzling tasks.You'll also encounter chatty cockroaches, buzzing dragonflies and other creepy-crawlies everywhere, which will not only make you smile with humorous pop culture references, but also have optional missions up their sleeves.For example, in each level, you can find a certain amount of golden pollen, which your friend Sikaru will use to brew delicious concoctions and also reward you with an extra bubble to float in. Thus, meticulous treasure hunters – in this case, eager pollen hunters – will sooner or later have advantages in fun exploring the exciting environments, as each new bubble will allow you to travel longer distances and thus reach new areas.With the help of a striking overview via spyglass you can see new and undiscovered missions at any time. If you want to collect every pollen, successfully complete all the main missions and finish all the side quests, you'll certainly be busy for around ten hours plus.Especially the concise 2D representations of the protagonists, who otherwise cavort in a three-dimensional world, are a nice eye-catcher. In addition, the positively playful melodies will surely animate you to sway along happily once in a while, and thus ensure a good mood.At first glance, Tinykin may seem overwhelming with its various mechanics and collectibles to find, but somehow the game keeps you moving at a steady, yet entertaining pace. As a bare minimum, you'll still have at least six hours of fun trying to get Milo home. However, opt. to complete in full, and you'll be able to extend the total game time by a few hours, or more, of satisfaction by solving increasingly difficult puzzles. And although it doesn't necessarily have that strategic component of Pikmin, Tinykin makes the most of its interpretation of the genre, while adding its own adorable mascots for one of the best 3D platformers of recent years, especially on Gamepass. This is hands down my personal GOTY 2022 and childhood dream wrapped in a superb collect-a-thon platforming experience.

_childDocuments_.review: The core loop is you go to a room, collect some Tinykin to help you solve a number of puzzles (move a thing, collect a thing, retrieve a thing, etc.) and eventually you collect a object that goes towards the game's primary goal and return to the centre of operations.  Each room is a platforming puzzle that as you go through it you'll unlock shortcuts to make it easier to move around, as well as having to take advantage of each kind of Tinykin.  As far as I got, each room introduced a new kind of Tinykin that would help you in a unique way: the first Tinykin and pick up or push heavy objects, the second can be thrown to destroy breakable objects, and the third stack to create an impromptu ladder, etc. It is quite like Pikmin, but it's been a long time since I played that so I can't get into the details.  If you liked Pikmin you'll enjoy Tinykin.It's got a very Cartoon Network feel with flat characters drawn in 3D spaces and a has nostalgic quality to it because of this.  The cutscenes are very cute as well.  This also goes for the sounds, it's very late 90s cartoony.Controls are intuitive, you get a double jump/glide right away, and a soap-based hoverboard equivalent plus things to climb up and slide down, but most of the movement is just running and jumping.While I think it's fun enough to finish I don't really see any replay value except for if you want to 100% it.

_childDocuments_.review: A Hat in Time gained a reputation for being a great alternative to 3D Mario. It certainly had solid writing, characters, and unique scenarios, but it wasn’t a good platformer. With its extremely restrictive moveset, basic platforming challenges, and collectables that quickly lost their purpose, it was more akin to an amateur’s first stab at the genre.Tinykin is essentially a weaker version of that title. Somehow, it’s more rudimentary while also lacking most of A Hat in Time’s redeeming qualities.Every single mechanic in Tinykin can be traced back to a better title. The game’s namesake are the most obvious example, functioning as Pikmin that don’t require babysitting. This is fine for a platformer, but of the five types of Tinykin, only the green variety enhances the platforming in any way. The rest are used for puzzles that essentially solve themselves.The core moveset is a lot shallower than an open-zone 3D platformer has any right to be. Take the jumping. Milodane barely has any hang time, so he drops like a rock after peak jump height. It really doesn’t pair well with his ability to glide around like Bunny Mario. The soapbar is decent, but there’s so little to master outside of the time trials. At the time of writing this, I haven’t played Tony Hawk’s Pro Skater or Jet Set Radio, the clearest inspirations for the soapbar’s physics, but it doesn’t take a pro to see how much more effort those older classics put into their movement systems.The more I played Tinykin, the more I wondered what the point of it all was. The hub and spoke level design is neat at first glance, but the theming is just for show. Take away the wallpaper and each level plays exactly the same, even down to the number of side quests available in each one. The numerous collectables do an adequate job making the player feel like they accomplished something, but why bother collecting everything when there’s no system to help players find those last few collectibles you’re missing? The least it could do is be more friendly to completionists than Super Mario Sunshine.Between all of that is the most uninspired platforming I’ve seen in a long time. Incredibly simple jumps and sparse use of hazards that barely punish the player to begin with. Calling it a B-grade platformer would be an insult to non-Mario platformers that actually bothered to engage the player like Banjo-Kazooie, Sonic Adventure, or Pac-Man World 2. Even A Hat in Time’s weakest challenges were more involved than this.The story is whatever. I think it would have been more interesting if there were only a few characters that needed to learn the house’s inner workings rather than dozens of NPCs spelling out everything or telling bad jokes. Not much else to say really.I’m willing to bet everyone reading this grew up playing at least one 3D platformer that delivered an unparalleled feeling of wonder. Given all the advancements in technology and game design, I think it’s fair to expect modern representatives of the genre to recapture that excitement. If Tinykin accomplished that for you, then please ignore my whining and be happy! I’m not here to upset readers. However, I’m not going to apologize for being honest with myself. In a world where 3D platformers are unpopular among indie and AAA studios, I cannot help but be disappointed with Tinykin’s mundanity.

_childDocuments_.review: Update: Comments were made on my review by a certain developer who shall remain unnamed that were rather rude and chlidish sounding. They either clearly agreed with this sentiment or where told off by a fellow dev on the project as the comments are now deleted. I'll take the deletes as an admission of guilt, or at least being somewhat self aware of the negative look and let bygones be bygones, but I'm leaving my comments below and this here for context regardless. I'm not one to endorse any bullying or witch hunting but that wasn't cool.Not a No that I enjoy handing out, but I think this game is getting too much praise for what it is. It's a cute fun romp through some neat levels, but the entire experience is shallow as a water drop on pavement. Most of the challenges and problems presented are simply resolved by walking around and finding more tinykin, or just walking from one end of the room to another. Problems solve themselves as there is only ever one solution, with no room for player creativity, ingenuity, or expression, short of the ladder tinykin. It's a shame that the ladder tinykin rear their head, because it shows that the game is NEARLY able to let the player do something creative, but never steps further than that. If you're looking for something akin to a walking simulator, then you might find fun here, but the game seems almost like a prank on anyone who wanted to actually play a game, rubbing the scent of Pikmin in our face and then ripping it away once you know what's happening. Add on laughable 100% achievements that are built on random useless tinykin being hidden around every corner, and the game just feels like a slap to the face.This really just feels like someone played Pikmin and Chibi-Robo and completely missed the point beyond a surface level """charm""". Pikmin was enjoyable and slightly challenging due to a (rather generous) time limit, on top of very alien creatures that kept you guessing how things worked, despite the familiar earth setting. You needed to protect your Pikmin and grow more of them, mistakes causing you possible days, making you care much more about the carrot things. The lack of any real danger, threat, or failure state means I often didn't even keep track of how many tinykin I had. Additionally, the roles of the pikmin make an infinite amount more sense and are much more interesting. Why can only the pink tinykin pick things up? There's a reason Pikmin didn't do that, because the three colors had multiple roles, thus reducing an amount of bloat that would otherwise be caused by needing a new Pikmin for every role, like tinykin does. As such, the tinykin end up feeling much more like a set of tools that have limited uses. I don't know how you expect me to care about them when I'm throwing them at the wall to blow them to gibs, but they're not willing to carry a bit of mail.Similarly, Chibi-Robo thrived off the battery limitation being a natural gate keeper, encouraging you to play the role of a cleaning robot to earn money and upgrades, pushing you towards more enjoyable platforming that opens up with new tools and your actions causing changes in the house and with other characters. The actions you were forced to take put you in the mindset of Chibi, building a personal bond with the house and all inside. Tinykin feels more like I'm just playing a GMod map, noclipping around only sometimes being stopped by needing to press E on a nearby object. Not only am I not being challenged in any capacity, but I feel that my input is meaningless as both a player and as the character. Nothing I do couldn't be done by a bug if it weren't for an arbitrary usage of tinykin.The story is the last strike against the game. You've filled the game with so many individual bugs that all have their own dialogue, stories that continue between rooms and quest that build on each other, and instead of making the story about them you decide to suddenly pull some horribly convoluted BS about time travel, multi-world stuff, and whatever the hell was up with the ending cutscene. I liked the bugs, I don't give a damn about the one other human character or his plight.I'll suggest this game if everything I've said doesn't bother you that much and you just want to walk around a cute world with little bug things that make funny faces, but even then not at 25 dollars. That's theft for the amount and quality of content on offer. Get it at least 50% off.

_childDocuments_.review: An exploration-focused 3D platformer with the core gameplay of , the level design of , and the mission structure of old-school collectathons; all tweaked to streamline and optimize the fun factor. Its launch day version needs a few minor bug fixes (namely bugged achievements), and it would benefit greatly from a post-game collectible tracker to avoid the tedium of finding those last few collectibles; but both are hopefully resolved in due time. With about an 8-hour playtime if you're a completionist--and just a bit less if you're not--it just might be the easiest recommendation I'll make this year.  is a 3D platformer about a human on the distant planet of Aegis named Milodane, who deduces that humanity actually originated on another planet and sets out to explore it. When his teleporter sends him to a suburban house on what we know as Earth, things aren't as they should be: his navigation equipment has been damaged, he's  smaller than he should be, the house is technologically stuck in 1991, there are no humans in sight, and the environment is populated by an array of intelligent insects. Among these is a species of hivemind-like creatures called tinykin that inexplicably see Milodane as their leader and respond to his every command, and he'll need to enlist their help to find a way home--and uncover what happened to humanity in the process. . Each of the game's six locations (corresponding to rooms in the house) hold a certain number of tinykin that you need to find and hatch from their eggs, and doing so will have them follow you around so you can throw them at things they can interact with. You can't take them with you into other rooms, but they will wait for you where you left them; so unlike the  strategy of grinding to build up an all-purpose army, you have to rely on the tinykin you're given in that room to accomplish your goals there. There are five types of tinykin total, each with their own special abilities: some are used to solve puzzles, others open new shortcuts or make it easier to traverse the environment, but all of them are valuable in the long run., focusing purely on "play at your own pace" exploration and platforming, and not on things like combat or sequences demanding fast reflexes. There are no enemies or boss battles to be found, but there are a handful of environmental hazards you'll need to watch out for, like water, fire, or simple gravity since fall damage does exist here. The challenge factor comes from the puzzle-platforming involved in main and side missions, though I wouldn't describe any of it as "hard". The only potential source of frustration might be in its "collectathon" side, namely in the hundreds of the collectible "pollen" to be found in every nook and cranny of the house. Collecting around 75% of the pollen in a room lets you buy a movement upgrade, but getting 100% of the pollen is just for unlocking achievements--though you could argue that going for 100% is the point of collectathons. If you choose to do this, know that you'll run into a problem that plagues many games in this genre: the frustration and monotony of running around to try and find those last few collectibles you somehow missed. , maybe as a post-game upgrade or a reward for finishing all the side missions so this issue can be avoided. They already have a function to switch to first-person view for a better look at your surroundings--complete with markers that highlight the location of mission ojectives--so hopefully it'll be expanded in a future update to also highlight missing pollen, and perhaps unhatched tinykin since there's an achievement for finding all of them as well.That's really the only frustration I had while playing, because . These are just a few examples I found while playing of little design decisions that went a surprisingly long way towards maintaining my enjoyment throughout:, but players who choose to avoid that last, tedious hunt for their final missing collectibles can still finish satisfied in a bit less time. The list of my favorite games growing up includes the likes of , , and several N64/Gamecube-era collectathons; and playing something that seamlessly combines elements from all three, while taking steps to remove most of the tedium from each one, makes for a game that does more than just feel nostalgic: it makes for a game that feels almost tailor-made for me. P.S. , showing missing progress even if you've done what's required. If this happens, revisit old locations so it re-checks your progress there and it should update properly.

_childDocuments_.review: I thought it's pikmin for steam. It's actually nothing like pikmin besides having cute little guys do slavery and commit sacrificial suicides for you. Tinykin is cute, has amazing graphic and sound design. The adaptive music makes my brain tingle.Movement is interactive and really satysfaing when you get the hang of it. Story and gameplay is goofy. _childDocuments_.review: Finally, someone brings a Nintendo formula to the PC.Tinykin is Pikmin.  I’ve seen people call it everything from Chibi Robo to Mario but this is absolutely a Pikmin clone. I’m always amazed at how few PC games are based on Nintendo Franchises, but Tinykin does this right and it’s fantastic. You explore a large house and meet various creatures that can accomplish different goals. At the same time, Tinykin is a bit short with only 6 levels. There are collectibles, and small challenges after the game, but it may only last about 10 hours. There’s not a lot of challenge either but it’s still quite fun. The gameplay is really solid, and the style is brilliant, every level is a different piece of the house, and the experience here is fantastic. Pick this up if you like Pikmin, or if you just want an interesting game where you explore a house. This should get a lot of attention and it’s the perfect game to play with your kids or just by yourself. I enjoyed this game so much that I bought a copy on Steam because I want more games like this. A small note, there does appear to be a problem with AMD graphics cards and this game. Not everyone is having it, but a friend of mine’s game is unplayable at this point, which is a shame because he also enjoyed the first level. Hopefully, they can fix that.

_childDocuments_.review: Tinykin is the game you get when somebody asks "What if somebody made a faster-paced Pikmin where you can explore in three dimensions?"The player is Milodane, a human space explorer who crash lands on a deserted human planet where he's insect-sized, in a house where the insects worship a long-vanished human named Ardwin. For no apparent reason, even tinier creatures called Tinykin have an irresistible urge to follow Milodane around and help him do stuff.All of this is a thinly-veiled plot device to allow the player to explore the different areas of the house, climbing onto and into the furniture, using the different Tinykins' abilities to manipulate the environment and incidentally help the insects while unlocking more areas of the house.Each area introduces a new type of Tinykin and coincidentally contains some obstacles that require their special ability to overcome.Tinykin streamlines the classic Pikmin gameplay in a number of ways:The different rooms are gorgeous and fun to explore, and each one has a cohesive theme. Additionally, there's plenty of optional stuff to find, collect, and achieve.I had a lot of fun, and the game ended before it had a chance to get old.If you like Pikmin, or if you like the  of Pikmin but the games themselves are too slow-paced for you, give Tinykin a try!
_childDocuments_.name: Tinykin

_childDocuments_.review: What. A. Game!I honestly can't remember when I spent so much contiguous time* on a single game and was utterly delighted by every** single moment. One of those games you really want to get through so you can see everything, while at the same time wish would never end.* Ignore my playtime; I didn't bother shutting the game down when busy with annoying but somewhat important distractions like work and sleep and eating.** As always, the bane of 3D platformers on a 2D screen is judging depth and the exact positions of things, and some jumpy bits got a bit frustrating at times.The level design and mechanics start off interesting, clever, and well thought out. And just keep getting get more interesting, extra cleverer, and better thoughter outerer.There aren't very many levels, but they are (especially the last few) exquisitely designed. The intro flyovers on the last few main levels took my breath away. And I was also immediately thinking "O.M.G. Where the **** am I even going to start with this one?!?". But in every case once you look about about a bit, gradually everything becomes clear, and shortcuts open up to make repeating things you've already done unnecessary to follow different paths.The dialogue of the characters is well written and sometimes pretty amusing. But there is a heck of a lot of it, to the point it becomes a bit distracting from the game's pace and mechanics. Fortunately, almost all of it is optional if you find it a bit weary-some. I did about half way through, but next play through I'll probably take my time a bit more and read it all.For maximum story effect, I recommend the approach I accidentally took. Don't look at any of the museum items until you have them all. And then look at them before getting into the ship at the end. Basically; I can't recommend highly enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Tinykin is truly a hidden gem! From the moment I started playing, I was hooked! The game not only looks wonderful visually with its colorful, cartoonish art style, but the gameplay is also just pure fun! Each level is packed with creativity and charm, making exploration a constant joy. There is also a fantastic sense of discovery, with every corner of the game hiding some collectibles or some other details or surprises to find. I had an absolute blast with every second I played it and would highly recommend it to anyone looking for a fun and unique platformer experience!

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible experience. Lovely art , game flow and level design. A dream come true for completionists. Not too easy to the point where you feel like you're getting a freebie but not overly difficult that it becomes a time sink to 100% the game. I loved every minute of this game and wish it went on longer. The storyline is surprisingly deeper than you would first expect when looking at gameplay. Only issue i had with this game is a little problem with achievement tracking which sorted itself out later on.
_childDocuments_.name: Tinykin

_childDocuments_.review: I got this in a humble bundle and didn't think much about it, there were other games in the bundle that I was more interested in. I was playing on my steam deck and was frustrated from dying multiple times a row in the game I was playing so I went to my library and sorted Great on Steam Deck by most positively rated and this one shot to the top, so I figured OK, I'll give it a shot. Oh. My. God. It is so good. I actually completed the full play-through (not all the achievements, but for me to complete a full play-through is practically unheard of) I was occasionally stumped, but the user base online with walkthroughs are good, and it's pretty easy to figure out where you need to go next. Which is not to say it's easy, it's challenging in a fun way. There are multiple ways to complete most of the puzzles. Failure does not put you back very far, which I appreciate. I could try things and fail and then immediately try a different idea without having to play through a bunch that I've already played through. After the first play session, I decided just to clear my schedule and play all weekend and complete the game. The storyline is complex emotionally if you want to engage with it, but you don't need to. The mystery unfolds elegantly and interestingly. The characters are cute and interesting and their problems are relatable. I think my favorite was the monster in the cabinet. The world-building is top-notch. The graphics are fun and well-built. I have a talent for getting stuck between polygons and not being able to move, and for once in a 3D open world, I did not get stuck once. I would highly recommend this game to anyone who likes cute puzzle games that makes you think and feel. It is not a long game, which I don't consider a downside. There are definitely opportunities for replay with various races and extra credit achievements. My only annoyance is that the Nintendo Switch version is practically impossible to find on a cartridge, and their stupid DRM system makes it so I only buy cartridges for my nephew, which is not a knock on the game but rather Nintendo :)
_childDocuments_.name: Tinykin

_childDocuments_.review: The level design is top notch. The writing and music are entertaining. The mechanics are solid, although you might eventually notice that you are doing the same sort of things in each level. It isn’t a precision platformer though. It’s exploration in an amusing bug-world. I only wish things were explained better in the ending. There’s a lot of well-written dialog in the game, and plot devices, why wasn’t this talent used to wrap it all up? But this feels like a quibble next to the 10-12 hours of a wonderful experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a sucker for platformer/collectathon games, and Tinykin certainly delivered. I thoroughly enjoyed playing it!The movement feels good, especially the "soapboard" to move around quickly. (think skateboard, but instead it's a bar of soap 😋) There are even races you can do with it, if you're into that.The art and sound are all very cute. And the soundtrack is nice too. I still have one of the songs stuck in my head. 😁Because of the genre, I wasn't expecting much in the way of story. But I was positively surprised, intrigued and even a little moved at the exposé at the end of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Tinykin

_childDocuments_.review: Playing a tiny character in a scaled up approximation of real world locations in one of my favourite types of environmental theming in games, and Tinykin just may be my new favourite. Journeying through all the rooms of the house as a two-inch explorer provides plenty of creative takes on settings that combine regular household objects into a selection of differently themed levels. It takes a smidge of inspiration from Pikmin in the form of the Tinykin, but recontextualises them in a 3D collectathon platformer space to marvellous results.Controls are smooth as butter, art direction is excellent, sound design is satisfying, and the music makes great use of dynamic tracks. Level design is not only visually brimming with creativity, but is laid out in such a way that it's satisfying to explore and get around and rarely leaves you searching high and low for one particular collectable for long. It's quite the feat for stages as huge as they are.Tinykin was one of the most enjoyable 3D platformers I've played in a while and I absolutely see myself coming back for repeat playthroughs in the future. It's quite a testament to its quality when the only gripe I can think of is that it's a little on the easy side.
_childDocuments_.name: Tinykin

_childDocuments_.review: This game was honestly just a ton of fun. A great mix of Pikmin and paper Mario without either of those two games' shortcomings. The exploration is fun, the world is cute, the dialog is funny, and somehow it manages to always feel rewarding. Never once did I feel like it was a hassle to collect every single thing in the game. That to me is a sign of a very good game. On top of that the challenge stuff is so frustrating but also super fun to do. Not normally into that stuff but I don't know how they pulled it off it was very fun in this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Tinykin

_childDocuments_.review: Tinykin is a 3D platformer that really manages to scratch that collectathon itch.You will go through six unique zones each packed with things to do in every corner and exploring them is just a delight, it's very satisfying to move around the room which is what you'll be doing most of the time. They really nailed the movement with the soapboard having you unlock rails you can grind on, as well as one of your abilities letting you stack your tinykin into a ladder allowing you more freedom of movement as you progress a level.It takes around 10 hours to 100% all achievements and it isn't very hard to do, I do wish there was an upgrade that helps your track missing objectives after you finish the game or something but I just made sure to fully explore everything before moving on so it wasn't a big deal.There's also extra challenge races that are not required for any of the achievements but are very fun to do and reward you with skins, and getting the platinum medals can be quite hard.(Note: there's a bug where to have some achievements unlock you need to revisit all levels, but it's barely an issue and the only one I encountered)Overall it's just a very solid game, highly recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing platformer than goes back to basics. It doesn't try to introduce any complicated new mechanics just refines ones that have existed for a long time resulting in this excellently crafted world. Pairing this with a beautifully told story and cute art style makes it into one if the best indie games this year if not one of the best games this year. 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: Ever since I first played Pikmin back in highschool I have always wondered what it would be like to have Pikmin style game play elements in an collect-a-thon 3D platformer. Tinykin scratches that itch perfectly. The movement system in the game is quick and snappy and really emphasizes your ability to chart your own path through the enviorment rather than the other way arround. Tinykin easily stands its own against its contemporaries and has an amazing sense of identity. Tinykin is a must play for all collect-a-thon fans out there.

_childDocuments_.review: Tinykin has no enemies, just a few obstacles which you easily overcome. Every time you advance within a new area, you gather a giant army of minuscule creatures, who can either carry heavy items, or build bridges or explode barriers. When you don't command them to do the above actions, they just follow you around aimlessly. Could have been used to push back hostile bugs (those shielded are everywhere!), help with boss fights (there's none) or I dunno - form walls for motion detected sequences (also non existent). Give me a damn challenge! :(The core play of Tinykin is checking all possible corners, ledges, hidden passages and multi level platforms. You never know what you might find - an objective item? a collectible pollen or a nice reference?However. Because nobody and nothing stops you from exploring or gathering story things, the play turns into a boring vacuum sucking activity and tedious search. Attention, memory! Have we checked behind those books? Did we bring that lost animal we spotted earlier? And what about those eggs we thought "oh we would collect them later...", where were they?

_childDocuments_.review: Polished, super cute 3D platformer with a satisfying gameplay loop.As a scientist from another planet, Milo wants to find out where humanity came from. For unknown reasons, his research makes him end up in a 1990s earth house, but shrunk to the size of a bug. He finds said house inhabited by lots of cute talking insects, but also by "tinykin", an even cuter species of tiny spherical creatures. Every tinykin species is very good at one task, for example, some are strong and can carry heavy objects, others can explode, and yet others can stack into ladders. For further unknown reasons, the tinykin really, really like Milo and follow him around, allowing him to use their help to get to otherwise unreachable places and solve problems.Milo sets out to explore the house and unlocks one room after another. He helps the insects with various problems and gets their help in return. When you first enter a new room, you have the liberty to go into any direction and tackle everything in whichever order you like. As you reach new places, you can release climbing and connecting ropes to allow you to later quickly return everywhere, often from a hub in the middle of the room. This makes it easy to move from task to task and also to climb to high spots to check the room for any missed pollen. This pollen is a collectible of which there are hundreds in every room. If you collect a certain amount, you can buy upgrades for Milo's flying suit, allowing him to float in the air for longer and longer times. I'm not sure whether you actually need these upgrades to finish the game, but they do help to reach every place.I had lots of fun playing this and cooing over all the cuteness (one favourite: a bunch of tinykin carrying an object together, with very determined faces and little shouts of "heh! hoh!"). The platforming difficulty was just right- motivating, not too easy, not too hard. I was shortly frustrated in two spots, but that's really nothing compared to the total playtime.

_childDocuments_.review: Pleasant collect-a-thon type game with great graphics, gameplay and soundtrack. The only fault is the game is very easy with minimal puzzle aspects, however it was such a pleasure to play that the lack of difficulty can be overlooked. This is the perfect game to play when you want to relax and turn your brain off for a bit.

_childDocuments_.review: Tinykin is a fantastic collectathon platformer, right up there with the likes of Banjo Kazooie, Spyro and Mario Odyssey. It makes good use of its "tiny character in a big world" idea with thoughtful level design and layouts that allow players to easily memorise their surroundings, and incorporate gameplay mechanics inspired by Pikmin, with its eponymous throwable minions, the Tinykin.The game follows Milo, a human inhabitant of a distant planet, who after learning his species didn't originate there, finds his way to Earth in the 90's. Once he arrives to investigate, we see that he's tiny compared to the humans on earth, and around the same size as insects. From here, he meets and communicates with insects, and learns about the mysterious Ardwin, who they revere as a god. From here, Milo encounters Pikmin-like creatures called Tinykin, each with different abilities and properties, and must aid the insect denizens of an abandoned home with the help of these new creatures, all while rebuilding a machine that can return him home. The game has the player travelling across 6 main areas within a regular human house, and finding a machine part in each. These areas will have their own unique mini-story to tell, and in order to get the machine parts, the player has to help the denizens of these areas with whatever troubles they're facing. There are also side-objectives that award the player some mysterious objects, belonging to a museum-keeper, and a whole ton of collectible nectar to find (collecting 900 per area will award Milo an extra bubble to glide with and allow him to reach areas he otherwise wouldn't). So right off the bat, there's a clear main objective, and side content for completionists and fans of collectathons to scour through. Milo can jump, climb ropes, skate on a bar of soap and grind on strings of silk, glide a short distance with his bubble, and throw Tinykin, which are used to solve a variety of puzzles and deal with various obstacles. Pink Tinykin carry objects and push obstacles out of the way, Reds explode on contact with any flammable or otherwise weak obstacles and destroy them, Greens stack on top of each other to give Milo a makeshift ladder to reach high places with, Blues conduct electricity from an outlet to a broken cable, and Yellows form a staircase for the Pinks to carry objects across. The game gets a lot of mileage out of each type of Tinykin, and they lend themselves very well to the exploration-based gameplay of collectathons. They hatch from eggs after being touched, and the more you have at your disposal, the more you can achieve in each area. The Tinykin you find in one area don't follow you to the next, likely to balance the game's difficulty and prevent players from trivialising the puzzles in later areas. The 6 areas, despite all taking place in the same house, are visually and functionally distinct from one another. The third area serves as the "water" area, since it takes place between a toilet room and a bathroom separated by a door, with one side's inhabitants being disturbed by the other's constant partying. And the 5th area is a kitchen with many sponges stacked on top of each other to give the illusion of a grassy field with rivers of water flowing between them, serving as the set-piece to a conflict between a well-meaning monarch and an uprising of disgruntled working-class ants. The way the developers refashioned every-day objects to create these differing insect societies with their own stories and problems to face is clever, and it's the sort of charm I've been missing since games like Clockwork Knight and Chi-bi Robo. While there are water and plant hazards that'll set Milo back to the last place he stood (in addition to fall damage that forces players to carefully consider where they explore), the game has a surprising lack of enemies to fight. Seriously, like an Icelandic man once said, there are no enemies. This is a neutral aspect, one that I'm neither for nor against, on its own, but it's clear the devs' focus was on the treasure-hunting and exploration. So in that regard, I'd say it was a smart call. And again, since the levels have various landmarks and points of reference, the treasure-hunting never devolves into finding a needle in a haystack, even if you have one piece of nectar missing. If you're looking for more of a challenge though, then the aptly-named Challenge Update and its content should suffice. This free update includes timed races across the 6 sprawling areas for the best time, with a medal from Bronze to Platinum being awarded depending on the player's time. They make great use of the areas, and give you a good reason to go back to them, as clearing each one will unlock new costumes for Milo to wear. While the platinum medals teter on the edge of ball-busting, they're still doable and fair enough to make the 100% completion experience worth it, and they made me put the soapboard to good use. The game's visuals are top-notch too, going for a toony impressionistic look. Surprisingly, Milo and all the NPC's in the game are 2D, similar to other indie 3D platformers like Demon Turf and Here Comes Niko! I didn't know what to make of this at first, this being my first foray into these types of games, but having played the game to full completion, I can safely say it doesn't detract from the gameplay one bit, as far as precision platforming goes. I initially played Tinykin on Xbox One via Gamepass, and since it never went on sale after my subscription expired, I got the Steam version. While it meant I couldn't continue from where I left off, it allowed me to play the game at an ideal 60fps, which was easily achievable even on my outdated hardware. I do wish there were a few more graphics options to adjust the draw distance and overall clarity, but the game still looks great as is. The sound design is nothing to scoff at, either. Each object Milo walks or lands on has a distinct, believable sound effect to make the game's world feel more lived-in, from scrunching sponges to the pings of steel cutlery. The game also features an up-beat, whimsical dynamic soundtrack, which shifts and changes depending on what part of an area you're in or how much progress has been made there. No expenses were spared, it seems, and the game has the overall polish you'd expect from a double-A or even triple-A game (ideally, anyway). Very impressive how much care, creativity and attentiveness went into the game, considering it was made by small indie studio Splashteam. My only real criticism is that the achievement for collecting all 6 glide-bubbles doesn't trigger unless you revisit each area. This really needs to be addressed or fixed somehow, as I didn't know what was going on until looking outside the game for answers. Other than that, the game is as close to a 10/10 as you can get, and in the 18 hours I spent doing everything, I was having a blast. One of my favourite games from last year, and easily a favourite among the many in my Steam library. Definitely get the game if you enjoy collectathon platformers, Pikmin-likes, or any games where a tiny bloke explores a human home. It's worth the full price, but it's an absolute steal on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked the world of It Takes Two this game is a must try.Otherwise just an adorable world to explore where you are tiny and the household things are big. _childDocuments_.review: This game is great if you are aren't a completionist, but tedious if you are. The main problem is that once you backtrack to an area you may get some pointers on side missions, but these are usually not hard to find either way. However trying to completely collect all pollen and tinykin is an awfully frustrating endeavor.you get no hints or rough area for where to search so it may mean you spend 9 complete scans of all your surroundings until you finally find that one pollen you are missing on a shoelace (climbable rope), or that one cluster of tinykin that just was just laying around on the side of the road. I even resorted to video guides for 2 of the levels and followed them around in 5 second intervals because it got too frustrating.Simple things like talking to an NPC and him telling you a rough area to search in, or the objective tracking goggles hinting at the location of collectibles once you found enough of them would have helped a lot but as it is now I regret 100%ing this game. It just wasn't fun.Even more frustrating was when I finally found all there is to find and due to a bug the achivements both ingame and in Steam didn't unlock. This is a bug that was known for years, while revisiting every location of the game seems to fix it, it just felt bad having to do this, it detracted from what little feeling of accomplishment there was.The story was, a little weird, leaves a bunch of things unanswered, some big mystery left pretty much unadressed. This is honestly fine and would make for interesting sequel plot.Speaking of a sequels, I do not recommend this game, but if it ever receives a sequel you should definitely check that out instead. This game was decent, but fell flat in the end.
_childDocuments_.name: Tinykin

_childDocuments_.review: This review is specially made for those who like to get all the achievements in games (minor spoilers ahead).Tinykin is an indie casual 3D platformer set in an oversized house with each level taking place in different parts of the house, each one with a special name and theme. The levels have simple puzzles that need to be solved by using the minions you can collect throughout the levels, each type with different abilities, but regardless of the puzzles the game is more about exploring the worlds and finding items to complete quests or gain artifacts.The story isn’t very developed during the game, having mostly just a few cutscenes at key moments, but the lore and culture of each species of insect that inhabits each level is unique. There are also a few other NPCs that give you instructions, requests or upgrades.The graphics are good and the 3D levels have lots of interesting details and objects, and some of them can be interacted with. The main character and other characters don’t have a 3D model, instead they are 2D figures, similar to paper mario, in a stylized and cartoony style. In general, the animations are well done and fluid, from simple movements to the different death animations.The level design also has a lot of depth and verticality, you have to explore the grounds as well as the top platforms located near the ceiling and glide in the air a lot.The music and sound effects are also fantastic. The songs change depending on what’s near you, the creatures sing and rejoice and overall the ambiance is very cheerful. Some platforms also have a different sound when you jump on them depending on the material they are made of, and that’s a very nice detail.Regarding gameplay, and as I have mentioned besides the puzzles there are a lot of items to find and collectibles to get, and if you want to 100% the game you’ll need to get everything. In each level I managed to get the essential items rather easily, but it’s very easy to miss a spot or interactable object and struggle to find the last collectibles you’re missing and they happened to be in most levels. After you complete the levels, there are a few races you can do to unlock cosmetics, and they are also fun, but very demanding, and if you’re trying to get the best medal, every move needs to be flawless.     43 Achievements. 10 hours, but I’ve also got some medals and some of the races. Easy. Medium. While the game is easy, getting every collectible requires persistence and a lot of attention so you don’t miss anything. No achievements are missable, but some can get bugged in the end and might require you to revisit every zone, including the “stairs” and “attic” to unlock. Tinykin a very fun to play indie 3D platformer with a lot of items to find and collect, in levels that are unique and beautifully designed. The music is also a joy to listen to and overall it offers a lot of content and things to do.

No less than half-price.Gameplay loop is not rewarding but other than that, what you see is what you get; a casual time waster.For this reason, I cannot give it a thumbs down especially given that I am not giving it a longer playtime.Maybe it gets better. I doubt it, but fair is fair.Platforming could be more enjoyable but again, the main appeal of the game is the puzzle-solving with your kins. _childDocuments_.review: I adore this game. It's beautiful, polished to a fine shine, each of the worlds feel brimming with things to explore. It also has one of the strongest first levels of any platformer I've ever played. So many little things in this game add up to an incredibly strong experience. For example, the soap-board that allows you to travel more quickly through each level, adds so much mobility to the game. Gliding around the levels is easy and joyful. That's just one example among many that create an excellent game. If it looks like your kind of game, pick it up even if it's not on sale. Just a joy.
_childDocuments_.name: Tinykin

_childDocuments_.review: A fun cutesy little game. I did 100% it and I would say that took me maybe around 8 hours or a little less to do so. There were some issues with achievement progress not counting but that was cleared up by entering and exiting the levels. Another weird thing about the achievements is that it hides info on what are some rather basic achievements that you may not necessarily run into while playing, such as get eaten by a plant. It has them as hidden in game and on the Steam Achievements page so with those either you stumble into them at some point while playing or you have to look them up at the end to figure out what you need to do to get those last few hidden ones even though you 100 percented every room.I definitely give this game a recommend and I hope to see some more Tinykin content or sequels in the future.

_childDocuments_.name: Tinykin

_childDocuments_.review: Good music, cute and whimsical art. But a very bland game, just a large collection minigame.Has a few obnoxious gameplay bits, including the inability to choose what type of Tinykin to use, general camera wonkiness while aiming, and soap bar being a little too unpredictable.Would have loved to see some actual puzzles, or the ability to use tinykin for more than just their singular use, very frustrating to not have enough pink ones just because you can't recall ones that are holding something on the other side of the map.I guess I was hoping for something more Pikminesque and got a cute but bland minigame.
_childDocuments_.name: Tinykin

_childDocuments_.review: This was a super fun collectathon! The movement and transition on and off of the soapboard felt very smooth. I've been able to find most of the collectibles just by exploring but there are some levels that I'm only missing a few items. The only thing I think would make this game a bit more enjoyable (as a completionist, not for everyone) would be an option to enable a Tinykin and pollen tracker once you finish the story.
_childDocuments_.name: Tinykin

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful game! The setting feels clearly inspired by Pikmin, but the game itself is very different. Tinykin is a collectathon platformer, with some solid movement mechanics conducive to exploration. Your main goal is to go around helping people in these different bug societies, and gathering parts towards the game's main objective. The Tinykin themselves are basically items to help you explore, there's no fighting system and they aren't at risk of dying.The thing I liked most about Tinykin was the level design. There is a ton of creativity put into the design of the world, and there's a lot in it to admire in the small details and in the bigger picture of each area and how they fit together in the game's world as a whole. The NPCs are well written, with a lot of work put into fleshing out their different societies and how they all interact.I had an excellent time finding all the secrets this game had to reveal, searching every nook and cranny to find all the collectibles, and completing all the sub-missions to achieve each level's major goal. It took me 19 hours to beat 100%, though a lot of that time went into these unlockable race challenges. Note: If you 100% it and achievements are glitched, re-visiting each of the game's areas in the same gameplay session should fix it, and won't take too long.
_childDocuments_.name: Tinykin

_childDocuments_.review: Have you ever played a game that is just pure joy? All around fantastic work by the team, from gameplay/movement and level design to audio/music and art/cinematic, it was a magical ride from beginning to end. I was already in love with the demo and this game delivers even more than I could hope for. Beside being an absolute blast for completionist - what a delightful and adorable game it is!
_childDocuments_.name: Tinykin

_childDocuments_.review: When I played the demo I knew immediately that it was worthy of a day one purchase. I fell in love with this game instantly and it made me remember why I enjoy 3d platformers so much. This game feels like pikmin but it uses its inspiration for puzzle solving mixed with exploration and is not a real time strategy game. One thing that Tinykin focuses on that makes it stand out from other platformers  that it focuses on vertical exploration combined with horizonal though the former being the main focus, as most 3d platformer tend to be an obstacle course design instead this game has a sandbox style of 3d platforming gameplay to it(similar to mario 64 in a way).It has goodies to collect and that makes exploring make addictive and I consider this to be one of the greatest indie 3d platformers I have ever played. Its art style and animation suits the game's setting as well. My minor complaint is collecting all the pollen which I wish they had a system similar to demon turf where you press L3 button to show an arrow  where you are missing the pollens, nevertheless this game is really fun and makes me glad there are creators that want to make 3d platformers while still standing out from other games in the 3d platforming genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Tinykin

_childDocuments_.review: Easily one of the best collectathon platformers on Steam, an incredibly polished and charming game akin to Hat in Time.Always loved the theme of being ant-sized in a human sized world, and Tinykin nails it perfectly. All the small details not only fit their respective rooms, but create a very fun playground. Hidden collectables under a crease in the rug, a wedge of cheese used as a ramp in the kitchen, smart usage of everyday items that always gave me a laugh when I noticed them.Speaking of laughs, this game is FILLED with funny characters with even funnier names. All sorts of references to realworld and videogame names are crammed into almost everything. I'd say thenegative point I have with this game is the painfully annoying 100% completion experience.Most levels have upwards of 1200 pollen (the primary collectable), as you zip-zoom around the levels you're bound to miss some. Not the end of the world, but coming back later to find the 3 pollen you missed in an enormous level with loads of hidden nooks and nothing to help you? Not fun.This could easily be fixed if they implemented something like the recent Spyro remake has; a button that gives you a ping to send you searching in the right direction.Overall a great experience, especially if you can get it on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Tinykin

_childDocuments_.review: Went in expecting Pikmin and ended up with an average 3d platformer with a garnish of Pikmin - a veneer, really. Three hours in, I didn't feel like I was exploring and building an army of minions naturally. Rather, the hand-holding between levels and the lack of meaningful upgrades meant I just couldn't finish this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Tinykin

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely adore this game. It gave me serious feelings of childhood nostalgia. I love the setting. Your about as big as an ant and you get to explore a normal sized house that's filled with life. Every room has a very distinct feeling to it. The bugs have very charming designs and the amount of references is insane. Gameplaywise you might think: "Oh its Pikmin" but its more of a puzzle-platformer collectathon. The movement feels smooth and the "puzzles" aren't overly tedious. Didn't put a lot of time into the races but the ones i did felt fairly challenging. Storywise the game is fine. Nothing new but still very wholesome with a nice "plottwist". Overall 9/10 wish it had more content (even though i know it has the perfect length).

Though I did not enjoy the story or characters involved until the very end. The gameplay feels super smooth and nice to control. Though it is weird that the player character is always facing towards the camera and never faces away. I was able to ignore it after a while but at first it really threw me off. I also didn't enjoy the main character's design. I think it's purely a me issue, but to me the main character looks like one of those rich snobby bully characters you'd see in a cartoon, rather than a smart scientist hero.But again overall the game is great. I would have enjoyed some more designs for the bug characters since those were great!

_childDocuments_.review: Played the whole game on Steam Deck with proton-ge, no crashes or anything like that.  Generally ran well on high settings, with some minor (but not unplayable) slowdown in the last few big areas. This game is absolutely wonderful. On the shorter end of things, took me about 7 hours for a not-quite-completionist playthrough, but they were 7 great hours. There's so much love and care put into this game. Artstyle is super charming, with these nice dry brush textures and these lived-in settings. If you like the micro-scale of games like Pikmin and Chibi-Robo, you'll be absolutely thrilled with Tinykin's rich and varied environments. Not a difficult game but it's not a boring one either, there's tons of charm and the levels are fun to bop around in. Seems like everywhere you turn there's something to discover. Buy it. An absolutely top shelf indie game. My favorite non-Elden-Ring game of 2022.
