_childDocuments_.review: Fuse Slay the Spire with a chain-3 game, and you have Demon’s Mirror.Key note. Chain-3, not Match-3. With Match-3, you swap the position of board symbols to create a 3, 4 or 5 block. With Chain-3, you drag a line through as many symbols of the same kind as you can, so long as they are adjacent, orthogonally or diagonally. Set aside the chain-3 board temporarily, and Demon’s Mirror follows the Slay-a-like formula closely. # Begin with a starter deck and a starter artefact / trinket unique to a character, which strongly influences what they are better at# Choose your path on a branching map of nodes with battles, Elite battles, rest sites, shops, events and deck manipulation sites# Progress through multiple acts, each act ending in a boss fight# Battles are a turn-based card-playing tightrope of trying to deal damage whilst avoiding taking damage, and wins result in card and coin rewards# During a run, you add, remove and upgrade cards, gain permanent passively run-changing trinkets and single-use scrollsThen what it does differently, which also changes all the card-based play, is give you a 6x6 board of gems, representing attack, defence, a form of power-up and a form of limit-break currency, 4 total. You have the 3 energy points, same as Slay, initially, but you split them between playing cards or creating chains. Each battle turn then presents a tactical dilemma, what is the best combination of cards and chains?Slay has a magical quality of a near frictionless sequence of card-select, drag to target, release, outcome, with immediate feedback and that little dopamine hit that accompanies it. Demon’s Mirror has that, 100%. Everything executes slickly and feels goldilocks, just right. Many turns give you a wonderful little tactical dilemma. On any given turn, you may have choices like these:# Play 2-3 chains but no cards# Play 3 or more cards, but no chains# Split your energy between chains and cardsWhich is the best will also change based on how you can change the board state *before* chaining, through cards – often 0 cost – that destroy, convert or move gems around. You have a LOT of scope for setting up over several turns for a huge attack, for example, by removing other types of gems from the board to create a long chain of attack gems, applying a vulnerable debuff to enemies, and a chain buff to yourself.Many cards can manipulate the board state, and it appears – initially – viable to really lean in to either a card-heavy or a board-heavy deck. The cards and the board interact with each other – a lot – requiring careful thought both in battle and in the overall deck building. Take the learning curve of any deckbuilder – it can be tough initially as you try and figure out what the heck makes a viable deck. This has that challenge AND then the added complexity of the chain-3 side. This is not necessarily a bad thing, but I could imagine that non-veterans of both genres might find the learning pretty harsh initially.Writing this only 3-4 run attempts in, I can say little just yet. There *are* things to unlock, including the core characters and buffs and debuffs that can be applied to an entire run to change the challenge level.
_childDocuments_.name: Demon's Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: One of a kind roguelike deckbuilder.It combines a connect-3 board with deckbuilding. Each turn you have a number of energy, and you spend that energy either on using your cards, or on chaining on the board. Rest follows the typical Slay The Spire formula. Move through the map with battles, random events, deck management and campsites.. 3 classes which have different mechanics. Enemies telegraph their turn, which goes after yours. And keeping your deck thin. It's quite difficult though, even at 0 ascension, so you'll have to use your brain when making your build.
_childDocuments_.name: Demon's Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: The deckbuilder genre is heavily saturated and afraid to innovate from its core formula. This game is fun, but I don't think the tile-matching is enough to overcome what is essentially the exact same problem-solving set in StS.The tile matching is a fun gimmick but the game focuses too much on the admittedly boring cards at the beginning of each run (pay 1 mana gain 4 shield, pay 1 mana deal 4 dmg etc.) and not enough on the games core feature of tile-matching. And I don't think a game where every run all I'm doing is paying 2 mana for 12 shield until I get some cool combos is something I want to ante up for the umpteenth time.
_childDocuments_.name: Demon's Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: Solid card battler rougelike with chain-3 mechanic. The Slay the Spire inspiration is obvious, but the inclusion of the chain-3 grid really adds to the decision making and puzzling out each turn. The game can be quite challenging, and some cards and enemies could probably do with a few small tweaks, but the vast majority of the content and core gameplay is very solid and exceptionally polished. I also want to say that the music has been excellent and card art is fantastic, especially ones with expressions on them; I've laughed at quite a few of them!If you're a fan of Slay the Spire or similar deckbuilders and the chain-3 mechanic intrigues you, this is a solid recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Demon's Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: A superb game that adds a new "gimmick" to the deck builder roguelite in the way of the match 3 board.Careful use of both your deck and the tile board are required in order to progress. The game takes a few runs to get into (I lost my first 3) but offers a good but beatable challenge rather than spamming a select few cards. The tile board also has enemy tiles that if left alone can damage you, curse you, heal the enemy or give them block... as well as a few other tricks on the bosses.Visibly it's pretty and each character feels different thanks to the unique bonuses each receive. Likewise, even the enemies feel somewhat unique with a number of them having special attributes or weaknesses. There's a lot of hidden control to these fights in using the weaknesses and traits against them. One elite does massive damage but is stunned by gaining enough of a specific symbol on the board, the barbed trait deals damage back to you when you attack them with cards but not with tile-chaining, and one enemy will change it's action based on your plays... and that's just a few, and doesn't even talk about bosses. While there are certainly a number of 'regular' mobs, there's still plenty of times you need to pay attention, adapt and actually think about your actions.It also has positive modifiers as well as negative, allowing you to fine-tune the difficulty to your liking.The biggest negative is that there's not a lot to unlock, and I felt I didn't get anything rewarded to me when beating the final boss and watching the credits roll. It would be great if each character had one unique unlock for that... but this is a SUPER minor negative.I'd love to see more YouTubers/streamers cover this game, as I truly think it stands out in the genre and I'd love to see them expand it further.
_childDocuments_.name: Demon's Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: Quite interesting mix of chain-3/match-3 with roguelike deckbuilder. Sharing the same pool of energy, you have to be playing cards and chaining tiles, being the most interesting part of the game deciding which one is more convenient to use and when. The deckbuilding mechanics are pretty default and not that engaging, but you have a bunch of new extra stats to make some use of the more unique part of the game, which I think is a great idea, because it is the more interesting part here.You count with 3 different playable characters so far, each one with different deck and stats, and overall there is a nice variety of different synergies you can build.Be aware though, runs can be pretty long (could take 3 hours depending on your build), so be ready for a long journey.Overall, a pretty solid roguelike deckbuilder 8/10. If you are curious here you have some gameplay
_childDocuments_.name: Demon's Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic and surprising mish-mash of genres. If you're a Slay the Spire fan, this is your next obsession. Three completely unique characters complement a varied and unique gameplay system. The match-3 is fantastically integrated. I only wish that there were more ways for the match-3 to affect the cards. I've had a great time with Demon's Mirror.
_childDocuments_.name: Demon's Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, now I feel bad I called out the devs for missing VSync option, the game is definitely good (was impressed last night it's pretty smooth on Steam Deck), so I am just gonna turn this review into positive, cause they responded promised to add VSync soon.Also, Match3, that's not a predatory mobile game with billion micro transactions AND it's a rogue like game for just 20 bucks? The world is slowly healing.
_childDocuments_.name: Demon's Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: A tighter, harder, and more mentally demanding Slay the Spire clone whose big gimmick feature is a match 3 taking up half the screen that can be used with your energy instead of playing cards to gain damage, block, build meter, unlock character abilities, etc. and honestly the blend of the two seems JUST barely not fluid but thats a hard thing to judge - the two elements definitely do not detract from one another.
_childDocuments_.name: Demon's Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: A thumbs up for the game and a sprinkle of #Ad I guess :P A well deserved one though, for an amazing channel/communityBeen waiting to try Demon's Mirror since I saw it played on Esty8nine's channel some time ago, it has been on my wishlist for quite a long time and it turned out to be an amazing game! A thumbs up 100%. If you are reading this please try the demo, you will get a good idea about the game. It is a little short in my opinion. You do not get to see how a fully built deck functions, and it is really satisfying towards the end of the run when your deck really scales. A really solid game!
_childDocuments_.name: Demon's Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: I've done several runs now. 2 with all the characters at least, Where the dragon seemed like the character I synergized the most with, being that you get free cards to play when you chain anything, as long as you keep your card requirement low. (Already incentive not to use higher energy cards, VERY BAD, DOESN'T Incentivize experimentation.)The furthest I've gotten is the third world. and I was royally screwed in my first encounter because there were two enemies that wanted to attack for an upwards of about 40 damage and that's literally impossible to block unless you have insane luck.I started getting to the point where if I had low HP and kept getting bad RNG on the board and cards, I'd just slog and end it early so I could start another run where I didn't make the mistake of picking up cool, but very niche cards that I'd never find a use for.The run where I made it to world 3 was one of my worse runs. but RNG kept giving me godlike chains and cards exactly when I needed them. it felt great until the run was over and I realized that this game isn't very skill based. you just get lucky, or you barely scrape by while trying to fight back against your terrible odds, and inevitably die to some BS in one battle because you stalled for too long.I see a lot of people comparing this to Slay the Spire... I wonder how true that really is because I never played it.>The mix of both worlds, Deck builder, and Chain 3 is very VERY well done. it feels good to get a big chain in the first world that just smashes enemies.>There are events that help you out on your journey, and there's a lot of variety. with shops, Treasure chests, upgrades for cards, removing cards, all to help customize the run on the fly.>Every enemy does it's own special thing to the Chain 3 board, there's a lot of different outcomes.>Each character has a unique playstyle that changes the way you play the game.>Characters are objectively worse than others. even though I played the Dragon the most it's probably the worst charatcer in the game.>If you have any cards that require 3 energy you won't use them period, by the time you can, you've already won the battle, and don't need it anymore because the threats are all dead.>Better cards require more energy and more often than not YOU DON'T GET MORE ENERGY TO COUNTER BALANCE THIS.>Most cards are too niche and require such a specific scenario that you're throwing your game if you grab them.>Some cards are so good that if you don't grab them you're throwing.>The game is boring when you're trying to min max and play effectively instead of for fun. (Burn bad cards, force less RNG.)>If you stall out a battle and try to be tactical, you get punished by buff stacking enemies. all enemies often have a means to infinity scale damage and YOU don't.>Some Elites tend to spam tiles onto your board and it makes getting big combos impossible. Setting up becomes tedious instead of tactical.>Trinkets do so little, honestly felt like half of them did nothing at all. And by the time you get one that would have synergized with something, you don't have the means to make it work.>Battling gives you so little in return, you'll get further avoiding all but the first 2 battles in your run with the same odds of winning or losing.>Some, if not most combat mechanics feel like BS. the lack of power scaling for your own character (like permanent upgrades for this run only.) don't exist. you're stuck with the hand that was dealt to you, no pun intended.>You have to get really lucky to have a good run. and you have to beat impossible odds to win.>The game isn't hard, it's unfair. Hades is hard, but fair. Spirit Fall is hard, but fair. Backpack Hero isn't Hard, but it's Fair all the same and can be made harder with challenges.>The game has a Challenge window, but good luck getting to the point where you unlock any of them.>I'm probably not even listing all the flaws for this game.The game has a Challenge window, among those is things that can make the game easier. but like I said before, it's all down to RNG so... I enabled all of them and died to my first Elite enemy. when I've killed 3 Elites in a row without those settings before.Might play a few more runs but honestly this game needs changes NOW.Want a fair game that won't make you feel like you're bad and it's your fault your bad? don't play this game.Want a game that's skillful and implementing strategy can get you a flawless? don't play this game.Masochist? play this game :)
_childDocuments_.name: Demon's Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome idea, very clunky and boring. It makes me irrationally angry that the developer had such a wonderful concept, but somehow managed to make it unfun to play. Costs 2 energy to do the match 3, but you only start with 3 energy? Why doesn't it just cost 1? Why is every single fight tedious and boring? At least the things blatantly copied from Slay the Spire are decent, but it's just not enough to save this game in it's current state. I really hope either this developer figures it out and makes it fun to play, or someone else takes the reigns and makes a fun match3/card game roguelike, because it's a great idea.
_childDocuments_.name: Demon's Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: Full disclosure, the developer of this game is a friend of mine. But that hasn't stopped me from trash talking or giving a bad opinion before.I think this is a really worthy Spire-like. It really gets the ontological side of things, little lore drops and a vague feeling of unease. The tile-matching component slots in surprisingly well and really changes the dynamic of your deck. Cards I would never consider taking in Spire I would take here in a heartbeat. Draw is less important, the tiles are everything. Everyone has a satisfying gimmick for how they interact with the board (and let's be honest, the axolotl is the best. Hours will pass before you realize that you've been chaining those conductor tiles). I'm currently working my way up the difficulty modifiers, but I'll write a full report when I'm done. At a first glance, this is definitely worth your time if you're a fan of rogue-likes.
_childDocuments_.name: Demon's Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: Let's start with the fact that I love Slay the Spire-like games, and I also enjoy a good Match 3 phone game. As you can tell from 5 seconds of video from the game, this is a very close clone of StS but with a Match 3 board reminiscent of the classic Puzzle Quest. Given that and the care with which the game was made, I enjoyed it enough to give it an up rating.On the negative side, I think it's so similar in many ways to Slay that despite the Match 3 boards, I quickly mined it out. There's not much new to discover, and the three classes all play somewhat similarly. That's not to say it's a bad game -- I had a good time, and I'm upvoting it because I love the genre and this is a decent example of it, but if you are only going to play a few games of this type, there are a lot better entries to pick up. On the plus side, the art is pretty and the game is pretty well-balanced, in my opinion. If you are a frequent StS-like player, you'll likely find it to be perfectly balanced; if you're new to the genre, you may find it quite difficult to win. The cards are well thought-out, and there are a variety of builds to try, but a lot of it feels awfully familiar. It's often more fun to have greater diversity of experiences on runs but have a less tight balance -- maybe an unpopular opinion, but that's how I feel about it.
_childDocuments_.name: Demon's Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a big fan of these types of games, and since the release of Slay the Spire, the Deckbuilding Roguelike genre has been done to death with the same concept over and over again. There's a few good ones out there, and far more 'meh' ones.Demon's Mirror has been a refreshing take on a genre that's been frankly overdone. A second facet to combat makes things very different, and I've been having a great time with this game. Be warned, however, as this game is NOT easy at first, but that's not a bad thing, it's a fun challenge for veteran players. 9/10, would recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Demon's Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: I have really been enjoying this game so far! I find the first two characters you are able to play as (All I have played so far) to be very charming and distinct from one another. I adored Slay the Spire and I think this game does an amazing job utilizing elements that are similar to Spire, but also puts a fun spin on the genre. This game is very unique while also having those charming parallels, and anyone who loved Spire will also love this game. Super recommend giving it a try!
_childDocuments_.name: Demon's Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: This is Slay the Spire with a Match 3 element provided.  It works a lot like StS ... different paths, creature battles, random events, and campfires for healing, and shops for upgrading.  During battles, the match 3 board allows you to attack, power spells, gain shields, etc.  You draw cards for attack, defense and skills.  Some of those cards can change the board around to allow for more powerful combos.  The enemy can also add bad tiles to the board that you need to destroy or take some serious damage.  Use them in combos to destroy them.  There are mini-games, one of which uses match 3 and cards to gain gold.All in all, this is a pretty fun game!  It does have some bugs and things that I don't understand.  However, There are lots of things to considers as enemies and enemy board tiles have certain abilities that make things difficult.  There should be many hours to this game as I am still working on my first run...
_childDocuments_.name: Demon's Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: very replayable, and enjoyable. Great artwork and sound. I wouldn't say it's the hardest game to beat, so if you like brutality this is not for you - but that's why I love it. Now that I've beaten it, I'll be adding the modifiers to make it more difficult (the difficulty seems highly adjustable!). I got this game at full price, and will TOTALLY be getting my moneys worth. Got this to play while I'm sick at home, and I can see myself putting 40hrs into this over my extended weekend. If you think it may be for you, just try the demo - you've got nothing to lose!P.S - If you're stuck not having good chains, don't forget to use the tile damage cards to clear away unwanted tiles in an area to set yourself up for a great play the following round!

_childDocuments_.review: Very good deck building roguelike. The matching adds an extra level of depth that's very welcome. I've played so many games in this space and they often feel overly similar, this one feels fresh and new. I highly recommend it if you like Slay the Spire, Dreamquest, etc. Also the art is incredibly charming. It all feels very good.
_childDocuments_.name: Demon's Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty fun, interesting mechanics with the chaining stuffEdit: Won the entire thing for the first time after about 5 tries. I saw some discussions saying that it's a bit too hard but I think it's just right. If it's too hard there are modifiers to make it a bit easier. I'd like it to be a bit harder but that's easy to do with the modifiers you unlock.
_childDocuments_.name: Demon's Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: Just had to pause and write a review. I played the hell out of the demo and am stoked for the full release. This game is so well thought out with both methods of play working with each other it's amazing no one did this sooner. I love both grid-chaining puzzlers and card battlers and here they are in one! There are sooo many synergies it's insane. Going back in, kudos to the devs for such an awesome game.
_childDocuments_.name: Demon's Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: really fun deckbuilder roguelite. the grid-chaining puzzle elements fit in really smoothly, the art and music are good, and the whole premise is just really charmingEDIT ok i'm 20hrs in and this game is addictive. there is so much complexity to explore, so much depth to the tactics, so many weird trinket combos to try... every run i'm thinking about my next run. the music keeps playing in my head long after i quit the game and i like it. i've noticed a few very minor bugs but they're hardly disruptive and the overall experience is incredibly polished. the art and aesthetic are so delightfully strange and a lot of the card illustrations are downright funny. the board chaining stuff should feel tacked-on but it's so well integrated it just feels right. a real gem of a game, well worth the price
_childDocuments_.name: Demon's Mirror

_childDocuments_.review:
Demon's Mirror is the first game to combine roguelike deckbuilding and chain-3 mechanics in a way that creates a powerful synergy between the two. Like other deckbuilders, you battle enemies by playing cards to attack, defend, and gain powers, but in Demon's mirror you also battle opponents by chaining tiles. Certain cards let you manipulate the board in ways that will allow you to create longer chains. Mastering the strategic balance between playing cards and chaining tiles is what will ultimately determine your fate.

Demon's Mirror plays like a combination of Slay the Spire meets Puzzle Quest (but with a chain-3 mechanic).

name: Frostpunk 2
detailed_description: Digital Deluxe Edition About the Game Frostpunk 2 elevates the city-survival genre to a new level. Take the role of a Steward and lead your city through a cascade of calamities taking place in a postapocalyptic, snowy setting. Build large city districts with their string of endless needs and demands. Navigate through conflicting interests of factions that populate your metropolis. As the needs of the city grow and factional power at its core rises, only you can steer the society towards an uncertain future. The world is overtaken by an ever present winter, which makes expansion of the city the only way for the survival of mankind. In order to grow, the metropolis needs resources like coal and oil, just like its citizens require food and warmth. In Frostpunk 2, it's your job to tackle this never ending circle of supply and demand. The number of your citizens steadily grows, making the task of governing them and satisfying their demands all the more challenging. As the Steward you will have to maneuver carefully across the interests of many groups inhabiting the city. People of your city want to have a voice in how you run things. Each faction has its own ideology and ideas for the future, yet they also have one thing in common - insatiable thirst for power. Choose your allies in the Council Hall wisely. The story of Frostpunk 2 introduces a multi-chapter saga set in the frozen wastes. Spanning across the life of the Steward this campaign lets you feel the burden of leadership as you take the responsibility for thousands of lives. At the same time, the sandbox mode called Utopia Builder with infinite play time leaves you room for boundless social and infrastructural experiments. Frostpunk 2 comes with a comprehensive and versatile modding tool. FrostKit will let you create your own maps, models, and scenarios inside the game. Now, only your imagination can limit the destination your city is heading to!

_childDocuments_.review: Oh boy, this is a hard one. I've waited so long for the sequel to Frostpunk and have put over 400 hours into the original game, so my expectations were sky-high. Unfortunately, Frostpunk 2 feels like a bit of a mess.The game introduces too many resources to manage, making it feel overwhelming rather than challenging. There's no clear way to see important information at a glance, and the UX/UI is incredibly unintuitive. I found myself constantly struggling to find what I needed, which killed the immersion and made the experience frustrating.On top of that, the game isn’t well optimized. Even on a high-end system, I'm barely getting over 30 FPS. This makes it hard to enjoy the game's atmospheric visuals and adds to the feeling that this sequel lacks the polish and finesse of its predecessor.I really wanted to love this game, but right now, it just feels like a missed opportunity. I hope future patches can address some of these issues because Frostpunk 2 has potential, but in its current state, it’s tough to recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: A great sequel, with a completly new aproach to the known its-all-problems sturcture like the first frostpunk.I have some minor criticisms, but on the whole its definetly a great game.The only bigger issue right now for me is the performance, which certainly could be better.But heres to hope for some great dlcs like in the first one! Base game is already a hit.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who considers the original Frostpunk one of the best games ever made, Frostpunk 2 had high expectations to meet—and for the most part, it delivers. Just like its predecessor, Frostpunk 2 does not disappoint. While the prologue starts slow and feels a bit awkward, the game quickly finds its stride as you dive deeper into its core mechanics.Much like the original, the late-game experience shines as you can once again embrace controversial laws and technologies. However, the sequel takes everything up a notch. The tech tree is significantly larger, easily tripling the options from the original. Combine this with the expanded laws and the delegate voting system, and you're presented with a vast range of choices that affect gameplay. Additionally, the sheer number of buildings and their unique mechanics keep the game fresh and intriguing.  The game massively expands on the options available in the original. The combination of laws, technologies, and the delegate voting system allows for a more dynamic and replayable experience. The number of buildings and the mechanics tied to them are well-thought-out, adding layers of strategic depth as you manage your city’s survival.Despite its many strengths, Frostpunk 2 has a few drawbacks that impact the experience:     -> Artistically, the UI is impressive, but functionally, it's lacking in several areas. Heat buffs are displayed in blue, which is visually confusing since red is the conventional indicator of heat. There are many such cases where u wish to see certain map information only to not be able to.    -> The 's current time indicator is uncomfortably placed right at the edge, making it awkward to read.     -> The 's temperature icons turned white on my playthrough?    -> The  feels out of place compared to the old liquid thermometer from the original, which added more flavor to the cold, desolate atmosphere.    ->  could be better organized, with some key information hidden or difficult to access.    ->  also often appear off-screen, making navigation clunky. Centering the screen when opening a menu would greatly improve the experience. To optimize heat bonuses for districts, you're forced to build with maximizing surface area, which feels illogical and counter to real-world strategies of heat efficiency. The frostbreak mechanic is an exciting concept, but its lack of visual representation feels like a missed opportunity. Incorporating something like a tessellation shader to show the depth of the frost would have added to the immersion. Managing scouting parties on the map feels off. The fact that they can operate in a whiteout and somehow spawn directly at locations you want to explore doesn't feel natural or coherent with the game’s harsh world-building.In summary, Frostpunk 2 successfully builds upon the foundation of its predecessor, offering expanded gameplay mechanics and difficult moral decisions that fans of the original will appreciate. However, a few issues with the UI, adjacency bonuses, and certain mechanics prevent it from reaching perfection. With some patches and tweaks, Frostpunk 2 has the potential to stand alongside the original as a classic in its own right.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for a game that plays like Frostpunk 1, with more too do and new challenges and environments, Frostpunk 2 is not that game. I think a lot of people, like myself, were expecting a game with the same feel and gameplay as Frostpunk 1. Frostpunk 2 pulls the camera way back and scales up the city management is a way that makes your choices feel less important. Sometimes bigger isnt always better. Frostpunk 2 is a good city management simulator that loses all the charm of the first game. If you're looking for an experience close to Frostpunk 1, this is not that game.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: The sequel to one of the best games ever turning out to be an amazing game? "impossible" one would think, but this is everything that was promised and more, can't wait for the extra content and DLCs to be realised, i am certain that they will be as amazing as the DLCs for Frostpunk 1 were. Truly a marvel of modern gaming.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Playing Frostpunk 2, even in the supposed "easier" Citizen Mode, was far from a relaxing experience. I thought I’d start with this mode to get the hang of things, but it turns out managing the city is still incredibly challenging. Resources run out way too fast—just when you’ve finished building a new district, the previous one is already depleted. It feels like I’m constantly running behind, and I can only imagine how brutal the harder difficulties must be.That said, I have to admit the faction and City Council management is really well done. It feels super realistic, and the way they react to your decisions adds a lot of depth to the game. However, I found myself wishing for more help in-game. A proper tutorial or written tips on every feature would be great, especially in the Utopia Builder mode. It would allow you to dive into the gameplay without needing to complete the whole story first.All in all, Frostpunk 2 is intense, challenging, and rewarding—but definitely not easy. If Citizen Mode gave me this much trouble, I don’t even want to think about what the harder modes would be like!
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: As the critics say: Frostpunk 2 is not like Frostpunk 1, but that's okay, fine even.Frostpunk 2 feels like a mix of Frostpunk 1, Simcity/Cities Skylines and Victoria 3.Even more so: It feels like Frostpunk 2 manages a political system, as it should have been in Vic3.Frostpunk 2 plays in a larger scope, so you feel less like a part of the community, facing the decisions you make yourself as well, and a bit more distant.However the cruel decisions remain, as well as the consequences of each and every action you take.Other than many say: Frostpunk 2 fully remains a Frostpunk game - in my opinion. And it's way more than just a batch of further DLCs for Frostpunk 1.Only negative aspects:- The technical performance of this game could be improved (a computer running all games so far, seriously struggles in the late game here.) (But apparently it's being worked on.)- Some translation mistakes (including placeholders) in German language- Some functions/aspects are (despite a Tutorial system) really unintuitive and will only be figured out after 1-2 playthroughs.I'd also recommend not to buy this at full price, as it roughly grants 10-12 hours of play time to finish both Story- and Utopia mode. So for everyone who does not intend to do multiple runs, test multiple things and hunt every achievement, it's most likely not worth the full price.For everyone else: go for it!
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Bought this because of my good experience with the original Frostpunk, but the brand new game mechanics in Frostpunk 2 proved far less attractive and addictive. Also ran into quite a bit of performance issues with a great deal of lagging as well as a lot of problems starting up the game. A substantial proportion of these 27 hours were recorded while waiting for the game to boot.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Is it different from the 1st Frostpunk? YES. Instead of feeling more "down to earth" with the individuals in the city and focusing on the "center core" with little hubs, you are now "progressing" into the metropolis of things that happen "after the center core is established". _childDocuments_.review: This is a very very tentative recommendation. It's a good game, BUT there's some caveats. This is NOT the same as Frostpunk. If you were into Frostpunk for the story and setting, then I can happily recommend this. If you preferred it for the semi-Banished or other small scale city builder mechanics, I cannot recommend this. There is only one game I can think of that is proper to compare it to: Tropico. This game is cold-climate Tropico which has depression instead of humor. There's only a few individually placed buildings, but the story is good, the environment is good, and overall if you like Tropico but ever wanted it to be more serious, this is a good game for you.IMPORTANT NOTE: The store page recommendation fails to clarify something very vital. If you have an older PC, make sure that you have 8 cores minimum on your processor. I had 4 cores, and the game ultimately failed at a certain point. Others have 6 cores, and struggled. DO NOT BUY if you have less than 8 cores, as your game WILL fail.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to love this game but i dont and I am kinda surprised it got so many good reviews. The resource management part is kinda basic. There are very few goods to manage and only one currency thats restricting all your actions for most of the time. While that doesnt have to be something bad, if thats not the main part of the game there need to be something else and for Frostpunk 2 thats the politics system. And honestly thats great, at first. But it comes with some major issues:-  E.g. if dialogs force you to make decisions without being able to look up the consequences/alternative laws for the category. It also happens that even tho a fraction is supporting a change of law, they start raging because its breaking a promise you made before so you gotta keep track on your promises as the game wont necessarily tell you. - There are straight up  in the system. In my latest play through when i enforced captains law it froze the state of guided voting impact with all groups at extremely bad which caused tons of trouble for like the next 5h in the game. Than the whole politics system became stable (i still had worst relations with all groups, despite guided voting was the only negative impact for some of the groups) and stopped giving me problems to solve, so that i was left with a rly basic and boring although great looking resource management city builder.There are a couple  which can often lead to confusion and frustrations.Another thing i wanna mention is that in "endless", once you made it past week 400 (~5-6h) with a decent strategy, stacking effects starts kicking in and the week 400 - 2000 becomes easy/boring even on highest difficult level. Also the game runs into some serious performance issues in endgame where auto save and even build menu lag the game for multiple seconds. The whole endless mode feels more like BETA state. So in the end its not a bad game, but it lacks depth and at its current state it doenst feel worth the full price. Lets see what kind of bugfixes and DLC content we might get in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: First off, I would like to mention that I was following the development of this game, and that when making the choice to pre-order, I knew that the game would take a drastically different direction than the original. The first game appeals to the morally ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up side of you. You have to make tough decisions that shape every single person under your command. Mistakes can wipe out families, and the game makes sure you know the blood of every mistake is on your hands. You felt the weight of your actions through 2 medians: the building placement/city direction, and the politics. The politics of the game did interest me 100%, and added a rugged & bleak sense of humanity to this steampunk wasteland. Every policy you made would garner reactions from your people, and truly shape your society in tangible ways. This aspect was pretty much kept, and even expanded upon with factions. But the city builder part of it, and thus the intimacy, was kind of scrapped.In Frostpunk 2, instead of placing individual buildings and seeing your specific policies visually manifest themselves like in the first game, you designate plots of land for districts. You do get a few slots in a district to place specific buildings, but it is quite limiting. Despite my clear favoritism of the first game's system, both game's city building mechanics match the scale. The original has you running a small and desperate settlement with a few hundred people and bad heating infrastructure, so yeah, it makes sense that you have to micromanage where every single building is placed. In this game you're running a 'well off' city with a population count in the thousands, so its much more realistic that instead of buildings, were actually doing more broad city planning and zoning. The mayor of New York City would (rightfully so) have no business deciding where exactly a new diner or hotel should open, because the scale of those decisions is so small and irrelevant.This doesn't bother me THAT much, but when you have such a visceral original game where placement means everything, you can't help but feel it's a massive downgrade.Now for the society part. In the original game, shutting off the generator for a night could mean halving your population. It's brutal, and it meant that radical policies were literally commonplace. Signing children away to work in factories and mines is literally a law you can enact scarily early on in the game play, and you know it's necessary because you would run out of workers without it, but you still get that gut punch when a notification pops up that a 12 year old has just been mangled in heavy machinery. In this game: "250 bystanders have perished in protests..." Okay? And? That's a drop in the bucket compared to the massive scale of this game, and I have literally no reason to care, because if you only put in moderate effort, you can get immigration and childbirth rates to go through the roof, instantly replacing anyone who died in the last year. No matter how inhumane the policy is, it's hard to feel guilty. You can't really see these people, and they have no connection to you. So who cares if they die. If the game gave me an option to execute 5 innocent people a day just for fear mongering, I would totally do it because it's just 5 out of 3000 numbers. But in the original if the same rule was proposed, there would be some serious strategical (and true moral) concerns about it, because every day you'd be losing a noticeable amount of workers who have actual names and ages and families.Just to show you how extreme this can get, when we eventually needed to recolonize or scavenge winterhome, I decided on my first playthough to scavenge it for steam cores, but this would release toxic gas. I shipped out 6000 workers to mine for cores, and sure enough, a large amount of them just died. I lost like 4000 out of 30,000 total population I had at the time, but I just committed, didn't actually face many repercussions, and no joke, finished that chapter in like 25 minutes. In Frostpunk 1, you could lose the same percentage of people I did there by having a few less clinics than needed or not boosting the generator overnight. So those were like 'trivial' things that caused me to lose a solid chunk of my population, but in this game I lost the same amount proportionally, but it was to a MAJOR milestone that had to be completed for our survival.That leads me to my final major point, and while a little trivial, is kind of important. The game felt short, easy, and frankly, tame at times. I'll start my saying that throughout playing the full campaign in normal mode, I didn't fail a single time. It was incredibly easy compared to the grindfest I viewed the original as. Next, I feel as though the original game had a MUCH broader array of topics and issues you need to tackle. There were tons of completely different themes and problems with every section in the game. In this game, it ALL revolves around one thing, and to be honest, I cannot recall what I did in any of the 5 chapters except for chapter 5. In the original, I know off the top of my head every task, section, milestone, hardship, etc, in chronological order. Everything stood out because every section of that game was so challenging and memorable. The UI for every section of the first game was noticeably different and unique. But once again, in this game, it's the SAME STUFF in all 5 chapters. Just as an example, let me break down both games and the content in their campaigns.Section 1 - Starting to set up the basics of your colony, and the fundamentals of the game are introduced.Section 2 - You launch your first frostland expeditions and find Winterhome, destroyed and abandonedSection 3 - Citizens lose hope and join what is basically a suicide pact, attempting to leave and aimlessly try to return to London. This is obviously a huge problem, and you need to try to stop them by raising hope and lowering discontent. In this section you can choose a radical path of either a brutalist authoritarian society, or make up a fake religion/cult, which provide their own perks.Section 4 - After the Londoners crisis, you now have to accommodate a huge influx of refugees, which can destroy your city without the proper resources and housing.Section 5 - You now have to research weather technology, and prepare for the incoming storm.Section 6 - The storm hits, and you have to do what you can to keep your colony clinging on to life.Prologue - The concepts of the game are introduced and you find a food source. Very similar to the original's first part.Chapter 1 - Different city, but you're doing the same thing as you did in the prologue, with added politics & expeditions.Chapter 2 - There's a whiteout and you now use oil for power. You have to decide between adapting to or fighting the cold.Chapter 3 - Literally all you're doing is trying to locate Winterhome for cores to help upgrade the generator.Chapter 4 - You establish a colony in Winterhome, and now you have to mine the cores or settle the area. That's it.Chapter 5 - There is a civil war, which while being by far the most interesting section of the game, still comes across as tame. What they mean by 'civil war' is a few thousand pissed off people protesting in some districts, smashing some stuff, and dipping. Now you have to either eradicate a faction or make them co-exist. While it definitely serves as a climax to the whole factions aspect of the game, it's nowhere as impactful as the leadup to the great storm in the first game. This game COULD have been so much more. There are only 2 factions coexisting in story mode, but I was hoping for a melting pot of them, intercity warfare, and more extremism. I most of all hoped the scale was large but still intimate. Despite all of this, I highly recommend it. It scratched an itch, and was loads of fun. Just understand this is a political game, not a city builder anymore.

_childDocuments_.review: I love Frostpunk 1 as much as I hate Frostpunk 2. The second game unfortunately turned out to be a mess and a disaster:- The UI/UX is so bad and poorly designed. I literally can't see that little mouse cursor when you need it to react quickly to notifications. You have to read A LOT of small text on a white background - research screen will burn your eyes. Text and icons overlap images and another text on different layers. - The gameplay mechanics are unclear and extremely unfriendly. Since they have changed it completely from FP1, there should be a detailed introduction to each part. Or a detailed built-in tutorial and hint system. But here you're all alone with dozens of blockers where you don't understand what's required for the next action to move on. - Story and atmosphere are missing. You can no longer feel this post-apocalyptic world. There is no smooth connection to the FP1 lore. How did they find out about the oil in the first place when there was no mention of it in FP1? Also this "building-by-districts" idea leads us to were we don't give a f ... don't feel any responsibility when another 100 people die from a random event. You're moving hundreds of people between districts and you don't care who dies. I remember in FP1 it already felt like a tragedy when 1 man died. - I started the game on the lowest difficulty to be able to concentrate on the story and have fun exploring the world. But instead you have to do everything at the same time and the game throws you into a race for survival very quickly. At the lowest level, you don't have much time to think, you can't see the development of your settlements step by step, but you find yourself in the middle of a fire. So forget about having fun.All in all, I am sure that this game has been released too early. It has cool ideas, but they need more time to polish it and make it more user-friendly. And most importantly - this is no longer Frostpunk.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of Frostpunk 1, I was prepared to throw my wallet at anything with the Frostpunk title. Unfortunately it took me 5 hours, which is over Steam's refund policy, to realize that this game has very little to do with Frostpunk. The focus on the game is on politics. It's not a survival game, it's a politics simulator. If you are into that stuff, this game is probably your GOTY.I'll briefly sum up some things that bothered me:- Due to the large scale, the game feels soulless. A death is meaningless, there is no day and night, you can't even see your people going to work and going home. You are only looking at numbers, week after week of the same. You are not building houses, you are assigning districts.- Oil/coal and heat are almost irrelevant. It's the backdrop to what is basically a game about navigating several political parties who disagree with each other. In FP 1 the main problem was that people are freezing in the night and the hospitals get overcrowded. The biggest problem in FP 2 is that political party A is crying that political party B passed their vote. Yawn.- The UI is absolutely terrible. I hear they released some patches to fix some stuff so who knows, maybe it'll get better.- The game doesn't explain anything. Many mechanics aren't intuitive, and you will end up on google quite a lot. This isn't a showstopper but it was responsible for me rolling my eyes a couple of times. They could have handled this a lot better.Overall, it's brave of the creators to do something completely different, but it's not for me. I was very disappointed. It gives me the feeling that it shouldn't have been named "Frostpunk 2". It should have been its own name. I might give the game another go a bit later, after some patch cycles, and hopefully I'll get some enjoyment out of my money.

_childDocuments_.review: As it turns out, scaling up Frostpunk makes it not Frostpunk....if you loved the unique story telling of Frostpunk 1, this game is not for you.if you loved the way Frostpunk 1 made you care about your citizens, this game is not for you.if you loved the way you got immersed into the world of New London, shouting "The City Must Survive!" as you and your citizens take on the storm...this game is not for you---who this game is for.People who love the constant stress of decision making and 'sliding to the finish line'Where Frostpunk 1 focused on the story of New London as it comes to represent the human condition, the sequel takes out the soul and just gives you a steady drip of BS for the whiniest NPCs I've ever seen in a city builder.I never felt like I could breathe and admire the city, or sigh and think to myself “I need to find a way to solve this problem”. I am constantly trying to find food/materials/housing - and the moment I had everything balanced, some brat shank'd someone causing my citizens to demand a new policy, after which I had to do some research as a quid pro quo for the policy (that they wanted!),  After that I had to rebalance my food/materials/housing again. Then the funeral for the guy the kid stabbed caused some controversy because some people think funerals are a waste of resources and want the body donated to science causing another demand for policy - and then quid pro quo research, repeat.Where Frostpunk 1 was a nice introspective of "how far will you go to ensure humanity survives", and "how will we overcome this situation". This game is "how well can you juggle and multitask while people yell at you: the game".I leave feeling "why am I even doing all this? just to say I beat the game?". All that said, I encourage everyone who dropped it at the Prologue to power through Ch1. The Prologue is not a good showcase of the gameplay, it gets a bit better - but in the end, it's still not why I liked Frostpunk. Without those, it's kind of just a mediocre city builder....It's not a bad game, I'm not mad, I enjoyed some parts, but I am disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: The most unenjoyable "city builder" I have played in years, even considering its a 3 day early access. It is a travesty to even consider this is related to Frostpunk. It is a spin off. The only similarity this has with the original game is that they're in the same universe.The entire time I played this, I was comparing it to the original, and even reinstalled Frostpunk just to make sure I wasn't wrong. I put 3x the amount of time into Frostpunk over the past 2 days than I did playing this 3 day early access.Lets start with the graphics. There is nothing notably better than Frostpunk 1 (FP1). The only thing I noticed is that FP2 is horribly optimized, leading to regular lag spikes and average frame rate below 60 fps on medium graphics.Update: I wrote this in google docs yesterday and just to prove a point before posting, just for this game I decided to repair my computer that has a 4090 and i9-14900KF. With V-Sync enabled, constant lag, sub 60 fps. With DLSS and Frame Gen on, V-Sync off, I got a little above 60. I don't know how they managed to do this. Almost top of the line PC and still struggles.Next is the buildings. In FP1 you built buildings but in FP2 you draw districts. After placing these districts you can place a single building on it to increase output at the expense of using more workers, but its the only way to actually get large amounts of resources. You can expand a district to house ONE additional building. The housing district needs to be expanded to have a building, and can only support one. The game encourages you to plan your cities by having different districts give proximity debuffs. It is awful.If the city building was rather just placing buildings on hexagonal grids with proximity debuffs, or free form district drawing, I would probably have no issues, but this system is simply ghoulish to play with and not enjoyable to me.Next is the scouts. Unlike FP1, FP2 requires you to "frostbreak" (excavate) to the border of the map to build a logistics district. This will give you 15 "Frostland Teams". These are your scouts. Rather than have singular scout teams that can go everywhere, FP2 has turned it into a resource meaning some undiscovered areas will require more Frostland Teams than others to go to. There is also a new danger system for exploring that is useless as you can just research to decrease the danger. This system is flawed, but not really bad. Just needs some numbers tweaked to balance it out.Similar to FP1 Settlements, FP2 has outposts, settlements, and colonies. Outposts are found with your Frostland Teams, and can have a trade route established using some resources and your Frostland Teams. Outposts can be upgraded into Settlements for more Frostland Teams and resources. It will also take some population to construct it. The downside to Outposts and Settlements is that they have very limited amount of resources before they run out.Colonies are mini cities that you can actually build in and trade resources with. They're used for getting more resources from other locations after you run out in your main city. They are essentially resource depots. You can also shuttle your populations between them if you need more workers in the colony vs city. I don't like or hate the Outposts and Settlements, but I COMPLETELY adore Colonies. They are the most enjoyable aspect of the game by far.I'm not even going to bother explaining resources because I'm simply too dumb to. I don't hate the new system but I hate the resource balance and how buildings are required if you want to not immediately fall apart. I will say this though. Heatstamps are required for every building and district in the game. You gain them passively from people living in the city, and this number can be increased by producing ample amounts of goods. It is the worst "addition" as it literally is just there to impede progress. It is similar to the hospital death spiral in FP1. If you go into a deficit while not having enough goods and you can't get heatstamps quick enough, its game over. I found that 230 weeks in.That is all I can remember of what I would personally like to completely forget. I would add more but I've largely forgotten and will not be relaunching until at least the first patch. I don't hate this because it's different or new. I did like the outposts, but thats it. The best game I can compare this to in recent memory is Sins of a Solar Empire II. The planetary buildings and poor resource collection is very similar to Frostpunk II in my opinion.
