_childDocuments_.review: At the time of writing (1.0.2 update), a reluctant recommend; mostly due to consistent performance issues in late game, and I'm not even on old hardware anymore! (7700X/RTX4070S) Autosaves are the biggest problem; they just completely freeze the game (no pun intended) for about half a minute on my setup, starting from around week 400 or so. For reference, autosaves occur about every 50 weeks, and most of my story playthroughs took a little over 600 weeks, so the last third of the game had this issue.EDIT: Forgot to mention that manual saves also take forever when this starts happening.Besides the performance issues, Frostpunk 2 diverges quite a bit from the original Frostpunk. To many, this is a dealbreaker, as evidenced by the current 'Mostly Positive' Steam review rating, compared to the original's 'Very Positive'. You are no longer placing buildings in rings around a generator for your little community to survive; you are now stewarding a city of thousands towards a new future by placing districts outside the city center, and buildings inside those districts.The district mechanic is actually the fun part of the game for me. The map is made up of polygon tiles, mostly hexes and pentagons (and rarely squares), with districts being 6 tiles usually. Districts get bonuses when at least three tiles are adjacent to another district, or a hub. It seems simple but it just activates neurons for me. Unfortunately the mechanics behind the adjacency bonus is not clearly conveyed through gameplay nor is it in the actual tutorial, so minus points for that. I initially assumed that you'd get a partial bonus for one or two tile adjacency, but no, it's all or nothing.The other radical change is the communities and factions. The campaign gives you two of each, but in 'Utopia Builder' (sandbox mode) you get three and two respectively. Every law you pass, every tech you research will be aligned on one of three axes. Communities favor one side of an axis each, factions have three favorites. So pleasing everyone is impossible, although you can put in some effort to be on friendly terms with all of them simultaneously.For those of you who've played Frostpunk, imagine if you had the Londoners all game. And another group that opposed the Londoners. And either group will protest you if you make them too unhappy, or hold rallies to demonstrate their support if you've  built buildings and passed laws they support. Basically.This game, due to its scale, does feel extremely impersonal compared to 11bit's other games I've played, the original Frostpunk and This War of Mine. In those games, every illness can require you, the player, to shift workers around; there is a direct gameplay impact whenever someone falls ill (which is also probably caused by your action or inaction).In Frostpunk 2, though, you will never think about it outside of maybe one chapter in the campaign. "One death is a tragedy, a million is a statistic" - 11bit on Frostpunk vs. Frostpunk 2, probably.More specifically, the moral consequences of your decisions are conveyed purely through text only events, either an event to which you must respond or a blurb from an affected citizen. For example, passing the "only productive outsiders are allowed into the city" law will later give you a short blurb from . We all know how much gamers like to (not) read so I'm not convinced this was the best delivery method, despite them being pretty compelling otherwise.In spite of all that, this game is does feel like a sequel to Frostpunk. Aside from the campaign being an obvious continuation of the 'A New Home' scenario in the original game, playthroughs do feel similar between the two despite being mechanically quite different. Extremely constrained by resources early on, sending scouts exploring for resources, prioritizing and making compromises to reach stability, then finally autoplaying on max speed until the end. It is missing a lot of the emotional weight that comes from 11bit's other games, but perhaps that's by design.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Having just finished the story I can definitely say this:They nailed the setting, the atmosphere, the music and everything around it. It just feels like Frostpunk.But the gameplay is quite different to the previous game. So if you're going into this game expecting something like a new Frostpunk DLC, just bigger, than you'll probably be disappointed. While I personally like the gameplay, I can imagine that it's probably not for everyone.So you should probably look into the new gameplay before you decide if you want to buy it or not. Especially if you're a fan of the first Frostpunk.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: I thoroughly enjoyed FP1 and was excited for FP2.  I like that they did fresh game play (which makes sense chronologically and story-wise, to me), but still were able to keep the feel of urgency and that one or two wrong decisions can tank your city.  The starting levels might be challenging until you learn the mechanics, and just like FP1 there are multiple harder difficulties once you get those down.  Well worth trying if you liked FP1.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Choose your adventure: 1) "I can't believe this game isn't exactly like the first with some insignificant QL improvements"; or 2) "Devs just aren't creative anymore, all new games are just a re-skin"From a review standpoint, this game suffers from the same problem Darkest Dungeon 2 had-- it was following its own greatness. People want everything to be different and better but also the same and familiar.Frostpunk 2 is an awesome experience. The systems are complex, exciting and challenging. I'm enjoying my time working through the unique puzzles this game has to offer. An absolute treat! Thank you 11 bit :D
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk 2 is probably the best implementation of a sequal to a game I've ever played that keeps the same core feel of the prequel, while also expanding both the gameplay and continuing the story in a logical manner. It feels different enough from Frostpunk 1 that it's clearly got it's own identity, but like the next natural progression from just building one city in the frozen wastelands.Only con is that it's a bit short. It does have a bit of replay value though.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: I really love how this game took the concept and world of Frostpunk and expanded its scope in virtually every way. This is not the same game as the first Frostpunk, it trades off some of the granular gameplay elements for broader 'city-builder' like district expansion. However, if you spend some time you will find all the same balance of survival strategy that makes the franchise so special.I had major technical issues with this game on Mac OS when it launched. However after the 1.1 release I have to say everything runs great now! I have updated this review into an endorsement based on the continued investments 11 Bit has made into the game. I'm really happy that I can enjoy my experience fully now!
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: FP1 is you getting the handful of people together to survive. FP2 is years later when you are gathering thousands of survivors to make your empire. You are no longer placing a house to fit a family in, You are building a housing district to handle hundreds of families. No longer are you hearing a handful of people wanting changes, you are getting told there are thousands of people that think something changed.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Too buggy. I don't expect to crash to desktop doing ANYTHING in Windholm (i think it was called) to relocate a faction crashes to desktop and entirely halts progress. I was sad they didn't keep any of what I liked about the first one, and opted for this Hex/Civ builder, but despite them leaving the best parts of Frostpunk 1 behind here, was having fun through frustrations. The game fails to explain basic things or warn you. This ranges from small things, like letting you double up on all district buildings (building 2 of them in the district) but prevents you from doing that with deep wells, for some reason (and others only apply to top level resources), and to big things like preventing you from wholly abandoning a city (you cannot move the last 1k people, so they just have to die). This was annoying, since the dialogue and pop-up makes it sound like you can 'stay and harvest cores up to the last minute'. It was a smaller population, but little "WTF, why!?" were common and tooltips either further mislead, or just weren't helpful. Not recommending given the Chapter 5 bug preventing me from doing anything (crash do desktop) but would recommend with caution to someone looking for a strategy game that rubbed up against a board game, as thats what Frostpunk 2 feels like with the Hex building and 'chance cards' events. I came here because I loved Frostpunk 1, and found myself wanting to finish this campaign at least once so I could uninstall and play Frostpunk 1 again =D.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Just beat the game as of October 6th. Was hoping (after beating the first chapter) that at the end of the first campaign you would find yourself in another area, location, scenario. However that's not even the case. Spent 15 hours trying to get all these random factions in with me just for me to beat 5 chapters in, get to the end, and realize it's only a one scenario game. Can we revert back to the original Frostpunk 1? Where there were at least 5 campaigns and scenarios? Do not get me wrong, awesome play through I had. But come the ♥♥♥♥ on, these guys were already dead before I came and helped them. (Chapter 1)Give us more scenarios with no DLC cost. This is a great game just to have a downfall of a 20-30 hour play through to grind achievements.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: It's just not fun.Maybe it's because the scale is greater and you're further away from the action, so it's less compelling and harder to tell yourself a story about how you're barely scraping by day to day.Or maybe it's because I researched a hospital but I can't build it anywhere and I don't know why, meanwhile my workers are freezing to death by the hundreds even though all two of my poor little coal mining operations are working overtime to feed the generator at max capacity, on top of which the generator is in overdrive. Maybe there was a note I missed about other ways to increase heat, that I missed in the 900 other notes.More than anything I'm just confused and tired of looking for the fun. I made it about three hours in; maybe the game starts to get fun at five hours? I don't know, these days I quit books and movies if they're not interesting by the 15 minute mark, so I'd say I gave this game more than a fair chance.And now I'm off to go play some Frostpunk 1.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fresh not frozen. After the initial hour, going in with limited details about the game, I quickly realized this game is a different beast to the original. I feel like this game as a sequel is not intended to fully replace the original, (by superseding it with improved gameplay mechanics like traditional city builders aim to do), but to co-exist with the original, continuing the narrative, whilst providing a new take on the gameplay.Overall really enjoying it.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: So, I've been a big fan of the Frost punk games for a while now. I was really excited about this continuation- and I still am. It was an interesting expansion of the OG concept and certainly a challenging game. That being said- I was kinda hoping for more lore dumps. Do we ever get more on what caused the disaster? Was their a race to Antarctica for the global south? Also- Utopia mode. Its got three major scenarios, which were fun, but I did quickly exploit the whole map. I'm hoping there will be some updates and DLC options later down the road.Over all, I do recommend this game. Its fun, its a gorgeous city builder, and I love it. My critique is the core game can feel quick to play through once you figure out the mechanics and its replay to find hidden lore and gems feels to be wanting. I hope they add and build on- and I hope to see more out of this franchise.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: I expected a city builder, and first it was a disappointment. But after learning the game I realized, this is just amazing, extremely challenging and fun.Frostpunk 1 was like being an Individual Contributor, you had to micromanage your city, build roads, houses, etc.Frostpunk 2 is like being a Vice President or a CEO, you have to deal with more macro level challenges, and have a much wider influence. It is intense, it is different, but entertaining.So I would recommend, give it some time, learn the game and be the leader! Save the Humanity! Good luck!
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely Phenomenal Experience!Frostpunk 2 exceeds expectations and delivers an unforgettable gaming experience! As a seasoned player of the original Frostpunk, I was eagerly anticipating this sequel, and it did not disappoint. The developers have crafted a compelling narrative that delves into the complexities of survival in an unforgiving world.The strategic gameplay is challenging yet rewarding, and the intricate story adds depth and immersion, making every decision impactful. The graphics are stunning, capturing the chilling atmosphere with meticulous detail.Moreover, the soundtrack is masterfully composed, enhancing the emotional experience and standing out as one of the most memorable parts of the game. It truly complements the intense atmosphere, immersing you even deeper into the game.Overall, Frostpunk 2 is a masterclass in storytelling and strategy, a must-play for any fan of the genre. I wholeheartedly recommend it to those seeking a challenge and a rich, engaging story.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing sequel to frostpunk 1. They really fleshed out the QoL and city planning in this one. The new council and faction mechanics are also extremely cool and fun to play around with. The story mode can be replayed multiple times with favoring different factions and unlocking their special effects.The funniest thing is the efficiency programme employees that remove their arms and replace them with pickaxes, that is just pure dedication for work
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: I have to disagree with many of the negative reviews. For me, moving away from managing individual people to focusing on a larger scale feels like a positive change. The district placement puzzle may be a familiar mechanic, but it still works well, and I have no complaints there. In the previous game, I didn’t enjoy placing everything around the generator because of the autoscale feature, which felt clunky. The unpredictable heat zones from the extra towers were also not fun to manage. That said, the shift to the new model overall feels like a good direction for me. I definitely don’t miss the hassle of micromanaging individual sick workers based on their location.That being said, just like the original game, the developers still haven’t provided the necessary tools to plan effectively. In a game all about planning, where are the tools? There are none. You’d probably have to print out a map and plan everything on paper.There’s no way to keep hexes visible, no way to view the map without height interference, no way to force district borders to show, no way to pre-place or mark something. How are you supposed to PLAN your city? In a game where the core gameplay loop revolves around city planning, this lack of tools is a serious issue. It turns into an exercise in frustration.Maybe the developers expect you to plan hundreds of tiles in your head, or offline, or think it’s fun to play suboptimally because "planning is tough" - but none of that is enjoyable. I need the ability to mark the map, plan districts, and predict how things will turn out. The challenge should come from meaningful choices, not from a cumbersome UI. A bad interface is not a fun challenge. The first game could get away with a suboptimal UI because it was innovative. This game, however, has an even worse UI, yet relies more heavily on it for its core puzzle, and that’s just unacceptable.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Great deviation from the traditional Frostpunk. I see many reviews stating that this isn't Frostpunk anymore and I agree that it is vastly different from the original Frostpunk, but only in fantastic ways. (I don't see the point in releasing a second game if it's almost identical). This is a realistic portrayal of survival and continuation of the human race. Frostpunk 1 is survival --> Frostpunk 2 is survival + rebuilding/redefining society through your actions and choices with the factions.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: I personally really liked the first frostpunk game, and this sequel does not disappoint. Building entire districts instead of individual buildings and trying to gather enough resources to maintain the city is one thing, but also trying to opese the many factions who all have diferent ideas for the future of the city makes this a very challenging city builder.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: The decisions made for improvements from Frostpunk 1 to Frostpunk 2 are a downgrade what made the first unique. Bigger does not always mean beter and this is the case in Frostpunk situation, where it was a turn off for the majority of Frostpunk fans including myself. In Frostpunk 1 the deaths of people had meaningfull impact for the story and your gameplay, as in Frostpunk 2 its just like "yeah we will just allow some randoms in our City to compensate for the loses". What was cool at start were the different buffs and nerfs you can combine and role the dice if it will apply through the voting system. However it becomes boring fast and I mean really fast as it just RNG system similar as with slotmachines but you can influence or manipulate the votes in your favor. You are so busy learning and playing with these complex systems that you forget that you playing a survival sim instead of another sim city clone.I miss the tense situation I had with the last mission in Frostpunk1, where my small city was almost burning through the last  coals during a snowstorm with possible revolts could happen any time. My people still had hope and put all their trust in me as their leader. With tensions rising I made the decisions to become a dictator, where i made some unethical decisions, that resulted in unhappiness and revolts everywhere. On the brink of losing everything, and I had no options to turn the situation around anymore. The snowstorm ended and a notification came that we survived. I am still surprised that I finished the mission as I replayed the last mission many times and failed. Never knew the dictator route got me through this hard mission.If they ever make a Frostpunk 3, they should go back to smaller cities or towns, where the immersion and the impact of decisions is more visable and meaningful. We dont need another Sim city clone with slotmachine mechanics and badly implemented ai generated areas.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: i have over 70 plus hours on FP1 and loved the game. i was so excited about FP2 and man did you fail. i loved how you could see the heat zones and control the temp in FP1. i loved how you could see the people moving in FP1 but in this it feeks like a cheap 1990 game. look you had the right ideal with the voting and new settlements. i love how you can just keep growing the population but trying to keep the peace is annoying. you can prob save this game if you somehow put heat zones back into the game. just sad to see a monster of a game FP1 then this crap FP2 comes out.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk 2 pulls me back into its icy, unforgiving world, where leading a society to survival is both a strategic and moral challenge. This sequel shifts the focus to oil as a key resource, adding new layers of complexity and forcing even harder decisions. Every choice feels meaningful, making me constantly question how far I’m willing to go for the greater good.Visually, the game is stunning, with improved graphics and a haunting soundtrack that sets the tone perfectly. The expanded mechanics for city-building and resource management are deeper and more satisfying, though the difficulty might feel overwhelming for newcomers.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: It is not frostpunk 1, and i understand that's what a lot of people wanted.But I still get the same feelings that the first gave me. The tension building, the nervousness, the oh god i forgot to prepare for the temperature drops. All in all. It's not a carbon copy of frostpunk 1, but it still has the soul that gave me so many hours of joy before.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: They managed to keep the identity of the first game, while reworking the mechanics and giving it a whole new scope. I'm getting as involved in the game as I was in the first opus, trying to manage everything as best as I can to get enough resources, control the people etc... and I don't see the time flying and I don't want to stop my session ! Now you get to handle a much bigger city and the politics and factions aspect is much more prominent. I can't wait to see what the campaign has in reserve for me, and also to start a new game after that to see how much better I will do with everything that I will have learnt.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game is excellent - do not listen to the 2-hours-on-record reviewers who expected the same game as last time, with a new skin. This is how you make a sequel - you push the concept in a new and exciting direction while maintaining the spirit and feel of the old game! This is an excellent and deep city buidling, reminding me of the early days of the genre in the 90's. Yes, there is a deep political system to understand, but once you do, the system does a great work at puting the different factions in your city at odds with each other, with you trying to minimize the damage....or just taking outright control. Some people have complained about that the placement of buildings doesnt matter, that the game is simple to beat without spending time with careful placement. There is a solution to that, obviously...increase the difficulty. I have tried the highest difficulty, and trust me, at that point every single decision and buidling has to be very thought through. 11/10, would incarcerate, sterilize and exile the opposition again.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: This doesn't hit as hard as the first game. It's not a bad game in my eyes, but it lacks a clear vision. I personally don't like the direction the devs went in. I think all this game has to offer should have just been introduced into the first game. Such as establishing colony outposts and expanding beyond your initial city.Nothing really matters anymore. Death? It used to make me cringe everytime I'd hear the bell in the first game. Knowing there was a huge problem in my city, knowing that I was losing CRUCIAL workforce. In this game, whenever I hear the death sound I just don't care. People are endless in this game. You can find them all over the frostland, plus you get population growth. Also, the main plot? It kinda sucks honestly. At least the ending I got. I pledged to overpower the cold and restore a warm spot. But I didn't even get to see anything cool out of it! All the sacrifice, all the voices I suppressed. And I didn't even get to see like, plants growing or the local climate actually warming! All I did was burn extra fuel for literally nothing in return. Unless you call the game guilt-tripping me for suppressing other voices a reward. Look.. I get the idea behind the plot. You're supposed to listen to everyone. You can't create a "utopia" with one vision. Well guess what? It's STUPID. This is not a deep, enriching experience. The first game it certainly felt horrible when you crossed the line, this game it has no emotional impact on me. The soundtrack is kinda good, I'd still say the first game is better though. That's how I feel about the whole game honestly. "Kinda good, but the first one is better."The one thing about this game I love is the frostland and colonization. That's something I deeply wanted in the first game. Other than that though, I would prefer the first game.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a fan of FP1. I like the new political/faction system in FP2, but I hate the new building/district system, so much that I only played 9 hours and probably won't play anymore. I can't say it's a bad game, actually it seems like a very good one. And it is beautiful. I guess I had other expectations. I would have preferred to leave a neutral review.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: I don't typically write reviews, but both Frostpunk games are just amazing. This second game though at first I was a little disappointing as they went from micro management of the city to macro management, I was afraid I wouldn't get a similar experience of always being on the edge of my seat to barley missing catastrophes (be it environmental or political). The more I play Frostpunk 2 though the more I like the focus on not just the city, but the surrounding area (which was less so in the first game). You can still get the same feels of difficulty and balancing decisions that never truly everyone is happy with mixed with not just playing a Frostpunk with new paint on it. I think they did a great job on this second game, if you liked the first one I think you'll like the second one. Just give it a little time to get over the changes and for sure make sure to play the story first, it's a great narrative to play through!.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: There are other, more detailed comments that describe my problem with the game quite fittingly. But i want to summarize the main points for myself:Totally different compared to the first game and overall, i think that's a great idea. The setting is amazing and to approach the setting and story with a different gameplay is sooo much better than to just do the same again. Sadly the new approach didn't work for me very well, because: - The city building feels kinda boring and i can't really get the feeling of it being MY precious city (mainly because you only really see the districts that are planted and all the different special addon buildings are not worth mentioning)- Differences between the special buildings of the different factions are totally irrelevant... bit more workers, bit more output, bit more heat... that's all there is to it) --> i think there was to much focus on the really good politic system and the differences there - Campaign was fun, but so much less compared to the first game. There you had different settings, different objectives on different maps... here you just stay at the same point and if you play slow you are so strong at around chapter 2 or 3 that you can finish the rest of the chapters in 30min I really hope that the add-ons and patches bring more stuff to the campaign and more differences between the special add-on buildings (optical and mechanic)...  but at the moment there isn't enough content/fun for me to recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10 game. cured my OCD. there is a sTELLAR lack of long-term consequences for not being perfect in mid/late game no matter the difficulty & i love it. thousands of citizens may die while you're off in the frostlands twiddling your thumbs in 3x speed, but when u check back in even 10+ years later, theyre just still hangin in there, deposits depleted, freezing their butts off but still trusting you somehow??? nothing is unfixable even if you start torturing them on purpose for three whiteouts straight on capt. difficulty apparently LMAO. really giving me that much needed microdose of the 'man ig we still living' mentality all OCDers gotta snag.genuinely the game is so much fun, I cannot seem to put it down. 30 hours played in only three sessions since i bought it can tell you that much though LOL
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: What i wanted frost punk 1 to be but instead of being so intricate building roads and upclose with buildings ( kinda miss that part)  not done yet but the exploration is way more satisfying. Take a good pc for late game or turn it down but kinda looks cheese , make sure to put sharpness to 100% as it wont tell you but recommends!4/5
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Out of the 12+ hours it took me to complete the main storyline campaign, I spent more than half of that time with the sound completely turned off due to crashes that could only be fixed this way.As for the game itself, the sequel disappointed me. The game mechanics shifted the focus from planning, resource management, and city-building to micromanaging numbers. The story is weak, and the sense of weight behind decisions is gone. The balance on normal difficulty doesn't offer any challenge. The interface is very rough; it was radically changed and made worse, with some necessary and functional features from the first game missing. The tutorial isn't fully thought out—sometimes it was very unclear what to do to complete a story mission. Graphically and visually, I didn’t notice any significant improvement either.Conclusion: the game wasn’t polished at launch, but more importantly, the developers fundamentally took a wrong step in terms of game design, and unfortunately, that's something that can’t be fixed.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game lacks soul. The Frostpunk experience we had in first game is completely gone.In general I would recommend the game as a game, but I do not recommend as a Frostpunk successor. This game has no Frostpunk vibes, it's basically Cities Skylines: Frostpunk, just with some annoying politics overlay. Or maybe Civilization. Or something in-between.Frostpunk made us relate to, and care about our citizens. Every single one mattered. Every single cold wave made us fight for the survival of all of our fellow citizens. Deciding if we should lower heating in the hospital, or maybe in the food farm. Decisions, hard decisions.Frostpunk 2 is more like... excel balancing simulator. I do understand that time has passed and the city building is a bit on the bigger scale, but having tens of thousands people? I'm completely detached from them. They are just a number in a sheet. Hell, I can't even see them - the game just adds some Tron-like light-lazers traveling around the city. Also, what the hell is going on with the roads connections (the automatically generated ones)?I wish it was more like Frostpunk 1, just with maybe hundreds-to-thousands instead of tens of thousands of people? The politics aren't too bad, but they are a bit annoying and with the detachement from our citizens... Meh.Also, heatstamps. That's a hard pass. "We are staaarving! We have the resources to build food producing buildings, but we rather die than build it without getting those sweet, sweet heatstamps!" -_-...Performance also seems to be an issue.I have radeon 7900 XTX (24GB vram), Ryzen 7900, 64 GB RAM and 12000mb/s SSD.I'd expect this game to have a bit more than just 25-30 FPS on 4k resolution having everything on ultra. 90% of display is literally snow, doesn't seem to be super complicated to compute. There's no ray-tracing. Turning on FSR to Quality mode and turning on frame generation makes it better, 80-100 FPS, but dear lord, those options should be an addition for lower end computers, not a must-have on a non-raytracing game.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk 1 is easily in my top 3 games of all time, I loved it and got a huge amount of replay-ability from it. Frostpunk 2 is a great move on, the graphics and sound are absolutely gorgeous. The story is great and the NPCs have been really well thought through.  However, my one moan is that there is an awful lot going on that isn't explained. The help window is useful for some aspects but I felt like I was 'winging it' throughout most of the story play through because things weren't backed up via a tutorial. The tutorial that is included is very basic. I am now playing through endless mode and still loving it but I am learning far more in there than I did through the actual story. I would still recommend this if you are a lover of Frostpunk 1 as a challenging sequel but I think more need to be done to explain the new game mechanics.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: I am a huge fan of the original (1000 + hours) and I am in love with this sequel. The gameplay is quite different and yes there are some UI/ quality of life things that could be improved, however the world still has its richness, the moral choices are still there, and the story is fantastic. This is a new story building off of the original but it really does stand on its own and I have not found another similar city builder out there.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: An Amazing City Builder/Management game with a incredibly unique Theme and setting.the story mode does a great job at streamlining you through a well paced tutorial slowly teaching you everything you need to know before making your own fresh world state.even if your new to the genre this game would be a great start point.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk 2 is mixed for me. So I settled on positive with the assumption that the game would fix a lot of technical problems I'm going to complain about and that part of the problem is just me as a player.If you played Frostpunk 1(you don't have too to understand/play this game by the way) your skill is transferable. The scope here is much broader, you don't see individuals in the snow or machinery/automatons truck out to an area to clear it. The individualism banding together to survive the frost fades away into people having gotten a foothold and talking about politics and ways of life. People die but there are swaths in the Frostland to recruit making it numbers to refill over personal worry. Instead of four different types of workers(Worker, Engineer, Automaton, child) they are now one conglomerate workforce. The game wants to have 'gotcha' moments about peoples personal lives and health, much like the first game had 'did you cross the line' moments, but for players returning that can feel off. They'll probably notice that individual, close-knit intimacy with the cities survivors was gone. The game is run on bigger time scales, bigger cities, bigger and lofty ideas. It's a grand way to go for a sequel but I missed the intimacy of the first. Truly though, that's a me problem I just think others might have. It's good game with some:Technical problems. That would include bad UI placement. I'm trying to research something and click it but the game decides I actually clicked on the nearby but not overlapping map icon, bad. Or I interact with someone but the buttons available to do anything don't register unless I click on the far left side specifically. Researching grinds my gear a little, requiring Heatstamps(currency here) but not letting you see what you have without exiting and re-entering the screen. It also doesn't show what you're researching. You have to find it. For infinite resources you can place a Deep Drill onto a 'infinite' tile but it doesn't say that anywhere. Replacing a law doesn't tell you what effects are lost/changing, or if there's a law in place at all. The game stutters hard when autosaving and stutters some when going to the map via scroll out. Adaptation is laughably overpowered compared to anything else, the easy modes easy mode.The music is beautiful and the visuals, especially people and how it's stylized in pop ups, are gorgeous. The game oozes 'ends meet the means' in game form.Good game but if you're a Frostpunk 1 fan be ready for the changes. I personally would've been happier at $30. I 100% it, but I'm not sure if I'll be back beyond base game.Generic tricks and tips for the interested:-Build Housing Districts next to each other to lower heat requirement, and keep in mind Districts can be expanded so there's no need to go all out building like 5 housing Districts off the bat-Get prefabs. _childDocuments_.review: Let's get one thing of the way real quick: Is this a bad game? Not at all, there's a very good amount of work and passion put into it. Now, is this a good sequel to Frostpunk? Well, you can see the negative on top of the review, so let me break this down:First of all, the game has been streamlined substantially (And that goes past the logical consequences of having a game with a larger scale, mind you).Automatons and their unique playstyle? Now they are just additional workforce, if you happen to find them.Day-night cycle, with the corresponding differences in gameplay? GoneGranular system of healing, sickness and amputees? GoneManaging heat zones and individual temperatures? All has been combined under just "Heat". If you have positive heat, you're good, and if you don't, turning off individual districts is even more busywork than turning heaters off was in FP1.The city building portion is kind of a missed opportunity. They play around with the idea of tiles interacting with each other, but it doesn't go past "Huddle districts together for heat" and "Houses next to industries increase Squalor". There are some "valuable" tiles (Like crevasses that provide a Shelter and Heat bonus), but overall this system, while cool, is way underutilized. The buildings are interesting, but rather than developing unique buildings for different alignments like there was in FP1, the buildings are basically either “Regular building” or “Regular building+X bonus/penalizer”, which makes them feel pretty samey. Sure, there are alignment-specific buildings, but they are the exception rather than the rule.For all the comments about how much grander the scale of this game is compared to the first one, this game can be seriously micro-intensive. For the FP1 veterans who are reading this: Remember The Refugees, and how one of the challenges was having to deal with a constantly increasing population for the first half of the game? The whole game is like this. The population keeps expanding at a fairly ridiculous pace, both from births and from “people migrating to the city” (Fairly surprising, considering that we were supposedly the last city on Earth, but there we go). Losing due to a population boom is a very real risk, and you have to be constantly building new housing districts and infrastructure to support your ever-increasing population. It gets to the point that one of the most coveted late game abilities is one that can decrease your population growth.The first (and so far, only) scenario gives me mixed feelings. On one hand, it’s really nice to revisit the Frostlands and see all references to the previous game, but on the other, the scenario looks more like a beefed-up tutorial than an actual campaign, and the finale absolutely pales in comparison to the one in A New Home. Besides, the game absolutely railroads you into the events of the finale, and they can come off as really contrived depending on your actions throughout the game.Also, for all the big talk about the transition to oil, it is basically coal by another name. It doesn’t require any special infrastructure to store or process compared to coal, and other than focusing exclusively on oil for fuel (Which is optional), not much changes when you discover it.However, there are some actual improvements here too. Some laws can synergize with other laws or buildings to improve their function, and you can amend some laws to make them less extreme after passing them. The announcer, as well as the vignettes you get in response to certain laws and events are nicely written and help you connect a bit with the regular lives of your citizens. Also, while the game pretty much forces you to play with more than one settlement (At least in the campaign), having to babysit more than one instance is fairly nicely done and it did not make me want to punch my monitor like other similar games did, so kudos for that.As it stands, besides the bugs and poor performance (Which will probably get patched soon), the game is pretty deficient in content at the moment. Sure, FP1 did not have Endless at launch and only had 3 scenarios, but there is only so much you can do in Utopia before it starts to get stale (And this game is 50% more expensive than FP1, mind you).Unless they pull all the stops with their DLCs (Or bank on the modding community to pick up the slack for them), as it stands, I am not sure if this can be a decent follow up to Frostpunk 1. Keep your expectations seriously in check.

_childDocuments_.review: In fact, I have some ideas about new game.As it turned out, my expectations differed from the developers' plans. I don't know how much the changes spoil the new game, it's up to you to decide.The new game was created with an emphasis on politics, not building. Now there is no possibility to build a single building, as it was in the first game. In the new game, building is possible in entire districts or settlements. That’s I don’t like. Of course, it greatly expands the city, but in my opinion, manual building of single houses with a separate possibility of building districts would be more interesting.The interface has changed a lot, it has become less clear and convenient. The first half hour of the game I had to figure out the interface. The light background is somehow not very suitable for this game.Unlike the first game, the new game does not have such ultimate tasks as in the first one. For example, such as: "the end justifies the means" or "sacrifice everything for the sake of survival and the building of reactors." Now, instead of building a reactor as quickly as possible, you have to spend more time searching for resources and politics.I don't know if it worth making a new game with such differences. Personally, I expected a continuation of the first game, with approximately the same mechanics, but on a larger scale, variability and content.If the scale was possible to make in the new game, then the rest is questionable. Was it worth sacrificing the ability to manually build one-offs for the sake of scale? And the content  in the form of individual buildings, such as medical centers, taverns, etc., will not increase using district construction methods. Thanks to the advent of politics with variability, everything is now fine, but the realistic ultimatum from the first part is gone.The graphics in the game look good, but I did not notice any serious improvements compared to the first game.It is upset that the zoom only works on significant buildings that are built after research. That is, the developers did not work out the details of most of the buildings that occupy a vast area of ​​the map, so you won't be able to see them up close. By the way, the optimization at the start of the game can be called "normal" compared to many other new products in recent years :)Overall, I think it turned out to be a good continuation of the series with new features and a larger scale. Someone will definitely like the new product, someone, like me, will not like it because of the innovations listed. The quality of the game does not get worse from this, and the desire for something new creates new impressions and encourages interest. Therefore, I give it a positive rating.

_childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk was a game where you took the role as captain in order to save your city, save your fellow refugees, save seeds for a warmer earth that might never come. You personally ordered the construction of each and every individual building, every hot house, hunters hut, home to keep your people warm and safe, infirmary to treat your sick, Coal mine to keep the generator running, factory to make prosthetics for your people and automatons to work tirelessly, hot air balloons to try and claw back the world from that cold Indifferent death. Every law signed to respect the dead, advance Research, address issues, give your people a fighting chance, make the decision to rule with by law or faith. Every worker assigned to a hot workplace Where they would be safe, a cold workplace Where they might get sick and take up room in your infirmaries, a dangerous workplace where they might come back home in a coffin or be harvested for their organs or thrown in a corpse pit, assigned to a 24-hour shift where they may collapse and die. What was built, where people worked and how they worked, how Your people interacted with each other, how your people lived how, what would be done with their corpses, how you chose to face That indifferent white deaf which stole the world from you and every single person you will ever govern, all of them looking to you for answers, for hope, For a strong hand or a guiding prayer. Frostpunk is not a normal city builder, it Is a story of survival where you guide your people to live and adapt in a cold world that does not care for their lives, their hopes, dreams, cries, prayers or final breaths. Frostpunk is a game where you will care when for 5 people get sick, Frostpunk 2 is a game where you care when 500 people get sick. I like the game play of Frostpunk 2, it can be stressful and demanding yet rewarding to bring yourself out of the red and build up your city, but I did not feel a personal attachment to my people. I was not the captain, I was not a strong hand or the singer of a guiding prayer, I was an elected official who could just be as easily replaced as I was placed into my position. I was not the captain I was the steward; I was to govern the city by approving laws, construction of districts, research projects, and where to break and batter the frost that choked the land. I strongly recommend being a captain, if you like the idea of building up a city and watching it grow While dealing with demanding and stressful game systems but with good gameplay Then I recommend being a steward. I really love Frostpunk I think it's great, I don't Frostpunk 2, I like it I think they did a good job for a sequel but not a perfect one. Well maybe for others but not for me, that personal connection you had to the community you cared for was unique, it was something that separated the game from almost anything I had ever played. The art team sound team and every other team that worked on the game did a great job, I think it's a very good sequel but I think it needs more, more ways to connect you personally to the people of your community, to show you the effects of your actions, to show what politics is like in such a Cold Indifferent world. I think it needs more And I am Optimistically waiting for more content to come. Thank you 11 bit studios for making both Frostpunk 1 and 2, and thank you for reading my review.TLDR: A pretty good sequel that takes a very different approach from the original. 7/10

Compared to Frostpunk 1, where you had to deal with a significantly smaller population and assign each individual, the sequel is on a much larger scale. Although you could argue that this means the game has less feeling and heart in it, I disagree, looking at it from a different angle, its just as impactful. _childDocuments_.review: I've seen some reviews saying that this game is too different from Frostpunk 1 - and it's true, and I would say that's the whole point. If you're looking for a game that is essentially the same as Frostpunk 1 but with more features, this isn't that.This is not an upgrade of Frostpunk 1 - it is a sequel in the narrative sense as well as the chronological sense, and the mechanics reflect this - either you'll like that or you won't. Frostpunk 1 is about the immediate survival after the end of the world, where every life counts - Frostpunk 2 states it's theme openly "you've survived the end of the world - now what?". It imagines what happens after you reach the point in Frostpunk 1 where you've established a self-sustaining city, and carries on from that point. Suddenly your concern is not individual lives, but the lives of thousands, then tens of thousands - and all the complexity, politics, and needs that go along with it. So yes, this game is different to Frostpunk 1, it isn't an upgrade to Frostpunk 1, it isn't even a reason to uninstall Frostpunk 1. In my view the two games complement each other by telling the story of two very different eras of human survival - you'll either like that idea or you won't. You'll see people in the reviews on both sides of that - neither are unreasonable, it just comes down to what you're looking for in this game.But is it a good game? I would say absolutely - it's engaging, has depth, gives you challenging decisions of a different nature to Frostpunk 1, and has a fantastic atmosphere. So far I've thoroughly enjoyed it - but I can also see myself replaying both games, 1 and 2, in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: There is a lot to say about Frostpunk 2If you came into this game expecting more of the first game then you will be disappointed. Frostpunk 2 is an entirely different game than the first one.  Instead of desperately trying to survive against all odds with a small community and limited resources you are expanding into a full blown city builder with an economy, districts system, politics, logistics with outposts, etc. That being said, it is a *very* good city builder, and if you like this genre of gaming then I can wholeheartedly recommend this game to you.However, when comparing it to the first game it falls short. -A big reason the first game was so fun was the huge stakes with the small community, every decision mattered. In this game the story feels pretty scripted, and even the "major" decisions don't seems to have that much effect on the game.-In the first game, every death hurt. If you lost 10 people to a mine collapse that could cripple your settlement. Contrasted to Frostpunk 2 where you don't really care if hundreds of people die since population is a renewable resource, it really takes the stakes out it.-The economy/resource system in this game while being more complex, ends up being much easier than the first game. Once you have stable income on resources this game becomes a cakewalk, and you don't feel the struggle of trying to meet your objectives or the sacrifices you had to make to succeed.-This game feels *significantly* shorter than the first one. Instead of multiple, separate scenarios there is one large campaign that goes from one event to the next. Overall, the campaign feels slightly longer than one scenario from the first game. There might be more content on the way in the form of DLC's (like the first game) but it is still a disappointing lack of content for the base game.-So much of the charm from the first game is lost with this one, you don't see the people running around going to their jobs, automatons are not stomping around, snow isn't piling up in the cold areas and melting away in the warm ones. And the city planning feels much less important/impactful in this game with a lack of "heat zones" and instead treats heat (as well as sickness) as just another number to keep track of.So why am I still recommending this game despite all of the negatives I listed above? Because comparing to the first game is unfair, it is impossible to capture lightning twice and if you separate it from the first one this game still stands above many others in the genre. Despite the flaws it is still a very well-built, fun city builder that manages to capture the ~vibes~ of the first game while still being mechanically distinct. Overall I would rate this game 7.5-8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Ultimately the game is a really good city builder but it kinda lost a lot of its impact from the first game. somehow there are 6 factions but none of them feel like they have any impact at all. I felt no need to really interact with them or their special techs until the game artificially forces you to by forcing something that wouldn't happen if you had good relations with all factions and placated them all throughout.The district building is interesting but I liked the first game for the small scale of desperate small hold outs of humanity. not thousands and thousands of people which creates a sense that the people dont even matter anymore, previously every death meant something now it kind just becomes a pop up which hardly has impact at all.the law system by the end removed any sense of impact when things are voted on by people who can change it constantly. the first while it felt interesting but eventually with so many laws constantly changing I forgot what all of them did and began ignoring it other than when I needed influence with a specific groupresources feel really dumbed down, just found myself placing a new district whenever the last one ran out, no sense of urgency to get resources since almost everything resource wise is a mundane upkeep with only 1 actual "resource" being used for building.Sense of the heat was completely lost, maybe I just minmaxed without realising it but literally all my fuel that kept me going for the whole game was secured within the first year. I went back to the location to upgrade it maybe once.The big story event that is meant to create tension is a new whiteout similar to the first game, is a complete joke, no sense of impending doom, didnt even touch my resource count, I was literally still producing excess food and fuel throughout the whiteout which in the end was only annoying because it stopped me from scouting. I still seen everything and could interact my colony which was completely unaffected and still somehow was shipping fuel in what was apparently so bad a storm it is meant to bring everything to a stop.The other big story plot factor of either taming the cold or adapting to it was dull at best. I didnt feel at the end I had tamed the cold, I felt like that after maybe the first chapter? and in a "I have unlimited fuel" way not a "we are saving the world" way. The other route, adaptation really doesnt feel like adapting at all, sure the laws and research are stuff like foraging etc but I didnt at all feel like I was becoming nomads or really taking advantage of the wasteland.a huge amount of the story leans on locations from the first game too and not in a good way, there are locations like the prison ship which could be extremely interesting are literally just a little bit of text and a choice with 0 impact, you can find teslas experiments and even find a strange formation caused by it where you can "drill in to investigate" I got really exicted and interested but there was no flavour after that just a small amount of resources. Let me colonise these locations, continue the experiments, theres even mention of nuclear power from a group and then it isnt touched. Old locations return only for it to be tied to a choice and that you might just lose access to it after maybe 5 weeks at it which is such a short amount of time in the game time.Again even after bashing all these things its a good city builder and it does everything well for a city builder that is meant to be about making political bargains whilst also balancing resources but I dont feel like im surviving and hardly hanging on like in one, I dont feel like I am making deep choices that have huge impacts on my people like in one and I feel like thats what the heart of the first game was, it was a city builder yeah but it was a dark gritty survival game forcing YOU not some council to make the hard choices for your people. I mustve played all the scenarios of FP1 into the double digits over the years, I imagine I will only come back to this to play DLC which I have already paid for since I punished myself by avoiding any early access gameplay. The game scaled too much too fast and as I keep saying lost its character as the cost which for a game which people got for the character and environment is kinda sadI recommend this game but do not expect anywhere as much grit and atmosphere as the first one, its less frostpunk and more a city builder in a snowy wasteland now.

_childDocuments_.review: Would I recommend it? Yes. Have I played it enough to give a well rounded and full review? No. Am I gonna review it anyways? Yes.In the simplest of terms, the game is a solid city builder, with common resource management supply lines. The environment of the game is more unique than the core gameplay loop, as the snow and interesting post-apocalyptic steampunk look offers an interesting design and look. Compared to many other city builders it offers more on the story side of things. Gameplay loop and multitude of difficulty settings seems to offer good replayability value and challenge.How does it compare to Frostpunk 1? Would I recommend it to people who liked the first game?I would say the first game offers more variance and story with all the different scenarios. The first game was more focused on the individuals and the closer camera angle to your city and citizens made you feel more close to the people and their suffering. I personally also felt that the first game had more options in progression, with population based workforce compared to automatons. Frostpunk 2 has quite a good amount of research, map exploration, secondary colonies, etc. that are interesting changes compared to the first game.In my honest opinion, if you liked the story and personal connection of the first game more than the city building aspects, you might not like Frostpunk 2 as much. Overall it is a solid sequel that evolved in most aspects and stepped back in others.

_childDocuments_.review: I've never dropped a game so fast in my life after beating it.  There's nothing super wrong with frostpunk 2, it's well polished, it does exactly what its designed to do.  The problem is it's very shallow and soulless.  No matter how you're playing, your city will always look like the same general blur of ramshackle buildings.  If you see 100 different player's cities, none of them will have an ounce of personality or individuality because all the districts look extremely similar and blur together and there's no options in the game for any sort of creative design, decoration, or aesthetic choices.  Once you understand the core mechanics of the game and how to win, there's really no replay value because all that's available to you is doing the same thing over again.  Frostpunk 2 is a very simple puzzle game about adjacency bonuses and balancing resources and very little more.  Disappointing.  Worth a single 15-20 hour play through if you can get the game on sale

_childDocuments_.review: It is worth appreciating the creators for leaving their comfort zone, taking risks and not simply copying the original Frostpunk.I love the way the main storyline of the game is narrated, in addition to text inserts we also get shots of views of our developing city. The snowstorms look phenomenal, the prologue and the later reference to it are also brilliantly done, and the mention of Lily May (IYKYK) was no small surprise.This title is currently unique on the gaming market, something I have been looking for for a long time, because in addition to the typical elements of a city builder - building districts, meeting the needs of residents, we also have a highly developed system of politics and introducing laws in the city. A huge plus for the fact that compared to the first Frostpunk, the laws are not one-dimensional and can be tightened/softened based on the requests of residents - this provides additional immersion. The way the factions are presented can certainly be compared to how it looks in the real world, people with extreme views clash, extremist factions are formed - I don't know of any other title that would reflect the political system in such a way.The aspects of building a post-apocalyptic metropolis are also excellent - yes, the creators moved away from building individual buildings in favor of building entire districts, but this brings with it other mechanics worth refining (the appropriate layout of districts, building logistics centers, etc.).Sound has also entered the next level, or more precisely the "voices" of the residents, which change depending on how much they trust us and what relations we have with the factions, as well as the brilliant soundtrack.The only thing that can be criticized here is the optimization, I hope that 11bit will introduce a few improvements to the optimization in the coming months.

_childDocuments_.review: Really amazing example of a sequel. This game doesn't attempt to replace the original, so much as expand the experience in a new direction, and it is done very well. While the game is more abstract now, it also adds new and engaging systems that more than compensate for the shift away from the more granular approach of the first game. Edit Insertion: After reading some other reviews, I decided to point out here that it seems like your experience of Frostpunk 2 is largely shaped by your expectations. If you are expecting a 1:1 successor of the original, you will be disappointed. Frostpunk 2 is simply not designed to be the same experience as the first game, though I would argue it complements it beautifully. Personally, I love what 11-bit studios did here. Rather than make a sequel with the intention of replacing the first game, they preserved the uniqueness of the original and made a sequel that is a different game. As a result, some people who loved the original may not enjoy the sequel in the same way, but I highly encourage you to give it a chance. It is certainly different, but it is also extremely well done, and the losses from the original are well compensated for by the new systems, choices, and open ended story telling. End Edit.To me, the details of the political system, resource management, and stockpile system made this game feel like the best city management simulator I have ever played. It is beautiful, and there are many technical aspects that really prong the experience together, such as the seamless zooming from the city, to the frostlands map, to the colonies. Not to mention, as far as I can tell this launch had no noticable bugs. My highest praise has to be for the designers ability to make this game feel like it is rich with difficult and meaningful choices. From the small every day decisions of which Faction to support or appease, to the major long term choices like what type of generator you will use. I highly recommend playing this game on the highest difficulty you can. The game is at its best when it has an edge of desperation and constantly being short on some resources, as it really forces you to think about your choices.All in all, a fantastic game, and probably my most highly recommended city builder/manager. I still love the original, and recommend you play it, but this is a fantastic continuation of the experience. If you liked the original, you should certainly pick this up.

_childDocuments_.review: No Restart?2.5/5As a huge fan of the original Frostpunk, I was really excited for this, but I have to admit, it’s been a mixed bag so far. The game is stunning, no doubt about that, but the actual experience has been frustrating.Gameplay: 2/5The learning curve is way steeper than it should be, especially compared to Frostpunk 1. Without a decent in-game tutorial or solid online guides, you’re left to figure things out on your own—and it’s far from intuitive, even for a veteran like me. The real deal-breaker though? After messing up on the first level, I wanted to restart... but apparently, there’s no easy way to do that? Either the restart option is hidden deep in the UI, or it doesn’t exist at all. Both of these options are terrible from a UX standpoint.Graphics: 5/5No complaints here. The visuals are stunning and beautifully capture the grim, icy apocalypse we love. Every detail feels meticulously crafted, and it really pulls you into the atmosphere.Soundtrack: 4.5/5The music is hauntingly beautiful and elevates the mood of the game. It perfectly captures the bleakness and intensity of the world, making every decision feel even more significant.User Experience: 1.5/5Sadly, the user experience just isn't up to par. The UI feels clunky, and small but essential features (like restarting a level) are either missing or unnecessarily hard to find. It’s frustrating when basic functionality feels like a puzzle.Overall: 2.5/5There’s potential here, but right now, it feels like it’s being held back by poor design choices. The graphics and soundtrack are amazing, but they’re not enough to compensate for the lackluster gameplay and clumsy UI. A few patches could make this a much better experience, but as it stands, it’s a letdown for fans of the original.

_childDocuments_.review: I had been eagerly anticipating Frostpunk 2 for a long time and preordered the deluxe edition, but unfortunately, I’ve found it quite disappointing.1. GraphicsThe first game featured detailed models and captivating environments where every citizen had a role to play. In contrast, the sequel presents districts filled with small buildings and a lack of life—where are the inhabitants? We’re only given numbers to indicate living, working, and deceased citizens. In my opinion, the graphics have noticeably downgraded compared to the original Frostpunk.2. OptimizationThe optimization leaves much to be desired. Without using FSR 3.0, I struggled to maintain a stable 60 FPS on medium/high settings with my RTX 3080 laptop at 2K resolution and DLSS set to Balance. Why not to implement FSR 3.1, which offers better scaling and works with a separate frame generator compatible with DLSS, that was released in June? I can’t help but wonder why the game demands such significant resources without delivering the stunning visuals I expected.3. GameplayThe gameplay feels simplified compared to the first installment. There’s a limited variety of district types and resources, and many of the laws are reminiscent of those in the original game. The council system lacks excitement; it’s nearly impossible to gain a majority for votes, even with good relationships with all factions, withount negotiations. The thrill and tension that characterized the first game are missing.Additionally, the tutorial is quite lacking. How was I supposed to know I needed to expand a living district to build a Research Institute? I ended up searching online for answers, but couldn’t find any helpful information in the game itself.4. StoryThe story fails to captivate, lacking scripted events and feeling rather short and uninspired.Perhaps the game will improve over time with patches, additional content, and optimization, but as it stands, I don’t believe it’s worth the full price for now.

_childDocuments_.review: Very different from the first game but in my personal view, this makes sense. Let me explain..In the first game things start small. Clusters of people eking out an existence. Localised industry if you were lucky to find the things necessary. On a small scale one person or group could keep control. Now things have grown to a massive scale! More people means more industry. which in turn means more fuel...In addition one persons dream is no longer enough. More people means more ideas, more systems of thought. More factions. Hence the need for a Parliament like system of government. The need for oil and less reliance on coal makes sense when you realise your little community has/is heading for the next industrial revolution. With this context in mind...The new way Frostpunk plays makes sense on so many levels. Yes the first game felt more personal. You knew people and their names. Each person felt important, and you felt each and every loss deeply. But now, the city has grown so large, its not possible to have that close connection. Your only connection is through the representatives of these different groups who give you a rough idea of what is best for your city. The control of your citizens is more detailed as now the emphasis is not just survival but developing a new civilisation. In conclusion....If you are expecting the same game as the first frostpunk, you will be disappointed. But for the reasons i have given (in line with the lore) if you change your perspective and see why the changes have been made....you will LOVE this game. Its more in depth, more complicated, more detailed, more demanding to control your city. Before the Generator was everything, but now it has become the beating heart of this living, breathing, multi-headed beast...the city!

In this you can only zoom in at district centres and the lack of details in the animations are disappointing. Also the constant lighting trials zooming along roads (which you no longer choose to build) is a completely pointless flourish, just glitter to make the thing shiny.* Over complicated - The developers have spent a lot of time adding political elements which only serve to constantly stop you achieving anything quickly in building the city. There are so many of them you cant keep them all happy and strikes cripple you.* Difficulty - Now this may just be me but i found this game very difficult even on the easiest setting. Ive played a lot of games like these over the years but found as soon as a white out occurs the entire city was crippled and unrecoverable.* HEATSTAMPS!!!! - For me the stupidest addition to the game. Again another tool to slow you down from achieving anything in the game and it makes no sense that a post apocalyptic society would introduce a currency, they have bigger problems :)Overall i would say if you are buying this for the city builder element there are numerous better games then this. _childDocuments_.review: I absolutely loved FP1, but FP2 is just a totally different game. If FP1 was like Warcraft, FP2 is like a Total War game. It just feels totally impersonal. One of my favorite aspects in FP1 was the city building, but in FP2 that is totally gone. You don't place individual buildings, you just establish zones that have to be built to preset sizes. There is also a really silly feature to where before you establish any zone you also have to "frostbreak" the ground, it seems totally pointless and just like a silly way to add another resource sink without actually adding anything to the game. The UI is not great, and the game is not intuitive to learn like FP1 felt.The scale is much grander, I've seen a lot of people complain that people are just another resource in this game, and it's so true. I remember in the first one when people got sick sometimes I would remove them from work in their building to put a healthy person in, since that didn't automatically happen, they were assigned there until well. Now, there is nothing like that, people die and get sick in droves and just the workforce is automatically redistributed. I've gotten to chapter 4, and I'm just done. The game isn't fun or engaging or at all like the first. Kudos for making it so different I guess? FP1 was such a good game that was just missing a few things to make it fun to replay over and over, and I was really hoping FP2 would be an improvement on FP1 in that sense. Adding maybe more RNG features, more outside threats, different map/generator zones, more with the settlements, etc. There are some things in FP2 that would have added to FP1. The entirely different direction is both confusing and disappointing. To those that enjoy the new one, great, but personally huge let down and waste of money.

_childDocuments_.review: I generally liked the game and have enjoyed playing the main story, but feel it fell short of being as great as frostpunk 1 for two main reasons. One is as the game was scaled up we lost some of the immersion. We are fed some dialogue and pictures occasionally reflecting the decisions being made, but there is very little graphical reinforcement of this; we don't really see what's going on with the people or buildings as we make decisions and build certain things like transitioning to oil/steam or building faction specific buildings. Zooming in lets you see some things, but you end spending most of your time in the overhead view since that's where most of the game play is occurring.  Frost land exploration too was rather inconsequential for the most part with risk being easily eliminated by researching one or two techs. Generally speaking some of the immersive elements were there, but there were also a number of missed opportunities.Second, the game play loop is a little too simple/ easy even on harder difficulties. City building in general was a bit too simple with roads being built automatically and essentially replaced by a frost breaking mechanic that doesn't really provide much of a challenge. Building placement is pretty straight forward too in that you just build certain buildings like houses or industrial/ extraction sites together to optimize things. Building trails on the world map is mostly a connect the dots game which isn't very interesting. Overall, the core mechanics are good, but it's missing some substantial spice. I am still very much interested in seeing what the future DLC could bring to the game. Dynamic building graphics/ people and things would help with immersion. Introducing more logistical challenges like consequential trail placement (losing people/ materials if you place your trail somewhere treacherous, or if trails are too long resources trickle in slower etc.) and more consequential terrain effects in cities (widening negative affects, routing pipelines that could burst and pollute areas) would help spice up the game play loop. TLDR; Good game with some missed opportunities in regards to the game play loop and immersive elements--still a good solid game overall. Looking forward to the DLC to see if it might help resolve some of the short comings.

_childDocuments_.review: I really like Frostpunk 2.At the start, I was a little shocked at how different Frostpunk 2 is from its predecessor, and the new systems felt a bit confusing, but I started liking the game pretty quickly after the initial shock. (I also found the opening cinematic much weaker when it comes to storytelling and and emotional impact than FP1's opening, so it was a bit of a rough start.)Frostpunk 2 is a different game from FP1, but it feels like a natural succession: After surviving the initial challenges of "the end of the world", humanity starts to rebuild. More people, larger cities, and focus shifting from individual people and small groups to large groups with different ideologies. The increased abstraction (like icebreaking machines fading in and out of view out of nowhere) felt a little jarring at first, but makes sense at this scale.The shift in scale was really hammered home by a choice I made early on that said "some children will die", and it ended up being 109 kids. Whoops.Making ideological and moral choices feels much more robust in FP2; being able to make large-scale ethical and social decisions, like whether to privatize alcohol sales or housing, is a very unique experience I've never had in any other game. None of the factions completely share my own personal values, which I find great - it makes deciding which factions to favor much more interesting.Because Frostpunk 2 takes a step back and views the city from more distance (literally and figuratively), some of the personal stakes of FP1 are lost: the fates of individuals feel less important when instead of one worker getting sick or dying, it's tens or even hundreds. But for me, being able to make important decisions about the lives of a large number of people can also be emotional and interesting. Like providing free essentials to my citizens, or funding youth art initiatives.My advice is not to only look at the bonuses that different laws and different variations of buildings offer, but consider what kind of society you want to build (whether it aligns with your real-world political views or not).  At least for me, that is the most interesting and fun way to play!As a veteran of Frostpunk 1, the Officer difficulty feels right for me. I had to load an earlier save a couple of times somewhat early in the game to fix some bad mistakes, but otherwise I've felt challenged but not overwhelmed. Like the game also hints, I would recommend the Officer difficulty for first-time playthroughs if you've played a lot of FP1 (otherwise go for the easier difficulty).Overall, I'd definitely recommend Frostpunk 2! Making it so different from FP1 was a bold move from the devs, but one I've ultimately grown to like.
