_childDocuments_.review: For starters, I played the original Frostpunk for 250+ hours, easy to say I'm a big fan of the game. Before I first played Frostpunk 2, I didn't watch any gameplay before it officially released so I could experience it by myself. In the first couple hours of the game I was shocked at how different FP2 was compared to the first, which I initially didn't like. However, I stuck with it for longer and ended up being really invested in the mechanics and story of the game. Here are some thoughts I have of my first playthrough of the game:The scope (population, frostland, society, etc) is bigger and less intimate, but it is still faithful to Frostpunk's survival formula of hazardous weather, resource struggles, and a (much expanded) tech progression tree. The main innovation of the game is the political / faction system which makes signing new laws more complex. Some factions support a law, others are against it, so you may have to compromise to achieve these goals. If you aren't a fan of democracy as a form of governance in New London, rest assured you can always become a dictator... to a certain extent! This new system is very fun to me and just adds more replayability to the base game. However, there still are some things that could be improved in my opinion, such as the abilities; I spent a long time trying to figure out where I can activate abilities like "recruit more guards." I figured it out eventually but it was still annoying. The tech tree is pretty overwhelming; I feel like the tree format should be tweaked to better separate the different ideas of opposing factions (ie. make them more apparent / distinct). Also, I feel like once you research one faction's tech you shouldn't be able to research the opposing one's tech. For instance, it seems redundant to me to have two different kinds of oil extractors in the same playthrough even if you wanted to appease both factions. There are some minor glitches here and there: sometimes the resource display disappears, which I fix by reloading the game, and the autosave function is pretty laggy, but nothing game-breaking. I'll end this review with a big positive, one of my favorite things about the game by far is the MUSIC. It was well composed and did an outstanding job of portraying the world of Frostpunk all over again in a more sinister tone.In my opinion, there are many pros and few cons to FP2. For those of you who are hesitant to buy because it is different from the original, I urge you to give it a try regardless. It is faithful to the original game and expands upon many aspects that made FP1 amazing, albeit less intimately. The game is well-made and you can tell that the developers poured their heart into it, just like the first game.

_childDocuments_.review: BLUF: If you like FP1's world, and don't mind a broader scope at the cost of micromanagement-focused gameplay, this is a solid title.As a big fan of the first game, I enjoy the return to the frozen wastes.  This game is absolutely not "More of the first game", but is instead a cousin of the first game.  While it takes place in the same setting, it focuses more on macro-management of your society to include multiple outposts and exploration/exploitation of the wastes as opposed to micromanagement of a single city.  Some may find this "wide and shallow" as opposed to "narrow and deep" but I'm enjoying the change of scope -- If I want to micromanage, I'll fire FP1 up again.Looking to the fit and finish of the world, I'm enjoying the look of the game in general.  The graphics are compelling and fit nicely with the world narrative and lend an appropriate atmosphere.  The soundscape is similarly well crafted and helps add legitimacy to the atmosphere the game is portraying.  The aggregate of these accurately conveys a grim world where survival is a struggle.I find the story to be compelling, and the political management to be entertaining and interesting.  I enjoy that many of the decisions you'll have to make effectively amount to a "trolley problem" sort of situation where there is no perfect option that satisfies everyone; It's all shades of grey.  The game does well to point out both sides of the outcome of your decisions, and similarly to the first, doesn't shy away from some horrifying moral choices, such as sending the kids into the mines to increase efficiency.The UI/UX integrates nicely with the bleak narrative, for those who don't want to go snowblind with white UI elements there is a dark mode that is in beta within the options, however it does have a disclaimer regarding not all menus looking appropriate -- I have not dug into this and can't comment on how well it actually works or doesn't.  The only UX gripe I have is that clicking a district will move the camera to show the district's information card, which can be annoying when you're just trying to toggle/adjust something on that card and wish to do it quickly.Performance is adequate, although it could use some polish/optimization.  In my experience many Unreal Engine games generally optimize well in the post-launch world as successive patches are brought forward, I'm not terribly concerned about this aspect going forward.  I have encountered some small bugs with buildings and resource generation math not adding up correctly, but I feel these will be fixed in time.I feel satisfied with this purchase, for those who enjoy the world of Frost Punk and don't mind having a higher-level view of the society to manage, I'd say this game is a solid purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk 2 ventures boldly into new territory but may stray too far from what made its predecessor a standout. While it retains the core premise of survival in a frozen wasteland, many of its changes dilute the essence of the original.The expanded scope of New London introduces a plethora of systems focused on faction politics and diplomacy. While intriguing in concept, these mechanics shift focus away from the intimate survival experience that defined the first game. The addition of a parliamentary council, for example, transforms the player from a decisive, lone leader into a mediator juggling competing interests. This results in a loss of the tight, personal connection to your city’s survival, replaced by political wrangling that can feel more tedious than engagingCity-building has also been overhauled, with districts replacing individual building placements. This streamlining sacrifices the intricate planning and tactile satisfaction of designing your city in favor of efficiency. The new system may appeal to some players, but for fans of the first game’s hands-on approach, it feels like a step backwardFurthermore, while the narrative complexity of faction interactions adds depth, it can overwhelm players with micromanagement and obscure the urgency of survival. Balancing the needs of various factions often feels like a frustrating distraction rather than an organic part of city leadership. The faction system also leads to outcomes that feel scripted, diminishing the sense of agency that was so impactful in the originalVisually, the game is undeniably stunning, and the updated graphics bring the frozen wasteland to life. Yet, even this improvement can’t shake the feeling that Frostpunk 2 has lost some of the raw, emotional grit of its predecessor. The emphasis on scale and politics distances the player from the immediate human struggles that made the first game so impactful.For veterans of the original, Frostpunk 2 may feel like a game trying to do too much, losing sight of what made its predecessor a genre-defining masterpiece. While it’s ambitious and offers new ideas, it risks alienating those who cherished the more focused and intimate challenges of the first Frostpunk.6.5/10

Also for real endless mode you NEED to play 2000 weeks of Utopia builder, which is rediculous since most of the game is done by 1250-1500 weeks, so you just sit there barely doing anything OR struggling for resources because your city just grows and grows, sucking up all the finite resources of the game...And lastly the design is pretty sad, as I said the districs look samey, buildings literally all have the same skin (of one type) no matter what tech. Your laws have 0 impact on the visuals of the city. No parks or decorations to really give a feel of thriving. Nothing to do but "Make city bigger, more people!" and that's pretty sad. You cannot fulfil or at least REALLY further any factions goal, you cannot REALLY heat the city, or colonize the frostland past 3 colonies and a few settlements that will probably vacuum up all your food anyway forcing starvation (so no "conquering" the frost there). There's is just barely anything to do past the very unbalanced resource and dilpo management. The city building is reduced to plop down districts around "Hubs" that boost certian things, like less heat consmption or mats, less tenstion etc. But that makes you have weird district shapes to minimize the burning of your resources, not helping the street/building placement that is automatic, ending in ugly clip fests.All in all, wait 2-3 years, like a lot of people did with Frostpunk 1. It's currently a glorified Early Access, but has a lot of potential.Do. Not. Get! (For now or more than 25$/€)

_childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk 2 is a stunning follow-up to the original, taking the core elements that made the first game successful and pushing the boundaries in every direction. Whether you're a fan of the first Frostpunk or completely new to the series, this game has a lot to offer, and patience will be your greatest ally as you discover the depths of its gameplay.Set in a harsh post-apocalyptic environment where freezing cold dominates and survival is precarious, Frostpunk 2 continues the struggle of humanity, but this time it introduces a much broader scale. The city-building, decision-making, and moral dilemmas return but with more layers, more depth, and more ambition. You don’t need to have played the first game to enjoy the second, as Frostpunk 2 does a great job of easing newcomers into its mechanics. However, the sheer scope of the game can be a lot for newcomers, so taking the time to learn and absorb everything is key.What really stands out is the developer's ambition to not just rest on their laurels but to expand on everything that made the first game memorable. The scope of the sequel is bigger: the map is larger, the decisions are weightier, and the consequences are more far-reaching. You’ll feel the weight of every decision as you manage your city, balancing resources, managing the emotional state of your citizens, and trying to maintain hope in a world where every day brings new challenges.One of the most impressive aspects of Frostpunk 2 is how it weaves its storytelling into the gameplay. The choices you make as the leader don’t just affect the numbers—they have profound impacts on the world and the narrative. Every difficult decision has moral implications that challenge your leadership style and values. Will you favor the needs of the many or the individual? Will you be ruthless to ensure survival, or compassionate and risk jeopardizing your city? These narrative threads create a gripping, immersive experience that pushes the genre forward.The introduction of new resources and systems like oil exploration brings an exciting dynamic to the city-building genre. These resources fuel both the literal machines and the figurative social machinery of your city. You'll face challenges not just in managing the cold, but in keeping the political and social landscape stable as the world’s demands change.The sense of growth is palpable: while the first game had a tighter focus on survival, Frostpunk 2 has the confidence to expand beyond that and explore themes of industrialization, society-building, and the conflicts that arise from progress. The pacing of the game allows for a steep learning curve but also rewards experimentation, making it accessible to both returning players and those new to the genre.The developers, 11 bit studios, have taken a bold leap with Frostpunk 2, and it’s clear they aimed for something grander in scale and vision. Their dedication to world-building, intricate systems, and thought-provoking moral dilemmas has resulted in a game that feels massive, but not overwhelming. They listened to the feedback from the first game and crafted a sequel that not only builds on what worked but also pushes the boundaries of what a city-building survival game can achieve.The production values have also stepped up a notch, with even more detailed environments, beautifully harsh landscapes, and a hauntingly atmospheric score. The improved graphics and fluid animations make the cold, unforgiving world of Frostpunk 2 feel alive and hostile in ways that are chillingly real.Whether you're a returning fan or a newcomer to the series, Frostpunk 2 is a game that demands your attention. It takes the original's formula and supercharges it with more complexity, a larger world, and deeper, more nuanced moral dilemmas. The patience required to master its systems is well worth it, as the rewards for perseverance are rich and satisfying.Frostpunk 2 isn’t just a sequel—it’s an evolution. By expanding its scale and ambition, it hits just the right balance between honoring the first game and pushing the genre into exciting new territory. 11 bit studios have outdone themselves, delivering a game that stands as one of the best in the genre.So, brace yourself for the cold, prepare for tough choices, and get ready to lead humanity through the harshest of winters—Frostpunk 2 is an experience you won’t soon forget

_childDocuments_.review: People complain about how this game is not a true continuation to the first one - but i think this is fine in itself, i can deal with the changes developers have introduced.Instead of beating that horse, i want to talk about something that has greatly disappointed me - the political system. In pre-release notes it was hyped up as a main feature of the game, an expansive system that would represent a diverse landscape of political thoughts in your population. And what do we get in the end? A bland, static parody of what could have been a pure gem in the gaming industry.You have 4 factions in the campaign and 5 in free-play mode. There are also Colonists, but they don't take part in politics and exist only in your secondary cities so you can safely ignore them. Existing factions are divided into 2 camps - pro-progress and pro-tradition. That's the whole political complexity, the end. No, seriously, there is no intermingling of ideas between them, no situations where 1 group wants something and 3(4) others are strongly against it. You don't even get your own gang of loyalists once you become a Captain. Those groups exist only as statistics, equally spread among your living districts.  They don't try to push for any agenda on their own unless you really piss them off - and they won't fight with one another (with the exception of the campaign ending, but that's spoilers).Overall, the political system is a major disappointment. It could have created a layer of gameplay of its own, but ends up being just a distraction from city management - which was not as captivating as I hoped. It starts great but falls off closer to the endgame, where the difficulty goes out of the window. You have so much resources that building colonies feels pointless - your main city + resource depots on the map have enough of everything to win you the game. You don't even need oil if you manage coal properly - and steam is not even available properly in the campaign!I also must admit that swapping between colonies does not feel great. It is too tedious once you get to 3 or 4, and i ended up just making every single one into a self-sufficient hub just so i don't have to manage resources there. At least in free-play, you can name them (but not the permanent outposts for some reason). Also, as I mentioned before, there are no factions in your colonies, only nameless colonists that would be fine with you proclaiming to be god-emperor and stealing their kneecaps. Lots of wasted potential over here, something like dynamics between colonies-capital city based on your approach towards local resources, or perhaps population that was forced out of comfortable capital and now forced to live in a frozen hellhole once again.Overall I enjoyed some parts of the game, it was a pleasant experience. But Frostpunk one felt much more memorable when compared to this. If there was a neutral score I would give it, but for now, it is a negative one. Maybe updates and DLCs would make the situation better, Frostpunk 2 is very close to being a good game.

_childDocuments_.review: Masterpiece. Game of the year for me.I didn't play the first one, but heard much about it. So I'm not comparing it to anything, but to me this game is a masterclass in immersion and natural as well as guided storytelling. The mechanics are great and feel different from other games. It's original. The game doesn't hold your hand, the prologue serves as a tutorial, but doesn't feel like a tutorial: You're immediately fighting for survival, but the game never feels unfair. Here and there I wished the consequences of my actions were clearer, but you can always reload, and I suggest making multiple saves. I never got soft locked, but I'm sure you can.You explore the world as you explore mechanics and the story unfolds. The story feels very authentically interlinked with what you do. When factions were mad at me, they had good reason to, and they all have reasonable stances, that just happen to conflict very often. Moral choices are nuanced.You will be managing and balancing dozens of things at the same time, have to make sacrifices, sometimes heavy ones, but you always have clear and realistic short and long-term goals. Some self-imposed, some from the game's plot, and some just to keep your people alive and if possible, happy. For a city management game it's extremely exciting. Oftentimes I barely scraped by.Other developers can learn from this. How to trust your audience: show them the basic with more show than tell, then throw them into the cold water and let them figure it out.Special shout out to the the graphics and sound design. It's actually a very pretty game and I wish I could zoom in more (the zoom-in on generators doesn't do it for me).Now that I finished the campaign I can't wait to play the sandbox mode, which seems pretty fleshed out with 7 starting locations and completely different factions from story mode.

_childDocuments_.review: All right, the good... the bad... and the ugly.First, the good.  This sequel does what so few are able to do - it captures the spirit of the original without being a beat-for-beat retread, and does it with real respect for the original.  It also manages to sidestep the one thing that caused my negative review of the first one (no matter what you did, you were a horrible person).Now, the bad.  One of the key elements that made the original great was managing the city around the heat source.  In this one, you don't have to do that.  It's a major loss to the strategy, and also makes it significantly less of a game.  Yes, the original had additional heating towers you could build to change the layout from concentric circles to a venn diagram, but in this, the districts can be haphazard and irrelevant to a heat source.  This pattern repeats in the game - there are automatons from the beginning, which changes the entire dynamic.Finally, the ugly.  Factions.  While the original fell victim to the false dichotomy of moralities (or the choice to follow neither of the two presented options) the political game in this version of balancing factions and keeping them all both in check and also approving of you destroys the immersion of a dangerous world requiring hard choices.  It's a political sim now, not a survival sim.  And that loss is sad beyond measure.

_childDocuments_.review: Everyone is saying that if you liked Frostpunk for its intimacy and smaller scale, you may not like Frostpunk 2's grander design/strategy as much. This has been gone over a lot already, but I will say that this is true. I love the direction they took the game. Everything from the resource planning, district planning, managing research and the council, the differing factions -- they are all things you have to think about and balance at once, which makes coming through the tough times that much more rewarding. However, this game is not perfect. Firstly, I feel that while the faction origins are different from each other, they generally fall in the camp of "far left group, moderate left group, moderate right group, far right group" in terms of social spectrum. while there isn't anything wrong with this, I had a hard time telling apart some of the factions because while they had different ideals, they wound up supporting the same ideas all the same meaning they didn't feel different. But by far the biggest issue with the game is the stability. Quite frankly, releasing a game this unstable is just unacceptable. There are way too many crashes, and they can honestly happen at any time but it usually happens when navigating the map. I've lost a lot of playtime due to having to either re-trace my steps from my last step, or having to save consistently because i don't want to lose a lot of progress. While I trust they will get this fixed, in the meantime i would recommend saving after every important action you take, even if it feels monotonous and isn't something we should have to do, it will save you for now. Overall, great game. the campaign does a good job introducing the core mechanics for endless mode, and im excited to see what story elements they introduce next as DLC. 8/10, will be bumped up to a 9/10 once stability is fixed.

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: if what you are looking for is just a review of the game, look elsewhere. I want to share my story, and this is where it will happen.It all started with me watching Frostpunk playthroughs on youtube. And I don't mean playthrough as a series, multiple episodes and such - the ones that do well on YT. I watched, what were essentially, stream vods. Many hours, 6 to more than 9 depending on what was exactly happening. I fell in love with the game. It's design, lore, gameplay. But I wasn't able to play it. Then, a few years later I managed to score a discount on Epic (or was it free? Don't remember, sorry). I sat down and, even though I had school on the next day, played through the opening scenario in one sitting - still have the recording from that one.I never was a big fan of trying to 100% a game, playing endless modes or rouge-like titles. I love watching people play them, but I'm not really into playing them. The same stood for Frostpunk.I picked up the game again when the sequel was announced, got all the DLCs and played through the whole game. I'm not a very hardcore gamer so I played through the scenarios only, and on the normal difficulty. After that, I got the pre-order for this game and waited. Once it released I sat at it again, and didn't leave until I finished the story. Granted, it took me more than just 5 hours to finish it this time.And now the review part of this "review".I, personally, love the game.To me, it kept the spirit of a Survival-City builder while changing things up. It's not a direct sequel. By that I mean it's not like a direct continuation - think the Dark Souls series (these have tiny story/location/equipment changes, but the games are essentialy the same). This game is placed in the same universe, and it's similar enough that I would call it a spiritual-sequel. A similar example to what happend between FP1 and FP2 would be Darkest Dungeon - the games are set in the same universe, same background lore, but the gameplay and style is different (also, I know that many people say they like DD1 more than DD2 [same as here] but I actually like the 2nd one more).To me I like that, since the scope of the cities/colonies is different, 11 bit made the decision to make this a different game, rather than an overblown DLC to the first one.A lot of people are complaining/moaning/are upset that this game is so much different from FP1. What I have to say to them is: Instead of spreading hate and negative energy because you don't like the 2nd game. Just play the 1st one. And if you're bored of replaying the same maps on endless for the past 800h, maybe just look for something different?To conclude,I like both games, so far I have played more of the first one - simply because there's only one story/campaign/scenario mission in the 2nd one. _childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk 2 attempts to build on its predecessor’s success but falls short in several key areas. The game introduces a more complex political system, which, while ambitious, often feels more frustrating than engaging. Players are forced to navigate a labyrinth of faction demands and political maneuvers that can feel like busywork rather than meaningful gameplay.The game’s pacing is another significant issue. The early chapters are relatively easy, but as you progress, the difficulty spikes in ways that feel arbitrary and unfair. For instance, factions frequently push for counterproductive laws that can cripple your city’s progress, making it feel like you’re constantly fighting against the game’s mechanics rather than working with them.Additionally, the new frostbreaking system, which requires clearing tiles before building, adds unnecessary tedium to the city-building process. This mechanic slows down gameplay and can make even simple tasks feel like a chore. The inability to reposition single tiles without demolishing entire districts further exacerbates this issue, leading to a lot of wasted time and effort.Overall, while Frostpunk 2 has some interesting ideas, its execution leaves much to be desired. The game often feels more like a test of patience than a rewarding strategy experience

_childDocuments_.review: Gameplay is quite different than FP1 but by no means is it worse. _childDocuments_.review: This review is just my personal opinion, not intended to convince anyone of anything. Right off the bat, before I dive into the details, I want to say that I liked Frostpunk 2. I don’t think the game is a failure in terms of design, although I recognize that many players may not agree with me. That said, before we get into the main points, I should mention that I bought the game with my own money, and on top of that, I own the Deluxe Edition. I’d been eagerly waiting for the release, especially since I loved the first game in the series. Sure, the delayed release was a bit of a letdown, but not a huge deal — at this point, that’s all in the past.So, Frostpunk 2.I got the chance to play it three days before the official release (thanks to the Deluxe Edition, as mentioned earlier), but the pre-release didn’t go off without a hitch. The game wasn’t available for download on Steam for about half an hour. In this case, though, I’m more inclined to blame Steam itself. The release of another game, The Casting of Frank Stone, by a completely different studio, had similar issues. From what I’ve heard, this isn’t uncommon, and users often run into these kinds of problems. Interestingly, I’ve heard that players on other platforms, like EGS, didn’t experience any delays with the pre-release. Of course, I might be wrong, but for now, I can’t fault 11 bit studios for something out of their control.Now, let’s break things down.**Single-Player Campaign and Story Mode**The story mode opens with beautifully stylized cinematics that capture the essence of the Frostpunk universe. These cinematics accompany every chapter of the campaign, and they’re just a pleasure to watch. As a fan of the franchise, I couldn’t help but appreciate the visual and audio design. Is it stunning? That’s subjective. But the visuals perfectly convey the atmosphere of the world — total despair in frozen wastelands where all that awaits is frostbite and death. It’s pretty impactful, especially considering the leap between the first and second games in this regard. The campaign is divided into chapters, starting, of course, with the Prologue, which does a great job of fleshing out the game’s lore. I have no complaints about the storytelling; the delivery of information is smooth and engaging.**Graphics**While graphics aren’t the main focus in a game like this, I have to say the visuals in Frostpunk 2 are solid. It’s not groundbreaking or hyper-realistic, but within the context of the genre, the game’s graphics hold up well and leave a positive impression.**Optimization and Bugs**This is a big topic for many modern games, and I’ve even heard people say that Frostpunk 2 suffers from poor optimization. Personally, I didn’t run into any issues, either in the pre-release or afterward. The game runs smoothly for me, with stable FPS, no stuttering, and it all works like clockwork. As for bugs, I didn’t encounter any, and while I can’t claim they don’t exist, they didn’t affect my experience. From my perspective, the studio did a good job here.**Gameplay**The heart of any city-building strategy game is the gameplay. It’s the core of the experience, and Frostpunk 2 delivers. I’m not going to do a direct comparison between Frostpunk and Frostpunk 2, because gameplay-wise, they’re quite different games, even if they share similar mechanics and ideas. The first game feels more intimate, almost cozy in a way, while the second one is more complex and global in scope. I’ve described Frostpunk 2 as a mix of Frostpunk and Cities: Skylines, with some added faction management and political elements. And I like that. I can’t say whether the second game is better than the first — it’s hard to compare because they offer such different experiences. But the new mechanics and their blend with the old ones definitely gave me a lot of enjoyment, and that’s a win in my book. Speaking of politics — relationships with factions are a bit simplistic. I’d have liked a deeper system for more hardcore gameplay, but for a broader audience, this simplicity is probably a plus. And despite that, the game still retains its brutal, frostbitten challenge, making progression much tougher.In conclusion, I honestly don’t get the negativity toward Frostpunk 2. The game has evolved, becoming bigger, more ambitious, and more global, without losing its hardcore edge. At the same time, it’s added elements that make it accessible to a wider audience, so both casual players and hardcore fans can enjoy it. Thank you, 11 bit studios — I loved the first game in the series, and now I’m really happy with the second. I hope the market situation improves soon, and your company continues to thrive, bringing us new projects, including future installments in this franchise.

_childDocuments_.review: Did you love Frostpunk? Then good, news Frostpunk 2 is nothing like it!Gone is the unique circular city setting, gone are the heat generator upgrades you desperately need to expand towards resources, gone is the value of the lives of your preciously limited workers.Building is now done on a hex grid, with most districts requiring 6 hexes to build and heat bonuses being applied if you put a certain amount of hexes in a specific spot.Population is now a necessity to even construct new production buildings. No planning ahead allowed.Heat is no longer governed by the generator or steam hubs, but is now just a currency to be paid to every new district, expensed by putting down new coal mines/oil wells. Resources are no longer infinite, including food! This is the first city builder I've come across where food is a limited resource.Community demands have been replaced by council interests, who will put forward suggestions for new laws. This should have been more interesting, but you have a limited way of interacting with this system which can prevent you from developing your society the way you want.Overall, I felt very disconnected from the feeling of the game, like I'm just pushing numbers around on a spreadsheet. Rather than trying to build a civilisation, I'm putting pieces on a puzzle board.

_childDocuments_.review: Mixed emotions of the game.First of all, this isn’t FP1, except for the recurring themes of ruinous cold and the stupid morality tied to your decisions.When it comes to gameplay, I’m disappointed by the so-called "infinite" resources. Massive numbers aren’t infinite, and I realized this in my last playthrough—my oil ran dry, and my city collapsed because I’d invested in oil-only generator techs. While some resources like food and materials might feel virtually infinite if they would last for 170,000 weeks, oil is definitely not one of them; it runs out very fast. After about six hours of gameplay, my oil colony became dry.Then there’s the annoyingly bleak interface with many shortcomings. For instance, how can I figure out how many anti-squalor buildings I need? What buildings produce squalor? How do I highlight districts to quickly see what I already have? There are so many little things missing here. And else, and else. In comparison to FP1, the interface sucks. Buildings. Why are we limited to building only within districts? It’s absurd that I can’t place anything outside a district, and if I need an extra prison, I have to build a whole new housing district just for it.Factions conflict seems pretty but feels underdeveloped. There’s so much potential here, but it’s hard to say exactly what would make it better.The game is nice, but it needs a lot of patches and polish. Better to wait for DLCs, maybe?

_childDocuments_.review: Like many Frostpunk 1 players, I did not enjoy this game at first. I would go as far as to say that I resented or even hated it, because this sequel took away many features from the original that I enjoyed (e.g. actual city planning/building, not this district thing) and it was difficult to understand what I was doing at first.However, after a certain amount of time spent trying and failing, everything will eventually click for you (it took me about 5 hours before I really understood what I'm supposed to do). After that it was pretty much smooth sailing, and I did end up enjoying the story mode overall, even if endgame feels a bit underwhelming. The dev team's commitment to expanding the "lore" of Frostpunk with this sequel's story mode is definitely one of the game's strongest positives in my opinion, and the various decisions or paths you could go down were equally compelling. The Parliament feature and vote-based technology is also a fresh addition to this type of game.My advice is to not give up on the game too soon; maybe it still won't be your cup of tea in the end, but you should at least come to understand the mechanics/strategy before determining whether you like it or not. For me, I'm invested, and I am excited to try out endless mode as well as whatever DLC content comes out in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: I still remember the first time I send the people to gather coal in Frostpunk, the emotions I felt when I saw them walking through that thick snow, it immediately made me think "these guys (the devs) nailed it". That sensation is missing from Frostpunk 2. The social/moral choices don't really matter. For example if you follow the merit path and try to keep your people focused on their individual strenghts, you'll end up creating a servant faction! How does that even make sense? Are the devs trying to tell us something? The game feels pointless, there is no urgency, no impending doom no real sacrifise.At the end of Frostpunk you felt that there was hope, even if you made hard choises (like sending children to fix the generator moments before everything collapsed). It was a masterpiece in every way. This game is a generic city management game covered with snow.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: The game is a straight up upgrade from Frostpunk 1. The politics and managing factions is an excellent addition. Nothing from Frostpunk 1 comes close to the feeling of manipulating the council into giving you more and more power until you eventually seize it all. The resource management and balancing act between your different colonies, exploring the Frostland and finding all of the locations from the first game are all very well done. The research makes you pick who to side with, and if you only lean on one side you will anger the other faction. However maxing out either side of the tech trees gives massive bonuses. You can definitely try to be a paragon of diplomacy and peace, but where's the fun in that?I can only imagine what modders will come up with, but the replayability is already here with an endless mode featuring completely new factions and communities not seen in the main story.

_childDocuments_.review: its a great game and had a smooth launch. better than what alot of AAA games can manage these days some nerfs/buffs are needed for a few things but the game itself is solid.though for its price its a bit short. i finished the story in about 16 hours, i would recommend picking it up when the DLCs start releasing and when its on sale the UI does need some work, its not terrible but has a lot of minor issues that can easily be fixededit) the game starts too stutter and freeze when auto saving in the late game (only major issue i felt worth mentioning)

_childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk 2 is very different from Frostpunk 1 in a lot of ways. _childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk 2 is good, albeit not as excellent as Frostpunk 1. I suspect that's the main reason for most negative reviews here, because on its own Frostpunk 2 is a very decent city builder/survival game. But indeed, it doesn't quite "hit" on the same level as the previous Frostpunk, where you were faced with the consequence of your choices on the lives of individuals. Frostpunk 2 is more detached, less emotionally involved, but also has more strategy. Frostpunk 1 was more like boxing, while Frostpunk 2 is more like chess. I love chess, but don't expect you'll be punching people when you buy this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: I won't comment on concept and design choices, because people will say it's subjective, but for a game that's so ambitious in scale/scope, it has a horrendous user interface. That's a fact that most people can agree on. You click on so many things by accident, and the explorer map is so clunky to use. It just drove me mad how many meaningful choices I made by accident because of the UX/UI. It drove me mad exploring the surroundings on that clunky map that you can't zoom out of and that you can't click on without popping an undiscovered zone menu. Changed my mind. I'm actually gonna comment on a design choice, which I think is plain bad, and made me so mad when I encountered it. When I discovered the first oil outpost in story mode (the outpost from the prologue that's supposed to teach you the game mechanics in the 2 hours you need to play before you can't request a refund), I got so mad because I realised that you have to manage multiple cities at micromanagement level at the same time, in real time. That's ok in a game live CIV6 or HOMM, which are turn-based, but not in real time. You end up staying more in pause mode, which is not fun.I also had very serious performance issues. Very laggy to the point that it stalled and had to restart the PC. It got so bad that the game became unplayable, so I quit the game and requested a refund (which I probably won't get because I played more than 2 hours of it while doing the prologue). If they fix the game, I'm gonna try it again, but from my pov they'd have to do a complete overhaul on many game mechanics, which I don't see being feasible. I hope that I get that refund, so that I can buy the expansions for the first game.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: the game is breathtaking, I think some reviews are unjustified and definitely super uncool. I am having so much fun playing, and I want the game to do well :) With that out of the way:I was a bit weirded out when I started playing. It's true the prologue isn't great at explaining some core concepts, and the game has obviously favoured a "grand strategy" setting rather than the personal, closely-knit small cities we are used to building in FP1. But that is not a bad thing. Far from it. In fact, I think it's probably the best direction they could have gone in.I do think many of the negative reviews are unjustified. Many of them having spent between 2-3 hours in-game. Others less. This really isn't enough time to appreciate the game if you're coming from FP1 and wanted something similar. You have to appreciate the game for what it's trying to accomplish. And what it tries to do, it does really well. These people have been very quick to dismiss Frostpunk 2 and should definitely give it a (real) chance. it might change their mind.My first 2 hours in-game felt a bit weird, but when I started getting into it... I was blown away. I'm playing on hard difficulty and am having so much fun. Juggling the factions, expanding my city, going back to Winterhome, the Dreadnought Colony, just... New London with over 40k citizens. Everything is so beautiful and you can tell it's been made with so much love, passion and care. The Frostpunk universe is so goshdarned pretty I could just tear up.No, this is not like Frostpunk 1. And that's a good thing. It's an entirely different game that emphasizes the disconnect between leaders and their people. Emotions are different. You still care about your people, but in a different way. Everything is on a Macro scale now. Hopefully someday we get a Frostpunk 1 Remaster, with better graphics and new stuff. But Frostpunk 2 is not the place to get that experience. And I love it for that.It's a great game. Definitely worth a buy!
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Yet again, Steam not allowing for anything in-between "recommended" and "not recommended" makes this a bit misleading. I can't say I don't recommend it. But it's a wildly different experience from the original Frostpunk (FP1). That being said, I can boil my complaints down to two point:1. Everything has been abstracted to the point that the entire game is now a logistics management simulator, it is no longer a city-builder. Sure, you have the ability to control what districts are placed where, with up to two buildings per district (think of them as two bonuses you get to pick for each district), but your choice of placement matters little. Sure, there are minor bonuses and minor penalties for said choices, but I can't say they truly impacted my gameplay.2. The story is short. Painfully short. This is clearly designed to be a vehicle to sell DLC. Just as things start to get interesting, you start unlocking interesting tech, and you solidify your rule over the city... the game ends... WITH NO OPTION TO CONTINUE PLAYING IN THE CITY YOU JUST SPENT 8 HOURS BUILDING. "But this was the same in FP1!" Yeah, it wasn't cool then, and it's less so now, both the DLC model and the inability to continue playing.Ultimately, it's a decent experience. The art style and and vibe is faithful to FP1. But it is lacking the soul of the first game. Too much abstraction in an effort to bring the game to a grander scale has simply led to the feeling that one is only controlling numbers, keeping them from going negative.Wait for a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk 2 takes the ideas and the mechanics of Frostpunk 1 and examines them with the eternal question of: what do we do now? Humanity survived the Great Frost and 30 years of intermittent storms, but now thousands of people rely on a power source they don't understand or even think about too much. They have their own lives, born and bred in the frost. And so Frostpunk 2 challenges you to think about scale, to think about how everyone has their own opinion on you and gives morality a new front. After all, with that many people, someone's always supporting those dangerous ideas. Some of them might even encourage you. The rest can be convinced, if you're willing to see what happens.Yes, it's visually very different and uses a hex based system instead of a grid, but fundamentally the same principles apply. There's not enough of anything and it's your job to try not to let the city collapse under its own burgeoning weight when people start having problems. Approach with an open mind and you'll find some very interesting experiences inside...

_childDocuments_.review: I have completed the story mode once so far, on Officer difficulty (2/4) and this game is amazing. I was pretty slow with my game play, spending a large amount of time paused planning but it has been some of the most fun I've had playing a game in a while. I will say this, if you aren't ready for a difficult game, or are expecting more of Frostpunk 1 then you came here for the wrong reason. Frostpunk 2 has so much detail and strategy, ever decision you make has consequences and you WILL feel them. Without spoiling anything, towards the end of the story mode I began questioning who I had been siding with politically between 2 different factions, as they demanded more extreme measures that I didn't know if I could allow. There were multiple times where I didn't think my city would make it out the other side, but just barely it clung as the weather began to lighten and began to heat up its cold cold houses. I can't wait to try out the utopia builder mode and later replay the story on harder difficulties choosing to hold different values dear as I lead my people to thrive within this never-ending winter.

_childDocuments_.review: As a dedicated Frostpunk fan, I eagerly awaited the release of Frostpunk 2. The game held so much promise, and while it delivered on some of the bold changes, it fell a little short on other aspects. I want to highlight a few notable differences. The council and the factions system are a thrilling addition to the game, adding a new layer of depth. They are not needlessly complex or bothersome, especially on lower difficulties, but these decisions inject a fresh element into the game each time. I loved the romanticism of the first game, where I knew most (if not all) of the workers. The scale of this game is different. It doesn't feel like Frostpunk anymore; it's more like Cities Skylines, which removes a lot from the intimacy and being nervous about the little helpers that throttled through the neck-deep snow to get to a worksite. People die for all sorts of reasons, and this is just meh... it's all automatons everywhere, and there's no personal touch. Regardless, I like the city manager aspect, and this is a change I welcome. I'll be honest, the idea tree is terrible. I have difficulty finding anything there; the UI isn't easy or intuitive to use. The old-school research system was so much better to see through and plan with. I understand why it looks like this, but it could be represented much cleaner and more searchable.: While I haven't seen any game-breaking bugs so far, there are slight UI issues here and  there. The most annoying is that the extra buildings tab sometimes renders buildings that shouldn't be in that category and makes it hard to see what should be there. Apart from the UI issues, the game's performance is subpar, it stutters and has a hard time playing without weird throttling even on an Ryzen 7800X/GeForce 4700. Even on a high settings there's a blur around everything.

_childDocuments_.review: This isn't Frostpunk 1. It's a sequel. Too many sequels are scared to try anything new. This one makes a bold choice to add elements of new genres. This time around the game feels like a grand strategy game. This change has caused much butthurt in a small, crybaby sub-population of gamers. They seem to have expected to be spoon-fed an exact replica of Frostpunk 1, like toddlers in a high-chair afraid to try more than apple sauce.If the essence of Frostpunk 1 was theme and story and choice, those are present in abundance here. Frostpunk 2 has added an entirely new layer of political drama. Now it is less game-like and more realistic: you are not so much a dictator who can click out orders freely, and instead a leader who must balance the threats and desires of competing factions.Contrary to the silly "it has no soul" reviews, there is plenty of thematic flavor: you can click a magnifying glass to zoom-in to the center of districts to watch a close-up portrayal; city-wide announcements warn citizens of events over a public address system; there are thought bubbles/dialogue bubbles that pop up over districts where people voice content or discontent; and event and choice screens often come with an individual citizen's portrait, age, background, etc. If you're familiar with a game like Crusader Kings 3, that's an analogous level of detail. The focus is on strategy, but it has splashes of narrative color.PROS:* Gorgeous visuals, an overall cohesive and effective style (music, artwork, writing, etc.)* Many impactful, difficult decisions to make your playthroughs unique* Fresh political mechanics for people who want to explore realpolitik versus idealismCONS:* A few mechanics can be confusing or under-explained (e.g. Why can't I place the Research Institute in an expanded Extraction District when it shows Empty Building Slots? What's the maximum output of the generator? Why does building frostland trails from settlements feel awkward?)* Even on my modern rig, I get micro stutters at times and have to have DLSS turned on to have a solid 60 FPS* UI issues like overflowing text in descriptions, no notification for frost-breaking completion, being unable to skip the Prologue on new playthroughs, and the UI feeling "floaty" and nauseating as it jumps around a lotOVERALL:* The game feels worth buying for strategy game fans. It has rich choices and a flavorful, thematic presentation. There are a few issues present. But if the studio can improve the explanations of unclear mechanics and squash the technical glitches, Frostpunk 2 feels like a solid platform on which to base years more content.

_childDocuments_.review: Its good, the gameplay is different than the first one and a bit more complicated so dont go into this expecting a 1:1 of the original - my only complaint is that the tile system can be a bit wonky and hard to manage at times. It lacks a bit in the cinematics department and is generally less focused on individual people aside from pop up events - which i think makes it a bit less engaging than the original, though it still has pretty good moments and great writing behind it. The politics is decent, it can feel clunky and a bit restricted but its still fun to work with. Soundtrack is very good but some of the audio cues just seem to be missing or way too quiet, like scouts finishing their missions. One thing I do like is the sheer scope of the game, it has a lot more replaybility and options than the original one had at launch. I also like that they've continued their focus on a stable and completed singleplayer experience (not a single crash yet), which is more than most companies can say nowadays.When everything is said and done its rough around the edges but still worth a buy.

_childDocuments_.review: Not currently recommended. Might change with a lot of patching. It is a great game except for two very important aspects. The tutorials are very confusing and generally unhelpful in most cases. This adds quite a lot of frustration since following the instructions on screen do nothing, but any number of youtube videos show the actual way to do things immediately. If an online search is not only more clear, but faster, then the in-game instructions are just very poorly put together. I am certain there are people who like this kind of treasure hunting, and there are some who understand exactly what the tutorials are trying to say. But tutorials should be very clear and require as little time to use as possible. Whatever guiding structure is behind the creation of the tutorials in this game, it was not to be helpful and concise. And then there are so many bugs that playing the game is like rolling the dice. Want to spend resources building something? Sure, but it might not get built, just eat up resources and space. Gotta tear it down and start over again. Want to expand to other areas and connect with them? Keep adding connections. Because doing it once might be enough, but maybe you need to do at again. Or again. Or again. Taking the resources each time just to gamble if it'll work. The worst bug I encountered is that districts wear out and need repairs. Fair enough, lets repair them. But the devs seem to have forgotten to add the repair button consistently, So you have to hope things don't wear out(they will) and when they do that you have the button to repair.If you don't have that button?Well you can't remove the districts, can't repair them, and that effectively means you are locked out of that area forever.Either these things are intentional gimmicks to keep resources down, which might be true there are a lot of resources in this game. But more likely it is just a very polished beta release. Give it a few years before you buy the game. It will probably be reliably possible to complete the game by then.

_childDocuments_.review: A perfect sequelI found that most game sequels play it safe, following a very similar route to its predecessor. However, Frostpunk 2 is different, it stays true to the core idea of the first game but also completely overturns the gameplay into something new and fresh. The graphics are stunning, to expand the city all the player has to do is select a handful tiles to become a certain district. The game will then build up the district with unique buildings and tracks that all connect to create a natural, detailed design. This game isn’t just a city builder/survival like the first one. The cities population is split into different factions that all have very different ideas of what a utopia is. The frostlanders believe in adapting to the cold as well as equality for all. The New Londoners believe that technological supremacy over nature will save the city, also believing in ‘merit’ whereby only the best of us are given the resources to excel. You’ll have to navigate this political minefield carefully as laws passed and technologies researched will impact your relationship with these factions. Later in the game these factions split of into extremist groups that will protest and riot against an unpopular ruler. This game really comes to life when temperatures drop to -100, you’re running low on coal and oil and suddenly your city is ablaze in red fire as riots spill out of control. This game is completely unique, your morals and ideology will be tested. Will you put the needs of the city above all else? Are a few hundred deaths worth it to secure your city? Will you reconcile with hostile factions? Or crush them with force?The city must not fall

_childDocuments_.review: As with the first game: I highly recommend.While the scale may be larger, Frostpunk 2 is still very much a Frostpunk game. While you may not place individual buildings anymore, the core of what makes Frostpunk: Managing resources, both human and more mundane, prioritisation, and the ever present feeling of desperation (And the hard choices that come with it), are all present and better than ever. Do you focus on getting a roof ever everyone's head, or do you ensure they are fed first? Do you put off manufacturing goods to ensure you're making the maximum heat credits, or accept the loss to ensure you keep the deathcount as low as possible? I also think the political system added on top only enhances Frostpunk's strengths, and adds even more depth and choice to a playthrough.And at the end of the day, while the game is hard, it is fair. If you are good enough, you can even minimise how many hard choices you have to make.Phenomenal game. Cannot recommend enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, the story has several great improvements, like a parliament, a new major resource, and a more complicated system of laws. A whole new political game takes place within your game, where you have to balance the relationship between factions, and make deals to pass your laws. If you are looking for a unique city-state builder, this game has got it.Why a negative review? Minor nitpicks concern the game's UI, or design of the buildings: this just doesn't feel as gritty as the first game. Instead of planning individual buildings, we are placing a whole district in tiles of an arbitrary number. Sure, that's fine, but I can't plan my city as closely. On a larger scale, the greatest negative departure from the first game is the lack of connection with your citizens. Unfortunately, this game doesn't feel as personal as the first Frostpunk, which I loved. The fact that I can't see individual settlers, name individual automatons, or customize them in any way - is a major downgrade. The game is stressful, but it could be worth it if you could connect with your citizens on some level. I used to name citizens after my friends, or I made up fictional characters with background stories about them, which gave me extra purpose to keep them alive. In Frostpunk 2, some council members have generated backgrounds, but you have no control over it. They just felt like faceless, nameless numbers, a statistic and nothing more. Death of 60 people due to frost shouldn't feel like an annoying notification in the early game that you just brush away with annoyance.

_childDocuments_.review: If you are looking for Frostpunk 1.5, this is not it. The city is dead, long live the city!Decades into the future, the concerns of your citizens remain the same; food, shelter, health (now split into health and squalor). But now they don't agree on how to go about fixing them. You are therefore in a constant game of 3D chess, in which you want to stop your population from freezing to death, but that blast coal mine you just built means those pesky Pilgrims are up in arms about you making the city dirtier.in FP1 you noticed every death and illness, now you measure them by the hundreds, and accept it as the price of doing business. I have no doubt that this is deliberate - forcing you to make the difficult choices; childhood apprenticeships vs mandatory schooling, mass exile vs public execution, healthcare focusing on teaching and research vs treatment.You lose that personal touch that made FP1 incredible, but in exchange you face much grander decisions, and strike out into the unknown in the pursuit of riches unknown, and have to balance the needs of near and distant requirements.The UI could do with some cosmetic work, it feels a little clinical, even though I know the colour palette is deliberately stark. The extra work on tool tips and text prompts were worth the wait, but some Ideas and votes could do with more direct explanations, and I predict some are going to be pushed and pulled to rebalance the choice to make it more even (there some genuine no-brainer choices unless you're really into a moral roleplay paythrough).I can well imagine many FP1 players howling in annoyance at how far removed this is from its progenitor. But these are older and younger siblings, not identical twins. If you're willing to embrace that, this game has a lot to offer, and I would argue decent replayability.

_childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk 2 is not going to be everyone's cup of tea, especially for folks expecting a similar game to the first game.While the first game focused on a more microscopic scale where you actually get to see each and every citizen's names and status and it feels very personal; the second game presents itself in a more grander macroscopic scale where deaths and tragic events feel less personal and more "by the numbers". At first this seemed very jarring to me and honestly turned me off from the game.But then I finished the Tutorial (which you can absolutely fail even on the easiest difficulty, mind you) and I started playing Chapter 1 of the story. At that point, the vision of the devs and the highly complex mechanics CLICKED for me and I got immediately hooked. This is the point of the game where I would imagine many players would get conflicting opinions on, so bear that in mind.One of the greatest aspects of the story is that it is divided into several chapters rather than several missions. This means that the progress and state of your city from the first chapter will be the exact same when you start the second chapter, and all the other chapters after that. What this means is that the decisions you've made, be it in policies pushed, factions supported, districts laid out, or even people lost have significant consequences to the rest of your game; either making it easier or harder for you.Frostpunk 2 is highly unforgiving, complex, challenging, and very stressful. The way I see it, the game plays very much like a mix between Against the Storm, CIVILIZATION, and the first Frostpunk game. There are so many resources, systems, factions, and situations that you need to be mindful of and it is easy to get overwhelmed quickly if you do not pay attention to the game. For some, that would be a dealbreaker, but for many, that would be a draw.

_childDocuments_.review: Very disappointed.  It doesn't have the tight balance of the original, which was what made it one of my favorite games of the last several years. Completely unlike the first game which managed to be challenging and intense throughout.The story mode is also very very short, and you'll be done in 2-3 evening of play.  It's a shorter game than the first one, it's less balanced and fun than the first one.  Just added a bunch of complexity for complexity's sake that isn't tweaked properly so isn't fun.  Thumbs down.

_childDocuments_.review: This is not a clone of the original Frostpunk but it's amazing in a new way. It's more of a society builder than a city builder. I personally loved the first game and I feel like the sequel lives up to the legacy while still being its own game.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible. Everything you could ask for in a sequel. _childDocuments_.review: So far a great follow up to the previous Frostpunk!I've come to expect some great things from 11bit studios, always managing a captivating blend of earnest and engaging thematics, supported by some very strong designed games. One of the best in making "fun", commercial, challenging games, while at the same time pulling in some of the more "serious games" parts by asking some real questions of the player.This one doesn't disappoint, 11bit did it again, expanding beautifully on the established themes in the previous Frostpunk, where they asked "why do people survive and how far are we willing to go?" This time bringing in the delicious mechanic of politics!! Different factions are all part of the council deciding on which laws will be passed, making you wheel and deel between different viewpoint to keep everyone happy.Can't wait to see how the rest of the game shakes out.
