_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: If you think this is just more of the same then you need to look again. This game managed to rip out nearly all mechanics from the first game, do something completely different and make you think "Yep, this is definetely Frostpunk".Gone is the building to building custruction of a small town, now you are plonking down entire districts which have a minimum size to them. Instead of being in charge of a handful of people they are in the hundreds and thousands. You are basically moving from micro management to macro management.This is also the only city builder series I am aware of that manages to pull off a story mode while being a city builder. The game has factions and voting on policy by said factions. You can negotiate to get the factions to vote for your ideas (or against ones you allowed a faction to pick) by making promises. I started this like probably many would: oh we will keep it balanced, find compromise and see how democracy goes, only to end up basically being a despot that forced his will to make sure everyone is alive and isn't killing each other. Not sure I've seen another game do that...There are some minor gripes as they make the UI unintuitive, such as heat demand. It's practically a resource like any other, you have to meet the demand. Unmet demand is a negative value. The thing is, when you try to research something you might see a sentance state: -20 Heat demand in red. What does that make you think? Will it satisfy some of the demand or will it increase our demand? If it's the latter congratulations, if it's the former then you, like several others I know, have read it wrong. It doesn't help that heat supply is more or less a function of how much fuel you have, so if you have no stockpile and unmet fuel demand it's just straight unmenet heat demand, which often makes you feel that both values represent the same thing. All in all minor gripes, the game is well designed and polished.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent successor to the first game. It's more accessable than the first, with less focus on micromanaging every scrap of land, but it makes up for it with puzzle gameplay based around hubs and adjacency bonuses. The visual and sound design are top notch, especially when things start to collapse, and balancing the interests in the council can be very engaging. Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: I wanted to like it but didn't. Turned from survival city-builder to city-builder survival. Due to increased scale the game feels nowhere near as immersive and people's deaths are no longer a true problem, just a minor setback that has no real weight.I'm going to be honest, I don't like Frostpunk 2. I know that for someone it'll be GOTY, and that's fine by me. I do not want a sequel to be a direct clone of the previous game, and I know they spent forever working on this to make it interesting. It has amazingly fleshed out political mechanics, a robust research tree, and a sprawling overworld to explore. This is also where it falls short for me.To me, this isn't Frostpunk 2. This is at best a spinoff in a similar genre in terms of gameplay. Whereas before it was just you and your small city versus the terrible expanse of a frozen world where you do only what is necessary to survive while trying not to lose yourself and the few people left in the process. Now, with society progressing again, people become a number. Deaths can easily count in the 100s and make no real long-term difference in your run. This is no longer a survival city-builder, but a city-builder survival. The priorities feel flipped, and now it's closer to Cities than it is to Frostpunk 1 in terms of scale.I really wanted to like this game. I really, really did. I just can't bring myself to. It isn't a game for me and not what I feel like it should have been so I can't recommend it, but I know that there will be people who will love it. While each mechanic is amazingly fleshed out and interesting, even as someone who loves his color matching Grand Strategy games I feel like there is simply too much going on at one time and when combined doesn't feel natural and homogeneous but instead a jumbled mess.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk 2 is an excellent evolution of the first game through both gameplay and themes while retaining the core ideas that made the original special.Gameplay:This is still your gruelingly difficult steampunk cold fighting city builder game - but at a level higher than in the previous game. Instead of micro-managing a workforce of a few hundred, you are in charge of thousands organizing workforces of hundreds through districts. Furthermore, you can expand the interests of New London to new locations. The game has a clear influence on some of the mechanics introduced in the "On the Edge" DLC from the first game. Logistics is everything. Ensure there is enough housing. Ensure your new districts dont overwhelm your heat demand. Ensure your new population is fed. Ensure your buildings are being maintained.Along with this, the tech tree is now split on ideas by the factions you will encounter. Each have some interesting benefits or setbacks that have their appeal. Some techs will require a law to be introduced and passed by the council.The council is able to pass laws that attend to issues in the city, though you do not have the same authority as in the first game. A bill can be proposed as a law, and depending on the different delegates' worldviews, it will or wont go through. Some of the laws that need to be researched first can be a bit out of the way, or rarely encountered and is one of the main criticisms I have for this mechanic.I find it hard to believe that it takes about the same amount of time for my researchers to understand machinery used to recycle heat as it does the idea for privatized alcohol.Sound Design and Music:Much of the appeal of the first game comes from its presentation in sound and music, and that carries over the the second game. The light groaning of the generator in the first game has been replaced by intimidating sounds of machinery that echoes through the much larger city. The music in a similar vain emphasizes the change in scale. This is no longer a small group of survivors. It is a prospering well ordered city.The music also happens to be very good.  I still find it amazing how 11Bit's music makes a city building game as intense and stressful as it is. They. Do not. Miss.Performance:This game is incredibly well optimized. I am amazed at the ambition and scale of the game, and yet it is crammed into a mere 14GB of space. In an era of games being bloated and performing poorly, Frostpunk 2 stands out as an example of coding prowess.The crowd simulation is, as ever, detailed and impressive. The city feels alive; you can see people walking around, trains zip around the city, and the lights really makes the city feel alive.TLDR Summary: 9/10FP2 is an excellent, intensely difficult city building survival game wherein your survival and reign as the Honorable Steward depends on your ability to fend off the cold and appease the delegates of the city. Your vision of the city will be opposed, and the political discourse will escalate.The city is past survival - Now, The City Cannot Fall.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is like the awkward middle Evolution of a Pokémon.Pros: - Actual sequel: It's not just the first game but more of it, it's actually bigger and more complex in scope- Factions: people want to have a say how their city is being run and thus organize into opposing factions. You can influence these factions, so you still techically fully control the city.- Variable tech tree: The factions have their own solutions to some problems. Buildings researched in the tech tree have variations depending on the faction researching them. For example, adaptation based pathfinder scouts decrease terretory threat level, while progress based pathfinder scouts decrease scouting time.- Bigger frostland: Biggus dickus no complainus have returned in teams, ready to explore a bigger area of the frostland. Instead of investigating points of interest, they explore areas at a time and all PoIs within them will be uncovered at the same time.- More fuel types: no longer do you have to rely on coal to fuel your furnace. You can find ways to power it with different resources, like oil or steam.Cons:- Music is ok, not as memoriable as Frostpunk 1 and it certainly does not have an amazing opening level- The weather takes a backburner. No longer do you stockpile for regular whiteouts, instead you're only concerned about pleasing the bickering factions. (unless that does happen in later acts. However I haven't seen anything like that during the early acts or during the endings. The only instance I know of where the weather has a story impact is during the very short prologue)- City building isn't as personal as in Frostpunk 1. Instead of planning building spaces and roads and decorations, you just plop down districts and that's it.- One super long campaign, instead of 7 different shorter campaigns. This decreases the variety of challenges and scenarios you can play.- The UI looks boring and lacks soul (like those simplified logo memes you've probably seen), and sometimes is hard to use (like you gotta play a round of twisters with your fingers to have an overview of the heat demands of the city etc).- Sometimes overwhelming: at some point the game asks you to build outposts. Unlike in the first game, they are not autonomous points on the map, but actual cities that need to be managed just as well as your main city. Multitasking between them takes away from the fun of the game.Should you buy it?:If you want Frostpunk 1, but more: No. Go play Frostpunk 1.If you want an evolution to Frostpunk 1: Yes.

_childDocuments_.review: So long as you didnt come in expecting it to be exactly like the first game ( which they did not advertise it as a clone of the first ) and you take the time to learn it, it's actually really fun! So far there's some issues with performance in mid - late game but I'm sure it'll be patched soon enough.RTX 3070ti with a i9-1900k, 64gb of ram. It lags even on the lowest settings possible toward the mid to late game. I think this performance issue will be patched or it might be part of the CPU bottleneck they're currently working on. I didn't have this issue on the early access testing but I also wasn't computing a city of 20k, an outpost, and the entirety of the frostland during that time.My only recommendation is to make the instructions a lil more clear ; emphasis that the council and the research are separate for the most part, and that research unlocks other parts of the council that aren't yet accessible. And for a tip for newer players: If you're looking to build a facility on a district, but don't have enough workforce for it, turning the district's workforce down to build that facility will net you more than just the facility itself. Adjust accordingly and don't be afraid to put places at less than maximum efficiency to work around the workforce limit. Also, build storehouses. They're fantastic.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, you've expanded the city building and management parts of the game. But you've ignored, and in some parts regressed, what I consider to be the main attraction of Frostpunk, the survival. Because you're not surviving anymore, you're rebuilding society. That means you can have 100 children die in a mine and apart from some blurbs, nobody really seems to care. But you don't pass a law that's clearly just a net negative for everyone even the faction proposing it? Well that's cause for a riot. That and the whole law system feels totally unbalanced. Exploration feels hollow with no real dangers, just another "resource" I have to keep track of. I lose more explorers ferrying people back home rather than when I'm sending them out into the unknown. Nothing really interesting happens out there, and when you think you might've found something interesting it's bait. As in you get some resources or people and nothing else happens.The cold means nothing, people dying means nothing, it's all about those sweet sweet Heatstamps. Want to build a trail and you can't rob any of your factions? Guess you're gonna wait a couple weeks doing nothing. Not building, not researching, not even frostbreaking. You just sit there, waiting. Should've prepared better I guess.Don't even get me started on the UI, the Tron lasers people have, or overall atmosphere of the game.I'm gonna keep playing it a bit more. But yeah, hopefully it gets better come the first DLC. Because balance changes and quality of life updates aren't gonna cut it for me. By the way I like that you went in such a different direction from the main game. Too bad this ain't it.

_childDocuments_.review: I might be slightly biased when i say this, but this game is incredible. (spoiler warning further down, rest is safe to read. :D )You remember the first game? Pretty much all the faults of that game went out the window here (Except optimisation on release, but that'll get fixed eventually) Due to how the storyline mechanics work, there are many, many endings to the story scenario, both good and bad, so you get plenty of replayability value (both with self-imposed rules, difficulty, and political choices)Great stuff from the first game:-Tough moral choices (also improved upon) It's quite scary if you get self conscious enough to see that you're going mad with power of your own volition..... Like trying to push a radical law even though it isn't necessary.... To see yourself become a monster like all those 'evil politicians in the news'....Yeah, that's good game design, thank you 11bit; I have anxiety about politics now.-Rewarding the player for strategizing (much more recognizable in this game's building mechanics)-Good skill floor for new players with plenty of room for error-Godlike music (Listen to the main theme please, it even has the violin solo from the first game's climax music track, it's amazing)-Exploring the frostland (much more complex here, but the game doesn't tell you to RUSH LOGISTICS DISTRICTS ASAP... a free tip from me :P )-British humor in a citizen's speech is so good to see.-Plenty, plenty more amazing stuff that I don't really have the energy rn to write. I havent eaten lunch yet. :>There are cameos of places from the first game's DLC's! Yayyyy!Now, for some of my gripes, but more like suggestions for balance changes or ranting about small issues that could use some polish (pun intended) -Optimization..... My Pc was almost burning for the 7,5 hours I played this on medium-high settings. (A little over exaggerating here, it's not as bad as with cyberpunk, but y'know...) Working on optimizing the game wouldn't hurt.... even though i think it's already pretty well optimized on lower settings, and ppl playing on ultra are coping their 2006 laptop can't run it smoothly.  :P-Tutorials ain't exactly accurate, or more accurately: they're incomplete. Like with heat surplus. How does it benefit the city??? Also, on a more personal note, please tell people to not sleep on Logistics districts or something, it's a huge lifeline that can provide very efficient supplies with minimal workforce commitment. It'd do this game much good if it became common sense in the community..... and save a game journalist a couple braincells :P-UI is a little bit clunky at times, and you end up clicking research instead of a hub building you want, or deadlines being very imprecise (it shows how many full weeks you get to do something, but not days, so it might get confusing)(Scary wall of text ahead  D:  ) (A tip included)-Balance change proposal: The Fervour  and faction relationship is... very weird. It has no cap, so if you keep antagonizing one of the radical factions for a long time, it is almost impossible to know how many points of fervour a faction has accumulated (and the biggest consequences are at fervor 3...... i got to something like +10 i think) -(Tip for beginners, use at your own risk) You can easily cheese the political system by repeatedly denouncing and antagonizing one of the radical factions to reduce their size and support, thus weakening them..... Yes, you can turn a political party into a harmless chiuaua this way; and make a 'powerful fanatical guard dog that'll follow you through hell and back' out of the other one. If you manage your city well, you can try out one of the laws under 'Rule' category that requires like 2/3 or 3/4 majority to pass... and having a unflinchingly loyal faction helps a bit. And if you succeed... the council is a cakewalk from then on (not really, you still gotta keep the normies happy enough, so they'll let you get away with everything). TLDR: Suppressing a faction from the beginning of the game makes it much easier to play, but limits your choices later on. Recommended if you start your first game of frostpunk on officer difficulty. -Suggested fix: Change the fervor mechanic into something similar to the favorability mechanic, or give larger punishment for maxing out the fervor. Add caps to the favorability and fervor mechanics, so that it doesn't go past the max... give it a bigger bad event, or some other penalty except tension (Fightclub or two can fix that easily.) (on the other hand, favorability is fine as it is, because you can keep raising funds from your loyal fanatics..... yeah keep it cuz heatstamps are very difficult to get in a pinch. :>  )  SPOILER AREA AHEAD:-SPOILER (Stalwarts): it's kinda sad that you don't get to keep using the second colony after the civil war hits if you go with dismantling it for cores and build the last upgrade too early. (ngl, if you can afford that thing, something went very right, and there isn't much left ahead.) -Also, some of the cores are very hard to access due to elevation or ravines, and sometimes it's simply too late to realize that you can't access that deposit because of elevation shenanigans, even though the district you just built is directly bordering those sweet steam cores. I might add more stuff as I play through the other endings.(SPOILERS OVER)Not much else, this is fun as all hell, politics included! If you read this entire damn thing, I salute you, and let it be known that Polish people are built different, Polacy górą!

_childDocuments_.review: I have read a large number of negative reviews of this game, which led me to chime in with my thoughts.  It seems the most of those disappointed are those who pre-bought the game, not knowing how it would turn out.  There's a lot to be said for the loyalty of the fans of the first game that paid out immediately upon pre-release,  I am one of them, paying up front, without any  knowledge of how the game would turn out.Am I disappointed?  Maybe a little.  As with some people on here I have hundreds of hours played on Frostpunk.  I completed the new game in 30hrs or so.I did, however, enjoy it.  It is not a repeat of the first game.  The devs said from early on that they did not want to just make a copy of the first game.  The also postponed release date after receiving feedback from the fans that were given access to the early version of the game.I was bewildered with the early version and pleasantly surprised at how much better the later version was.  It was much less confusing and carefully laid out.  So much so that finishing the game felt like I was just finishing a tutorial, or first scenario.  Perhaps this is a pre-cursor for upcoming DLC.  Which would make sense, but seem a bit unfair.  I think that the devs should compensate those fans that bought the game early, and had to wait longer than announced, by giving them free DLC access.  Assuming there will be DLC.I think that the game play is excellent.  There is so much to keep and eye on.  Pretty much like the first one, but on steroids.  Which makes a great deal of sense for a follow up game.  Similar, yet different.  I like the factions, vying for control.  Having to placate them at times, defy them at other times.  The way they react to each other's credo.  Very cool, and almost like a mini game itself.  Despite the time involved in making this game though, some aspects still feel rushed.  It's as though all the individual pieces work great separately, yet don't meld as perfectly as they could.  What do I mean?Well, it just feels like there should be more to it.  For example, the above mentioned factions.  I barely scratched the surface if laws available to implement.  The same goes for the research tree.  Also for map exploration.The conclusion that I came to is that, perhaps, the real experience from this game comes from the unscripted endless mode.  Which is what I am going to try next.  I am not sure how it will work out, but I am hopeful that this allows me to experience much more of the game.  I will update this review after I do that.To sum up, for those on the fence about buying the game.Firstly, it is not the same game as Frostpunk.  There are a lot of similarities, but, also a lot of differences.  For those who managed to complete the first game and all the DLC, this game is not as unforgiving as the first.  You can come back from mistakes.  In fact, I liked that aspect, it was very rewarding to realise that you are doing something wrong and be able to fix it.  A lot better than save scumming!Secondly, as I mentioned earlier, the campaign, or story mode, is relatively short,  It make take longer for some.  I am not trying to say that I am better than others at the game.  But, we all play differently.You will have to decide if the price tag merits that little time.  Though, as I said, maybe the time comes from the endless mode......  I will let you know.

_childDocuments_.review: It's the resource management gameplay of Frostpunk 1 abstracted one level higher than before.  You don't manage individual people and buildings, but instead districts and factions.  There's a trade-off here, and depending on what you valued in the first game, you may find the change an improvement, or off-putting.City design lost a lot of granularity. Painting down districts on the hex-based maps lacks that cozy feeling of sculpting and optimising layouts just right and the limited positioning of special buildings definitely feels less impactful. You will also likely miss that feeling of getting your tents and coal thumper snugly inside the heat radius in the first game, instead getting abstracted adjacency bonuses from tiling certain districts together or building area of effect hubs and awkwardly positioning  your city around them.The game gained a lot of such granularity back in its law system however.  No longer a selection of black and whites, laws and research have been opened wide up, with different ways of tackling problems which can be researched and proposed by different interest groups.  Not only are the options widened, but your motivations for choosing accordingly are made more complex.  Perhaps you want to extract oil and quickly as possible with fracking because the storm is approaching and coal is almost depleted, but your faction of damn hippies want to pursue a less destructive method and are too close to protesting your rule for you to slight them further.Music and visuals remain good, although in both cases are not quite matching up against Frostpunk 1 which had a more focused, immersive and useful UI along with a more impressive sound track.The frostland exploration is on a much larger scale than in the first game, with more considerations about how to explore, budget your time and safety concerns for scouts. Additionally there are colonies, including buildable colonies you can establish out there.  If the lack of additional colonies bothered you in the prequel, this could be for you, although personally I found that management of multiple colonies a clumsy situation, not aided by the lack of useful information on the interface. Overall, it's a different playing experience from Frostpunk 1, but hits the same notes of fighting for survival in a grim, resource-starved information.  While I don't think it will make quite the splash that Frostpunk 1 did, it's an enjoyable game in its own right.It took quite some resolve to write an actual review instead of just putting "Get back to work!" here.  I trust it will be appreciated.

_childDocuments_.review: 11bit's highly anticipated sequel to their smash hit Frostpunk is finally here. This game is a far more ambitious title than its predecessor, and it does not disappoint. Instead of building only individual houses and industrial buildings, you are now responsible for planning entire districts, with specialized buildings within them. Creating your city requires even more careful planning, as there are bonuses for having symbiotic districts next to each other, such as housing/food, and extraction/industry. The Frostland exploration is now done through Logistics districts, with specialized buildings providing bonuses to safety and exploration time. The law system has been entirely reworked, where before you could simply sign a law and it would take effect, now a council of 100 will vote on every proposal you put forward, which may require some careful negotiation should you not have the votes outright. New laws also have to be researched, but they don't require any resources to do so, aside from time. Your citizens now belong to factions, and those factions will influence how your city develops. If you ignore one faction for too long, tension develops, which can boil over into a full blow riot. The research tree has also be reworked, with buildings requiring heatstamps to research. Each faction will have specialized buildings, each with their own bonuses and costs associated.The economy system has also be reworked, requiring not just materials, but currency as well, in the form of heatstamps. Your citizens provide heatstamps, but if their needs are left unmet, the amount you receive becomes lower and lower, which can cause further issues when attempting to expand. This new, more complex gameplay system is incredible. 11bit swung for the fences, and delivered on almost every point. However, the only drawback is you have lost the individualism from the first game, as you used to be able to click on each individual citizen, and they had a name, and a family. You have the ability to zoom in on districts, and see your citizens working, but you no longer have that connection with them. Overall, 11bit took a massive risk with this title, and it payed off. I can see myself playing this game for hundreds of hours like the previous one. I can't wait to see how they develop this world further.

_childDocuments_.review: Usually when you hear about a sequel its a toss up between "here we go again" or a "Wow! They really improved it." What the devs did with Frostpunk 2 is revamp the game to be almost a new game. You feel the constant pressure of your choices. Everything is on the brink of collapse as you try to balance the politics, failing machinery, and ever encroaching cold with resources that are few and far and between. This truly feels like a "survival, post-apocalyptic setting". You desperately need more food, you finally find some frozen food stores under the ice. So you go to build an extraction district to try and pull the resources out. Some of the workforce mining the coal out of the ice died from starvation or the frost. Now you do not have enough workers. So you pull from another area. Some of the children start to go feral as the city starts to descend into anarchy. The coal mine is not producing coal as it dries up, so your generator holding the cold barely at bay is running out of fuel now.  You make a deal with a colony for some of their oil to keep the heat on for a little longer. In doing so, one of the rising factions in the city begins to oppose you because they do not like the deal you made. Its a constant struggle of back and forth that makes you feel you are really on the precipice of extinction and about to go over. Game play is outstanding. Graphics and audio are great. Some audio sound bite loops (such as when you click on one of the factions) can get old fast. Minor nitpicking aside, this game is absolutely fantastic. No you do not need to buy the first game at all. This is well worth the 45 bucks to a somewhat small studio for game play that is infinitely better than any of the sludge the "AAA" studios will ever produce.

_childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk 2 is by far the best city builder, colony game, and strategy game I’ve played so far! Most, if not all, of your actions have consequences. Your moral compass and how far you are willing to go to achieve your goals are often tested throughout a playthrough. My favorite aspect of Frostpunk 2 is that it allows you to see a snippet of each person’s life, even though there are thousands of individuals. Unlike the first game, where you had to worry about Hope and Discontent, now you must manage Crime, Trust, and Tension. Crime rises with food and goods scarcity and a lack of guards or buildings. Trust falls when promises aren’t kept, due to discontent factions, or certain buildings. Tension increases as factions gain and lose power or due to specific buildings. If you don’t manage all three of these aspects, you will fail. Heat-stamps (money) are arguably one of the most important aspects of your city. Unlike in the previous game, you must now face the conundrum of money: how to pay your workers and how to collect money. Do you give everyone equal pay or merit pay? Another intriguing feature, and one that adds a whole new layer of difficulty and strategy, is the public image system. Unlike in the previous game, where you could sign any new law into effect with little public backlash, you now face severe consequences if you’re not paying attention to your public image. Even with good intentions, you will face riots and possibly assassination attempts! If you really screw up, you could cause a civil war, prematurely ending your playthrough. Most importantly, your laws can be rejected. I was surprised by the Colony and Outpost feature. I really like the outposts because they grant you infinite resources, and if you upgrade them into settlements, they even operate in a whiteout. Colonies can be built once you research colony furnaces; a colony is basically a new generator site. Squalor or industrial waste adds an interesting touch to the game’s mechanics. Managing or using this waste can define a playthrough. Whether you use it for more materials or just store it is up to you. But if you do nothing, your structures will begin to fall apart. Managing families was something I did not expect to do in this game. From mandatory marriage to family apprenticeships, these directly affect the city. Do you allow children freedom, or do you make them work? Do you allow mothers to do more than just take care of children? But this is only the tip of the iceberg. There is so much more to this game, and I love every aspect of it. Frostpunk 2 requires a stronger PC than the last game, but it runs just fine on an NVidia RTX 2060s All in all, I believe Frostpunk 2 is more than worth the price.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game received a fair bit of backlash due to differences from the first one, but from my experience so far all of the changes make sense. First, politics. In the first game, everyone was desperately struggling for survival, many were left dead on the way to the city, they are willing to go above and beyond and are all unified in their struggle against the cold, at a pace not sustainable forever, but that they are willing to bear for the month or so in-world that games usually lasted.In this game, many years have passed. They likely remained unified under that one leader who got them through the hard times, but that character has died, and after their death rather than choosing a new person as essentially a benevolent dictator, they chose more of a hybrid solution with a parliament in which delegates from the various factions within the city vote for new laws, to decide whether the Steward should stay in their position after a bit of a trial period, and so on, then a Steward who has sole control over most decisions related to building, expending resources, choosing what work should be focused on, and research, with some special amendments prepared to give the Steward more powers if it turns out to be necessary.This new system makes sense, allowing the people more of a say in the city while still allowing for a quick response to the changing threats and avoiding stalling the operations of the city in bureaucracy and red tape. It does mean you are no longer an all-powerful dictator and have to play politics a bit with the various factions, and some people dislike that, but I feel that the mechanics associated with that actually add quite a lot to the game and make sense.Same with districts, before you built individual buildings, now you essentially build multi-tile buildings that can benefit or be harmed from their proximity to others, location, and so on. I honestly don't feel anything was lost here compared to before, the system is more engaging overall, and these districts also each have individual building slots you can make the more traditional buildings in. The change in scale also makes sense since decades have passed and what was your entire city in the past is now only a small number of tiles in the center, with a lot more people, a lot more resources, and a lot more expenses.Another thing that changed from the previous game, and that I kind of miss as well, is how the generator worked. Before, it was a constant race against time to upgrade the generator to produce enough heat to keep people warm, while the temperature drops lower and lower. In this game, the generator could generate as much heat as is needed, you just need enough fuel for it. I do kind of miss how it worked before, but this also makes sense for the world. You already upgraded the generator for heat as much as you could in the first game, then the city had 30 years to further improve on that, it makes sense that now it is mostly a matter of fuel and efficiency, and that the people have developed systems to pump the heat wherever it needs to go rather than relying solely on proximity to the generator. That sort of thing was already possible in the first game through steam hubs, I think now steam hubs are essentially just standard for every district and probably a bit better than they were before.For the next, very big, change, there is scenarios vs story mode. In the first game you had multiple different scenarios where you play as different people responding to the frost in different ways, and in different locations. You might be building New London to survive, be a group of scientists with a huge amount of steam cores, their own personal generator, and the sole purpose of preserving a bunch of plant samples and seeds to help the world recover when the frost is gone, only to have to balance that against helping a nearby struggling city, you might be the people desperately trying to build the generators pre-frost for people to evacuate to, and much more. The scenarios were each pretty replayable and often had a couple different routes you could take, and were great.i would honestly consider this to be one of the few ways in which Frostpunk 2 actually is behind the original. There is just one scenario, Story Mode, that has a bit of replayability and a couple different routes you can take, but primarily serves as an extended tutorial, just as the first scenario of the previous game did. I am pretty confident the devs will add new scenarios with the DLCs, and I expect them to be pretty good, but there will likely still be fewer overall and not having as many different perspectives to play from is unfortunate, with more of a focus on Utopia Builder mode (roughly equivalent to the endless mode of Frostpunk). To be fair though, 30 years have passed and things have stabilized a fair bit, there are likely to be fewer groups with completely unique goals and motivations, having already resolved those in the past few decades, with the goal now being survival, rebuilding, and expanding.So far I have just been comparing some of the biggest complaints I have seen about Frostpunk 1 vs Frostpunk 2, now let's talk about what kind of game it actually is for those who are not coming over from Frostpunk 1 (though I would honestly recommend playing Frostpunk 1 first for lore and context, it holds up very well, is a great game, and they are different enough that Frostpunk 2 won't just be more of the same).In Frostpunk's setting, a roughly steampunk industrial age world fell into a horrific ice age. Various countries were able to recognize this impending threat in advance, so took measures to help their people survive, in Frostpunk 2 you only really see what the British Empire did, finding sheltered locations with ample resources in isolated areas and secretly constructing massive coal-powered generators for their people to be evacuated to and build new cities around. Thirty years passed from then, now that people have survived the Frost, they want to expand and start reclaiming what was lost. No longer content with the extreme emergency measures that they went through at the start, they also want to live more comfortable lives, shape the city towards their visions of an ideal future, have a say in the laws that are passed, and work towards the future rather than desperately struggling to get by just one day longer.They still make plenty of sacrifices, but there is more hope than there was before. In terms of mechanics, it is an atmospheric survival city-builder where you constantly search for new resources to replace ones that have been drained or support an ever-increasing population. There is a pretty big and interesting law and research system, much expanded compared to before, and you have a lot of different options and your people have clearly come very from the first game in terms of what they are capable of developing with enough time. There is a series of "zeitgeists" that essentially represent the direction of the city, Adaptation vs Progress, Merit vs Equality, and Reason vs Tradition, all with their own pros and cons, as well as their factions supporting or opposing those directions. Laws can get extreme, but many of them also eventually offer you an option to reform them to be more moderate (i.e. paid essentials gives you the choice of offering indefinite unemployment pay for those who can not get a job, thus allowing them to still get by as long as they use their money wisely, at the cost of reducing the heatstamps bonus), so there is a pretty big range in terms of how reasonable or extreme you can have your city be.The various factions, depending on their zeitgeists, also offer different research options to you, in terms of both laws and buildings. There is a pretty good trade off of pros vs cons, though in some cases one building may just be clearly superior to the alternatives. I have apparently hit a character limit, so I will end here. Very good game overal

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a great evolution of the first Frostpunk, but it is quite a departure from its predecessor. Many sequels these days stick to the same mechanics, and just expand on them. This game looked at Frostpunk and asked "what makes this game fun at its core?" Well the answer is brutal city building that requires delicately balancing resources, often on the brink of starvation or freezing, along with tough decision making to try and keep people happy, leaving the player morally justifying their choices in real life. I often found myself saying out loud things like "Well... making kids work in the factories isnt great, but at least they're with their parents while they do it..."Frostpunk 2 took those core concepts but radically re-contextualized the rest of the experience. This game focuses on a larger scale version of the snow-pocalipse. You no longer build individual houses and roads, and you no longer build bespoke upgrades for individual buildings. Now, you build tile-based districts, and upgrades take the form of specialty buildings in the district. You don't build city streets, you build skyways and trails to outposts in the surrounding frostland. The tile-based nature of the game presented in the first chapter at first had me worried that the experience had been dumbed down, but I was quickly shown otherwise.This game maintains the spirit of brutal resource management, and additional complications in keeping the populace happy in a very enjoyable way. At the same time it takes the survival experience to a much grander scale, moving the story of the first game forward in a very satisfying way.The faction system for your city's population was honestly what blew me away with this game. Each city is divided into several factions that affect every mechanic of the game. trying to keep every group happy requires thoughtful decision making, as what will please one faction will often frustrate another. This translates over to the technology tree, which, despite its appearance at first is substantially more complicated than Frostpunk's. Instead of researching specific technologies, you are presented with problems facing the city. when you click on them, different factions have different solutions to these problems that each have their pro's and con's in terms of resource consumption and side-effects. on top of that, doing research aligned with one faction could upset another faction which added in a level of decision making I did not expect. Deep into the game i found myself looking at the research tree saying "Well this is option is the exact one that will tip resource management in my favor, but picking this one may tip me over the brink in my relationship with a certain faction"While I miss some of the more micromanaging elements of the first game, Frostpunk 2 had a clear vision for its unique gameplay elements and it nails it! This game is incredible! Strongly recommend for any city-building sicko's out there.

_childDocuments_.review: So far, a nice successor to the first title. It's a different experience, which is what sequel titles should aspire to be, though the mechanic changes may not interest those who are expecting a much-improved version of the first game. This is more like playing a different game set in the same universe and should be approached with that in mind.Whereas Frostpunk was a colony management game that dealt closely with placing buildings, micro-managing heat districts, selectively managing citizen placement, and a very close watch over resources, Frostpunk 2 tackles colony management with a bit of a broader scope. Resource management is still an important part of the game, but you deal far more with districts, factions, and voting politics than you do with individual people. In my opinion, this doesn't necessarily make the game better or worse than the first installment—it just gives it a slightly 4X feel—but it might not be your bag if you enjoy a closer style of colony management.The game is missing some QoL options and basic tooltips. An option to invert middle mouse camera control, for example, would be really helpful but is absent from this game. Short tooltips on where buildings need to be placed (within their building description) would also cut down on learning curve time. It took me a little bit to figure out how to build a research institute, for example, because there was no clear statement within the building description that it needed to be placed in a residential district post expansion. These are very small additions that would go a long way toward better accessibility.An enjoyable title despite its differences to its predecessor, still with great worldbuilding, visuals, and music.

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, Frostpunk 2 falls short of expectations. It has deviated significantly from the original game, which could have been a positive change had the developers focused more on testing and refining the gameplay. The choice between settling colonies and drilling into deep ice deposits feels superficial.We either settle colonies in the frozen world, or stubbornly drill ice to reach deep deposits. The question is, what are deep fertile soil deposits? Why, having such advanced food production technologies, do they even need fertile soil? Spoiler – whatever you do, you'll know that your city will die of starvation, as by week 600 you realize that all the food on the map is not enough to feed the growing population because the soil is finite, and you must finish the game earlier. So why is this a bad game design decision? Because it prevents us from being able to unlock technologies to drill deep deposits or settle colonies. If you're playing as the technocrats, you still have to connect outposts to the main city until the resources are exhausted! This is purely artificial limitation that contradicts COMMON SENSE, which you're supposed to embrace if you choose the technocrats. Meanwhile, creating an oil settlement isn't against their "religion," but creating one or two more is taboo (because it's a dumb script)! Don't you understand how artificial and cheap this looks!? I played on Captain twice. And you know what? The colony route is much easier! You have colonies on the map that bring infinite resources, and you absolutely don't worry about their housing, morale, etc., just sending them crumbs of food and oil. And even founding a colony is cheaper resource-wise than building a district with a deep mining upgrade! These colonies steadily provide you with resources despite all the riots in the main city, just like the two other cities you personally control, but if the district with deep mining riots, you risk losing the upgrade and have to rebuild it! Now to the factions – the funniest part is you can easily maintain good relations with both opposing factions (even on the highest difficulty)... IF IT WEREN'T FOR THE DAMN SCRIPTS! The game is heavily scripted, and the first part suffered from this too, but in this one, it's just insane. In the last chapter, all factions go off the rails regardless of your previous relations. And even with this, the game is very easy! I got the 0.3% achievement "Checks and Balance" (not passing any captain's laws) on my second playthrough as soon as I found out about its existence! There was no survival challenge, just idiotic political squabbles over which I had even less control due to the achievement run. I passed most of the scenarios from the first game on Survivor, and that took effort, knowledge of the game, but here it's not required. And yeah, developers, where are the achievements for Survivor difficulty? Why should I play it if the highest achievements are only for Captain difficulty, and there are no others! As a buyer of the premium edition, I am extremely disappointed. I saw the game's problems back in early access, and unfortunately, they were not fixed but left as the game’s concept. I'll check the DLCs they release later (I've already paid for them... the cactus hurts, but I keep eating it...), but I don't have much hope for improvements.

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked the first part, chances are high that you also like Frostpunk 2.You get the same setting and feeling, without the micro management and a lot more reactions to your decisions.Like the first game, it's difficult. But the difficulty is so high that it is very unlikely that you make it on Captain difficulty on first try. Even if you are an experienced Frostpunk player. The reasons for that are the mechanical differences from the first part and that you can't forsee which consequences you're decisions may cause. And if you are not prepared that can easily end your game. You almost won't be able to correct anything on a bigger scale.If you beat it on max difficulty you can still crank it up with survivor mode which wont let you pause or save the game, besides autosave on quitting.The city building part feels like a puzzle game, which isn't a bad thing but people that like a more structured approach on building a city won't get the most out of it. You are constantly looking for synergies no matter what, otherwise you lose.The social and political part is good, but in some phases of the game I hardly noticed it, it could be that this is a personal thing or something with my city. But ingame, half a year went by without me visiting the captain's hall, which seemed strange. Also I wouldn't recommend the game solely because of these mechanics. There are games out there which are way more interesting in that regard. Still, it adds a nice touch, makes the world more believable and I'm glad it exists.The Frostland part feels really good, because of being able to build outposts, trading routes and other stuff that was also present in the first part. I am exicited to try the sandbox mode. So far the campaign feels like a very long tutorial which you can fail.Frostpunk 2 looks good with everything on maximum and runs very smooth, even better than in the beta.But to be honest, the game doesn't need that, you will also enjoy it if you are on a slower machine.There are a lot of details which are completely unnecessary, serve no gameplay functionality and are just there for your entertainment, like the detail view of districts or buildings.So far I really enjoyed it and also like it more than the first part. There are some minor complaints I have about the interface and also about events not being displayed clearly enough, but I'm sure that will be fixed eventually and isn't a deal breaker.

Highly recommend the Frostpunk series! Also, people complaining about it not being like the first Frostpunk should go back and play that! It's called Frostpunk 2 for a reason! _childDocuments_.review: Great strategy and management game. The visuals and music are as usual gorgeous. A few comments :- When you vote for a new law, it would've been nice to also see the law you will be repealing in the process. - The relation to the cold is way less present than in the 1st game. It's almost banal in this version. And become obsolete at the last stage of adaptation. - Death means almost nothing when you can survive quite well losing 250+ people every few weeks. - The campaign is nice, but has little replayability. I don't see any reason to go through it again except for achievements. Overall the game is more "macro" than its predecessor. Cold and death has little impact to how you manage your city. Most of your law and technology choices are made to please the different factions independently from their actual bonuses... That and top obtain the last upgrade of the City direction you chose to improve. I have great hopes for future expansion to provide new types of campaigns and choices ! This edition is a solid foundation for more various gameplay experience.

_childDocuments_.review: A fundamentally broken and frustrating game that doesn't quite know what it wants to be.First and foremost, it's not a city builder. Sure it has traits of this, but fundamentally, it isn't.It's a narrative puzzle game.And this is where it fundamentally fails.It doesn't matter how well you have managed to balance the various factions within the city, the story requires that conflict happens in the final act, and so conflict does.And the final act is a drokking nightmare of battling against the mechanisms of the game to try and do what you need to do.This could have been an excellent game, and 11 bit studios should be applauded for trying to genuinely make a new game, rather than release the same game with better graphics (cough TROPICO cough) and a bit more playtesting might have realised this vision.But as it is, it's a frustrating pain in the arse where you don't quite know whether you are having fun or not.

Not worth removing everything that made the first game unique just for some extra sales on consoles. sad.cannot begin to express how disappointed I am without writing a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ thesis on it.Do not buy

_childDocuments_.review: WAIT FOR THEM TO BUGPATCH. There's a lot to like in this new vision for Frostpunk. Whether you like this new flavour (or not) will come down to your preferences, but I gave it a proper shake as I'd love to write well of it. However, I've ultimately come away frustrated, drained and with a bad taste in my mouth. I can't recommend anyone buy it until they patch it some. Among the things to wait to be fixed are:-  PATCHED AND FIXED (26/09)- Absence of really commonplace city-builder QoL features e.g. 'cancel construction'. - Abominable performance in the later stages - the game wants to hold onto its fore-bearer's prettiness, but it's utterly unoptimised for the 'scale' of city that the narrative demands. What is 'pretty' in your first hour will become irrelevant clutter by your fifth hour, FPS-destroying obnoxious noise by your 8th... and then it'll get worse from there. - Outposts are a key part of this version, which makes the Dev's choices about what information to provide, and what to hide, utterly bewildering. Have you got infrastructure that'll handle 600 units, but it won't handle more than 4 if those units are materials? Any idea why? Might as well guess - the game won't tell you anywhere. Been waiting so long and patiently for this - I'm really disappointed. All the worst because I spent my playthrough stumbling over these QOL shortcomings going "oh, okay, that's an early release bug" only to fight my way to the climax and have to give up due to a bug that makes it impossible to finish (or maybe it's just a catastrophic failure of UI design? The forums haven't worked it out yet)I do really want this game to succeed - so I'll keep an eye and be back to update this review when there's word, fixes or updates on the worst of these problems.

_childDocuments_.review: Before writing this review i have completed frostpunk 2 on steward difficulty. And I wouldn't say that I'm a fan of Frostpunk 1. But maybe because of that liked this game even better. I always wanted something of a proper city builder, but with some difficulty. In short, it's different from the first game, but i wouldn't say it's worse.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start by saying if you are looking for Frostpunk 1 with updates: YOU WILL NOT FIND IT HEREFrostpunk 2 is an "evolution" of the original in the truest sense of the word. The question of "how do a group of stranglers survive the collapse of the word and the oncoming frost?" have been thoroughly answered by the first the game. The humanity defining conflicts that were so difficult to make every time you made them, are now a common occurrence. Where in the first game you could try your hardest to hold on to what little there was to hold on to of sanity and morals, NOW, after 30 years, those decisions are now monthly, or weekly, or even daily. A group barely surviving the frost, now desires to conqueror it, tired of barely surviving.The mechanics of everything have been changed, overhauled, and streamlined from the first game, turning in it to the scale operation needed. But the heart and character of frostpunk, "humanity vs the frost" that is told with so much love, is told all the better here.

_childDocuments_.review:
Frostpunk 2 is the sequel to the highly acclaimed, BAFTA-nominated society survival game that blended city building, strategy and management gameplay, creating a brand new genre. Its successor takes place 30 years after the apocalyptic blizzard storm, and Earth is still overwhelmed by the icy climate of neverending frost and harsh weather.

Demands and expectations of various factions will raise tensions and evoke conflicts, but will a cold-blooded rule and a Machiavellian approach to politics be necessary? As the everlasting cold continues its grip on the city and outside threats arise, you'll need to make sure your people are united, driven, and ready for difficult, unavoidable sacrifices!

_childDocuments_.review: As a big Atlus/Persona fan, I never thought I'd refund a Persona game ever. It was a painful and difficult decision.I cannot recommend the game as it is right now. The PC Port is really bad to the point that it ruins the game experience.If you take a look closely at the Steam reviews, almost all positive reviews are just people simping for Adachi. Most of the real reviews of this game are negative due to the terrible port.P4AU itself is an incredible game, very fun to play with excellent characters and a very colorful, flashy and vibrant visuals.My PS3 broke due to a power surge that came from the network cable in a stormy day about a month after P4AU got released 9 years ago so I could never play it since then. I was really excited to finally be able play it now in current-gen hardware, especially on PC, but unfortunately the awful port ruined my experience of this great game.There are several random crashing issues in different modes, very inconsistent audio volumes that are either inaudibly quiet or freaking loud, plus video playback issues (init render and separate "active movie window" pop-up).The developers didn't even bother to upscale the game graphical assets from 720p to a higher resolution.Online matching crashes when searching for rooms with more than 2 slots and when it finds any rooms there are like only 3 people available. Ranked works but I can only find like 4 people with a 0 bar connection. I understand that this game is not popular in my region but I was expecting to find more than 7 people online at launch day.Lobbies have been removed in this version for no real reason.Atlus completely trolled us all at launch by unlocking the game 5 hours after the Steam page release time.The game is expensive for a bad 9 year old "remaster" and doesn't have regional pricing. I decided to buy it anyway because I'm a big Persona fan and I was really excited to play this game that I could never play for 9 years. The game itself is excellent, but the terrible PC Port and the big number of issues alongside a bad delay based netcode completely ruined the enjoyment of the game.Maybe I'll reconsider buying it again once rollback is implemented and the issues are fixed, but for now I can't recommend P4AU in it's current state. The negatives are greater than the positives and I felt a big disrespect from Atlus this time. I wasted too much time waiting the game troll release time, trying to fix the port issues, and trying to find people with acceptable connection online.It was a difficult decision, but I had to refund it unfortunately.

_childDocuments_.review: As I’m only okay-ish at fighting games like this one, this review will focus on the story modes of  instead. However, I don’t want to stick to just reviewing this time and instead also share some information on how to correctly approach the story modes – so you won’t make the same mistakes I did.The most important thing to know about the story of  is that it’s a canon continuation of ,  (+ FES) and  (+ Golden). And I do mean “continuation”, because  will spoil the events of both games for you - if you aren’t already familiar with them. I can’t emphasize this enough: If you’re even remotely interested in the story of , make sure to experience them before engaging with the story modes of . In fact, stop reading this review, other reviews and leave the store page and make sure you’re prepared before coming back.Still here?Already know what happens in  (or just don’t care)?Good. Here’s what else you need to know about the story modes of .If you’re opening the “story mode” part of the main menu for the first time, the game conveniently selects “Episode P4” for you to play. . What you instead want to check out is the bottom option, “P4A: Story MODE”. This is where the story really begins, set between the ending of  and the epilogue of . But why this confusing mix-up?To keep things simple, here’s the short version: Initially, this game only released as  in 2012 – and it only contained the story mode that’s now called “P4A: Story Mode” in the main menu. Two years later (at least in the West),  released as an updated version of the game, containing more content and other refinements. And yes, this includes new story modes, which serve as a direct continuation of the original  storyline. However, for some reason, the main menu put these new story episodes on top the menu – quite confusing. Anyway, tldr;  .Alright, let’s talk about the story of  then. In short, you’ll have to play through a few character stories in order to unlock the whole story. Here’s the problem though: Considering you’re exploring (mostly) the same events only with a different character, you’ll quickly get tired of seeing the same events over and over again. So here’s the shortest way to unlock the actual ending of :1. Play through the story of Yu, Yosuke, Chie or Yukiko until you reach a “to be continued” state. This unlocks the story of  or .2. Play through the story of another character until you again reach a “to be continued” state – it doesn’t matter if which story you pick as long as you got two stories in a “two be continued” state. This unlocks the stories of  as well as .3. Now, reach the “to be continued” state with one of the  characters. This unlocks the story of .4. Clearing the story of  finally allows you to continue past the “to be continued” state of all . Get to the real end of one of these character’s stories and you are now able continue past the “to be continued” state with the remaining characters.5. You guessed it, reach the real end of one of the  as well and you’ll unlock the last character story: .You can still reach the ending of the remaining character stories if you wish to do, but again, that’s going to be one hell of a repetitive task. I’d suggest going for the bare minimum instead and then continuing with the story mode the game initially wanted you to play: “Episode P4”.This story is, thankfully, not asking you to experience the same things over and over again. It’s actually pretty straightforward and getting to the end should be no problem: you can even let the AI fight for you if you don’t want to battle yourself (although this doesn’t always work well. I let the AI play against the final boss a few times to see how it fares and it actually lost quite often).After clearing “Episode P4”, you’ll unlock two more story episodes:  and .However, in true  fashion, there’s also a true ending to the story of . This unfortunately isn’t just unlocked by beating the story modes of . Instead, .That’s it, you beat the story of  in the correct way!No, for the review part: Should you even bother doing so? That’s mostly depending on how much you enjoy spending more time with the characters of .  really is mostly fanservice and while I enjoyed one of the new additions to the cast (), the story really only works if you’re invested in both  games to the point you’d even play a fighting game to see how the story continues (again, this is canon). did a better job at serving as a connection between  than I thought (longer as well, took me about 11h to see the endings of ). However, the game really likes to keep you busy with the same events, which can make it a real slog to play/read through at times. I feel like going for a linear campaign would’ve been a way better choice here, even if it meant having less content to play through. But well, fighting games and story modes …Anyway, you want more ? Check out the story modes here, even if they are longer than they need to be. If not or if you simply dislike unnecessarily long or repetitive fighting game stories, maybe just read through a Wiki summary. Also, keep in mind that this isn't even canon the end of the  storyline - that'd be , a rythm game. _childDocuments_.review: Just know that this review is only negative because of the quality of the port, and not the game itselfI'll open with this, P4 Arena quickly became one of my favorite fighting games when I first played it because it has all the things I look for in a fighting game. It's fast paced, frantic, technical, has a large and diverse character roster, and is just plain fun. This is on top of being a love letter to personas 4 and 3, with a fairly decent, and canon, story mode to play through as well. With all of that being said I was very disappointed in this port having the issues it does have, because I wanted to see this game get a second chance in the spotlight. While I haven't ran into nearly as many issues as others have, there are still some very OBVIOUS issues that ANY PLAY-TESTING would've revealed instantly. Very bad audio mixing making the FMVs and random sound effects incredibly loud compared to the rest of the game, and generally poor online performance. From my experience it was mostly fine during matches although due to not having rollback yet, random stuttering will happen, and that is not ideal at all for a technical fighting game of this nature. If that wasn't bad enough, simply trying to get into a match and find players who you haven't played against before can be a real hassle. Also the game ran perfect from my experience, but I have friends who had the game run unplayably slow, despite having great PCs. This sucks because not only is it a gamble on the game FUNCTIONING for you, but for whoever you may want to play with as well. I just straight up can't play this game with some of my friends until they fix the optimization or whatever is causing this. All of this being said, it makes me very upset that this game wasn't handled with the respect it deserved, and was clearly rushed to meet a deadline. The player base is already pretty small, and I can very well see these issues making people drop the game or not want to pick it up entirely. TLDR, fantastic game, but buy with caution

_childDocuments_.review: Serving as a direct sequel to both Persona 3 and Persona 4, Persona 4 Arena Ultimax is a  2D anime fighting game with its own canonical story mode following the events of the two games mentioned. Taking place 2 months after the end of Persona 4. The story itself is mostly told through a visual novel style presentation split between fighting segments. If you're picking this up for story you're gonna need to be ready for a lot of reading as there's a lot of dialouge between fights, for better or worse that's what they went for. The game meshes casts from both Persona 3 and Persona 4 into a unified story and fans of both games will be delighted to see the interactions they form, lots of fanservice to go around in that department. The game includes the original Arena story and its subsequent sequel Ultimax. As for the plot, the new character Labrys is a fantastic introduction and her origin story was delightfully tragic. The callbacks to Persona 3 feel very nostalgic. Sho Minazuki not so much.  The story is very dependant on you knowing/having played their one of/both of the respective entries for you to understand it so that's best done before getting into this if you plan on playing through the story. Story mode also features an 'Automatic' mode for you to toggle if you just wanna experience the story but don't want to do any of the fighting and just let the CPU do it for you. Gameplay wise it's a very fluid and enjoyable experience as far as 2D fighters go. There's a lot to work with here in terms of the skill ceiling while also being incredibly easy to get into even if you never played a fighting game in your life. The character roster is distinct and comes in many flavors that you can bet at least one of them will be to your liking. As far as offline content goes it features a serviceable arcade mode that does its job but nothing on the level of Tekken regarding quality. The multiplayer is mostly dead last I checked unfortunately. In my experience you can easily enough invite a friend to play a few rounds with and the connection is fantastic, results vary depending on connection quality of course. Lots of fun to be had if you can make it work! A solid 8 if you like fighting games and enjoy Persona. Probably less if not so much.

_childDocuments_.review: In keeping with tradition, ATLUS has decided to skip over Persona 5, 3, or any other mainline entry and give us the fighting game instead. Having played it now though, I can’t say I’m complaining.Persona is usually a JRPG series, but this is a fighting game and it’s one developed between ATLUS and the prestigious Arc System Works - who brought us classics like BlazBlue and Guilty Gear. This game plays a lot like those two, but does so while incorporating a ton of elements from Persona and honestly, it’s a bit brilliant how it all works out.Each character has moves of their own, but also has their persona with unique moves on top of that and the game basically revolves around combining these two to build up some nasty combos. It is a very cool mechanic and, while complex on paper, I managed to pick it up pretty quickly.The base combat is some incredibly polished stuff too - before you even get to the extras like personas or super moves. It’s fast, fluid, responsive, and way more fun than I thought it was going to be if I am being honest. Maybe it’s because I am just coming off of playing Phantom Breaker, but this one just feels good to play. It has that perfect blend of move variety, gameplay mechanics, and audiovisual feedback to give the combat that unique Arc System touch and it makes for some very satisfying gameplay.You’ve got arcade mode, score attack, lessons, training, challenges, and this RPG-like endless mode called Golden Arena. In that one, you basically fight to earn XP to level up a certain character’s stats and even unlock abilities for them. It’s nothing too complex, but it’s a nice touch over the “endless mode” that we usually get.The story is also notable - both for its length (around 18 hours of VN scenes and fighting) and its insane entry barrier. Not only is this game a direct sequel to Persona 4, but Persona 3 as well and you will get spoiled on major plot points for both if you just jump in right here. I would speak on the quality of that story - but I am going to be honest, I have not completed either Persona 3 or 4 and don’t want to be spoiled myself, so I did not play through Arena’s storyline.At launch, the game is not going to have rollback netcode, but the devs have announced that it will be implemented in an update sometime this summer. A bit odd that they didn’t just do that right off the bat, but at least there is official confirmation. I was unable to test the netcode as it is because I played before release, so hopefully it’s at least decent enough to hold out until summer.PRAU is a solid fighting game all around, bunch of stuff to learn and master, yet still not this massive wall to get into. It looks great with that flashy Persona aesthetic, has that similarly great music, and also runs just fine and I had no technical issues whatsoever. I will note that while I did play at 1440p, the game is actually locked to 1080 internally and only scales up from there - disappointing to see.Persona 4 Arena Ultimax is a fairly easy recommendation to make. If you are a fan of any of Arc System Works’ previous fighting games, then you’ll likely have a lot of fun here. Persona fans too or even just fighting game fans in general. The story might be lost on that latter group, but the gameplay, the characters, the mechanics, all of that is incredibly polished and this is definitely one that will be on my fighting game rotation for a while. Now please just give us Persona 3 and 5.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

_childDocuments_.review: Summary: Persona 4 Arena Ultimax is a very fun fighting game with lots of style, but the game being dead with no one playing online ruins it. If you are a Persona fan, buy it, if not, don't.     Persona 4 Arena Ultimax is a very fun but flawed game. Positives of this game include having the story mode from the original Persona 4 Arena, having great music, stages, and characters, and being a very fun fighting game. The fighting mechanics are kind of complicated at first, but if you have played a traditional fighting game before, then they are very familiar, once you learn the mechanics, it is surprisingly fun and in depth. Games such as Dragonball FighterZ and Street Fighter are very similar control wise as well.      But once you actually get more into the game, the cracks start to show. Minor issues such as load times, difficulty, and overall how confusing the game is for newcomers. Load times can get upwards to a minute (for me at least), the game also has major difficulty spikes in the arcade and story mode and to change the difficulty, it's hidden away in the options, and lastly the game does not give you a proper tutorial, you have to go and find lessons, which is over 70 and took almost an hour, not to mention over half of them just give you button combos.     Those may seem like minor nitpicks, but the major issue of the game is the lack of support. Other successful fighting games continue to have support in ways like adding new characters, stages, or even having a battle pass (which i'm not saying battle passes are good, they just help the game stay alive). These are mainly excusable considering this was a PS3 game from 10 years ago, but the fact that the online for this game is dead just ruins it. There is absolutely no one online, i'm not even exaggerating, I waited an hour for someone to join my match, no one ever did. Online matches are a huge factor in keeping a game alive, just look at Super Smash Bros for example. When the game came out there was not Rollback Netcode, which pretty much every fighting game has. This lack of Rollback Netcode let to the game being dead on arrival. The game being dead is the most major issue that plagues this game.      So, should you buy this game? I would say if you are a Persona fan, like myself, just buy it, the game has interactions between much of the Persona 3 and Persona 4 cast, making it very fun for fans of the series. But if you are a fan of fighting games or haven't heard of persona, don't buy it unless it's on sale for less than $10. And lastly, if you want to get into persona and choose this game, first of all don't, second this game is very "fan-servicy", third, you should buy Persona 4 Golden instead because it's $10 cheaper, and will provide much more playtime, and is a proper introduction to the series.But it has Adachi 100/10

_childDocuments_.review: Easily one of my favorite fighting games of all time. The characters are unique and fun to play as, the system mechanics are unique with the persona system, status effects are simultaneously so cool and so awful depending on if you're the one with a status condition, and with the addition of rollback it finally has playable online. People overrate the difficulty of this game a ton, all of your specials and supers are quarter circles and the difficulty of most combos comes from properly timing tight links rather than having to do a bunch of crazy inputs. Of course if you play a good player you'll get smoked but that's true of every single game on the planet, you can't get around the skill gap.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fighting game fan, its pretty good, feels good to control, very fluid, characters are fun. Roster is a bit limited, but since all the characters feel drastically different that's fine. I'm a casual fighting game enjoyer, so i don't know all the terms, but overall it feels great to control, and the online isn't half bad either (if you find a match). I would probably give it a 7.5/10.As someone a persona fan, its pretty disappointing, the story mode is repetitive, the inner monologues are boring and mostly just there to fluff out the story mode, and in my opinion, although the new characters are interesting in concept, the execution was lacking and i ended up not liking any of them that much. It was fun seeing the different casts interact, and it was especially fun seeing how the p3 cast is doing after a 3 year time skip. The base story is not bad at all, if it was just streamlined and cut short it would be a good 7/10, but due to all the fluff they added for no apparent reason (other than to extend game time i guess) it goes down to a 6/10 for me. If the gameplay looks interesting, buy the game (on discount though) its worth it. If you just want to experience the story mode, just watch it on youtube. Overall rating is 6.75.

_childDocuments_.review: Easily one of my favorite fighting games to play, I played the hell out of this(and the original arena) back in the PS3 days And I was really hoping that it would come to steam and modern consoles, and I was beyond hyped to see that they finally done it, instead of being locked away in the previous generation of consoles and entertainment.Everything about the game is just so damn fun, The gameplay is very unique and awesome with the ability to summon your guardian angel called a persona in battle, much like jojo's. The content is in-depth and filled to the brim, and of course the graphics and presentation are fantastic too, Don't let the games age fool you, this game plays as good as it looks.With rollback, there's never been a better time to start jumping in and having some fun with this incredibly underrated fighter, you don't have to be a big fan of persona to enjoy this game, so tell your friends, show off this game to the FGC, and experience the most unique entry in arc system works history of fighting game collabs. The only thing that would make this much better is crossplay with PC and PlayStation 4, which I hope they would add in the future. In the meantime, get this game now and enjoy, you will not regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: Perfect game, amazing port, don't be fooled by the negative reviews from people experiencing obscure issues that seem to purely be on their end and not the same problem for most players.I've played this game online and offline for about 20 hours, I legitimately have no idea what people are complaining about with this port with the exception of the audio. Yes, the audio is kind of all over the place in this game where it gets way too quiet for most of the game and then it's way too loud during cutscenes for example, but it's genuinely not a big deal and I imagine it will be fixed in future patches.But seriously, other than a bit of audio problems, this port is fantastic, and Ultimax is an absolute masterpiece just like P4G. The current netcode is very playable too, I played over 80 matches with my friend who lives about a 2 hour drive away from me and we had short instances of lag about 3 times in total out of those 80+ matches. That being said, I can't wait for the rollback update this summer! That's when this game's online play will really take off.Overall, the game runs perfectly, no crashes, no "broken cutscenes" (although they are loud), etc. It's just excellent. Don't believe everything you see just from one or two negative reviews, the majority of us Ultimax players know it's a solid port that could use a few little improvements, but is currently perfectly fine as it is.PS. Chie best girl.
