_childDocuments_.review: Let me preface this by saying that I loved the Danganronpa Series of games, but always felt underwhelmed by the fact that it never was a true "social deduction game", those games had a pre-determined story to tell and nothing you did had any effect on the outcome. It's probably why very few people are fond of the VN tag/genre, because most of them lack gameplay..There are visual novel elements to the game, however it is paired with quite a mechanically deep "social deduction game", where you're pitted against characters with different behaviors (thanks to their intelligent AI). The game expects you to pick up on each characters unique characteristics, some of which can be very subtle, others can be extremely blunt () and this lends itself to making each character feel more "real" in their personalities and the way they would behave. Whether you lose or win, the game doesn't end instantly. Instead you are rewarded with EXP (in which you can level up certain characteristics to help you win) and sent to another "loop", where your relationship with every character and role shifts. One run will never turn out exactly the same, so you'll have to rely on your own deduction skills, abilities and rational thinking in order to survive. With each loop you also get the chance to progress the story, and learn more about characters via VN sections (yes that's where the VN bits pop in). The plus side for most of you who simply care about gameplay is that these sections are short and sweet, so it doesn't take long before you're back into some social deduction action. However, with how strongly written and unique the characters are, you'll WANT to learn more about them and spend time with them- both from an emotional standpoint and gameplay standpoint. Learning more about these characters will help you win loops, and choosing not to do so will simply make your life harder.As for the music, well there's not much to say besides I love it and how unique it sounds- and that the art style is equally as superb. I'm no arts/music major, I simply like what I see and hear here.One more thing before I leave my final rating- for those of you who decide to try this game, don't be discouraged by losing loops. Like every other roguelite, you'll get stronger via levels and better yourself at deducing each character and situation. Trust me, this game is worth the patience.I would honestly recommend almost anyone to atleast try this game out once for yourselves, as I truly believe this game is a unique hidden gem, and my one wish is that more people will notice it and applaud it for what it is. This is the most fun and refreshing experience I've had with a video game for a very long time, and I have the utmost respect for the people who worked on this.For those still unsure, I'd recommend watching gameplay or streams  to get a feel- or better yet bum it off a friend for a bit and purchase it if you like it!The game's a solid 9/10 for me in the 7 hours I've played it, and I can't wait to play even more in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: The beloved game has finally arrived on Steam! Described by many as a combination of Werewolf and Among Us with a heavy dose of Anime nausea is a visual novel that surprised me in several ways as I played through it, while its comparison to Among Us is valid with all of its characters being on a space station with one or more of them being an imposter of sorts, that's generally where the similarities end as while this game came out after Among Us, its original release in Japan was way before it became the sensation that it is now, so if anyone is looking for a similar experience they're going to be a bit disappointed.In Gnosia, you play as a faceless protagonist whose only discernible characteristics are their gender, name and whatever symbol or color you decide to associate with them you are soon introduced to some of the characters that you'll be interacting with throughout your adventure, only to learn that some of them are what are known as Gnosia. I can't really divulge too much about their goals without spoiling part of the story but let's just say that they are an imposter of sorts that will kill someone every time the ship goes through warp speed, if you've ever played the game Werewolf you'll be able to see the similarities. As a crewmate you must try to figure out which of your fellow crewmates are lying and put the traitors into cold sleep, after you succeed or fail to find out who the Gnosia is, you'll eventually go through a time loop and will once again need to find out who each Gnosia is but this time with a slightly different group and with everyone's roles jumbled around, these loops act as rounds in the game and are integral to the game's story and they're what allows you to replay the game over and over again.During your playthrough, you will meet all 15 members of the crew including yourself as well as learn about the different roles that each of them could have, besides the gnosia you have engineers who can suss out who is human and who isn't, you have guardian angels who can protect one person per night and prevent them from being killed, doctors can check on anyone who has been put into cold sleep to see if they are actually gnosia or not, AC followers are basically a wild card whose main goal is actually to let the gnosia win even though they are not gnosia themselves, there are characters who will have been on guard duty who cannot be gnosia as the gnosia cannot lie about being on guard duty so you can guarantee that anyone who says that they were to be genuinely human and the final role in the game is the bug, bugs are characters that shouldn't exist in the timeline they are in and if the gnosia or humans end up winning their loop and a bug is still alive its very presence can cause the universe to fall apart at the seams, so yeah, bugs are bad. These roles are explained a bit more in depth in the game but generally no role in particular is overpowered as there is plenty of counter play depending on which roles are in play during each particular loop. Eventually you will begin to realize that while the Werewolf game mechanic of restarting loops over and over again is important it isn't the true goal of the game, what you're actually trying to do is obtain as much information as you can about everyone who is on board the ship and by doing so figure out some of the mysteries that pop up as the story progresses. Going after this information can lead to some unusual situations, including a gnosia member sacrificing themselves in order to save everyone else on board while another may have you and a member of the gnosia working together when something goes horribly awry, the thing is sometimes these tidbits of information only come up if very specific circumstances are met and they aren't always guaranteed to proc unless you know exactly what you're looking for luckily after a certain point you'll be given the ability to automatically have the game set up a loop where a segment could occur making it where you don't have to randomly keep guessing what you're looking for. When going from loop to loop the frustration with the game comes when you're trying to complete these extra objectives and the characters that should theoretically be your allies in this situation does their best to mess up what you're trying to accomplish.If the above doesn't sound like it's going to scratch any particular itches with you, then Gnosia may not be the title for you but for those where the idea of a single player Werewolf style game as you slowly uncover an overarching mystery sounds appealing, Gnosia may be right up your alley!
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: Gnosia is a bit of a rough little gem - an attempt to take a game framework that relies on human social deduction and interaction and turns it into a single player affair, to largely successful results.At its core, Gnosia is effectively a Very Weird Sci-Fi take on a Werewolf/Mafia simulator, where you play through a number of loops of the game with a variety of NPC crew members present; the gameplay revolves around debate sessions where the crew decides who is a probable Gnosia (the werewolf analogue) and tries to stop them by voting them into cold sleep, while the Gnosia eliminate people off the board each night. As you go through these loops and various permutations of role assignments for the crew, you see a number of events; some give you background on the crew, some teach you skills you can use during the debates, and some flesh out the broader mystery of why you and another crew member are time looping and how to stop it. There's also the complication of a special non-human/Gnosia role known as the Bug, effectively a walking paradox; if the Bug makes it to the end of the round without being put into cold sleep or scanned by an Engineer, they win by destroying the entire universe.  It's an interesting twist to throw a role into the mix that the standard "teams" are both required to play around and address ASAP.In the moment to moment, Gnosia is a fun game. The actual debates can get a bit repetitive in terms of dialogue since there's a relatively limited pool of statements each character has, but the developers did a really great job at actually designing the characters and giving them specific strengths/weaknesses and personalities that you have to learn to work with - and around. One character is incredibly adept at spotting lies but is effectively doomed the moment they have to try to tell one. Another character has high overall stats but is erratically insane so he doesn't use any of them well - but can still surprise you with his skills. Another character has good logical and analytical capabilities but is so abrasive that they'll often get voted out purely because nobody wants to deal with them. Another plays almost entirely on emotion and if you get on her bad side, regardless of whether or not you're on the same team, look out. Learning the character styles fleshes out the debates, because you have to decide how best to handle each round - who's a threat, who's a potential ally and who's just acting weird. If someone everyone tends to hate suddenly has a bunch of supporters this round, they may well all be Gnosia - or if everyone is dogpiling someone it's entirely possible they spotted something about their behavior that you missed. This ties into the fact that you get to choose your own stats and build and decide the approach you want to take; I went extremely high in intuition (spotting lies), performance (telling lies) and logic, but was generally weak in terms of keeping below the radar and lost a bunch of sessions because I made too many folks angry even when I was right about something.  You're not locked in though, with a fairly easy set of criteria to trigger a character stat reset to allow you to change what you feel isn't working.Ultimately, Gnosia is worth a look if you're curious how a well handled single player social deduction game would play out, or if you just like weird sci-fi settings and narratives.  The cast and crew are very interesting and fleshed out well and it's fun to just interact with them even if one of them might stab you in the back the next day.  The art and character design is bright and colorful and neat, and the music is gorgeous and strange with just a hint of friction.  Gnosia plays well and each loop is pretty speedy, and the game has a nice feature where you can have it set specific round parameters that can potentially trigger new events for you to help you progress. It is, however, very much not a visual novel at its core and just uses some of the trappings; Raging Loop is the flipside where the focus is the VN and the Werewolf games are more set dressing.  Approach Gnosia as a cool framework for a set of variable logic puzzles and you'll have a good time.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: Gnosia is an unbelievably fun Visual Novel style game about surviving on a ship with Gnosia infectees using a Werewolf-style mechanic. The crew must find the Gnosia, the Gnosia must eliminate the crew with each phase taking the shape of 5 conversation-type interactions and then a vote. You can defend allies, call out enemies or even betray your collaborators.Each of the Crew have their own personality and discussion style, be it Raqio's purely logical approach, Yuriko's ruthlessness or Shigemichi being... well... Shigemichi. Meaning you have to truly know and understand the characters you're on the ship with to be able to read them for deception.There is story, with a wide variety of loop endings depending on both what roles you had, who survived and what actions you took, with plenty to do to unlock the mystery of the characters within.The art style is nice, characters are visually distinct and whilst I could've done without Comet's underboob, it really isn't a focus of the game.Gnosia is exceptionally fun and really rather well made. The achievements are also not obnoxious, and I personally had a lot of fun with this.

_childDocuments_.review: Do you know the true rage you will inevitably feel when the collective intelligence of the town hits rock bottom because your fellow townies couldn't figure out a mafia member if h...Wait...Do you know the true rage you will inevitably feel when the collective intelligence of the spaceship hits rock bottom because your fellow humans couldn't figure out a gnosia even if it hit them in the face? Yeah, that. The game is exactly that.It is a werewolf party game with more roles. You play as an amnesiac protagonist who has to piece together information as you go jump through the loops (literally). Since it is a single-player game, the game gives all of the characters unique skills that the player can also learn and outlevel everyone (yes, you can grind). This way, the game offsets the problem that is Artificial Unintelligence so you will not be forced to pull all of your hair but only some locks here and there. My main criticism is the overall weirdness and RNG-based progression system. Yes, there is a tool you can use to maximize your chances but you still have to rely on luck and more absurdly, you will need to betray your own faction in order to get a specific ending. All in all, good game. Much better than I expected, but not a masterpiece that left me speechless.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: The main selling point of Gnosia is the absolutely gorgeous art by Cotori. The game is a visual treat from beginning to end. As an actual game, it works, but not spectacularly well. You'll play somewhere around 150 somewhat short rounds of gameplay trying to find the Gnosia hidden among the crew or working with other Gnosia and to take down the crew yourself. There are a few other wrinkles to add complexity but they aren't terribly important. As you go through these rounds, repeating the same loop over and over again, you'll gather information about all of the characters and finally solve the underlying mystery.This hunt for secrets is what makes the game actually compelling to play- especially once you level up your abilities to the point that you're almost invincible and you can lead the debates whatever way you wish. The game does some things behind the scenes to point you in the right direction but whether a round of gameplay will yield anything new or not is kind of a toss up. Raging Loop was a much more interesting way to tell a story like this because it was fully scripted without any of those random elements. Because this one is randomized, you'll hear the other characters repeat the same lines in their debates over and over again and seeing the same general outcomes over and over does get a little tiring. I still found myself getting attached to some of the characters and there are some legitimately emotional scenes. But I can't help but think that this could have been a legendary game with a different approach. I still have a soft spot for it and I recommend it for anyone looking to enjoy the beautiful visuals and spend time with this crazy cast of characters.

_childDocuments_.review: Gnosia is basically a singleplayer among us, with a story.There are different roles crew member, gnosia (enemy role), engineer, doctor .                                                                                 You will unlock event search after the tutorial. You can play it to uncover the story, and learn bits and pieces about all the characters.You can also create your own custom games, choose what role you want, how many crew members, what roles to include, how many gnosias (max 6).                                                                         It's a lot more fun than i expected it to be.                                                                                   As for the gameplay itself                                                  You basically are stuck in a time loop, yet every loop is different. The core of the gameplay are conversations. You can doubt, defend, become allies, or the npcs can doubt and kill you too. At the end of the day everyone votes on who they find to be guilty. You can lvl your abilities, and learn skills in order to help you survive and win. Despite being a visual novel, it did not feel like one due to the engaging game mechanics.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played this game before on the Switch (finished at Loop 129) and the best thing I can say about it is that is excels in the uniqueness of the mechanics it uses: while it is true that you are stuck on a loop of days playing a variation of the popular Werewolf/Mafia game, the story/progression offered not only by the events of the game  as the degree of consistency of the characters and their respective personalities make this VN an excellent and easily recommendable experience, as long as you know what you're in for.I believe this latter point on the characters being consistent is very much worthy of praise, considering the circumstances for every loop are 99% randomized . I find it amazingly cool that you can start developing your own biases like being annoyed a certain character has been the Gnosia for 3 consecutive loops, for example.It is also worth noting that, as you will be relying to some degree on luck, especially at the very start (and towards the end), the game can feel slow at the beggining. I recommend playing at least around 25/30 loops to decide if this game is for you, if you are by any chance as turned off as I was in the first few loops — the initial segment of introducing new characters and mechanics certainly does not represent the entirety of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: To say that I liked my time with Gnosia would be an understatement. It quickly became one of my favorite games of all time. The very emotional story is accompanied by great characters and an unbelievable soundtrack.The art style seemed weird at first, but as I got used to it, the urge to buy an art book was irresistible. Unfortunately, there is no art book (yet), but hopefully, they'll make one at some point.It's one of those visual novels that are very easy to recommend to genre newcomers, as it's partially an RPG. It's challenging at first, but as you unlock more skills, it becomes progressively easier. The endgame is a breeze, serving the purpose of unlocking various character scenes and exploring different outcomes.I really hope that it'll get a good remaster with voice acting in the future. It absolutely deserves it.

_childDocuments_.review: this is one of my favorite games of all time. has your brain been completely and irreversibly damaged by time travel stories? did you play mafia once in high school and got way too into it? does seeing the phrase "among us" used seriously make you laugh? this game is for you. be the most suspicious person in your efforts to point out that someone is very clearly an impostor and get cryogenically frozen for your crimes. be the most suspicious person in your efforts to throw everyone under the bus because you're the impostor and wring your hands as everything goes according to plan, until the dolphin in a space suit reveals she's actually not supposed to exist and the whole universe collapses. these are just scenarios that will pop up in the basic gameplay loop, which, while it can get repetitive, holds a surprising amount of complexity in the individual personalities of each character you will come to understand throughout the game.the story is a whole other animal, and I won't discuss it here, but I will say it made me ugly cry. this is the game of all time. its soundtrack makes my chest hurt. big thanks to my wonderful friend who gifted this game to me. i am now going to probably buy a switch copy just to display. please buy this game

_childDocuments_.review: Underrated gem.Very consistent art style, addicting gameplay loop and nice narration. Contrary to some other reviews, I haven't had to spend too much time hunting for events, wrapping up around loop 90, but I still feel compelled to run it again for more gameplay (achievements are requiring to win in some tough configurations) or for any missed optional events. Also the game looks gorgeous: there are absolutely no elements which would look out of place.Few tips, because you deserve something good if you've read this far:- If there is Yuriko, then either make sure that you're BFFs, or plan ahead how you'd get rid of her. She can be a ton of pain to keep around, and she won't hesistate one bit before throwing you under the bus even if you are on the same side. Even more so on the late game, when she gets retaliate: if you desperately need for someone to survive, make sure they don't get hit by it, even if it means you defend Yuriko immediately after she is accused by them. - Raqio is opposite, utterly useful to keep around. Same for anyone universally hated: being able to focus votes on someone may be your only hope in certain situations.- AI never makes two gnosias assume the same role. There are AC follower and bug, though...

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely well done story-rich game. The storytelling had well done twists and turns, and even with the game's nonlinear progression, all the story points fit in well together, like a carefully crafted puzzle. It's also just a fun werewolf/mafia game if you want it to be- very unique singleplayer setup that makes the game play unlike any multiplayer werewolf or mafia game. _childDocuments_.review: It's a unique game which feels like 70% social deduction, 20% RPG and 10% visual novel.It has a low story-to-gameplay ratio and is quite grindy to unlock the various story and lore bits.I repeat: do NOT play this game assuming it will be a visual novel with some gameplay. You should approach it as a roguelite RPG with (fairly repetitive) "encounters" with backstory, special events and dialogs sprinkled here and there.The social deduction mechanics, despite playing against AI, is quite fun as the AI characters have behaviors that fit their personality and game rules have enough randomness and quirks to keep it interesting through many runs.Art is fine, music is great. My main gripe is that character lines get repetitive very fast during normal gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: This'll be a different review than what most people would expect to find in a negative review.First things first: I like the characters and the story, let me make that clear.The OST is, although very experimental, quite nice. It definitely creates an unique atmosphere, especially when combined with the art of the game.I would give this game a 7/10. However, I would never recommend it to anyone.What the game gives to me, in exchange of the effort I put on it... Is absolutely not worth it.This game's constructed nature easily rejects smooth pacing, script writing, dialouge depth and realism; by sacrificing these elements in exchange of making the interactive gameplay work. And how that happens? Due to the fact that these elements are evolving around the interactive gameplay.You're definitely "playing" a story and its characters, for sure. But in this case, it's a torture. Spoilers are ahead!I hope I could clarify my frustration enough. Basically, the game won't reward you enough, not at all, for all of the effort and time you put into its gameplay. And some of its problems could be fixed so easily too...For example, if I fail, let me press a button that'll reset things. Another example, let us save the game at times. What about more examples? Let me have a skip button. (Maybe there's one and I'm dumb. But CTRL not working says a lot in itself.)According to steam, I've spent 24 hours for this game(probably longer since I played it offline too), and a lot of it came from the gameplay.Please, listen to me. There are richly written stories that are like this one, but way more relaxing to go through. Way more focused, paced way better, given way more depth to its dialouge and etc.These types of VN's reward the player for simply experiencing their stories. I could recommend them to you, and you would have a much better time than having to endure what gnosia makes you do.It's... Just not worth it for your time and effort.Gnosia's gameplay is flawed; It doesn't think of the player's comfort at all. It asks way too much, even though there are alternatives to its type of story that are way more comfortable to go through.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: I did not expect to enjoy this as much as I did, I fully expected to get tired of the loops as many reviews before had stated. Instead I was hooked and for the two or so weeks that it took for me to complete this game, I was well and truly hooked. When I didn't play at the time, I wish I was. When I couldn't be playing at the time, I thought of ways to get to it. What makes it great? The way the social deduction type of gameplay has been integrated into the story. Inbetween gameplay segments you're able to experience character events. I think this is a wonderful way to combine gameplay and story and in the end, combined with the stats page of each character, the backstory and the way everyone acted in gameplay, the characetrs truly came to life in a way that no other game has really done for me. It lets you connect the dots to an extent, as you slowly understand each character's way of acting, who you can and can not trust. The events were frequent enough that I never felt as if I was grinding for it, apart from the very end, where it was still fortunately a brief stint.The dev team seems to be so small, but I loved every aspect of the game so much, the art, the music, the gameplay.. it managed to throw in scenes that were outright horror in their nature as well as a few laughs here and there. I highly, highly suggest this game. Thank you, Petit Depotto and Playism <3  One of my favourite games of all time. I really appreciated the nonbinary representation of this game as well.

_childDocuments_.review: Originally released on PS Vita and Nintendo Switch, Gnosia is a social deduction game in the form of visual novel. Inspired by ,  and , this is a compeletely single player experience that proves how social deduction games can be played alone. Gnos, an unknown alien parasite, has infected the crew members of a drifting spaceship. Stuck in a never ending time loop, they are now forced to re-live every moment trying to find who the Gnosia is. Each day the crew will meet, discuss and vote the most suspicious person who will be put into cold sleep, while every night the Gnosia will kill one member of their choice. It’s up to you to discover why all of this is happening and how to stop this alien lifeform from taking control of the ship.The Gnosia is not the only threat though. There is another dangerous enemy known as the Bug, which apparently can destroy the entire universe. If the Bug manages to survive until a winner has been decided among the humans and Gnosia, the victory goes to the Bug. Apart from this, there are a few other roles that are crucial to the gameplay. The Engineer can scan a player each round to detect any sign of infection, while the Doctor can discover the role of those who have been put into sleep. A Guardian Angel is able to protect a single crew member (but not themselves) from Gnosia attack, while an AC follower is a devoted person who would do anything to make the Gnosia win.At the start of the game you can choose your name, select your gender (male, female, non-binary), pick an avatar and tweak your initial stats. From there, each loop will gradually introduce you to the gameplay mechanics and I can fairly say that everything up to the 20th loop can be considered part of the tutorial. After these introductory loops, you can finally setup your own game, choosing the number of crew members, the number of Gnosia infected and if you want to allow any other role in your game. You can also choose your own, of course, and it’s best advised to play them all to unlock different scenes.Each meeting is made of five rounds where the crew members can suspect others while defending from accusations. You can also stay silent, which is a good strategy if you don’t want to raise any suspicion on yourself. At the end of the fifth round, a vote is held and the most suspected member is put into cold sleep. After the vote, you can visit one location of your choice, speaking to others, getting closer to them and adapting to their unique traits. During the night, someone will die and the next day you will have a new meeting, until either the Gnosia or humans win. From the main menu you can always check discussion logs, voting results, crew data, engineer and doctor reports, which will help you to better understand your crewmates’ behaviour.The game follows a roguelite structure, with fragments of the story being unlocked progressively by knowing more about the characters and filling the “special items” section in the crew member tab. To unlock these special items you need to succed at certain events, which only appear when some conditions are met (like playing with different roles, having a high level of affection for another character etc.). It certainly takes many loops and a bit of luck to progress further with the plot, but once you get to know your crewmates you will be deeply absorbed by their stories. You can even team up with another crew member to collaborate and find the Gnosia. This is also one of the fastest way to trigger events that can improve your relationship with that character. It’s recommended to collaborate even when you know your teammate is lying, as this will still unlock special scenes you don’t want to miss.There are some stats that you can increase by gaining experience after each loop: Charisma, Intuition, Logic, Charm, Performance and Stealth. They all can be improved when leveling up, with new skills being unlocked after reaching a certain threshold. This way you can become more convincing with your actions and detect liars more easily. Each gameplay loop offers interesting situations and while it’s hard to survive at the beginning, due to the low level and lack of abilities, it will become much easier to debate and prove your point when you have increased your stats enough.The AI does a good job at creating difficult situations, but it’s not immune to failures. One time the remaining crew started accusing me of being Gnosia and one character jumped to my defense, but soon after he voted against me and I ended up being frozen (too bad; I was indeed the Gnosia).I must confess that the game is far more enjoyable when played in short sessions. Each loop can take from 5 to 15 minutes, depending on the events. The game was meant for mobile devices after all and it should be perfect for Steam Deck. This doesn’t mean that it’s not enjoyable on PC, but after playing for a few hours it obviously shows its repetitiveness due to dialogues that rarely change during the voting phase.Graphically, the game includes detailed backgrounds and art. Characters look fancy and the camera zooming in and out helps give a decent sense of animation. Unfortunately, there are no voice overs and the recurrent soundtrack is nothing memorable.I’m personally not a fan of visual novels, but Gnosia trapped me with its social deduction mechanics, making me way more interested about my crewmates than I first thought. Its addicting roguelite formula offers a good sense of progression and makes each playthrough different. While the setting is not new, the story becomes more gripping as you connect with the other characters and unlock new scenes after each loop.

_childDocuments_.review: There's aspects of this that are alright, and the concept is neat, but there are two major problems:1. The game itself, the social deduction aspect, is just... bad. It's not really based so much on logic and reasoning as it is a stat grind, and even then, there's no real... logic arguments made, you just point fingers and hope your pointed finger is more convincing than the other pointed fingers. Answers could be blatantly obvious - a detective who got two gnosia voted off catches the third gnosia but because it's someone the AI "likes" they will vote the detective instead. The entire game operates off vague feelings and only once in a blue moon do you get to make a logical deduction. And for the longest time, the game will punish you for even trying to play, because "talking too much" gets people to tell you to shut up and then almost always voted off for it. This can be the first time you talk in a round, until you raise your stats high enough to diminish this, anyways. You're basically not playing the game at all until like two-thirds of the way through when you actually start to gain influence and the gnosia are often so transparent that finding them isn't especially satisfying.2. This is the worst progression system I've ever seen in a VN, hell, in a game ever. Do you like waiting for randomly triggered events to show up? What if it took over an hour? What if you're convinced the game doesn't work right unless you do a fresh boot literally every time you start a new round? Or how about the more convoluted ones, like getting two specific people to counterclaim, or covering a person whose always barely a part of the conversation and not really worth even considering most of the time? Or two specific characters both being a specific role? Progression has absolutely /nothing/ to do with the game itself most of the time, there's a few events related to winning games but most of them are just luck and convoluted nonsense and the pacing is abysmal because you'll be seeing new story once every half hour at best, meanwhile playing the same mediocre social deduction game over and over and over.The story itself is... fine. The music is pretty good, some of the characters are likeable (and some of them are complete voids of personality - hello chipie) but actually playing the game is excruciating and once the initial charm of the first hour or two fades you're left with another 20ish hours of tedium and frustration and I have to ask myself why I even bothered playing all the way through this one. And I don't have a great answer. You can do better, skip this.

_childDocuments_.review: Short version: I absolutely love GNOSIA and can't recommend it enough. I am just gonna tell you to get it. Buy it. Enjoy it. If you want more details, see below.In GNOSIA, you find yourself playing a game of find-the-impostor/detective where every time you succeed (and fail, though to a lesser extent) you get XP to tailor your characters to what you think is your strongest point, or more useful, in helping you survive the day. It blends rogue and RPG elements into a visual novel format, which makes it strangely compelling to play.Every character in this game is unique in their own way, and tend to be deeper than what you see on the surface (you know, actual good writing?) and it is up to you to discover all of their personalities. _childDocuments_.review: GNOSIA is an intriguing detective-visual novel style game set in a sci-fi universe, with a very charming and unique art style. After escaping in a ship from a GNOSIA infested planet, you must deduce the crew members who have also been infected that managed to get onto the ship. The main game play is a lot of fun, as you learn the various personalities of the characters and their mannerisms when the debate is going on. Each character has their own stats, which will affect how they will act during a debate. This is further expanded upon as more roles open up and more characters join with each debate. Though, as the game goes on, the mechanic will start to get stale, and with the abilities you gain as you level up, the deduction will become a lot easier. By this time, the main thing carrying GNOSIA is its story. Each character has their own background, which is revealed little by little through the game play loop itself. These backgrounds contribute to GNOSIA's overarching narrative, which does a good job of slowly revealing the surface of a deep, interesting, and well expanded universe.Unlocking the character events can become tedious and annoying due to some RNG, but there's a way to get around this by maxing out your stats, which lets you easily manipulate the characters into the outcomes you need.When the game play does become stale, I recommend either farming exp, or manipulating the exp values with something like cheat engine, to level up all your stats to max. This will stop the game from becoming stale and save you time. This, along with a walk-through, will make it easier to get all the events for all the characters, which you will eventually need for the true ending.While GNOSIA has a pacing issue due to story events being locked behind a somewhat annoying RNG game-play loop, I wholeheartedly can recommend this unique game because of its great art, story and characters.Also that soundtrack hit pretty hard :^)

_childDocuments_.review: GNOSIA is a visual novel styled type of game that plays like the communication games of "Werewolf" or "Mafia". I'm only familiar with the former, and it felt like a similar game but with an altered scenario to it. These games usually require a group of people to play, so GNOSIA manages to turn it into a single player experience by having a skill system that allows the player to strengthen their skills with experience they gain from playing, and additionally by having a cast of characters with set personalities and behavioral patterns. The key to victory alongside understanding the rules of the game is to master playing around the different characters, knowing when to trust or doubt them.The gameplay loop asks the player to continue to experience "actual loops" of the situation they find themselves in, trapped in a spaceship where a contamination from Gnosia has been confirmed. There is a main plot which revolves around finding out new information about the participants and the loop itself, progression is presented with special events that trigger at the beginning, throughout or at the end of loops. I found the story to be really engaging even if it isn't incredibly strong. The whole suspense that's caused by the continuous loops was really captivating.A little bit of luck on your side is required for the progression, as certain events require specific situations to trigger, which involve certain events to happen during discussion and specific characters to be around. This COULD be annoying but the game provides a feature that will make it more likely to discover something you lack. Once you're in the right track, even if you fail to meet some situation through the end, you'll be left with a clue on what to replicate to get it again. I personally didn't really struggle finding the events and I did enjoy the discussion game, so that kept me entertained even if I wasn't finding something new every loop. Recommended for fans of discussion games of this type.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an unfortunately buggy port of an otherwise fantastic VN. At least, it's supposed to.Gnosia on steam suffers from a plethora of progression related issues in it's current state. The game's event system and the RPG elements tied to NPCs completely fail to progress if you play for extended sessions, requiring you to restart loops and reload your save over and over until the game "snaps out of it". Given the trial and error nature of some late game mechanics it can be hard to tell if you are having bad luck or if the game is broken. Chances are, it's actually broken.I did manage to get past the bugs with about an hours worth of time wasted exiting to menu and reloading my save and the story is so unbelievably rewarding that I'm still giving it the thumbs up but if you don't want to deal with bugs I'd give it a few weeks.Couple side notes:is it horny? _childDocuments_.review: Not only do i not normally edit reviews i definitely dont edit them a SECOND time, but it must be said that throughout my casual returns and playing the game i finished it by accident, and it has by far one of the worst, most shoe-horned "noble sacrifice" endings ive seen in a game in a LONG time. horrendous execution and nonsensical explanation.I don't normally edit reviews, but after going back and playing a bit more ive a few things to say, i still dont recomend this game whatsoever really, but something must be said about the sheer impressiveness of the character design and programming thats put into this, each character having their own stats and tendencies make the loops feel a bit less up to RNG and like a mystery you can genuinely solve. i will probably keep coming back to this  game now and again just for that alone but i have NO plans to properly finish it as its just not worth the slog.OP Review: TL:DR getting exactly what you want for Christmas, but it's wrapped with metal.Gnosia is, what i believe to be, the first of its kind, A Story-packed Social deduction game, but also a rougelite? _childDocuments_.review: I played this game back on Switch and rebought it for steam because I loved it so much.For those interested in this game, it is a single player werewolf sim, where you need to find and seek out the Gnosia. The Gnosia seek to destroy humanity. However you and a character named Setsu are looping through time over and over. Each gameplay session has you loop to a new scenario with different crew assigned to different roles. The crew must vote out one person per night and the Gnosia can eliminate one person per night. There are other unique roles such as Engineer that can identify the Gnosia etc. You also get exp to put into stats that alter how characters perceive you and what skills you can use during discussions.The game focuses on looping over and over and finding discrepancies among the crew while trying to figure out why you are stuck in a time loop. Even when you lose, you still gain exp and may even get story content that you couldn't get otherwise which is nice because at the beginning you will lose a lot as you learn how to play the game and each individual character's behavior.  If you have any interest in sci-fi, time travel, visual novels or werewolf/among us type of games, I highly recommend trying this game.

_childDocuments_.review: A social deduction visual novel where you have to figure out which character is the enemy and put them into cold sleep. The game takes place within a time loop with the overarching story revolving around gathering information in order to escape the loop. In each loop characters are randomly assigned various roles granting them different abilities to help them detect the enemy, but whether or not those who claim to have taken on those roles are genuine is up to the player to deduce. An impressive game with quite a few moving parts going on behind the scenes. As a social deduction game, it's not simply about being right, it's about convincing others that you are right too. This can be quite difficult to do at first, and it may seem like characters are throwing out accusations at random, but the key to success lies not only in your ability to deduce the logic but also your ability to understand and interact amicably with the characters as well. Some characters operate purely on logic, while others can be more emotional. Knowing how to treat these characters and pull information from them as well as understanding their individual strategies and how they operate will massively influence your chances of winning. The randomly assigned roles can sometimes lead to some fairly chaotic situations, but more often than not they lead to incredible moments of emergent game play which produces some genuinely entertaining logic puzzles. Using the collectively available information to figure out and prove definitively to all the other characters that someone is lying is incredibly satisfying. While other mystery-style games are usually designed so that you will always eventually win through trial and error, that isn't possible here. The possibility of making bad choices and failing to interpret the information correctly makes figuring things out so much more rewarding and provides an experience not found in many other games.

It's difficult to compare it with another game specifically, it combines social deduction with RPG elements which make progression feel great, you'll have to start out hiding behind other characters and supporting their statements without having much repercussion, but as you get more EXP and unlock more abilities you can create your own build and specialize in several fronts. Other characters also level up their stats and unlock new abilities each time you advance their stories, so this prevents you from steamrolling everyone late game and keeps discussions fresh.The events that advance the story are great, I have to admit more than one made me say "What the f*ck was that?!" out loud. The only negative I found is that 2 or 3 events can be pretty difficult to obtain, you're either gonna get them by pure luck while playing or you'll have to look up the wiki, and the game can get monotonous if you're just playing aimlessly and trying to win every single round instead of interacting with unusual situations, that's why it's important to read the "How to play" section in the pause menu, which explains everything in extreme detail and it's a 10 min read at most. So yeah, definitely give this game a try, probably my favorite of 2022.

_childDocuments_.review: On one hand, Gnosia is a mix of two genres I don’t particularly care about – a social deduction game and a visual novel. On another – it’s so shockingly fascinating and well put together, that I was engaged until the final ending of the game.You read that right – this is a mix of two genres that don’t seem compatible. Social deduction games (like Mafia or Werewolf) tend to be multiplayer titles with little to no story, like its popular video game adaptations – Town of Salem or Among Us. While Visual Novels are almost exclusively singleplayer games about telling a linear (but often full of divergent paths and choices) story. So how can this work?The main gameplay is all based around the Mafia-like process, except all of the characters involved (apart from the player) are NPCs. To make it interesting, all of these NPCs have lots of special traits and skills to them, meaning that whenever they are an enemy (titular Gnosia) or a human of any supporting role, they have certain “patterns” to them. A lot of this isn’t extremely obvious, to not make the game boring, yet a patient and attentive player will start noticing the specific choices and elements of behavior between the loops.Oh and yes – the loops. The overall structure of the game is based around a time loop of several days, after the presence of Gnosia-infected humans is discovered until the victory of one of the sides, after which the loop resets. The properties of each loop change, so people usually change roles and you yourself will get to play all roles as well. The game will explain all of this (and much more) via the story driven interludes between the arguments about who suspects whom, which play as a Visual Novel.And eventually you will be given a lot of freedom in how you want to play the game, while also searching for special events that can trigger with different properties. Some of which tell more about the characters and the overall story. And some might unlock the NPC skills for you. Because you get a set of skills and attributes of your own to affect the gameplay, since you’re dealing with the NPCs and not real players. It’s a very simple, but a very engaging concept and if you like the social deduction type games, you will probably love this.If you don’t… Well, I have to say that the game does take a bit too long to go through the story, if you care about it first and foremost and I do wish that some of the story events weren’t so hard to trigger. It does get easier with leveling up and your own experience, and it does seem like the game gets progressively more lenient on letting you achieve the goal, although maybe I was imagining things. But if you don’t like the main gameplay loop, you might start getting a bit bored at a certain point. I’m very glad I went through it to the end. But I won’t keep on searching for non-vital events and unlocking the last skills.Gnosia is a shockingly good game with really awesome soundtrack, simple but engaging gameplay and story and memorable characters. It falters from time to time. And I wish it didn’t do the typical “everyone is horny about the player” visual novel thing at several points. But it wasn’t enough to detract from my enjoyment and I definitely recommend checking Gnosia out.

_childDocuments_.review: A very engaging and surprisingly deep story in what could be summarized as a 'single player Among Us' visual novel, featuring a time looping story of mystery and social deduction mechanics. How does this work? Well, be prepared to likely either get killed or be voted for cold sleep a lot early on, while you work on stats and slowly get an idea how everyone thinks. Events trigger randomly, depending on who's alive, their roles, and how they react to you, but slowly gives you clues to help you find answers as you navigate through the loops and the mystery behind it all. As long as you use the 'search for event' feature, you should be able to keep subtly making progress in case you're lost, or at least give you an idea. Story driven loops also happen, where you may need to do something with unique conditions like winning but a certain person needing to survive alongside you.Despite the gameplay taking up the majority of your time, the characters have a lot of depth and backstory to them with limited dialogue, although some can get weird as heck. It's mostly in a good way. Setsu's story though, being the most important character beside you, can hit pretty hard. Some characters's stories can get heavy with some events in their life.They are a few iffy designs or eye-rolling moments (mainly Comet I think, but the general art and other character designs are great), some bad endings that are brief and subtle but maybe uncomfortable. As you get closer to the end, getting the last events may be harder to figure out without a guide, or if you're being a completionist, although I still enjoyed going after them. Enjoyed it to the point where I actually got every achievement and even did the optional pure gameplay challenges it mentions. Ended up being one of the most memorable stories I ended experiencing, with its very unique take on gameplay. Took me a while to get to this because it barely ever goes on sale, but well worth it at any price.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is spoiler-free.For those who still don't know what Im talking about, here are the basics:You and up to 14 other people are trapped in a spacecraft. Unfortunately for you, some fellow crew members were infected with Gnosia and they want to kill everyone on thatship. You can't really distinguish them from others by looks, the only way to do so is through social deduction. Each day, everyone shares their opinion on who they think the Gnosias are and, at the end, all of you will vote on whom to put into a cold freeze. Each night, however, Gnosias act as well, as they will decide who should disappear without a trace. There are multiple roles characters can have that give them some sort of special ability or purpose (for example: the Engineer can check each night, whether or not the selected person is human). Once all impostors are frozen or half of the crew are Gnosias, the game ends. But when one game (or loop as this game calls it) ends, another begins, with different role assignments and different situations. Not only that, but you can also choose to play as those malicious Gnosias, completely changing your approach to the game.That's the general idea, but these types of games are always played with real people, so how does this singleplayer system work? Well, each day has 5 rounds, and each round you have numerous actions to perform. For example, you can doubt someone, everyone then can defend the person or agree with you. You can also do nothing (which you will be doing the most, since talking too much or not talking enough makes you suspicious), allowing someone else to state their opinion, letting you react with different skills.These actions are called skills. They can range from simply defending a fellow crewmate, through starting a collaboration with someone, all the way to making small talk, tricking Gnosias into thinking you are either useless or not a threat. There are around 40 of these skills, and each does something unique, even if it doesn't appear so at first.Each loop, you gain experience points and you can spend them on developing your 6 stats which will drastically change how you play. For example, you can level up your Performance, making your lies hard to spot, or you can opt into Charisma, making it easier to convince others into believing you. These taught and visible mechanics alone aren't really worth the term “complex”, but there is a ton of stuff going on behind the scenes. Take the friendship meter for example, everyone likes others more or less and it drastically changes how they interact. To this day, after 30 hours in the game, I still discover completely new mechanics and special situations that can occur thanks to them.Each crewmember has their own stats and skill set. I have played around 150 loops, and, thanks to the characters, I remained fully immersed in all of them. Not only are the characters really interesting, but each and every one of them has a unique personality. The best part is that a character's personality is not only aesthetic but also plays a huge part in how they act. For example, we have Jonas, who has a very high overall statline but due to years of loneliness cruising through the galaxy, is very chaotic and eccentric. So he rarely puts those good stats and skills to use. On the other hand, we have Raqio, who has absurdly high logic stat, making them a fearful enemy, or a powerful ally in the late game, where there is a lot of information from previous days. That is if they can get into the late game, since they tend to be put into a cold sleep early, due to their playful nature and unlikeability. Throughout the game characters also improve alongside you, unlocking new skills and improving their stats. So you never truly know what to expect from them. However, the best part is, in those 150 loops, I could not ever figure out or cheese the AI. It always feels real and absolutely never acts against one’s personality. Even occasional logic flaws are delivered to you by people on the more foolish side (yes I'm talking mostly about Shigemichi), you can still pinpoint these flaws and correct them, making you feel like you are playing with actual human beings that can make mistakes. Especially when they are more or less connected to the ongoing…While most of the players pick this game up out of curiosity and interest in its mechanics, I can still confidently say almost everyone stays for the story. The developers actually acknowledged this - at the beginning there is little focus on world building and character development, letting you familiarize yourself with the main mechanics. Only later, after several dozen loops, do you slowly begin to uncover the story. Which, without getting into spoilers, is one of the most interesting and memorable tales I was able to experience in my life (I truly mean it).Each character has several events giving you some information about them. By collecting this data, you can progress through the story, but you also get a lot of information about this universe. Where the game can get a bit frustrating, at times, is how you come across these events. For each one, in addition to requiring a specific situation to take place, there is also an aspect of randomness. You can not encounter a specific event, despite having all the right conditions repeatedly. This is not a problem for most of the playthrough, since the sheer amount of events ensures if a specific event doesn't happen, another will. Still, towards the end, getting the last few pieces of information you need to get the ending, can be a bit time consuming.While not particularly groundbreaking, character sprites and special scenes with them are very well drawn. Getting a random event almost always means a new special image, and, trust me, there are a lot of these in the game. The UI is also really fitting and somewhat minimalistic, not overwhelming the player that, at first, already has a lot to take in.In terms of music, there are only around 5-6 tracks, but each and every one of them is not only special, but high-quality as well. Once again, nothing outstanding, but always fitting the mood, which  is very important for the soundtrack - and this game never fails to do that.Gnosia is not a game for everyone. That said, I think it is simply a masterpiece. Very rarely am I able to play games that I actively want to forget, just so I could experience them once more.This visual novel is just on another level when it comes to interesting and unique characters, exciting and emotional narrative, as well as absurdly fun and complex game mechanics. This is not only one of the better stories I read, but also one of the most fun I've had in a while. Gnosia is an amazing game, completely worth your attention and money.

_childDocuments_.review: Playing through Gnosia was a roller-coaster for me in more ways than one. Plot-wise, it threw me for loops that I thought were only possible in games by Kotaro Uchikoshi, who worked on the Nonary Games and AI: The Somnium Files. My enjoyment of the game also felt like a roller-coaster, as well. When I had first heard about the game during a Nintendo Indie World, I was already enticed and had decided on buying the game once it had come to Steam. When I actually played the game though, I was a bit disappointed. The gameplay mechanics were different than I had imagined, and the writing style was awkward and prevented me from forming bonds with these characters. Yet, once I had got into the meat of the game -- once I had all members of the crew available and had a heartwarming event with one -- I was enticed to keep playing. I wanted to find out all the info on these characters and figure out how I could manipulate the roles to favor me learning about specific characters. I think that's what the game does best. By allowing the player to experiment with the game to create paths that favor learning about specific characters, the game gives the player enough control so that when they do find information, the player feels rewarded. This is especially shown with more intimate events that are more tricky to get, as they feel like a better reward. The game also makes it easier on players who may have trouble setting up these paths or do not want to bother with it by having the "event search" option, which has the game lay out the paths for you. There are special events, however that can not be gotten as easily, which personally makes me feel like they're a reward to clever players. All in all, I think the premise of Gnosia is an interesting one: a visual novel with rogue-like gameplay, with the details you learn about characters being rewards for each successful attempt, and I think this premise is well delivered. However, the writing still leaves a lot to be desired in terms of letting me create a full and complete bond with each of these characters. Do yourself a favor and try it out! (8/10)Also obligatory comment on who's my fave: WOOOOOOOOO SETSU

_childDocuments_.review: Perfect game if you enjoy Mafia/Werewolf but don't have enough friends or don't want to bother bringing them all to play together. And even though it's not a story-driven work like Raging Loop, Gnosia has dozens of unique events that make you want to learn more about the characters and the situation. Some of these episodes appear pretty ?? at first, so you can't help but play more, trying to solve the mystery. I also liked the writing. It can be funny and clever, but it also never bores you with long flashbacks or something like this. Someone can tell you about their past, but they do it casually and briefly like you'd do it yourself. This way you never get the full picture and fill the gaps with your imagination. It might sound weird, but it works surprisingly well at making you feel like a part of the group and not a center of the world that gets all information in every single detail possible.I can talk a lot about Gnosia, so I'll shut up and just say that it was a unique experience. I could wish for a more emotional conclusion, but it has so many strong parts, and I don't feel like complaining about something.From my . _childDocuments_.review: I get tired of rogue style games quickly, I have a like-hate relationship with Visual Novels, and I'm not fond of social deduction games like Secret Werewolf and Among Us.  Despite those, I still wanted to give Gnosia a try because it sounded so unique and hoped it would hold my attention.  And for a bit, it did.  Unfortunately, I began to get tired of it and started getting annoyed at it's random design.  Since its a single player social deduction game without voice acting, you're more reliant on your stats than any deductive capabilities to survive each loop.  Which means you will at some point have to start grinding up EXP so you can appropriately level up stats.  You only get EXP at the end of a loop, and you get significantly more if you "win" in the end.  So grinding in this game is very tedious.  As far as the story is concerned, the overarching plot is not the real focus.  Instead, its about the learning about all 15 of the characters.  Literally,  you have to learn more about each character in order to progress in the plot.  In order to do so, you have to meet certain criteria in a loop in order to trigger an event (like certain characters get voted off, you have to play as Gnosia and keep someone who isn't Gnosia alive until the end, etc.).  However, because this is a roguelike, there's several things that are just random and you have no control over.  You are able to customize SOME aspects about a loop, but unfortunately, you can't customize everything, which means you could start a loop where you don't have all the criteria you need to trigger the specific event you're after.  There's other random elements as well that could completely screw you over.  Like if you need to keep a specific character alive until the end, that character could just get randomly killed while progressing the loop.  There's also the fact that several of these characters I just didn't find interesting enough to actually want to know more about.  Yet in order to progress in the game, I had to put up with random BS in order to try to learn more about this character I don't like.  Another thing, and admittedly this may just be me, but I never liked being the Gnosia in this game.  That could stem from me just not liking being the antagonist in social deduction games, but I also just in general don't want to be the evil character killing off these characters because I don't have any grudge or reason to want to kill them off.  Again, that's probably just me, but since you have to play as the Gnosia (or play as non-Gnosia and help the Gnosia win a loop) to learn more about certain characters, I was at an impasse.  The game is also in general bad at explaining things.  There's a lot of tips and things to know about how to play this game in which it just doesn't properly explain in the game and you're forced to either look it up online or read through the many pages of explanations in the game's pause menu.  You should always properly explain the mechanics of your game in the actual game itself and not relegate it to a menu or an outside resource that someone else made.  And if your game is too complex/complicated to do that, then just make your game simpler for cripes sake.  Plus, there's some criteria for advancing the plot that I don't believe ANYONE could ever figure out.I think the game has some lovely artwork, I appreciate the ambitious attempt, and there are some character I did genuinely like and wanted to know more about.  Unfortunately, I was only on like Loop 16, and many people were saying you'll need to do like 150+ loops to beat the game, and I just couldn't bring myself to keep playing with all of my grievances I was having.

_childDocuments_.review: Gnosia is a visual novel where a large chunk of it is playing social deduction. This genre should be familiar, as it's appeared in board-games like Werewolf, and video-games like Among Us.The main gameplay can be boiled down to finding the Gnosia(s) of the given round. But what makes Gnosia so interesting, is that the mechanics behind each character is very well thought-out. People are complicated, and in Gnosia the mechanics overlap perfectly with the character being presented. If it feels like someone is a bit naive, you'll see it in the rounds for finding the bad guys. The only thing missing from playing Werewolf IRL, is that you can’t try and guess whether a person is lying or not based on their body language. However here, there’s a mechanic for that – and even if you’re “perfect” at it, you’re not going to identify people lying all the time.There’re multiple layers of mechanics behind everything, which means that you pointing out that someone might be a Gnosia, has consequences in the short- and long term in the given round. In addition, other character’ abilities and personalities bounce off each other. All of this mixing together, means that it’s never easy. I’ve tried multiple games of noticing 1-2 people lying early, only to have a really hard time getting them voted out because it’s only me that knows about it. And if I do get them voted out, I rarely survive the night. Your goal isn’t just winning a given round, it’s surviving to the end as well.If all of that sounds interesting, the next order of business is the story behind all of this. Personally, I feel it’s very well thought-out and makes perfect use of all kinds of people trapped in very unfortunate circumstances. The vast majority of the characters are unique and has both strengths and weaknesses that’s all in display both while playing and while experiencing the story. The main story becomes complicated and is meant to be interpreted to fully comprehend. So, I wouldn’t recommend the game to someone below the age of ~18~, or you’d probably be more frustrated and confused than thinking and brooding. At least I would in that age. The story is fun, scary, wholesome, depressing and thoughtful.Finally, there’s the aesthetics. I very much enjoy the art and visual style – it’s manga-based, but far from manga-like. You’re not going to find manga tropes or clichés: This is very much its own thing. Something that’s not immediately obvious, is that the soundtrack is amazing. It doesn’t distract you when it doesn’t need to, but helps elevate the mystique/confusion/drama. But, when it needs to, it knocks it out of the park: The main theme, different themes of certain recurring plot elements and credits are all absolutely amazing.My playtime as of writing this review is the time it took me to get 100%.I severely recommend this game to anyone who likes social deduction. But if you’re not, and more of a visual novel fan, I can’t recommend it: The vast, vast majority of the game is about social deduction.

_childDocuments_.review: I certainly did not expect to enjoy an indie game made by literally four people in their basement this much. Look at this playtime. I spent 73 hours on it and it felt like 5. Of course, there are other factors at play, but overall the game is absolutely solid and just for that I should give a thumbs up. The story revolves around a space-time loop. The core of the game sees the player, a customizable character (through stats and some story-related choices) facing off an unknown alien enemy called Gnosia who can infect individual humans and desires either physical violence or control over the human race. Why is Gnosia a thing, who created it and how is set in the background, as the player needs to determine who among fifteen other members of a spaceship have been infected and eliminate them one by one through daily debates and subsequent voting to put the suspects into cryo sleep.The Gnosia infected of course wont stand back and watch, and will actively try to murder the player and his allies during the night where everyone is forced in their own quarters due to the spaceship warping.The player is able to gradually increase their stats inside their own quarters, gaining experience every time they complete a loop (either after eliminating all the Gnosia infected crew members, being murdered, or destroying the current universe - yes that's a thing). The story progresses by acquiring certain notes from the other crew members, and these require you watch specific events unlocked throughout the adventure by setting up the composition of the crew, how many enemies will be present and other parameters. The game generously guides you towards your goals via a convenient button called Event Search so you're not blindly looking for random events (mostly). It's still hard to find the patience for completing each task though, because failing a loop, being murdered in the middle of acquiring a note or having your quest givers killed can halt your progress until the next loop, which is also random, adding exponentially  to the time requirement on the player's part. Simply put, while it does work both in-context and as a game mechanic, it is just not that fun and a bit tedious.This "should" be a 10 hours game, but instead it ends up becoming a 30-40 hours game because of its randomness factor and a series of events that you HAVE to watch and there is no way for you to comprehend how to achieve them unless the player reads a guide.That is the single most frustrating thing about the game as a whole. Everything else simply just works. The entirety of the gameplay revolves around conversations and how the different personalities of the other crew members operate, it feels very rewarding and fun to play around with conversational tropes and try to stir the debate, shift the blame onto others, collaborate to put someone else into the freezer, conspire to eliminate someone or protect potential targets. It feels a bit like Danganronpa but the atmosphere and danger is more immediate, perhaps more tangible, and way less cheesy.I have no doubt in my mind that if this title had any budget whatsover, it would have become a masterpiece in its own right. As it stands, it is "just" a good game. CGs are well drawn, sprites and backgrounds are pretty good, sounds and music are serviceable (they loop too often, pun not intended, it really is apparent where the budget cuts were applied) and the storyline has a satisfying beginning, middle and ending although I would argue they REALLY pushed for all the possible sentimental buttons a bit too far. It's hard to pull at your heartstrings with a story like this, I'll admit. Perhaps if there was more meat in key aspects such as characters' backgrounds, which were often way too vague to justify that kind of attachment. Of the 15 participants, perhaps 5 or 6 were relevant, everyone else was there to fill in for diary entries and worldbuilding.Still, I did not feel disappointed and I will keep playing the postgame for a while longer. Hopefully it gets remastered with proper voice acting, a graphics overhaul and an expanded story.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not usually one to leave reviews on games... but I'm going to make an exception in this case, because Gnosia absolutely deserves a shout-out. It's a fascinating game that is far more than just "Among Us, but as a single-player visual novel with roguelike and RPG elements". Like yes, that's the basic idea, but it's not what makes this game shine.The thing that REALLY makes Gnosia great is the writing. It's hard to say too much about the plot without spoilers, but let's just say that it tackles a notoriously tricky subject to get right and does a great job with it. (Are there some unanswered questions? Yeah, there are. But the plot is pretty solid on the whole, and I cared enough about finding out how the game ends to keep playing through over 34 hours and nearly 200 runs, which says a LOT for this gamer with ADHD and access to a bunch of other shiny things to distract me.)Like a lot of VN-type games, the characters are the core of the experience -- if you get sucked into their stories, then you're going to love the game (even if you HATE some of the characters themselves). And for me at least, Gnosia nailed it on that score. Everybody has a backstory (some more complex than others), and you slowly unravel more information about everybody's deal as you play. NPCs have different habits, personalities, and ideologies -- there are multiple characters who are non-binary and the game handles that really well, making it a part of who they are but not the ONLY thing that those characters are about. They feel very "real". The art and sound design are really good, as well. There are a lot of subtle touches like changes in facial expression that are really well done, and really help bring the characters to life. And the music is inoffensive enough that you won't mind it while you hear it over and over again, even if it's not super-catchy.Is the game perfect? Nope, it has a few minor flaws. As play through repeated runs some of the dialogue does get a bit repetitive, although admittedly there's a lot of variety to it so the experience still feels fresh even if some lines do get old after a while. And because some NPCs have better stats than others, trying to take down certain characters who are infected is WAY more difficult than others, which can be frustrating earlier on before you build up the stats and abilities to crush them. (And when you do get that power, BTW, crushing those NPCs is incredibly satisfying!) Also, at times it can be very hard to figure out how to advance the game's metaplot (I confess I did end up checking a spoiler-free walkthrough at one point for hints about how to trigger the next step forward). And as noted above, some things just never get fully explained, either .But despite those issues, this is the most I've been sucked into a game in a good while, and I can't recommend it enough even to folks who aren't into VNs. At the end of the day, the way that I judge whether a game is truly great is this: does it stick with me even when I'm not playing it? In Gnosia's case, the answer is definitely yes.

_childDocuments_.review: I played a ton of Gnosia on its switch release and this port seems solid on my machine, some UI polish issues aside.This game is incredible. An innovative take on visual novels and interactive storytelling structure that I consider a must-play for any game designer. The basic premise is as follows: They took Werewolf/Mafia and made it a single-player skirmish against AI opponents. You play multiple matches and over time you're unlocking narrative scenes that advance a meta-plot that runs across each match.The details in the execution of this premise are what make it so compelling. Each match, there's a chance for some cast members to be human, some to be Gnosia (the mafia or werewolf equivalent), some to have special roles, etc. However, each member of the cast plays each role differently, and they each have an associated stat block (as do you) that determines how well they play said role. As you play, part of the mastery of the game is learning the quirks of each character and how to play around them. Some characters seem to lie constantly and competently, making them dangerous as a Gnosia but even more difficult to trust as a human. Some characters fold immediately when they're Gnosia, and others go for big lies to cause chaos. Clear archetypes start to emerge that will feel familiar to anyone who's played social deduction games with a consistent social group will recognize.The key here though, is because of how the game has carefully structured both its perfect and imperfect information, you never really "solve" a given character. You know if this one guy is Gnosia he's always going to go for broke and claim the Engineer role to sway the game. If he's saying he's the Engineer, he's probably lying... but what about the times where he isn't? You can't trust that behavior completely, because if you do there'll be games that you throw completely by doing so. It becomes one tidbit in an ocean of information when you're making high-stakes decisions, and there are *15* completely unique characters with gorgeous designs and their own quirks and patterns.Characters will share information with you, with each other, cast doubt and accusations, defend others, catch liars (including you), and they will be doing this with hidden motivations based on their role and what information they have. It's remarkable how "human" they feel as you play this game with them, to the point where I've gone on mutli-page tirades about how angry some characters make me. (♥♥♥♥ you Raqio, you beautiful piece of ♥♥♥♥.) That's kind of the most fascinating thing about this game to me--the characters don't feel like NPCs, they feel like fully realized people when I'm in the middle of a match, people I'm actively trying to persuade, outsmart, and outplay. When a match is going bad in Gnosia, a computer isn't ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ me over. They feel like cardboard cutouts who say the same stuff loop after loop.  Never before has a game made me feel in my own flesh the tedium of being trapped in a time loop like this one has.
