_childDocuments_.review: Have you ever wanted to play Among Us, but with more anime nonsense, and less having to interact with actual people? Then look no further than Gnosia. Unfortunately, however, the burn on this game is just too slow, and if you don't play it the way the game wants you to, you will lose again and again, which will only make the burn even slower, because to unlock more plot, you must both win and lose in very specific, frustrating ways that even if you know what you're aiming for, you can still miss out due to bad luck. And even then, these little plot nuggets can feel completely redundant or insultingly obvious. Oh, really? The guy who kept skipping meetings has a problem with authority? Thanks, never would've got there on my own. This game has a few hours of content spread out over more hours of gameplay than I cared to grind through (over 18, if Steam is to be believed). Save yourself some time and money and just read a plot synopsis.

I had noticed that in the latest update the game is now locked at 60fps, despite being able to go up to 144fps previously (on my 144hz monitor, at least). _childDocuments_.review: Really wanted to like this game since I enjoy werewolf, mafia, 9 doors 9 people 9 hours, zero escape, and danganronpa (strongly recommend looking into the last three if you want legitimate social deduction game), and this game was giving me a similar promise in the premise and art style.The entire thing is just chaotic and random with little to no logic or evidence.  You basically just rely either your role or an intuition check to see if someone is lying, without actually checking what they've said.  In fact, the log of what people say is so bare bones, you can't even seen anything besides the main actors so you are less likely to notice multiple people taking contradictory positions in back to back accusations.I was interested in the promise of the overarching plot, but based on other reviews, I shouldn't waste my time trying to grind potentially hundreds of niche scenarios is get scraps.The ham-fisted gender politics didn't help.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: Ehhhh.... So this feels like an Among Us fangame trying to capture that in a single player setting. So I guess if that's what you're looking for, go ahead. It *does* manage to capture the idea of a single-player mafia game to some extent.However, the main story is almost completely absent and drip-fed to you extremely slowly. It's there I guess, but I don't feel like playing for 40 hours to see it. Almost all the time you spend in this will be doing the same thing over and over.There's essentially only one or two characters who have any personality at all. The main character who is your friend and remembers the time loops is Setia (everyone else has their memory reset), who's extremely uninteresting and you're supposed to like it because it's "non-binary". There's also a kind of a glimmer of personality from a few others (alien bro Sakaguchi is funny, Ming is just an arse to everyone and somehow gets away with it), but basically they're just there to be pieces of artwork to look at while selecting a response. Even if you're curious about a character you never really have a chance to interact with them outside of one or two canned scenes on repeat and some out-of-nowhere scenes where a character shows up and is like "I love you let's have sex".Maybe something interesting will happen if you grind through 100 games or something, but at the pace it's going it feels like a massive waste of time. You have to really enjoy the core gameplay loop to push through with it. And... well... I don't. I can see why some people might like this because there's nothing else out there quite like it, but it's neither Danganronpa nor is it Among Us, it's just a waste of time. At least the art is nice.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: Needlessly confusing, just throws you into the game. My character somehow knows everyone's name, with amnesia. Though I will admit it's really the player (you) who knows, but why should WE know? We know as much as the MC, right? I have no idea why a Gnosia is bad, or why the ships AI will turn on the HUMANS IT'S SUPPOSED TO PROTECT if there's half or more Gnosia onboard. Why are they bad? How do they appear between warps? Why do they kill the crew? If they can assimilate or replace the crew, do that every warp instead of killing. A little intro would be nice, and if all the text didn't scroll by way too fast and the screen didn't black out making it impossible to read the character's dialogue that'd also be nice. The loop system seemed cool, but I had no effect on the story. It's still a he said she said thing, and at no point could my character say, "I'm a time traveler and I know the future." Bad option and it'll make you seem f**king crazy, but allow us to try and fail!

_childDocuments_.review: This game originally appeared to me as I was looking for visual novels that fit the niche of death games that I have become completely obsessed with. And, considering this basically is just Among Us in a visual novel format, I expected that I would be refunding this game on the premise of trying it and finding it not original or story-driven enough. But, once I started playing it, I didn't slow down until I'd beaten a majority of the main story because I found it a pleasant surprise how addictive the game really is.So, the plot is still really similar to Among Us/Mafia, in which you wake on a ship where there are Gnosia (this game's version of Impostors/Mafia. You've gotta figure out who the Gnosia are by holding a meeting and voting on it before you all split off for the night, allowing a murder to happen. If you're looking for a completely original premise, then this doesn't present a completely unheard of plot. But it's the way that this game tackles the whole idea of playing Mafia that appeals more than these party games. Whilst in any other of these, if you wanted to play another game, you'd simply set up the cards/start another game, in Gnosia, you encounter a time loop that ends every time you die/have won. Whilst this may make the game seem repetitive, unlike how you may expect time loops to work in which everyone loses their memory bar the player, another character, Setsu, who acts as the supporting character, is able to recall some of these loops, giving you an ally in this game. The reason that this game gains much of its points in my books is that it really does well at fleshing out its characters. Setsu's mindset is explored in detail, about how she wants the loops to end but has no clue how to end them and all characters have much to learn about them which unveils why they act the way they do, which adds replayability as a player seeks to find out everything they can about their favourite characters. Plus, there is an element of skill retention in which a player can continuously increase their skills, leading to a greater ease in retaining skills such as gaining influence in the meetings, allowing them to best the strongest players such as Yuriko. To add to this, there is no issue with getting frustrated at being provided a certain role, as before a player begins a game, they can choose their role and which roles are at play, which makes the game much more replayable. As well as fleshing its characters out, the game manages to insert some strong comedic relief characters such as Jonas and Shigemichi, who in one scene somehow end up announcing that they are Gnosia in a certain loop despite this meaning their 'death'. The story can be lackluster in some runs due to you not finding the key to activating the advancement of the plot but the ending of the game and the way in which the story is captivating to the extent that I'm glad I beat the game in its entirety and unravelled the mystery behind the time loops. However, one issue that I feel is only fair to bring up with the game links to an issue caused by its premise. By having a social deduction game in which none of the characters are played by actual humans, there are bound to be limitations as to the mind games that can be played and the range of dialogue. Whilst there are many unlockable special events, some of the meetings can feel dry after a certain point, as characters repeat preset dialogue to express their opinions, an issue which becomes especially prominent when you become so overpowered that when you make a suggestion of who is Gnosia, you are likely to gain the votes needed without much strife.Whilst this can take away from the game somewhat, I still feel that the game is worth playing on the whole, as it offers a fun game of whodunnit where you get to learn the ways in which people act and to discern who is innocent and who is not through mind games, getting close to the members of the diverse cast you want to in each loop.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: Honest truth here: This game was hard to get in to be honest, I found this game frustrating especially with some of the game mechanics. Gnosia was annoying to me... but ever since I actually figured out I needed to do and the strategies to win, GOD DO I LOVE IT!!! Gnosia is very talented game, a couple flaws there and there but other than that... It's perfect! The story is amazing, I love the Sci-fi direction they went for and I love social deduction games and it being single player really made it a lot better from someone with social anxiety! The characters are very likable, of course some more than others. The only character you would hate is Shigemichi and who doesn't hate Shigemichi? Hell, even some characters I used to hate (Sha-Ming, Otome, Raqio) became lovable if you just got to know them well! Now, I understand the problem with some of the social deduction aspects of this game. I hated being Gnosia and went out of my way to not BE Gnosia but honestly you just need to find statergies which I love in this game, instead just lying your way and killing someone random. I took my time and killed people I felt like needed to be killed. Also with the stats, I felt like I was actually thinking about what I needed to level up instead of randomly clicking one. For Crew stats, I went for Stealth, Charm, and Intuition but when I play as the Gnosia, I went for Charisma and Performance and for Skills, Logic! I felt like I actually needed to think and what I needed to play as next!I do have to point out I felt like there was some plot holes there, how repetitive the gameplay and dialogue were, how much the first/normal ending tipped me off... and there and some of the characters wasn't doing it for me... uuugh Shigemichi... but if you can not notice that or accept the fact it kind of becomes the perfect game.And always... Play for Setsu..And maybe for Yuriko, SQ, Gina, Stella, Sha-Ming, and Raqio.

I thoroughly enjoyed yelling at the crew members freak out about the wrong people while the Gnosia were getting setup to do their Gnosia things. _childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: A singleplayer werewolf game with an intriguing story. Gameplay is fun and AI are mostly logical, with each character having unique tactics. Gameplay loop gets slightly tedious near the end but the characters and their backstories are fascinating, drawing me to push through and find out more about them. Simple yet heartfelt moments can be experienced in between gameplay loops. The highlight of the game for me is the creative character designs and their distinctive behaviours throughout the game. Highly recommend if you're into this genre of games.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: Very engaging game! This interactive visual novel with exciting character build-up and unique story unwrapping. I heard good comments about this years ago and finally got a chance to play it myself. I wish they could make more content to fulfill the stories. The mechanism itself is one of a kind: unlike other visual novel, it requires your own input and action to complete the story. I spent a couple of days trying to figure out what would happen next and they didn't let me down! I got it in simplified Chinese.

_childDocuments_.review: A very good game about finding moles on a ship. At this point I have spent about 6 hours with this game, but I will easily reach at least 20-30 hours. The biggest advantage is the level of difficulty. Just when I thought I was going to win, I was sent to a cryogenic chamber - a dozen times. Satisfying and frustrating at the same time.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: It's a singleplayer social deduction game that somewhat works. Conceptually interesting enough to warrant a playthrough.Conversations (even hunches picked up by the protagonist) are driven by stats and progressively unlocked boiler-plate dialogue options (eg. 'xyz is suspicious').I was pleasantly surprised by how focussed this game is on its gameplay. You gradually unlock story sequences by playing the game with different parameters (roles, team balancing, ...).Not such a big fan of the characters and the writing, still think it's worth full price. Not seeing myself ever playing this again, though. The gameplay gets too formulaic after a while.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: Gnosia took everything I love about social strategy games, and made a singleplayer version that is surprisingly satisfying.The characters are fun to get to know, the mechanics are satisfying (using a skill tree to affect your influence over time is a really interesting idea, and I think it helped the game not feel too stale from run to run) and the artwork is beautiful.Recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: Gnosia is a fun game. While the story might not make all that much sense, the character interactions in events are interesting. My only problem with this game is how you have to rely on RNG to start a game with certain characters having certain roles to trigger some events. I still had fun playing it. I give this game an 8/10.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: Gnosia is definitely not for everyone because of the repetitive gameplay, but I really enjoyed it!It has elements of a visual novel, but you can't really interact with the characters as each round is different. Nevertheless, I recommend it wholeheartedly. It has great graphics and the soundtrack is very soothing <3.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: A gorgeously illustrated series of games of Mafia with a slowly unfolding mystery behind them.Social deduction gameplay is the bulk of the game, so if you're looking for a relaxed, dialogue driven visual novel, this isn't it. The gameplay can also be a little frustrating early on, before you get the hang of it and while your main character's stats are low. But if you give it time to get into full swing, I found the core gameplay pretty fun, and the way the story slowly plays out over many iterations is interesting. The characters are lively and the illustration is top notch. Probably the best character sprites I've ever seen in a visual novel. The vapourwave beats are also pretty good, and help flush out the aesthetic.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: I'm kind of dumbfounded.It's really simple gameplay. Single player "Among Us". But the time loops, rpg mechanics, and mystery of what the bigger picture is really draws you into the story. I'm fascinated and enjoy the quick pace, even if it is a tad repetitive.This is a perfect "on sale" game, though I doubt you'd be too upset at full price. I'm enjoying myself and really like the casual nature of the game. It's intriguing and I'm hoping the ending pays off.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: Less repetitive than it might seem albeit the not so consistent character behavior makes it fairly hard to read each character aside from very specific mannerisms. I would say in general that the game is more engaging than a repeating barebones werewolf and has progression linked to story although given the randomness and difficulty involved, I highly recommend using a guide.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed my time with it, but it had some notable flaws.I had fun exploring the games systems/interacting with the characters/ and experiencing the overall story.-Unique idea of mixing Werewolf-like social deduction gameplay with visual novel storytelling and -You can build your characters stats to focus on your priorities during gameplay (stealth, manipulation, logic, lying etc.)-Unique characters that are fun to interact with, you spend enough time with them that you feel like you get to know them.-Knowing the characters and understanding them is also useful in gameplay, as knowing each characters behaviour and skills/weaknesses is really useful during the debates,  and makes you deal with each character somewhat differently. -It plays with some fun sci-fi tropes, which are just fun (and which I'm not gonna spoil) .-It has a pretty unique identity with its visuals and soundtrack.-Your options to interact during the debates are very limited at the start, you might feel ineffective while your stats are low und you don't have the active skills as additional options.- The games structure/themes/plot results in a lot of repetition, it makes sense in context, but it can get a bit tiring.- Sometimes randomness can be frustrating, especially when you need to rely on it to unlock story scenes. The game later adds an option to pretty much ''rig'' the requirements for new events to spawn, but even then the requirements for the event can seem opaque or counterintuitive.(To the games credit, I only had to look up the requirements for one character event..That felt frustrating, but at least the rest occured somewhat naturally over the ''rig'' option).- Some of the sci-fi stuff felt a bit too incredible to feel believable in the setting. At least for me. I think it's a pretty cool game that hasn't gotten much attention,I only found this game over a throwaway comment in a video that was talking about another game.I don't think the game is something everyone is going to like, checking out the first few minutes on Youtube might be somewhat advisable. ''Menu Gameplay'' and some of the characters weirdness, might not be something that clicks with everyone.The game isn't exhaustingly long, or annoyingly short. I clocked in around 15 hours before I completly finished game.It's probably worth it if you buy it on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: It's a social deduction game of similar vein to Town of Salem and Among Us, but in visual novel form. (Actually, this game predates Among Us, but I digress.) Despite the limitations of being styled in a visual novel format, logic and observation are your tools to succeed. There is an RPG element in that you gain XP to level up stats, which help your chances of success and survival.That does make the game grindy at points. I found some of it frustrating at times, but the game offers good laughs and intriguing plot-lines along the way. It's a well written game.7/10 for me, get it when it's on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: I'll recommend it, but still buzzing my face over this one. I don't know. Try it out and decide for yourself. A very unique one. Visual novel roguelike is the way I understand it so far. There's some elements missing. Still a beautiful visual style and interesting deductive choices. I'm sure the experts of this game can offer you a better analysis.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely amazing adventure! It's single player werewolf, but with a few twists and turns to keep you on your toes. Over the course of many, many games, you'll start to get attached, and Fore pick up on their tics.Combine that with an interesting story, with just a splash of sci-fi sprinkled in, and an ending that similarly amazed me, You've got a recipe for an obsession!You get the whole experience of werewolf, without having to have other people!Right down to being mad that everyone isn't listening when you know the answer!10/10Definitely recommended for anyone who wants a unique story, or who wants to find their new group of characters to get irrationally attached to over the course of 14-20+ Hours.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty fun if you enjoy Werewolf. The story doesn't run very deep and mostly just consists of the characters and what you learn about them as you progress. The gameplay can very easily get repetitive since you have to play through many times over to get every necessary scene for the ending. Also, although the game is like Werewolf and should consist of evidence and critical thinking, the gameplay is more or less just playing the blame game back and forth. None of the characters use any real logic and whether or not you're able to convince them of who you think is evil is purely based on your stats that you can level up as you continue to loop. Overall, the game is fun and the characters are definitely interesting but don't expect a thriller story or logical discussions in gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most interesting and unique gameplay experiences I've ever had. A single player social deduction game with effective and believable AI, great art, a killer soundtrack, wonderful character design, and a nice overarching mystery that you solve as you play.Super enjoyable, and highly recommended for both social deduction enjoyers and visual novel fans.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game. The level of polish this game has is pretty crazy considering just how small the dev team was. The main gameplay loop is just so much fun. It's quite complex but very intuitive at the same time. The characters have well written and properly developed story lines and which flow so well that you really only notice just how crazy some of the reveals are afterwards. The timelooping in this game is pretty much perfectly implemented. The off-chance that something weird happens on one of your loops is just high enough that you can reasonable keep an eye out every time for something new, and up till the end will be discovering most events organically (with the use of the even finder which you unlock by finishing a loop with Setsu alive and on the crew side). The art is fantastic and the soundtrack is also realy good. Just wish it was longer but only because what is here is just so good.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, I've finished the game now and I have to scrap my first review, which was also positive, because I horribly undersold this game. It's absolutely gorgeous and the soundtrack does a great job setting the mood for each scene. It's a really fun mystery-solving game, both in the typical way of a "find the traitor" game, but also in modifying the game conditions to try to discover things about the characters.And speaking of, the story and characters are just amazing. It deals with time loops well, and has progression based on how much you discover about the characters in each loop. It's funny, unsettling, touching, and heart-rending, in turn. The game made me cry a few times, it was an incredibly memorable experience.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: Such a good game, the story is incredible, and the social deduction mechanics are really cool and super fun to play - since the people who are Gnosia change with every loop, you're always left guessing who might be Gnosia. Plus you eventually get options to affect the difficulty, so you can play your way and at your own pace.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: This game is incredibly addictive so don't make the mistake of playing it during exams like I did. I absolutely loved the entire cast and the way the fun gameplay elements tie up into a stellar story is incredible. Also, although we don't get too much info about the worldbuilding, the tidbits we do get are really tantalizing pieces of info. A must play for ANY one who enjoyed stuff like Danganronpa and Raging Loop.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: Not without it's flaws, but an incredibly unique and mystical game. With each loop you find out more about the world, your predicament, and the other unfortunate souls you must work with. The nature of the threat and how different characters react to it, either when fighting against it or becoming apart of it, is the highlight of the game. If nothing else, the soundtrack alone is worth the entry price.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: Really fun social-deduction game with genuinely good AI, and an overarching story to tie it all together. Lots of mind-games to be had. Really fun deciphering what everyone is thinking, and there are a lot of conversation skills to be unlocked that allow you to influence the debates in all sorts of ways. Loved the art and (very surreal) music as well, it fit the game very well. Great game. Make sure to get the true ending (the end is not the end).
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: Gnosia is a game that takes the game play from games like Mafia and Among Us and gives it a story line. From the moment I turned this game on I was captivated by its striking art, colors, music, and plot.Gnosia starts off with you, the main character, being woken up by your friend Setsu. Throughout the first few missions it is explained that you are stuck in seemingly an endless loop. Each time the game loops, the Gnosia changes and you must discover who they are. The game often likes to change this up and make the rounds end early or a special way. This helps you learn more about each character and about the world. I will not spoil some of the later missions but one early one during the tutorial, SQ is revealed to be the Gnosia and has a terrifying change in model.This brings me to the character design; each character feels unique and has their own personality. For example, Otome, is a whale that can participate in the games. She often is happy and trusts those around her. This ends up translating to her doing the same thing in the mafia style matches. However, Yuriko does not trust others and often points out flaws or inconsistencies with things going on around her. Again, she brings this to her game play. Each loop the player experiences, the player learns more about the characters and more about the world while gathering experience to get better at detecting lies, lying, persuading others, being able to stay silent unnoticed, and other abilities. Speaking of the game play, this game is like Mafia without the toxic players. After a bit of time, you can control what roles are available in each loop. There are several roles, each playing a unique role, doctor for example, can protect someone from being killed each night. Engineer can review a player and determine if they are Gnosia or Crew. Change these roles changes the complexity of each match but also can reveal more to the story and world. This can be a bit frustrating if you trying to finish your character logs but the game includes a “story hunt” option that sets suggestions based on what information you still need to gather. The music is very calming during matches however, the game has some sound effects that play too often and are a bit jarring. In the grand scheme of things though it’s more of a minor nitpick.I would love to write more about this game, but in doing so I would end up spoiling this wonderful game for others. I ended up beating the game in about 110 loops and the ending was the perfect finale for this wonderful masterpiece of a game. If you enjoy games that are psychological thrillers or intense drama, I highly suggest buying this game. It’s by far the best visual novel I have ever played.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing gamereally fun gameplay loop that will get you hooked for hours, great art (albeit limited) and great musiccharacters are interesting and getting to know them is an awesome half of the game, story is pretty good and the ending is emotionalone of my favourite games now and I give it a 9.3, anyone who enjoys ace attorney or danganronpa should check this out because it's better than all of them
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: This game is basically yelling at your family at the kitchen table trying to prove the other people wrong, but instead of having access to the internet to back anything up, everyone is in the dark about what they're arguing for/against. You're not making deductions based on evidence or logic half the time, just gut feeling and an RNG to be reckoned with. That being said, I would willingly subject myself for days trying to get these people frozen because of how absolutely braindead they are defending me (I'm looking at you Sha-Ming you asshat) and will do it again to see Setsu judge me on my priorities on this godforsaken clown car of a spaceship. 10/10, suck my butt Yuriko.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: If you like visual novels, and you like mystery solving with a dash of backstabbing, GNOSIA has what you need. The concept is quite unique, with elements from games like Among Us and Goose Goose Duck, but in true story form. With a colorful cast of characters, and a genuinely interesting and intricate story to unravel through the course of many successes and failures, GNOSIA genuinely entertains, frustrates, brings joy, and brings sadness. If you consider yourself a person with a lot of patience, don't hesitate.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely phenomenal story, gameplay is quite slow at first and the very last 5% can be *agonising*, but it's all worth it in the end. Takes about 20~ hours for a full playthrough, more or less depending on how quickly you learn to game the mechanics. Don't recommend if you aren't the type who can put up with repetitive stuff.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Extremely well-made and carefully thought-out, awesome game go play itTo be honest, I was not sold on AI being able to be a satisfying opponent in a game of Werewolf. I was so bloody wrong.It is astonishing how efficient writing and smart programmation makes a character feel compelling and intelligent. Characters never voted for someone on guard duty, there were charismatic leaders who would sway public opinion and controversial figures who got voted off by default, extremely talkative characters and extremely shy ones, and so on. The beautiful artwork added to each character’s personality and charm.I was worried that the game would run stale after a while. Most reviews I read prior to playing mentioned this issue, especially since the game requires you to go through a ton of loops (unless you’re speed-running the game, you’re going to reach the 100 marks). However, I didn’t get bored of it at all!The game is pretty good at reinventing itself. You can mess with a ton of parameters like what roles are available, what you play as, and the number of players/Gnosia. What’s more, as you gradually start unlocking more info about the characters, they gain new abilities making the “day” part of the game loop change with time. Additionally, . The main goal of Gnosia isn’t to get rid of the Gnosia (ironically), it’s to unlock ‘notes’, pieces of info about every character (between 4 and 7 per character). Unlock conditions are extremely varied and range from very easy to super hard to attain, and so around loop 80 or so my view of the game completely changed: it was no longer about winning, but about having to keep x or y character alive, make sure I was Gnosia alongside someone, make sure someone died, etc. All of that to say: when you reach the point where you’re no longer able to randomly unlock notes, do not be scared to pick up a guide, it’s 100% going to make your experience better!

_childDocuments_.review: It took some getting used to, but I really got into Gnosia. It's basically PvE amogus against a bunch of interesting characters instead of real people. Each round or "loop", as they're known in this game, is for the most part, randomized. It feels more like a game than a visual novel. This is where Gnosia is different from Raging Loop, which is more of a visual novel where the rounds are pre-written and linear. Gnosia also has a bit of pre-written story sprinkled here and there, but to progress through it, you have to keep playing more and more randomized rounds of among us to encounter events unique to each character that can only be seen under certain game circumstances, i.e, you and that character are both imposter and you both make it to the end, etc... I didn't like this method of storytelling, as gating story progress behind RNG is never a good idea and there are only so many rounds of among us you can play until you get sick of it. The game also does not tell you what the conditions for unlocking these events are until you've done them, so you're just playing rounds over and over waiting for the next story event to happen by accident. I'm on loop 25 and I'm already getting sick of the amongus gameplay. I've heard from a person completed the game that it took them 150 rounds to beat it on their first playthrough. Y-yeah...That was the bad part of this game The good part, however, is as follows:The concept of an endless, dynamic, and randomly generated PvE amogus game is really interesting. The crew AI that they made for this game is very unique.They don't play 5D chess against each other like people do, and they can seem kinda dumb or random at first, but as I got more rounds in, I noticed that they do have some pretty intricate logic programmed into them, and they can actually use quite clever tactics to bamboozle the player. Each one of them also have programmed-in personality traits that make them feel like unique human players too, i.e, one is really sensitive to lies but can't lie very well, while one is not good at arguing but is good at deflecting suspicion and staying alive for really long. Over time, you start to think of them like real people, and it is quite a fascinating experience. There are also roles for the crew and other bells and whistles that comes with these kinds of games. Game rounds can become insane cluster♥♥♥♥s when you have the maximum number of players, which is 15. Among these 15 is an engineer, a doctor, a guardian angel, a traitor, a bug, two guards, and 4-5 imposters. Once, I had a round where 4 people came out as the engineer and 3 people came out as the doctor. You get the idea. This is what makes this game unique and worth checking out, if you're into amogus/werewolf/town of salem social deduction gameplay mixed with some light visual novel elements. It really makes your head spin when it's at its best.EDIT: I beat the game. It took me around 100 or so loops. I know I complained about the endless among us gameplay, but it actually became strangely zen after a while. Yeah, it actually became kinda relaxing. The game gives you a lot more debate tools to use later on so you have much better control over the outcomes of rounds. You start to figure out who the imposters are and breeze through rounds like clockwork. The game also has a built-in search feature that generates rounds for you that has the highest chance of triggering events you haven't seen before. With this feature and the help of a guide, you will eventually find everything and complete the story. I'd say it was worth it. The characters, setting, and writing are very unique. You know it's good sci-fi when throughout the game, you never actually leave the spaceship you're in, but you always feel like there's a much bigger world out there. The diverse lives and backgrounds of each crew member, and the constant world-building that they give you really expand the game beyond just ship they're all occupying. The characters really are the backbone of this story, and I genuinely wanted to see what would happen to them at the end. After 100 rounds of among us with them, they really felt like they were my friends. TLDR: I'll give Gnosia a 9/10. It has a great overarching mystery, and its cast of characters is consistently a joy to learn more about. The gameplay, while slightly repetitive, does its job well as a means of engaging the player with the story beyond just reading text like most visual novels. The artwork is also really nice. Buy it, play it, and become a god at among us.

_childDocuments_.review: A very solid loop-type game with quite a few interesting mechanics. There is  going on underneath the hood here, and it culminates in a unique experience that definitely leaves room for replayability.The core mechanic of the game is the rounds of werewolf the player must play. To keep the game from getting monotonous, there are different abilities and skills the player can unlock to spice things up. For example, you can just keep doubting the obviously suspicious eboy for 4 rounds of discussion, but doing so might put a target on your back, or make you seem annoying to the other characters, thus lowering your overall persuasion. Instead, it might be better to bait the eboy into doubting you instead, and then hitting him with one of the many counter attack skills. A lot of options open up, and while by the endgame you should mostly have all skills, the intermittent time allows for most character builds to be viable. It also adds a satisfying feel of progression. At the beginning of the game, you're gonna find yourself cowering behind your protective enby a lot of the time to avoid getting voted off. But as you acquire new skills and learn more about the other characters, you're able to get yourself advantages in discussions for you and allies to pounce on. Overall, the skill system is probably the best way an AI vs Human social deduction game could go.On the topic of characters, learning about them is how the story progresses. As you learn more about them, you fill out rows on their stats page called "notes." Filling out notes will provide insight into the characters, unlock story events, and even increase their stats (which is a good way to keep the debate rounds interesting instead of falling into a clear power creep). As mentioned before, there is a lot going on underneath the hood in regards to the characters. They are constantly reevaluating whether they like the other characters and the player themselves, which makes for a different feel for the game each time you play it. Choices you make in previous loops might affect how they subconsciously view you in others. For example, creeping on a woman in the shower locks you out of getting her "Love" ending later down the line (as it should you weirdo). For a game genre where character writing is usually pretty bland by consequence, Gnosia does a good job at making the 15 characters unique among each other, and a lot of the events that get unlocked provide really interesting insight that explains their actions, as well as their hinted reasons for interacting with other characters the way they do. It is genuinely one of the more interesting ways I've seen NPCs interact with each other in a video game.As others have stated, the gameplay loop can potentially get pretty boring, especially when you need to unlock the final few notes. While it is  random when said notes show up, it's pretty easy to change the settings using the Event Searcher to more or less manipulate the RNG. I would recommend using the  if you're stuck on a particular one, because admittedly a few are convoluted or just kinda stupid to get.Don't get it twisted, however. Gnosia is an incredibly unique game that doesn't have much in terms of peers. I didn't even get into the excellent atmosphere or in depth mechanics of the loops themselves. It is worth playing if the concept even remotely interests you, and I hope we see more from the developers in the future!

_childDocuments_.review: ===== Positives =====+ A really smart game in terms of gameplay, though it dumbs down a little once you have high stats because you can pretty much muscle through in many cases+ Complex mechanics. Contrary to some reviews, you do not actually need to stat grind to win, but you need to understand social deduction and the game mechanics. No amount of stats can save a player who make logical fallacies that lead to characters declaring the player as "Definite Enemy". Similarly, no amount of stats can save a player who is playing the role of a "bug" if the player fails to masquerade the needed role and actions. This game is not easy to learn and certainly not easy to master. You will be juggling a lot of information at the start to get used to the game. But this gets easier later once you get comfortable at tracking the information for deductions. People say it is a stat-grind because they do not understand the social deductions needed. This game does not hold your hand, though the character Raqio will explain some of the logical fallacies to identify lying characters, which I myself admittedly could not think of. + Art is very very good.+ Story is amazing and intelligent. The setting is very atmospheric even until the end. Characters are really interesting and you will get familiar with them as you will be seeing the different sides of them a lot. You do feel that you are trapped in space and time. This game actually has a true ending that will explain a lot of characters and events that happened, so be sure not to miss it.+ A fresh and unique take on a super futuristic human future after earth's space exploration+ Futuristic soundtrack creates immersion.+ Counter-intuitive strategies and some luck are needed when fighting against a certain character on a boss map in the mid game, because *she* will wreck you if you face her head on. *She* will continue to be a dangerous character even in late game, but you will learn strategies to pick her off in other ways. (Those who played will know who)===== Negatives =====- No skipping of matches or forfeiture if you know the game is already lost for some maps- Takes a fair bit of farming if you go in blind to try to unlock certain events for certain characters===== In Sum =====A very strong 9 / 10 - I am having difficulty uninstalling it after maxing its achievements. This game is very close to a masterpiece work.[As a benchmark, the non-social deduction mystery VNs of Stein's Gate and Stein's Gate Zero is a 10/10 score for me because they were tear jerking emotional roller coasters. Gnosia falls short of that, but its events and its ending will tug slowly at your heartstrings, give you feelings of a good long journey, and leave you wanting for more Gnosia after that]All in all, well worth the price tag, can buy this with or without a discount. Highly recommended to play this game. It is a gem that doesn't appear often in gaming history.

_childDocuments_.review: GNOSIA is a great blend of sci-fi worldbuilding and werewolf-style deduction gameplay. The main gameplay loop is that you have a bunch of crew members gathered in a discussion, but some are randomly selected to be infected as "Gnosia", which choose one crew member to eliminate each night. The entire crew must also vote on one member to be sent to "cold sleep" each night, which effectively removes the member from that loop. Aside from crew and Gnosia, there are a variety of other roles that can investigate the status of crew members, or who otherwise have their own goals and objectives. GNOSIA's greatest strength is the complexity and diversity of its characters. Each character behaves in a unique way that is supported by their stat distribution (logic, charm, intuition, etc.) and their surprisingly intelligent AI. For example, one character might have very high intuition that allows them to easily pick out liars, but they stand out due to their low charm, which often causes other crew members to dislike them. Another character often plays the victim whenever they are accused, making it difficult to get people to vote against them. A big part of the game is learning how each character behaves over time, as their personalities remain constant over each loop. This will allow you to better determine who is infected -- or if you're one of the Gnosia in that loop, you can use that knowledge to manipulate the AI into voting in your favor. The story of GNOSIA is told through mostly random events that happen if the conditions are right in that loop. While I did enjoy the overall narrative, I will say that it can be frustrating to cause these events to trigger sometimes, and the circumstances of that loop may not be favorable to completing the event. For example, you may be tasked with protecting a certain crew member, but that crew member coincidentally is Gnosia for that loop and will actively seek to eliminate you. You will likely need to try these events more than once to complete them. Aside from that, one of the negatives of the game is that the gameplay loop may become stale over the 100+ loops that are required to complete the game. Some players may easily become bored with the repetitive dialogue and player dialogue options. For me, this was saved by the aforementioned random events that gradually reveal more information about the characters' backstories, though are more interesting than others. If the gameplay doesn't bore you, it will definitely suck you in as you try to master it. Overall, I enjoyed GNOSIA and the story that it had to offer. It's not for everyone, but if it hits, it hits hard.9/10

_childDocuments_.review: + A well-executed single player video game version of the Mafia / Werewolf social deduction party games.+ Multiple roles to play which mixes up the gameplay.+ Wide range of skills you can learn from other characters to employ throughout debates.+ You can change the settings each round, e.g. number of players, number of Gnosia, and customise it to how you want to play.+ Fun to try and figure out who the baddies are and who's just misguided, or alternatively trying to twist discussions and deflect onto others. It can feel quite realistic to actual Mafia / Werewolf games where someone can get completely dogpiled by everyone and voted off despite being a goodie.+ Really good music and artstyle, has a very distinctive feel to it and meshes well.+ Some really interesting characters that you find out about piece by piece.+ Characters have different stats and skills and lead to different playstyles which are fun to learn over the course of the game.+ Interesting sci-fi concepts and world.- The AI is largely pretty consistent, but on rare occasion the AI will do something strange e.g. Setsu acknowledges SQ is a Definite Enemy but then tries to cover for SQ even though Setsu is Crew.- If you play for long enough you will get such high stats that you can essentially dictate each game. A level-cap would have helped negate this problem.I really enjoyed Gnosia, the core gameplay works really well as a single player Mafia / Werewolf style game, with added stats and skills to employ that blend in really well. The characters and story are really interesting as well and quite different. The main thing I’d caution is that if you’re here for pure Visual Novel, bear in mind that you get delivered snippets of the story at a time, in between the gameplay, and towards the end you may have to play a lot of rounds before you get the next snippet. There are also some scenarios that have very specific criteria to trigger, although there is an in-game setting to help you find the next story snippet, and there are guides online if you are particularly desperate for a specific note or two. If you like games like Zero Escape, Danganronpa or Ace Attorney, this should be right up your alley.

_childDocuments_.review: Gnosia is a solid game for those who wanna have a so-called "social deduction" experience without the social aspect. That may sound bass-ackwards but trust me, it works.  The player character has 6 stats that influence different interactions throughout the arguments. Levelling these stats to certain thresholds grants you the opportunity to start using new abilities during the arguments. This gives the game a bit of a rogue-lite aspect, since the stats & abilities will persist across all sessions. The player gets XP at the end of each session - win or lose. There's a debate/argument phase in which all the characters try to cast doubt on one another in hopes of voting the gnosia off (ie the imposter). After that takes place, the player is able to level up their stats & run through any available conversations w/ NPCs. Note that there isn't a whole lot of action. Apologies if that's a given with the "Visual Novel" genre - as I don't have a lot of experience with such games. Regardless, don't jump into the game expecting to take out the trash or swipe key-cards in your spare time. There are 14 NPCs, to be exact. It turns out that you can play against all of 'em in a single session. While the story never gives you a chance to learn a whole lot about the characters, what little you do learn about them is fascinating. There's a guy who has a cat attached to his neck, and even a talking dolphin. The game gives you "just enough" info on the characters to help them feel like more than some random AI but it doesn't go further than that. So if you're like me, you'll be wanting "more", but you won't get it.On the topic of characters, another thing that really helped them stand out was the AI behind each of 'em. They each have AI patterns that help reinforce what kind of character they are. So you'll see the quiet characters who hardly ever speak up. You'll see the characters who speak more than they think. You'll have the characters that everyone always suspects, and the characters who everyone forgets. And while this may sound like a minor detail, I will say that I was pleasantly surprised when I noticed this. Once a session ends, you're given the opportunity to start a new one, and as you progress through the game, you'll unlock new options to customize the session to your liking. A couple of examples of such include the ability to control how many NPCs show up & how many of them are gnosia, or imposters if you prefer. The roles for all characters are randomized, meaning you can't just assume that the gnosia from the previous session is  a gnosia in the current session.: There are roughly seven roles. There's a basic crew member & basic gnosia, and then there are more complex ones like "the bug" & the "engineer". The bug simply wins if they survive to the end; they don't necessarily need the "human" side to win (or the "gnosia" side, for that matter). The engineer, which was my personal favorite, is able to investigate one person in-between argument sessions & in doing so, they immediately know if the character is human or not. Furthermore, if the engineer investigates a bug, then the bug disappears (which is one of two ways to get rid of bugs). These weird & quirky rules help make things a fun mess.  Some of the dialogue options result in the player character more-or-less confessing to one of the NPCs.  To be clear, you can play through the game without really focusing on this aspect, and that's honestly what I did. I just kinda stumbled through the dialogue options, and occasionally ran into a character who liked the protagonist. It never really felt like the game was trying to railroad the player into those kinds of scenes. But regardless, I don't think most of those scenes really "fit" in the story.  To progress through the story, you need to have certain conversations with the NPCs. But sometimes, those conversations require both you & the NPC to have certain roles (like being human vs gnosia). And so there's a bit of RNG involved in whether or not you'll be able to advance the story during each session, since NPC roles are randomized. It's not a  issue, but it becomes much more noticeable toward the end-game whenever you only have a few conversations remaining. In fact, I ultimately used a guide to figure out how to trigger the last five-ish conversations I needed to see, since the game doesn't spell it out for the player (and it turned out that a few of them required a different play-style than what I preferred). Again, not a big deal, but from what I can tell you aren't able to "finish" the game until you've seen those conversations, so just know that it can be a stumbling block

_childDocuments_.review: Gnosia is a visual novel-slash-solo social deduction game, where you're playing a game of effectively werewolf against computer opponents.The game is simulated... Fine. Each character has preferences and skills, so some are easier to spot lying than others, some are easier to convince than others, etc. It's a pretty good simulation of Werewolf with computer opponents. It's a lot simpler, of course - you select who to doubt or cover, and who to agree with or argue with. There are some additional skills, but the nuance of actual werewolf isn't there.The game has a stat system; the more games you play, the harder it is for NPCs to spot you lying, the less attention you draw to yourself, the more you're able to speak before people get annoyed at you for dominating the conversation, etc., and you get new abilities such as being able to ask certain roles to step forward.It's pretty interesting, but tbh if all you want is to play werewolf, just play among us or town of salem, with real people.But that isn't all this is.Your actual goal is to learn why you and Setsu are trapped in a time loop, learn about each of the different crew members, and escape the loop. It's a detective game. The werewolf game just lets you gather evidence.Sometimes you need to kill people that are on your side, to learn more about them. Sometimes you need to let your opponents win to get more information on them. Sometimes you need to make sure certain crew members survive, or make friends with specific crew members even if (especially if) they're being suspicious, because they might open up to you.The route to get the ending is kind of a collectathon, since your ultimate goal is to find all the (relevant) scenes, which can be time consuming, but there are ways to increase the likelihood of finding scenes, and each scene is interesting and says a lot about the world and about the characters.The game has a good bit of positive nonbinary representation - there's two NB characters, one of whom is the secondary protagonist, Setsu, and you can play nonbinary yourself. The nonbinary representation is mostly incidental in a good way - ie: characters happen to be NB, sometimes they bring it up, but it's neither made a huge deal out of nor is it demeaned.8/10 would recommend

_childDocuments_.review: Sometimes, you might get a game that ends up clearly not being for everyone, but it absolutely appeals to your personal tastes and you end up loving it in spite of, or because of its flaws.Gnosia is that game for me.I've played this game twice now. Once on Switch last year, and once earlier this month. A hybrid between Visual Novel and a social deduction game, Gnosia is one of the most unique experiences I've ever gone through.Unlike Raging Loop, which mainly uses the Social Deduction game as its setting while being a more traditional VN overall, Gnosia uses it as the core gameplay. Every loop, you get thrown into one of several roles that are equivalent to the roles found in games such as Werewolf. More often than not, you end up learning more about the cast and story that plays out.And that's your goal: Experience as many loops as you need to in order to learn everything about the (wonderful and extremely lovable) cast, for it is your only method of continuing the story, and by extension figuring out how to break the loop and returning to a normal life.With this comes a certain caveat: GNOSIA is one of the most repetitive games I've ever played. You'll eventually be able to choose your own role after the first few hours and for the rest, roles are randomly distributed among the characters, but every loop consists of "discussions", voting, and hopefully getting more info several times. The actual story is, for lack of better term, dripfed, and you may not learn anything new for several loops at a time. That dripfeed however, was spaced out just the right amount for me to say "Alright, gonna do a few more loops and see if I can fill out another entry". But this may not be everyone's cup of tea. With this dripfeed also come new abilities you can use during the discussions, such as using logical deduction to pinpoint someone as a guaranteed ally or enemy, which gets quite fun to use, and the other characters all behave differently, favouring different tactics.GNOSIA is a story all about the journey and its cast, rather than the destination, but the journey is filled with a ton of repeats, most lasting about 10-20 minutes. Both playthroughs took me between 120-130 loops before reaching the end, and if you can't stomach its admittedly repetitive nature, you're probably better off staying away. However, if you don't mind a bit of a grind, and are curious to see what's in store, you could do a lot worse than spending 20 euros on a 20 hour journey with one of the most memorable and diverse casts I've seen in all of media. If you're on the fence, you could look up the first half hour of a playthrough on youtube and seeing if it's something you'd like. But if you ask me, GNOSIA's in my top 3 VN's. There truly is nothing quite like it, and it gets my wholehearted recommendation to anyone willing to try it out.

_childDocuments_.review: I got  the secret ending in gnosia so I feel this is a good point to leave a review. Gnosia is one of the most unique and interesting VNs i've ever played, not that I played all that many. Every character is deep and the story includes all of them quite nicely. The writing in my opinion is fantastic and it grew to life in individual personalities of each of the 14 characters in Gnosia. The gameplay is social deduction "Among us" Style mystery but with RPG elements, Dynamic dialogue, and outcomes that your decisions affect. There's a rogue-lite element to it too with loops being procedurally Generated. Something to note is when I picked this up on steam, I never played the switch/vita version of Gnosia and there were some bugs in the steam release. I recommend Gnosia to anyone who enjoy mystery games, Visual Novels, Rogue-lites, and a good story.

_childDocuments_.review: Gnosia is a rougelite rpg themed around mafia/werewolf social deduction with a bit of visual novel thrown in. While that sounds like nonsense, it actually works. Each game the human crew has to pick out the traitors, while the traitors kill a crewmember each night. You level up your stats to be able to do various aspects of this more effectively, while getting a handle on everyone's personality and strengths. At the end of the game, time loops and a new one begins with you retaining memories of what happened. The catch is that in this new loop, roles are changed (randomly generated). This includes not only the traitors but the roles of the crew (one can protect someone from harm each night, some can investigate, etc.) The question is if you can figure out who you can trust before you get stabbed in the back, and even if you have a hunch, can you win over the rest to your side without painting a target on yourself? The more you play, the more you figure out each character's story and the larger narrative underlying all this.

_childDocuments_.review: Social deduction game, but without real people. Characters are cool. They all feel different and play certain ways. For example, one character is good at spotting lies, but is bad at getting the others to listen, one is willing to throw games to get the people they don't like in that round out. Stuff like that.  The overall story is okay. Interesting enough but does not get very deep. You won't come away knowing much about the world, and lore is scarce. But it is good enough to keep you playing. The objective is to try to fill each characters' character notes, which are received by completing events. They have specific requirements, such as eliminating every other character besides you and the target character. The tough part is, you have no clue what the requirements for scenes are. The game can try and set you up for them, and you will stumble across most, but once you are down to a few, there are plenty of spoiler free guides are out there. Use them. All in all, fun, easy to play just a round real quick, or several if you have time to kill.

_childDocuments_.review: game is really cool.  it takes some time to get going so don't be discouraged if it seems ♥♥♥♥♥♥ early on; the tutorial rounds have preset roles and there's not enough nuance to do anything except second-guess the writers.  later on it becomes more interesting.i didn't think a single-player werewolf could work but it does.  the basic accuse/defend can raise or lower people's trust, just the usual werewolf "everybody's yelling at each other" kind of gameplay, but once other roles like doctor/engineer come in (which gnosia and their human confederate role can falsely claim) there are opportunities for logical deduction, plus the characters' persistent personalities can help or hinder.  e.g. shigekichi the ayylmao guy is a charisma moron, he's basically acting at random but it's hard to take him out in the vote unless he makes obvious logical mistakes because people tend to implicitly trust him.  conversely yuriko and raqio basically never leave themselves open, so they're much more dangerous as gnosia.  you can beat gnosia ayylmao by using logic skills when he does something stupid like claim doctor when there's no way he can be, but you'll probably have to make emotional appeals to beat raqio cause she'll never leave a logical hole.the AI knows how to play, that's probably the biggest plus for the game, along with the weird timeloop story it's what keeps it interesting.  the AI plays to win and at least some of the characters are extremely good at winning.  there's a lot more to it than random guessing, even if it feels that way early on.  early on you have to trust the game, trust that it's more nuanced than what it's showing you, which is kind of an interesting meta-element since it's a game about suspicion.

_childDocuments_.review:
The Gnosia lie. Pretending to be human, they’ll get in close, trick and deceive, and then eliminate one victim at a time... The crew of a drifting spaceship, facing off against a mysterious and deadly threat known as the “Gnosia” and having no idea who among them is really the enemy, formulate a desperate plan for survival. The most suspicious among them will be put into “cold sleep” one by one, in an effort to rid the ship of Gnosia.

Gnosia is a Sci-Fi Social Deduction RPG in which you will engage in discussion with a variety of unique characters, with the aim of identifying the Gnosia among the group. Players will have to use what information they can gather during the discussions to ascertain whom they think is Gnosia and then vote to put them into cold sleep. As you progress, your abilities will improve - but so will those of the crew.
As the numbers of crew members, Gnosia, and various “roles” increase, it will become increasingly difficult to determine who is telling the truth. Work in collaboration with or against other crew members to ensure your survival until the end.

・Repeatedly play through “loops”, triggering special events to unravel mysteries in a uniquely original narrative. Certain events will unlock new commands for you to use during discussions.

・Step into a variety of roles to develop different character builds. Your stats will determine how effectively you can sway the group’s opinion or lie, and will also affect your likelihood of being selected for cold sleep.

・Engage with an engrossing and eclectic cast of characters and experience randomly triggered events, each one unique to its subject. Character events will reveal information about your crewmates in the form of special “Notes”.

name: OTXO
detailed_description: MORE FROM US About the Game OTXO (pronounced oh-cho) is a violent top-down shooter with roguelite elements. Play as the protagonist entering an inexplicable mansion in search of his lost love. As you venture deeper into the Mansion, more of its secrets will be unveiled to you. Featureless, unnamed, and without memories of how you came here… but you remember why . She’s waiting for you somewhere in this Mansion and you cannot leave until you find her. Cut your way through various unique areas and meet new allies as you delve deeper into the mystery, face your inner demons, and annihilate them . With a massive variety of guns, over 100 abilities, and Focus to dodge bullets at your disposal, kick down doors and eviscerate the variety of enemies standing in between you and your mission. ◼ Tons of replayability: OTXO will take the player through 8 areas with a randomly laid out selection of rooms out of the over 150 hand-crafted rooms built in the game. No two runs of the game will be the same. ◼ Customization: Find the setup that’ll help you break the cycle from a whole selection of unlockable weapons and over 100 acquirable abilities from the game’s enigmatic bartender. ◼ Playstyle: With the slow-mo mechanic, Focus, at your disposal OTXO will make the player feel powerful and in control. However, be careful because the variety of enemy types thrown in your way can quickly turn the tides of the combat if you don’t adapt accordingly. ◼ Soundtrack: Fully immerse yourself into the brutal noir-esque murder ballet through the gritty pulse pumping soundtrack composed by the developer himself.

_childDocuments_.review: I immediately bought this game after seeing Youtuber's Raycevick's glowing review of the game. And much of what he says is true. This excellent addictive little game distills the essence of Hotline Miami into a perfect arcade like experience. It also refines it in a lot of aspects, having health does make the game feel far less of a system of just repeating the same bite sized stage until you get it just right. At the same time I wouldn't say this game is inherently better than Hotline Miami and there's a few important reasons.1. This game doesn't have the crazy story of Hotline Miami. That's not a bad thing but part of what made the Hotline Miami games so damn memorable was its crazy surreal story. I still remember practically every storybeat from those two games and it has been YEARS since I played them. They're in the top tier of video game storytelling bar none. 2. While I do think Otxo's roguelike game design is an improvement death does feel too punishing for a gamer like me with average game skills. I think replay wise doing an arcade system where you have 2 lives per run would be a marked improvement, this would make Game Overs still feel like a kick in the pants and yet give you a much welcomed second chance. Raycevik does note there is a work around, if you quit the game before dying and then select continue you will start back at the beginning of a stage with full health, a "cheat" that I'm highly likely going to abuse the hell out of because I know already I'm super addicted to this game. But still doing that does feel cheap on my end and I just think a lives system for this game would be such an enhancement to the gameplay. Fingers crossed that maybe we'll see that in a sequel???3. The Black & White (and Red) visuals are definitely visually appealing and the sprite work is fantastic. But I must say I still do prefer Hotline Miami's Neo-80s acid washed colors. This doesn't make it bad but man if this game could just steal Miami's color scheme that would be so awesome to me. But anyway I'm very happy to discover this game, the gameplay is addictive and no game was ever hurt by having a bullettime mechanic. If you loved Hotline Miami you need to check this game out because I can't see how any fan of those games wouldn't be engaged by this lovely little piece of top-down mayhem. This is definitely a sleeper hit of 2023 and if you'll excuse me I'm going to playing more as I listen to podcasts.

_childDocuments_.review: In 2015, The indie game Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number once released, has achieved great success with its refreshing and hearty pixel aestheticization of violence, and obscure yet profound plot. Even now, it is still favored and praised by many players. Regrettably, the developer never made a sequel for it. Many enthusiasts from the community have spontaneously tried to make standalone mods for it, one of the most anticipated and famous of those is Midnight Animal. However, because the developer tried to incorporate many inappropriate Persona 5 elements during the later development process, Midnight Animal was finally canceled under excessive criticism from the community. Since then, there has never been any spiritual sequel as topical as it until the release of OTXO. At first glance, the game's top-down perspective, familiar gameplay, and presentation make it hard to not be reminiscent of Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number, but rather than being a spiritual sequel, OTXO is more like a reference and tribute to it in terms of gameplay and mechanics, its core gameplay is completely different.OTXO uses red, black, and white pixel graphics, its biggest difference from Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number is the shift from linear level progression to incorporating core Roguelike elements. OTXO itself also incorporated many mechanisms and designs, like dodging, health bars, bullet time, killstreak counts, etc. That makes it much more easier for players to get started, but the difficulty of it will continue to increase as you face more responsive, powerful, and diverse enemies. The unique drinks system can be said to be the core of OTXO, could bring change and reshape the gameplay in a variety of interesting and crazy ways, like infinite kunai throwing, grenade clearance, ammunition endurance, increased firing rate, and counter-attack bullet. With these interesting options, coupled with dynamic and exciting in-game music and thrilling boss battle experience, there is no doubt that OTXO is neither lacking in joy nor challenge.As mentioned above, the core of OTXO is Roguelike gameplay, which is fundamentally different from the Hotline Miami series, so much so that in the minds of some fans, OTXO is not worthy of the title of a spiritual sequel. Additionally, Roguelike games usually require players to accumulate experience through continuous failures, but OTXO's level design is quite homogenous, with no other changes except for the map order and enemy positions. That means as the game proceeded, increasing familiarity with enemies and maps would make the game boring, with the highly random drinking system being the only way to maintain the player's interest. Furthermore, since enemies in late levels would react faster and more tanker, and once dead the player must start over, the use of bullet time will become very frequent and vital, which greatly diminishes the game's exhilaration. In addition, the game's plot is extremely straightforward and lacks substance, coupled with the low scene recognition, the fixed and rigid pathfinding logic of AI enemies, etc., these issues have greatly damaged the player's gaming experience.In essence, OTXO is more like a big mix of many games, with Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number being the largest component. The core of OTXO's gameplay is mainly Roguelike, which may disappoint some players who come here for it due to it expecting similarities to the Hotline Miami series. However, OTXO is still qualified as an Indie game, also it can be considered the most outstanding Hotline-Miami-like game in recent years, it is worth a try for players who are interested in such theme and gameplay, and also relatively tolerant. Unfortunately, the playthrough of OTXO may only be enjoyable in the first few hours, as players go deeper, the lackluster gameplay becomes more apparent. The difficulty in retaining players for a long time is the game's biggest and most fatal shortcoming.

But certain issues within Yen's life happened and the pressure built on him and lack of communication within the fandom lead to disaster and the death of Midnight Animal. Then OTXO came along where Spencer Yen himself assisted in the creation of OTXO where you can see certain creative liberties by him and even an easter egg was left as a way to respect Yen. OTXO is a fun game and surprisingly difficult where despite me finishing this game over and over, I still die at certain points in the game due to the fast pace combat. Overall OTXO are the remnants of Midnight Animal but is still a great game by itself. Story is kinda all over the place though.

_childDocuments_.review: The brainchild of Hotline Miami and Hades. If you liked both of those games, you'll like this.It has the art direction and play "feel" you'll recognize from Hotline Miami. Plus the color palette of a newspaper, and an appropriately energetic soundtrack for its genre. The gunshot sounds are punchy, the enemies are stupid (but plenty lethal), and the level design lends to an impression that while you may die and die again, THEY are trapped in this labyrinth with YOU. The progression strongly reminds me of Hades, with boosters, challenging fights, and the goal to reach the other end of the underworld (mansion) without dying.Gripes so far:Characters and dialogue aren't great. The tutorial hand-holding and general "I guess I should introduce myself"/main character amnesia are a bit painful. But the gameplay makes up for that as far as I'm concerned. When you die you don't have the R to Respawn option immediately. You gotta wait, skip a screen, and choose where you wanna spawn back in at. This could be streamlined. Please let this be streamlined. PLEASEGud game. Will continue playing

_childDocuments_.review: Otxo is a top down roguelike shooter with a lot going for it. As someone who usually doesn't enjoy roguelikes, I bought it on sale and initially played maybe 15-30 minutes at a time of this game but quickly found those sessions building up until hours had passed in a flash. Now I would happily recommend this game at full price.The gameplay is fast paced and feels so satisfying. Many people compare it to Hotline Miami and it may have even been inspired somewhat by it. However, OTXO is, from a gameplay perspective, superior in every way. Where Hotline Miami has its masks, OTXO has drinks except you can stack all the effects which makes every playthrough feel different. What really makes OTXO stand out though is Focus. That's the name of the slow-mo mechanic which the game straight up tells you to use as much as possible. It doesn't lock it behind a long cooldown or some consumable etc. and it feels great to use.In terms of story, there isn't one...or is there? There are notes to read and NPCs you can talk to which provide some exposition for the world you find yourself in, but it's purposefully vague and mysterious like the mansion itself. There are also some unlockables of which there are two types, guns and trophies (not sure if they're called that or not). The trophies are just little characters I assume from the dev's previous games and as far as I can tell, they don't do anything. The guns you unlock are added right into the hands of the enemies however so you can get to using them straight away.If I had to give some criticism, I'd say some of the bosses are maybe too easy or at least too repetitive. They would benefit perhaps from having multiple phases à la Dark Souls. It would also be fun to have challenges to complete. There are a few achievements that get you to complete some interesting feats but this could be expanded to further increase the replayability.

_childDocuments_.review: Surreal and brutal, OTXO is a game I never knew I needed.While the roots are obvious, Hotline Miami and all, it does quite a few things differently instead of simply retracing the same steps. For starters, levels are randomized each run, so gradually building up a plan solid enough to get you through is no longer an option. You have to improvize on the spot, and you better be damn good at it.Thankfully, there are means to survive. Apart from many, many guns to find, shoot and throw, you now have an actual health bar  can slow down time. Does it make life easier? Not really, but it sure changed my approach to gunfights. I can afford being  the right amount of careless when entering a room full of baddies, even eating a shotgun shell or two, and still get my ass handed to me if I go a bit overboard. Not once has dying felt cheap or unfair, it's all on me.Add dozens of stackable modifiers (get the attack dog!), AI tweaks, and seemingly minor stuff like being able to reload weapons — and OTXO is really a beast of its own. It has a much more flexible nature that lets you experiment more freely, customize your play style and have fun your way in general. Flexible doesn't mean merciful, though: if your way fails, it's back to square one, no excuses.And yet, despite all the differences, this game is the closest experience to Hotline Miami I've ever had. The insane tempo with split-second decisions, the perpetually violent dynamic, and the satisfaction from turning crowded interiors into a pixelated bloodbath — all of these things are fully present and waiting to suck you into an elegant bullet ballet. With John Woo-like slo-mo doves, no less.I only finished one run so far, but I can see myself coming back for more soon. Regardless, those 3 hours packed so much action, style and adrenaline that I wouldn't care if it ended there for good. I enjoyed every second.Oh, and good thing I played it just in time for the Steam Awards — because  does that soundtrack slap hard. Easily the best thing produced this year.
