_childDocuments_.review: I don't really like writing reviews for games very often. This will be an exception.OTXO is a top-down, fast-paced shoot-em-up game. A lot of people have been comparing it to Hotline Miami, which is valid in some respects, but ultimately an inaccurate comparison that taken at face value, gives the wrong impression: while the genre is the same and the inspirations taken are present, its predecessor places emphasis on slow, careful gameplay and one hit kills, OTXO is a game about fluidity, speed, style, and grace.The way this game works in large part is by putting emphasis on rapid ultraviolence: you are given currency for killing enemies in rapid succession, and given multipliers on your income if you perform quick, non-stop combos. This money gives you the powerups (presented in the form of rare liquors) that will ultimately enable even faster-paced, wilder, more reckless gameplay. Towards the end of the game, I honestly sometimes felt afraid to blink, lest I miss some pesky floor-lizard or suicide-vest maniac barreling towards me at 800kmph. The game oozes style with a limited color palette, which keeps your attention trigger-wired and primed on the things that matter: enemies, health, damage being dealt, the level of focus you have remaining. The music is excellent, too: moody, driving music that remains in the background but sets the mood with a cool bass-riff - sort of reminding me of Jesper Kyd's work, but faster-paced and with a little bit of electronic influence. The pacing is also really good: beat three levels, and then stop at the bar to ponder your upgrades. There are also boss fights interspersed between every two bar visits, which feel essential to keeping the pacing interesting, although sometimes they drag on for a bit - mostly just because you can't wait to get back to the main levels again.There's a lot of content. Ten or so different 'worlds' or 'biomes', some ~hundred different upgrades, probably at least fifty guns, a good number of boss fights. A lot of these are inherently locked behind in-game currency, at times means you need to be willing to slightly sabotage your present run in order to unlock new stuff - weapons, especially. This ultimately doesn't really matter much though, as regardless of what weapons or upgrades you have unlocked,the game generally more or less plays the same, which means you're not missing out on too much if you're not much of a completionist.I'd been keeping an eye on OTXO for a good while during its development phase, and oftentimes with a lot of skepticism that it would meaningfully differentiate itself from the other games in this space. Playing it now, that skepticism was clearly unwarranted: this is a very well designed game that takes the hair-trigger shoot-em-up so many people have been itching for and executes it flawlessly. I would strongly recommend you buy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I have to say that I know about it from Raycevick's video and I agree with most of what he says there - it's fast paced, skill based and similar to hotline miami in core gameplay but changes and adds enough to the formula to have identity of it's own. I was suprised how customizable it is by changing the available weapons through the nun character - you can make the game very different and have a range of difficulty just by e.g. restricting guns to one category and getting all the drinks for it or getting all guns and revel in more randomized experience. I heard people saying that drinks are boring but i have to disagree 100%, I love them :D. Also the 666 update is great, I'm going through the challenges it added right now and it adds a lot of replayability to the game. On the other side I must say that the color pallet is sometimes confusing for e.g. spotting enemies (it happens rarely, but it does happen), some bosses are a little clunky for me (Deabrua, Ehiztaria), but overall these are minor complaints to an otherwise great game. It's really impressive that this is a work of one guy, thanks Nate ;)

_childDocuments_.review: OTXO seems aware of its predecessor and is built not to change but to tweak and enhance how the Hotline games played in a way that makes a lot of sense and feel in line with what those original games could have done; albeit some being obviously necessary changes to balance the higher consequences that now come with death. The addition of dodge roll with I-frames (I think?), and straight up health bar are examples.Even the story of OTXO plays around with memories of Hotline Miami that you might have - though in often very symbolic and more abstract ways. Visually the game robs of the bright color pallets present in Hotline Miami - leaving a stark black on white with splotches of red that is all about contrasts. This all creates a dream-like aesthetic, and indeed: each 'run' through the game's succession of progressively complex combat levels begins with the player character awoken upon washing up on the shore of a beach inhabited by a sailor, a nun, an artist (?) and a person who has the head of a praying mantis.If you don't mind being sent back to the beginning when you die and enjoy the roguelike / roguelite (there are permanent unlocks that persist between runs) thing - you should really play this game. Especially if you know you enjoy the type of twitchy top down combat that Hotline Miami put a particular feel on. It has its own surreal vibe that can be creepy while having the range to also dish out subtle bits of humor. It's cool enough that I just sat here and wrote all this, but this rough draft of a review doesnt do OTXO justice - so,

_childDocuments_.review: OTXO (Pronounced Ot-Cho) is a Hotline Miami-inspired roguelike with a banging soundtrack. That's the gist of it, both good and bad.The plot is somewhere between vague and non-existent. You play as a nameless male character that puts on a mask and ends up on an island with a large mansion situated in the middle. There's a few NPCs you may interact in the hub area, however all they say is that the island is a kind of purgatory.The game smooths out some of the annoyances Hotline had, such as enemies one-shotting you from across the map via addition of a health bar and a rolling mechanic. In addition, there's bullet time, which is meant to be used conservatively. My only gripe is that it suffers from the general issues other roguelikes have, in that RNG dictates most of your run. The floors are largely static with similar enemy positions, but the upgrades (served as drinks at a bar) are random and end up shaping you run. The overall gameplay loop consists out of going through the floors until you find some new enemy or boss and get sent back to the first floor, occasionally finding a new weapon that can be utilised in later runs.One part I'd like to commend is the sound design, specifically the weapons and the OST. While Hotline had a lot of smaller artists doing the individual tracks, OTXO has a single composer with a more coherent techno beat. It's genuinely pretty good club music. In addition, while I appreciate the limited colour palette, it did get somewhat excessive in later levels where the low contrast areas made it basically impossible to figure out what is going on.I'd say it's good fun, but the game could use a few quality of life features. For example, the roguelike element is somewhat jeopardised by save scumming. It would be neat if that got patched out via autosave system, but would still offer a more "forgiving" mode for people that want to see all the levels.

_childDocuments_.review: The moment to moment gameplay is very satisfying and tight feeling. Its got a lot of cool details and I think the reload animations are great. I enjoy the overall pace and spectacle of the game. It takes Hotline Miami's formula and turns it on its head so you're NOT supposed to die, but instead live out your roguelike John Wick power fantasy. This comes with a lot of sacrifices to the general HM mechanics but I think it works for the most part. I recommend this if you're looking for a similar experience to HM, but something more casual you can play without having to sweat too hard. It's great for when I have like 30 minutes to kill between irl responsibilities. Some gripes I have:  The black, blood red and white aesthetic is uncompromising, to the game design's detriment. Things like windows, and the AOE goo NEED to be more visible. In chaotic situations it is very easy to lose track of what's happening because you, the guns, the enemies, and the goo destroying your health is all black and white. Bullets come out of your muzzle so in said chaotic situations you can be shooting over enemies and not kill them. Bullets should come from the player's origin point when your hitbox touches an enemy.Surviving a fight but being left on extremely low health is when the game becomes tedious. You have to basically cheese the rest of the floor by abusing corners and the slowmo to not lose upwards of an hour of progress. A small health regen back up to a max of 15-20% health over time might help the pacing be less impacted. Health drink help this bit it's RNG if you get them.

_childDocuments_.review: This is everything a spiritual successor should be.  At a glance you know exactly what it's paying homage to, but the gameplay and artstyle shake things up enough for it to stand on its own.  The black and white noir aesthetic fits perfectly for this kind of game and the booze perks give you a lot of new ways to approach familiar obstacles.  This is awesome!EDIT: Beat the game.   After playing for much longer I can go deeper into my thoughts on it.  The main problem with this game is how much it forces you to rely on the Focus (bullet time) mechanic.  Some choke points and overcrowded rooms can result in a huge chunk of unavoidable damage if your Focus runs out.  Even if your reaction time is perfect, you'll get shot several times if there's more than two enemies.  The invisible guys that show up during the Vast Library aren't too fun to fight against either, the black and white artstyle makes them blend into the background and will get some cheap damage in if you don't slow down to scan a room before engaging.  The Goldeneye liquor helps with this a little bit, but it's still annoying.  I still definitely recommend this game to anyone who loved Hotline Miami and wants more of that style of gameplay, but it's not perfect and at times you will experience some cheap deaths.
_childDocuments_.name: OTXO

_childDocuments_.review: A game that gets compared to Hotline Miami a lot due to it's violence and top-down combat but it really stands on it's own, all while offering a mysterious loose plot about a mansion that may be an afterlife or an otherworldly dimension.The reason it gets compared to HM so much is that it's a high-lethality, fast-pace romp throughout levels killing everyone in your way, all top down and picking up guns from the ground. Which is definitely inspired by Hotline Miami, but then the differences kick in, like both you and enemies being able to soak some damage instead of dying from single hit, and there's a very stylish and useful slow-mo mode you can use frequently that helps you dodge shots and aim better yourself, which makes it feel like a whole damn big load of cool movies. Another big but less obvious difference is that enemies here are so, so much smarter - they will run at noises you cause, but they will also take cover to fire at you from, or ambush you, provided you didn't jump on them by surprise, and even though you can soak up some damage, if enemies anticipate you they're going to shoot you as soon as they see you, so it's a very risky approach to jump at them head on instead of trying to find a flank or using dodge roll or slow mo to get an edge. Oh yes, there are dodge rolls here, but also you can make cool leaps over stuff like tables and sofas like in a movie, which also counts as making you immune, and some of roguelite aspect upgrades give you temporary bonuses for rolling or leaping over environment details.Talking about upgrade part, there's a variety, not too big but varied, of liquors you get at a bar, that in standard roguelite fashion you get to make a choice of after some levels, and there's some predictable boring stat boosts or super situational gimmicks, but also a lot of super handy heals and income boost effects, or damage increases, or even companions to assist you in combat, not to mention stuff like turning all of one-handed ranged weapons into dual-wield variants or extremely risk and rewardy ones that half your health but double income. Oh yes, income, nothing comes free here, the drinks cost and you gotta kill enemies quick and rack up combos for biggest payouts - which means taking risks, so you have to go all in on speedrunning individual levels and soaking up bullets if it means finishing everyone fast enough. But nothing stops you from buying multiple or all of them if you do well enough, especially later on, and there's also gachapon balls you can get useless toys or variety-increasing new guns for enemies you encounter ingame - and also yourself! Whole thing is build on playing safe or risking and gambling, like, you unlock new drinks by investing into them during a run, and if you die you won't get to use the money you got, but you may as well need that money for something else as you play - and same with gachapons, are you gonna get a toy or increase in shotgun variety that synergizes with your current build boosting shotguns? Or would it be better to not risk it and keep hard-earned cash for reliable barman drinks instead?Betting feels like a major plot in this game. Like, the place you're in is called a mansion but it feels more like a casino or some shady mafioso-run hotel sometimes, and the story implies you were a pretty bad person for your fate to bring you there, risking life again and again to save your beloved. And there's lots of tiny minutia details adding to the feel, like how you must drop a gun away before bartender offers you a drink. It creates a really interesting, auteurish feel to the mystery world and the mystery plot even if it's just a game about running around and shooting people for booze you'll take a sip at most of. Soundtrack is also a banger, very much so.So yeah, if you love running fast and shooting? Consider this. Don't get put off by big chunky pixel art style and seemingly derivative gameplay, this game rocks and has it's own vibe and really really nice flow.

_childDocuments_.review: In a few words: Low-effort yet enjoyable.OTXO mostly piggybacks off the success and lasting effect of the HLM games by not only drawing a ton of ideas from it, but also by attempting to make the game conceptually associated to it. Even though most of its players have caught the bait, you'll notice none of them denounce it as neither a copy nor a worse version of it. That's because it's not. It's just uncomfortably similar.Beside the visual design, perspective, flow, storytelling and many gameplay elements, the game is practically its own thing. May sound sarcastic, but trust me it's a genuine, honest statement.Emphasis on the "practically" though! Because that's the main point I'm trying to make.You see, these two games share one too many things, yet they feel and play extremely unlike each other.The literal reasoning for this is of course that OTXO is a 2D top-view roguelite with health mechanics, some permanent progress elements, weapon stats, bosses, progressive difficulty, unique enemies, blah blah.On the other hand, Hotline Miami is just a 2D top-view shooter with instant death, quick restart, one-shot enemies, weapons separated mostly by their capacity and range and a simple scoring system.Quite obviously, both games have significantly different gameplay and are not and cannot be the same. Props to the dev team for being able to add all elements required for this thin line to still stand between these games rather than making a modernized knock-off. That settled, the game has plenty of issues besides the striking similarities it has with another game series, which is what actually made it stray from the path of true excellence. That said, games that take too much inspiration from others don't always fail, and sometimes it is in fact what makes their success, wether long-lasting or not.However, the dull visuals, inconsistent artstyle, uninteresting and short plot, poor balance, lacking soundtrack diversity, small pool of floor designs, painfully linear gameplay and many other nitpicks I'd rather keep to myself, well, they really hurt the replayability and objective quality of the game, as well as its artistic, non-surface value. Sure, as far as I'm aware, it does what it's supposed to, giving you a quick adrenaline boost and at the same time some incentive to keep playing, with the collectibles and floor progression, but it's just good enough, if even that.Yet another, larger-scale issue with a game that takes so much from another game is that drawing an audience other than that game's is difficult. I have rarely seen non-HML players invested in this game or its release, and all articles I've read on it just compare it to other roguelite games, if not HML itself. This could seriously damage its potential and reach, if it didn't already.If a game struggles to separate itself from another, it cannot expect the players to do so.Never said I didn't like it though! 8/10. Tons of fun. Buy on sale. I look forward to DLC or updates in the near future.

_childDocuments_.review: OXTO markets itself as a Hotline Miami-inspired roguelite. It's a cool idea, and if you enjoy a grind and you don't mind a bit of repetition, this game might be for you.It's unfortunate that Steam doesn't offer a neutral review option because, while OXTO isn't for me, fans of the roguelite genre and those who enjoyed Hotline Miami may find something to appreciate—provided they can overlook its shortcomings.However, there are several issues that make it hard for me to give it a positive review.Limited Field of View: Enemies have a line of sight that extends far beyond the player's, leading to frequent hits from outside your field of view.Repetitive Soundtrack: The soundtrack is limited, which contributes to the overall sense of repetition.Aesthetic: While the game's aesthetic is pretty sweet to start with, it quickly loses its charm and is in the middle of action often tough to navigate. You'll often find yourself stuck on furniture, shooting through some objects but not others. The screen can turn into a fast-moving grey mess, making it difficult to keep track of the action.Inconsistent RNG: The RNG can be frustratingly inconsistent. Some runs feel like a breeze, while others are punishingly difficult (like facing armored enemies in the conservatory).Slow, Repetitive Grind: The game's grind feels slow and the gameplay quite repetitive. I gave it a few shots but every session it quickly lost me. There's really not much to pull you back in for another run.If you like HLM and Roguelites, I would reccomend giving it a go if you can pick it up on sale, there might be something here for you. But if any of the points above put you off, it's probably not for you.

_childDocuments_.review: What does it mean to be a man? To be a protector? Warrior? Provider? Father? Leader? Hunter? Poet? Sage? Playboy? Or something else altogether? Whoever you ask - both those who embrace classically understood masculinity and those who reject it - will probably agree that a man should be strong. And even then, what does it even mean to be strong? It really is a pointless conversation; everybody is "supposed" to find their own answer, but let's be honest, people aren't good at this kind of stuff. So we fall back on what's unspoken, and return back to square one.To talk about OTXO is to talk about masculinity. You are with your girl. You pick up the mask. You put on the mask. Now, she's gone, the mask is stuck to you, and it's up to you to save her... by laying waste to an army of enemies, their blood being the only colour in this accursed mansion.It's Hotline Miami, but it flows better - because you don't die in one hit. And can't get sniped from off screen (ok, you can, but it won't kill you). You know that state of playing Miami when you just mow down enemies, dancing with death on a split-second knife's edge? This is what the entirety of OTXO's gameplay is. At least once you learn the ropes.I'd say the game is pretty hard, partially because it's a roguelike. While there is some meta progression, generally you're going to win using your skills; you won't suddenly unlock an upgrade that will grant you more max health or anything like this. All you'll get is more weapon options, and more drink options. The difficulty comes from the fact that the enemies -will- get stronger, and their variety will increase as you go. You need to keep up. You can increase your own power by buying drinks - each drink is a helpful perk, such as higher fire rate on SMGs, higher throw power on grenades... but also game-changers such as the ability to dual wield one-handed weapons. Double Uzi fire? Not much will be left of whatever you shoot at...Now, to earn money to get these drinks, you need to do well in fights. Kill fast, in varied and interesting ways, and avoid getting hit. But mostly it's about the speed. So you must learn to enter this flow state and stay in it; otherwise you'll find yourself outmatched.Yeah, there's more to this game than just shooting. Believe or not, there's even some lore, and of different kinds, to boot. I won't bore you with the details, let me just give you the, shall we say, vibe of it.A man wants to protect. A man wants to love. But he ends up being a wolf. Not a proud beast, but a starved survivor, fighting at the end of his rope. Your face doesn't matter. You don the mask. You're interchangeable. And once you're drained of everything that you once were, another will come.The game oozes the aesthetic of wounded masculinity. It -knows- it's senseless and hurtful, but it's the only thing you know. Nobody told you how to be anything but a wolf, so that's what you are. Now go; grab a firearm, down a drink, and get back into that meat grinder.Or maybe it's just me. Not that it's a bad thing. It fits, it know what it is and what it isn't, and that's a good thing. The music is banger - in fact, I use it for workouts sometimes - but I wish there was more variety. There are quite a few tracks, but latter areas have the same music as the earlier ones. The only moments where you'll hear something new is when you fight a boss that you haven't seen. Luckily, in order to beat the game you have to literally go through every single boss, so no worries, you'll hear it all.There's also this interesting mechanic. As you play, you'll unlock new weapons. How do you get these weapons, once unlocked? Well, the enemies will be carrying them; so every new weapon can make both you and your opponents more dangerous. Sounds risky? It is - but you are given fine control over which exact weapons will appear during a run. So if you see that some weapons just don't feel right in your hands, or give the enemies too much of an advantage, turn 'em off and you're golden. Finding the right set of weapons to play with is also part of learning the game.Took me 52 hours to beat. Not many people beat the game, though - 85% of players have the achievement for dying for the first time, but only roughly 10% have the achievement for winning. I'm not surprised, there were times when I felt like there's no way I can ever get any further; but eventually I managed to get just the right combination of drinks, weapons and not-being-an-idiot-s and it just happened.I recommend it, of course - I really liked it. It's a little rough here and there, but it's a fantastic evolution of Hotline Miami's formula. And even if HM wasn't your thing, I'd say this is worth checking out. Even if you don't identify with the aesthetic!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Choice for January 2024, and this is part of my coverage of the bundle. If you are interested in the game and it's before February 6th, 2024, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.A mad shoot-out of black and white, and red all over.Otxo takes the fast-paced combat of Hotline Miami, gives the enemies bigger guns, and larger areas, and then creates a rogue-lite where players are forced to travel through 40 rooms of a mansion to save someone close to them.  There’s not a lot of plot or story, but there’s a ton of action and combat, which is the driving force of Otxo.I don’t like this title, but I also am going to say I think it’s mostly because it’s such a fast and twitchy shooter.  The combat seems over the top but the entire time I just wanted a second to make each decision.  There is a focus mode but I needed more than that.  Mostly I found myself flailing around against enemies.   The only way I was able to find success was to line up shots to kill multiple enemies as I kicked doors open, and maybe that is the way it’s intended but it never felt natural to me. Pick this up if you loved Hotline Miami but wanted more guns, faster gameplay, and a rogue-lite rather than a story-based game.  I’ll be honest, I’m probably too old for this game and my reaction times have dried up, but since I never was as enamored with Hotline Miami’s gameplay, I’m not surprised I didn’t enjoy this one either.If you enjoyed this review or want to know what I think of other games in the bundle, check out the full review on or subscribe to my Youtube channel:

_childDocuments_.review: The best top town shooter I've played since the first Hotline Miami. The visceral gunplay, the slow-mo, the bossfights and rogue-lite elements work really well together.Here are some improvement suggestions to consider for future patches:- The blocky bullet tracers look a bit too abstract, I feel it would be more immersive if they looked a bit more realistic.- The gun sounds are very good overall, but they feel a bit rough on the year. This makes it tiring when playing a longer session.- Speaking of sound, I believe adding a chill tune after finishing the enemies in a room would add to the atmosphere.- The Liquor UI would benefit from continuous scrolling when holding down a direction key, you have to spam left/right quite a bit if you have a lot of effects on you to search through them.- It would also be nice if the Bartender menu would stay active after buying a drink, so you don't have to talk to him multiple times when you're buying more than one drink. - I also see no point in having to drop your weapon while talking to the bartender and supplier. This might be fine for npcs that you visit once or twice but not someone you talk to regularly.- The liquor drinking animation could use a bit of a speed-up or a skip option, it gets a bit annoying waiting for it when speedrunning.- The chapter after the first bossfight is a bit too steep of a difficulty jump, it should be toned down just a bit.- Pistols and Rifles feel a bit weak compared to the OPness of LMGs, SMGs and some of the shotguns. They could really use a buff, at least so they are good enough for bossfights, especially considering they do show up in the rooms before the bosses.- Grenades should probably be some kind of separate consumable, I barely ever bothered picking them up.

_childDocuments_.review: OTXO is basically Hotline Miami 3  ! ! !Oh-Cho is the unofficial successor and a worthy surreal action game on its own.Dennaton Games never wanted to make Hotline Miami 2,their hand was forced by their own success/ fans/ publisher. _childDocuments_.review: First off, I want to get something clear. I generally dislike roguelites or roguelikes or roguevanias or any other permutation of the rogue-slop. My major exception is Necrodancer, and I haven't tried Hades yet but it looks cool. It's always the exception rather than the rule with this cursed genre. That being said- this game has been frequently described as a roguelite, and I simply don't think that's true. This game has some structural similarities to the genre- it's based around singular runs where a victory state is a start-to-finish deathless completion; rather than a predefined set of levels, you enter randomly chosen layouts and gain randomly chosen boons that power you up as you progress in hopes of being able to sustain progress; and it has some elements of making permanent progress in the form of persistent upgrades.That's where the similarity ends. Map layouts are not randomly generated, rather, there is a pool of premade and quite nicely designed maps for each tileset, and they all flow fantastically with nice, consistently designed encounters that remain challenging even as you learn what to expect. You don't get loot within the levels, but rather, there is a regular and guaranteed structure for boons, so you're not running the risk of being snubbed by RNG that just doesn't produce enough chests or whatever. Instead, you gain a steady flow of money from completing the levels, increased by maintaining the combo meter, and after a set amount of cleared levels, you enter a bar where you can buy drinks with the money you're guaranteed to have that confer passive and active boons. It ensures that you will generally always be able to get SOMETHING.If I had to compare this game to anything other than the obvious, it would be Smash TV for the NES. This game feels like a hyper-advanced take on that game, as a top-down shooter structured around clearing rooms.This game is, honestly, quite amazing and I think its quality should be upheld in its own regard rather than in comparison to anything else. The shooting is fun, and the guns are nice and well represented. It's a rare game that really does respect the danger a gun represents while also being able to make some guns feel more powerful. A pistol can typically down an enemy in two shots, but it will still feel comparatively weak next to other guns because of its ammo capacity and other traits. It's really smartly designed.The drinks system has a lot of fun flavor and is really tightly balanced, and it allows for a lot of build flexibility. There's great mixing and matching to be had. I love doing shotgun runs with El Cycle and High Roller in particular. If I had any criticism of the system, it's just that I wish rerolling the drinks was a bit cheaper, or increased in value slower.The art style is amazing. I can't really even go into detail other than to say it just looks nice and I don't mind that it rotates objects out of line with the pixel grid.The story and lore are vague, but not at all bad. The forefront is definitely the characters, they're all great.Highly recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I have five or so hours in this game as of right now, so might as well write this. OXTO is good. It's really good. It's basically a modern refinement of Hotline Miami as a roguelike, and I love every second of it. Although here's a hot take you might not be prepared for. I don't like Hotline Miami. It has nothing to deal with the violence of the game, because I've played much worse. Miami is about the violent nature of man and it captures it wonderfully, but playing the game itself is not great. Enemies with guns kill you at point blank, it's hard to see what's coming off screen, some encounters you have to cheese, and sometimes you get killed by stray bullets. Some of which are from off screen. Not very fun and the sequel is more frustrating. OTXO looks at this and makes Miami fun for people like me. You have a health bar now, but to compensate enemies come in bigger numbers and rooms are larger. However, you get more room to move around and it's much easier to tell where things are since enemies always have a distinct look and color. Guns come in a variety of flavors, can be picked up easily, and used easily. High accuracy, understandable quirks, and gorey damage. You have a focus ability to slow time down to a crawl and lay down bullets like Max Payne. Making stressful scenarios much easier and allowing for more strategical play. Your health refills when you get the score multiplier up and this encourages you to play fast and violent as possible. The game has a fantastic combat loop overall and I keep coming back to it for more. There are some flaws though. The bosses aren't very great and often find you pumping bullets away at a weak spot. The drinks, otherwise perks, you get during runs range from being really useful to "When would I ever waste coins on this?" The game has a really strange difficulty curve midway through each run, so sometimes you're doing really well and you get killed instantly. Yet, this is the fun of roguelikes. Going back in and doing better, so not much complaint. Oh yeah, I don't know if this game benefits from being a roguelike. On one hand it's really fun like I said. On the other tredging through that first area over and over again gets annoying especially when you mastered it, and I don't know if there's enough variety to give it endless hours of replay value. I haven't beaten the final boss yet, the furthest I've gotten is floor 20, and I wish the game would end soon. I do recommend OTXO, strongly. It's a modernized Hotline Miami and it even contains accessibility options for those who have visual disabilities and such. It's hard, but it is fun and rewarding. One of the hidden gems of 2023.

_childDocuments_.review: Very Very Good for what it is. Is it the next hotline miami? No. Is it worth the $15? In my opinion, yes. If you like the action of hotline miami and the game design of roguelites this is PERFECT.There are a lot of things to break down about the game design but overall I'd say many of the choices the designers made are clearly well-thoughtout and manage to take Hotline Miami's frantic combat while still making it playable as a Roguelite. The player has a proper healthbar, and its pretty generous, too. You can't really have a roguelite if you had Hotline Miami's "dying every 5 seconds" mechanic. It still manages to be extremely frantic as the Combo Meter directly increases the coins you get, which then helps the Roguelite aspect. Honestly it's impressive how the designer has broken fundamental staples of Hotline Miami and Roguelites and still managed to get the best of both worlds.Pro-tip: I don't know if the tutorial explained this, but you can Kick with both the Left Mouse Button AND the Middle Mouse Button. You can even middle click while holding a gun and you can kick without having to drop the weapon.

_childDocuments_.review: "OXTO" is an intense, adrenaline-fueled, twin-stick-shooter-roguelike with similar graphics and gameplay as "Hotline Miami", but with its own gorgeous style and the addition of bullet-time, dodgeroll and (a much needed) health bar.The visuals are viscerally noir, the soundtrack slaps you in the face just right, the story and lore of the mysterious entity manifesting as the mansion and the Sisyphus-like task at hand (which is a meta-comment for the genre) is told well and with a grain of existential dread.Unfortunately, the first area of the game can get old when you already did various runs and then it is very hard to die to the first boss, which seems a bit of a chore. Also some of the drinks (skills) seem superior to others, but these two complaints are just a minor setback.I still wholeheartedly recommend this for any fan of these genres or stylish games in general!

_childDocuments_.review: Rougelite Hotline Miami with some small yet smart changes from the admittedly very easy comparison. When only a few enemies remain, they are highlighted in the room to make finding the last stragglers far easier, making the search for those few guys you missed a lot less painful. All of the guns (I've seen so far) can be reloaded, allowing you to hold on to a favorite gun a bit longer at the cost of slowing your momentum by having to wait for the reload animation.The dodge roll can be used to traverse small pieces of furniture, making awkward room structure less of a hassle to traverse while allowing you to still avoid damage.You have a health bar, but the game feels like it's balanced around it accordingly. Enemies are more alert and can also take more than one shot before dying.If you're a HM purist then this all probably sounds like blasphemy, but for everyone else this is loads of fun. Oh, and the soundtrack absolutely slaps.

Due to the closeness, I'll be comparing this to Hotline Miami, so bare with me. In Hotline Miami, getting hit is usually able to be avoided easily, due to being able to understand what and how an enemy will move and do, but in OTXO is can often feel like they can hit you when they shouldn't. _childDocuments_.review: Okay so its basically Roguelite Hotline Miami. If you enjoyed Hotline you will very much enjoy this game.However keep the following in mind:This game is much more lenient. Where as Hotline Miami is one hit deaths where you need to have quick reaction time this is basically its adrenaline doping cousin. You can take hits. You can spray 'n pray your way through rooms. You can outright customize every weapon that can appear in runs which includes what enemies have (outside of a heavy sniper rifle which can always appear on certain enemies and you always start with a Garand)However this isn't exactly a copy. I'd say its more like... Lies of P compared to Bloodborne. Both are very very similar but have their own clear identity.Best way to describe it is both OTXO and Hotline Miami are games based on being quick, being efficient, and being ruthless. However Hotline is more reaction based while OTXO is more instinctual based. Honestly thats the best I can describe the differences between them.Hotline you can think out your strategy and use what is available to you. You ran the level before. You know the threats. You know the patrols. You pick your mask and go but be careful because death is always right there.OTXO is pick what you want going in then just... GO. Screw strategy outside of the drinks you pick. You can take hits and have slow motion powers. BARGE IN THAT ROOM WITH NO THOUGHTS AND JUST PULL THE TRIGGER ON YOUR GUN.To actually understand this gibberish from my weird mind you have to have played both.Also this games sound track, while not having as many tracks, goes just as hard at Hotline Miami.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't leave many reviews at all - As this is my first ever on a game like this. However, OTXO's OST caught my attention and I loved it. In my view, negative reviews that are mostly literal cope about the enemies from OTXO (Unless they're of course meant as a joke-review, then it's something different) usually indicate the lack of actual interest in improving their skills in the game. _childDocuments_.review: To be clear, this is NOT Hotline Miami 3. It has the same aesthetic and shares some features, but health bar, focus (slow motion mechanic) and liquors (gameplay modifiers) make HLM and OTXO feel completely different. But if you like both HLM and rouge-likes this is no brainer. Try this game. The music is great, tonn of guns, the gameplay changes slightly depending on what liqours you have purchased with your hard-earned money. Keeping your combo meter high is the key to fun and more gameplay possibilities and gimmicks. Each new stage features a new type of enemy, which is added to the general pool of enemies and gives your foes a new difficulty modifier. Mid and late bosses hit like a truck. _childDocuments_.review: I wish I like this more, but there's some fundamental issues that hold it back.First the positive: - The combat feels great, the guns are punchy and when things are flowing nicely it's easy to fall into the zone and cause chaos, and at the end you're left with the blood-splattered evidence of the carnage you created with a sense of pride. - The music is a perfect compliment to the chaos. While it might not have the same identity, variety and personality of the Hotline Miami OST, it does a great service to the mood of world and gameplay.However, I have a lot of problems that keep me from thinking this game lives up to it's potential.- While the  monochromatic aesthetic showcases the viscera perfectly, it also makes the enviroments very difficult to read, especially when you're in the moment and trying to keep up the momentum. I would frequently bump into furniture during tense firefights, particularly large rectangular objects that aren't immediately recognisable as a rug or a floor pattern, which breaks the flow and got me killed multiple times.- While the rogue-like structure might make the gameplay seemingly "infinite", it often makes levels feel carelessly structured and occasionally unfair. You will absolutely still find situations where the rooms and hallways are so large that you'll be shot by enemies you can't see even when you're looking in their direction. It also means that unlike Hotline Miami, there's no way to learn the levels through repeat attempts, so a bad seed and unfair level layouts will probably result in your death with nothing to learn from the experience.- While some liquors are interesting, many of them aren't impactful enough to make repeat runs feel interesting and distinct from each other, so if the base loop isn't enough to keep you interested, you'll be bored after a few runs and the slow progression of importing more liquors makes it feel like you need to grind your way out of the problem.- The bosses are uninspired, and can largely be defeated by just firing in their general direction while circling around the room.6/10. If Steam let me give a more middling recommendation I would, but I don't think my feelings on it are positive enough to give it a full endorsement.
_childDocuments_.name: OTXO

_childDocuments_.review: I came to this game as a Hotline Miami enjoyer looking for a longer, more gameplay focused experience. Ultimately, I don't think that's what this game is. It is something better.At first I thought the departure from HM's one hit kill system was to the game's detriment, but I have come to find it creates a completely unique gameplay loop that allows you to be a complete and utter maniac. Where in HM (especially in 2) every move needed to be carefully calculated because every misstep meant death, in OTXO you can sprint into a hail of bullets, send your own back in return and come out covered in blood, feeling like God's gift to the firearms industry.The best advice I can give someone who isn't immediately hooked by this game is: learn to play like a maniac. There should be no downtime. You should never be stopping. You should always be shooting.My only complaint is the boss fights. They are bullet spongey and are more reliant on knowing attack tells and safe strategies as opposed to the normal combat loop which is 100% off the cuff improv. Luckily they only show up every 6 rooms or so.This game is fantastic. You should play it.

AND THE MUSIC, the music speaks for itself even if you don't play the game the soundtrack is worth it on its own. While taking second place to the gameplay, the world and story are VERY intriguing, and there are still secrets in there to find. I can not recommend this game enough to anyone who likes high-octane action games or rouge-likes 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: If you want Hotline Miami experience, you probably won't get it here in the way you expect it.Pros:+ The gameplay is fun.+ The soundtrack is good.Cons:- The fun from the gameplay is completely overshadowed by the amount of repetition you're expected to do. You will die a lot, but this is not the issue - the problem is that you'll have to look at the same 2-3 rooms again, again and again. It got stale after the first 4 hours.- The repetition of the soundtrack due to you dying again, again and again will make you resent the music very fast.- The story is complete and utter garbage. I'd say that it's mediocre, but compared to similar games it's a beat up corpse.- The difficulty is absurd. This, by itself, would not be a problem if the game would respect player's time - but it doesn't. You don't get any checkpoints, and late game sections are difficult enough to where it's reasonable to assert that average casual player would not be able to complete them. Unlike some games of this type, OTXO does not provide you any difficulty-reducing accessibility options, aside from the "show enemy markers when X enemies are left" setting.OTXO aims to provide you "roguelike"/"roguelite" experience, while completely missing the point of Rogue and roguelikes in general. Roguelikes are popular, because they provide you a gigantic toolset to solve problems, and each run is often incomparable to the previous one due to their VAST amount of parts for procedural content generation. This, paired with the toolset the game provides, makes each run very distinct. This does not exist in OTXO, where, by the game's nature you have only two major mechanics - shooting and Focus ability. The drinks (enhancers) provide nowhere near enough replayability, because the game still feels almost completely the same, which is antithetical to the core of what a roguelike is. This leads to gaming experience, that does not feel rewarding in the slightest. if you fail in a roguelike then chances are that you failed to utilize the entirety of the toolset provided to you. You also don't need to be an expert in all mechanics of a roguelike to beat it. On the other hand, if you fail a run in OTXO, this is very likely because you haven't mastered the very limited toolset you've been provided, and you are expected to master it to actually beat the game.I wish I could recommend this game, I really do - I liked the gameplay a lot - but I just can't. It's not worth your time and effort if you actually intend to beat it.

_childDocuments_.review: Getting the comparison out of the way, I've held Hotline Miami (and Wrong Number) as some of my favorite indie games of all time for years. Naturally, with the retro-pixel top view gun-switching ultraviolent fast paced shooter action going here, this game had enormous shoes to fill. So my first few runs made me think "this is just fresh enough. Some good ideas, nice visuals... Yeah, this is good".And then I got into a boss battle with a giant mecha snake with machineguns. In my 4th run. And that was awesome. "Hotline Miami, this is not".So yeah, for anyone like me that might have been worried that this is "just bringing some decade old game with more modern considerations", I'm pleased to see that it differentiates itself positively and extremely early. With "bullet time" to slow down the massive amount of bullets on the screen, a fresh variety of enemies and bosses early on, and a generous healthbar that will likely deplete after strings of poor decisions and bad planning, each floor has a lot of adrenaline that doesn't reward "trial and error", but instead, planning how to approach each room.Yeah, planning is rewarded... but so is keeping a high combo multiplier to get more money to make your run better. So there's a lot of high-risk high-reward decisions at every moment. Play too safe and you won't be able to afford upgrades, yet play too reckless and you'll end up surrounded with no "bullet time" to even the odds.It's very good action, extremely fast paced, and while it can feel a bit clunky early on due to the unusual controls, waltzing in and painting this black and white mansion red is very gratifying.So yeah, recommended if you like fast paced action, punishing but fair gameplay, are okay with its violent themes, and if you like roguelikes in general.

_childDocuments_.review: It's Notline Miami.Perfect to get that fix of fast-paced, top-down ultraviolence if you've been itching for it, but without the narrative breaks or trippy story. What OTXO offers is a roguelike experience that boils the Hotline Miami formula down to its essence and packages it in distilled, short bursts of nonstop action. You get a combo meter that rewards you for killing enemies fast, pressuring you to keep pushing pushing pushing. Taking a breather means losing out on cash, which means less upgrades at your next pit stop. A thumping soundtrack that keeps urging you to move fast and be rough. It's amazing.The only thing I really consider a downside is the almost-greyscale artstyle. I understand it's a stylistic choice, but it does at times make things hard to distinguish from one another, allowing enemies or weapons to blend in with the environment, corpses or debris. Fairly minor complaint, though. This ♥♥♥♥ rules.

_childDocuments_.review: Huge fan of the gameplay, music and atmosphere. A small tip for new players, there's a firing range where you can test the DPS of different weapons. Significantly helped my experience.In conclusion, if you crave more of the Hotline Miami top-down shooter formula, OTXO's great as it not only recreates it, but actually pushes it further with interesting new mechanics. _childDocuments_.review: A part of me kinda feels that reviewing through comparison - in a way - does a disservice to the thing being compared. It's that anxiety that instead of judging something on its own merits, I "taint" my review of it by leaving a reference point in the reader's head......but what should I do when the game does not shy away from its influences at all?Indeed, if you've scrolled down to the review section, you probably will have seen that OTXO's store page mentions positive opinions comparing it to Hotline Miami. Hell, knowing the impact that HM had on the gaming industry, you probably didn't even need anyone to tell you that this is a similar game. But simply drawing the comparison doesn't really describe what makes OTXO stand out from its inspiration. And oh boy, there is  of stuff to go over – and unfortunately I myself will have to fall for that trap and talk for a bit about the other game as I discuss this one.Suffice to say, we are never getting another Hotline Miami game from its creators. Though Dennaton have struck gold with the gameplay formula of being a glass cannon and having your reflexes tested alongside your ability to strategize on the fly, the plot of the games never glorified that violence. Instead, the developers had made a point of portraying most of the main cast as pathetic creatures unleashing death and misery on the world for various selfish reasons, with violence itself leading only to a pitiful end for those who choose to take part in it.And even though the core message chastised the bloodshed, the series took the gaming world by storm because its rendition of violence in gameplay and presentation was . Divorced from the plot and the setting, Hotline Miami offered a  solid experience and a great challenge, with just about the only downside being its linear structure.And so it didn't take long for OTXO to figure out what the good parts were and how to iterate upon them.On a mechanical level, we're talking about another fast-paced top-down shooter which requires good reflexes from the player. However, the first immediate difference is the toolset available to the player. One of the major elements in OTXO's gameplay are the drinks. Every few floors you will run into a bar, whose bartender will sell you liquors which carry different effects. What sets them apart from HM's masks is the fact that you can (and likely will) take various different drinks during a run in order to stack their benefits. A liquor which makes killing enemies with SMGs yield more coins? Neat, let's mix that with a drink which makes you dual-wield one-handed guns – which, conveniently, includes SMGs. Add a few more just for variety and you'll build up a truly formidable otxo.Some of those drinks even interact with your Focus – another major mechanic. Much like Max Payne, you get the ability to slow down time. This allows you to correct positioning mistakes, react faster than your enemies, or even just get the buzz from seeing bullets cut through the air.Another tool is the dodge-roll, which was also present in Hotline Miami for some characters, but OTXO escalates it to a regular gameplay mechanic. Rather predictably, this lets you reposition and dodge some of the projectiles flying your way, but also vault over furniture such as tables and chairs, unlike HM's static props cutting off movement but letting damage through.All of this may sound like it's easy to become really powerful in this game. Make no mistake though, OTXO is no cakewalk. These tools are given to you because the enemies  do not forgive. As you proceed further through the Mansion, its guardian demons will have their own attributes augmented, perhaps most notoriously through shortening their already quick reaction times. Though the game gives you a health meter, letting yourself get caught off-guard and not checking your surroundings will probably cause the meter to deplete completely from an SMG-wielding enemy unloading an entire magazine into your back. And once you die – because you highly likely will, even with prior experience with the genre – you will wake up back at the Beach in front of the Mansion again, with a reminder that the only way to get out and break the cycle is to destroy the Heart of the building. On your way you'll be able to talk to the Nun, who will let you select which weapons will appear during the run as part of the enemy arsenal, or the Girl inside the bar, who handles liquor imports and expands the inventory of drinks that the Bartender may offer.In recent times I've discovered that I'm really fond of roguelite games – and here I found something that managed to scratch that exact itch that's been missing for all those years. Hotline Miami was already an excellent game, but OTXO looked at what worked, and decided to try to do it in its own style. The end result is a remarkable experience, lined by a distinct "red-accented monochrome" artstyle and a truly vicious soundtrack (composed by the one-man studio behind the game! Yes, all of this was made by one person!). HM made me aware of many different artists and introduced me to some really energetic tracks that I still enjoy and listen to even outside of the game – but the soundtrack to OTXO, by the virtue of having one composer for all of its soundtrack instead of licensing different tracks not originally made for the game, feels a lot more cohesive, collected, and concise. And . ( is easily the most violent and vicious track I've heard in , perfectly fitting the high octane bloodbath – and it's not even a boss theme or anything, Despite all of these comparisons to Hotline Miami and the amount of times it's been mentioned in this review, I feel like out of respect for both of these IPs I cannot say that one is flat out better than the other. What I  say, though, is that OTXO – despite being iterative upon concepts we've already seen – manages to stand for itself and carve out its own identity. My very first session in the game, despite me having gotten my butt handed back to me multiple times, had me feeling like I, too, was becoming a prisoner of the Mansion. There was that urge to go for one more run, be the star of another action movie shootout sequence, push onward and conquer the Mansion.And if a game manages to make me crave more  from , I feel like it more than deserves a positive review from me.

_childDocuments_.review: The nature of hotline miami is that it's interesting puzzles/setpieces that are set up in a progression that is satisfying.  I have found games like Hong Kong Massacre to be enjoyable in the same vein, and the addition of things like bullet time are nice in those various games.  I seem to recall Katana Zero did the same, but in a sidescroller format, and I also liked My Friend Pedro, but not quite as much as the ones noted above.I get what this game is trying to do, but it doesn't really use space in interesting ways early on, and given the roguelike nature of it, I wouldn't expect that to change.  It's a good chance that if you just absolutely want more Hotline Miami combat, and you're cool with enemies and  yourself tanking damage more, then this is for you.  It's possible I will come back to this at some point in the future, but in the short term it was asking me do master some controls that felt a bit awkward at first, and not really giving me the same "sense of place" or theme that the other games above have.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, this is really fun for a small sized little Hotline Miami-esque shooter. The gunplay is very fun and engaging and keeps you on your toes. Soundtrack is fantastic, and the sound design is meaty and each gun has a unique feeling of oomph to it. The arsenal in this game has a fine mix of both classic and modern weaponry, ranging from a G36C to an ANM2 Stinger machine gun, and to a damn Blunderbuss. You start off with a small handful of weapons that you can toy with before discovering ways to unlock more as you go. You also have a companion in the game who alters what weapons both you and the enemy can use, which you can use to your advantage. The AI is very smart and differ from Hotline Miami greatly, as you need to either make enough noise to hear them or simply be in front of them, allowing for perfect stealth opportunities. The enemies also get a different and completely random "attribute" for every major area of the Mansion you progress through (think stuff like faster movement, faster reaction time, faster fire rate, etc). The art style of this game is also quite unique although a bit dull on the eyes since its all black, white, and red. This game might be up your alley if you liked Hotline Miami. It isn't a 1:1 clone, but it certainly replicates some aspects well while giving a unique twist to the original formula.

_childDocuments_.review: Lobotomized Hotline Miami.OTXO feels like a game that overcomplicates itself from its source material and misses the points that made the Hotline Miami games enjoyable while not committing fully to its roguelike design, resulting in a confused game that lacks cohesion.The music is great and the game has some nice fancy visual effects. The particles, the environmental debris, the lighting, the shadows, and the ragdoll physics all add a lot to the game's feel and visual feedback. Unfortunately, I can't say the same for the overall presentation. The monochrome visuals resulted in a very dull and samey-looking environment, which was a lot of the appeal I felt with Hotline Miami where each level had a distinct color palette that made them immediately recognizable even beyond the level design. Not to mention visual clarity is also lessened as the white bullets just blend in more with the monochrome backgrounds.The problem also extends beyond the presentation, as the procedural generation of the levels despite the handcrafted rooms just results in everything feeling uniform and derivative. It's usually just a bunch of rooms on the left side and right side of the map, and a big open hallway in the middle. This also doesn't flow very well and clashes with some of the more enjoyable aspects of Hotline Miami, which is to try and fully combo the entire level as you figure out the best pathway in getting through the enemies in succession. The whole scoring aspect is pretty much gimped too. You do still want to keep up high combos for the coins so you can get more abilities, but with the way things work, it's more reliant on having a lucky seed of RNG rather than mastery of the levels and mechanics. Outside this, it's a lot less exciting and inconsistent to score, which again is a shame since I felt this is one of Hotline Miami's main sources of fun.Then we get to one of the biggest offenders which is the whole health system. I feel a lot of the flow and intensity of Hotline Miami came from the almost-always-one-hit-kill system. OXTO opting for varying damage and health makes sense for a roguelike, but it still clashes a lot with the overall feeling of the combat which undeniably does still take a lot from Hotline Miami. All the guns sound fantastic and punchy, but it's such a disconnect when they take 2 to 3 hits to kill someone, and there's a lot less feeling of danger when your character also can tank bullets for the most part. Some weapons can one-hit kill, which extends to the fact that the game ultimately even contradicts itself with the mechanic that allows you to remove weapons from rotation, and only select the ones you want. Thus you have the option of keeping only the weapons that can one-hit kill and negating the whole damage system in the first place.The roguelike design overall just doesn't work with Hotline Miami's style, since another large part of what made Hotline Miami work is the quick inconsequential punishment of death where you can just instantly restart, and learn the level like a time-based puzzle where memorization and then execution comes into play. In OTXO, when you die you start from the beginning, and you're more reliant on getting good RNG with abilities that can help you or layouts that aren't too much of a mess. I did finish this game thrice, with a run that didn't involve using abilities, but most of it devolved into abusing mechanics like the bullet time and dodge rolls. Especially as you get further into a run where all the enemies have different modifiers and they all get stacked haphazardly with no real design in mind how they placed.This then extends to the other poorly thought-out element, which is the boss fights. They're neat on paper, but poor in execution. Except for one samurai-themed boss, most of it comes down to spamming the dodge roll and waiting for your bullet time to cool down, while avoiding the same three or four attack patterns over and over again because the bosses are bullet sponges.There's an unlockable 'Impossible Mode' that makes it feel closer to the original Hotline Miami games, with damage raised across the board, which translates to all guns pretty much being one-hit kills and survivable by two to three through lucky shaves. I wish the game was designed with this mode in mind as it resolves the bullet sponge problem with the bosses and retains the fast exciting pace of Hotline Miami. The rest of the problems are still here, but this is where I had most of my enjoyment. I feel like this game would have been better overall if it's just a linear campaign with a dozen levels or so with an upgrade system slapped onto it. There are some neat elements with the systems here, but they just don't work well together. As a Hotline Miami clone, it lacks a lot of the original game's flow and intensity. As a roguelike, it lacks a lot of the extra systems and mechanics most roguelike games have, including permanent upgrades. Outside some modifiers and the ability to unlock guns and select which of them spawn during a run, there's little progression within the systems themselves.If you're itching for a top-down shooter with some roguelike elements and a Hotline Miami flavoring, and you're willing to look past the shortcomings, this game is mostly fine. But if you just want more Hotline Miami in general, there's a whole bunch of well-made and creative campaigns, levels, and mods out there in the modding scene, even in HM2's Workshop alone. Not to mention the massive overhaul packs and standalone projects. And if you want a roguelike in general, there is a whole sea of them nowadays that also pretty much does a lot of its dedicated systems better.Also, OTXO's a stoopid name.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a decently fun game but I can't recommend it. It is locked to 60FPS, so moving the camera around feels a little juddery if you are used to playing games at high refresh rates. The enemy AI is very primitive. If they see you, they start blasting or navigating around the level geometry like Pac-Man ghosts. I fundamentally don't like how your weapon inventory is handled, either. Basically you pick up dead enemies' weapons and they come with 1 extra mag. Kill more enemies, take their weapons. You can't just go in with your favorite gun and keep it the whole level. What this means is that you'll often be using guns you don't want. Later in the game, you can meet a nun character to limit the weapons the enemies spawn in with, which effectively limits the weapons you can use, but having it be two-sided like this is not fun. For example, on a recent playthrough I limited the weapons to JUST the 9MM pistol. I got very far in my run because the enemies also use the pistol and it does bad damage compared to other weapons and isn't as accurate long range. Let's say you want to use an LMG or a shotgun on your playthrough... all the enemies will spawn in with these weapons and they will mow you down very quickly.You can get upgrades from a bartender but they only last as long as your given session - I would have much preferred some sort of system where once you bought a perk it was always in your inventory and you could just roll with a set of like 3-5 of them. Also, many of the bartender upgrades aren't really upgrades. They're more like sidegrades or weird game modifiers.And then of course, there's the artstyle. It's black and white and very basic. Finding fallen weapons can sometimes be a bit difficult because of the lack of color contrast. And while the game's style works for what it is, I quickly found it boring.Conceptually, the game is good. And for the most part shooting feels alright. But I feel like the developer fumbled the ball with some obtuse design decisions. And the caveman-level AI ultimately makes the game feel sort of cheap as opposed to intelligently challenging.As far as top down shooters on Steam go, you could do worse. But it is annoying knowing how good this game could be with a few different tweaks - uncapped framerate, more color in the art style, more interesting long-term progression, smarter AI, etc. As it stands I can't give OTXO more than a 6/10.

Most of the upgrades (drinks) feel underwhelming, some are simply useless- it doesn't feel like there is even remotely as much synergy as I wish there would be, most upgrades are boring and only directly or indirectly buff your DPS, Durability, Speed, Focus, etc.  It has some rogueLITE mechanics where you can progress in between runs, but it requires you to spend the currency you need to buy upgrades during the run- so you're essentially forced to hinder your current run or ignore long term progression.Honestly, it's worth your time if you've already played and gotten bored of all the other Roguelikes, Hotline Miamis, Katana Zero, and all the good games like them. _childDocuments_.review: OTXO has two sides to it, the first is the actual gameplay, where you go around shooting enemies and cycle your guns to always have ammo, which i must say is fun, altough is very much lacking depth, the game plays the same 1 minutes in as it does 30 minutes into a run, no matter the unlocks you have. There is also a insentive to play agressivly and stylishly with the combo meeter that duplicates all the coin enemies drop, unfortunetly the way to stylishly kill enemies is limited both in variance, and in opertunities. I think kicking down a door to kill someone may increase your combo more than shooting them, but if it is, the amount of extra combo opertunities is enterely up to enemies choosing to stand close to doors, and the reward for doing so is miniscule (which is why i am unsure style is even a factor, cause i haven't noticed much of a reward). Instead the combo meter is best used by chaining togheter kill, this in combination to semi random layouts means that the skill of keeping the combo is not to play agressivly, but to not miss enemies to keep the combo going, and that hide and seek like minigame does not really play into the power fantasy the game is trying to sell.The other side to the game is the economy, you collect coins by killing enemies and keeping your combo up, the rate at which you get coin can also be affected by perks you buy with said coin, however perks are random so it is all up to luck of wether you can stack enough economy boosting perks early in the game to have a significant advantage late in the game (over those runs where all your perks are combat focused).Furthermore coins are also used to unlock things, so the player has to choose between runs they intend to win, and grinding unlocks while falling behind in power due to the lack of perks. Even worse, the system where you unlock perks functions as a bank, where coin you put into it saves between runs, and once you fill up the investment you get that perk for "free". This encurages a strategy where you invest into these new perks untill you get 99% there, stopping just before you unlock it. Then next run you can get the perk for a pittance by paying for the last 1%, functionally giving you up to 3 almost free perks, this strategy works untill you have bought all of the unlockable perks, making them the most usefull as almost unlocked.If anything i can see why other rouglikes often choose conditional unlocks (do A, unlock B), and/or have a separete currency to actually unlock things, that only can be spent between runs (so no freebies). Since nither of those solutions undermine the actual goal of winning. The solution of some perks boosting your economy is often in a lot of rouglikes offset by giving you free stuff (item rooms in isaac), or just making it so that more damage = more kills = more coins (think risk of rain 2), instead of hard limiting the amount of enemes, and thus coins, in run progression.Soundtrack is a banger tho.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game, but I figured out how to cheese the game early on, and it's not fun anymore. The other problem is even if I don't do the cheese, the shooting mechanics just aren't that fun to me. The main problem is with the slow motion ability, and how the rooms are sectioned off pretty distinctly. So basically I hit slow-mo, then immediately kick the door in, kill everyone in the room, deactivate slow-mo, wait for it to recharge, rinse and repeat. Some rooms are shaped in ways that make this a little more interesting, but almost every situation seems to be pretty much the same, just taking everyone out as soon as possible. In larger rooms this mechanic still plays out, but you are instead just using obstacles to get your slow-mo meter back to do a quick trigger of the slow-mo as you or the enemy comes around a corner and comes into view, kill them real fast, then disable the slow-mo before it eats too much of the meter up, rinse and repeat until the room is fully cleared. Sure you don't have to play this way, but with how fast the enemy responds it really does feel the game is designed to be played this way, at least to some extent. I feel like if enemies next to the doors leading to nearby rooms were alerted, that might make this game a lot more interesting.As far as every other aspect, like the story, the awesome roguelike type upgrade systems, and overall feel of the game is excellent. But unfortunately I just can't remain interested, even with the cool bosses they throw at you.

_childDocuments_.review: A less melee and tactics focused Hotline Miami with some roguelike elements that gives you a quick to recharge slow motion toggle and dodge move to fight quick reacting enemies.Your characters puts on a mask and suddenly finds themself washed up on a beach near a mansion where he is told he can't leave or die and that he needs to fight his way to the deeper part of the mansion to destroy the heart. You will fight through rooms where you will need to kill all enemies to proceed. To do that you pick up, shoot, reload, and throw guns at enemies, kick enemies and doors with doors near enemies being able to kill them, toggle on slow motion, and perform a dive move that can avoid bullets. The base mechanics are fine but I don't enjoy the enemies that take multiple hits to kill and your own large health bar. Mostly all your trying to avoid doing is destroy too many doors or glass windows that can lead to larger groups of enemies engaging you or sneaking up on you, as long as you don't break open a door or window enemies are unable to get through them.Every three areas and in the first area of a new run is a bar where you can spend coins (first one of the run is free) that you get from killing enemies and maintaining a high combo for higher rewards on different types of alcohol that give you passive bonuses. The abilities you can gain from the bars might do something like allowing you to do more damage when stationary, reload faster, recharge your slow motion ability faster or they can give more targeted buffs to certain types of weapons or give you abilities that allow for unique playstyles like allowing you to block bullets, gain a kunai if you roll while holding no weapon, transform kunai into a throwing axe that you can summon back to you, etc. As the bars are limited to only three kinds of drinks unless you spend even more to restock you could easily thing that your likely to be stuck with completely useless or contradictory things for your runs most of the time but one of the only positives I can give the game is that if you get to a bar and choose to save and go back to the main menu and then reload it will change the drink menu, actually allowing you to pick up skills that might make the game more fun or interesting for you, if you don't mind rerolling drinks as many times as needed.The available weapons can also be changed up by toggling what guns are available or not in your next run which also means it effects what weapons enemies will use. Trying to do an all pistol or sniper rifle run might be fun but you do have to keep in mind that doing so might make boss fights much more difficult. Once you get through six stages you will fight a boss before moving to another area with six stages and a boss, the new area might introduce a new enemy or give enemies a bonus like having extra armor. Every boss is a tedious bullet sponge with a small number of attacks that become easy to predict over time, while the main enemies aren't as much fun as they lack the more visceral nature of the kills of your opponents in something like Hotline Miami or even other slow motion using top down games like The Hong Kong Massacre, these bosses have no reaction to being shot at all and are some of the worst bosses I've seen in a genre like this.Fighting the main enemies is ok but not as much fun as similar games I've played in this style. The bosses are terrible. I personally hate the music. A lot of the guns and abilities just aren't that fun to use. You can, in an inefficient way, tailor a run to work more in a way you find interesting which seems more like an unintentional feature or engine issue (like not being able to use the mouse on menus, not being able to save Steam screenshots, not being able to change the mouse sensitivity that are related to the game engine) as it certainly isn't something the game tells you. If you don't reload for abilities you end up with frequent terrible choices that can have either nothing to do with your playstyle or you might want to play in a certain way but it requires having multiple abilities together that can take too long to find otherwise. There also just isn't that much content and what there is it pretty much wants you to do all of in one run, by the time I was done I didn't even have anything practical left to buy as an upgrade and the logical endpoint of the run should have come around three sets of stages prior.Screenshots:

_childDocuments_.review: There's a good game hiding here, but you wont find it at the time of this review.--- 3/5OTXO is a game of high potential and with beautiful presentation, hamstrung by misguided design decisions. Fans of Hotline Miami and other fast-paced top-down shooters will find some entertainment here, but OTXO is no memorable experience and unlike its stronger companions, playing it again and again requires the willpower to do so, rather than its systems seducing you into "just one more run".--- 5/5OTXO has a very strong stylized black-and-white-and-red presentation, chunky gun sounds and excellent music. I have nothing bad to say about how great the game presents itself, and it's wonderful to see the effects of your gunshots blow up every imaginable debris possible within the mansion.--- 2/5OTXO suffers from a story which wants to be interesting and mysterious but fails to be neither by overexplaining concepts, characters that are flat and bad dialogue. Intentional obscurity, and characters that push that fact in your face doesn't serve to create interest in the player - rather it feels snobbish and I care little for the story.The background story serves its purpose, and I must admit that I was initially intrigued, until the first character emitted a waterfall of cliché dialogue. There is mystery to be evoked from the beach and the mansion, but the characters must support this mystery and must speak more like real entities living here, instead of strange pseudo gameplay devices too eager to tell the player how lost and mystified they should be.While I wasn't very entertained by the narrative, I do admit that it is wholly unimportant to the experience, and a good narrative would only be sprinkles on top.--- 2/5Giving the gameplay of OTXO a bad score hurts a lot. It is so obvious that the developers have spend tremendous effort to make the gameplay loop as smooth and entertaining as possible, and indeed it is, but the problem lies in the 'meta' roguelike aspects of the game.Upgrades are so abysmally tiny that they feel absolutely horrendous to pick up. 20% extra coins if I kill an enemy while standing still? Slightly increased chance to deal damage to nearby enemies when a foe is dropped? These upgrades are so incredibly boring I started skipping the bar entirely towards my later runs. It's a roguelike! Give the player something fun every time they play, something that lets them change the way they play and actually feel powerful! It's okay, they'll lose it all as soon as they die, and if it makes the game too easy simply put in more enemies!Examples for drinks that would actually be interesting could be "Standing still gives double damage" or "First bullet can penetrate doors", "Killing an enemy gives 50% increased movement speed for 3 seconds", "Holding the trigger down ramps up damage", "Rolling into enemies knocks them down"The combo meter is also good, but falls just short of excellent. Racking up a large combo is awesome, it was awesome in Hotline Miami and it's only better in OTXO since you are rewarded coins for it. But why limit it arbitrarily then? Let it freeze when you complete level instead of resetting your combo between each level. Let skilled players rack up gigantic combos if they are able, racking up 7x, 8x, 9x as they smash through levels keeping up their combos.My last great point of contention is the fact that every boss is the same. It seems you must fight the snake guy first every single time, and the same enemies up until that point. A player will go through that boss every single time they play the game - variety is badly warranted, and it becomes daunting to start a new run, knowing that you'll be treading the exact same steps as before,  considering how your upgrades are going to be as useless again.I would like to say that I appreciated the gun nun, and choosing how you wanted to form your opponents/weapons through this mechanic is excellent.

_childDocuments_.review: It's decent, but feels very light on content and thus replayability.
