_childDocuments_.review: Updated Review:This game is fun, and I generally hate this sub-genre. I decided to give it a try and am going to allow an exception in this case and say I love this game.One piece of advice is to check your marines traits to see what they are inclined towards, since these are unique rolls to each character. After playing through the tutorial once I now disable the tutorial and restart the campaign until I get at least 1 marine I like. In my case I re-rolled an Interceptor with Omnissah's Chosen which will allow me to fully min-max this character, even more important since I'm playing my entire team around having a pimped out melee Interceptor. I'm planning to roll augmetics as many times as possible since he will double their effect. For your opening build I suggest either 3 Judiciar 1 Interceptor with maxed WP on the Judiciars for Honour the Chapter to feed into the Interceptor. OR you can go 2 Judiciar and 1 Apothecary with the Interceptor. The apothecary is only there for Iron Arm to buff the stun on the interceptor so you can chain executes. 3 Judiciar is more of a 'sure thing' but the Apothecary addition is more fun in my opinion. You can sub out a Judiciar for either a Chaplain or Librarian later; both have their merits with Chaplain improving the rewards for Executes, and Librarian making it easier to execute with a very good aoe stun spell.For some reason, I haven't had a game hang since I started playing with Grandmaster mode (this game's name for Ironman/ forced auto save only) disabled, which is weird, unless they have since patched it.The game is fun and I haven't had another campaign ending bug and am now on my second campaign. I decided to restart on Legendary since I felt I had learned enough on my first attempt on normal to do it properly. The game is pretty brutal but I found normal to be waaaay too easy. The AI in this game is pretty bad so the only way it's going to challenge you at all is if they have such insane overwhelming numbers that they can walk into you and eventually kill you if you don't play well.On Legendary, you're often fighting 15+ enemies which at least means you get punished for every misplay.Original review below:Fun game, would thumbs it up but for some reason, like many games in this sub-genre, it has issues where the game gets hung during the enemy turn. Basically every Turn Based Tactical RPG I've played had this problem, not sure why Developers can't figure this issue out.For me, the game got stuck on the third mission but my friend was like 15 hours deep before it happened to him. We are both playing on Ironman mode (autosave only) so this means our campaigns are ruined. My game got permanently frozen when the Cultists were revived.Game is good but you must be able to save scum to avoid this bug ending your campaign.

_childDocuments_.review: Going to give this a reluctant thumbs down. Here's why:1) Abysmal UI. The worst kind of UI - obfuscates important information, doesn't display other important information, makes it easy to mis-identify and mis-click units, draws needless attention to itself rather than translating in-game action. The skill trees are some of the worst I've ever seen. Sub-menus within sub-menus with no quick way to navigate.2) Terrible balance issues. Your Grey Knights - some of the most elite fighters of the most elite units in the Imperium - are outgunned and outclassed by a bunch of scrub chaos cultists. Who the hell knows what happened to Storm Bolters and Power Armour. They are garbage. The grunt units have (a) better weapons, (b) more range, (c) more reinforcements and (d) better armor and/or more health (sometimes both) than your supposedly amazing Knights. You'll enjoy spending turn-after-turn cowering behind loading docks avoiding simple enemies. Overwatch is garbage because you have to deal with (a) critically limited range; (b) limited action points; (c) limited ammo.3) Limited tactical possibilities. You will face a near endless stream of warping-in enemies that will constantly arrive behind, infront, to the sides, etc. Its impossible to predict where they will be and (a) when they do arrive they all get free movement to move into cover and go on overwatch. Your weapons won't have the range to take them out, so you very often need to get in close in H2H - which will then trigger the other enemies lying in reserve just beyond initial mouse range. Every battle after the first 2-3 becomes a grueling slog.4) Wound time is a joke. Take 6 damage. Wait 49 days to get better. Oh, bloom happens every 10-12 days it seems.5) Random events to kick you while you are down with no explanation of repercussions. I had no idea what making some choices in the campaign would entail - only to get locked with no ship movement for 30 days while bloom increases. Fun.Overall, I love the 40K setting but this game feels terrribly unpolished. It has potential but if I was you I'd wait (a) for mods or cheats to solve some of the annoying issues or (b) get it on sale and enjoy it for what it is before inevitable frustration sets in.

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to like this game, and there are things to like, especially the combat. TLDR, it's AP based and you can regain AP from executing enemies/abilities, so you can wipe whole enemy squads in one turn. Once you master that system, then the game doesn't pose much of a challenge. It's very similar to Gears Tactics in terms of how it plays. The real issue with it is that lack of mission variety and limited enemy variety. It trips up the entire core game play loop and fatigue sets in pretty quickly. You quickly realize you're just playing the 2 mission types(3rd added later on) against the same enemy pods across 4 to 5 maps. The UI is terrible, moving around the ship or equipping your knights takes far too many clicks. There's a good game buried here, but it really needs polishing up.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is as flawed as a game as you can get. I am a great fan of tactical turn based games (XCOM, UFO series, Mechanicus etc) and am a giant 40k nerd so, in theory atleast,  I should be overjoyed playing this game as it strives to combine 2 of my favorite things. It does do that to some degree but what it fails utterly at is being a fun game. Having finished the campaign, I promptly uninstalled it and will not touch it again, barring a major rework or such. The base tactical game is fun and engaging enough and the builds and classes are all varied, or atleast they were until the devs decided to nerf alot of the possible builds into oblivion. These heavyhanded and shortsighted approaches do not bode well for the future of this game. The final mission is the pinnacle of uninspired game design - repetitive, bland, filled with artificial challenge and gotcha moments, a pure reflection of the game in its entirety.To conclude, I am writing this not out of spite, but rather dissapointment in seeing a potential great game ruined by bizzare design decisions and balancing. It is as if the developers are devotees of Slaanesh and derive pleasure from the suffering they inflict on their player base.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first review I have ever posted and I leave it here because I am disappointed by the patch the developers dropped (in the very first week of the game) for a single-player game to "balance" it. Holding off on the what the balances consisted of for now, the major issue with it technically is that it broke my saved files. I was on day 673 before the patch, afterwards I was forced to return to day 500-odd as it was the only old save that worked. Annoyed is an understatement as it meant I had to grind through all of the same missions again and hope I picked up some decent gear in the mission rewards lottery. The game is a slog, the steep learning curve over the first 20 hours of play left me thinking "surely, its going to get better. Surely, I will unlock some decent strats and combo's and be able to make good progression". And you do, it was absolutely rewarding levelling up my knights in the mid-game and combining them together to maximise efficiency. And trust me, you will want to do this too, as it is otherwise quite boring and repetitive. The "balance" consisted of nerfing some combinations that did actually work to improve efficiency and making already weak classes even weaker rather than adding new combinations that could have allowed for different strategies. Not only did they do this but they also do not allow you to re-spec your current squad meaning that all the time invested in leveling them up is wasted. I requested a refund and was denied. The patch destroyed what I thought was an entertaining and otherwise well executed game and has made it more boring and tedious. Would not recommend in this state at all. Do not buy

_childDocuments_.review: This is... an incredible game. I want to just tell you a story of my last mission. It is a typical go in and grab the *REDACTED SPOILERS* and get out. We get the first item, my terminators loping forward soaking up the damage whilst my purgators melt the enemy in a hail of fire. My glorious deed of killing 8 enemies with ranged fire ticked off quickly. I kill a second patrol and damage begins to rack up, I regret the lack of apothecary and only bringing two servo skulls. The final group is revealed and I audibly groan as the enemy space marines are revealed. I start trying to figure out my strategy. As soon as I grab that last item the item's protectors will warp in, using overlapping fields of disruptive fire my terminators take out the item carriers buddies. Just then the warp surges, reinforcements. Bugger. Okay new plan, we whack the last guy. This triggers the reinforcing parties for the hold out. 2 groups of space marines to add to the horde of pox walkers. Crap crap crap. I realise the map is quite long, maybe we could... you know run away? So my terminators break towards my purgators who manage to keep the enemies just far enough away to do any major damage. The minute, and I mean the minute, I turn the corner at the top my terminators come face to face with another bloody patrol... They carve into the enemy but one terminator goes down severely injured. Behind them the purgators both fall to superior numbers. Its' down to Thule! He smashed aside some pox walkers and dashes into heavy cover with enough ap to cast aegis shield (fun fact I had actually forgotten about this ability but I digress). A hell storm of fires pounds into him and his cover leaving him a slice of health, as my turn begins... *EXTRACTION BEGINNING COMMANDER STAND BY* I let out a breath i didn't know I was holding.If you wanted to know what it would be like to command a force of psychic space commandos fighting galactic black mould look no further! There is crew management and a base to manage with limited resources, every loss hurts and every serious injury compromises your ability to succeed. This game is ROCK HARD and I love it! Obviously there are easier settings so you do you! It really is a sensational game that rewards the risk taking, I mean I could have played with iron man off but where's the fun in that now?? The graphics are very pretty with some occasional performance loss but look for that to be patched out ASAP. THE EMPEROR HATES INDOLENCE BROTHERS, LET US NOT DISAPPOINT HIM!

_childDocuments_.review: it´s fun , I like it. Similar to x-com , gride based squads, an "overworld" map where you float around in your ship deciding what missions to do,what to research yadda yadda. But ofc it´s warhammer 40 so all the characters look and sound really cool.So far there has not been an very large enemy variety but it´s still fun as new types show up ever so often and I see some new abilities of , at least new mixes of old stuff often enough to keep me entertained. Ofc the guys you play as get new stuff all the time so there is enough depth here IMO.Also a bit of variety between mission difficulty is nice, sometimes I have a couple of fairly easy missions then I get one where I really need to think about how to proceed or I end up swamped in enemies and it can snowball fast.How all your abilities work together to form the combat and you managing your "resources" (limited number of grenades, whatever it´s called that let´s you use abilities, it functions like mana you loose it when you use an ability and get some back when you kill things, servitors ( robot skulls that can do various things ) etc got enough moving parts , it´s fun.There´s a "bloom" meter that fills every turn and using certain abilities makes it fill faster and some enemies can make it fill faster as well, when it hits 100 bad things happen, like extra enemies get teleported in, you get debuffed, enemies get buffed etc,it can do this several times per mission. At first I felt stressed by it like I was supposed to rush things to keep it from "blooming" but after a few hours playing it clicked with me how it plays into the mission dynamics and the random stuff (it´s not really random as there´s a limited list of things that can happen) adds to the mission dynamics and it´s fun having to roll with whatever comes up. Storyline and characters is also well done and I really get into being the commander of a group of grey knights on a mission. Really hope to see more of this  .  Hope the devs make more games with the same basic mechanics but other hero/enemy factions and so on. Lastly it´s got a few bugs, so far mainly some fps hanging around 40 even though I had both gpu and cpu headroom. And some minor issues during missions but nothing a save/reload didn´t fix so no progress lost.Load times are good on a ssd.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish there was a meh or ok rating. The core issue is Warhammer 40k itself. It's nearly impossible to have a good plot and story line in Warhammer 40k when there's no real hope.It gets repetitive. _childDocuments_.review: + Grey Knights vs Nurgle minions+ Squad customization+ Boss fightsMasterfully crafted Warhammer entry for sons of Titan. Chaos Gate is turn-based tactics set in Warhammer 40,000 universe which puts Grey Knights' finest against Nurgle minions.Game is played on galactic map where your ship (Baleful Edict) moves between missions and encounters.Your ship serves as base of operations and can be fully upgraded but also maintained if it's damaged during the game. There you can talk with your companions, research new stratagems or mission leads and customize your squad. When time passes, random events occur which can bring both positive and negative effects depending on how you handle them.Beginning of the game is quite challenging but once you unlock new classes, level up and upgrade your squad and ship, you can play at your leisure.I would point out two things and that is great tactical combat and squad customization. There are all known Grey Knights classes (Justicar, Interceptor, Purgator, Paladin, Chaplain etc) from Warhammer game and you can fully customize them with appropriate weapons and equipment. If you actually play Grey Knights faction you'll be very happy with level of customization.In combat, you deploy squad of four and fulfil different objectives. Only downside is that these objectives get pretty repetetive. Occasionally, you get boss fight where the final one is trully epic. Environment is quite destructible and you can even use it against your enemies. Once you find your ideal squad composition it's real joy to kick Nurgle's ass.

_childDocuments_.review: I tried to enjoy the game. I really did. After around 30 hours I posted a negative review, but then removed it and gave the game another chance. Kept pushing.A terrible disappointment.The first 10-15 hours feels good and rewarding. Sometimes it's challenging and I almost lost a grey knight, but you know, I play on normal difficulty, so it's fine.After around 15 hours, after discovering more seed types, the game became unbearable and unplayable.To make things clear:Space Marines are "foremost amongst the defenders of Humanity, the greatest of the Emperor of Mankind's warriors. The are barely Human at all, but superhuman: having been made superior in all respects to a normal man by a harsh regime of genetic modification, psycho-conditioning and rigorous training.Power Armor of a Space Marine "integrates with him. It can take many solar decades to forge a single suit of power armour, and each is maintained with absolute care and devotion by skilled Chapter serfs or even the Space Marines themselves. Each suit is a unique artefact with a spirit and history deeply valued by its Chapter."And finally, "The Grey Knights are a secret and mysterious Chapter of Space Marines specifically tasked with combating the dangerous Daemonic entities of the Warp and all those mortals who wield the corrupt power of the Chaos Gods. [...] They have the honour of being implanted with gene-seed engineered directly from the genome of the Emperor Himself."Traitor Guardsmen - "These traitors, unlike other mutants and other vile Beastmen, have not completely lost their military skills or sanity, forming a reasonably reliable core force amongst the slavering hordes of the Lost and Damned armies."In this game:Grey Knight in Power Armor - 0 armor, bolter deals around 4 damageTraitor Guardsman - 0 armor, bolter deals around 3-4 damage.You have 4 Grey Knights.When the game difficulty peaks, you fight around 8 squads of enemies, out of which a squad of 4 guardsmen is the easiest.Guardsmen get repetitive mutations. For example each guardsmen gets 5 armor, resurrection, +4 hp, etc. A friendly reminder - Power armor gives 0 armor. Terminator armor gives 2 armor (the starting ones, later on you could get 3, maybe 4).Other Nurgle units get 11+ armor (it stopped showing armor icons, just a number...)I understand you want to make the game challenging, but I don't have time to sweat over that completely losing the feeling of Grey Knights - my beloved Chapter.A strong negative. Shame.I will drink a glass of piss, change the difficulty to the easiest and just watch the story.

_childDocuments_.review: Look, its just not polished, in a few ways.It lacks the theme-ing that all good WH40k games have. It  like a mobile game, in the way it plays, the cut-scenes, the dialogue..... Even the font is just... lacklustre. A little more attention to detail and it could be there. The bones of a story are there, but the dialogue is pretty uninspired, and the pacing is all wrong, so the lack of polish stands out far more than it should. Honestly, if there were some well voiced and animated cutscenes to tie all the goings-on together, it would have rounded out the experience far more.The gameplay is surely XCOM, but that all it is. Its not enough to draw you in, and make you feel like you are playing a 40k game. I honestly had a better XCOM-like experience with Mechanicus. At least that felt like a game unto itself. This has no originality, right down the the little cut-scenes when you discover the enemy. Its all the same. It doesn't  right in the way the matches flow. There's no impact to anything you do. Just the same old zoom-in-for-a-kill-shot deal. Just a itty bitty bit of love and it could have elevated the whole thing.The graphics are a bit janky too. For a game of this era, where are the particle effects, or interesting plays of lighting? It looks a combination of over-saturated and flat. The maps feel very boxy and cutout, with little depth. The models and the textures just aren't quite there, so it looks sub-par. A crying shame.I would bet London to a brick that it started as a mobile game that was over developed onto PC, which is why all the little things are missing.I refunded the game, and not because its something I simply cant play. Its just not worth the money.

If your knights get injured they will be down forever (a few in-game months) and if critically injured you can forget about using them for the next few hours of actual game-play. Injuries have such high repercussions coupled with the fact that enemies never miss and spawn forever makes this game annoying to play as you are locked into set play styles without much wiggle room: if and enemy group spawns you have to rush them and kill as many as you can the turn they spawn, rinse and repeat. It's extremely boring.Lore wise this game is disappointing: you have grey knights wearing cardboard armour struggling to kill corrupted human and poxwalkers... honestly could have just given us guardsmen.

_childDocuments_.review: I can absolutely recommend this to anyone with an interest in either 40k or games in the vein of X-COM.This game is broadly respectful of the lore it draws from and serves as a wonderful look at the Grey Knights chapter.  The art direction is beautiful and the environments are richly detailed.  The gameplay is compelling and while I do have a few bones to pick about the AI, the fights were sufficiently varied, and tactically demanding, that I always felt engaged.  In particular, the ironman mode made for some real nailbiting moments.  In short, if you think you are undecided about whether or not to pick up this title, don't hesitate. _childDocuments_.review: I tried very hard to like Chaos Gate through two different attempts. The game seems to promise so much, the experience of deploying some of mankind's greatest supersoldiers against a variety of inferior, but more numerous foes. But for all that I might feel that the game, with all its skill and equipment and class upgrades, might eventually become something like that, it continually holds it out in front of you, like a greyhound chasing a rabbit. Except the rabbit here is more like a tortoise, slow moving, not very deadly, and for all that armor, not very well protected, either. It's a difficult game, but more than being difficult it's stressful, because you're always under threat of bad consequences. Whether it's your characters being wounded because they took 1/3rd of their health as damage, whether it's enemies that can hit them regardless of their cover or armor, whether it's waiting to see if the next boom cycle will be trivial or will make the next hour of your life miserable. It feels bad. And though the flavor of it all is great WH40K, there are better turn based tactical games out there.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, but I just can't in good conscience recommend it.Gameplay:1) The game is a grind. Very much three-steps-forward-two-steps back. You are constantly beset with 'random events' which are pretty much universally negative, can persist for weeks of game time, can overlap with one another, and can radically alter the difficulty of even 'easy' missions.2) You often find yourself in a position where the ideal way to play a given mission relies on particular abilities / classes that you just don't have. Naturally, there is no way around this - you have to just do your best to slog it out with what you have.3) If you make a mistake, the game punishes you by making the next mission / round even more difficult. In missions with a lot of enemies, you spend more time waiting than you do actually playing.2) If you fail a mission and want to reload a save, there is so much unskippable blah-blah that it's actually quicker to ALT-F4 and reload the entire game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is probably the worst XCOM style game I have touched in a hot minute, and I’m genuinely impressed by that fact alone.In short, Chaos Gate is a game that seeks to wage a prolonged war of attrition against you. Except instead of whittling down your forces it instead insists on whittling down your patience, and it does this by being that kid that goes “My Death Guard are actually Grey Knight proof and have four dreadnaughts and can kill your Terminator instantly.”Warhammer 40,000: Chaos Gate Daemonhunters has plenty of interesting concepts that work decently in gameplay. The atmosphere during cutscenes and overworld map feels authentic to the vast world of 40k, with the dynamic between the Grey Knights and Inquisition being put right in front of you. In representation, the game absolutely nailed it in this department. The Grey Knights finally get represented in a way that doesn’t visualize them being covered in the blood of the Sisters of Battle. Their traditions, lore, and general concept of this mysterious specialized force are all presented in a very interesting light. While the story suffers from some writing shortcomings, there was a strong focus on what differentiates the Grey Knights from other chapters and that made most of the game bearable. The environment interactions are an amazing touch and change the tactics of battle from just being pure positioning. These interactions can range from shooting down statues to kill enemy units, to something as simple as throwing a manhole cover at a 5’1” manlet who doesn’t shower. Criting an enemy to slowly dismember them and change their combat effectiveness is also a plus, making crit builds have more depth than simply doing more damage. However, if this game was all that, the review would be positive.This game suffers from an identity crisis. In a desperate attempt to separate itself from the evermore successful Mechanicus, it chose to copy some of its ideas but failed to implement them in balanced methods. For instance, the awakening mechanic from Mechanicus is here, but slightly modified to accommodate the Death Guard. Each battle there exists this overarching meter called the “bloom” meter, wherein the more rounds that pass (and more abilities you pop) adds a certain amount to the bloom meter. Once it reaches 100, a random mutation occurs on the battlefield to force you to swap up tactics. In theory this is great, Mechanicus did something similar to force you stay mobile and complete your tasks before more Necrons arise. Except here it changes from more powerful enemies spawning to completely immobilizing one of your units, buffing the defensive characteristic of every enemy unit up to ridiculous heights, calling in enemy reinforcements nearby, decreasing your entire squad’s HP by 1 for the rest of the mission (this effect can stack with other abilities, by the way), and sometimes even flat out causing a mass resurrection of every dead unit on the field. These are all random, and there are only two stratagems to decrease the bloom level, otherwise it will constantly go up to 100 regardless of your playstyle. Speaking of resurrection, it’s here as an ability too. Some daemons of Nurgle will choose to respawn themselves after being slain, which isn’t horrible. Except once again making the Mechanicus comparison, you can effectively double tap the Necrons to ensure they do not respawn, either by ranged or melee attack. Here you have to run up to their corpse and waste an action to “cleanse” the corpse. So, if you kill a plaguewalker from range while taking cover from his allies actively shooting you, you must run out of cover just to cleanse and leave yourself exposed if you don’t want to deal with him again. Trust me when I say you do want him to stay dead because otherwise he will run up to you and proceed to melee you twice – Once for damage and once to strip any armor you have or applying a harsh debuff. Your fault he was able to resurrect himself and run with impunity, so reap what you’ve sown I suppose. Perhaps the devs intended for you to only fight in melee, as most ranged weapons aren’t worth their punch. Overwatch has a very noticeable problem, that being your knights (and even the AI) can accidentally position your firing cone to shoot exclusively at birds, allowing units to . It also doesn’t help that most of the loot you find barely aids in your fight against Chaos, with my current run having maxed Armor and Melee Weaponry requisitions only for missions to drop Level 2 equipment that barely change my status quo. I won’t get into the story because it’s the basic “Grey Knights go fight demons and Inquisition woman does unorthodox stuff but its for the good of mankind this time honest.” If you’re familiar with 40k’s writing, you probably already know how this story ends. I wouldn’t buy this game at $45, or even $20. If the game ever goes on sale for $10 then at least consider it. Just remember to have a guide open on a second monitor so you don’t mess up an arbitrary decision and it ends up ruining your run. Once I'm done subjecting myself to this torment, it's getting uninstalled and shelved right next to Dawn of War III.Edit: The Final Mission is purposefully designed to waste at least one hour of your life. You are not fighting anything special, the game just drags out combat cause it feels like it. I pray the devs never touch a project like this again.

_childDocuments_.review: The number of enemies per battle is too damn high! Sure, 40k fans will love the setting. However, even on easy, the battles... take... aaaaages.......... The balance isn't right for a casual gamer. God forbid, I might have chosen 1 of the 3 higher difficulties, let alone the ironman mode. Dios mio! I got exhausted/bored by the sheer number of enemies. If I had selected a harder difficulty, I'd expect to be sweating it out and feeling constantly overwhelmed. But if I ask for my eggs easy, I don't want my nuts hard boiled.Plenty of negative reviews for the DLC and marketing strategies. Couldn't care less. I want to recommend the game, but this is one of those instances where a 3 out of 5 would have been more appropriate as I really want to nudge the developers to improve. _childDocuments_.review: This is a fairly good tactical turn-based strategy game with a relatively engaging story based on a very interesting background universe.Perhaps what the game does best is presenting an interesting experience in the Warhammer 40K world by putting you in the shoes of one of its most interesting denizens: the Grey Knights, a caste of genetically modified super soldiers, of even more prowess than the 'normal' genetically modified super soldiers.You control a cruiser from the Order of Grey Knights, going from one disaster zone of the Imperium to another fielding your team of Grey Knights to deal with threats that nobody else in all human kind could deal with.Your schedule as a Grey Knight is basically 'Why look at the time, it's time to purge, like always, until I die'.Of course, in terms of game-play, it is inevitable to compare it to XCOM, but instead of forcing careful tactical approach, this game really preaches the best defense is a good offense idiom by rewarding extremely aggressive tactical approach allowing you to feel like true armor-clad super human exterminators as you plow through legions of heretics and demons (As long as you know what you are doing).Randomness is minimized in actual combat. If you point a gun or raise a sword, you are told the exact damage you would do, but factors such cover, angle of fire, statuses, etc. influence the final exact damage number. This design makes it so that the core mechanic of combat is about chaining coordinate attacks to keep the momentum going and not risk breaking the chain due to someone missing a 99% chance to hit a target. This turns the game into series of impromptu puzzles as you try to figure out what series of actions in what order would allow you to wipe out all oppositions on the map while incurring minimal damage.Team building is also a fun exercise, as you try to optimize your team of 4 exterminators to be able to deal with any situations. The variety of enemies, battlefields, and battle modifiers makes it a need to balance your team or build it with specific tactics in mind. There is a surprising depth to the combat system, as every team member must be well designed with each other in mind to ensure you can beat everything.Overall, this is an excellent 40k game that brings a solid take on the tactical turn-based strategy game genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Warhammer 40,000: Chaos Gate - Daemonhunters

_childDocuments_.review: While very similar to "a certain other game", Chaos Gate really comes into its own after a few hours. I do recommend buying it, provided the following issues don't bother you that much: Gameplay:The game really favors a very aggressive style,  which does mean that it may be a bit too bland and limiting for hardcore strategists. The enemy variety is lackluster for now, and it does take a while before new enemy types are introduced. Also, sending wounded marines to combat leads to a trivial debuff which means that you can just pick 4 favorites and not change them at all (with some exceptions).  The mission variety is not great either, and some missions do feel a bit like a grind, but there are a few very fun surprises thrown here and there which do make it worth it in my opinion. Another annoyance is that you can't re-spec your marines, so if you make a wrong choice or recruit a new high level guy, you are stuck with whatever they have.Story:Theme-wise, this game feels a bit too cheery and goofy for the "grim darkness" of 40k (and not in an Orky way).  The characters are made to be relatable and too "human" for my liking.  One of the worst offenders here is the Mechanicus tech priest which has metal eyebrows and a vox box mouthpiece mimicking a human mouth to achieve what I can only describe as "cuteness" (a similar thing can be said for all other characters).The crew's (and Inquisitor's) behavior is far too childish for the grizzled veterans the story suggests they are and you will feel like a babysitter at times.Power fantasy wise, this game also misses the mark, with some silly situations like a non-mutated human guardsman punching a power-armored space marine and dealing damage, or a terminator armor clad knight walking through some pitiful bit of burning oil and setting himself on fire (yikes).And finally, although it breaks my heart to say this, this game is another one in the long line of media misrepresenting the bolter. The poor bolter is once again little more than a glorified assault rifle instead of the stupid and awesome auto-cannon/rocket-launcher hybrid that it is in the lore.Performance:The game is decently optimized, but it has some significant frame rate drops in certain menus or certain combat arenas. Even though my rig is relatively good, I did end up lowering the graphics quality on certain missions or while interacting with certain ship menus (the second bit was especially annoying and odd). Overall, I still think the game is a lot of fun, and would recommend it to anyone but the most hardcore 40k purists (so that your eyes don't roll away from your sockets). But even for the purists, it may be fun to have a look at this game simply to see an outsider's interpretation of the franchise (just don't take it too seriously, you nerds).I am currently still progressing through the game, and will update this review if anything new or interesting comes up.
_childDocuments_.name: Warhammer 40,000: Chaos Gate - Daemonhunters

_childDocuments_.review: It's like XCOM and WH40K got drunk together, and had babies without the defective random hit gene that causes you to miss a headshot at 99% accuracy. Instead of a stationary HQ, you have a ship that's extremely damaged and requires repairs to get everything going again, in a tiered progression of various new resources (like prognosticars, which psychically tell you what's up in that system while reducing the corruption there) and upgrades (like your barracks, which allow you to recruit additional team members for when one of your favorite guys is really messed up and missing most of his HP) that will send you flashing back to a bunker where you organized assaults against Xenos rather than daemons in a galaxy far far away from Terra."Acts of Glory" are an optional hard mode that you can commit to before the start of a mission, essentially for the glory of the Imperium, which nets you extra requisition points for supplies and upgrades. One example is to finish a mission without any of your squad dropping- another to complete the mission while taking less than 20 damage.I haven't completed the story yet, but from the get go everything draws you in - and I, at least, was immediately set on edge by just how coincidental it is that this inquisitor appears to commandeer your ship at the precise moment you completed the intro mission against BBEG. Sometimes you have to make choices that make one person happy and another upset, and each of these people can give amazing benefits or crippling debuffs depending on who you side with. The game very much accomplishes the gritty 'everything sucks but we're the empire of man and we're going to rock at it anyway' atmosphere I associate with the WH40K universe. You are a disposable cog in the machine, as are all your fellow troops, and after sufficient repairs, this is further reinforced by the fact that when your troops fall, you can harvest their gene seeds to improve your surviving troops. In a darker universe like this one, I can't help but think to myself; I should train up some of these troops -specifically- to send them on a suicide run and combine their genetics with another to make the *ultimate* knight. And that moment right there? For me, that's how I know they did it right. Dark and twisted as it is? That's WH40K - Glory to the emperor!

Its too large at 4k so some scaling options would be nice, also more tool tips on icons and better navigation for the equipment screens would be good improvements.

_childDocuments_.review: Some remarks beforehand:* Game needs a bit of polish. * The models and animations look like they are from an older era (which has its charms, for sure. But its nothing like Total Warhammer 3 for example). * The weapons and balancing of the armor might need a revision. But all in all, a title i'm already quite enjoying. And while not 'as' in depth as an Xcom 2 game 'yet' (so far for me at least), I'm enjoying it. Solid mechanics idea's so far that really seem to work.I LOVE the fact that i can change minute details about my Knights, down to the voices, armour details, last names ( which are spoken aloud as well as be displayed on the knight on certain places). It really makes me care more about them, instead of 'generic marine nr 5'.I have played several 40K games who have all tried their own spin on this genre of Xcom like gameplay, from mobile to PC games. And this is the first one where i'm actually enjoying myself.Each class of knight has their own feel to them and has a varied roster of traits they can unlock in a tree.(so far, no idea if one Knight can have all of them, but hey.)It feels like Xcom married Dawn of War 2 in terms of loadout mechanics but expanded heavily on them. Such as the ability to unlock upgrades for your gear. I would love to see this kind of game (with perhaps a bigger budget), with other chapters. Could be the same setting for all, with minimal narrative changes or references, so long as the chapters have their own styles or changed options/gameplay. Such as Black Templars (Templar visuals with correct colours, no psykers, themed weapons and traits, stratagems etc) compared to Blood angels or even Imperial Fists and so forth (just some founding chapters would be enough in this case, or possibly to create your own generic second founding one). Just roam about the galaxy, doing missions, trying to beat back a warp event/invasion or other xeno races. Leveling up your Marines, building up your base/fleet in a freeplay scenario. Expending resources or requisitioning more from your chapter/the imperium. Collect gear and personalise all of it like in this game. Heck, a system/game like this with an expanded roster choice to also play as a strike force of Imperial Guard, Sisters of Battle, etc. I would be amazing to have the choice to play as a different faction for another playthrough. _childDocuments_.review: The Short Answer:How would I assess this games progress?Fun, but flawed. Game breaking bugs with place holder comments from development of the game isn't a great look. Save your $50.00. Wait for a few patches, and a price drop (I would expect these issue from a game that cost less).The Long Answer:I beat the game on Normal with no issue on my first play through, and enjoyed the game play loop (and the random events). Then started a second play through on Grand Master Mode, Ruthless difficulty (single save file only). I got to a Grand Master report (on day 688, I was 2 stratagems from unlocking all stratagems to get the achievement, then planned on progressing to the final boss levels), and all four questions for the Grand Master Report are:"How would you assess our progress in the war, Inquisitor?"All four answers are:"Bloom Seed Thingy" (This must have been place holder comments left over from game development, funny/sad that it shows up in a game breaking bug in the final game)On the same Grand Master Report screen, in the top left corner, I got what appears to be a random encounter with a Death Guard ship at the same time (which no DG ship is in orbit of the planet I am around). No matter what option (of Bloom Seed Thingy) I select the game does not progress, and freezes (Yes I loaded the game back up four times to test it). I have overall enjoyed the game, however being right toward the end and having a game breaking bug on a single save file play through is frustrating (not even mad, just let down).This sadly switches my opinion of this game, and I would not recommend this game. The lack of balance in classes didn't deter me (Paladin is poorly designed and should not have been released in this state). The flawed concept of taking stratagems away at times (or all together like in the last mission) didn't bother me. It forced me to approach maps differently from time to time. The random encounters, and having stuff stolen out of my inventory/bad things happen that I had no direct control over didn't even bug me. I like the difficulties that these things created, and had to overcome. But game breaking bugs is where I draw the line (and yes I know I chose to play a single save file game. No one forced me too do that. But, if it is an option the game gives me, I shouldn't be punished by a bug for choosing it).

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fun game.  At first it seems like a shameless X-com 2 knockoff which feels super cheesy, so my expectations were low to start-out.  However it surprised me how fun it got especially towards mid-game where resources are tight and every battle matters.  Another surprise is that gameplay is actually VERY different from XCom in that the gameplay pushes you towards uber aggressive-style play vs extra strategic, stealth or ambush-style set-up type of play.  The aggressive in-battle gameplay has a lot of similarities to Gears Tactics, but the out-of-battle strategy is FAR superior to Gears Tactics (i.e. striving to attain key resources of your choice from successful battles to support and enable your overall campaign style and choices) and this is totally what makes the game a blast.  I would highly recommend it to all fans of the turn-based tactical strategy genre!

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this game. Although I was slow getting into it, it is a great quality 40k game, and there are precious few of those (and I own most of them).As an XCOM type game, I like it a LOT. It doesn't have quite as much going on as something like Phoenix Point, but you have many, many options in combat, and what happens in battles makes sense. I never liked the original percentage based hit formula because it would often be just stupid, like shooting something at near point blank range and missing because you only have a 98 percent chance to hit. None of that here. You can clearly see what result your actions will have before you commit to them, and there is good strategic depth. I rarely if ever feel cheated by the game or that my loss was simply bad luck instead of bad tactics.On the 40k side, it is pretty good. I read quite a bit of lore and some of the books, and it feels right as a 40k game. I've heard complaints that your Grey Knights aren't as strong as they should be lorewise...maybe those people just haven't gotten far in the game. They are pretty weak at level 1 or 2, but by end game, a single knight is wiping whole squads of enemies in a single turn, so they aren't THAT weak. It has to be balanced as a game, and generally, your knights feel like the badasses they are supposed to be. The game presents plenty of the challenges, and the story is good and fits well with the series.The two biggest issues I have are how randomly punishing warp surges can be, and the general ridiculousness of injury recovery until you invest in the medical upgrades for the ship, but these are small issues clearly meant to balance challenge and game pacing, and they seem to have been a little smoothed out since launch. Optimization is slightly lacking. I had to reduce graphics to medium in order to smooth the game, but honestly, it looks great on medium anyway, so it wasn't a noticeable loss of anything.I greatly, greatly want to see more DLC and campaigns added. There is a LOT of Nurgle in this game, basically its all Nurgle, and some variety added would greatly help. If you like a better version of XCOM, you like 40k, and you want to bash demons with a team of cracked space marines. Then this is your game.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: As a long time victim of Xcom and a reasonably well versed fan of 40K, I had been keeping my eye on this one for some time. I'm happy to say that the game provides ample lashings of both the brutal turn based Xcom gameplay we all love to hate, and the grim darkness of the far future that we all hate to love.For more details, feel free to continue reading my rambling, loosely connected opinions / early observations below. We'll start by addressing the common talking point of the campaigns' difficulty, and see where we go from there.The gameplay will be familiar to many fans of the genre, but the challenge of even the early 'trash' enemies makes you feel like you are on the back foot right from the outset -mirroring the early gameplay of a typical Xcom campaign. The game does at least partially justify this through recent events the Knights have endured, some of which you actually get to participate in during the tutorial mission. Nevertheless, it can still feel jarring from a lore perspective to have your Grey Knights pinned down and shredded by a handful of giggling lunatics with rusty autoguns and basic armour. In fairness though, it certainly does make for a satisfying early difficulty wall to punch through. Using these early foes as actual threats rather than laughably dismissed nuisances, (as lore accurate Grey Knights would likely do), forces you to experiment and engage with the suite of tools available. And you WILL need to effectively use those tools when the bigger threats start to ooze out onto the field. After you have some beefier Knights and more powerful wargear to swing around, you can start to take some bigger, bolder moves that you'd expect to see from our boys in Grey. The first time I group teleported my team right into the middle of a full swarm of cultists, priests, plague marines, and a mini-boss target ... but managed to take them all down in one turn? Yeah  felt like the Grey Knights the lore would suggest -and I felt the game had built me up to earn that success.Needless to say of course, things continue to ramp up. I am (at time of writing) roughly 180 days into the Ironman campaign story on ruthless difficulty after having suffered one campaign restart already. New threats and objectives are steadily introduced to keep you invested in the struggle without ever getting too comfortable. While I'm sure that the difficulty will eventually level out and the pendulum start to swing the other way, these early hours with the game will feel like you are on a knife edge. Having said that the game does absolutely provide the means for a power-fantasy playthrough, with the the 'merciful' difficulty option beefing up your team dramatically for a much more relaxing, gung-ho purging spree if that should be more your style.The story, (at least what I have encountered so far), is solid enough to provide a lore friendly reason for the steadily building threat -viewed here in terms of an infection of the sector. This infection is spreading between systems and becoming increasingly more virulent, making it harder to control and simply hold ground, while also desperately trying to research and understand the foe to devise an effective counter. The forces of Nurgle fit into this role as well as you would expect, and they feel like a credible looming campaign-wide threat just as they cause difficulties on the individual battlefields as discussed above. Your principle NPC allies consist of engineering, research and military focused characters, as well as a monthly report from a distant authority figure effectively ranking and rewarding you on your progress. Again, an obvious mirror to the Xcom structure is in place, making the setup familiar. These are each well acted and presented, giving credible lore-appropriate character types to flesh out what are effectively a series of upgrade menus. These are further explored in campaign cutscenes, where we do see some conflicting ideas about the best direction to focus your efforts. Choosing to follow the advice of one will often disappoint another -leading to some interesting cost/benefit decisions. Not being able to see the full outcome of such choices before committing, (as far as I have been able to tell), can lead to some unexpected calamities, and could potentially have been made clearer.An odd quirk is that the flavor dialogue presented by these characters is often only partially voice acted -which I have found distracting. Main cutscenes don't tend to suffer this, but the optional conversations regularly have the character speaking only a single sentence from a much longer speech shown in the accompanying text... how and why this happens I have no idea, but it does feel offputting.Speaking of flavor, lets talk about the look, sound, and feel of the game universe. Mainly.. is this 40k appropriate? The visuals may not be bleeding edge, but such things have never been a requirement in my eyes. They are stylised around the almost comically horrific visions of the future which fans of the universe would imagine, and fit the tone as can be expected. It's rare to see a high budget release of a Warhammer game which gets this wrong, but it is always pleasing to see it done right, with the world brought to life in a way that feels lifted right from the pages of any official released material. Likewise, sound and music design feel right at home. Meaty bolters, stoic battle chatter, heavy treads of terminators thundering through the environment.. it's all good stuff. Perhaps the cultists lean too heavily into the giggling madman voice acting style, but this is down to personal taste. Just as you would expect from a 40k game lots of ominous chanting, bombastic horns & orchestra work is the order of the day. Much like the visuals, the 40k soundtrack is something we know what to reasonably expect by now, and has been competently delivered.Tonally, I found that elements like the description of the ship upgrade to speed up servitor production by 'optimizing the lobotomization of ', or seeing the nightmarish results of even a mid level nurgle infestation on a planet and its' inhabitants help evoke the overboard horror of 'life' in this universe. And having access to the unlockable ability to destroy entire planets if you judge them not worth saving? As the good guys? Yeah, this is 40k.More directly, I have also experienced the commonly reported performance problems during some missions. Oh! and the UI can be a struggle to read / navigate sometimes. Like, why can I not immediately see when I select a knight if they are out of ammo? Or why can I not consistently use the same option to back out of a particular view / menu? Why does the UI have to be so big, and yet somehow clunky and unclear? These do not push the game over the threshold for a thumbs down from me, mostly because the turn based nature of the game means you can work around both of these without direct time pressure, but they are surely blemishes which I hope to see addressed sooner rather than later.So let's try and make a sensible conclusion to all this. Game is good -possibly great. If you are a fan of Xcom or 40K, you may want to give this a try. If you are a fan of both, I can honestly encourage you to pick it up. I doubt that you will find the game wanting. If you are troubled by the current in-game issues, perhaps wait for a sale a few months down the line after a couple of updates have been rolled out. If you are understandably holding out for a more fundamental change to the policies surrounding the game, (which I have not touched on here for space reasons, but do fully acknowledge as valid points of concern), you have my respect and support. I hope that someday you will be able to enjoy this game without the negative trappings that taint the release in its' present form, while still being able to support and stand behind the dev teams who make such games possible in the first place.

_childDocuments_.review: After a few hours of play, I think it is time to review Chaos Gate - Daemonhunters.For the record, I am a big 40K fanboy, and I loved the original Chaos Gate (OG Chaos Gate from now on).Chaos Gate - Daemonhunters mixes the tactical gameplay of Gears of war tactics with a strategic layer like in XCOM.If you have read a few other reviews, you'd probably have come to the conclusion that the game is unforgiving.Except in theme, the game has very little in common with the original Chaos Gate from SSI. It is further apart than the newer XCOM were from their inspiration. Combat is closer from the new XCOM formula, with enemies "pods" that get triggered when you are in visual range of them.The game also relies a lot on special abilities (as in XCOM, the performances of your knights are night and day between a fresh one who just graduated from supplicant school.The immersion is good. I miss the old choir of the original chaos gate, and Nurgle lore is really weirder than Khorne lore, but the game makes a good job of conveying the fact that we are in the 40th Millenium.However, your Grey Knights will suffer from gameplay/lore mismatch: Their survivability is much lower than you would expect, even when faced with mere cultists, and it is one of the areas where OG Chaos Gate got it right:A dozen cultists will be a major threat to your squad of 4 knights, to the point you'd rather face 5 Chaos Space Marines, because their standard power armor offers no damage reduction. I was initially annoyed a lot by this fact, but I learnt to live with it. after all, in the original Chaos Gate, you could just ignore every cultist, and every Chaos Space Marine that didn't wield a heavy or special weapon.I would have preferred a better compromise (like CSM being equipped with anti armor rounds, and a few cultists with special weapons).This result in the early game being quite brutal. The difficulty has been one of the major complains about the game. But it is actually one of the parts I liked the best. Many complained that it was more unfair than XCOM.But it took me a lot of campaign retries to survive the early game in both XCOM 1 & 2 at the highest difficulty level(60 or so for XCOM 1, and around 30 for XCOM 2), before cruising to the end game.Unlike in XCOM 1, I never felt like I had to memorize the maps in Chaos Gate in order to survive in ironman mode. The game difficulty is also front loaded, but not as much as in XCOM.Overall, I agree that the game is difficult, but I don't think it is unfair at all (I completed it on the highest difficulty level in grandmaster mode), and is comparable to XCOM.You have a higher chance to love someone in mission, but the game gives you tool to recover from it (your knights can usually survive getting to 0 HP a few times in their career, and if they don't, their spirit can give boons to their brothers later on).Another issue with difficulty is that the game features a lot of random events whose outcome can be very negative. Unfortunately, it is sometimes pretty hard to make an informed decision without refering to the Steam event guide (or reloading if not playing ironman), which is pretty annoying.The game also likes hiding information that would be really helpful.It won't tell you that you need 8 geared and leveled knights to handle the final battle, but it really should for instance.Surprisingly, there is also quite a lot of randomness for a game that boasts to not have hit chances : the gear you get access to is random, the warp events that give boons to the opponent vary a lot, and there still are many rolls in the game to trigger some abilities, or critical hits, which make a huge difference. It seems rather negative so far, but I really had a blast with this game. It is actually my game of the year on Steam for 2022, because the combat is really satisfying.- You know the location of enemy pods, so you have less surprise triggers (even though it is not as true with the DLC, as some maps get pretty cramped).- The ability can be really fun to combine, and there are many ways to build your squad, depending on the gear you get.- As I wrote earlier, having ways to mitigate your losses really helps compared to XCOM- it focuses a lot more on melee combat, which makes it much more satisfying to use than in XCOM2.To me, the main weakness of Chaos Gate is the lack of variety, both in maps and enemies. The maps in XCOM felt much more impactful, but here, you end up charging in melee most of the time anyway, so the maps don't make a huge difference.The game also lacks mission variety: I liked the set battles, even though I usually don't like boss battles in tactical games, but you only have 3 versions of the repeatable missions, which is an issue the game shares with its main inspiration, Gears of Wars: Tactics (but GoW:T had more hand crafted missions).It departs so much from the original game that it is very hard to compare both. It still has a great atmosphere, but it feels much less faithful to the Codex Astartes (not that Grey Knights follow it), and the character count is much lower (4 instead of 15). It is a downgrade, but on the other hand, a good part of your squads were basically cheerleaders, because there was little more they could do with a bolter against CSM armor.I also preferred fighting over the whole map, than having mini skirmishes with individual pods, like in XCOM 2012.But the choice of equipment, strategic layer, and customization of each knights really adds a lot for me.OG Chaos Gate also had a memorable soudntrack, while the one in CG:Daemonhunter is just serviceable. I still remember some themes from the original, but I would be unable to do so with the new game, despite having freshly spent 200 hours on it.But the choice of equipment, strategic layer, and customization of each knights really adds a lot for me. I like Chaos Gate: Daemonhunters, but I loved his predecessor, so it is similar to the X-COM vs nuXCOM situation for me.So overall, I can only recommend this game, but we warned it is pretty unforgiving, and the first playthrough might seem unfair, especially if played ironman without spoilers.It is my preferred of the tactical or strategic 40K games that have come out in the last 10 years.

_childDocuments_.review: This review comes after a complete playthrough, start to end. You play a Warhammer 40,000 faction, the Grey Knights, battling a Nurgle threat.The good: + The grim-dark Warhammer 40,000 setting for an X-COM-like game is a fresh take on the genre. Unlike X-COM, it does away with much of the random throws (although there are plenty of other random elements).+ The core of the game is solid, turn-based gameplay that rewards tactical planning and smart, considered but aggressive play styles. + The turn-based game play takes place over six or seven varied mission types, not including the unique campaign missions, and it is important and fun to pay attention to the different objectives. + The simple campaign mechanic of time passing while you try to quell a growing existential threat is well handled.+ Most of the mechanics in the overarching campaign (the various currencies and rewards) mesh together well. Managing them requires the type of trade-offs that reward a thinking playstyle. + The Nurgle enemy units are varied and full of character, especially the bosses. + The narrative, plot and characters are engaging and well voiced, although the dialogue is clunky. + The art style and sound are excellent, balancing immersion and distraction well. + For the most part, the difficulty levels are well balanced. + You start with a basic squad of Grey Knights who can be upgraded into super-powered, elite psychic warriors as the game progresses. + The different classes are satisfyingly different from one another and can be combined in interesting ways, meaning that in theory you could try different class combinations in different playthroughs. + Similarly to other games in this genre, your Grey Knights' appearance can be customised, as can their load-outs. + There's around 50 - 80 hours of satisfying gameplay for a single run through of the campaign, depending on how you play it. + At the time of writing, the game has been well-supported by the developer and is refreshingly free of bugs. But: - In the base game you can only play one faction - the Grey Knights - and not as the single enemy faction, Nurgle (which, to be fair, is usual in the genre). - The random events on the campaign map feel like a weak point, interrupting the narrative with opaque, irritating consequences that usually prove very limiting. - Random factors feel arbitrary, meaning you can suddenly find yourself without the currency needed for essential research or upgrades.- The limited numbers of mission types can become repetitive towards the end of the game. - I feel the narrative-driven campaign and repetitive missions limit the game's replay value, a general problem in all the X-COM-alikes. - Most of the scripted plot-related missions spike the difficulty considerably. For example, the final boss mission is a lengthy repetitive grind with no prior information given to help pick squads. It requires careful preparation and thought, which the game does not warn you about. - Other games in the genre have innovated the core formula in more advanced ways, such as turn ordering (e.g. in the excellent X-COM 2 War of the Chosen DLC) , squad bonds and allowing more units in a squad. - No sandbox skirmish mode. A mode allowing you to craft a squad to test which abilities are best combined, so you don't have to play an entire campaign over again, would be a boon. - No multiplayer mode.- No mods or workshop.This is not a casual game. Overall, it's a satisfying way for a gamer who wants a demanding mental workout to scratch the tactical turn-based itch, even if the setting isn't your thing, and it's worth the money.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a great tactical rpg with plenty to love. But in this review, I'll focus on the negatives other reviews have listed rather than the big positives. If you like tactical rpgs, you'll probably like it. A tiny bit about myself: I adore turn-based strategy in all forms it takes. Though I've never managed to finish any X-Com game. I take my time with them and eventually something new comes along before I can wrap up my 100+ hours campaign.The twitch drops are forgettable. They're all simple T1 gear, and none of them have particularly exceptional looks, either. They give 10% crit chance or +1 crit damage. You will get similar and better gear the moment your missions start rewarding gear (about 1h into the game). The pre-order hammer and book are more substantial, but hardly overpowered. You get similar gear about 4-12 hours into the game, depending on how hard you rush the requisition upgrades that boost your loot drops (it's a very simple system).I like them. The enemies are somewhat cartoony, but that seems adequate, given that they're Grandfather Nurgle's jolly hordes. Your knights look badass and not cartoony at all. The simpler graphic style also means you can easily tell at a glance if enemies have mutations (a system that makes basic enemies more dangerous as the game progresses), and that you can play it very well on weaker hardware and have it still look fine. I play on max on my desktop and on minimal on my ♥♥♥♥♥♥ old laptop, and while max is prettier minimal still looks pretty decent.I've played on normal difficulty so far, and while it took me a few missions to get used to it, the game seemed straight forward enough once you get a hang of the mechanics. Basic enemy cultists hurt a lot if you're out in the open and they have the numbers advantage, but once you realize they waste their action on a really weak punch if youstand next to them, and that their guns deal next to no damage if you're in cover, you very quickly figure out how to dismantle encounters. Another important trick is to realize that once you kill the last enemy, your entire squad immediately reloads all weapons and recovers full action points. So you use up all your ap to heal and reposition before finishing off the last enemy and then immediately move to trigger the next encounter. It's possibly to finish some of the easier missions on smaller maps without the enemy ever getting even a single turn, once you levelled your guys a bit.If a knight takes even a single point of damage, they suffer a "minor wound" after the battle. If they take more than half total hp in damage (regardless of healing during the mission), they suffer a major wound. If they go down, they suffer a critical wound. Minor wounds reduce max hp by 3, major wounds by 6, critical wounds by 9. Your average knight has 14 hp (though it's fairly simple to get them to 20+ total hp around my current playtime, and presumably even more later). Wounds take from 14-60 days to heal (depending on severity and some RNG). But here's the thing. Nothing stops you from continuing to use an injured knight. And if they are, say, recovering from a major wound, suffering another major or minor wound wont extend their recovery time at all. A critical wound will, though. So it's a system that incentives not letting your knights take too much damage, but not overly punishing if they do. The max hp reduction hurts somewhat, but is far from a run-ending handicap.I have no idea where this comes from. The UI gives you all the information you need during a mission with very few clicks, and I've never really noticed it "getting into the way". The only minor gripe I have is that you cant go directly from the gear screen to the skill tree or swap to another knight's gear screen without first having to exit out of the gear screen. But that's not really that much of a problem?

_childDocuments_.review: You command a squad of Catholic priests who are juiced up with Space Jesus' seed but not in a gay way. A very manly way. After taking command of your squad because of reasons you're tasked to eliminate the Covid 19 virus and it's ever expanding variants. If you're reading this review you've probably just rage quit after your third attempt at a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mission and you're looking for someone to reaffirm your masculinity. I can't do that unfortunately but I can give everyone else an honest review of Chaos Gate Daemonhunters.Fans of Warhammer 40k and Xcom are the target audience for Demonhuntahs. If you're coming from either series you'll likely find plenty to pick at. For those that slept through hard mode Xcom2, you'll likely struggle in regular mode here. Many of the mechanics echo but they don't rhyme and a semi complicated UI can fuddle the learning curve even further. If you're someone that already struggles with Xcom, you'll be happy to learn that there's a "Restart Mission" button and like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in the shower, only the bravest among us are willing to admit to resorting to such extreme measures.Gameplay wise, you'll recognize the core gameplay. ♥♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥♥♥, you're trying to un♥♥♥♥ the ♥♥♥♥ and your success will be based entirely on how well you respond to new ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥ through tech building and research. The initial (and probably final) Squad size is four people which means you'll be utilizing the Justicar class until you realize that Purgators can bypass armor if you turn their talent tree into a John Madden playbook. Then you'll use three Justicars and a Purgator until one of them coughs with a little too much enthusiasm and has to spend the next two months learning to walk again.The UI has some real fantastic design if you went to school in Japan and you enjoy reading in whatever ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ direction the wind happens to be blowing that day. For the rest of us, you can enjoy finding new things to gripe about like being informed that you have infinite melee attacks but you have to hover over your shoot button to figure how much ammo you have left. The AI has a few tricks up their sleeves as well. By that I mean that the AI knows how to do exactly three things based on the enemy type and one of those things is typically overwatch. I'd make a fantastic joke about Blizzard here but some of the missions can be outright exhausting and I still haven't gotten over that whole thing with Tracers ass. Speaking of ass, the tutorial. You'll probably decide that tutorials are for OTHER PEOPLE and you'll end up skipping it. That's a mistake. It's also a mistake to play it because like the Governor of Florida, it really doesn't handle transitions well. For fans of the lore/tabletop, go write your own ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ review that talks about how Swordbearers don't make any sense for the gameplay and the distinct lack of eighteen Dreadknights in ever mission really pulls you away from the experience. I don't know what you want from me it's a Grey Knight themed game, I need this and you better not take it away from me.Graphically the game is fine. It has this weird Borderlands ♥♥♥♥♥♥ World of Warcraft vibe without actually over utilizing either of their art styles. The game likes to randomly run like ♥♥♥♥ for literally no reason at all but like my previous relationships, it doesn't stick around very long. Looking forward to mod content so I can finally have eighteen Dreadknights rolling around the field and maybe a larger squad size from a different Brotherhood.All in all I give it an eight. Could be eight out of ten, could be eight out of a hundred. Go figure it out for yourself.

The presentation is a bit too colourful and cartoony for my liking, but it's a very good expression of the chosen aesthetic. The interface seems like it was designed for a console game and is a little clunky at times, but perfectly servicable. I became very invested in the story and characters, and the difficulty hit me just right to engender a sense that I was progressing mechanically and upgrading my ship and squad, while at the same time falling behind an increasingly mounting threat, and that I had to hurry in order to save the galaxy.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: While the below is still true and I still enjoy and recommend this game, there's a really big need to fix some of the early game balancing. Your guys are too weak and take forever to heal and the enemies are too plentiful to avoid damage. TL;DR 40K-Com which suffers slightly from not being as high budget as X-COM 2 or Gears Tactics but is still well worth playing if you like Turn based tactics games.I love X-COM and I love 40k, so this game is tailor made for me. The standard Games Workshop games issues are obvious though, and that's lack of budget. The core of the gameplay is really solid - which is the most important part. It plays well and features a good range of enemies and load out options, even only 2 hours in. It's not quite as hardcore as X-COM but in a lot of ways that just helps make it less frustrating. The presentation leaves a little to be desired though, the graphics are quite heavily stylised and cartoon-y. I don't mind this, but Grim Dark this isn't. The animations are passable and the sound design is eh (which is a big let down after the glory that was everything audio in Mechanicus). The UI is also pretty weak. I currently recommend this game, it somehow manages to remind me of the original Chaos Gate despite having little to do with it. The important part of the game is great - that being the tactical layer and the characters are fun too, it just needs some tweaks which hopefully will come in patches down the line.

_childDocuments_.review: Chaos Gate starts off with a great impression. It is a gorgeous game that spares no details, from battle worn armour, to all the beautiful lighting, colors and effects. You start the game right in the turn based strategy of the action, as the game walks you through the basic commands, actions and abilities your space marines possess. After that very first battle you're boarded back on the ship, where the story of the campaign begins to unfold and where you can select your missions. Playing through the game's missions, it's been fun gaining ability points for each of your Grey Knights and improving their abilities, or selecting new ones to make them more effective in battle. You can also gain requisition points for completing bonus objectives. For example, completing a mission without grenades. You can select different loadouts for each character, gain new characters during the campaign and more powerful abilities and weapons as you go along, so the game has a lot of depth. You can even select different graphics on parts of your armour. Naturally, the game has even more depth as there are many different ways yo can approach battles depending on your team and its loadouts as well as the type of enemies you encounter. One of the main enemies is The Bloom, which can spawn enemies in unexpected locations and also give them random buffs. While this keeps the game intense, it can also be frustrating because you also have enemy encounters that are already guaranteed on the map. I do recommend this game, but make sure you save early and wisely. Also, you'll need to learn how to best equip and use your team. This game is no cakewalk. I haven't been faring so well later in the campaign and I think I'll have to start new and relearn how I've been doing things.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been a longtime fan of Warhammer 40k, both for the games on the PC as well as on the tabletop (I've even had the opportunity to play in a weekend tournament at Warhammer World in Nottingham, UK), and currently I have spent 275 hours playing this game at the point this review is being written. So, to save some time for those who would reply "TL;DR", here's my summary: - Very aesthetically pleasing- Great game mechanics- Superb variety of classes- 2 out of 3 of the DLC (Duty Eternal and Execution Force) are worthwhile getting unless everything is in a saleIn more detail:- The graphics of this game are stunning, and my 4080 runs at around 68*C with all settings on max and on 4k resolution. The only downside is that there is no native DLSS option, which would significantly improve temps and FPS. But as it is winter right now, having my PC act as a heater for my office is quite handy! Sorry, I'm digressing. In all honesty, having painted tabletop miniatures for years, I can appreciate the time spent on the level of detail on the models used in game, and not just the knights, but those from Chaos as well. All in all, a solid 9/10. - The game mechanics are very similar to the tabletop. As I have very little free time, the tabletop games can run from 3-6 hours each, depending on the size of the army, so being able to just jump straight in and play a virtual tabletop version of the game with excellently rendered scenery is a godsend. As for those who have moaned about "Urgh, Dawn of War is faster, this game is too slow!" the DoW series of games were enjoyable, but this is much closer to the tabletop version and makes you think about your choices a lot more than DoW ever will. Every choice you make, every move taken, has an impact on your progress, and one miscalculation can end it all, necessitating a reload from an earlier save point. - The variety of classes available to you is vast in the vanilla edition, with different roles available to each class, allowing you the opportunity to decide how you wish to use your knights. IMHO the best combination is the Justicar, Interceptor and Apothecary. Apaart from acting as the tank for the squad, the Justicar can gift your Interceptor 3 move points and an extra willpower point.  The Apothecary can boost the Interceptor's critical chance percentage as well as keep your knights healed. With these two bonuses applied, the Interceptor can then teleport close to a group of enemies, then use a second skill called Teleport Strike to whizz through the warp, hitting a string of enemies close to each other, and sometimes take out an entire group before they can even fire on your knights once! The fourth spot in your squad can be then filled by whatever knight takes your fancy, or, not a knight at all, which leads me to.......- The DLC. Having read about the Castellan Champion, I couldn't see it being worth the full price cost, and err'ed on the side of caution and saved my money. So I can't comment on that. However, the other two DLC (Duty Eternal and Execution Force) are very much a worthwhile purchase. Execution Force gives you access to four types of assassin, my favourite being the Culexus due its absolutely game breaking abilities (closing enemy reinforcement warp rifts before they open!!!) and outright brutal attacks. Duty Eternal provides you with access to a Dreadnought on specific missions, a techmarine for use on any mission, and a very, very welcome second ship in the form of a Gladius frigate that you can use to send another squad to complete a mission when 'The Bloom' spawns. There are multiple negative comments and reviews out there about the lack of availability for deploying the Dreadnought except on certain missions. To be fair, I understand why; if you could take the dreadnought on every mission, the game would be too easy, even on harder difficulties! Keeping it for use on Technophage missions provides a challenge, but without making the game too easy. The techmarine is also a handy tool in the right situations, with their ability to take along a servitor that can be armed with various different ranged (and melee) weapons.All in all, a solidly built game, one you REALLY need to learn to save regularly and often to avoid any game issues, it really is worthwhile buying the base game and the two DLC noted above, eschewing the Castellan Champion unless it is on sale; at £13 it really isn't worth the cost based on the description of how it works in game.
