_childDocuments_.review: Teaboy's Basic(ish) Reviews....I read a lot of reviews when looking at games on Steam, and it quickly gets tiring – those who write involved, down to the micron scale reviews, although helpful, end up like looking at War & Peace when you’ve only got time for a quick 5 minute dump!  This is middle of the road and to the point – not easy for me as I tend towards sesquipedalian loquaciousness!  Vociferously Verbose?  Alright, verbal diarrhoea.  (Although I hate panning a developer’s work and all the time, effort and love they put into designing these – it is their life after all – this is my honest, personal opinion of my level of enjoyment.  Sorry devs!).  A note on time played:  My Steam clock does not seem to work properly, indeed, it even minuses time on occasion!  Plus, I have a tendency to wander off and leave games running at times, so time played may not be entirely accurate!  Teaboy’s Tonsil Titillators or Toenail Titbits!  (Rating)  Tonsil Tickler (Totally Tops):  The frenchy of which you always dreamt!  To quote a master, “She’s got a tongue like an electric eel and she likes the taste of a Man’s tonsils!”.  An absolute masterpiece and joy to play.  The Tits (Terrific):  Everyone loves playing with these!  Not THE best bit, but such fun on their own you can be lost for hours....mmmm.  What most games you really like score – perfection is so rare after all.   Torso Teaser (Taker of your Time):  It’s a flat stomach....sure it’s nice to look at, run your fingers over, slobber on a bit, sometimes that bellybutton gets your motor running....but it's just basically the corridor between the two ‘gaming rooms’.  The definitive ‘Meh’ - the middle ‘sideways thumb’ option for which everyone on Steam cries.  Todger/Tadger & (scroTum) Taters (Tedious):  Is it an ‘a’ or is it an ‘o’?  Who cares!  The meat can be fun to play with for about 5 minutes of your entire day, the rest it just hangs there and generally gets in the way of doing something else.  The main problem of course, is the two veg sticking to your inside thigh.  This is what this game feels like – the occasional/rare bouts of fun, the rest bobbing like a 19th century British Policeman (now you know why!).  Toenail Tornado (Total Toss):  A playthrough so appalling it’s like being trapped in a Turkish sauna with the ugliest, hairiest, fattest, sweatiest beast of a neolithic hominid who’s trimming his toenails using pliers and the splinters are reminiscent of a scene from the Normandy Landings.  My god how did this get released!?  Teaboy Touts (Score):  Torso TeaserThe Review:  Slow and sad.  But a lovely tribute to a dear friend and thought-provokingly executed.  I would be proud to have a game like this made of me - you can feel the love and deep heartfelt sorrow of the friends who have lost their companion.  There's not much to the puzzles in way of brain usage, but this just means it's relaxing and not frustrating in any way, which is the point - the people behind the game wanted us to know the feelings involved and the love they had for their lost bandmate.  It's a journey of remembrance and recovery, of the person departed and the struggle of the heart with loss.  Beautifully done and a dear tribute, as dear as the soul it's attributed to.  Well done and thank you for sharing her with us.

_childDocuments_.review: 7/10The game is a bit confusing untill u know the story behind the game and what its all about.A band of friends lost their friend and lead singer (Emma Ninel) and is afterwards struggling with depression, despair, guilt and everything else that follows the loss of someone u love.And its about returning to the other things in ur life that u love and moving onwards,The whole interview story stuff is a bit weird and unique when u first start, and its a weird 'story' to a game.Until u find out what its about and that its a game made from real life as a tribute to her (Nina in the game) I didnt know what to expect from this game and i generally dislike jazz with a passion lol, so the game has been a thorn in my eye for a while now when browsing for puzzles and indie games.But I finally gave in and gave it a try, and im glad I did, its an underrated masterpiece tbh!That being said, if ur a hardcore puzzler and here simply for a puzzle challenge, dont pick this game. The puzzles are easy and not the real point of the game.This game deserves more recognition and playthroughs than it currently has!It takes about an hour to finish.Great indie with a great but sad story.Been listening to her songs and as others mention, her voice was amazing and its such a shame she wasnt recognised at the time, the songs are simply amazing and her voice too.Be sure to check out Emma Ninel on YT (like on Tumai999 channel).You know you made an impact and was loved when someone makes a game about you.*If you enter this world knowing you are loved and you leave this world knowing the same, then everything in between can be dealth with.* - MJ

The premise of the game is really interesting and the puzzles were fun to figure out. Definitely worth the play through if you're looking for something easy and relaxing.

_childDocuments_.review: I like puzzles, and I found some simple ones with not too much complexity.You can finish them within 1 hour, which is strange as developers avoid games shorter than 2 hours for the sake of not getting the game refunded after finishing it, and I respect that there are not much of "fillers" to extend it to 2 hours, but you could add some more puzzles.Also, it is not clear why I light street lamps, there is not even a single achievement for it, or do I just turn them on always but the level will not be completed without them, I don't know lol.The graphics, story, and audio are nice.This game is not worth the full price, though.Recommended (with discount) 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: Nice little game you can finish in 1 hour. It's about grief, as many other games (Gris, RiME, Zau), but this time you play the dead character! The singer of a quartet comes back as a ghost to help her band to bear their mourning. The backgrounds are beautiful and the puzzles interesting. Maybe the final could be stronger in emotions.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forest Quartet

_childDocuments_.review: A soft, short game about loss, grief, and finding reasons and the will to continue. The gameplay centers about the spirit of the singer, Nina, getting the band back together for a final concert. Movement was satisfyingly smooth and floaty, and the puzzles were relatively simple, though occasionally it was difficult to tell what was a path, which delayed finding a part needed for the solution. (Singing often helped, by lighting up the surrounding darkness.) The story and music were the main draw, with each section having a theme befitting the band member, and a very lovely final send-off that tied it all together. Overall, a very chill, at times sweet and somber, experience.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forest Quartet

_childDocuments_.review: Game was quite enjoyable, with about 90 minutes of playtime. The soundtrack and audio is phenomenal, which definitely contributes to the atmosphere and emotions. _childDocuments_.name: The Forest Quartet

_childDocuments_.review: Oyunun arka planındaki hikayeyi en iyi radyodaki sunucumuz açıklamış: "Nina akli dengesi yerinde olmayan jazz müzisyenlerinden oluşan bu üçlüyü buluyor ve hepsinin ormana taşınmasını sağlıyor." Grubumuz şehir hayatını terk etmiş ve ormana yerleşmiş bir jazz grubu. Oyunda grubun solisti, yeni ölmüş Nina'nın ruhunu oynuyoruz. Ölümümüzden sonra, her biri farklı bir mental soruna sahip olan ekip arkadaşlarımızın düzelmesi için bölümleri puzzle çözerek geçmeye çalışıyoruz. Bölüm tasarımları ve bahsedilen akıl sağlığı sorunları güzel eşleştirilmiş. Özellikle Fransız kontrbasçı arkadaşımızın sorununda duygu ve hissin çok iyi yansıtıldığını düşünüyorum. Oyun süresi kısa ve puzzlelar basit. Fakat geliştiriciler film yapımı kökenli bir şirket. Asıl odak noktalarının oynaması basit, sinematik açıdan zengin oyunlar yaratmak olduğunu söylemişler ve bu oyunda amaçlarını gerçekleştirmişler. Oyun değil de film ve hikaye odaklı bakan insanların daha çok beğeneceği bir oyun olmuş. Şu anki indirimli fiyatıyla tavsiye ederim.The background story of the game was explained best by our radio host: "So, the story goes, Nina found this trio of mentally unstable jazz musicians and made you all move into the woods." Our band is a jazz band that abandoned city life and settled in the forest. In the game, we play the spirit of the recently deceased Nina, the lead singer of the band. After our death, we try to pass the levels by solving puzzles to heal our teammates, each of whom has a different mental problem. The level designs and the mental health issues mentioned are nicely paired. I think that the emotion and feeling are reflected very well, especially in the question of our French double bass friend. Game time is short. But the developers are a company with filmmaking roots and they said their main focus is to create simple-to-play, cinematically rich games, and I think they achieved their goal in this game. It is a game that people who focus on movies and story rather than games will like it more. I recommend it at its current discounted price.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forest Quartet

_childDocuments_.review: In my garden, all is peace. Grass so green, so soft under my feet. Wind that sways, so sensitively.Nina has passed on. Depression, anxiety, and anger issues - Nina was the glue that bridged the quartet members and eased these tensions. Her final act of love before moving on completely is bringing her friends together for a last performance out in the woods.Lovely game about forests, mental health, and grief. 11/10
_childDocuments_.name: The Forest Quartet

_childDocuments_.review: Expressing what grief feels like is unanimously hard to do. Pain and loss is a unique experience and interpreted in a variety of ways but I think this game does that beautifully. Taking into account each persons perspective, relationship, and sound - this game captivates both the sadness and beauty that comes with life and death extremely well. If you want something to help you get through a similar experience, or even just to grow and reflect by coming to understand themes of life and loss a little more, then this one's for you. It's relaxing overall, has a good OST, and is paced well. A lovely story with even lovelier tunes and the art is pretty, too.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forest Quartet

_childDocuments_.review: The Forest Quartet may be short, but it's an experience that will stay with you long after the final notes fade away. This game is a true masterpiece, offering a poignant journey through a world filled with beauty, mystery, and emotion.From the stunning visuals to the haunting soundtrack, every aspect of The Forest Quartet is meticulously crafted to draw you into its enchanting world. As you explore the forest and uncover its secrets, you'll find yourself captivated by the game's atmosphere and entranced by its melody.But what truly sets The Forest Quartet apart is its ability to evoke genuine emotion in such a short amount of time. Through subtle storytelling and evocative imagery, the game manages to convey a depth of feeling that is truly remarkable. It's a testament to the power of storytelling in games, and a reminder of the emotional impact that can be achieved through simplicity and restraint.In conclusion, The Forest Quartet may be short, but it's an experience that lingers in the mind long after you've finished playing. Whether you're a fan of atmospheric games or simply appreciate beautiful storytelling, this game is not to be missed. Take a moment to step into the forest and let yourself be swept away by its melody—you won't regret it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forest Quartet

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely beautiful game. The sound, the visuals, the effective use of light and shadow and particles, all tied together with the intuitive but interesting game mechanics and the heart warming story. Loved the final concert as well.  The portrayal of the various issues of the band felt authentic and reflected each members challenges well. 10/10 would recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forest Quartet

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very cute lil indie story with a fantastic soundtrack!Pros:- The puzzles are neat- Every band member has a great unique theme to them- The art style is greatCons:- It doesn't utilize the game mechanics well throughout- Parts of the story I feel could have been handled a bit better- Sometimes the movement got a bit slowIt was a good adventure with some nice puzzles and decent game play and the focus is def on the narrative. I think it has room to improve in a lot of categories to be top tier for sure but I think it did a good job as well across the board. i give it 3/4 band mates
_childDocuments_.name: The Forest Quartet

_childDocuments_.review: - Fantastic, artistic aesthetics. Great axonometric 3d graphics with dark color palette and atmospheric lighting conditions.- Amazing eerie world. It has a lonely, peculiar, kind of surreal atmosphere. The forest looks haunted and it's like it was taken from a fairy tale or a dream.- Great animations. The movement of foliage and things in the world around you is so fluid. Character's and creatures' animations are so smooth. Interactions are very pleasant too.- Simplistic, but good and responsive controls.- Awesome jazz music that enhances the mysterious atmosphere and fits perfectly to visuals' vibes.- Great voice acting performances that feel realistic and emotional.- Perfect minimalistic audio design with creepy environmental sounds and cool electronical sound effects during interactions with the generators.- It doesn't have a classical story structure, but it's mostly an atmospheric experience that speaks about psychological states and grief after the loss of a close friend.- It's so calm and relaxing.The bad- Puzzles could be better intergraded to the plot. They are distinctive sections inside the forest separated from the story and the characters. You mostly solve them because they are there and just to continue the dialogues.- Simplistic gameplay. Puzzles are well designed visually but they're shallow pattern matching ones with not much creativity or challenge. You just solve them mechanically.- It's too small and most importantly too personal for the average player to manage to engage with it. It's probably a personal statement or a farewell by its creator.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forest Quartet

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for a puzzle that will challenge you then look for something else.But if you want a short, sorrowful, atmospheric adventure of grief, with a tinge of angst and hope, then this might be for you. The game is really gorgeous and never hampers you into shabby symbolism or any boorish oversentimentality. Pretty straight forward puzzles that never roadblocked me.I have refunded it though since it was free on Epic the next week LOL. In good faith I would like to proclaim its well deserved praise on Steam
_childDocuments_.name: The Forest Quartet

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderfull little gem! Very pleasing to play, super relaxing and just the right amount of challenge set to a beautiful soundtrack. I love this game, the sound design is so full of detail, the game plays so smoothly and the story is so moving. The perfect game for a casual semi impatient player, such as myself. Thank you for this game, please make more sound and music centered games like this!
_childDocuments_.name: The Forest Quartet

_childDocuments_.review: Well that was a beautiful tribute. I wouldn't call this a puzzle as much as a point-and-click story, though there are some basic puzzle elements for beginners. It is shorter than I expected, I would have liked a bit more of the chatter of the group together or an understanding of what made some of these characters themselves.Either way, great game, definitely recommend picking this up and checking it out.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forest Quartet

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful little story about a jazz band dealing with the passing of one of their members. It is a short experience, but with a very compelling and emotional conclusion, so it doesnt feel like it needs to be longer.The gameplay is simple, but rewarding. As you solve the puzzles you learn more and more about the members of the band and also the ethereal ghost you are playing as. Any time I felt like something was missing, or felt like something didnt fit the game, I ended up being surprised, because it the end it all fit together so nicely. I only had very small issues during playing, mainly some inconsistencies regarding whether i could fly somewhere or not. Having invisible walls stopping me when my character is cabable of flying was one of the few less elegant parts of the experience. But it didnt take away much from the game.I recommend it to everyone who is looking for a short, linear, and very well made experience.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forest Quartet

_childDocuments_.review: This is a wonderful little gem of a game. I couldn't have spent my Saturday evening better than playing this from start to finish. The sound design is so creative and mesmerizing, just playing around with how the sound changes when you move objects was sooo satisfying! Also: the jazzzzzzz is so gooooood. The music only plays during relevant moments, which makes you look forward to progressing through the story even more. The graphics are a wonderful balance of weird, like the pulsating organisms and charming, such as the anxiety monsters running away from you but curiously approaching again when they hear the tone of the voice.The story is told through bits and pieces with brilliant voice acting. It's relatable and moving and doesn't feel over the top at all.The gameplay is not very difficult or challenging, but that's also not what the game is about. I personally enjoyed not getting frustrated at puzzles when all I wanted was to vibrate with the world and immerse into the story - which worked perfectly for me.Overall I greatly recommend The Forest Quartet for a quality interactive story experience on a cozy evening!
_childDocuments_.name: The Forest Quartet

_childDocuments_.review: The artistry, in every aspect, was beautiful. There's a depth to the simplicity of this game, that made it thoroughly enjoyable to play.The game moved itself in that it is very easy to see what your next step is as they introduce the controls. The puzzles were fairly simplistic, but the artistry used to depict the mental states of Nina's pals gives even more insight to who you're helping in each moment.Also, MAD credit to Nina's song voice. Gave me goosebumps for the whole concert. Absolutely wonderful!
_childDocuments_.name: The Forest Quartet

_childDocuments_.review: A great little game or I should say a good bye letter that you can play.Great music, I just wish there was more of it at the end.Visuals are lovely. I loved how anxiety, sadness and anger were presented.The puzzles are simple, you will not get frustrated with them.Loved the radio interview parts - it was very much needed to have those jokes so the whole thing isn't too heavy.It's a bit on the short side, but fits the "good bye letter" style. The only thing I miss is a longer concert at the end with maybe 2 more songs or so.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forest Quartet

_childDocuments_.review: I took my time with this little gem, purely so I could absorb the atmosphere, style, and most importantly - the Music. On the surface, this is a puzzle game with several different mechanics that shift as you move through the three chapters. There's nothing particularly challenging about the puzzles themselves and the mechanics are silky smooth. The game never sticks you with a section or a sequence too long, and at no point should users feel like they're forcing themselves through these sections. A big part of this is because these puzzles aren't the main part of the game. The story is.It's short - I'd say 1 to 1.5 hours in length if you don't dilly dally like I did. Definitely playable in a single setting. But it uses the time perfectly to tell a story. Ultimately, this is about the shattering of a creative collective and the untimely loss of the glue of the band. Each of the members in the band have their own struggles to push through in order to make it to the final show, to honour their singer. The voice acting is absolutely on point. Having spent time with jazz groups and ensembles, it felt so natural and organic. The interview sections as a retrospect was a wonderful story telling tool, with a new segment offered as a reward for completing the various puzzles.The final act is outstanding, with a phenomenal piece of music and a dedication to the singer of the song - Emma Ninel. I'd not heard of Emma, nor her music, but was floored by the song chosen for this piece and have been listening to her work on repeat since finishing the game.The Forest Quartet is a perfect example of short story telling in video games. It's short, but it's full of heart with equal parts light and darkness which is paramount in a true jazz tale. The final piece I will say is the art style is exceptional. The colour palate of dark greens mixed with the shining gold lights is magical, the shadows playing are fantastic, and each level felt familiar, yet unique. This game was an excellent way to spend a Saturday afternoon.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forest Quartet

_childDocuments_.review: Full gameplay: This game is a short journey of what we go through our lives as humans, struggles, depressions, sadness, happiness, ...It was a beautiful game with emphasis on understanding we all are humans with our problems. Visually game is looking really good with some easy puzzles that are enjoyable to solve.The only negative side of it was the amount of gameplay, I wish there was more of this story telling and telling more about each band member.
_childDocuments_.name: The Forest Quartet

_childDocuments_.review: ~Simple but satisfying puzzles and a story that will move you to tears.~     I loved how you get to know just enough about each character as you play and the way each emotion was portrayed in the environment really immersed you in what they were feeling. Top that off with some fantastic music and you've got yourself a game that's absolutely worth playing!

_childDocuments_.review: The Forest Quartet is a puzzle adventure about a gone, but not forgotten, lead singer. Play her spirit and travel through 3 acts unique to the members of her band for a final farewell concert. Face their emotions, solve puzzles and fight the corruption plaguing their souls.

detailed_description: Atelier Sophie 2: The Alchemist of the Mysterious Dream Digital Deluxe Edition In this set: - The main game 'Atelier Sophie 2: The Alchemist of the Mysterious Dream' - Atelier Series Legacy Swimsuit Set A set of six swimming costumes based on designs introduced in past Atelier titles, one for each character: Sophie, Plachta, Ramizel, Alette, Olias, and Diebold. - Useful Weapons Set A set of six weapons with useful effects such as 'Normal Attack Count +2' that you can equip from the beginning of the game, one for each character: Sophie, Plachta, Ramizel, Alette, Olias, and Diebold. - Useful Items Set A set of useful items that you would usually have to wait to acquire in the second half of the game, including three types of talismans, Traveler's Shoes that increase your movement speed, Victor's Charm that increases the amount of Cole earned after a battle by 4%, and Training Charm that increases the amount of EXP gained after a battle by 10%. Note: Costumes can be changed in the 'Changing Room' at the desk in the atelier. The DLC items can be obtained from the Container in the atelier. Weapons and talismans can only be used after you progressed the game to the point where you can change your equipment. Please visit the official website for more information. Please beware that the main game 'Atelier Sophie 2: The Alchemist of the Mysterious Dream' is currently also available for purchase separately and in the 'Atelier Sophie 2: The Alchemist of the Mysterious Dream Ultimate Edition' set. Atelier Sophie 2: The Alchemist of the Mysterious Dream Ultimate Edition In this set: - Atelier Sophie 2: The Alchemist of the Mysterious Dream Digital Deluxe Edition - Atelier Sophie 2 Season Pass Access to 14 DLCs that will be added in the future. The Season Pass content will become available starting from March 2022. - Season Pass Bonus: Sophie/Ramizel's Costumes 'Grandma's Outfit (Matching Set)' A pair of costumes for Sophie and Ramizel based on a special costume previously released for 'Atelier Sophie: The Alchemist of the Mysterious Book DX'. Included in the Season Pass: 1. Sophie's Costume 'Alchemist of the Mysterious Journey' 2. Plachta's Costume 'Haute Couture' 3. Ramizel's Costume 'Ertona Hunter' 4. Sophie/Plachta/Ramizel/Alette's Costumes 'Bunny-Eared Salesgirl' 5. Recipe Expansion Pack 'The Art of Synthesis' 6. Recipe Expansion Pack 'The Art of Battle' 7. Gust Extra BGM Pack 8. Sophie's Swimsuit 'White Canvas' 9. Plachta's Swimsuit 'Clivia Nobilis' 10. Ramizel's Swimsuit 'Agapanthus Romance' 11. Alette's Swimsuit 'Rainmaker' 12. Olias's Swimsuit 'Vegetable Garden' 13. Diebold's Swimsuit 'Knight Commander' 14. Extra Scenario/Area 'Atelier Plachta' Note: Items 1 to 7 are planned to be released before the end of April 2022, and items 8 to 14 are planned to be released before the end of May 2022. Items 1 to 4 and 8 to 13 are individual character costumes. Costumes can be changed in the 'Changing Room' at the desk in the atelier. Items 5 and 6 add new recipes and catalysts that can be purchased from Gnome at 'Crystal Sparkle Pavilion' after progressing the story. Item 7 adds new in-game BGM tracks that can be changed at the desk in the atelier. Item 14 will feature an additional story episode with young Plachta as the main character, set in the time after she arrived in Erde Wiege and before she first met Sophie. Players will play as Plachta, with Diebold and Ramizel available as party members. This DLC will also feature a unique area and new items. The content of the Season Pass, release dates and order are subject to change without notice. Please visit the official website for more information. Atelier Sophie 2 Season Pass and all items included in it can be purchased separately at a later date. Please avoid making redundant purchases. Please beware that the main game and other sets featuring same items are currently available for purchase separately and in other sets as well. About the Game A mysterious story of a mysterious dream ... This is a story about one of the adventures Sophie the Alchemist had after she left her hometown of Kirchen Bell. It is centered around Sophie's quest of searching for Plachta after they are separated in a dream world of Erde Wiege, and the new friends they meet there. Main features: - Evolved Seamless Turn-Based Battles This game incorporates new multi-link turn battles that feature six party members divided in two teams and begin seamlessly when players encounter enemies while exploring. The combat experience is enriched by a multitude of special effects and actions, including special Dual Trigger skills that involve two of the team members attacking in unison. - Two Types of the Panel-Based Synthesis This game features an accessible puzzle-like synthesis system where you place ingredients on a panel to create new items. Players can choose to use either the Standard Panel or the Restricted Panel, which will increase both the difficulty level and the rewards. - Manipulate the Weather to Open New Paths While each region of Erde Wiege has fixed weather, you will be able to change this with the help of special tools. Changing the weather will allow you to not only change the scenery when visiting the same area but also gain access to new, previously inaccessible places. Perhaps the weather will affect even the materials you can collect? Note: Please visit the official website for more information. Please beware that the main game is currently also available for purchase in the 'Atelier Sophie 2: The Alchemist of the Mysterious Dream Digital Deluxe Edition' set and 'Atelier Sophie 2: The Alchemist of the Mysterious Dream Ultimate Edition' set.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, 29 hours and I decided to stop. I've tried the Atelier franchise several times now, and this is by far the furthest I've gotten.I can see why the people who like this franchise like it. It's cute, it's pretty, it's content rich, it's mechanically deep. I... I just can't immerse myself when the plot is essentially, "we're cute! Watch us be friends!" At hour ten, I started skipping side character cut scenes, and at hour twenty started skipping main plot cutscenes. All characters, main included, are paper thin. They have a singular 'thing' that they are about and their entire presentation resolves around that one quality. Olias for example, is the cocky, "world's best bodyguard." Every conversation with him is about that. "Don't worry girls, world's best bodyguard here to protect you!" or "Life's really busy for a bodyguard as talented or popular as me!" The guy is just about incapable of having a human conversation. Everyone else just talks about that topic too, in conversations with him.I also got pretty frustrated by all the male characters jumping into danger shouting "don't worry, we'll protect you!" to all the female characters.The story itself is basically just, "my friend is missing, let's go look for her!" And then they wander around the world doing cycles of, "is she here?" "no... awwww" "let's try the next place!." I played through the entire previous publication by this company, blue reflection:second light and its story was so much more heart wrenching and detailed.Bascially the characters and the story really just don't resonate with me.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright here we go, 100% achievements reviewI'm gonna start by saying that I started the Atelier Series with both Ryza games which I LOVED and also 100%'d with no complains and relative ease.For my fellow Ryza lovers this is a warning, this game does NOT play like the Ryza games.the game's crafting is completely different and compareable to a tetris type board and requires a lot more thinking.Rather than Ryza's just start from a simple blueprint item and build it to the 5th blueprint and get stupid strong substats and quality, Sophie 2 requires you to do each item separately and item quality and traits instead come from trait combinations and puzzle combos such as getting 8 yellow combos to add another item to the crafting etc.The combat is once again NOT like Ryza. Ryza combat is real time turn based, meaning your turns are based on your speed, but are reactive and the fight keeps going as you take your turn. Sophie 2 is basic turn based. you still take your turns based on speed, but plays like a regular turn based whereas time stops when you take your turn. Which for me is a lot less hands on for tougher fights and ends up being less fun. the collectathon and craft gameplay still allowed me to overlevel and craft in ways that  normal jrpgs do not allow, which is of course what I loved about my previous 2 atelier titles. The only difference for this game is that the crafting is much slower and requires more though and ingame time and in my own experience makes item usage less important, even in my final battle (achievement for beating the final boss on very hard) to not require hardly any items.I genuinely think the crafting in this game for my own playstyle overstayed it's welcome, the achievement for crafting requires both Sophie and Plachta to reach level 99 alchemy. unfortunately, this eventually led to me making All craftable items for both girls and still having level 94 for Plachta. So I ended up making 52 necklaces to compensate for this, which took at least an extra 30min-an hour to get her to 99.The story of Atelier is, same as the others, of no real consequence. The gameplay far outweighs the simple story by leaps and bounds and you could literally play this game with no fx or voice and sound and get the same gameplay experience.I WILL say however, that the ending story payoff was wayyyy better than either Ryza games and made me tear up. After 75 hours that ending really kinda touched my heart.1 huge warning for people that want to 100% the game. you do NOT return to before the final boss after the ending so make sure you save your game! otherwise you risk screwing yourself if you don't get her on very hard!last tip is that changing the difficulty to very hard for the final boss achievement seemed rediculous at first, but with patience and strategy, got me to 100% completion and was actually insanely fun to me, considering how easy these games are!Overall this game played wayyy longer than either Ryza game, but with a few breaks I still managed to easily 100% the game. I will definitely play the next game in the series and 100% it too!I did still really enjoy this game, so this review is simply an information block for Ryza junkies, hope you enjoy the game and give it what it's worth! let's go Atelier series!

_childDocuments_.review: Before we start, let me explain why I think this game is very important for the JRPG genre considering the current state of the Japanese gaming industry. A lot of JRPG developers these days are currently more focused on bringing new players, especially from the west, and because of this strategy, many of them are completely throwing away the past and tradition of their games in order to appeal to the new audience. A lot of JRPG franchises that used to have anime graphics and turn based combat are now real time action with realistic graphics. This strategy has been working really well for many developers considering the sales numbers of recent games, but I'm not a big fan of this trend and I think it also divides the fan base.Sophie 2 doesn't follow this trend and is both a gift and a love letter to the long-time fans of the Atelier series. It keeps the traditional turn based combat and alchemy system while improving even further with excellent animations and a lot of QoL options. Sophie 2 shows that Gust actually cares about both long-time fans of the series and newcomers that joined after the Ryza games.There are a lot of Quality of Life additions that make the gameplay experience much smoother. Gust did a really good job with the gameplay in Sophie 2. It's a very refined experience without stress and no time wasted. Fully turn based and makes good use of the elemental weakness system. All 6 characters participate in battle, 3 in the front and 3 in the back, and even the characters that are in the back can participate actively with Dual attacks. The combat is an absolute joy to play. Really fun with incredible animations and character poses. Smooth transitions between field and battle without loading screens. There's also a turbo mode with up to 2.0x speed to make farming stuff even faster. Very smooth item gathering with one button. The maps are really big and all of them are interconnected with a lot of points to interact and discover new items with different tools. The weather changing system is very creative and add a lot of depth to the exploration since it can change the enemies and the items you can gather in the same map and also unlocks paths to new areas. It's a rich and big world with a lot to discover. Sophie moves fast, the items you can get and points of interest are properly indicated on the maps, there's a very handy full map overlay, and you can get different materials with different tools without the need to change them every time like in Ryza.  An improvement based on the Mysterious trilogy. It's pretty much the same puzzle-like grid where you have to make links and increase the items level based on each element to make more powerful proprieties to appear and then transfer traits to the new item. It's the best alchemy system in my opinion and I had a lot of fun creating new items. The progression is also really good. The recipe book gives some tips on how to unlock new recipes and they give the player a really good incentive to fully enjoy what the game has to offer by creating a certain item with a specific propriety, defeating a certain enemy, doing certain things during battle, etc...Item duplication and auto-restock with Pirka is very handy and makes everything crafting related much more manageable.The story in Sophie 2 is pretty much what you would expect from an Atelier game, but it's more than just "cute girls doing cute things". The story has much more depth, meaning and emotion, and it kept me engaged all the time. It's still first and foremost a friendly story between Sophie and the other characters, but it has good pacing and some mystery behind the world of dreams. The main aspect that makes the story interesting is the characters, they are great, have good personality, and each of them have their own dreams they want to fulfill.Playing the first game is not necessary but there are some references that only those who played Sophie 1 will understand.Every single side character has a storyline across each chapter and a conclusion to their story with fully dedicated screen time in a very long emotional cutscene by the end of the game. It doesn't end in a cliffhanger and properly connects to Atelier Firis, which is the next game following the chronological order.The game took me about 58 hours to finish.The graphics in Sophie 2 is based on the same engine of Ryza 2. Everything in this game looks very lively and colorful, it's definitely a beautiful game driven by excellent design and art style. Gust has stepped up their game with animations this time around. The facial expressions show a lot more emotion and the movement of the characters are much better than in previous games making the cutscenes much more enjoyable to watch.The battle animations are the real stars of the show in my opinion, especially the Dual Trigger attack animations that put many modern JRPGs to shame. The character poses when selecting skills are also really cool and a very creative part considering that in most games you just look at the character's back in idle animation while selecting an attack.The battle poses and win poses are one integral part of JRPGs and Gust nailed it in Sophie 2.The soundtrack in this game is excellent, as always. Gust never disappoints when it's about music.There are multiple battle themes and all of them are great. I think it was very interesting how they managed to make the game sound familiar to the fist game while also making a completely new different set of tracks. It's not just a rearrange of music from the previous game.Voice acting is also excellent in this game and the seiyuus great work really help bring the characters to life. Yuuka Aisaka, Yuka Iguchi, Rie Takahashi and Reina Ueda are all part of the cast and I'm sure you've probably heard their voice at least once if you're into anime/JRPGs.Yes, it's the usual Koei Tecmo thing. Sophie 2 PC Port is pretty much on the same level of quality of Blue Reflection 2.I did not encounter any bugs or crashes during my entire playthrough. It's perfect.The problem is really on the performance side. I was able to play the game on a GTX 1050 Ti at 900p Standard quality and Ambient Occlusion Off at 60fps with drops to the 40s in heavier areas. The game still looks good even at this setting and it runs at 60fps most of the time.They still need to optimize their engine for PC, but just being able to play this at 60fps with acceptable quality on low-end hardware such as the 1050 Ti is already a pretty big deal over PS4, which runs at 30fps.Sophie 2 is a 10/10 for me. It's the best in the series across all aspects. No wonder why it has overwhelmingly positive status on Steam reviews. Gust outdid themselves with Sophie 2. It's a love letter to long-time fans. Excellent full turn based combat system, good story with emotions, a lot of gameplay QoL options, excellent and very refined alchemy system, a great cast of characters, a very good soundtrack, excellent battle and super attack animations, win poses, and the list goes on!The game keeps a very familiar feel and the traditional JRPG style while also improving literally everything. Gust showed how a modern JRPG is done. They showed that a good JRPG doesn't need to be open world with real time combat and ultra realistic graphics.I really hope they keep making more games at this level of quality, keeping both the Sophie style and the Ryza style concurrently in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: After being very disappointed with Atelier Sophie 1, I was hesitant to try this one, but I'm pleased to say that Sophie 2 eliminates almost all of what I disliked from Sophie 1 while keeping the same sort of cozy feel.This game bridges the time between the events of Sophie 1 (there's a nice video summary at the title screen if you didn't play it or it's been a long time) and Firis.  It takes place in a dream world/dimension, so it is mostly separated from the main Mysterious storyline.  The game is more for giving you insight into Sophie's past and relationship with Plachta.Graphically it's a great improvement (as expected as the first Sophie was from 2015).  The graphics look very similar to the Ryza games, and all the game and graphical settings are in the game (same as Ryza 2).  A lot of the terrain and material objects are directly copied over from the Ryza games, but the terrain has a bit more variety.  The widely varied terrain is fitting with the dream world theme.  One late game dungeon is absolutely phenomenal, looking like you're in space among a series of floating islands.Exploration is also far far improved over the first Sophie.  There are large maps with some verticality as in the Ryza games, the gimmick this time is weather manipulation.  You will eventually be able to switch between 4 different weather, and each one can have a different set of pathways open up or close.  Monsters and gathering ingredients available are often different when you change the weather, making it a puzzle to access some of the more difficult nodes.  Not all maps support all weather.  Weather control uses items with charges, and those charges get used up pretty quickly.  You'll need to regularly recharge the weather control items with crafting, this can be frustrating.  Make sure you have enough charges as it's very easy to need a long chain to open the way to the next teleporter/door/gate but run out, making you have to go back and recharge and redo all that progress.  The charges are removed VERY late game, after the "point of no return" warning.Music is great as always, it retains the same mellow piano feel that Sophie 1 had, while giving you at least a little more excitement during battles.  It's quite different from the music of the Ryza games which is a nice change of pace, differentiating the series from one another.  One regions track gives me a feel reminiscent of Atelier Ayesha.  Sound effects are pretty solid, though some are obviously taken from the Ryza games.  Voice acting is all Japanese, while expected for any more recent Atelier game, I really did find I missed Sophie and Plachta's English voice actors.  The Japanese voices are good, but I found the English ones (especially for Plachta) far better.Gameplay replaces the not-great system of Sophie with a new turn based system that I found extremely enjoyable.  There are 3 active and 3 reserve party members.  It's pure turn based, the gimmick this time is that doing actions will fill a bar, and allow you to issue dual actions.  These allow two characters to attack at once (one active and one reserve).  The reserve character will then swap in to the active party.  Since you can't manually swap in or out characters unless dead, you will be using the dual attacks often to get the characters you need.  There are also support blocks, using the same meter that fuels dual attacks.  These support blocks work similarly to the ones in the Dusk games, but since Sophie is pure turn based, you don't need to react at all.  You'll instead see the enemies action and can decide to use a support block or just let the attack through.  You have two alchemists in your party, each of which has a general focus and can use most of the items in the game; while the other four characters each specialize in a different element and damage type.  Element, damage type (magic or physical), status effects, and knockback all matter quite a bit for the new aura system that enemies have.Enemies can put up auras, bosses can put up several during a fight.  These auras are shields that reduce incoming damage until broken.  They have some sort of weakness, depending on the type of aura, such as wind damage or magical damage or status effects.  They also are often immune to certain types of damage, like an ice aura takes no damage from ice.  Finally, they often have a type of damage or effect that triggers a devastating counter attack, you definitely want to avoid doing that.  Hitting the auras weakness or applying debuffs will remove stacks from the aura and eventually break it.  A few other effects, like blocking with certain talismans and a few late game skills will also reduce aura stacks.  Being able to efficiently break auras, which stuns the enemy, is vital in more difficult fights.Crafting uses the grid based system, it's a lot less limited than in the first Sophie.  You start with the ability to rotate pieces, and most ingredients contain multiple smaller "chunks" to fit into the cauldron.  The item links and general nature of the crafting makes a lot more sense than the original while still having a high skill ceiling.  Learning recipes by killing monsters, doing certain actions in combat or exploration, collecting ingredients, and crafting certain items with certain effects returns.  Learning feels a bit easier than some of the very difficult ones to unlock in the first game.  It remains in a "skill" tree where you have to unlock some previous ones to unlock the next ones in the tree.  You have 3 different trees this time, as you have two alchemists each with their own levels and their own unique recipes along with a tree of "common"/shared recipes.  You need to level both alchemists, as there are storyline gates requiring certain crafting levels.Crafting is very important, these turn based battles can get really difficult.  If you do not work hard on your alchemy, you will get destroyed.  Even with fairly high end gear and around 1000hp on my characters (Diebold 1300), I was getting nearly 1-shot by some late game boss attacks.  Debuffs are also vital, it's a great idea to make an item that applies lots of debuffs as that will be what keeps you alive late.  Good Breezy Aroma items (AoE healing) will also be important to make.  The turn based nature of the game makes it so the difficulty can be way up, and you need to both prepare and execute the puzzle like nature of the fights well.The story is better than Sophie 1, but just like with all Atelier games the best part are the character interactions and scenes.  Sophie's a lovable character as always.  Sophie gets to meet another Plachta, and Ramizel is an important character to Sophie's past.  Both of these characters are excellent.  The other characters are all fun as well, I'm personally fond of Diebold and his (mostly) calm supportive strength.  Only Elvira can feel a bit grating, but she's still a decent character overall for the story and plot.Overall, excellent Atelier game, definitely among the top ones in my opinion.  The improvements made over Sophie 1 and some aspects of Ryza 1 make me hopeful for future entries in the series.  I really wasn't fond of the Mysterious games before, but this one is excellent and worth a buy.  Excellent combat, very good crafting, good exploration, and good character interactions make up for the weaker (but still decent for an Atelier title) story and frustrations with constantly recharging your weather control items.
_childDocuments_.name: Atelier Sophie 2: The Alchemist of the Mysterious Dream

_childDocuments_.review: Atelier Sophie 2 will be the most memorable game of the Atelier series for me hands down. The cast is wonderful, the theme of the story is handled delicately, and it touches on some very human issues without being too cringy about it like many anime JRPG games tend to do. Story aside, the gameplay has never been better. There are several quality of life changes, and the best of them is what they did with the tools. You don't have to swap to them anymore. All tools have been consolidated to a single button. If you have it equipped, it doesn't matter if it's a rock you need to mine or pool of water to fish from, you will pick it up with a single click.I have little to comment about combat other than I hate so much the barrier mechanic. You could tell they wanted to try something new with combat, but it fell flat because most of the times you are forced against playing how you want to, and are pigeon-holed into playing a certain way. You MUST bring down the barrier when it comes to boss fights, otherwise you will deal little to no damage.Progress far enough into the game, and you will begin to constantly come across mobs and bosses with barriers. There are multiple kinds of barriers that mitigate overall damage, requiring certain elements, effect, or damage type to reduce X amount of times. Why is that bad you say? Because the beefy item you and I have so affectionately crafted to max out does 95% less damage to the boss. It gets easier a little later when you round out your crafts and weapons though, so it doesn't become too bad if you put in the effort to learn them.That being said, crafting in Sophie 2 is the most fun I've had in a while. Oh, I love it. There are hidden effects that you must combine in order to discover. However, these are the VERY VERY strong kind of effects, and not at all necessary to craft strong items with. It is mainly for those who really want to take it a step further.The recipe tree, on the other hand, feels incredibly regressive and sometimes outright frustrating. It continues to use the same mechanic in the previous games: You craft an item or progress the story, then the adjacent craftables unlock. However, the added component of "Gather Item: X" often leaves you scratching your head.Imagine, you have gathered item X possibly enough times already that you don't need to pick up anymore. Any future crafts that require X you don't need to go out and find anymore because you have plenty of it. But wait! Suddenly, you have unlocked a recipe that requires you to gather X. Unfortunately, since you have previously gathered enough of it and it has gone to the back of your mind, you don't know for sure where it is. There are hundreds of gatherables to remember all of them after all, it can be in a dozen different areas, and upon going to the right map you have to scour the entire place. BUT WAIT. Since certain gatherables are unlocked behind certain weather patterns, you have to sort through another instance of inconvenience.No, the gathers are not retroactive. Just because you gathered it hours or days ago, you don't earn credit to the recipe until it pops up in the book for you to go figure it out. Do that about 40 different times and it becomes very tedious.I forgive those flaws because crafting is just so much damn fun in this game, but I would be lying if I said they didn't sour the gameplay a little for me.What I love most about Atelier Sophie 2 is it becomes increasingly clear that this game is a love letter to the devs themselves and to you, the player. The whole premise and theme of the game is about dreams. No, not the ones when we sleep. The dreams you have. Your aspirations. The goals you strive to achieve.The cast comes to life by embodying those at different stages of following their dreams. Some have failed and lost it, others have achieved it, many are in limbo in what to do or in the process of achieving their dreams, and there are plenty who are still searching. it all comes full circle because we know Sophie's dream is to become a licensed and great alchemist that helps people. And you help her do exactly just that.It is even more beautiful when you remember who one of the most important people in Sophie's life is, which is her grandma. The culmination of the touching story actually made me teary-eyed when it completed her character arc, thus closing this chapter of Sophie Neuenmuller and possibly the era of her series.
_childDocuments_.name: Atelier Sophie 2: The Alchemist of the Mysterious Dream

_childDocuments_.review: Same satisfying gameplay loop of the other Atelier games. Atelier Sophie 1 was actually my first in the series, and it's crazy to see how much improvement they've made. Before characters barely animated, NPCs rarely had anything useful or interesting to say, voice acting was minimal (though that did allow for localization unlike this one), cut scenes were practically nonexistent, and the game didn't bother to teach you that making gear was more important than leveling up. Now their battle camera is dynamic, characters you aren't interacting with all have different idle poses, even randos in town have voice acting, and there's a new in-engine cut scene every 5 minutes with several facial expressions and lip sync.Overall, if feels like they took a bunch of the mechanics from Atelier Ryza 2 and brought back the old cauldron mechanics from Sophie 1. It's a good mix, and making different exploration tools that increase in efficiency as you get better at alchemy and find better materials does add another satisfying layer to the gameplay loop.The series has come a long way, and I'm glad they are getting a bigger budget to expand their audience. The one drawback to that new success may be the costumes. I feel like they are a lot more "fan servicey" than they used to be. Female characters show a lot more skin - especially cleavage - in this one. If you don't have to worry about your wife walking in at awkward times (like I do) that may be purely positive for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Another year, another Atelier game. This is now the 23rd entry in the series and it might just be the best yet.As someone that literally finished the first a couple weeks ago and then played through this sequel - I wouldn’t say it’s really all that necessary. Not that the first game is bad, but just that its story is particularly weak for an Atelier game and the fact that the entire thing can be summed up in a roughly four minute recap video tells you all you need to know about how complex the story was there.So if you do want to jump in right here, it’s completely fine and the recap video will serve you well enough.The Tetris system makes its return and is somehow even better than it already was. Now, instead of having to swap cauldrons around to do things like rotate ingredients, you’re able to do that right off the bat and in its place you get some other neat features like link pieces, super successes, catalysts, and even an outright second alchemist to use.It’s somehow much easier to understand and pick up than in the first game, yet maintains that same level of complexity - if not more so. The bulk of this is likely due to the new UI, which makes it much easier to identify ingredients, elements, etc. Whatever the case, I found myself really getting into it, trying to get the perfect ingredient spread to fill up all the spaces without overlapping, rotating the pieces just right to get the maximum number of links, and really just trying to min-max my way to some stupidly powerful items.Honestly, it might be the best I’ve seen in the series yet and this is coming from someone that has played nine entries.Taking cues from Ryza, the game world is now this big, inter-connected thing. It’s not necessarily open world, but each area is large enough on its own that it kinda gives that impression. It’s not one of those “empty” open worlds though. There’s hills, forests, caves, ruins, and these are all flooded with enemies, items, treasure, and other stuff to find.Ingredients are actually visible on the map this time and the combat now takes place without any loading screens. The game may have dropped some of the additional exploration tools introduced in the last Ryza game, but in its place introduced a new weather system.The weather system was pretty cool at first, but I can’t deny that I became a bit iffy on it as the game went on. Having to cycle around the different weather settings to get to where I needed to go can be a bit tedious and it doesn’t help that the weather items have a set number of uses before being depleted.The game does provide waypoints on the map that can be traveled to once activated, so it is not as annoying once you’ve explored an area, but I would say this new addition is okay at best.Compared to some other genres it might not be the best, but for an Atelier game the graphics are absolutely some good stuff and comparable to the quality we got in the past two Ryza games. Actual level geometry, buildings that aren’t just giant blocks, and the character models are noticeably more crisp. Great news, as Sophie might just be my favorite Atelier protagonist design-wise.Combat is yet again another area of improvement and it feels really nice to finally get back to the tried and true turn-based formula of past Atelier games. For one, it’s fast-paced. Because entering combat requires no loading screens, you’re thrown right into it and can immediately start duking it out. Animations can be sped up to 2x and that was pretty much the default for me. The animations are already fast enough, but keeping it at 2x makes battles go significantly faster and you can easily get the materials you need from certain monsters within a matter of seconds.And if you do want to take it slow, there is a good bit of depth here. Twin actions, type matchups, skills, abilities, changing the weather mid-battle, and of course, all of the different items that can be crafted and then used in battle. It doesn’t go too out there in terms of complexity, but it’s not this dead simple thing either.In the first Sophie, it felt like I was constantly doing the same basic process over and over - unlocking a new recipe, crafting it, then having to hunt down the next recipe to craft and so on. There was little actual story content until the end and a lot of the time I was doing guesswork trying to figure out which NPC, item, area, or whatever triggered the next recipe idea to allow me to progress.Sophie 2 pretty much does away with this system entirely. Recipe ideas are still there and get triggered as you do stuff, but I hardly ever found myself locked behind some mystery gate for hours trying to figure out what to do. Instructions are not as vague, relevant NPCs, items, and monsters are marked on the map, and the game in general doesn’t waste your time grinding out recipes.The story this time is actually NOT terrible. Not only is the writing better, but the plot is weaved in and out of the gameplay in a manner that doesn’t require it to all be dropped at the end to wrap up in the time remaining. From the start you are constantly getting new cutscenes, character backgrounds, story events - the entire slate. There is much more dialogue this time around, but I also found it to be more interesting.I won’t sit here and tell you that it’s the best around - I mean, Atelier games generally aren't known for their writing - but it was engaging enough that it didn’t feel like an interruption to the otherwise excellent gameplay.Running at max settings, 1440p and 144 fps on my 3080 Ti was fine and I didn’t have any stability issues there, but the UI has this weird bug (I assume it is a bug) where whenever certain menus open or close, the game dips to 30 fps for a split second, resulting in a visible slowdown.This is best demonstrated when opening a recipe for crafting or opening your storage container to view ingredients. Doing so immediately dips the fps before climbing back up again once the menu is visible. However, I also noticed the issue when gathering items on the map. When doing so, items are listed on the left side of the screen for a few seconds before disappearing and, unfortunately, when they do vanish from the screen, the game microstutters.Otherwise, the PC port is fine. Runs well, no crashes, and even has a good amount of settings to change - at least for a Koei Tecmo port. Controls on a controller are flawless, but the keyboard and mouse controls were practically unplayable for me. There is no mouse cursor for menus, the mouse is not locked to the game window when controlling the camera, and it jitters constantly. This is definitely not a game I would recommend if you do not have a controller to play it with.Atelier Sophie 2 is the best in the series yet, combining the elements that made the first Sophie fun with the recent advancements in Ryza to deliver a familiar, yet modernized Atelier experience. In-depth crafting, fun turn-based combat, great graphics and music, a story that is actually not terrible - there’s a lot of good to say about this game even if it may have a few technical flaws and some iffy elements. For newcomers, it still might be best to start with Ryza, but Sophie 2 is an easy next best choice.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!!

_childDocuments_.review: After the gruelling suffering that was Elden Ring, Sophie 2 is a great relaxing JRPG. More of the same ol' "cute girls doing cute girls" and I couldn't enjoy it more. My autism was augmented with alchemy crafting and while sometimes the slice of life style stories of Atelier games can be a bit boring I enjoyed all of the characters and bits here right up to the ending.Even though it's Sophie 2 I don't think you miss all that much by not playing the first game first, and it seems very friendly to newcomers of the series.10/10 again, I'd take Atelier over CoD for a yearly release any day.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wish I can say I really love this game but the reality is, there are too many unnecessary elements or functions in this game that makes it not as enjoyable as the other ateliers. I personally really do not enjoy changing the weather numerous times while exploring a new map, not to mention sometimes you change weather just to get a treasure box. I find it really annoying and time consuming, not in an enjoyable way. You spend so much time crafting those weather stones and it feels dumb. To me, there are many clumsiness in the game play, which does not make it more fun or satisfying. Also, system requirement is too high for the game and I don't think it necessarily looks a lot more advanced. The mixing method is also just so-so, it's quite difficult to achieve a high level of excellence (I am not a pro and I already set my difficulty level low). I might be very critical but for this price point, I expect it to be more fun than it currently is. I still find joy in playing, after all I paid $70 for it, though I find it hard to believe it is worth the price tag of $115 for dream deluxe. Atelier series is always very special to me as I have had many fun playing them and I own more than 10. However, Sophie 2 sadly is not one of the most polished atelier games for me. I wish they make a sequel of Lulua as I truly enjoyed that one. It's not that I do not recommend this game, I just want to give it a more neutral review.

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost:  I tried to go back and play it after nearly finishing the main story and it was torture to suddenly lose all of the quality of life upgrades that the main story has. The inability to fast travel in the DLC story feels physically painful when you've spent 100 hours fast traveling all over the place lol.That aside, atelier sophie 2 is pretty gratifying and does a lot of the same things right that it did in the first game. I took my time with this one but there's still a good chunk of things I could do if I still had the interest after the fat chunk of hours I've spent on it.

_childDocuments_.review: Best Atelier game since Shallie.  I vastly prefer the classic combat to the slow plodding combat of Ryza.  Sophie herself is as charming as ever and the overall game is fun and packed full of recipes and fun areas to explore.  The soundtrack is really, really good.   That said, it's an anime game.  So you will have to pay the usual anime tax of installing Special K to fix all the frame pacing and sloppy port issues.  It runs like a dream after that tho.   For me that's a small price to pay since literally no one else makes a game quite like this.    Strongly recommended, especially for fans of the pre-Ryza games.

_childDocuments_.review: 21 hours later and only about halfway through the story, so take this review with a grain of saltAltier Sophie is a very enjoyable game set after the events of the first game (obviously). Sophie now finds herself in a dream world that allows her to meet new characters and even a few surprise characters from the original game. That's about all I'll say about the story as that's all I cared to follow on it. Being perfectly honest here, I haven't been that impressed with the Altier games stories. I don't know if it's the dialogue or the heavily recycled/cheap animation shortcuts they take, but I just can't get too invested in these characters or the story they're involved in.Thankfully where Altier Sophie lacks in story, it makes up for in it's game play loop. You are an alchemist (again obviously) so you wander the maps in this game gathering up various resources to meld them all to create you're latest mad experiment, be it weapons, armor, explosives, cra... I MEAN medicine. As a gamer who hasn't played many games with this style of game play, I find it to be enjoyable, rewarding, and relaxing. My one sole critique with this one part of the game is the board that is used to combine the ingredients is very one note. there's no variation in the board itself so your not presented with much challenge outside of how to arrange the actual ingredients.The combat of this game is also enjoyable in it's own right (take it from the guy who usually doesn't enjoy turn based combat) neat party swaps, fun animations, plus the option to speed up the combat speed to make grinding feel a little less tedious (thanks to whoever pitched that idea) Honestly I preferred the seamless combat in Altier Ryza, but this one is still good. The only downside is the difficulty spikes you encounter with each boss battle, you'll be going through the dungeon area and not even realize you're about to come up on a boss battle.  The other annoyance is that you can't flee to grind levels or get better geared for it.Not a super technical gamer, but the only trouble I've run into is the occasional PERSISTENT frame drops, makes the game feel choppy, but tends to go away after loading a new area. Which reminds me... the load times in this game are actually VERY QUICK. I know people expect nonexistent load times, but with how fast you can go from your cozy home to the current dungeon is a great touch.all and all, I give this game an 8/10, worth your time if you enjoy just a fun slice of life adventure. No huge complex plot (by JRPG standards) lots of quirky characters, fun game play loop, and a decent combat system. Plus plenty of cute potential waifus (again.... obviously)

_childDocuments_.review: Don't let the cover art fool you.  This is the kind of game where you're taking notes in a notebook while referencing spreadsheets on another screen, only for hours to pass and still not have made any headway into the game.  The Atelier series is all about min-maxing crafting equipment.  As far as RPG goes, it's pretty basic fare, not much substance.  But that's not what the game is about.  The game is about crafting super powerful gear that can one shot the final boss on the hardest difficulty.

_childDocuments_.review: I had a lot of doubts about this game and didn't expect to like it too much. Having a sequel to the first game after the trilogy completed? And in "it's just a dream" isekai setting? Also, I expected it to be mostly a reskin of Ryza 2, since it's the same engine. I din't like Ryza 2 so much I gave it thumbs down. I also didn't like the Mysterious Painting game, so I thought I got burn out on Mysterious formula.Well, I'm happy to report the game is actually very good. It FEELS and works like Mysterious series, and is much more fun than the Painting ever was. It's starts rather quick, introducing the characters and throwing you into the first dungeon... But it is also slow. Literally. Because movement speed is unbearable the visit to the first dungeon can alienate the player from the get go. Fortunately as you finish the first dungeon you unlock the recipe for boots of fast walking, which make the speed acceptable. It doesn't help that the first dungeon requires a lot of walking back and forth to go trough. Be warned, and also it's the first and last place where you'll have to suffer.The game introduces stones that allow you to change the reality, which mostly is limited to changing the weather. They are used in variety of puzzles, that you have to solve to get trough each map. I was worried it would get old pretty fast, especially on revisits to older maps. Except for the first dungeon it's actually quite a pleasure to work with and doesn't require much effort. You have limited uses of each stone, but I had to refill each stone (you do it with alchemy) only once during the whole playtrough.The crafting system is pretty much the same as in Mysterious series. You unlock new recipes by following the idea trees. Do some simple task and you'll unlock a new recipe. You have 3 trees to go trough, which made the process more streamlined, as the tree never got really big. Some of the last recipes are quite tricky to get though. This is different to Ryza series, where you unlock most recipes by "change crafting" existing ones. I like Mysterious system more, since the things I have to do are more varied. The crafting itself allows you to choose around 4 ingredients, and then you arrange them in tetris manner on the grid. As you progress you unlock bigger grids, grids with obstacles (but bigger bonuses), and ability to merge tetris pieces etc. The game hides from you the fact some items can be even better than they initially are until you're ready to craft those better versions, so you don't waste time in the initial hours obsessing on getting better items than possible. Crafting of the items is quite involved, but for throw away items you can just let the game throw in tetris pieces at random. For more important items you can spend dozens of minutes trying to get perfect properties. As typical for Atelier series the true power also lies in Traits, which you can transfer trough multiple item chains to get them on your final equipment.As far as traits are concerned, the game is much better than some other games in communicating to the player which traits are good. You have star ratings of the traits. You have info which traits are merge traits. You get number on trait potency, when applicable. Instead of just saying "this trait does a bit of damage" you will also get the actual power number. You also can easily check which item category this trait can be transferred to. You can also preview transferred traits before you start putting in the tetris pieces, so you can make sure the traits merges will go as you want.The one problem with interface is - there is no way to search by text, and sort by different categories. It's very likely because it's also on consoles, but man, having an ability to search for item you want to make instead of browsing a list of hundreds of recipes would be awesome. Filtering for ingredients also leaves a lot to be desired. If you want to filter by some traits you want you need to find that trait on potentially very long list. At least the list is filtered only to possible values. This point could be improved.This evolution of the crafting system also comes with passive skills that you activate by making piece links. Really the key to crafting in this game is making enough links, to trigger all the skills, which make you more links, and ultimately also allow to put in more ingredients. I found it very easy to make ultimate equipment without guides this time. Also, you have undo/redo buttons (a godsent), and you can make greatest items even before hitting max alchemy level(unlike, say, Ayesha).One thing I didn't like was the fact there were two alchemists to choose from, but there was no real reason to use one or the other. Their only difference was a slight number of unique items. All it meant it was harder to find the recipes you wanted to make, if you didn't remember which alchemist could do it. Fortunately the game doesn't force you to play the game twice, once with each Alchemist (unlike Shallie or such). You can get everything in one go. Yay. Another issue with having two alchemists is the fact alchemist#2 starts at level 25, and making each recipe once puts her around level 80, even if you used her a lot you might end up below 90. That means that to max out her level you have to mindlessly do the same recipe over and over to farm exp. Sophie can get to 99 quite easily.The game has much better maps than Ryza series. They can be traveled with more ease. Teleport spots are more useful. Their size is still too big for comfort, but oh well. You can quickly see which items are possible from given gathering spot, so you can only collect what you need, and basket size is appropriately big. There is also set of gathering minigames (different minigame for each gathering tool), which allow you to get items with specific elements and more links than usual. Those minigames aren't hard, and you don't do them often enough to get irritated. You can also choose which item you're "gambling" for so it's easy to get what you need.I had no issue getting the best traits with traits gatherer XL property on all tools. The seeds are also overpowered, allowing you to get great ingredients without much farming(despite the fact you plant seeds on mini-farms). Duplication costs in this game are paid in Cole, instead of some mobile-game-reminiscent unique currency as it was in Ryza. The costs are low - just 100 Cole or so for seeds. Even ultimate armours cost like 30k to duplicate, and best metals maybe 1k. You get tons of Cole from simple requests on request board, so it's really not much of a cost. The request work pretty much exactly as they did in Mysterious series.The story is... much better than I expected. Much more happens than in Ryza 2. The characters are much more fleshed out, and more interesting. There is that initial barrier where you might not care much, knowing it's only a dream. But because everyone knows it's just a dream they can focus on things that will be permanent even after leaving the dream world. The interactions between Sophie and two other alchemists are, in my opinion, enough to consider this a true sequel to Sophie. But I'm not gonna hide the fact I would have preferred something that would use more of the existing Sophie/Mysterious cast.The game uses the same engine as Ryza series - which means it's not a very good one. On Steam Deck you need to install community dlls to fix the bad optimisation. The game also crashes a lot on SD, making it, in my opinion, not worth playing there. On my 3080 it worked fine, but two times I suddenly started getting 40FPS instead of regular stable 60. That happened on maps that normally worked well, and leaving the map and going back magically fixed the issue. It also had very uneven frametimes in borderless mode... but in fullscreen mode it worked fine. _childDocuments_.review: Just beat the game on Very Hard, filled up the guidebook (mostly) and acquired all of the character "abilities".Very good overall, though this PC version could use some help with its graphics. While the story is simple, the speed of game mechanic progression is appropriate, and exploration of synthesis can yield superb results, literally. ;)I jumped straight into Sophie 2 right after Ryza 2, and I played through Ryza 1 also. Ryza 2 was a bit... hasty with things. Especially with DLC. This game is much better paced.No recipe morph, early Crystal Element or Philosopher's Stone for you this time (unlike Ryza's Secret series). Synthesis capability is largely frozen until you beat  key boss fights. You also have to unlock recipes the old-fashion way: story grinding, field objectives and massive amounts of enemy monster destruction. This keeps the game speed consistent. In fact, Synthesis appears not-easily-breakable this time. The puzzle system for synthesis is far harder to work with than the Secret series' bubble/node system. Just having the ultimate maxed out synthesis support items isn't enough; you really have to  the game features and plan well to synthesize the best items. Gust isn't playing nice with your 5+ year old graphics card anymore. My 1080 Ti could  get a consistent 60 FPS on 4K except when absolutely NOTHING was going on. Indoors. Outside was capped to 48 FPS constantly, with all the graphics settings maxed out. But this is fine. What isn't good is how they programmed the item selection graphics. Depending on what 3D objects are behind a 2D menu that you go through (like when selecting ), the FPS can drop to the 10's.  This happens a LOT during synthesis, and having tons of items to display in item pickers tanks the FPS dramatically.
