_childDocuments_.review: This is pretty a much kingdoms of amalur inspired/knock off game that has a HEAVY focus on parrying until you beat the 2nd main boss.The "souls like" tag is one of the most over used tags in gaming, plenty of rpgs out here cosplaying as a "soul like" this being one of them.Overall the game is fine,more of a side game than a main game to play but it's probably a 2.5/5Pros1.Being able to dye your outfit without having to pay real money for it unlike in a lot of other games. 2.The art style is overall nice.3.The voice acting is solid.4.The executions are decent enough.5.Doesn't hold you're f*cking hand like a lot of triple A games do(mostly sony games),you don't have to worry about a your npc sidekick constantly talking about nothing nor do you have to worry about him solving anything for you unlike in other games where you literally walk into the area & the god d*m boy instantly tells you how to do said puzzle because sony thinks it's player base is too stupid to figure out their brain dead puzzles on their own.Cons1.Has loads of bugs, most of them being minor like visual bugs where bojis back pack will be swapped to his chest just floating infront of him, worst bug so far being the infinite loading.2.Combat is inconsistent, Example being able to send a higher tier enemy flying yet being unable to send a lower tier enemy flying with the same hit until it feels like working.3.The game's different factions refuse to fight each other doesn't matter that the narrative says the 3 factions are at war nor does it matter that they completely ignore the wild life & vice versa.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed the game a lot more than I was expecting.Game has its fair share of issues, though none that are game breaking or too intrusive, few colision problems and enemies clipping in the enviroment etc. Performance could also be better but it is manageable.The combat could be more polished, the enemy animations are stiff and sometimes they kind teleport at you instead of smoothly move around.Exploration is perhaps the most interesting aspect of the game, with big areas with secrets and things to find. _childDocuments_.review: Writing this, while my memory is still fresh. 1st of all? It IS a good game. Especially, if you need something to play for 30 minutes before work. And now to the details. Lets start with saying, that I don't appreciate Unity games. Most of them are lazy and were not played by anyone, before the players themself... not even the developers of said games. This one... is much better. Graphics? I played on all low and only needed to correct my gamma to brighten the game in dark places, and it looked stylish. Perhaps, if you have 30-series or higher, you will be able to experience th whole majesty of this game... or not, because it's unity.... Combat? Most of the fight-related things are near-perfect. From hit-boxes to dificulty of enemies, to their numbers. (Although, I wouldn't recommend you killing every enemy on your way to glory) Battles? Questionable. AI for 2 and more enemies behaves strangely. Long-ranged enemies will still aim and hit you, while melee-enemies will only attack you, when you look in their direction. Camera? If you can, play on PC. If you don't like spinning things to the point of nausea, this game is not for you. As, about, every enemie deems it right to jump into the skyies or in any other way spin your character and camera, if you lock on to targets. And if you don't lock-on, you will miss 98% of your hits. Exploration? Great. But! Spikey plants suck as much as the one, who thought, that adding them into the game was the right idea, as they fling you over 2 screens, if you, oh so much, as don't dodge-predict their lightning-fast strike. And falling into the water is a death sentence in this game, for some never-explained reasons. Character development? Passable. It's kinda innovative and interesting to craft and level-up new weapons to upgrade your Hero. I've seen some of it in RPGM-games, but not much. On the other hand, all perks besides Stamina and health add almost nothing, of nothing that can be noticed with the naked eye... which is strange. Have to say that Bo(h)ji-related skill-tree is trash, beacuse of it's instability. As it completely relies on random.Weapons? Some of them are good, and 2-4 are fine enogh to be your weapons of choice. Now for some tart in this honey-pot: Weapon attacks are good. Weapon skills are useless. Weapon-opiented skill-development is good, but getting your weapon (not only) blueprints is random. And even by the final fight I had 1 weapon not found. even though, I had my LVL maxed-out ( 50 ). Which is complete bull5hit. Runes are nice, but 2/3 of them do not work, and of all that remain, only 3 work in boss-fights, all the while, only 1 gives you buffs, rather than questionable risks.  Bo(h)ji skills are random, don't change the course of the battle and are completely useless on bosses. Literally. Your own, elemental, skills are only effective against regular enemies, which isn't much. Especially. considering, you can't play and enjoy your 3rd ability, since all new enemies are IMMUNE to it's effects, and you don't even need to activate it to hit them :( Bosses? I played on 1.0 health and 2.0 damage. I died 3 times on the snake. (1 time fair and square. 1 time she decided to dissappear right from the center of the platform and the next moment I fell down, without any chances to crawl out.) And around 5-7 on Erray. Mostly, because I still had my double (-edged) damage, with 1 stack left, still on me, and couldn't get rid of it (and you don't resurrect after boss-fight, but return to the point before you fist entered it). erray is fast, strong, comes and goes whenever he pleases, has some undodgeable attacks and nearly invincible in 3rd phase. Overall, he is the only good boss of the game, but is still too easy for my liking). Ressurections? They. Are. Long. And become evenlongeraftermeetingBo(h)ji. I am not joking. Before Bo(h)ji, it takes 5 seconds to revive, after - 15. Unskippable. Useless. irritatingly long. Seconds. Plot is nice, but you can skip it and not loose much. Dialogs are voiced and pleasant to hear. I will give this game 7/10. 10$/my wallet. 15 seconds-revival/30 minutes before work.

_childDocuments_.review: I am 5 hours in and I am loving it really much. Everything has cozy PS2 feeling. The Leveldesign is a bit like Spyro Reignited Trilogy mixed with Soulslike fighting system.BUT this is not a Souls Like game. Despite the dificulty, the stamina system and the checkpoints, its more like a Action Adventure mixed with some RPG elements.What I really felt in love with is the world which changes after some of your actions. For example on your way you killed all soldiers in a camp. When you return to that place, monsters destroyed the camp and eat the corpses. This happens multiple time throughout the game and motivates me exploring so much.Until now, Iike the story and the characters. But be aware there are nearly no animated faces. Everyone is wearing mouth covering masks or helmets. Only thing I recognized were that the main characters weapons clip through the cape while running or fighting.For me it's a GotY candidate

_childDocuments_.review: The great knigthReleased on April 20, 2023, Stray Blade is an action-adventure RPG game. The game features well-crafted cinematics and voiced dialogues. The utilization of Unreal Engine 4 is a strong point of the game, resulting in beautiful visuals and a richly detailed world. The environments are pleasant, and the characters have a unique visual identity. The epic soundtrack and well-crafted sound effects add immersion to the audiovisual experience.Regarding combat gameplay, the parry and dodge system is creative and rewarding. The game's audio, including the soundtracks and combat sound effects, contributes to the immersion in the experience, providing fun for the players. However, the game has some flaws. The movement animations are stiff and seem outdated, contrasting with the beauty of the universe and the graphics.The talent tree is limited, offering only passive buffs related to weapon mastery instead of providing new abilities and combos. Additionally, the game has some bugs and glitches, such as enemies disappearing or the AI failing during combat. However, everything mentioned here may change.Despite these issues, Stray Blade still offers a stunning visual experience, well-developed characters, and rewarding combat. Although it doesn't reach its full potential due to its flaws, the game still provides fun for the players.
_childDocuments_.name: Stray Blade

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good game. Combat is a good mixture of parrying and dodging enemy attacks and striking when you have an opening. Every weapon in the game feels different and most are viable from start to finish, with a few that are definitely better than the rest. The different armors are cool, but there is one piece of armor in each category that is just better than the rest, so if you want to look a certain way you are likely to sacrifice armor and energy efficiency, which are the only 2 stats that armor effects. It is required to master each weapon to acquire permanent buffs to your character, which is fine as mastery only takes a few fights and can be made shorter by equipping a specific rune on your weapon. Speaking of runes, the system wasn't very well explained, but is very useful in making your weapons more powerful. Runes are temporary buffs applied to your weapons (3 max.), some become useless by the end of the game, and 3 of them just seem like the best choice. The biggest issue with the game is the camera, which is set to always recenter whether playing with m&k or controller. It was tolerable to me, but not ideal, and has been a deal breaker for many others.Overall I recommend the game, but maybe wait for a patch if the camera issue is something you don't think you can tolerate.
_childDocuments_.name: Stray Blade

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great. Best fun I've had in years. The combat is fun and difficult enough to be rewarding. The characters, although few, are great. The atmosphere, soundtrack, graphics, make for a really warm setting. And the whole idea behind the story is original and refreshing. I also like that it's a 3D metroidvania. Not so many of those around.I'd still say most of the complaints people have are valid. But most of them are nowhere near serious enough to make me not enjoy the game. The camera recentering/stuttering needs to be fixed ASAP. It CAN make you feel dizzy and nauseous, mostly when you are exploring, when you are supposed to enjoy the world around you, not fight back a seizure. I'm honestly surprised this one thing got into release in this state. Other stuff, like tiny bugs and sometimes awkward targeting I'd say are pretty normal for games these days and really no big issue (and will hopefully be gone soon).Overall, I'm having tons of fun with this one.

_childDocuments_.review: The game was much longer than expected. Did not feel too long or short, it was a nice sweet spot especially for the asking price. The controls were very strange when it came to parry or dodge, it felt pretty bad. Enemies were tough for me in the beginning but as I got the timings down, combat became much easier.There isn't a whole lot of content in my opinion, not as many opportunities or reasons to go exploring as I had hoped. Mostly just followed the next objective, one after the other. The crafting system is pretty lacking and wish there was much more you could do with it. Each weapon having it's own unique fighting style was really nice and allowed me to try out many different weapons, even ones that I would normally not use.Overall I think the game is pretty decent, it has a lot of room for improvement and hope to see some additional content at some point.
_childDocuments_.name: Stray Blade

_childDocuments_.review: The game is a bit of mixed bag, one moment very fun and then suddenly very frustrating in a blink of an eye.Pros:+ Gameplay is simple but overall satisfying, enemies have varied movesets that are fun to learn (and there is just enough of them to not make things too boring, even if some like spiders are present the entire game)+ Varied weapons, not so many armors but all can be customized color-wise+ Sizable map, a lot to explore.+ Fine, non-intrusive storyCons- Parry and dodge windows are rather narrow and fighting many enemies can lead to semi-unavoidable damage (that kind of fights happen more often in later stages of the game)- While varied in moveset, many weapons are simply unusable due to enemies having very particular stagger system. What that means is that heavy and very heavy weapons (3/5 of all weapons) are unfun/unusable for the most part and are easily outperformed by lighter ones (I recommend using any sword+shield weapon type as all of them are at least good).- The worst part about armors is that their stats are very unbalanced and the best (stat-wise) are found early which kinda makes finding more later on disappoining.Overall I had fun even if some of it was a bit jank, but if someone is coming into this and is expecting Elden Ring etc. they will most likely not be pleasantly surprised.
_childDocuments_.name: Stray Blade

_childDocuments_.review: I was a little but hesitant to try this one. On one hand the visual style and combat looks fun, on the other it’s been released to mixed reviews. After deciding to give it a try, I can recommend this game, it’s really grown on me.Visuals:Love the art style, it’s got this El Dorado vibe that is really fun. Textures and lighting are on point and they leaned into the art style in a beneficial way.Non-combat Gameplay:Outside of combat the zones are what I would call “open area”; mostly straightforward but with avenues for exploration and collecting. At first glance the skill trees can be confusing because skills are gated behind weapon mastery, what if you don’t like a particular weapon? However, if you read the tutorial on skills you would find that upgrades apply to all weapons. The system emphasizes exploring other play styles but has enough freedom to let you choose what you like. Oh, and once you clear enemies from an area completely, they don’t respawn. You also don’t seem to loose anything on death.Combat gameplay: This is what will make it or break it for some. The combat is very much focused on 1) Recognizing when to block and when to dodge 2) Learning attack patterns and 3) exploiting 1 and 2 to go ham on an enemy until they are staggered and can be executed. I found that once I really leaned into this combat system instead of treating it too much like a souls game, it was very enjoyable.Performance:This is where I think some improvements could be made. I’m running on a Ryzen 5 processor and 3080ti at 4K maxed settings and getting 30-40 fps. I can get a solid 60 if I drop the in game resolution scaling slider, but it feels like my system should be performing better. The AMD superes doesn’t seem to do anything and I’d like to see dlss. Other than that, no crashes or performance degradation.Bugs and other:I had one bug where I could no longer attack. I was able to resolve this by pausing and resuming play. Other than that, it think that the ui could be scaled a little better for playing on pc with a 4K tv.  Lastly, sometimes movement can be a little “janky”, not sure what to point to other than sometimes it feels a little offConclusion: I’m really enjoying this game and the combination of art style, light hearted dialog, combat, and exploration. I like that the skill system encourages exploration, but seems to let you decide which play style you like. I look forward to future updates and content.
_childDocuments_.name: Stray Blade

_childDocuments_.review: Great game for an early access game. Very few bugs, most were a pop up of a weapon stats that shows in the inventory, showing after a cutscene. but after opening the inventory it went away. Didn't always happen either.31 hours of play and exploring and finally beating the story.Gameplay: Souls like combat, God of War style world where you have to come back after getting skills to get to spots left unexplored. Different degrees of difficulty. Bosses were good and unforgiving at times.Weapons: Each weapon in the game plays differently, and there are 30 weapons. Some are slow and heavy hitting, some are fast and agile. Each unlocks with finding a blueprint. some after leveling up. Mastering each weapon lets you learn 1-2 passive skills that make you stronger, more HP, etc.Armor: is the same as weapons. lots of blueprints to find. There are the main armor, shoulder and helms. each with a different look and varying armor and energy effective levels.World: the world has varying landscapes from green forest to snowy mountains to caves. the enemies in each area have a fun mechanic. when you clear out an area of Beasts for example, the next time you come back, it might have been settled by some soldiers that made camp there, with buildings and such. clear those soldiers and the next time the camp is kind of destroyed and beasts or other wildlife may have moved in again. so the same type of enemies are not always in the same places. Enemies do not automatically respawn when activating a life tree spawn point. they will after leaving the area far enough and coming back.Overall a great game with lots of fun, 31 hours into it for $27? definitely worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Stray Blade

_childDocuments_.review: I'm gonna be honest here, I like the gameplay. Once I got the mechanics down and the timing for block-dodge-parry down, it was a lot of fun, combat feels rewarding. I'm going to keep playing post-review as well. The only issue I have is the auto-centering camera, it centers too fast or.. something. It just sort of caught me off guard and continues to do so. Maybe its too close to the character? If I could pin it down I could, but something with the camera is bothersome. That being said.. the core gameplay loop is fun, I like the block-dodge-parry stuff a lot, and the different weapon choices. Hard upvote for the price. Worth every dollar.

_childDocuments_.review: Stray Blade after learning the mechanics is a good game.A souls like, metrovania with a twist of its own. The graphical style is pleasant with crafting mechanics and various materials spread across the large map that adapts to the player with a large tree of unique skills to unlock.The game's problems are basically reduced to small gameplay details for souls like players mainly.I tried playing on the hardest difficulty and quickly realized that some mechanics needed to be changed.The game is based on a parry and dodge mechanic. Parry works well but dodging has a very small field which makes it frustrating at times.Simple mechanics like backstabbing should be immediate death to a single NPC but in this case it relies on a single hit, making stealth mode useless.The game has a lot of potential and it's a good game once we learn the mechanics, a few simple changes would make the game brilliant.It takes a long time to start a new game on the Steam Deck and games keep crashing.Not playable on Steam Deck!

_childDocuments_.review: Visually, the game looks really good. Despite its more toon like appearance, they did polish it really well. The environment is large, colorful, and sometimes hazardous. Characters/enemies have unique designs, I haven't seen any rinse and repeat so far. Nothing ground breaking, but I'll take a solid design over being the next best thing.  Audio is solid. The ambient sounds is relaxing, decent voice acting, and overall in game chatter is fun.Combat has a risk & reward setup similar to the Souls games. I don't think its anywhere near as unforgiving, but I do believe you Souls guys would still enjoy. You have your standard light/heavy attacks, dodge, parry/block, and ultimate attacks. You have the ability to lock-on to focus on a desired target. Enemies will glow according to what type of attack is coming next, which you have to decide on a dodge or parry at that moment. There's also a stun meter, which can stagger an enemy, giving you a window to unleash some free attacks. However, you're governed by a meter that's a resource for attacking and defensive maneuvers, so duel with caution. Upon death, you're treated to a revive at the last checkpoint you visited, with a little help from Boji. Weapons feel weighted accordingly, each with their own abilities and properties. You grow your character via skill trees, which you acquire points for as you level.  Equipment is also upgradeable, craftable, and can receive modifications to suit your needs. Stray Blade comes off to me as a marriage of Kingdom of Amalur's world and design, and a mild version of Souls' combat mechanics.  Don't come here expecting the next best Souls game or a ground breaking entry. Story seems pretty standard, but I'm OK with that, seeing as the game focuses on it's combat and character management. If you're looking for something that's fun and challenging, give it a shot.
_childDocuments_.name: Stray Blade

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fun and relaxing game that takes me back to games like Kingdoms of Amular. There is plenty to do and see in this world and you are rewarded for not following the the main path. At 17 hrs in, i'm still not halfway through the story as I squirrel a lot, but that's not necessarily a bad thing in my opinion. You are meant to explore in this game. I've never felt the "it's a walking game". No matter what I was doing, it felt like I was moving forward. Going back to previous places was refreshing as the world areas change as you progress through the game, sometimes in interesting ways. Eventually you'll unlock quick travel points which will help with the world traversal.The combat takes a little getting used to, and the camera angles are sometimes a hindrance to the flow of the fight, but it was never a game stopper for me. There is a good selection of weaponry to choose from and I found that some suited me better than others, and it also depended on what I was fighting. Crafting is simple, nothing too complicated. Resources are a little hard to come by early on, but if you explore you'll soon have more than enough for whatever you may need.The story and lore is well told through exploration, dialog, writings, and interactions with the NPC's. I can enjoy the game without having to face walls of text to understand the world. This made the game-play more fluid and allowed me to remain focused on being a part of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Stray Blade

_childDocuments_.review: Like the game so far. Dodge/Parry mechanics are a bit old school, pre-Souls old school. Probably not for everyone but, meh, can't please all.Game hits a number of high notes that I appreciate in an RPG like this. Companion that isn't an annoyance in combat but still talkative and cheerful to lesson the loneliness for the gameplay. Crafting requires slaying mobs and collecting materials from your surroundings, but otherwise you'll likely get all the blueprints you need on your travel. The map isn't sandbox or super open world, you have a solid direction to go, but still plenty of space to look around and explore areas you've been.As far as "souls like", it's kind of not. Variable difficulty setting so you can play the game in story mode if you want, or up the challenge when you feel like it. Clearing all the mobs in an area means they won't return if you die and run back, allowing you to freely explore the area without slogging your way through endless hordes of noodles. You gain experience from kills and just keep that experience. There's no penalty (like respawning mobs) for using the shrines to do mundane stuff like level or save the game or whatever.Really, this is a good RPG. Like, the way RPGs are supposed to be. The closest example I can offer might be Fable or maybe Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning. Really, the only difference is that you're revived when you die rather than loading a previous save or checkpoint.

_childDocuments_.review: Maybe I'm bias because I mostly play Souls like games, but I'm playing it at max difficulty and it feels good, loving the combat, the diversity of weapons.Don't get me wrong, the game is rough around the edges, probably needing few more patches, but if you are like me that like to play challenging games, then go for it.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall a fun experience. I think with a few more patches and fixes the game may end up being a lot of fun for the right audience.  The story is average but the world has a fun art style.  The combat is where I has some issues.  The combat can be quite difficult, which is not an issue on its own. The issue is more that the game seems to be overly reliant on the parry mechanics.  As someone who prefers sneaking or dodging even when I play a souls like, it felt a bit frustrating. I also found that a lot of enemies can be cheesed pretty easily with certain weapons.  Overall a fun experience and the devs are definitely listening to feedback and making improvements.

Prove yourself in this action RPG and master intense combat while exploring the ancient ruins of a mysterious civilization.

name: Oceanhorn 2: Knights of the Lost Realm
detailed_description: A GRAND ADVENTURE Oceanhorn 2: Knights of the Lost Realm, set a thousand years before the events of the first chapter, takes you on a magical journey across the vast world of Gaia, brimming with mythology and lore. A young Knight faces an impossible challenge, as Warlock Mesmeroth has returned with a formidable Dark Army. Will our hero be able to unite the Owrus, Gillfolk and Arcadians in a fight for the fate of the world? THIS TIME YOU’RE NOT ALONE You will not be taking this journey alone. Trin, the granddaughter of Arcadia’s leader Archimedes, and Gen, a mysterious robot wielding an old samurai weapon, will join forces with you, and fight at your side against Mesmeroth’s Dark Army. Contextual commands will allow you to direct these allies into battle, or have them help you with the solution of the game’s most clever puzzles! FIGHT, SOLVE, EXPLORE Bigger, better, and packed with new features – Oceanhorn 2 is not only one of the best-looking adventure games out there, but it also builds a unique experience on the shoulder of classic video games. Collect powerful items, wield the Caster Gun, solve the mysterious puzzles of the ancients, and discover all that Arcadia and its neighboring kingdoms have to offer! Accept the challenge and become a true hero. THE COMPLETE EXPERIENCE This version includes all QoL and Content Updates. FEATURES An epic Action RPG spanning 20+ hours of gameplay Massive boss fights test your reflexes and combat skills Dozens of side quests grant incredible rewards Clever puzzles to solve and mysterious dungeons to explore Beautiful graphics paint a world of legends and wonders

short_description: Sequel to the critically acclaimed action adventure. Experience a gorgeous new third person 3D view and embark on an epic journey that unfolds the mysteries of what happened 1000 years ago.

_childDocuments_.review: In Oceanhorn 2: Knights of the Lost Realm, players take control of a knight on an adventure to deliver the three sacred emblems to each nation. The game's intro cutscene begins promisingly: on a rainy night, a baby is placed in Master Mayfair's care. Eighteen years later, the young man will be put to the test that will determine whether or not he will become a Knight of Arcadia. To do so, he must return to the Island of the Outcasts and retrieve a box stolen from Master Mayfair by pirates. After obtaining the box, he discovers that his hometown has been attacked by dark knight invaders who pose a threat to the entire realm of Arcadia. The main goal of the game is therefore to stop evildoer Mesmeroth from attempting to take over the planet with his army of dark knights. Thus begins a quest to unite the peoples of Arcadia, which is also the setting for  (sequel story-wise) a 1000 years later. Anyone who has played the original Oceanhorn will recognize the universe of Oceanhorn 2. Despite the 3D transformation, enemies and places look familiar, even though you now control your hero in third person. The mostly linear, partially free-roaming game environment provides more options than the previous game. As the journey develops, you'll find yourself in larger locations that you may explore at your leisure without losing focus. The key reason for this is a mini-map that makes it easier to go to interesting spots. Not only will you face diverse foes, but you'll also have to solve interesting puzzles in order to locate the many hidden prizes or to simply advance the plot. The hero has a number of abilites at his disposal to do so. Running, climbing, and, of course, the fighting system, which is symbolic of The Legend of Zelda, are all there. Real-time battles allow you to slash your opponent immediately by pressing a button. Holding down the action button allows you to launch a strong series of strikes, but it will take a few seconds to recharge. Not only do the foes differ in appearance and attack style, but they also have unique vulnerabilities. Some foes, for example, take many strikes to show their vulnerability, but others require just one attack from behind to gain the upper hand. You may even sneak up on enemies via the dense grass and deliver a surprise attack that deals more damage than usual.Aside from fighting, the extremely low stamina is a hassle, especially when traveling long distances. Many pathways are needlessly long in general. It's also sad that the travel system is so restricted, relying on only a few portals. At the very least, there is a useful map function that automatically tracks where treasures may be found when journeying. On the other side, I had to become accustomed to unintended automatic jumping. You can't leap on your own; the hero does it for you on the edges, which was kind of frustrating at times.The riddles and trials in the game are undeniably the highlights. The flexible magic gun is used in addition to the standard switches and keys. You can not only use fireballs to destroy enemies, but also certain obstacles. Frost missiles may be used to either freeze a foe or to create a standing surface in the water to help you navigate dangerous shoals. Lightning ammo, on the other hand, may be used to shock opponents and activate electrical devices. You can also use standard ammunition to target opponents, or other things.As you move through the story, you'll also discover numerous shards that you may attach to your equipment to gain a boost in stats. So, despite the real-time combat, there are tactical parts that are well worth your time. During your mission, you will either find new shards in one of the numerous treasure chests scattered around the game, or you will be able to purchase them in one of the numerous shops or vending machines found in each town. Various in-game challenges are also rewarded with experience points, which grant you extra ranks and rewards; however, there are no conventional RPG leveling increases accessible. Instead, like in The Legend of Zelda, you'll be searching for heart pieces to gain more life points.Oceanhorn 2 features a few issues, whether it's the absence of manual jumping, checklist or the relatively rough controls/battle system. I certainly encountered a few issues as a result of unintentional jumps, but after I got beyond them, I was rewarded with a world I couldn't help but explore. The narrative is enjoyable, albeit slightly too predictable and the dungeons and riddles in the world are varied and just the right degree of challenging. It also doesn't hurt that the game is visually amazing. Oceanhorn 2's genre-blending gimmicks assist to elevate it beyond its shortcomings. Even if there are some hiccups along the way, this is an adventure worth embarking on and especially supporting.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to recommend this game because I loved the first one. I'd recommend getting it on sale and not full price though. I tried playing this on my iPhone when  it was released via Apple Arcade awhile ago and didn't like the controls. I attributed it to being on mobile and me never enjoying mobile gaming that much. The controls are still wonky on here and the auto-jumping is atrocious. So lo and behold it's released on steam and I've been following it intermittently in anticipation. The game itself looks great though I personally prefer the old art style. I won't say the game is bad but to me, it isn't worth $30. (Maybe buy it when it's 50% off) I don't remember how the first one played since it has been awhile but overall the game just seems empty.  I have to go to the menu to view the map and even then, the collectibles aren't displayed. If you're a completionist like me, have fun going to every area to find your missing collectible. The companions SUCK. I have to wait quite a while for them to respond to my actions if I got somewhere quickly via climbing or .Another gripe is there are (few) side quests but no quest log to read it unless you want to scroll through every dialogue you've had in the game. So really, your side quests are based off your memory or you opening the menu and scrolling through past dialogue to find it which is tedious. The card game is meh. There are times where it's a close match and I lose the 50/50 every time.  I'm still going to  complete the game because it isn't terrible but I regret buying it for full price.Update after completing the game: The over-world or whatever you call it is empty. You travel from point A to point B and find very little monsters to kill. Later on you unlock a faster way to travel this land but it is BORING and there's no creativity in it. The card game is just a big NO for me. "Experienced" NPCs have nothing to do with skill. They have the same OP cards that you do that it ends up being mostly "50/50" and like I mentioned before, I've gone 10+ times in a row losing my 50/50s. Which I get, it's not mutually exclusive but talk about annoying. Sure, maybe once I grinded my way to max the most OP card I would beat everyone. Overall a huge decline in quality compared to the first one. I'll reiterate the auto-jumping feature sucks on this game. I've fallen to my death multiple times because the game will auto roll and jump off a cliff.

_childDocuments_.review: I liked Oceanhorn.  I really wanted to like Oceanhorn 2.  Unfortunately it is worse than the first, just littered with poor design choices.  There isn't one central problem just a feeling of endless papercuts preventing enjoyment.One of the devs wanted to make a movie instead of a game, so you get tons of cut scenes, 90% of which are meaningless.  Most (but not all for some reason) are skippable.  Some scenes when skipped will immediately continue into a second cut scene.Map.  Map bad.  Bad map bad.Chests.  Ugg.  There are chests to find.  Opening them takes you into a nauseating 360 degree camera spin.  Most chests only contain gold.  Gold is nearly useless.What finally made me quit was the XP pickup.  Not only do you fight endless amounts of the same 2 basic monsters, but you don't auto-collect XP ???  After combat you have to run around even more to pick up the XP gems so you can get 0.1% closer to the next level.   A level that will give you barely any advancement anyways.

_childDocuments_.review: Set a thousand years before the events of the first chapter, the evil warlock Mesmeroth threatens to send the world of Gaia into perpetual darkness. With the help of new alliances and the cooperation of warring factions, you embark on an epic journey to save Gaia.Main quests and side quests are easily identified on the map, and navigation is made simpler with a mini map on the main screen, which also shows the positioning of enemies and chests.Apart from driving the story forward, completing quests gains you experience points, which earns you extra ammo slots, more spells, and replenishes your health. Collecting heart pieces can gain you permanent health boosts. There are no fetch quests or combat based side quests, rather challenges. Most involve collecting special keys to open their corresponding chests, but it is a bit of a hassle trudging around the area looking for some of these chests as they are not marked on the map. There is an interesting bounty hunter type challenge where six escaped convicts are wandering Gaia and you can hunt them down and kill them, but other than that they’re not very imaginative or add any story elements to proceedings. Most exploring is done on foot, but occasionally you can sail a boat or pilot a plane to faraway locales. Once found, you can also open portals for quick travel. There are lots of things to find and collect like sixty blood stones scattered throughout the world; Chests, containing either treasure or upgrades; Fifty Taroch cards, needed to play the Taroch game; and nineteen mysterious daggers. In each area of Gaia, the game screen shows how many blood stones and chests are left to collect, although this can be deceiving as some are hidden indoors and only show when you enter that area. If you’re not sure there is also a percentage explored in the menu which will indicate if you have got them all. There’s enough stuff to collect to appease collectors, and there are achievements attached to them.If you acquire the grappling hook you can launch up to predesignated points and swing between them. This can save a lot of time and is quite fun to do. Towards the end of the game, the diving helmet is found meaning you can dive under water and find chests, cards and treasure previously unreachable. Underwater scenes are done very well. There is a plethora of items to pick up, and plenty of pots, barrels, and sacks to destroy to reveal items too. I never had a shortage of ammo or magic because there was always something around, and it always seemed to give you what you needed most. There are no skill trees, but you can upgrade your gear or spells with shards located in chests. These improve damage and recharging speed and can be configured to your liking. Synthetic shards can occasionally be found in shops for a very high price and are often more powerful than anything you will find. Combat is very easy with most foes being dispatched without problems. The grappling hook can be used to grapple on to enemies from afar or in high places, or you can take them out with long range weapons, and even command your allies to attack, but they will fight without prompting. There is a shield which can block attacks but I never needed to use it, as rolling away is more effective. Magic can be used to attack also, with fire, ice, and electric spells but they travel very slowly and opponents can easily dodge them. There’s also the ability to heal yourself. Enemies and collectibles re-spawn if you leave and re-enter the area, which I always find annoying. Puzzles mostly require magic to succeed. Symbols in the areas usually denote which magic is needed, like electric to start up generators, fire to destroy wooden gates, and ice to create floating platforms in water. Bombs can destroy certain walls revealing new passageways. There are some puzzles that require dexterity and timing, like running through spikes, and the usual switches and lever types of puzzles. I got stuck on some of the puzzles and others required some thinking, but once you understand the mechanics, as they’re not explained, it becomes easier. On the whole they were imaginative and enjoyable to solve.

_childDocuments_.review: Very sad to give this a thumbs down, but it sorely lacks the magic of Oceanhorn 1 (OC1). Questing feels like a chore through barren open worlds rather than jubilant but carefully guided and curated exploration. Combat is repetitive and unrewarding. Navigation between islands is slow and uneventful; no shooting minigames (tetraodds or boxes) across the water with airborne travel equally hollow. Such a missed opportunity. Worse, the excellent, extremely enjoyable hovercraft is only accessible for specific plot-progression points and can't be used to explore freely (not even as a 100% completion prize). Even the music, a triumph of the prequel (especially Gillfolk's Drop and Sky Island) could not save Oceanhorn 2 (OC2). OC1's puzzles were better designed and somehow the story (with less VA and no friendly AI to help you press buttons) was more compelling. On the plus side, OC2's third person camera is great and far less restrictive than the isometric viewpoint of OC1. The hookshot was a fun gameplay upgrade and the bosses were decent (originality wise the fire bird 'chora tuyk' was definitely the best). But these good bits get swallowed up by the unnecessary enormity of everything...Ron Gilbert once said "constraints and limitations can sometimes be a driving force for inspiration", so if/when Oceanhorn 3 gets made, I hope it's tiny but mighty like OC1.Oceanhorn 1 review (game review copy provided for free):

_childDocuments_.review: I almost hate to give this a "no" because there's nothing terrible about this game. It's actually quite polished and it does deliver a game.It's just that, rather than anything being BAD about the game, nothing is particularly GOOD. Everything from the graphics to the combat to the puzzles and world design feels like it's just "good enough to be a game". This would be fine if there were one or two things the game excels at, but it really excels at nothing.The game has this weird "default Unity mechanics" vibe with its mechanics, like what you'd see in one of those clickbait videos like "I remade Simpsons Hit & Run in Unity". Sure, they WORK fine, but they feel very uninspired. That said, I don't want to give the impression that this is an asset flip or something. It's an actual game with actual original art and content, and the music is pretty decent too.If you're REALLY clamoring for a Zelda-like, particularly older 3D Zelda titles, this might be fun, though don't get your hopes up thinking that this is nearly as good as those games are.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a breath of fresh air.Baldaurs Gate just released (which i've owned since Early Access) and yet somehow i find myself wanting to play Oceanhorn 2 instead for now. That isn't a knock against Baldaurs Gate but its just that this game took me by surprise and delivered a feeling that i didn't know i needed to feel so badly. Just a pure sense of childish wonder and glee that recaptured how i used to feel as a kid when playing video games siting on the living room floor infront of the TV getting lost in some fantastical world.The franchise leans heavily into its influences (the main one being the original zelda games) but there are traces of other game sin here too.  Oceanhorn 2 manages to capture their charm incredibly well while at the same time being its own thing.Oceanhorn 2 offers some significantly updated visuals and a much more immersive 3rd person camera position compared with the first game and really feels like a way bigger and better game as a result.Everything about this oozes charm. The music, the color palate, the character, creature and environment design. Its all really well done and is quite wonderful to play.  The graphics are simply stunning. It really is one of the best looking games with this type of art style. It is just so crisp and vibrant. It makes me feel happy and cozy just playing this game and looking at the scenery.In a flood of overly gritty and realistic titles that more often than not try to be punishing for the sake of it, it feels fresh to play something that is so care free and charming. The puzzles will tickle your brain at best. The enemy encounters are fun and enjoyable without making you smash your controller and the world is interesting enough to want to explore.Its very much a cozy game wrapped into a gentle RPG experience and i'm quite satisfied with what they have done here and glad that we finally get to play this on PC.The game runs flawlessly for me on both my high end PC and on the steam deck.

_childDocuments_.review: As many have mentioned before, if there was a "Maybe" option rather than the customary thumbs up or thumbs down that would no doubt be the option I would choose for this game. It seriously had the potential to be GREAT, but judging by the story and some of thein game encounters it was clearly released in a state where the dev's true vision for the game was not fully represented in the finished product. I don't think there is any debate about this and that is what is so frustrating. Examples:1. There are major enemies that clearly don't belong in the fantasy setting the game takes place in, and as far as the story goes they are clearly unrelated to the main antagonist. The game never explains why they are there, or where they come from. There is also something you discover in the 1st 3rd of the game related to these characters that CLEARLY should have been explained, but nothing. Mad frustrating! I suspect they were supposed to play a major role originally, but that story had to be cut out due to the game being rushed. There is no other explanation for them even being in the game. 2. Late in the game you visit an area and find townsfolk in a state that is not "normal." This is never explained. It's not even brought up. Smh.Those are just two of many, but I really don't want to spoil much. Here are some pros and cons to finish things up.Pros- Game runs very well. 200-300 fps @ 1440p using FSR (Ryzen 5800 X3D - RTX 3070). - Clean and simple graphics. Perfect for the story and setting.- Controls for the most part are smooth, even the auto jump which some have an issue with I found it gave me no    problems.Cons- The story is not complete. I know it's a prequel, but there are still many plot holes. Very disappointing. - Combat is way too easy. Boss fights are not difficult, just annoyingly long for the sake of being time consuming. - Experience is gained by collecting diamond shaped objects from defeated enemies and these sometimes get lost in    unreachable areas. So annoying.- Money in the game is virtually useless. You never really NEED to buy anything. Don't waste much time chasing coins from    defeated enemies.- Side quest rewards are VERY underwhelming since you usually get money (See the above con). Stick to the main quest    for the things you actually need.- Your companions don't help much during combat, but combat is so easy it really doesn't matter. - This is not truly an open world game, it is very linear even though there is a world map. In closing this game left a bittersweet feeling in me. I enjoyed it enough to finish it, but did not enjoy it enough to play it again. Catch this on a deep sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Hi, this review is mainly directed at the game devs. As such, it is going to be nothing but spoilers from start to finish. Therefore I recommend you first play this game yourself before reading, as it is genuinely a gem among gems, but I have a few criticisms. I will format this so they take turns with praise :).Criticism 1. I am going to start off with Tarock. I already made a community post about it, so I will keep this brief- Acquiring strong and rare cards is way too easy, to the point where I went from using level 2 cards to using level 8 cards, jumping over all the rest. It also seems like a pointless thing to gather since the enemy will always have the same level of cards as you (so even if you have all cards, if you play with only level 1 cards, so will they, no matter who they are)(only exception is their hero card they give you when you win)- The randomness factor of the coin toss throws all skill and tactics out the window (along with the coin), as a few bad coin tosses in a row can ruin even a 8-1 winning game- continuing on this, restarting games takes too long, you need to exit out of the whole conversation, select all your cards again (i really wish there was a deck system) and retry that way.Praise 1. It absolutely nails the Zelda Aesthetic.I see everyone compare this to breath of the wild, but i have to disagree with that one (despite the technological enemies). It feels a lot more like Skyward sword, with temple/dungeon design, wind waker, with traversal, twilight princess, with tone (especially in the final level, its boss, and the final boss), spirit tracks, with how princess zelda actually joins you, etc. Theres also a triforce, zora, rito, master sword, lack of a blood-family, silent protagonist and not to forget the heavy use of items:- bombs- ranged weapon used for puzzles- THE GRAPPLING HOOK (turning into spiderman in the white city is something the zelda series could actually learn from). After getting this, traversal becomes a lot more fast and fluid, and its very clear a lot of attention went into designing it.- Diving helm - Cards (you can challenge anyone you want)- Fire arrows, ice arrows, lightning arrows (also used for puzzles)criticism 2, the extremely limited overworldI know i cant genuinely compare this indie game made by a few friends in their spare time to the polished quality of triple A, but I can't help but feel like more was planned for it. The starting village doesn't even connect to the overworld, and the only way to reach it is by train, boat, plane, or fast travel ("only"). When I see the terrain from the plane, I can see clear points where it could have been connected after certain story elements have passed, even if its only through a tunnel and a loading screen. The game does encourage exploration, especially after the owl temple, by removing the possibility of boat travel, forcing you to go by foot, but i still reached the city in around 10 minutes (or I would have if i ignored the miniboss). Speaking of which, while the sidequests present are stellar (hats off to the court of monsters), there is also a distinct lack of them. There's not even a quest log, because it is simply not necessary. A navigable overworld map would also have significantly shortened my time pointlessly looking around for missing chests and bloodstones (but maybe you dont want less playtime)Praise 2: the artstyleI already made a point of this, but I wanted to talk about the non-zelda features. The world is truly bright and vibrant, and a breath of fresh air from the drab brown and gray games that seem to be popular nowadays. The enemies are also still charming, though not too much, opening the market to younger children. A few great locations that stood out to me were the ghost town, with the statues being poised like they could come back to life at any moment, and the soft sound of the heartbeat in the background, implying that the people were still alive, but trapped, in limbo. The final level, the dark lords castle, especially with the being struck down and stripped of all your gear, recovering them one by one, and finding your way through the halls and hallways, until you encounter the final boss, who despite appearances, was not really evil, but had righteous intentions (although the means did not justify them).criticism 3: there were some really unpolished parts to itFor instance, the default robot voice you can find yourself, used for when the guards talked when trin is imprisoned, despite them having plenty of voicelines with an original VA, or when oceanhorn talks during cutscenes. The airplane animations, especially when it lands, need some serious reviewing, since it just looks like the way a child puts down a toy airplane. The diving, I thought would open up specific maps to more exploration, but even the parts you can see, are ugly and brown, and when you press the re-emerge button, you just appear back on the surface (as long as nothing is above you) no matter how deep you were. You also swim very slowly with no speed boosts available. Think of skyrim swimming.praise 3: The gameplay is a lot of fun- The leveling system is entirely optional, but challenges you to go out of your way to explore, complete challenges, and even be addressed by certain NPCs according to your rank in it (each level is titled). - Combat offers options, you can pull yourself towards enemies with the grappling hook, parry attacks with your shield, shoot them in/between the eyes to stun them, just place down a bomb (they are infinite but on a cooldown, which can be decreased using power gems), but you still need a certain degree of skill. The shield only blocks forward attacks, and you cant block when shooting or grappling (obviously). - You can easily cycle through items and ranged spells using the arrow keys, so you dont need to enter the menu every time (although I wish the game had told me that, and i didnt need to find out by accident)- Command companions to hold down buttons for puzzles or hit switches you cant reach with their boomerang (because honestly, zelda boomerangs are a drag and are shelved forever once you get the bow, which you get at the beginning here. In this game, your companion can boomerang without you needing to switch to it)and now some random smaller praises and criticisms, unrelated to any large topic+ the dungeon design is always unique, and features simple but clever puzzles- nobody ever addresses you by name, even though you are given one in a cutscene: Theo. instead you are known simply as "hero"+ the companion banter is fun, and rare enough to not be obnoxious- Some Tarock card descriptions feature serious spoilers for the story (gen for instance)+ The mystery and the plot twists are well done- The ending, though understandable why, leaves a lot to be desired. What was it all for then? I thought it would go the Dragon Quest XI route, seeing how much it borrows from that game as well.+ The voice acting is well done, and the voices always fit the characters- The bosses are aesthetically well designed, but they all feature the same boils that spawn infinitely until the health bar is depletedI don't want to give it a rating, because I know im too old to be playing it anyways, but I know child-me would have absolutely loved this game. A lot more than he would enjoy playing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ starfield or whatever the newest FPS is. This game still has the magic that I thought games didn't have anymore.If you are still reading and you are not the dev. PLAY THIS DAMN GAME!! SUPPORT THE CREATION OF MORE GAMES LIKE THIS!!! STOP BUYING 70$ SLOP!!!!

_childDocuments_.review: It's not a bad game, but it's also not great. Get it (in a sale) if you want an old school, pseudo-zelda experience, otherwise, don't bother;Pros:• The world is really beautiful;• The game works out pretty much like a pre-BotW Zelda: some sort of semi-open-world metroidvania, where you grab a item that works like a power-up, giving you a new ability (and so you backtrack to get to some items/areas you couldn't before lol);• The Overworld mechanics feel really nostalgic all the while incorporating the action-adventure style into it;• I really liked how "random encounters" were incorporated here. They don't interrupt your game and you can just ignore the enemies and run if you don't want to fight them. It could use some spawning animation, instead of just falling from the sky, though (and had more enemies in the pool).• Dungeons and caves gives off a Mega Man Legends vibe;• The dungeons are really interesting to explore (too bad you don't get many rewards out of it);• The hookshot is more fun that it should be;• The mini-game, a hybrid between FF8's and FF9's card mini-games (Triple Triad and Tetra Master, respectively), is addictive and gets fun once you get some better cards;• So far, it's the closest to a 3D Zelda-like experience the PC ever gets without emulators;Cons:• Combat feels clumky: there's no real difference between combat mode and non-combat mode, you can miss even when locking on (it only locks the camera, not the character's orientation) and parrying is really not worth it as it drains a lot of your own stamina only for it to drain the opponents stamina;• Please, let me change camera sensitivity for the controller;• The spells are really useless in battles, even with maxed shard stats on it;• Puzzles are meant for a 3yo;• 90% of chests aren't really worth it (Chest Opener Simulator 2023);• Overworld is too big with little places to explore (could've added more places/caves);• Characters have bad design (both visually and storywise);• Trin is by far the most annoying character ever, with silly quips and inconsistent personality;• The pacing of the story is veeeery slow at first, but then it gets too fast too quickly and suddenly the world is ending and protags are lovers, when they had no previous implications of such;It just... it works out for the game, I guess, but nothing very memorable. It's not  OST, but it gets the job done.

_childDocuments_.review: It's obvious where this game draws it's "inspiration" from, and in that regard, it does ok. Just ok. I first attempted to play this on Apple Arcade a few years ago, but quickly dropped it bc I hated the touch screen controls for a game like this. And honestly, you can tell it started out as a mobile game first. The options are very scarce, with hardly any of the typical PC settings to tweak. There's not even an option to turn off the subtitles. Biggest complaint tho: traversal is just SLOOOOW, especially due to the quick-depleting stamina gauge that nobody asked for. There's no fast travel, per se, only some shortcuts you can unlock as you progress, but exploration will feel unnecessarily sluggish for the most part. The map may as well be drawn on old parchment, bc there's no way to zoom, you can't set custom waypoints, or interact with it at all really. The minimap will keep you pointed in the right direction to progress the story, but as far as trying to go around and collect everything, well, I just wouldn't recommend that. They really could've done a much better job making this a true PC port, with some basic quality of life improvements that we've all pretty much come to expect. I get that it started out as a mobile game that needed to be simplified as much as possible for touch screen controls, but ppl who don't know that would just call a lot of this bad game design. I'm only recommending it bc it's pretty slim pickings for 3d Zelda-likes on Steam, and in THAT regard only, this game does alright. It's a pretty solid 3D Zelda clone, gameplay wise. I believe it's a prequel to the first Oceanhorn, but it doesn't really matter bc the whole story SUCKS. Do yourself a favor and just skip all the cutscenes, life is too short. I actually watched 'em and I still couldn't tell you a damn thing that happened in this story. All I kept thinking was how much the art style looks like those characters from Team America: World Police. It was kinda funny to see this game's dollar store versions of the Zoras and the Ritos tho lol. I got it on sale for 30% off, and I feel like maybe I should've held out for a bigger discount. Idk, it's decent I guess. Just not $30 decent.

_childDocuments_.review: Oceanhorn 2 is a very fun and colorful adventure game that closely follows the older 3d Zelda formula. It accomplishes this extremely well with a lively world and engaging, albeit shorter, dungeons. Is it as good as Zelda? No. But it does scratch that itch quite well.  There are some issues with the game. One is a map that was not interactive and not very helpful. Another is a story that at times was hard to follow and ends rather abruptly in confusing fashion. This game is a prequel to the first Oceanhorn, but that still doesn't really explain why the ending happens the way it does. Lastly, there is no way to quickly travel throughout the world. There are warp points to find for fast travel, but there is no means of transportation like in most adventure games. Early on, there is a hoverbike chase segment that made me think I would unlock that bike as a way to travel around the world, but nope. There are 2 chase segments with it in the game and that's it. Seemed rather bizarre to create the vehicle model/controls/etc but then barely use it.But overall, Oceanhorn 2 is a fun and satisfying adventure that is worth going on.

_childDocuments_.review: Upon finishing: This gets a thumbs sideways due to the really poor ending. No spoilers but it makes very little sense. I wasn't sure what to expect at the start. I delayed buying it but I like it overall. It's a really simple game hack/slash with a gun that casts spells instead of YOU casting spells. It's not perfect but it's pretty well made and entertaining. Hints: Chop up all the barrels, storage sacks, small shrubs around the map etc. that you see. You get your ammo and cash there along with health aid. Not sure how assorted ammo comes from a bush but hey, it's there. I guess people hid coins in bushes as well (shrugs). As you progress you learn to NOT CHOP THINGS UP NEAR LEDGES. Because a serious flaw in the game is, it literally throws the loot off the ledge. You don't just pick it up as you hit the bush or coconut. It THROWS the loot away from where you are. You have to chase it and collect it. Oh yeah, these locations respawn so you can pretty much cash in on loot /coins if you want to grind. Dig up a coin behind a tree, walk away to talk to a couple people, come back and the dig up spot is back there glowing again. CON: Defeating any enemies doesn't get you XP. You have to go grab the XP that it drops or you don't get it??? I don't know why but a bug seems to have maxed my levels within the first 1/3 of the game. No cheats used. I collected lots of loot grinding for a bit, beat a couple random enemies on the map and when I got back to town it kept raising my level 2-3 times each time I got to a new location until I was a legend after only a couple quests. Seemed pointless to keep collecting XP after that. The first map it puts you on has a decent basic tutorial for how to navigate and fight while you complete the first task except is says to go to the yellow arrow. There's a book on the beach with a bright yellow arrow over it. That's not what it's referring to so it's confusing. Books and things to read have a yellow arrow over them but the main quest marker is actually orange/yellowish.  Game system control settings say "Right CTRL" is for running but any CTRL button works. In the first town, there are little glittery hidden spots to dig up loot. Once you leave the town, they get MUCH more spread out and harder to find. Not sure why they're plastered EVERYWHERE in a tiny town. Inconsistencies. There seems to be a "find the daggers" hidden on the map quest but there are 19??? I'm not going back and searching for 19 of these things. It puts an X on the map if you're near them but I was all over the map and only found about 8-9.Map markers where to go are very clear where you can go for primary and secondary quests. Yellow/orangish triangle marker is for primary and green triangles/flags are for secondary quests. I was NOT happy that there are 2 locations you can't even go to even though they are RIGHT THERE. One was Faroah. Your friend talks about it and you can go to the crypt outside the town but if you swim around to the town itself, there's nothing to do and no people. It's locked behind a gate. There was another town in the desert area. I tried to walk to it and it has a fence. It's RIGHT THERE. There's nothing to do in the desert area but land your plane there and beat a centipede. Con: In the beginning, halfway across the sea to the owl city, I decided to stop at a small island to find a missing sailor before going to the next city across the map. After finding what happened to the sailor, the game defaulted to send me all the way back (fast traveled) to the very first town where the sailor was from to complete the quest. It doesn't ask you if you want to go back there. Now you have to get back to the boat and sail across the sea again to the primary quest/city instead of just halfway from the small island. It didn't do this for any of the side quest criminal monster hunts though. It forces you to go all the way back to White City to the prison to collect your bounty. After you beat the 5 main lower criminals, speak to the guard near the message board. He gives you the key to the last boss. It's on one of the islands just outside the main port. Specific location is online.  Minor annoyances like; You learn that if you can climb something like a smaller box, just walk into it. It'll auto climb if you can. I was trying to use spacebar to jump (like all normal games) and it kept dodge-rolling and then climbing. It was annoying at first. Why make it auto climb and not jump for boxes but you have to use spacebar to jump over holes/gaps or from ledge to ledge? It also just jumps with spacebar in some locations but roll/jumps for others? This inconsistency was REALLY annoying. If you fall off a cliff it usually grabs on to pull yourself up and it's a LITTLE frustrating when you WANT to walk off a ledge. Not a big problem, just a small annoyance. If you are jumping from one block to another, there's no edge grasping feature if you fall. If you get too close to the edge, you just fall off. It's like it's punishing you where you need it most. Especially if these are timed areas like a door closes if you don't cross in time. It makes you fall down and start over every time. More than once, I just ran through a maze to beat the timer and ignored the glowing/dig spot loot areas. It wasn't worth going back for. It's usually a low amount of coins. I only concentrated on the chests or keys. Puzzles like connecting electric shots from one conductor rod to another were easy enough to figure out. Some places have more than one way to get to chests so it's not nearly impossible to get to them accept ONE spot, the warehouse in the port. It's nearly impossible to get the chest behind a wall in clear view (inside the warehouse). One chest is easy to get to. The one in plain view is nearly impossible. I skipped it.  One more CON, it takes forever to load a more powerful gun the game upgrades you to. The reg ammo is the quickest to fire and works on many enemies. You learn that freezing and then hacking some enemies kills them in 1 freeze shot then one hack. I ONLY used electric ammo for puzzles. If you hit a stunned/electrified enemy, YOU get stunned??? Bad design there.   Learning to command my friends to go places took a little time to figure out.  Just aim at a spot and then either hit TAB to choose who to send there or on the screen it'll have "1" or "2" for each friend. You just hit that number and that person goes to that spot you're aiming at. I think this works for attacking too. You aim at a enemy and hit 1 or 2 to tell the friend to attack them. But you're getting attacked at that time so it has it's drawbacks.Fast travel huts: I found all but one. I looked everywhere. If you go into one that you DID open, you can go to the multiple doors and see through what it looks like. It was forest/hills. I couldn't find the last one. Not required to finish the game but it tells me there was a place I never saw/found yet I flew and walked all over the map.  Again, it's a simple hack/slash/shoot game but a cute, pretty entertaining one until the ending.

_childDocuments_.review: Though rough in some areas, I thoroughly enjoyed Oceanhorn 2.The story actually got me hooked, especially considering I played the original Oceanhorn over 8 years ago and have fond nostalgia for it. However the writing can and voice performances vary, with some story beats being predictable and obtusely written, while others had quite the impact for me, especially for the kind of game this is. There are some funny instances of voice performance mess ups, like some clearly placeholder text to speech dialogue from some robot characters which are inconsistent with how they sound in other lines, or Mayfair hilariously mispronouncing "Calliope".I didn't have many problems with the platforming system, but I agree a manual jump button would be an improvement. The combat is also simply serviceable, however I did really enjoy parrying enemies with a perfectly timed block, and the grappling hook's use in combat.The music is very good, ranging from whimsical and upbeat like you'd expect from a kid-friendly game, to surprisingly dark with the "Source Theme", which marks the beginning of the game's shift in tone at the final act (which I very much enjoyed).I would recommend Oceanhorn 2, and I feel it's underrated.

_childDocuments_.review: While not the worst Zelda-like game on steam, i have to say get this game on a sale. There are so many things I just don't understand about this game. It has 4 ways of traversing the nearly-open world. Straight up walking, taking a boat, taking a plane, and using a teleporter as fast travel. For some reason, to go so Submeria (creative name), a set of islands in the center of the map, you can't take a boat, you have to take the plane. That's just one of a myriad of strange game design decisions I have here, but nothing that defines whether I'd recommend this title or not.For another thing, this game for every room (yes every room in this game has its own map), handles the map by way of 'fog of war.' What I mean by that is that every map is blank at first, except for a small circle around the player, the more you explore, the more map you see. There are 2 MAJOR things wrong with this idea.1. You CANNOT unlock every part of most maps, leaving a permanent space of unexplored map forever.2. Every map is a screenshot of the overhead land you will uncover, not an illustration. That means that the maps covered in trees, are useless, you can't see the paths because the trees cover up the entire map. The same goes for maps inside caves, any rocks that are above you but not quite the ceiling, will cover up what you should be able to see.Every map should be unlocked from the beginning, there was 0 reason to use the fog of war method, besides to cover up unused plots of map that will look jank but if that's the case just make an illustration! And not every room needs a map!Story is whatever, the game's antagonist and thus his henchmen really only start to rear their heads into the picture 75% into the game. Why?? Plus every explanation of anything had me rolling my eyes as the attempts to world-build is laughably boring. If there are no stakes, no interesting characters, no meaningful dialogue, the world has nothing to offer. They took the Zelda formula and watered down the basic necessities for the already simple story.Mechanics here are WEIRD. Like, some are really damn cool, while others are introduced and sparsely used. For instance, I think the diving helmet is a neat idea. It allows you to go underwater for an infinite period of time, goes from a 3rd person perspective to a first, and allows for neat and new traversal. I said the idea's cool but the execution is lame. It's basically just a transitional item for world traversal, the game hand picks bodies of water you can and cant dive in, and there's nothing to do underwater outside of going through water to another room or opening the occasional chest. The spell gun, works in some ways but mostly doesn't. The basic fire is new for a Zelda-like, I mean, It's Link with a gun. Getting Ammo is the part that mostly doesn't work. Basic ammo is fine, it drops from most things, like barrels, pots and bags but the more interesting spells, also need ammo? Besides basic bullets you have fire, electricity, and ice. I've never once needed to use the healing spell I still don't know what that does, because health drops are too frequent to need it at all.Ok, fire makes a ball of fire, cool? Ice freezes enemies and creates ice platforms, neat? And Electricity really only allows you to do these stupid electricity ball 'puzzles', unnecessary. The only one I can see myself using the most is ice, it makes platforms on water and in the early game (without the diving helmet) you die in water, FAST. So that can be useful! One problem, you have a limited amount of shots, wtf happens when you run out? You grind barrels pots and bags that's what. These spells, shouldn't need ammo, there's no reason. I can see the basic fire needing ammo, but the electricity spell? Tf were you smoking? Hell- the BOMBS DON'T USE AMMO. The entire BOMBS that one-tap most enemies, are only cool-down???? You get an infinite amount of those, but no, you need to get more ice particles or whatever.There's plenty more I don't get but that's all I care to remember. It's fine, I recommend it very slightly, but ONLY ON SALE.

_childDocuments_.review: We have Zelda at home.Zelda at Home:This is a hyper-ambitious game from a very small studio, and you can really tell they put their all into building it, and I'm down for any team making such a direct 3D Zelda-like. Objectively, this is definitely like a 6-7/10, but the whole package just comes together to feel like video game comfort food.Positives:+ The game's structure is a straight forward implementation of the OOT->Skyward Sword Zelda games with dungeon items, keys, boss battles, and heart containers, etc.+ The music is pleasant and captures the vibe.+ The color palette is vibrant and feels cohesive.+ It seems like there's a decent amount of side content including mini-dungeons, optional bosses, and even a card game that is very reminiscent of Triple Triad/Tetra Master that seemingly every NPC will play with you.+ There's a lot more voice acting than I expected, and while not the most dynamic voice direction the character voices all pretty much fit the characters.Negatives:- The animations and character models are quite janky.- The combat is just serviceable. There are actually some fun interactions using your items and skills in combat, but everything just feels really clunky, and some of the physics based actions are really off like there's no weight to any of the items.- No side quest list and pretty unusable map on the pause screen.- The companion AI is VERY finicky sometimes not responding when you ask them to do something you need to solve a puzzle.- The game is extremely bright with the default settings with no brightness slider.  I had to edit the Engine.ini file to set gamma to 1.8 (default is 2.2) to make the image feel like a comfortable level of brightness.Not a universal recommendation, but I think if you go in with reasonable expectations and are just looking for a 3D Zelda-like experience you'll probably have a good time.

_childDocuments_.review: A Nostalgic Journey with Room for GrowthRating: ★★★☆☆"Oceanhorn 2: Knights of the Lost Realm" takes players on a delightful journey reminiscent of the Nintendo 64 era's Zelda games. While the experience was undeniably fun, I couldn't shake the feeling that it was over too soon. If you've been yearning for a nostalgic trip down memory lane, this game delivers.The storyline, while enjoyable, left me craving more depth. The characters and plot had potential for further exploration, and a bit more narrative complexity could have added an extra layer of engagement. Similarly, the combat system felt somewhat lacking in terms of depth and variety. While it gets the job done, a bit more complexity could have elevated the overall experience.Comparing it to its predecessor, I found that "Oceanhorn 2" didn't quite capture my interest as effectively. The first installment seemed to have a certain charm and intrigue that kept me hooked throughout. That being said, this sequel is not without its merits. The graphics are vibrant, the puzzles engaging, and the adventure itself is undeniably enjoyable.In conclusion, "Oceanhorn 2" is a worthwhile purchase, especially if you chance upon it during a sale. It provides a satisfying nostalgic experience, though the potential for a deeper story and more intricate combat may leave some players wanting more. If you're a fan of classic action-adventure games and can overlook its shortcomings, you'll find an enjoyable quest that harkens back to the golden age of gaming.

_childDocuments_.review: It was really interesting how much this feels like the first game even though there is a new style to it, as I just finished playing the first game when I started this. My biggest issue was just with exploration and a tracking of events, the stamina bar empties quite quickly while running around and it can take quite a bit of time to cover ground, you do get more as you level but even towards the end it felt sluggish having to slow down to let it recharge often.As for tracking there is a good feature of showing you whats in each individual zone and they blink near the radar when you are looking in the direction it's in, but it gets worse with for example in a village the tracking only shows outside it doesn't include what's in each building which has it's own independent tracking for it's own items and there are some fairly well hidden areas that were hard to find, so going for the 100% zone completion can be a little hard for some zones as you might not know where exactly the missing items are.

_childDocuments_.review:
A GRAND ADVENTURE
Oceanhorn 2: Knights of the Lost Realm, set a thousand years before the events of the first chapter, takes you on a magical journey across the vast world of Gaia, brimming with mythology and lore. A young Knight faces an impossible challenge, as Warlock Mesmeroth has returned with a formidable Dark Army. Will our hero be able to unite the Owrus, Gillfolk, and men in a fight for the fate of the world?

THIS TIME YOU'RE NOT ALONE
You will not be taking this journey alone. Trin, the granddaughter of Arcadia's leader Archimedes, and Gen, a mysterious robot wielding an old samurai weapon, will join forces with you, and fight at your side against Mesmeroth's Dark Army. Contextual commands will allow you to direct these allies into battle, or have them help you with the solution of the game's most clever puzzles!

FIGHT, SOLVE, EXPLORE
Bigger, better, and packed with new features Oceanhorn 2 is not only one of the best-looking adventure games out there, but it also builds a unique experience on the shoulder of classic video games. Collect powerful items, wield the Caster Gun, solve the mysterious puzzles of the ancients, and discover all that Arcadia and its neighboring kingdoms have to offer! Accept the challenge and become a true Hero.

FEATURES

- An epic RPG main quest spanning 15+ hours of gameplay
- Massive boss fights test your reflexes and combat skills
- Dozens of side quests grant incredible rewards
- Clever puzzles to solve and mysterious dungeons to explore
- Beautiful, handcrafted graphics paint a world of legends and intrigue
