_childDocuments_.review: Caveats:1. I have Stellaris and much of the DLC2. I have not played the existing Star Trek Mods which are freely available and highly toted by others3. I have picked this up on the pre-order and played through to just shy of the 2hr limit as I contemplate a refund. Star Trek: Infinite is based on the Stellaris UI/Clausewitz engine. It behaves and feels much akin to Stellaris. The downsides to this, and granting this is a new game, is that it feels like Stellaris after they removed some FTL options and before they got some actual polish updates into the overall system.The interactions, Star Trek shell notwithstanding, feel VERY sterile and underdeveloped when compared to Stellaris (again DLCs and longer development history notwithstanding -- this is comparing to other historical iterations of Stellaris).There is currently only a single stock medium map -- with systems/empires placed at incorrect locations relative to cannon. There are Governor ships instead of just using a Governor in systems (why this is a thing vs. how other leaders operate (both within Star Trek: Infinie and when compared to regular Stellaris)  I cannot fathom). A planetary/system Governor should simply be assigned to a planet/system -- having them fly around on ships relative to a science vessel akin to their anomaly missions to trouble shoot the empire is certainly not intuitive and seems illogical (relative to how other leaders operate/are assigned and relative to Stellaris proper).No racial customisation also "feels odd". Yes it is Star Trek: Infinite but it's not very infinite if you can only play as one of 4 major Star Trek empires and must be shoe-horned into certain behavioral traits 100% of the time.I had hoped that Star Trek: Infinite would be a "rebirth" of Birth of the Federation (one of my favourite 4x games - Star Trek notwithstanding). However, even Birth of the Federation BOTF (released ~1999) at release had 5 major factions (they also included the Ferengi Trade Union) vs. Star Trek: Infinite starting with only 4.BOTF did lock you into certain ships, traits etc. but it still feels more polished and intuitive. Star Trek: Infinite currently lacks either the raft of options available in Stellaris or the polish and nostalgia of BOTF.I remain very disappointed with this title/launch. The overall vibe being the taking of a much loved IP and a relatively popular and successful back-end (Stellaris/Clausewitz) and smashing them together with the least amount of input possible (I am not saying that is what was done, I am saying that is how the product feels/behaves after 1.8hrs of playtime).Will this improve over time -- very likely in the short term.Will this have continued publisher/developer support -- debatable given the clear competition vs. Stellaris proper and the lacklustre state at launch. I'll be holding out to see developer responses over the balance of the refund grace period -- without going over the 2hr limit to try to gauge how this may improve, however, for anyone who does not already have Star Trek: Infinite in their library, this is NOT a buy -- wait to see how things develop and/or wait for a substantive (minimum 30%) sale.

_childDocuments_.review: It feels a bit rough at times, which is not totally surprising for a Paradox launch? Some of the tooltips are not clear, and not all the things I remember from Stellaris are working the same way in ST:I, which makes for an occasionally frustrating experience...HOWEVER, it feels like a really good branch off of the mainline Stellaris platform? Like, we have Warp drive again rather than starlanes, which is a huge change. The starting zone is pretty fixed, with the good ol' cluster of Romulans, Cardassians, Klingons, and the Federation all together... each with "advanced starts" relative to Stellaris. Warp drive and multiple starting planets (partly to accommodate the Federation's multiculturalism) are better than the starting setup for Stellaris where it can be easy to get locked behind someone else's set of starlanes.No, it's not BOTF... but I feel that people have overly fond memories of the clunk factor in BOTF's turn-based setup and Civ-lite style.This is still a "simplified" Trek, not built for the minutia of 20 classes of Starfleet Frigate through multiple eras of TV shows and movies and video games... so if you're going to be irritated by a limited flavor of Starfleet, play Cardassians or Romulans.Like Stellaris, the potential is there for a launch title. It's an inexpensive Paradox launch title as well, especially given the license and the feature set it lifts from a later-stage Stellaris branch. For as much as the Astral money grab annoys me as an expensive Stellaris DLC, ST:I feels like a very inexpensive start of a Stellaris-like experience.Buy in for the potential and the Warp drives.

_childDocuments_.review: This game could be good, perhaps great but I feel a lot of work needs to be done before it should have been release on a lore and game play perspective. Posties: it is filled with trivia and lore that is accurate, the voice acting is superb and the art work is amazing. It is a beauty to look at and it is worth the price alone. Also the narrative is great and responsive when playing with options you would not see in Stellarais I hope the custodians implement some of them. Being able to assassinating leaders or running sabotage mission due to coveting the populace with brilliant idea. Also able to add districts is a much great game play method that should be implemented in Stellaris as well.The negatives: the game is balance for early Stellaris, which is a problem when gathering resources for the game does not provide the player a chance to gather as many materials as Stellaris due to planets being smaller and fewer resources you can mind from space. One wrong building and you have to spend 10 minutes working to fix your economy to stop it free fall, especially when it comes to energy credits. Also there is a lack of depth as you do not get as many ships to play with, technology being very straight forward, and lack of things to do after the mid-game and before and after the crisis. It also hurt it has some game breaking bugs or things allowed. For example, Bajor being assimilated by the Cardassians with a Federation that cannot declare wars to iberation to free planets from Cadrassian control. Along with no anomalies showing up to prevent completing of the Federation mission tree on the Enterprise. Not to mention getting certain mission within year 10 before you have a chance to research technologies to allow for more options in the game. Finally, there is just not enough factions to play with and lore is lacking in areas.So here are some suggestions I feel would greatly improve this game:1) Re-balance nearly everything to create more diversity. Starting with varying technology and ships to give players more options. In addition, I recommend planets on average have more directs, and/or gather mroe resources to making it easier to mange then a pain. I also suggest allow cruisers to serve more as mission all capable as science, construction and ambassador ships when traveling alone to be with lore. 2) Each faction start with cruisers, destroyers, frigates and corvettes and are research better versions and more diverse ships hulls to be able to make a diverse fleet. Like in the cruiser section fro the UFP, the starting is the Constitution as a close range ship and Excelsior is a mid range ship, and later research Promethus for close range combat, and Akira is a long range artillery ship.3) Removing the aging mechanic and the ability to die due to old age for key characters tied to mission tree. It was pain to get that point only for the missions tasks and make sens for some to die of old age (like Data). In fact, with how costly it is to get commanders, I suggest leadership is unlock through research and the person gains someone from the shows, video games and books to fill the role immediately once research.4) Resemblance the AI so they are more likely to diversity their one planet so they easier to assimilate instead of sending the economy into free fall doing so (which is necessary as any of the factions, especially the Federation). Also makes it easier for the player to convert the planet and allow them the empire to remain relevant as they are not running low on materials.5) Add more diversity in game play like the mission tree should be expanded. Like have more then one hero ship with missions and expanded tree. Also tradition tree could work to diversify with possible 2 more branches at least for its a case of more is needed.6) Remove trade and research agreements only viable for empires of equal value. You will quickly outpace other empires, and it removes a good way for factions to gain resources and increase likable to assimilate them.7) Add not only factions but also different game mod. Right now it only has four with making them more or less balance to each other. I think that is a mistake and should make a lore version with power being very different to reflect their actual versions. See below for example.8) Try to not only add factions but maybe change them up so they feel like their own and really stand out while increasing replay for different play styles. Again, see belowFor example:The UFP could take from their lore and by the 24th Century is the largest faction with vast territory rich in resources and a number of home worlds with various species. In fact they have not only four found species, but also the Betazeds, Bolians, Caitians, Denobulans, and Saurian as already assimilated members, with five multirace colonies. For species the UFP know and enticing for membership is the Trill and Bynar. They are also the most advance among the four and wealthiest. However, they are least developed and focus with few additional colonies and planet districts distributed evenly to not lack. In fact, you get penalize for trying to focus planets into one resource planet as the UFP wants each planet to be able to survive on their own with planets only focus on making specialized in specific rare materials, research or training worlds. There military is diverse but small for a empire its size so its player job to expand the Fedeartion and build it up to be a great power before others decide to try to take chunks out of Federation space early game.The Romulans is if playing as a tall empire. They have a small territory but unlike the UFP a highly focus economy to maximize returns, large number of cruiser size and up ships, and highly defended territory. However, they start off as isolationist with only after reaching a certain military threshold can they communicate and conquer outside their the empire. They also lack the smaller ships so they can be vulnerable to small fleet if you don't get first strike outside cloak. They are also the most sneaky and get the most spy master and bonus from spying on other species, specifically in acquiring technology and resources. Also the Romulans should have the Remans on their moon as a slave species with possible others as well.The Klingons, they start off the largest faction military and the most developed planets being the oldest empire. However, they also get the least from their own resources and research for being a warrior species. To compensate, they can be very charming and intimidating when meeting with other species, so they can get far more in trade deals, research agreements, and vassalize other empires. Meanwhile, species assimilated in their empire and more productive as well. As the Empire, you want to make friends with the more technologically advance UFPs or Romulans while vassalizing smaller powers which the player starting with the Orions (resources and trade vassal) and Ferasan (research vassal) from the start.Finally the Cardassians should be hard mod for players. They are smallest and least of all the other empires. However, as the under dog, so they deal more damage against stronger players, especially in their territory and are good in all areas instead of the focus areas like the Federation, Klingons and Romulans. So they best not get the attention of more powerful factions or they will face the consequences.Factions they need to add or think about adding: the Dominion, Tholian Assembly, Gorn Hegemony, Tzenkethi Coalition, and Terran Empire.

_childDocuments_.review: When I got this game, I went in expecting to be a little disappointed by what I found.There are some issues that I ran into. Day 1, there were UI scaling issues (I have my main display set to 150%) but that was easily fixed (but this could have been fixed). There are some notifications which don't make sense (like the Cardassian Union assimilating itself, apparently). The leader for the Trill Assembly has seemingly gone on vacation in my game. But none of this actually stopped me from playing the game.You play one of four galactic empires from Star Trek. Note that while it may help to complete goals in the Mission Tree, this isn't required for victory. A lot of the things you need to win come from researching technology in three areas - Physics, Society and Engineering. You don't progress along a tech tree, instead the game will give you several random choices of things to research.It can be a bit of a research roulette, but I found that if I stacked up research bonuses and made sure my empire was generating lots of beakers, I was able to progress quickly enough to eventually get the technologies I wanted. For a while there, I was trucking along with the Tier 1 reactor on my ships (one step above the starting reactor) which didn't let me power a lot of things, especially on the starting ship class.Speaking about stuff you can add to your ships, there are a few things which bug me, like how small quantum torpedoes need tetryons to build but medium and large don't. There also isn't a massive difference in damage done between small and medium torpedoes, but that isn't a big deal.You also need to manage the rest of your empire too. The populations (pops) of your colonies have needs, and you also need them to make resources for your empire. One of the mistakes I made early on was not adding enough mining and energy districts.Speaking of districts, if you feel like you made a mistake or, you assimilate a minor power who have a bunch of districts you don't need, you can replace them with other districts, but you will be making the pops working them unemployed. I realised late that this was a bit of a problem, so it led to a crime problem. Whoops. I eventually added some buildings which had jobs which they could move to. Having a governor working on keeping the crime in check also helped. Crisis averted.All in all, this game has plenty to keep an aspiring galactic ruler busy. I haven't played the multiplayer part so I have no idea how good that is, sorry.Is it a good Star Trek game? If you suspend your disbelief, yes. One of the mods that I noticed on the mods page for this game is one to stop Data dying from old age. So, that's a thing. Also, the sounds and music don't exactly do well to sell it as a Star Trek game. But they aren't awful, either. Except for the ambient sound in the galaxy map. Either there are too many sound layers or they're too loud, which led to me turning the ambient sound slider down to almost zero.Overall I'd give it a score of 7.5/10. 1 full point off for the UI scaling issue, and then half a point off each for other problems.

_childDocuments_.review: Space Administration Simulator just isn't very interesting.  All of the depth is sunk into micromanaging planets and resources and not into, say, diplomacy or missions.  This would be fine if there was some payoff, but there isn't.  You spend hours and hours doing that and all you get are random pop-ups.  The war system is terrible.  Random fleets go missing all the time because of a too-common random pop-up event.  Wars end and you don't even get a notice.  Wars should end at least with a pop-up where you can accept or reject terms, or change terms.  Why do I have to set claims and war goals in the beginning and then smash an opponent to bits and only come out with 3 planets and not more or the ability to add demands?  And if you have to push deep into their territory to win, the map resets and you end up with unmovable fleets trapped in their space for at least 10 years.  This is just a silly way to do things.  There's no flavour to the game, everyone gets the same threat.  It's a shallow bland timesink with zero payoff.  Watch somebody play it on youtube, it's equally boring but at least it's free.

_childDocuments_.review: God I wanted to love this game.  I love Star Trek.  I love Stellaris.  Unfortunatly this game needed more time in the oven, breakdown below.1. Borg are a letdown:  The Borg make there presence known early, but before you know it the Borg which are the "endgame crisis" are dealt with quite trivially.  The game starts in the 2340's and by the 2390's the Borg are dead and gone.2. Attempts to stay true to the "original" story get in the way more than they help:  Events will happen only because they happened in one of the shows, not because they make any sense given what is actually happening in your play-through.  The Maquis will show up, despite no demilitarized zone with the Cardassians existing for example.  The Borg will show up and kidnap Picard... despite the Enterprise being on the other side of the quadrant from the Borg.  I'll spare the list of examples, just know they continue.3. Game systems don't mesh well: The normal give and take of Stellaris just doesn't exist here.  Where you normally need to decide where to focus in Stellaris in this game you can just do everything from the jump.  Make a big fleet, send out a ton of research ships, research welll, etc.  There is no real decision you are making and at a certain point I just started ignoring my economy because it didn't matter.  When I wanted to do something I would have enough resources to do it, and if I didn't want to do something right then it could languish on the vine until I did and be fine.  This is because of....4. No one is there to stop you:  The other powers just leave you alone unless you start something, and why would you?   There is plenty of room for everyone to expand for centuries so there is no reason to fight over resources like in Stellaris.  With no need to fight, and plenty of smaller powers who pose no threat to you to trade with, you can just ignore the other "major" powers entirely.  There is no reason to fight.  There is no reason to talk.  Every major power might as well be playing their own game of solitare.5.  Bugs:  There are a lot, like a lot a lot.  I'll spare the examples, check reddit if you want some good laughs though.TLDR;  Like I said on the start, this needed more time in the oven.  You can see what they were going for, but nothing comes together in the way it should for this to be recommended by me.  Get Stellaris, find a good Star Trek mod for it (there are several) and check on this game in a year or two.  Paradox has a history of working on games for years after release so here is hoping they can salvage this.

_childDocuments_.review: I sadly have to not recommend this game.While there are a few likely fixable issues such as bugs, annoying pirates that really just force you to have fleets near everything or loose an outpost, a less than perfect UI that is somehow much worse than the Stellaris original, my chief complaint is actually the Star Trek bit.You have 4 Empires - Federation, Klingons, Romulans, Cardassians. Leaving aside the weird idea of Cardassians as a major power, that's all you can play. All else are minor Empires. Their start positions (aside Bajor) are entirely randomized, as are many systems, so you get strange things like Trill being on the far side of the Romulan Star Empire rather than between UFP and Cardassia. Not that it matters much - they're largely inconsequential aside offering a minor conquest or integration target.You start at around the time of the Khitomer Incident. Despite this, you can only build Miranda-class ships. If you're lucky like me, you might get the USS Cerritos from Lower Decks shortly thereafter - just that ship - and 30 years later you build your first Intrepid. Somewhere along the line you might complete the Enterprise mission goal and get the Enterprise-D. Only that one, no other Galaxy-class ships. Another 30 years, and you get... Excelsiors. Right now I'm well past Picard-time and have just upgraded (?) the Enterprise-D to the E with another mission. This mission also unlocked the Defiant-class (the class, not the specific ship) which is the equivalent of a Stellaris frigate and weaker than a Miranda. I'm also finally researching the Galaxy-class. I have been told the Sovereign exists but haven't seen it, nor any other classic ships aside those - well, and the Oberth science vessel.Onwards - equipment. I'm sorry to say that space combat looks nothing like any of the shows. No classic phaser beams and photon torpedoes, just a variety of differently coloured teardrop shaped energy blobs.Missions - I somehow have to liberate the Bajorans (but cant declare war as UFP, and Cardassians never accept a liberation request) to get missions to help out the Romulans and their supernova. I'm literally stuck there because of Bajor, even for completely unrelated matters. Overall - it's really all over the place and feels like a worse version of Stellaris with a botched Star Trek skin placed ontop. Compared to Star Trek mods like Star Trek - New Civilizations, I really wonder why I should play this when I could be going for the work of lore-accurate love that STNC is.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a Stellaris conversion, which is expected. What's unexpected and disappointing is that it's JUST a total conversion mod for an older version of Stellaris, with minimal changes and adaptations to the Star Trek universe. There are only four factions with no customization options, but that's okay, Star Trek factions SHOULD be quite unique.For example, the Federation technically should not have separate military and science ships and fleets, all ships capable of serving both science and military purposes depending on current needs. How did they implement this in the game, especially since Stellaris relies on highly specialized ship roles and clear distinctions between military and civilian units? Perhaps they could have come up with some clever solutions like science modules or combinations of admirals and scientists? No they briefly mention in the tutorial that technically all Starfleet ships are science vessels, but only some can shoot, great.It's somewhat understandable in a fan mod, but not from a game studio with salaries and access to the Stellaris source code.However, it's not all bad. The UI looks pretty nice, and the core Stellaris gameplay is still should be fun. I hope to check it up in future maybe they will improve it, but for now, it's better to play the regular Stellaris.

_childDocuments_.review: Decided to post a quick review here after a short first session playing this game after it crashed. So... Yeah, there's obviously some smoothing over to be done here by Paradox but don't let that deter you!The game sure does look great with a fresh coat of paint over that Stellaris core this game has. If you've played Stellaris, you'll feel pretty much at home here. Much of what makes Stellaris Stellaris is alive and well in this game. Many people like to refer to this game as being "DLC" for Stellaris but it truly is its own animal and is a standalone game in its own right and will probably have its own DLC and expansions (I would for one, LOVE to be able to play one of the minor powers or make our own civs!).Now for the elephant in the room: Star Trek has its own look and feel and if you've watched the shows and movies as much as I have, you're expecting to see and hear certain things and while the game delivers to an extent, it does fall short in the sound effects/foley department. Its like Paradox managed to get the rights to various characters and designs, names and such but cheaped out and skipped on the sound effects. I personally love the phaser and photon sounds and the game just doesn't feel like Star Trek without it. I really do hope someone mods these in or Paradox updates the game to put them in.Overall, I feel this game gets a solid 7.5/10.In my opinion, Paradox should focus on game stability and then on the (from what I've seen...) common complaint about sound effects and music in the game missing the mark. Then, I would hope they would expand the galaxy/civ settings so we have more than one galaxy to work with so we're not bored after playing through the four major powers' stories.

I really love the TNG Era Star Trek, and this game is all about that. It has this excellent classic Star Trek vibe that I love so much. Because of the fact that the tutorial is extremely basic, and you wont find a wiki about this game, mastering it takes a lot of time, with a lot of trial and error. I strongly believe that the game has a huge potential, if Paradox is willing to pick it up and improve on it. It could use a lot of polishing, DLC-s and new content. The four main powers (Federation, Klingons, Romulans and Cardassia) of the Alpha and Beta quadrants are playable, each with their unique playstyle. Regarding to content, the game draws a lot of inspiration from the best classic tv shows like ST:TNG, DS9 and Voyager. You can build all the best classical starships, like the Oberth, Miranda, Excelsior, Intrepid, Galaxy and Sovereign class. The legendary alien designs are also here. The klingon B'rel bird of prey, D7 and K'tinga battlecruisers, the Vor'cha and the Negh'var. The T'varo bird of prey, the Valdore and the D' Deridex from the Romulans. The Hideki, Galore and Keldon class of the Cardassians. You can micromanage each subsystem on them. Plus you can manage your star empire to the smallest detail. The Borg appears as the end game crisis, and they are a huge pain in the neck. The problem with them is that you can encounter them very early, when you have no chance against them. Pro Tip: The Borg quest line only starts when you visit any warp highway node. So as long as you stay clear of the warp highways, the Borg wont come and you can focus on dominating the other three major powers. Dont go near the highways until you have at least Tier 4 starships in your fleets like the Galaxy, D'Deridex and Vor'cha battlecruisers!The game undoubdtedly has its flaws, but if you are a huge trekkie like me, you should not miss this game, and buy it on sale!Also, there are great ship mods available in the steam workshop.They integrate into the game flawlessly, you just need to click on the 'subscribe' button on their steam workshop page.This way more starship classes become available, like the Constellation, New Orleans, Ambassador, Oberth, K'Vort, Kamarag, and the Romulan Bird of Prey.

_childDocuments_.review: Should my opinion change as I intend to revisit this game in 6 months,  I will update this review.In a nutshell I do not recommend this game. It isn't ready in its current state. In fact for the price paid, it's absolutely daylight robbery.There are several things I am pretty upset about;1 - When playing MP some of the diplomacy options between you and other players are permanently greyed out. You cannot do certain things with them, no matter how long you improve relations. This seems to be deliberate over a bug. Why? If me and a friend decide to play coop and then fight it out once we're the last 2 standing, whats the problem with that? Why have the game prevent that? Makes even less sense when you consider the Federation and Klingon's were allied anyway during the show....2 - Lack of ship / stations designs. It's Star Trek, we were never going to have the customisation Stellaris gives us, fine. However, a full tech tree unlock gives you 5 ship classes to play with, 1 defensive station, some weapons that fit in universe but the majority just don't, and ZERO effort on providing a adequate name pool for said ships so you end up with "U.S.S. Name XIV" for a ship name, which is absurd. Not only that but the Defiant isn't even in the game. So they either lied (and continue to lie) during their promotional campaign, or it's only available behind some sort of paywall that I don't have access too. Either way, I won't be purchasing anything more to support this product. 3 - You're expected to micromanage EVERY planet you colonise or conquer? I started to lose track at 20, and the universe has hundreds. What the hell.Overall, it's bad. They could have taken Stellaris, gave it a face lift and injected the Star Trek in to it and released a fully complete game with all the lessons learnt from Stellaris already baked in. Instead they've taken version 1.0 of Stellaris and gave us the bare minimum so they can fleece the fan boys some more with DLC's. The sad thing is people will STILL pay KNOWING they're being fleeced. If you want a Star Trek strategy game, buy Stellaris when it's on sale, download the Star Trek mod and play that. This is a waste of your time.

_childDocuments_.review: Having waited for the successor to 'Birth of the Federation' for 20+ years, I'm happy Star Trek: infinite has arrived. It was just too complicated.'Infinite' makes things a lot easier with some systems completely dumped from stellaris, as it wouldn't make sense in the star trek universe. Along with my passion for all things Star Trek, this made my life easier to get into the game. Further quality of life stuff like handing planet micromanagement to the computer (once you've selected the planet's speciality), reduced the stress of managing the empire, less tedious for me.All this helps me enjoy the story of the game and the in-game events. It's fantastic to carve out your own little episodes of star trek, while trying to conquer (peacefully of course :P ) the galaxy.I'm running this game on a geforce 1050 (2gb) video card at 1440p, and it runs just fine (75fps on galaxy map) ...  but we'll see if it chugs at end game chaos.It's a great game for its price. I hope it is successful, as I would love to see other empire's in the game, like: 'The dominion', krenim imperium, Breen confederacy and Orion syndicateI haven't had any crashes, and if there have been bugs, i wasn't paying attention.See you all out there, in the stars :)

_childDocuments_.review: After a few months of bugfixes, I can now recommend this game to any Star Trek fan that enjoys strategy games. The setup, events and especially the artwork and models make the game quite immersive. It's not too expensive and gives you quite a few hours of fun in our favorite universe.There are still a lot of obvious opportunities for DLC, such as adding the Dominion/Gamma quadrant and the Delta Quadrant and more DS9/Bajor related events. Anomalies and random flavor events seem to dry up in the mid game, even with many systems still unexplored. The flavor events that are there fun and wel thought out though.The mission trees could really be improved; i'm afraid the current ones don't make too much sense and quite easily become impossible to fully complete. The devs also made some debetable choices that i hope will be changed or refined in the future, the most prominent being the selection of Federation ships that is anachronistic (you get Intrepid class ships before you get Galaxy class ships) or not true to lore (you get the Defiant class quite late, which is fine, but it isn't even close to being as powerful as a Galaxy class while it really should be). I also dislike that the big 4 factions all get the same weapon techs. The amount of weapon techs is overwhelming and frankly just makes one defer to the auto-complete function for outfitting your ship designs. Lastly, i wish the borg ships would be bigger. At the moment, even the cubes are smaller than the Galaxy/Negh'Var/D'deridex cruisers.All that aside, the game is fun, immersive and not expensive. We should support this release and show Paradox that there is enough interest in the game to warrant future development.

_childDocuments_.review: So, I really wanted to like this game. I played Star Trek Armada and Armada II, Stellaris, and many other strategy games. If this was an early alpha I could recommend this game. In its current form I cannot recommend this game. There are just aspects that are missing. You are honestly better getting stellaris and just getting a star trek mod. Pros:* Ships look good. * Each faction is different* Art Looks fine.* It has mostly Stellaris gameplay. * The Lore is fun.Cons:* Some of the stuff is hidden in strange places. - For example, as the federation there is a way to claim a system. It just isn’t as intuitive as the other three factions. * Missing basic features- Why can’t I let my science ships just auto start anomalies like I can in Stellaris? If there is a way, then it is hidden going back to my first point.* The UI IS SO BAD!- Okay, even the devs acknowledge this problem. The text is just awful. There is a mod that was shown to help with this problem but this should be fixed sooner rather than later. We shouldn't need a mod to fix it. * Only 4 factions- You got Federation, Romulan, Klingon, and Cardassian and that is it. This is a bit disappointing as I would hope for the dominion, breen, borg, and more factions. I know this game just came out but we have models for minor powers, why can’t we use those? I would hope this isn’t part of some DLC money scheme. Which brings me to my next con:* You can’t make a faction- You are stuck with 1 of the 4, which I understand. This is a Star Trek game and so they want you to play one of the main factions. Why can’t we have the option of playing a minor faction that have ships like the Klingons but look like Romulans? (Remember when Klingons and Romulans had similar ships?)* Only one map- I wish there was a choice to play the star trek universe with different maps other than the same map over and over again. * Lore- While lore can both be a positive and a negative for this game, I have to put this as a negative here. The map is boring. I wish there was the ds9 map. The Romulans get screwed. They took the thing where they lose their home world and bam they get hurt hard pretty quickly. Romulans, regardless of the difficulty, seem to be always losing. * Pirates- There is nothing wrong with pirates. I know some people would like it if they could be turned on and off, but I am fine with them. I actually like the pirate feature. Now here is my complaint about them. My problem with the pirates is that the warning for them get lost in the notification for everything else. I wish the notification would show in the center where you get notifications for needing to do research, traditions, or your tree. * Ship problems- Not every ship in factions are equal. The Klingon bird-of-prey cannot have shields…. WHY? Also just the way you get ships from a lore perspective is strange. For Federation you get the Miranda class and then the intrepid? Why? Then you get the excelsior class? Why? Klingons are fine but the federation is just awful. * Mission Tree- I like this idea but some of the stuff is not really intuitive. I think the mission tree could be more refined. For example, with Enterprise you have to do missions. Which means you go to minor factions and hope they give you a mission that the Enterprise can do instead of the 6th one where you have to repair another of their ships that broke down like some cheap car repair business.* Borg- The borg would have been a fun thing but instead of them feeling like a mid-game or late game crisis like in stellaris, they feel like a minor event quest. You do some minor things and it is over. * Romulans- I have to mention this again. They are the worst faction. They have a slow population growth and they lose their home world. I feel like I am kicking a person while they are down every time, I deal with them. ALSO, they need to build little singularities for their ships and I swear they treat these things like oil in a car because at times you just start going in the red. Why? This is such a poor mechanic that I tend to always leave troops on the ground and then when I need them to invade, pull them up, fly them over, and then invade. All the while I am going through singularities like it’s coffee or something. * Loyalty- This is so stupid. I cannot fathom why I would lose population in my federation to go to the Cardassian and become slaves and then die there. WHY? I really dislike this stupid population loyalty system.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a Star Trek fan.  Not a convention Trekkie, but I like the shows and watch them, often.  I also love Stellaris.  And I'm of the generation of kids that saw the first advertisement for "Birth of the Federation" in CGW and waited years for it to launch.  Then it had bugs I never was able to resolve with my meager teenage funds.In other words, I had every expectation in the world and I had no expectations at all.  No clue what that means?  Then you haven't been playing Star Trek video games long enough.  I read the reviews,  They were mediocre-to-bad.  I waited.Over the holidays, I finally picked it up.  It is great.  Will I complete more than one mission-centric play-through for each race?  Yes, but very little unless there is a solid DLC or mod community.  There have been complaints that the "canon" events always occur at the same time.  I'm okay with that - those events make the Star Trek universe what it is.  That said, it would help for replay, especially in the event that there is no DLC or long-term support for this game, if it was possible to turn those events off entirely or randomize them among the species,  As-is, after three lengthy games in various factions (UFP, Klingon, Cardassian), I feel like I have one more in me (Romulan) before this goes back on the shelf waiting for some DLC, a good mod, or a sleepless night with TNG playing in the background.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR:  This is an unfinished game, do not buy yet.I'm a long time fan of Star Trek, and Stellaris is my most played steam game of all time, so I'm pretty much the ground zero target audience for this game.  What we get for the purchase price is a pretty enough Star Trek mod for a version of Stellaris which is several years out of date.  The gameplay is fine.  The story elements are okayish.  The graphics are very pretty, although puzzling in a few places (like, no LCARS?  Seriously?).The biggest issue with the game is its pacing.  It rushes through TNG's story elements extremely quickly.  It feels like we've barely gotten started, and suddenly Romulus blows up...  There's no tension with the Cardassians, and suddenly Bajor is conquered.  There's exactly one short little event for Locutus, and then the Borg invasion bugs out and doesn't launch properly.If this were a DLC for Stellaris for $20, it would be a great deal.  But at the price of a full game, it's an unfinished, shallow, and buggy mess that I cannot recommend.  Come on Paradox, you're better than this.

_childDocuments_.review: So having played through a Federation "campaign" well towards the end of the tech tree, the pacing in the game is terrible. The majority of the quests are supposed to be done quite early, I never managed to upgrade the Enterprise as anomalies disappeared and Troi's counter kept resetting.... I didn't even have the heavy transports in time to rescue Romulus as you can't focus the tech tree towards specific goals, you have to research what it provides. The fact you cannot change your war philosophy as Federation also makes late game combat more difficult (and terribly boring), because it's relatively easy to out tech your enemies just after the story completes, as that's when you finally have enough resources for your colonies to upgrade well, and unless they attack someone you are protecting, they won't engage you and you can't claim territory from them. The ship scaling and pirates are totally bananas compared to both resource production in the "early game", specifically for alloys. There is no reason I am using Miranda and Intrepid ships before the Excelsior class, no reason why fleet size is so restrictive relative to power (the pirates attack you with 2.1k dmg fleets and you need at least three or four fleets in the early game to defend against them), and if I can fly the enterprise around, why can't I build other galaxy class ships.... The idea behind the game is sound, and it could have been a lot more fun if they had scaled the time/resources/ships more appropriately. I would really hope there will be a balance patch to fix the pacing a bit but given the price of the game I doubt one will come. NOTE: I have not played the Stellaris star trek mod before, so this is only from playing Infinite.

name: Still Wakes the Deep
detailed_description: STILL WAKES THE DEEP is a return to the first-person narrative horror genre for The Chinese Room, creator of critically acclaimed games such as Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs, Everybody’s Gone to the Rapture, and Dear Esther . You are an offshore oil rig worker, fighting for your life through a vicious storm, perilous surroundings, and the dark, freezing North Sea waters. All lines of communication have been severed. All exits are gone. All that remains is to face the unknowable horror that’s come aboard. GAME FEATURES Explore a stunningly realised offshore oil rig in 1970’s Scotland that evolves throughout the story World-class visuals, audio, writing from award-winning studio The Chinese Room Star-studded cast of voice-actors: Alec Newman, Neve McIntosh, and more World-class, haunting soundtrack by Jason Graves Six hours of terrifying gameplay Brace yourself for a symphony of action, trepidation and awe LIVE THE HORROR An immersive disaster story aboard an authentic North Sea oil rig Face a terrifying, unrelenting foe Pray that, one day, you get to see your family again Experience the beauty and ferocity of the sea, as it rips apart one of humanity’s strongest structures and its steadfast crew ESCAPE THE RIG Avoid, distract, and sneak around in best attempts to survive No weapons. No powers. Just your wits and determination Run, climb, and swim through the flooding corridors and storm-lashed outer decks Struggle for survival, as one wrong step could be your last

GAME FEATURES Explore a stunningly realised offshore oil rig in 1970’s Scotland that evolves throughout the story World-class visuals, audio, writing from award-winning studio The Chinese Room Star-studded cast of voice-actors: Alec Newman, Neve McIntosh, and more World-class, haunting soundtrack by Jason Graves Six hours of terrifying gameplay Brace yourself for a symphony of action, trepidation and awe LIVE THE HORROR An immersive disaster story aboard an authentic North Sea oil rig Face a terrifying, unrelenting foe Pray that, one day, you get to see your family again Experience the beauty and ferocity of the sea, as it rips apart one of humanity’s strongest structures and its steadfast crew ESCAPE THE RIG Avoid, distract, and sneak around in best attempts to survive No weapons. No powers. Just your wits and determination Run, climb, and swim through the flooding corridors and storm-lashed outer decks Struggle for survival, as one wrong step could be your last
short_description: 1975. Disaster strikes the Beira D oil rig off the coast of Scotland. Navigate the collapsing rig to save your crew from an otherworldly horror on the edge of all logic and reality.

_childDocuments_.review: WARNING, DO NOT USE FSR 3 IN THIS GAME OR YOU WILL EXPERIENCE CONSTANT CRASHES AND FREEZES! Still Wakes the Deep is a fantastic, linear, story focused horror game that tells an amazing, emotional story, and provides stressful and fun gameplay. The visuals are fantastic, the sound design is amazing, the voice acting is superb, and the experience doesn't overstay its welcome and tells its story within a crisp 4-5 hours. Totally worth the money to support this team and the fantastic game they made.
_childDocuments_.name: Still Wakes the Deep

_childDocuments_.review: Still Wakes the Deep is a psychological/survival horror game that has a linear, but deeply engaging story line. It has elements of Lovecraft's cosmic horror, the more personal body horror of John Carpenter's "The Thing," and play mechanics similar to "Alien: Isolation." To me, all of these comparisons are good things and leave it game itself it's own unique cinematic experience. It's first person and you have to play in a stealthy, puzzle-solving way as you try to survive on the Beira D oil rig in the middle of the North Sea after the drill releases an unknown entity onto the platform. It either kills or absorbs members of the crew, making them another obstacle to try to survive. The story had be bawling by the end. Although marketed as a "walking simulator," the location of the story makes it make more sense and the feeling of being limited or claustrophobic is part of the horror. The only issue I had with the gameplay was the swimming. The swim mechanics aren't great and if you need to press A to lunge through the water, you have to be angled right and time the button press right to move forward. If you get frustrated, just take a break. breathe, and then try again. Read a more detailed review on my blog Second Unit Reviews:
_childDocuments_.name: Still Wakes the Deep

_childDocuments_.review: I wish there was a mixed review for this to be honest. For starters the game is actually really good or the story not really the game because there isnt much game at all. it just felt like a very long interactive movie and to be honest that is where my problem starts with this game. The game is VERY short. i completed it in around 4 hours and thats me taking my time and looking at everything i can. the game is very linear and there is no other paths besides the main paths. i wouldnt mind this at all if the price tag for this game wasnt almost $40. its not like youll be coming back to replay this game because theres nothing to replay. what you play through is what you get nothing more and nothing less. there is no replay value here. if the game was $20-$25 i wouldnt mind this at all, for me that is what the value of this game is. Overall though the story is really good and i enjoyed every second of it. its just not worth almost $40. if you can buy this game around $25 or below then thats when i can recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.name: Still Wakes the Deep

_childDocuments_.review: It's good, not perfect, but still good.It Isn't the scariest game, it isn't too intense, but it gets the job done.The story is the pinnacle of short linear story telling so don't expect bonus endings. The voice acting is incredible and all the characters are very human.7.5/10, wait for a sale since playtime spans no more than 5 hours.
_childDocuments_.name: Still Wakes the Deep

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know how to feel about this game. It had sooooo much potential. It just fell so short. I love the general setting and feeling of the game but it just seems so vacant. its boring. its DEFINITELY a walking simulator with very little sneaking. It's wayyyyy to easy and wayyyyyy to short. I beat it after 6.6 hours and for half of that I was afk. The voice acting is great though. truly the best part of this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Still Wakes the Deep

_childDocuments_.review: I'm terrible at reviews, but I'm going to try anyway.I love this game.It has a fantastic premise, that of a North Sea oil rig that hits something mysterious while drilling, looks and sounds amazing, has well developed characters and a well told and touching story. It uses atmosphere and tension to create a building feeling of dread and horror without resorting to cheap jumpscares.Some will probably say it's too short (I wrapped it up in just over 4 hours), but for this kind of game I think it's just right. Any longer and you run the risk of it beginning to drag, lessening the horror elements.I couldn't recommend the game more. Well worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Still Wakes the Deep

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent story-focused horror game.  The atmosphere, visuals and especially the writing/acting are all top notch.From a game-play perspective, this is more of a "playing a movie" sort of experience. You do not have any significant agency in what happens. You either do what is required of you at each step, or you fail and try again. At no point are you managing resources or much in the way of risk.The closest the game place gets to that is some Alien Isolation style segments where you do a bunch of hide-distract-dash.  But mostly you just follow the obvious yellow thing (if it's painted yellow, it is probably something you go through, climb on, etc.)None of this is a negative, though. That is just the style of game they went for, where the game place is more about driving a narrative. And that it does exceptionally well. Super great pacing, it never wears out its welcome, and pushes hard to getcha in the feels by the end.Except about 7 hours of game play.  But a very immersive 7 hours.
_childDocuments_.name: Still Wakes the Deep

_childDocuments_.review: This is rated by price of, length of, and quality of game per hour.  That means if a Game is 15 dollars and takes 3 hours to complete, it's 5 dollars per hour of entertainment.  If said 5 hours of entertainment are good for the cost, I recommend the game.  I paid full price for the game bringing the average to about $9 an hour.  For said price, the experience was not bad until the mid portion that felt extremely padded out, where you go here, fix this, go there, hide from that, over and over and over again.  There is no combat or inventory system, and while the voice acting and map quality is actually quite high, I can think of a good number of games that did a much better job of capturing and retaining my imagination for less than a quarter the cost.  In short, its an above average game for the style of game that it is.  It is simply not worth the price point.
_childDocuments_.name: Still Wakes the Deep

Great voice acting, horrifying lovecraftian monsters, although the narrative focus on the protagonists personal issues without investigating the behaviour, purpose, effects or origin of the main monster by the end kind of left me with blue balls.Main downside for me is the game play is so linear and simple (With a literal yellow paint trail leading you through the whole game) It may as well have been a movie, but it was a great experience none the less.

_childDocuments_.review: This game, with is beautiful acting, music, writing, Foley, and a great atmosphere brought by the creative team, stumbles for me because of it's gameplay. It walks the fine line of being a stealthy story-filled "walking sim" along the lines of Edith Finch, but really lacks in any variation in that. If I were to ask for any changes to this game, it would be gmaplay revolving around "elekky" work, and more seamless integration of 'the assimilated'. Exploring the cantina and bunks was such an amazing beginning and having the opportunity to explore these fleshed out characters lives before seeing them was amazing. That all being said, i think the gameplay and a steeper price point leaves more to be desired and lessens what would otherwise be an amazing peek into a world so close to ours.
_childDocuments_.name: Still Wakes the Deep

_childDocuments_.review: Haven't beaten it yet but at almost two hours again in everything I've seen is solid. Graphics are great, story/dialogue has me invested enough to want to stay up and be miserable at work tomorrow to see more, and the setting is amazing. One thing I really love is that so far a lot of this is actually taking place during the day which is rare for most horror games. So far the monster designs have all been The Thing levels of body horror and while the scare sequences definitely feel on rails that's just how it is with the genre of chase/unarmed horror. Stuff like Soma or Outlast was a lot more open ended with how you handled hunts but it all still boiled down to run and hide while completing an objective then have a chase, this game just cuts the fat with that and gets on with the story. Seen people say it takes a bit out of game play to give stronger set piece moments, but lets be real the hide and seek loops of other chase horror games aren't really deep enough to offset a good experience and I like the faster pace in this. Moving from one thing to another and not spending 30 minutes under a bed makes you feel like you're actually on a time crunch to figure out a solution to your situation.Overall strongly recommend. Glad the games getting good reviews and hope with the success of this we see more devs try their hand at eldritch horror and deep sea/oceanic settings.
_childDocuments_.name: Still Wakes the Deep

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game. Just what I expected and maybe a bit more. Interesting setting, well realized, with good sense of place. You really get to know the rig and seeing it change throughout the game is pretty cool.Loved the characters and accents. This game has great voice acting. Sound design and music are great too. Which is really important for a horror game. Story is interesting and I'm very happy with how it all ended.Also a good showcase for UE5. Good graphics, good HDR. Giving main character a real body, grounded in the game world, with all the animations etc. is really cool. Kudos for that.I would also like to thank the Devs for adding Story mode. It would be much harder for me to beat this without it. Greatly appreciated. I hope more developers implement something like that in other "walking simulator" horror titles.
_childDocuments_.name: Still Wakes the Deep

_childDocuments_.review: They nailed the Voice Acting and writing for this game, I've never seen a game nor really much media that has properly encapsulated Scotland as well as this one has; because even trainspotting sidestepped how Scottish people generally think about the union at all.Also this is the best game The Chinese Room have ever made with quite tangibly engaging gameplay and nailing that perfect atmosphere and setting perfectly.
_childDocuments_.name: Still Wakes the Deep

_childDocuments_.review: Still Wakes the Deep is a fantastic cinematic experience. It is a beautiful game with marvelous environment design. The game does a tremendously good job of making the player feel small and weak within the massive oil rig. The visuals, sound effects, and weather effects all complement the narrative, which is as distressing as each cranking corner of the slowly deteriorating structure. The voice acting is also brilliant, with each character feeling alive as you descend into madness throughout the story.However, the linear progression is too limiting for the overall experience to be truly satisfying. Still Wakes the Deep is essentially "The Thing" on an oil rig, but it lacks the absolute horror that the movie delivered and fails to offer anything that encourages the player to explore more. It’s a shame that such a gorgeous map feels underutilized simply because the player is forced to follow one path. As someone with a low tolerance for scares, I was disappointed to find very few genuinely frightening moments. Although the monster designs were wonderful, neither the psychological horror nor the scares lived up to expectations. Even in the darkest areas, the monsters felt too easy to avoid and applied almost no pressure. It is almost as if SOMA failed to turn its encounters into frightening experiences.
_childDocuments_.name: Still Wakes the Deep

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game but it just isn't very good. I'll try to keep it as spoiler free as possible but there are too many issues that add up to ultimately being a 2/5 game at best. Starting with the good. The voice acting itself is very good, and the environments are occasionally very pretty and almost always quite atmospheric. Now for the bad. The story is an interesting concept but is not executed well. The main character makes next to no decisions for himself and is just doing what hes told all the way to the end of the game. The supporting cast also will make nonsensical decisions just so the can end up in the right spot for the plot when needed. I will cry at most emotional moments in games and movies but I felt nothing during what should've been a pivotal moment. Basically take the plot of The Thing (1982) but make the characters only try to escape rather than ever fight back in any way. This causes the story to fall flat for me despite having a solid core idea. The first time you see a monster it's quite unsettling but be prepared to see essentially that same design for the rest of the game with the exact same gameplay loop of move from hidey hole to hidey hole. You'll also get a good long look at each of them causing them to lose any real sense of unease or fear. The pathfinding is also hilariously bad at times and I'm pretty sure monsters got stuck on the environment more than once letting me casually complete a section. The game also misuses mechanics that would fit in a more open design like a classic resident evil game. You will occasionally unlock doors, lower ladders, and close valves to shutoff spraying fire or gas leaks. There is also a one time use mechanic of being able to kick open a door. Now the misuse of these mechanics come from the fact that this is a linear game with zero back tracking so if you have to lower a ladder you aren't unlocking a shortcut back, you are just momentarily inconvenienced by hitting a button literally next to the ladder you are going to climb. Every blocked path is unlocked within feet of the block adding nothing to the gameplay except making you press X or hold right trigger and then tilt the left stick. I've seen a handful of complaints about all of these things but the vast majority of people seem to not have any of these issues, which truly surprises me.
_childDocuments_.name: Still Wakes the Deep

_childDocuments_.review: I understand the criticism this game gets, similar to the one A Machine for Pigs got.Are the gameplay mechanics paper thin? Yes. Would you say this game absolutely fits the 'walking simulator' genre? Yes, can't argue with that.Is the game still worth it? Absolutely yes.The environments and atmosphere are great. Maybe it's a me thing, but I love the oil rig as a setting, and how you traverse all of it, in and out. I liked the characters and especially the VAing. The creatures are pretty interesting too, very The Thing/Cronenberg inspired.I think that if you like cosmic or body horror media, this game is for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Still Wakes the Deep

_childDocuments_.review: A deep story driven atmospheric game one of the best of its kind for some time. The visual quality is excellent and there is a lot of attention to detail. Well done. The HDR was a bit hit and miss for me, some parts of the game like the lower levels of the rig look really good whilst others not so much, especially the upper levels where there is that grey misty background tone which was probably for atmosphere. 9/10
_childDocuments_.name: Still Wakes the Deep

_childDocuments_.review: Short and sweet game, excellent top-tier voice acting from the cast, good mystery in a fantastic setting (got this primarily because it reminded me of Cold Fear, iykyk), story overall engaging, scare and creepiness factor will keep you engaged and running - all 'round recommend honestly.Only things I'd say I was disappointed on was the lack of in-game collectables - there's notes and interactions giving characterization to everyone, but only really at the start. _childDocuments_.review: Great little game.Stellar voice acting and dialogue, absolutely sets a bar for it, better than 99% of videogame voicework and dialogue, feels extremely real.The level design of the oil rig is FANTASTIC, and really feels like you're on a real one, looks beautiful too.Good pacing! Many people complain about short games, I clocked about 5 hours in this playing at a normal pace, and was glad of the length, it fit the story and gameplay perfectly, and I felt I got my moneys worth completely.The horror elements of the game are rather hit or miss , the industrial and oil rig horror is fantastic, the  is pretty mediocre, but the dialogue and writing more than make up for it.The biggest stain on this otherwise good little horror game is it is optimised horribly and runs like crap.I'd give this a 7 or 8 out of 10 if you don't mind unstable frames. _childDocuments_.review: i played dear esther for the first time not too long ago, which got me really interested in this game when i learnt it was being developed by the chinese room. this is one of the best horror games i've played so far. the oil rig setting lends it a particularly oppressive, inescapable feeling of isolation, and the body horror featured here is some of the best i've seen, reminding me a lot of what appeared in motive studios' dead space remake. despite its 4-5 hour runtime it still managed to give all its characters so much personality, with phenomenal dialogue and voice acting. the ending made me teary eyed too, which is something only a handful of other games have ever managed. fantastic game. i almost wish it was longer, but i think it's actually the perfect length for what it does.

_childDocuments_.review: This really is a fantastic game, that delivers on all fronts. A gripping story with relatable characters, plenty of suspense and an incredibly immersive atmosphere make this an absolute must play for any horror fans. A big plus for me was also the fact that SWTD doesn't rely on cheap, predictable jump scares but actually delivers an unnerving sense of tension. The voice acting is also absolutely on point, adding to the already strong sense of immersion. Graphically the game is also a gem to look at and before all hell breaks lose on the rig, you could easily find yourself staring out across the ocean in menacing anticipation. I spent roughly 10 hours in-game and would certainly jump in for another round at a moments notice.
_childDocuments_.name: Still Wakes the Deep

_childDocuments_.review: Still Wakes the Deep is a really good and satisfying "Eldritch-Bodyhorror-Type" Game which is worth your time if you havent played it.Story 5/5The Story is really good, it is written so well and especially through the end it picks up and gets really emotional and engageing with it really catching your feelings. The Intro of the game helps so much because it sells the different characters to you, you will go "Oh man I talked with that guy before" or "No no no not him/her" many times and thats all because of the immersive intro. The Voiceacting is really great, Emotions and intentions of the characters are so clear because of this, you really feel emeressed and engaged throughout the 4 hours of Gameplay. The Voiceacting of the monsters is so good, from the pleading for help to the screaching and moaning. It gets so uncomfortable sometimes because you most of the time hear the entitys before seeing them. Graphics 4/5The monsters and the rig are really well made, getting you emeressed and creeped out with a feeling of dread. Beatuiful sceneary mixed with grey - almost hopeless looking - Graphics really sell the game and what it wants to create. I recommend playing with "film grain" on as it sells this dirty old 1975 look even more.Gameplay 3/5This is the biggest flaw of the game. Sometimes jumps or events really felt sluggish and not coordinated. This gets frustrateing sometimes but I can look over it for the most part. The swimming feels really bad, slow and all around just no polished. I sometimes felt like my inputs didnt do anything as the character barely moves underwater. The Controlls are the biggest weakpoint of the game.But the Horror, oh my the Horror. It is not in your face, it dosent need jumpscares to be scary. It just used these eldritch and deformed beings, you get really uncomfortable and start feeling the dread as you see one of the monsters. The story also gets really uncanny as u just feel hopeless throughout the whole game. This game is really good, it is worth the money and worth the time. If you have 4 hours to spare then please give this game a try.3,5/5
_childDocuments_.name: Still Wakes the Deep

_childDocuments_.review: It's important to stress out of the gate that this might not be a game for everyone, it's quite short and the mechanics are straightforward but it's an absolute masterclass in good acting, likeable characters and atmosphere and environment doing a ton of heavy lifting. With a game like this, you're going in for the experience more so than the gameplay and it certainly delivered for me personally. I found the setting and characters to be a refreshing change of pace. It was especially nice getting to hear some Scottish and British voices that weren't just cartoonish cliches dialed up to 11. The characters and actors felt relatable and I genuinely enjoyed a lot of the patter and found myself chuckling along on many occasions. The presentation and performance were also very impressive for me. I'm running a 4080 and a 7800x3D and I was able to comfortably run on Epic settings at 1440p with DLSS balanced and frame gen turned on hitting around 100fps most of the time. Baring in mind, the higher settings are using ray tracing for the reflections, GI and I believe shadows and maybe ambient occlusion. In spite of all these heavy settings, the game feels very fluid and I never felt like the game was chugging at any time and the visual returns are generally spectacular. If you can get over the short runtime then it's well worth checking this one out because it's a really neat and refreshing experience. More of this type of thing please Chinese Room!
_childDocuments_.name: Still Wakes the Deep

_childDocuments_.review: Let's make something clear, first:I don't play games like this very often (horror games, where you can't fight back). While I really like a well written story, I always want something more - an arsenal to shoot or slash the enemy, skills to distribute and/or choices to make - to use and/or to do.I'm most likely not the target audience, and if games like this are more to your liking, than maybe my points will not be as relevant for you. I will try to focus on objective stuff, so this review might end up being more useful.The very short summary of the game: you are on an oil rig, and something goes wrong, and now you'll have to survive.The visuals, the atmosphere and the voice acting is freaking awesome! The many little noises that you can think of are all there. Waves and rain from the outside, metal structures making noises - it's all done very well - I felt like I was there. The visuals of the game is great. The "grayness" gets you into the game's atmosphere immediately, and never let's go. The character models look good, and the enemies look very disturbing (I mean this as a positive). The only negative I can say (if I really wanted to) is some design of the "bad stuff" reminded me when some graphics weren't finished in a game, or when the models clipped - mostly in older games. In this games case, it wasn't a bug, or anything like that - it just reminded me of those things. I'd have gone with different (more "fleshy") design. But this, I'd put in the nitpick category.The voices got me liking the game from the first lines! Literally every voice actor and actress done a top notch job, and I really liked the accents! They conveyed the emotions - the panic, the hope and the despair - perfectly. Also, the voices and noises coming from the enemies enhance their creepiness. Made me want to get away even more.Now, get to why I can't recommend this game after praising it: IT'S TOO SHORT!Since there are no choices in the game, there is only one ending (as far as I can tell). There is no replay value - you can't change how to approach challenges, enemies, neither who to save or let die. Which is not a bad thing in itself. But then the game/story should've been much longer! I got the game on a sale for 26€ (with VAT) and even that feels much higher than what playtime I was able to put in it (and I was really not trying to rush). At full price you'll get 6-7 hours of gameplay for 36€. While it's pretty, that's irrelevant, if you can only play it for this long. The game either should be much cheaper, or they should've put in mechanics to at least create the illusion of choice and different outcomes (or actually provide multiple endings). I can sink in several hundred hours in games where I can create different builds and/or have different outcomes because of choices I can make. If I'd tried to price those like this game, they would cost thousands.I can't recommend this game, it's too short. I will still check the devs upcoming projects, because they sure as hell have talent - just either make them cheaper or longer!
_childDocuments_.name: Still Wakes the Deep

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't had a horror game that makes me feel real fear in a long time, I haven't felt my heart race out of genuine fear since I was 6 years old. A truly magnificent game with graphics that nicely emphasize the monstrosities contained within this creation. I've been anticipating the release of Still Wakes the Deep for a long time and it has not let me down. Amazing.

_childDocuments_.review: Still Wakes the Deep is the latest game from The Chinese Room, known for their critically acclaimed title "Dear Esther." This marks the final game written by studio founder Dan Pinchbeck. Set in the mid-70s, the game places players in the shoes of Scotsman Cameron McLeary, an electrician on an offshore oil rig, who is evading the police after a drunken pub brawl.The opening scenes introduce the beautifully rendered setting of the rig and its superbly voice-acted inhabitants. However, things soon go awry as the drill awakens an eldritch beast from the depths, threatening the rig's structure.Players must navigate the wreckage using first-person platforming to escape. As some crew members transform into monsters, McLeary must hide and run from his former friends to survive. The game predominantly offers a walking simulator experience, with players moving from one section to the next, interacting with environmental items, and occasional light stealth sections. Routes and interactables are clearly marked with the "yellow-highlight" method, making navigation straightforward. Those seeking in-depth gameplay should look elsewhere.Instead, the atmosphere and story are the highlights here, particularly the audio. While there aren’t many major twists, "Still Wakes the Deep" keeps you hooked throughout its roughly four-hour runtime. However, the lack of notes or similar items to discover along the way is a missed opportunity to flesh out the other crew members more.On a technical note, the game ran well on my 1080ti and Ryzen 5 1600X with FSR3, though I encountered an issue where the game would crash during a couple of loading transitions. Apart from this hiccup, I managed to achieve a decent frame rate of around 60-100fps.Overall, The Chinese Room has put significant effort into creating an edge-of-your-seat walking sim with good world-building and a fantastic cast of characters. It won’t be for everyone, and the higher price tag may deter some, but if this sounds like your cup of tea, I definitely recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Still Wakes the Deep

_childDocuments_.review: Eh, its a Chinese Room game, what else to say? If you didn't hate Machine for Pigs, you probably won't hate this one too, on a sale. If you want more from a horror game than just some visceral imagery, you should look for another one.It has a nice story and characters, atmosphere, good voice acting, but it is just a walking simulator. It has a few H&S and chase sections, but it would be disingenuous to call them tense. I initially wanted to give the game a negative review, just for how appaling the monster encounters are, but decided that it would be unfair. Especially considering that i didn't HATE anything else about the game.Visual and sound design of monsters is good, but the danger they present is an illusion. The game has no health or other damage system, so the monsters just instantly kill you on contact. You are not worried about spending recources to recover, so there is no tention from that. You also have no inventory and all of the puzzles are usually 1-2 steps long and do not require items that you can lose. The encounter sections are generally short and consist of you crawling from one hiding spot to another. So you have little to no tention from losing progress. The only thing left to scare is your own perception of monsters. Which crumbles to dust the moment you climb into a hiding spot.You see, monsters literally cannot harm you when you are inside a hiding spot. I found that out in the first encounter with a real monster, Trots. I was sitting inside a wide open cabinet, about a meter away from the monster, flashing the light directly into his mug, and he could not do anything to me. The monsters generally don't react to light, so you can safely crawl around with your lights on at all times. Even if you are noticed, you can hop into a hiding spot, put hands over your head in a triangle and say "I'm in a house!". They will growl and cuss, shake their hanging intestines in front of you but they will leave you alone. Later in the game there is a moment where a "hiding spot" is an elevator shaft with a wide open door that the monster could easily fit through, if it was a better horror game. Back in Outlast, Chris Walker would drag me out and rip my head off if i tried something like this.Besides Machine for Pigs, i was also reminded of a little game i played years ago called The Sexorcist, which had the exact same issue. Except the "monster" in that game was leaving traps around, you had multiple item-based puzzles around the house and only 3 lives to complete them all. An H-game with pre-bought assets made me feel more tense than a horror game by Chinese Room, because there was something to lose. If you get killed in SWTD, you are put at the exact same place. I think if you put monster encounters in your game you should put even a little effort into it, so it doesn't look like it was made out of begrudging obligation.I guess it is unfair to focus so hard on the monster encounters to the point everything else seems to be ignored, but had little reason to care about anything else. I don't feel that the characters are in danger, because i don't see the monsters as a danger. And i couldn't care less about the characters because i can't tell 90% of them apart. I remember Addair, , Rennick, , Roy and Finlay, who i assumed to be a guy for about half the game. Everyone else, including the main character, seems to be the same "wee Sco'ish bas'ard" who might as well have the same voice actor. A good voice actor, mind, but nonetheless.Like i said, it was supposed to be a negative review (and it clearly is), but writing it i realised that monster encounters are the only thing i didn't like about the game, and frankly the only thing i had anything to say about.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely recommended. If money's not an issue, buy at full price, it's genuinely worth it. This is an absolute gem of a video game, and one of those that stay with you long after the credits roll. Here's some remarks, if you're curious why I hold it in such high regard: Direction and design are positively outstanding. First time in a very, very long time, that I have engaged with a work of art, which truly understands cosmic horror - as a pure notion, and not as a deflated buzzword for 'tentacles from space'. The story is very good. It's engaging, the characters are memorable  and the setting is meticulously crafted. The rig feels lived in, realistic and interconnected in a shockingly immersive way. Some beats are simple and well-written, others introduce ambiguity and let the terror slowly seep in through the gaps in what you know and understand. Playtime is exactly what it needs to be. First playthrough took me about 5-6 hours and it included precisely zero seconds of downtime or padding. Subjectively, dedicating another hour or so to the buildup in the first chapters would be great, but if it were to come at a cost of anything else, then I don't want it. The gameplay surprised me with how involved it was. Promotional materials may or may not give an impression of a glorified walking sim, but that's just not true. You really do feel like a part of this game's world. Various threats can be usually dealt with in rather open environments, making the challenge fun. Of note is the remarkably competent inclusion of button prompts (that, for the first time in their history, make sense in context of what you want to do). I lost count of how many times my body physically tensed up to do something along with Caz, even though I was just supposed to press a button or two. From a technical standpoint, the game is quite tight. It ran okay for me, and while there are some small infidelities and a bug or two, they didn't take daway from my experience. One bit of jank towards the end of the game got me a bit upset, but I can't guarantee it wasn't user error. Quality is pretty high all throughout. The hraphics are really something special. I couldn't help but stop and marvel at them a whole bunch of times - literally, just stop and stare at the surroundings, sinking it all in. Framing is excellent, possibly on the level of Dishonored 1, and the environments feel 'made', rather than simply 'designed' or 'crafted'.  The audio is fitting, well made and immersive. Music doesn't overstay it's welcome, while the churning waters, the howling winds and the industrial ambience remain center-stage. Also, a word of caution: this game does audio cues. Pay attention to what you are hearing.
