_childDocuments_.name: Bramble: The Mountain King

_childDocuments_.review: The game is great. It is quite obvious while playing the game that it is inspired by Scandinavian folklore and also by the work of John Bauer, with some of his paintings in the game, as well as the character Tuva being taken from his painting called "Tuvstarr". The game sort of reawakened my fear of human-eating giants with its trolls that I had when I was little. I really recommend playing the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Bramble: The Mountain King

_childDocuments_.review: Bramble: The Mountain King is puzzle platformer similar to games like INSIDE or LIMBO by PlayDead while also using many elements (particularly the movement and traversal) from Bandai Namco's Little Nightmares. This game takes the strongest elements from all of these games (maybe a little too much in some areas) and makes them the main draw for this game alongside it's Scandinavian folklore art design and storytelling. Now, let's get into the Good, Okay, and Bad of this game.GOOD: VISUALS, MUSIC, AND NARRATIVEThis game is just a visual and auditory treat. If you are a sucker for Scandinavian folklore, fairy tales, or viking legends, this game will not disappoint. This game is punching way above it's weight in terms of graphical fidelity and art direction, which makes sense since Dimfrost Studio's previous game, A Writer And His Daughter, had some really high fidelity models for items and some nice lighting as well. It's been a long time since I've looked at water and thought: "Damn, that's nice looking water". This game also knows when to be scary. Since this is based on some really classic fairy tales, they know how to really frighten to inner child within. This game also has some beautiful and haunting music from Martin Wave and Dan Wakefield. They know how to really bring out both the cheer and fear within classic fairy tales, since they are meant to be both enticing and daunting at the same time. As for the story... oh man... it far exceeded my expectations. Typically, whenever a game opens up with a "Content Warning", I usually roll my eyes since it kind of takes a lot of shock away from me when I suddenly see the "Dangerous Content". I think a game like White Shadows really did a number on me for this exact topic regarding Content Warnings since I found their depiction of "Dangerous Content" to be very underwhelming. Bramble: The Mountain King... holds back no punches when it came to their subject matter. You will see very young children get mutilated, dismembered, and eaten alive. The amount of blood and gore in this game can be kind of nauseating in a good way. Now, for the story itself. I don't want to spoil it, but I will say that while the characters don't really talk, instead some NPCs have their dialogue described by the narrator, they give a good amount of character development to Olle, our protagonist, which needs to be experienced from start till end. There were some moments where I was genuinely shocked at what this little kid did, sometimes heinous, sometimes gross. He may not be the most developed character, but he has really good progression. Even his sister gets some progression, but it is mostly epilogue progression; the typically: "This character changed because of what you just watched, The End!" Kind of progression. This game is a visual, musical, and even partially emotional treat.OKAY: ANIMATIONIt is hard to find something that is just "okay" for Bramble: The Mountain King. But if I were to give it an okay on anything, it would have to be animation. NOW, before you disagree, I find the environment to be much better with animation that character models. I think that the character models unfortunately have a "Stiffness" to them at moments that can be kind of hard to ignore. Strangely enough, I only feel like this stiffness occurs in cutscenes rather than gameplay, since the controls are tight and the animations are really consistent and flow good when playing. But the cutscenes just have strange pauses and locking of limbs at times that is hard to explain without you seeing it. This is just okay since it didn't ruin the experience, but it was hard to ignore. But that environmental animation is top notch! Give the environmental animators a raise!BAD: COMBATI should start by saying that I do like some of these boss battles. Skogsrå being probably the best and is made even better for being a mid-point boss. Mountain King himself is also pretty fun with how he switches up his movesets mid fight, keeping you on your toes. Now, this is the thing. These bosses are really well-designed, but the amount of options you have in combat are extremely limited. Now, you might be thinking: "Well... it's a puzzle platformer!" True homie, but honestly, I would've preferred this either be shaken up just a little bit to spice up combat encounters (Don't want this to become an action platformer now do we?) or they just remove it entirely and make the combat a puzzle. But they want you to be engaged in combat since these boss fights give you a 3rd person perspective and have you aim at targets to shoot. It feels really... clunky. Like... trying to play a battle royale on your phone kind of clunky (I know what I said, I have no shame!). So I'm more favoured towards removing combat than enhancing it, and what they did was something... executed poorly.So overall, this game is an easy must play. I would put this next to Little Nightmares in terms of good puzzle platformers, but not as high as INSIDE since that game has just the best atmosphere I've seen in a game. In fact, I should mention that there are a lot of elements of both INSIDE and Little Nightmares you'll notice in this game if you've played it. Especially the scene in INSIDE where you fully encounter "The Pulse". If you know, you know. Congrats Dimfrost Studio on an excellent game!
_childDocuments_.name: Bramble: The Mountain King

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful environment with really fascinating and creepy folklore to get immersed in. I love that non-american folklore can get so dark, it makes it so much more interesting. My only complaint was that the controls were a little frustrating at times but it was a really fun experience over all, especially if you love folklore, fantasy, and horror!
_childDocuments_.name: Bramble: The Mountain King

_childDocuments_.review: Somehow the word I'd use to describe the game is "honest" and I'm not sure why.It feels like the developers really cared, but were limited by time or money to give it that final spit-polish to really make it shine. That is not to say that it's bad, looks like crap or anything like that, the quality is there but you just notice little things here and there that maybe should've been ironed out. The character doesn't move quite right when climbing diagonally, seems they forgot to detail the background in that one location, sound doesn't quite line up in that one cut-scene. Little things but they do add up to make the game feel a bit unpolished.Now that's said, the game is quite good. It really nailed that nordic fairytale aesthetic, the music, atmosphere, all of it, a real treat to see the old folklore from my childhood brought to life like this.I will say though, I'm glad I got the game at a discount, for just about 4h of gameplay, it's quite pricy.
_childDocuments_.name: Bramble: The Mountain King

_childDocuments_.review: This game might not be for everyone, but if you like the idea of dark Norse fairy tales come to life, then this game might be for you. The game play is simple and repetitive. But what this games lacks in game play, it makes up in atmosphere and some. Summed up: a dark interactive fairly tale type game.
_childDocuments_.name: Bramble: The Mountain King

_childDocuments_.review: Feels like you're in the middle of a fairytale.  Fun, lovely graphics, and generally an excellent fantasy adventure game. Its main problem is the only time it's actually difficult is when you have no idea what do.  It's easy to miss some important detail because of the dark graphics, or some mechanic and then you end up running around until tiring of it and googling the solution.  The other problem is it's kinda hard to tell depth on a 2D surface and I think this game would benefit from being 3D (stereoscopic: VR/AR/XR/etc/etc).  But it was well worth buying on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Bramble: The Mountain King

_childDocuments_.review: This is my GOTY. Highly recommend.The music and graphic are beautifulThe difficulty is perfect.It's linear. No backtracking.It's not easy for a game to scare me (jump scares don't count), but some boss gave me the chill.It's more emotional, violent and gore that I thought. Do not underestimate the trigger warnings at the beginning if you are sensitive.It took me around 5 hours to complete it. It went fast.I was expecting a side-scrolling puzzle/platforming game with an implicit story, à la LIMBO or INSIDE. That's not it. The camera angle changes often, and there is a narration and a backstory (beyond "the brother has to save his sister").It makes me want to learn more about the nordic mythology.
_childDocuments_.name: Bramble: The Mountain King

_childDocuments_.review: I am happy that I bought this game, I think it's awesome! :)(Got it on sale, so I wouldn't pay the full price, tho. :/)The story is captivating and it's cool to have the narrator do all the talking.With that said:The voices of the little dwarf people were so annoying to me, that I had to turn down the volume. :xIf they were ment to be annoying - 10/10, well done.I honestly was surprised how dark the story actually got and how they displayed it, so if you're into that, do play that game. :)I know, that there are trigger warnings in the beginning of the game, but still... - had many games with those kinda warnings and they did not deliver.I was emotionally invested and it was the right kind of horror & suspension for me. Was really happy to learn about Skandinavien folklore! :)And the controls were easy enough for someone who doesn't play with a controller a lot!All in all a solid 8/10 from me. :)
_childDocuments_.name: Bramble: The Mountain King

_childDocuments_.review: I played the demo, purchased the full game, and played it all in one sitting. The pacing of the entire game was very well done, going from story to action to puzzles to drive the whole experience forward, never staying doing one thing for too long.The puzzles, including stealth sections, were clever and interesting without being too hard or too easy. They never took very long to solve, but they felt satisfying to figure out.Like the puzzles, the boss fights are also very well done and balanced. Sure, I died quite a bit trying to figure them out for a first play though, but it never felt like it was too brutal nor was I left wondering what to do.Scattered throughout the game are some storybooks. I absolutely LOVE these storybooks! The art is just wonderful, and somehow the pages feel like they have weight as you flip through them. Kudos to whoever worked on them!The overall visuals of this game can be amazing at times. There were moments when I had to pause and look up what engine this was running on because there were some scenes that made me think it might be UE5 (it's on UE4). I usually do not like film grain and depth of field usage in video games, but it served this title well. I found the controls to work well using a wired xbox controller. Performance was great - no UE stutters here.
_childDocuments_.name: Bramble: The Mountain King

_childDocuments_.review: Overall fantastic game.  It has a pretty extreme range from cute to disgusting and gorgeous to dismal and terrifying.  The storytelling and folklore is exquisite.  The music is great, especially the main pieces and it ends with a very familiar piece, for most people I'd imagine.  The gameplay is light exploration and platforming with a few brief puzzles.  Nothing overly challenging and yet failing is part of the journey and was quite entertaining in a lot of cases.  There are a few boss encounters that were fun, but again, not too complicated.My play time was just shy of 4 hours without any searching for the collectibles.  Even with the brevity, there were a couple of sections in the second half of the game that could have been cut down by 5 minutes and I think the game would have been better for it.  An excellent way to spend 4 hours if the trailers look intriguing to you.
_childDocuments_.name: Bramble: The Mountain King

_childDocuments_.review: This was such a little treasure. Really enjoyable gameplay, great visuals, fantastic sound track and a good story. One thing I found unexpected delight from was the atmosphere of the game. I grew up with my grandparents, whom would tell stories of gnomes, trolls and other Swedish folk tales. and for about thirty years my grandfather crafted wood carved paintings, depicting the scenes which John Bauer created. _childDocuments_.review: A fixed camera angle! Wow. I'm really been missing such a thing in modern games for quite awhile. I'm so ♥♥♥♥♥♥ tired of solely over-the-shoulder 3rd person player-controlled cameras or just another cramped first-person camera.I'm so desperate for another fixed-camera game. And this game has quenched my thirst for the time being until I begin to get desperate & claw at my neck until I begin to spray blood again.I love fixed-camera games.Also, the gameplay alone is so good.Much like games like , your movement is pretty basic yet snappy. The gameplay instead more-so being applied to how your character, Olle, interacts with the world through its unique, ever-changing ways to constantly have you enthralled in the game's magnificent gameplay.You never know what's next, what next to expect. Every area feels completely different & individualized by their personalized mechanics or themes. One area will  feel the same as the previous or upcoming one.This why short games are so unbelievably good, as they allow to cramp all its good stuff within a 4/5 hour long package, keeping the player constantly engaged and excited to experience the next part, instead of spreading the excitement out so thin by same-y experiences.It's like a huge pie but most of it is crust with only a few, yet delicious strawberries placed about. Absolutely lessening its impressive size, making the much smaller yet more delicious pie to be so much more noteworthy compared to its counterparts.Anyway, AAA open-world lite-RPG rant is now over.Moving on... I think one of my favourite moments in the entire game actually pretty late into it.I'll have to spoil a bit, but I think it's a worthy exception of such.But essentially there's a part where you wander into an abandoned house from the lowest floor. You see a staircase & a huge empty room only blocked by a wooden box that you can crawl over & through.Okay, cool.But walking up the stairs leads you into a nearly pitch-black attic with stray holes spread all-over it. And in the attic it's home to many enemies. You can either lure these enemies to accidentally fall into the holes by luring them or try to avoid them when crossing this area.It'll be hard to get by them because the area is so claustrophobic & cramped with enemies.But if you instead lure the enemies down into the holes... and you thereafter fall into said holes too while attempting carefully walk over them by balancing on small wooden logs... then you'll now be stuck in the huge empty room from the floor below, desperately trying to muster through a horde of enemies to the exit blocked by the wooden box that only you can climb through.That's such a perfect encapsulation of risk/reward game-play, where you try to balance enemies both above & below as to minimize risk in both areas as much as possible to your personalized will, that will possibly have consequences if you misjudge yourself.♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that's just amazing. I sat there with gauged eyes & hanging jaw the second I left that area. WOW.The bosses in this game are so good that they deserve their entire dedicated section.Each boss-fight plays out entirely differently, helping establish their individual characterization through their fighting style & methods; and also keep the game-play new & ever-changing.I don't want to spoil any bosses, as they each are so impressively unique & shocking that by merely describing them will ultimately desaturate & degrade first-time impressions from this that will  be reading this.But straight-up, they're all so good...I adored every one of them.My  complaint with literally any single of them would by the "skull" boss (not spoiling anything beyond that) & how I felt it could've benefited from adding an additional & new phase; and thereafter shorten their first phase, as it is a little too same-y after awhile & underwhelming considering their wonderful visual character design.Still though, the rest of the boss-fights vastly make it up for this sole underwhelming boss-fight.I don't even feel comfortable describing it as "underwhelming" as it's still a pretty alright boss-fight, it's just that stacked up against all the other boss-fights it sorely lacks behind, sadly.But with fights like the Nøkken one & the last boss-fight... yeah there's just no way all of them can stack up equally. That's to be expected.I also just adore how a lot of the boss-fights based on actual folklore & fairy-tales have actual in-game collectible fairy-tale books explaining their history in great & honest detail.All detailed with gorgeous artwork & great voice-acting.It's these small things that just greatly enhance so much of the game, especially to those who may not know all these creatures & beasts since they possibly don't interact with so much mythology/folklore/fairy-tales as peeps like I do.It's really hard to talk about this game & review it.Because almost anything I have to say would end up being constituted as spoilers, since so much of the game greatly just benefits and relies on the act of surprise. That's why I have had such a hard time trying to actually write a review for this game.Still, I hope I did it quite fairly for this gorgeous & wonderful experience.Utmost certainly one of the greatest games I have played this year.It deserves every bit of praise that it has received so far + more.Please check this game out if you haven't already!

_childDocuments_.review: Bramble is an A+ storytime wrapped in simple game mechanics, and takes quite a bit of nerves to stomach through some scenes.To start off, Bramble is NOT like Little Nightmares. The atmosphere and theme are where the similarities begin and end. Little Nightmares relies heavily on parkour and platforming, and opts out of potentially traumatizing you by stylizing a lot of their gore and horror. Bramble goes for the complete opposite. It wants to lull you into a promise of a dark fairytale puzzle-platformer, and then hits you over the head with realism that's oftentimes not for the faint of heart. On top of that, the platforming mechanics often inconsistent and pathing unclear.HOWEVER, as soon as I understood that i will be playing a storybook, and not something like LN, everything clicked. Bramble transports you to a time when fairytales were meant to teach children that the forest is not a playground. That curiosity kills the cat, and that creatures who live in the woods will most likely kill you. You are an outsider in a breathtaking ecosystem that will never be your home (a subversion I REALLY enjoyed).You play as Olle, a little boy who snuck out to explore the forest with his adventurous sister Lillemor. Everything starts off fairly tame, but as soon she gets herself into trouble, the story begins to show its dark and twisted underbelly. The story is, ultimately, never losing hope despite how dark and difficult life gets. Olle is forced to grow up in such traumatizing ways, and the fact that he's a silent protagonist ON TOP of being a child makes the experience so much heavier on the player.To end this haphazard review, let me highlight my favorite aspects based on which I'd recommend the game:1. The graphics are great, the atmosphere shifts super well throughout the game. The devs really play around with lighting and level design to tell the story.2. The narration is top-notch, wish you could choose Swedish to complete the experience <33. The folklore. That's it. Just. Wow.4. The camera work is a dead giveaway that this was intended as a storybook experience more than a platformer. The camera angles shift with every new scene, like in old Resident Evil games, for example. It really enhances the cinematic experience of everything you do. For me, this one shot in particular, where the camera is positioned as if you're someone inside a house looking through the window at Olle (while you're running around with him) was what hit the nail on the head.5. Last but not least - the boss fights. Oh my god, their design gets better and more visually striking as the game progresses. You never know what to expect with each boss, and it's all the more exciting when you experience the fights. The final boss fight accompanied by the soundtrack is done like a proper culmination of the entire journey. All in all, Bramble was the kind of game I really needed to play, and I'm thrilled that I did. For those who like dark stories and heavy themes, it's perfect, but for those hoping they'll get puzzles and platforming exactly like Little Nightmares or INSIDE, you miiiight want to scale down your expectations. Bramble is more about the story and atmosphere, bogged down by platforming bugs and inconsistencies that might frustrate you, especially if you're playing on a controller.

_childDocuments_.review: The very first thing to point out with this game is the control issues... On the Steam Store page it indicates FULL controller support and under that full controller support for Xbox controllers. However; when after the game is purchased and it viewed in your library, it then changes to "Mostly playable with your controller... The game is playable, but may show incorrect glyphs or require a keyboard at some points." With that in mind, this game to me is best suited to be played with a controller due to the platforming and having to move diagonally in many instances, which I think is much easier to do with a controller.  I used a Playstation 4 controller and the first night I played it, it showed all the correct buttons on the screen. The second night, it showed the Xbox ones. This was peculiar but not a major issue for me. What almost caused me to refund the game on the first night of playing was not being able to move at all at random times when climbing netting up a tree. It took me a while to try my keyboard for those situations just to move left or down or whatever direction was needed. This was extremely frustrating at the start of the game, which is where it seemed to be at it's worst. So my caveat for others is that if you choose to use a controller, be ready to use your keyboard at times, especially in the beginning of the game. The glyph issue happens in many games as most don't seem to support designating which type of controller is being used so that is not much of a complaint on my part, but would be nice to see improved. After that mini rant, the game itself beyond control issues, is very good. The graphics at times are amazing, the story telling is done very well. I appreciated the game taking time after a sequence of intense events to stop and open a book and recap the story. That was excellent for pacing and retelling as it is sometime hard to decipher the story when one is busy playing through action scenes. The story itself was interesting and unique. Audio effects were good overall. Game play mechanics were exactly where they should be for a game like this - diverse enough but not overwhelming where new ones are constantly introduced. As others have mentioned, the game is somewhat on the short side, so waiting for a sale would be a good idea as it is likely a one play through game. Overall I would definitely recommend the game, just with noting the control issues for those wanting to use a controller.

_childDocuments_.review: Bramble The Mountain King is one of those hard games to describe, mainly because it's far more about atmosphere and outlandish spectacle, than it is about meaty game-play.  It may also require some familiarity with Scandinavian folk-lore, as this covers quite a few things that seem to have no connection with each other and so just come over as filler encounters to pad out an otherwise pretty slim narrative.A boy wakes up in the middle of the night and his sister is missing. For some reason the game doesn't explain, she has rather stupidly gone running off into a forest absolutely jam-packed with giant monsters that make no attempt to hide their existence, despite her seemingly being ignorant of them being real and quite unfriendly. He sets out to find her, and once he catches up, they have a really nice old carefree time of it running about in the beautiful outskirts of the forest and playing hide and seek with some very cute gnomes.Then a giant troll comes along, pops the poor little gnomes like they were adorable zits, and yoinks your sister into a bag so he can go feed her to the bramble king. Now, it's unclear why she was even out there in such a dangerous location in the first place, given that it took all of about 5 minutes walk to go from being in a tranquil gnome village and finding themselves  in some serious sh*t.To me the plot boiled down to: My sister is a free-spirited f*ck-wit, or some kind of mentally sub-normal thrill-seeker, who got into easily avoided trouble for no good reason at all, but hey! ho! Looks like you gotta go rescue the dozy muppet. Along the way there are flesh-eating trolls and giants that allow for a large sense of scale in it's set-pieces, and some measure of dread. There are evil forest spirits, malevolent entities, and the dark twisted forms of dead babies. It's a magical mystery tour of that cultures most grim and gruesome tales, but the actual terror is fleeting, as it's never backed up by mechanics with much depth to go with the visual grandeur.Back in the days of the playstation 2 it was impressive seeing the likes of God Of War 2 doing humongous menaces that would smash through environments as they tried to grab the tiny player character. And then again a console generation later on the xbox 360 when Batman Arkham Asylum had you tripping your head off under the scarecrows fear gas, in hallucinogenic sequences. Only, by then it was more about how they managed to get this absurdity into a relatively "normal" game, rather than being impressed by the scale. Seeing it in 2023, albeit with glorious graphics and superb ambience, is somewhat weak given that there is very little difficulty or involvement backing up the spectacle. It's great that an indie studio can now produce titles that match 20 year old console titles, but not so great that they still can't beat 20 year old game-play, never-mind the fact that things like GOW / Spiderman are on pc with massive increases in both the action and the scale since then.  It's like "my first horror game for children" in terms of the tone and challenge, yet is pretty gory and disturbing when it comes to the content. Platforming is straight-forward, as are any puzzles, and it all just comes down to being engaged by the story and the visuals.And, yes! It looks sublime and evocative when it comes to telling this grim fairy-tale, but at 5 hours length to complete and with few sequences that are anything more than a simplistic minute or two of tension that quickly dissipates, well, it's a bit hollow. The only time these sequences take more than two or three attempts to finish, is down to slightly awkward fixed camera angles and some poorly sign-posted things you need to do.If you took a bit of the whimsy of Ico, then chucked in the scale of God Of War or King Kong, and then tried to mix that with Amnesia The Dark Descent (by quite literally nicking one of it's set-pieces and repeating it rather witlessly twice) you'd have some sense of the various things this is mashing together. You can take inspiration from other games, but at least do it as good as them, or preferably even better. This does neither for about 95% of it's run-time. That Dark Descent set-piece that it cribs? It was in first-person and had you trying to wade through knee-high water as an invisible enemy chases you. It was intense and scary, precisely because the point of view limited what you could see. You could briefly distract this enemy, and then the game would deliberately slow you down by making you have to turn a wheel to open a vertical door until you could get under. It knew how to terrify and how to turn the screw to sustain the tension.The developers here, do not. They do it in third-person, which inherently weakens it's potency to begin with, and it then just goes nowhere after that. You can see the threat moving around under the surface, and you just run to the next safe spot. Repeat this about four times and you're done. Having done this underwhelming sequence once, they repeat it again later without any changes whatsoever. It's probably more irritating for me because I played Moons Of Madness only a few weeks ago, and guess what set-piece it too is cribbing in an equally lame fashion...Yup!! The exact same one! Nor did I think it was any good when The Beast Inside nicked it and tediously repeated it, or Bloober Team with their dreary Blair Witch game.The Evil Within did a pretty good job though, but the point is that I can reel off oodles of titles that are "inspired" by this idea and then only do a pish, cheapo knock-off when replicating it. The one time that they do a genuinely good "boss" sequence it's still riffing on ICO and has maybe, I dunno, two whole minor differences between how that games final boss plays out. This is, what? 20 years later?To some this will feel fresh, but to me it is stitched out of other games that were done better, and this folklore was explored in more frightening titles such as "Unforgiving: A northern hymn" / "Through the woods" / "Apsulov". It is visually stunning and incredibly well-realised when it comes to the presentation, but as a game? Well.....what's here is engaging enough to pass the time, and nothing more than that.Every so often it does something creepy, every so often it does something where you're like "wow! indie games have come a long way technically". Yet, looking back at it, looking past the production values....it never succeeded in being pant-sh*ttingly scary, or ever sustained those moments of dread. The reason why is that any stealth is basic, the chase scenes are too short and easy, any other type of challenge is pretty straightforward, and when they do find an average level of success it's just repeated again with minimal changes.So, on the one hand: It's good if you're new to whatever you'd call this toothless "cinematic" kind of "action" and "horror", but on the other hand....it's a nothing-burger of a game in a nothing-burger genre. I love games like Limbo and Inside, and in some ways they are just as vapid as this when it comes to the game-play, so I do understand the appeal. If anything it's the potential for this to have been a "proper" horror masterpiece, like Amnesia The Bunker, that makes it somewhat more disappointing. They do have game-play here, but it's done at such a low level as to be equivalent to crossing a 3d platformer for babies with a walking simulator "horror" experience.  I don't regret my time with it, or the money spent, but having finished it, ooh, I dunno, half an hour ago, I can't name one sequence where it blew me away beyond the artistic and technical side of it. At 5 hours for £25, and seemingly with little reason to replay it (such as a branching narrative, or things to discover) it's good enough for a recommended, but only just for certain players, and most definitely not recommended for action or horror seekers.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay so first things first. I played this on the Rog Ally so will start this review by saying overall how the game was on the handheld. It ran smoothly for the most part. I ran it initially in "silent" mode to conserve battery. About an hour in a started getting glaring frame drops so switched to "turbo". The game ran between 30 - 45fps from there without many issues at all. A small number of occasions it dropped down to 15 -25 fps when there was much going on on the screen. Seems linked more into the light stone you find and use in the later parts of the game. As for the actual game: an absolute masterpiece. Do not let the art style fool you, this game is a fairytale from Swedish (I think) folklore that is deep, dark and disturbing. You play as Olle, a young boy in search of his kidnapped sister. The gameplay here is very simple. The game is very linear (I would have preferred some exploration personally) and plays very much like a platformer/adventure game. It does have elements of combat which is also very simple that is used in the boss, which I must say were very fun and unique, albeit easy. I certainly get the feeling that they did not want to make the game too hard, which works well. There are some very light puzzle elements here, collectable figures and story books that you can find that add the depth and the lore outside of the narration. The characters in the game first off are silent and the game is narrated beautifully, akin to someone reading an old fairytale. This was absolutely fantastic and really helped pull you into the story and the world. It really sets the tone from the off. Graphically the game is gorgeous, yet simplistic (in a nice way). The lighting is used incredibly effectively. The colours and characters pop out at you. Without spoiling anything and if you haven't seen anything of this the game is incredibly dark and grotesque and the overall designs are top notch. The game gets progressively darker the further you get. It starts out colourful and playful but quickly takes a sinister turn. This game has some truly terrifying moments. The sheer size and scope of some of the things here in comparison to Olle is breathtaking. A final note and something worth mentioning is the sound design and in particular the musical score. It's 10/10. The folky instrumentation and the breathy vocals add such an atmospheric layer to the game. It accompanied the visuals and storytelling in a way that I can only sum up as sublime. This game sits at "overwhemingly" positive and it's clear to see why. Whether you love horror, walking sim, platforming, story, this game is something to be experienced. At £10 it's an absolute bargain. My gametime is around 8 hours though some of that was on pause. The game is a 4 or 5 hour run through, give or take on how much you try explore/collect and how much you die. I highly recommend this game. It's crafted with such a love and care that the AAA and even some AA devs really need to sit down and look at themselves after playing it themselves. I hope we get more from these devs like this in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: 100% the lovechild of "Little Nightmares" and "Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons" (and maybe Limbo)The atmosphere of this creepy little fairy-tale is immaculate, the detail to the world and its creatures is obvious. My complaints however would have to be that there isnt much gameplay at all (mostly walking sim), besides the bosses. The gameplay itself doesnt really adequately prepare you for the sudden difficulty spikes that are the bosses... not that theyre particularly difficult, just different from the rest of the game's core gameplay, which is mostly inane and kinda boring.Really, the game is about the spectacle and the vibe of the world around you rather than having a game that is super fun or intuitive to play. Not to mention the world and level design are INSANELY linear. Like, no freedom to explore or choose a different path beyond something that is already set. Overall, it is a beautiful and creepy little game, that maybe has a few too many reviews praising it as nearly flawless. However, it's easy and gorgeous enough to absolutely make it worth playing at least once anyway.(Also what's up with the "no deaths no restarts" achievement, its a ♥♥♥♥ move to include it and it's nothing like any of the other achievements. Total BS to attempt)

_childDocuments_.review: Unique atmospheric dark fantasy adventure. I was quite bored the first hour or so and nearly rage quit having to pixel hunt the eight gnomes, but the game gets better as it goes on, and I finished in one sitting. Pros: Graphics, story, music, level design, art, bossesCons: Bad controls, hit or miss puzzles, fixed camera can lead to deaths and annoying platforming, expensiveThe controls are particularly bad if you use a controller. Don't use a controller. I tried with an xbox elite series 2 which uses standard xbox mapping and it's the worst controller adaptation I've ever seen in a game. The buttons tend to double press more often than not, and aiming is next to impossible. So I played with mouse and keyboard, which was an okay experience, but the controls still felt pretty clunky particularly during boss fights, given the limited camera angle when aiming and run toggle not being a true toggle, among other things.Also the game took me 7 hours to complete and I died A LOT. Someone good could probably do it in 4 hours. That makes Bramble fairly expensive at $29.99 for such a short experience, and I don't think there's much replay value. Buy it on sale if you can. 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: a perfect spooky season experience! I rly enjoyed this game~ it came onto my radar after seeing it featured in one of Jacob Geller's video essays, Games That Won't Leave The Dark, and i'm so glad i picked it up.this is a very grim and unsettling horror adventure through a beautiful & terrible world woven from Scandinavian folklore. first off, the visuals are absolutely stunning... everything is so lush, and the camerawork is so cinematic, every scene is just such a joy to experience. the love and attention given to even the tiniest details, like how a flower head bobs when you bump into it, the grazing moose you just catch in the corner of the screen, the raven flying by the window... it's just very magical. the textures, lighting... everything, so pretty. the way they utilize depth of field, the sense of scale and camera placements pleased me over and overthe sound is also wonderful, with some great sound effect work, very fitting & at times very lovely & haunting music (& yes the final boss music choice was absolutely fire hehe) and the vocal effects in particular stood out to me, they were so well done. the narrator also does a fantastic joball of it boils down to an incredibly immersive experience, one that gives you small tastes of the light before plunging you back into the horrors of the dark. I was delighted with every new terrible and/or beautiful thing that i came across- and they don't hold back! some pretty gruesome and twisted things are about in these woods, so be sure to check the content warnings. this is more of a disturbing and unsettling horror game as opposed to one that serves you jumpscares thankfully, as i'm not a fan of those, too scaredy cat /ᐠ｡ꞈ｡ᐟ\this game has offered me so many things that will forever be in my memory, esp a certain point where things got veryyy psychedelic and liminal, i truly tripped out for a few moments and then was buzzing with excitement! there was another wonderful, violently musical scene that i really loved, just so much good stuffthere was more gameplay to this then i expected, which is both a pro and sometimes a bit of a con. there are some puzzles, which are fairly straightforward yet usually satisfying, and then there are a variety of things like chase scenes, stealth sequences, some targeting and a handful of quite inventive boss fights, some of which could get a lil tricky, particularly the last one. other than that there's a lot of just traversing from one place to another along with some simple platforming. there's enough variety here that it never rly grew repetitive, tho i do wish there was a lil less stealth, but it's alright, it's very suiting for what's goin on.as far as the story goes, i went in expecting a kind of abstracted, myth-type approach, and that is indeed what they're going for here. there are actually kind of a collection of smaller stories/myths throughout the journey in a way, and there are these absolutely stunning books you can find at different points that i loved flipping through, with beautiful illustrations and narration that give more context for the things you're experiencing. one thing i was happy about is how much they got you to care about several of the characters, even with no dialogue and for ones that didn't get much focus.aphantasia-wise, this is a very linear game so no worries there, the cinematography guides you from place to place in a very satisfying way. none of the puzzles were reliant on visual memory so that was also smooth sailing. fully accessible for meeeethe only reason i'm not rating it 5 stars is simply just that a few of the gameplay elements were a bit clunky at times, even slightly frustrating in a cpl instances, and i feel the pacing & ending has a bit of room for improvement, but yeah i highly recommend u check this out if u want a dark fairytale experience <3 a very unique piece of art that i will definitely return to~

_childDocuments_.review: The game is atmospheric, whimsical and amazing visually.  There are some odd fixed camera moments and the plot seems to omit too much leaving chapters to seem barely connected and the player wondering if parts were somehow skipped.  The adventure is amazing but goes from being a smooth, storybook experience to playing an annoying side game.  The aspect that makes this review negative is that there are several bad choices at making the game challenging.  The boss battles really ruin the game.  I didn't enjoy one moment of any boss battle.  They are way too long and tedious.  Sometimes, the last boss battle especially, you will get killed only because you can't see your character or tell what the enemy is doing. (the screen is concealed by effects, do I duck or jump?  The concept that all games need boss battles is antiquated and they definitely didn't need to be in this title.  My guess is that too many ideas where applied to the game resulting in a game trying to be too many things.  The energy put into the boss battles should have been used to make the story longer.    The character's walk and run speed has so little difference it is barely noticeable.  Some puzzles you are thrown into with no real preface hinting at what or why you are even needing to solve it.  I would really be excited for a sequel if I knew that the aforementioned issues had been considered.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Overall, 10/10. A beautifully dark game with a satisfying story and refreshing gameplay experience. After about 6 hours, I can say Bramble is worth it - but get it on sale. I like to put in at least an hour per dollar I spend on a game, and you probably won't get 30 hours out of this unless you replay it.Graphics & Sound Design: 10/10Gameplay Experience: 10/10Story: 10/10Combat & Controls: 9/10NPCs + Characters: 10/10Bug-free: 10/10GRAPHICS & SOUND DESIGN. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. The Swedes know how to make a game. They put in my favorite sound in the world - külning - and I was sold. I kept commenting on how beautiful the ROCKS were, not to mention the trees, grass, everything. It's gorgeous, and they place the perfect things in the perfect places so you just enjoy every square inch of the game.GAMEPLAY. This is honestly one of the most refreshing games I've played. They change the camera perspective every so often, a small detail that adds so much to the fun and keeps it interesting. Bramble is a game for gamers; throughout the game there are things to interact with that you wouldn't expect - keep an eye open for little surprises! I read everything, interacted with everything, even translated the words on signs because they were so immersively designed. You will get sucked in.You will also cry a lot because it will scare the ♥♥♥♥ out of you sometimes. Especially when you meet Näcken...STORY. My god. Dark and eloquently told in the form of a storybook, and expertly woven to make your heart bleed. There is so much pain in this story, so much love, so much to overcome. It made me cry, and that always means it was good. The coolest part? Not a single character speaks. When you can write a compelling story without a single line of dialogue, and still evoke emotions...you've done well.COMBAT & CONTROLS. Combat is hella fun. It's a simple system, but inventive - and the bosses are challenging enough to be satisfying when you beat them. This goes for the puzzles and parkour too! The controls are easy until you need to use all your fingers at once, so you might want to use a controller. Otherwise, I was able to play through pretty effortlessly with keyboard and mouse.NPCs & CHARACTERS. Beautifully designed and memorable. I love that the names are Old Norse in origin, too!BUGS. 'Nuff said. 0 glitches, 0 hitches. Plays smoothly.

_childDocuments_.review: Do you like games like Ico, Brothers A tale of two Sons, Limbo or those sections in God of War where you are scaling/avoiding giants? If so then you are likely to enjoy Bramble: The Mountain King.This game gets very DARK in places with some mature themes and is NOT for kids.Graphics of humanoid faces are just ok (they went for stylised/doll looks), however the graphics of the creatures, monsters, forest and background areas/details are excellent. Well above what you would expect for an indie title.HDR is not natively supported (even though it would be a great game for it with its contrasts between light and dark areas) and I cannot recommend Windows auto-HDR as it creates a noticeable black crush/film grain type look in darker areas. SDR still looks good though, so would recommend using this if you have an HDR monitor (especially if its an OLED panel like an LG C1, alienware AW3423DW monitor etc).Gameplay involves exploration, light puzzles, light stealth, and light combat sections. Progression is linear (this is not open world).Without getting into spoiler territory there are many "boss" sections (that often involve means other than combat to resolve), with just the one boss that I would consider "annoying", however there are also 2-3  boss encounters which I would consider great (one of which is likely to make a few top 10 lists with the way its handled).Difficulty could be considered Easy-Medium range (this isnt Elden Ring/Sekiro), with nothing designed to road block you for long.Completion time should range from between 4-7 hours for most people who don't use a guide and just explore naturally as they progress.Music is great. Voice acting is mainly limited to the narrator, who does a great job (storybook segments are a stand out).Performance wise it ran at 4k 120fps Epic settings on a high end PC (even when using DLDSR to go to 2.25x it stayed above 60fps). Unreal Engine game but seems very well optimised (no stutter struggle for me).A great indie game from an indie studio and one that punches well above its weight.If I had to assign a score/rating: 8.5/10 or B+

_childDocuments_.review: I'd been eyeing this game for a while and ended up purchasing it as part of a bundle with two other games for a grand total of $12. If you wanted to buy this game I certainly would not recommend spending more than that, as there's really not that much here, and I found what content there is in this game to not be nearly as compelling as most of the reviews seem to indicate.My experience with the "horror platformers" microgenre is pretty limited. I played "Little Nightmares" a year or two ago and found it pretty frustrating to play, if visually interesting. My opinion on Bramble is pretty much the same, though I think Bramble is an overall worse game. I haven't played Limbo or Inside, which I gather also fit into this genre.I found the first half of this game to actually be pretty enjoyable. It offered some diverse (if unchallenging) forms of gameplay outside of the platforming. The platforming, at least to start, worked well for me. By the second half of the game the difficulty spikes rather suddenly with some incredibly tedious boss fights, and the wheels start to spin in place on the gameplay in general. The game starts repeating its least compelling mechanics and hence loses its sense of freshness. Visual design and presentation slips very dramatically. A good chunk of the back half is spent in a generic medieval village running/hiding from generic zombies. It is gray and totally unmemorable. This is a pretty big problem for a game that is, at most, 5-6 hours long.On the platforming. Your player character moves a bit like a boat, very floaty and imprecise. Which is fine to start. The platforming challenges are initially very generous. (Little Nightmares also has  the "floaty" platforming but by contrast, required a degree of precision that made it more frustrating than fun). By the second half of the game this generosity wears off and you're essentially playing a different game. This feels like an artificial difficulty spike for the purposes of dragging out the experience.The first half of the game has quite a lot in common with the "walking simulator" genre. There are a few relatively cozy puzzles and other challenges interspersed with some creepy imagery and dreamlike atmosphere. The problem is when the back half of the game decides it wants to be a "real game" and the lack of precision becomes frustrating as bigger challenges are put before you. There is a boss midway through the game that really epitomizes this shift in design philosophy. I understand that the game needs to become harder/darker as it continues, but with little on-ramp and generally poor controls, this difficulty spike felt needless and artificial.This game's narrative and theming left a lot to be desired. The story-book folklore stuff is neat to start, but the game does not really do enough with it for me to feel like its particularly memorable. There is nothing particularly interesting about making fairytales gruesome for the sake of making them gruesome (sure, some fairy tales are actually gruesome, but usually in the service of moralizing to children, something that is totally absent here). One of the dumbest choices the game makes it delivering narrative both through "story-books" you read in game, as well as voice-over narration that comes and goes. They should have stuck fully with the voice-over or bothered to animate more cutscenes. What makes the "story-books" fail as a narrative delivery mechanism is largely that they occur *after* boss fights. They exist to explain the "lore" of the boss you just defeated after you defeated them. This choice really demonstrates that the narrative and world here is an afterthought. Transitions between areas are likewise abrupt and unsatisfying. Really, what I see here is a series of set-pieces the developers created with very little concern for how to tie them together. The dream/nightmare/fairytale/folklore conceit allows the developers to play pretty fast and loose with overall coherence in this regard, but nonetheless I was continually confused by certain basic elements such as scale (you literally change size relative to your environment between segments for no discernible reason), narrative cause and effect, and overall plot themes. All of this would have been totally fine had there been some kind of larger arc to follow (emotional, thematic, story, or otherwise) but its really just a series of discrete experiences tied together with the barest suggestion of a story.Maybe this genre isn't really for me. I initially found this game to be quite charming because the world design and relative ease of gameplay and variety of challenges and mechanics. For a five-hour game to totally run out of steam in the back half and devolve into narrative/gameplay incoherence is pretty unforgivable. Extremely so when you are asking $30 full price.

_childDocuments_.review: Bramble: The Mountain King - A Captivating Journey Through a Dark Fairy TaleBramble is an enchanting experience that beautifully blends stunning visuals with a hauntingly immersive narrative. From the moment I stepped into this dark fairy tale world, I was captivated by its rich atmosphere and intricate design.The game's graphics are truly breathtaking, with lush landscapes and meticulously crafted environments that draw you in. Each area feels alive, filled with details that enhance the storytelling. The sound design complements the visuals perfectly, creating an eerie yet captivating ambiance that keeps you on the edge of your seat.The gameplay mechanics are intuitive, allowing players to fully immerse themselves in the story without feeling overwhelmed. The puzzles are cleverly designed, providing just the right amount of challenge while seamlessly integrating into the narrative. I found myself genuinely invested in the protagonist's journey, experiencing a rollercoaster of emotions as the story unfolded.What truly stands out in Bramble is its ability to evoke feelings of both wonder and fear, reminiscent of classic fairy tales but with a unique twist. The blend of folklore and fantasy elements creates a rich tapestry that is both familiar and refreshingly original.Overall, Bramble is a must-play for anyone who appreciates beautifully crafted games with deep storytelling. It's a haunting yet beautiful adventure that lingers long after you've put down the controller. Highly recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: Bramble: The Mountain King is a solid, short game.  It is, however, a prime example of how the "thumbs up/down" system is flawed and should be replaced with a number system of some sort.  I enjoyed the game for what it is: an INCREDIBLY short, captivating fable with gorgeous graphics and intuitive game play.  It is just so short that I can only, in good conscience, recommend it if on extreme sale.  If you just sit down and play with no interruption, you will complete it in 6-8 hours.   THE GOOD:-Stunning graphics and haunting imagery-Easy to learn and master game play-Horror done well (I still jump in my chair every time a bear trap I didn't see gets me)-Several checkpoints so you never have long to get back after a death-Fun, engaging boss battles-It's just fun!THE BAD:-"Death my camera-angle" - annoying and punishes players for no reason-As stated, really, REALLY short story line-100% linear with no true replayabilityI am giving this game a thumbs down because I am so torn and want to offer some balance to the reviews.  You will beat this game in a single afternoon, easily.  That is the driving factor in my recommendation.  However, if you don't mind the hefty price tag/hour played, the game is definitely worth it.

Buttons to interact with items would disappear forcing me to restart sometimes (I noticed there is a softlock patch out rn, this might have fixed the issue I was having), left or right control stick would not work but only when I was climbing on cages for some reason. _childDocuments_.review: I once heard that the greatest test of storytelling in visual media is the ability to convey your narrative through visuals alone, without relying on dialogue or exposition to communicate with the audience. In 2012, an indie gem blossomed, captivating players worldwide. With no dialogue and limited movement, the harmonious blend of visuals and sounds guided players through a simple yet profoundly emotional experience. That game was Journey. Since then, many games have attempted to replicate the unique adventure that elevated said niche PS3 exclusive to a multi-award-winning game. Now, in 2024, I believe I have finally found a game that satisfies the itch Journey left on me all those years ago.Released in 2023, Bramble is a game I successfully managed to ignore for over a year. Saturated with announcements of casual, "emotional," and "immersive" walking simulator games, I dismissed it as just another pretentious indie studio's attempt, supported by a marketing team eager to reach into my pocket. Whether I have become more demanding or the gaming landscape more cynical, I cannot say. What I do know is that for most of the decade between Journey and Bramble, I consistently dismissed these games as "just another one."That changed when I stumbled upon what I, in my ignorance, dubbed 'the credits song.' I have a habit of listening to video game soundtracks, with tracks from Bloodborne and Hollow Knight always on my autoplay. Then, out of nowhere, YouTube decided to throw something new my way. Curious about the unfamiliar tune, I checked to see what was playing. There it was, an impactful song proudly displaying the logo of a game I faintly remembered but had never investigated further.I have always believed that a good soundtrack can elevate a game from ordinary to extraordinary, and Bramble certainly supports this belief. To satisfy my curiosity, I explored its soundtrack further. Delighted with what I heard, particularly their remix of 'In the Hall of the Mountain King,' I came to the possibly naive realization that I had to play this game, even though I knew little about it beyond a few tracks. Thankfully, I avoided spoiling arguably the best song in the game, which we have the pleasure of hearing twice, beautifully paralleling the beginning and the end our protagonist's wondrous and equally challenging journey.Unlike Journey, Bramble is not completely devoid of dialogue. Even though our characters don't have a voice, the story is told visually, with the characters we meet along the way communicating through gestures. The game sets the mood with its beautiful graphics, sounds, and music. Occasionally, the narrator assists the player in understanding the events around them, doing so indirectly through the reading of illustrated short storybooks based on Scandinavian folklore. The story does a fantastic job of weaving together the childish wonder of exploring a world of fantasy, while also, very gruesomely, showing the reality of a world that is dark and full of suffering.We explore this world through the eyes of Olle, a young boy who ventures outside his house to find and rescue his sister, who sneaked out to explore the nearby ruins at night. This journey is as sad as it is beautiful, as Olle is forced to endure things no child should ever face in order to save the one person who gives him the courage to keep going—his sister Lillemor. The game is relatively short, and over its 4-5 hour runtime, we witness the arduous tale of Olle's growth as a character. Along the way, we also meet several other characters whose tragic stories—filled with love, despair, injustice, death, and suffering—directly affect the world Olle sees around him.Everything I've mentioned so far might sound nice and good, but what elevates Bramble from a good game to a fantastic one? One of the greatest achievements of Journey was its ability to create a visually mesmerizing adventure and communicate a simple but emotional story solely through its visuals and music. Bramble accomplishes this as well, but with adult themes like death, loss, trauma, and other harsh realities to set itself apart. Bramble is not a happy story; its ending is open to interpretation. Whether you have a more positive or negative outlook on its outcome, the tragedy Olle endures is undeniable and leaves a bittersweet taste. What really got me to write this review, was not only the amazing combination of sound and visuals, but the commitment the developer had to tell the story they wanted to tell, no matter how harsh and gruesome it might be. That is a rare thing to see and it is surely deserving of praise.But the year is 2024, and clearly, Bramble is not Journey. It wasn't showered with game of the year awards, and while highly regarded by those who played it, it hasn't yet achieved the same indie darling status. Over the decade, this genre of games has expanded significantly, to the point of oversaturation. Bramble excels at what it does, but we must recognize that it isn't something revolutionary. Back in 2012, Journey was fresh and different, offering respite from the growing trend of shooters and action games. In 2024, however, Bramble ends up being treated as just another game in an oversaturated indie market. Had it been released in 2012 instead of Journey, I might not feel the need to make such comparison.Bramble is a hidden gem that blooms for those fortunate enough to discover it. It leaves your imagination pondering long after a brief yet immensely rewarding adventure. Without a doubt, I wholeheartedly recommend experiencing this game. While its initial price may seem high for its brevity, the investment is truly for its exceptional quality. Here, we're paying for craftsmanship, creativity, quality and amazingly beautiful music, the developers unquestionably deserve it.

_childDocuments_.review: is a 3rd-person-ish 3D Adventure Horror game with some platforming elements. In it you play as a young boy who is trying to save his older sister from a troll, in a world inspired by Scandinavian folklore. If that sounds rather light and , this game is  It is not afraid to show violence and cruelty, even to children. In some ways you could compare this game to  or another Playdead game, in things like tone and gameplay. There are also some light puzzles, and even "boss fights," but nothing too crazy.There are many creatures and monsters that are taken directly from folklore. You have adorable little gnomes, the aforementioned troll, witches, Skogsrå, etc.The story is quite moving, even delivered as it is. The characters don't really talk, but their dialogue and everything is delivered through a narrator. That doesn't hurt it, as it really goes well with the story-book feel.Mechanically, it works well. Although (and this may be a skill issue), I sometimes find the platforming to be frustrating when camera angles change and you can't always see well. I also found the first person aiming to be a bit clunky on a controller, but almost everything else about the game was preferable on a controller. You could comfortably use KB+M, though, and I did early on.The music is absolutely incredible. The character designs and environments are all-around beautiful, and often terrifying.

_childDocuments_.review: Probably one of the best games ever made. To start off, the story is amazing. It is like the Brother's Grimm but a bit more disturbing, and not relying on conventional tales remastered into video game form. On top of that, while it did seem to stress my PC out a lot, playing on the highest settings made everything beautiful. The art in itself was awesome, and there were times when I was playing that I felt scenes could make amazing backgrounds or even pieces for an actual wall. The music too was also perfect, and at every turn it was there at just the right moment to kick in and give atmosphere.  When it came to the actual game-play, it must be said that a lot felt unoriginal. Being a fan of indie games, the stealth stuff felt all too familiar to others I have played before. However, there is only so much it can do differently when many predecessors have come before it. As far as this critique goes it is minimal, and may be a selling point to see these tropes used in a new setting. Further on game-play, while this too is super polished, there was one thing that really annoyed me while playing. This was how janky the controls are. There were many deaths that felt unfair simply because I could not get the controls to do as they were supposed to, or to get the character to move right. A lot of platforming sections felt awful because of this, but it is also super easy to look past given patience. Another thing, although rare, were the small bugs.  These bugs were minimal though, and took nothing away from the game. In short, it cannot be described how good this game was. While it is not perfect, as nothing is, it should be considered one of the best things to come out, and everyone must play it.

_childDocuments_.review: I have mixed feelings about this game. The story is the big selling point to this game. It is very immersive and the storyline is very emotive and sometimes very scary, being based in Nordic folklore. Despite any frustrations I had with the game, I continued because I wanted to know what was going to happen. I think it would be a hit with anyone who likes dark fairytales and horror games. The one thing I will say it is deceptively very cute in the beginning and part of me mourned that there wasn't more of messing around collecting up cute gnomes and meeting friendly giants. But it gets dark VERY quickly. And when I say dark, I mean really dark. At one point you are wading through entrails, you witness ritual murders and infanticide and by the end you are so desensitised to the literal dead bodies hanging everywhere that they become part of the background. And when your character dies (I died a lot), you get close up shots of this 7/8 year old boy literally being eaten or ripped in two etc. It is not a game for the squeamish, though the developers do have a content warning at the start of the game. I must admit at one point I was like "what else can they literally throw to terrify this child?" and then lo and behold, plague zombies made an appearance. Now onto the visuals, the actual backdrops are quite detailed and I enjoyed the art style. The actual player character isn't so well characterised and can be a bit jerky but it didn't detract too much from my enjoyment of the game. I think it is pretty good for a game of it's type. Playability is where I ran into some difficulties. The puzzles were great, I loved the problem solving and the platforming aspect of it. It is a pretty linear platformer, with very little variation apart from whether or not you manage to collect the statues or not. However, some of the stealth/fight scenes were a bit frustrating because there is literally only one way to do them and sometimes that is not immediately apparent and there is no room for error at all or an alternative way or route to doing it. I tend to play more open-world games like Hogwarts Legacy, so this might just be because I changed genre but it was frustrating sometimes to have to die a few times before I perfected a particular sequence because the margin for error was so incredibly small. I salute anyone who manages a run through without dying - I died a lot, particularly towards the end! Also, your player characters skill in certain areas seems a bit shady - you have to suspend belief that the kid can stab a monster but drowns the minute he hits water or dies straight away if he falls over, with no recourse to quickly recover from your mistake. Another thing to note is that the final boss battle seemed disproportionately hard compared to the rest of it. Some of the boss battles were based around a combination of skill, stealth and pattern recognition and you got the gist of it after a couple of run-through's. Usually you expect a final boss battle to be a culmination of all the skills and patterns you've mastered over the course of the game and other boss fights, thematically some of it tied in - like the flowers play a big part - but suddenly, pattern recognition goes out the window because the game style evolves into predicting your possible moves and targeting you that way, rather than you knowing where to go because you've observed the fighting style pattern. Also, the hitbox for the Bramble Kings weapons are really big compared to previous fights - the weapon doesn't need to hit you to kill you - you automatically die if the weapon is anywhere near you. This meant that it took me quite a few goes to succeed in the final battle, I am not a seasoned gamer though so it's possible veterans of this type of game will have a different experience. I just feel it's important to note because this is a game that might appeal to more casual gamers as well who like to pick up storyline rich games for cheap in the sales like me. Overall, I did really enjoy this game, mainly for the storyline. It does have some flaws but if you are looking for a challenge or something distinctly adult, this might be a good pick for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Bramble: The Mountain King is an a great title in the horror-adventure genre, taking the crown from similar titles like Little Nightmares and Limbo. From the very start, the graphics are nothing short of stunning—each environment feels alive, with intricate details that bring Scandinavian folklore to life in an immersive, hauntingly beautiful way. It's hard not to be amazed by the atmospheric landscapes and the eerie, yet captivating creatures that fill the world. Visually, Bramble stands head and shoulders above its peers, making it the best in its genre by a long shot.The storytelling in Bramble is top-notch, perfectly paced and deeply engaging. The game offers a dark and emotionally gripping narrative that pulls players in, even if it’s heavy with themes that might be triggering for some. But this is where the horror truly shines—Bramble resonates because it taps into the fears and emotions that we can all relate to on some level. It takes its inspiration from Scandinavian folklore, which adds a unique and fascinating layer to the experience. Playing out these ancient myths in such a visually rich and atmospheric setting is an incredible journey.In terms of gameplay, the puzzles are refreshingly simple, which sets Bramble apart from other horror games where it feels like you’re constantly wandering around trying to find the next clue. Here, the puzzles are straightforward, never frustrating, and blend seamlessly into the game. It keeps the focus on the dark narrative and the overall experience, rather than turning into a walking simulator.Combat in the game is also well-implemented, particularly the boss fights that require strategic use of projectile attacks. It’s not overly complex, but it works perfectly within the perspective and style of the game. The soundtrack is another highlight—beautifully composed and atmospheric, it enhances every moment of the game, pulling you deeper into its eerie world.If there’s one downside to Bramble, it’s the game’s length. Like many in this genre, it’s relatively short. I finished it in about 4 hours and 30 minutes, but that was while streaming—so it could probably be completed even faster. That said, the chapter select and easy-to-get achievements make it a dream for completionists. If you’re a trophy hunter, this is a solid 100% run with minimal effort.All in all, Bramble: The Mountain King is a phenomenal experience—a must-play for anyone who loves dark, story-driven games with gorgeous visuals and a chilling atmosphere. Despite its shorter length, it packs an emotional punch and delivers one of the best folklore-inspired horror games out there

_childDocuments_.review: Little Nightmares if he Nordic. Cannot recommend this game enough.Not only does it tackle Nordic folk tales in a visually striking way, it also seamlessly weaves the cute and wholesome with the morbid and macabre. While sadly there is no codex to compile all of the folklore you see, nearly every chapter revolves around a central folk tale which gets exposition via wonderful art and narration.While you see most mechanics in first third or so, they all receive their own chapter-specific mixup in unexpected ways. In that sense, the game is very accessible (although the final encounter might give you some trouble if you're a very casual player) and worth it for the Nordic flavour alone.In a way, the game doesn't necessarily innovate any one genre; it doesn't have a hidden subtext about depression nor does it have any mind-blowing twists. But it's so masterfully crafted, complete with an amazing soundtrack and at least one encounter that's hard to gush about without spoiling it, that I really think it's worth the admittedly fairly high price point for the 5 hours it's going to take for you to clear it.This is one of those cases where a game is excellent because it does one thing and excels at it.

_childDocuments_.review: I already know that I’m going to be the unpopular opinion and I don’t expect to get any fans from this review, but I can’t help but feel like a lot of the aspects of this game that bothered me are being overlooked in lieu of the graphics. Story: The atmosphere of the game is well developed, and progressively becomes more ominous as the story progresses. Even though this is a horror-lite style of game, that relies heavily on gory visuals to unsettle the audience. It was nice that the story was voice narrated. This helped to reinforce the idea of having a story read to you. Pacing: The game is relatively steady depending on how easily the player overcomes different types of obstacles or boss fights. The somewhat janky controls for the character’s movement often lead to frustrating delays by not responding well to player input and command.Visual: It’s obvious that Dimfrost poured a lot of their attention into the visuals for this game. It’s beautiful. I don’t dispute that at all. I can’t help but wonder how many people can play this game on high or ultra graphics like it is supposedly intended to be seen. The average gamer doesn’t have high end graphics cards and so they’re paying for this gorgeous game they can’t fully enjoy because it won’t run without lagging all over the place. The animation style is well selected and fits the game. Soft, fantasy-feel, and creepy. And don’t forget all the inclusion of gore details from wading through intestines and other internal organ refuse, to repeatedly shanking a demon woman in the heart (100 times in a row for an achievement) and having blood spray all over a little boy’s face with every stab.Audio: The ambient music seems to fit the setting well enough. In contrast, I absolutely hated the screeching and squalling of the little gnome children. It hurt my ears and grated my nerves to the point where I had to turn the sound off when I interacted with any of them that were crying. Like forks scraping across a ceramic plate, oof. Gameplay: I noticed the reuse of mechanics in the game. It’s not a long game. The same use of hide from the light, hide from the sound, hide from the troll, hide from whatever is overused. There are lots of things you can do in an adventure game, add in more variety! That same thing is employed in at least three different areas and it’s only a four-hour long game. The lack of variety is really disappointing to me. As I mentioned before, the ability to control the movements of the character was more than a little loosey-goosey at times and downright infuriating in some instances. I feel like if the controls had been tightened up a little to be more responsive on the interface, perhaps that would have been a little less irritated when the character repeatedly ran in a direction I wasn’t aiming.I will say that the “boss fights” are very well done. Those are unique (mostly) and I thought they are clever and in theme with whatever is going on at the time in game. Kudos there, awesome job. Wish the innovation of those battles was brought to the rest of the passive gameplay. Accessibility: I will say this, Dimfrost did step up and put in an option for colorblind people. And not just one option, but several different types of colorblindness. Very cool of them to do that. They also had subtitles available for those who are hard of hearing or just like subtitles, and an assortment of languages to choose from for which the game could be played. Conclusion:I can’t shake the feeling that the developers leaned too heavily into the graphics and neglected the gameplay and controls part of this game a bit. Perhaps a few more hours of polishing would have really made a difference. The price is about $30 dollars for a four-hour game. That’s a bit rich for my blood. I won’t be recommending this game unless you really don’t care about the price, and you want to stare at something pretty. The story is alright. The boss fights are great. The gnome children cries are absolute torture for your ears…Overall, the game is very attractive, but I ran into a lot of hangups that really rubbed me the wrong way. Don’t get this game unless it’s on deep discount. 4/10Bonus:Does the game have achievements? Yes.Are they tedious/impossible? There is one that is tedious but depends on how much time you want to spend trying to get a perfect run.Are they fun/worth your time? All except the “perfect run” are relatively reasonable. As for the last one: In my opinion, life’s too short.Are they easy, playthrough only achievements? No, perhaps a handful are story related. Many are collections you have to look for, and a few more are random things some players might get without trying if they enjoy playing around.Other: There is chapter selection if you want to hop back though the chapters to get to an achievement that you may have missed without having to replay the whole game. That’s always nice.Liked the review? Looking for more? I'm a curator! Check me out:
