_childDocuments_.review: Everything The Plucky Squire tries, it tries successfully. Whether in or out of the storybook, every moment of this game is a delight.Inside the book is a top down 2-d Zelda clone with the gimmicks of changing nouns and adjectives to shape objects, as well as tilting and stamping the book itself to solve puzzles. It all comes together wonderfully and the controls feel really good.Outside the book the game adds a little more (but admittedly not as much as I thought) platforming into the mix, and takes a page from Mario odyssey and A Link Between worlds, wall mechanics to meld into the pages of anything hand drawn to progress. I genuinely loved when the game told me I needed to leave the book and find an item, because whatever shape the desk you explore took was exciting. Jetpacking in a space themed desk or scaling a dinosaurs tail in a Jurassic one, really it’s tough to decide which form of gameplay is the best.Between both sections there’s also a lot of gameplay diversity in some fun mini games. Punch out, puzzle bobble and even rhythm heaven, these moments are really great and none really stink (though I had a controller issue with one or two)All of this is packaged in one of the most appealing art styles I’ve played through in a long while. The storybook just looks so freaking good. Outside the book doesn’t slouch either, with life size objects reminding me of finding objects in Pikmin. Style can go a long way to boosting a games quality and Plucky Squire doesn’t let you down…where it DOES let me down is the length. This game took me 6 hours and at a $30 price tag, I’m prepared to say that feels a bit steep. The game is mostly a straight shot of linear game design (also very easy I should mention) with the only bonus objective being finding concept art and glitch birds. Miss any and you gotta use chapter select to go back and look. Even with this though, I feel like there should be more game here. One could make the argument that if that happened, the game could end up feeling bloated as a result but considering things stay the same level of quality throughout, I think a few more hours could have worked.After all, of the games 9 chapters, only 5 of them feel like full length levels. The other 4 are actual minutes each which can lead to some really weird pacing problems. If every chapter was an equal length I’d think to call the experience complete.Of course if the only argument I have for the game is in its length (and admittedly a few bugs and lag spikes) then clearly the journey with Jot and friends is worth taking. A wholesome family friendly experience that succeeds at what it set out to do. Current game of the year (but UFO 50 drops tomorrow and Zelda Echoes of Wisdom next week so…we’ll see how long that lasts)(This review is a copy of my review from

_childDocuments_.review: I really wish I could recommend this game. It has an awesome concept, and some very fun core mechanics. The idea of mixing 2D and 3D gameplay is genius, and the storybook aesthetic is extremely charming.Actually, to focus on the positives, the graphics really are beautiful, especially inside the storybook. All the art is really well-made, and the tiny effects that make it seem like this is really all a book on a table, including a little crease in the middle of the book, really bring it all to life.The problems however, start when you actually play the game, and it is insanely handholdy. Anytime anything happens, the game stops you out of nowhere so some character can say a one-liner or blatantly over-explain something you already figured out. Even opening doors gets tiring when each and every time, the game takes away control to show you a painfully show (but very pretty) animation of the door sliding open, and when this happens for everything, you get tired of playing very quickly. I was really hoping this game would be good, but unfortunately it seems it's too afraid to trust its players. Would probably be great for kids though.

The game does very seldom let you explore and find out what to do next, it just plainly shows you where to go, and then doesn't let your do anything until you've done it. You are taken on a tour of a beautiful world that you'll never get to enjoy.I can't recommend this game, sorry.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is my personal Game of the Year.So many games don't hold my attention long-term. I might play an hour here and there and move on. This game, with its creativity and unique puzzles; I couldn't wait to see what was going to happen next or how the next boss battle was going to work. I'm an old school gamer and loved that the boss battles were inspired by other retro games so instead of just 'slash your sword the most while avoid getting hit' they all had something unique to them changing up the gameplay completely.It says 8-10 hours. I probably put in 14+ just exploring and trying random things to see if it might work, just for fun. To me, it's a perfect game. Perfect length and already hoping for a sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: I’d been looking forward to this game for a while, and when I finally got to play it, the first impression was just as amazing as the trailers promised. The vibrant storybook visuals and fairytale-like narration are really attractive, and the puzzle mechanics were fun and engaging. The way the game is presented is also genuinely amusing. But when it came to jumping into the 3D world, I was hoping for something a lot more exciting. Instead, the limited interactions, weird camera angles, and clunky controls made exploring feel less fun. Some of the puzzles were super interesting, and I wanted more of that, but they kind of just ended too soon. The combat is smooth enough, but it also lacks that satisfying depth. Overall, it’s a decent experience, but it could have been something truly great with a bit more polish

_childDocuments_.review: I want to preface by saying that this game is incredibly charming. You can feel every ounce of effort given by the devs and I really hope it finds commercial success (especially with younger audiences). With that being said, this game ended up being a pretty underwhelming experience for me. Its hard to describe exactly why but I guess I was just expecting a bit more. In hindsight this sounds pretty silly, but I never considered the possibility that this was supposed to be a simple puzzle game aimed at a younger demo. I was super drawn in by the style, the mini games , and the cool looking puzzle mechanics that I figured this would be a more engaging experience. But the mini games ended up being a bit too easy for me to have to engage in any meaningful way. The puzzles were cute and sometimes would get close to being clever, but they never required much thought and largely felt very restrained (which is the exact opposite experience I was expecting). And the story had some very touching themes but more often than not only served to slow down what was already a bit of a tedious experience. It probably sounds like I hate this game, but I really do see the value in it and I hope that this team continues to create from this foundation in the future. It really seems to have the bones of an amazing game and will probably be enjoyed by many people. And because of that I don't feel as guilty not recommending this one. Ultimately I think you should give it a shot if you think it looks cool and want an above average 8 hour experience. Even better if you can enjoy this with your kid or younger family member. But if you happen to be someone like me who was  expecting something else, I would consider holding off for a sale.
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: Nothing makes me more sad then to rain on someone else's parade, especially when so much heart has been put into it. While the game's art and sound design is brilliant the actual game play is a total chore. Not only is the combat clunky and the platforming awkward but there is no trust in the player at all for the entire game. From the puzzles to the exploration. Everything is hamstrung by a lack of belief that the player can figure out anything for themselves. I get that this game is aimed at a younger generation, however I believe even they would benefit from discovering mechanics and ideas for themselves. The story itself and dialogue are simple and passable with some creative flourishes here and there. Now I will say, the way the light and texture of the 2D Pages is rendered is nothing short of spectacular. The crease in the middle of the page, the effects popping up, and even the pages flipping. The 3D sections are cool as you hop back and forth between the book and the room. Yet no matter how nice it looks it never feels like a connected experience.Unfortunately Jonathan Biddle did not learn from his mistakes in Momo's Curse and seems doomed to repeat the same mistakes of unsatisfying game play ruining an otherwise stylish experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Have you ever pondered the profound influence of the stories you read as a child? The heroes you admired, their teachings, the courage they displayed in perilous situations, and their sense of justice. These characters and their choices have shaped us, influencing our career paths, friendships, and, ultimately, our identities. But what if these stories had never existed? And what if brave squire Jot, a character from 'The Plucky Squire" was erased from the life of a young aspiring writer, Sam?That's what The Plucky Squire is about. It is a brilliant tale about the importance of stories and the courage they instill in us.Jot is an unblemished hero, a knight who fights against the evil Humgrump with the help of his friends: Violet, the sorceress, the troll, and Moonbeard, the sorcerer who is fond of disco music. But Jot is not only a brave and loyal warrior but also an excellent writer. It is not that he likes fighting all that much; it is by writing that he delights his fellow citizens with bestsellers that make clear his heart and great imagination. This is paradoxical since Jot, Violet, Humgrump, and all the others are characters in a children's picture book, The Plucky Squire.The work is the favorite story of little Sam, who has an absolute mania for Jot. So much is his love for this character, and so much gratitude for the joy this book is giving him in his formative years, that thanks to some magic (we are still in a fairy tale), we get a peek into his future: Sam will become a children's book writer, and his stories, like a kind balm, will touch the lives of so many other kids, inspiring them. Teaching them that evil never pays. In The Plucky Squire, no matter how ruthless and Machiavellian Humgrump's plan is, Jot always manages to prevent it. This aspect of the book not only entertains but also educates, instilling important values in young readers and inspiring them to become storytellers themselves.What happens if Humgrump, after becoming aware that he is just the character—moreover, the villain—of a children's book, manages to find a way to eliminate Jot from the story? In this terrible scenario, Jot will have to fight to return to his home world and prevent Sam's future from changing irrevocably, and thus that of millions of other boys.That of The Plucky Squire is a simple story, but one capable of touching deep chords. You could imagine it as a kind of Toy Story meets Harry Potter, The Little Prince, or whatever your favorite book from when you were a child. Its strength lies in realizing how these works touched our hearts and how manipulating their direction, even slightly, could have made a big difference in our lives. The genius of The Plucky Squire is that this "manipulation" doesn't stop at the theoretical level but comes in the form of dozens of gameplay ideas that leave the player continually dumbfounded.In its first moments, The Plucky Squire is a Zelda on paper. Printed on the glossy pages of our beautiful little book, Jot moves between the boards, as if in a magical flip book. Trees and florid vegetation, fantasy characters, and colors so vibrant they seem to pop off the page. We are already in a world that is inside another world. Like a window overlooking a universe we are privileged to see, the edge of the book acts as a frame, hinting that something else exists outside that story—a tangible universe made of scissors, sharpeners, and paper clips.The book is also not just a book; it is instead one of those astonishing graphic projects in which, every time you turn the page, you are left speechless at the author's visual inventions: pages that read from top to bottom as our hero descends deep into a cave, others dark (so black that you can see the texture of the print) that color as Jot goes through them. It is a display of styles and ideas that make for unique navigation.The Plucky Squire is the book of a warrior writer who is so ingenious that he can change his universe. In fact, one of the first ideas introduced in the video game is the ability to change illustrations through writing. Many environmental puzzles are solved through a system similar to that seen in "Baba, Is You?" We will find small sentences on the page describing the environment, with some keywords that you can substitute to alter the situation. For instance, a parched riverbed can become utterly full of water, and a giant road-blocking bug can be transformed into a tiny road-blocking bug. This process of looking for words within the page often involves us in layered puzzles involving classic levers and locked doors. When our Jot becomes capable of traveling between dimensions, things change quite a bit.When Humgrump succeeds in expelling Jot from the story and, literally, from the book, our hero finds himself in another dimension: the one outside, the three-dimensional one, which responds to totally different physical rules. At these junctures, The Plucky Squire loses its 2D identity and becomes a three-dimensional adventure, where the colorful fantasy settings are replaced by a world of giant tools, toys, and furniture reminiscent of Andy's bedroom in Toy Story and the home levels of Pikmin. In this new setting, Jot as much as the player must change the way they approach environmental puzzles and navigation: everything becomes tied to more precise jumps or physics, with objects to be moved or dropped to use as trampolines. This transition from 2D to 3D gameplay adds a new layer of complexity and excitement to the game, challenging the player to adapt to a different set of rules and strategies.The creative apotheosis comes at the moment when one acquires the ability to enter and exit these two dimensions through special green portals that allow one to transform Jot from time to time from the hero of the book into a kind of animated action figure and to make the two realities interact in every possible way.It is a gimmick that we have already seen and loved in The Legend of Zelda: A Link Between Worlds, and which, in some ways, especially in its ability to play with the two-dimensional nature of paper, also reminded us of the Paper Mario series. The most exciting aspect is that often, to solve puzzles in the book, you have to go out, look for an object in the "real" world, and bring it into the story. Similarly, in the three-dimensional world, some obstacles can be overcome only by the characteristics of the paper, taking advantage of gimmicks such as the folds in books and the verticality of posters. It is a continuous dialogue between two dimensions that talk to each other, intersect, and play with a physics that is there and then is no longer there. It is almost as if two different games continuously meet in a continuous exchange, enriching each other."The Plucky Squire" is a fun approach that, in each session, manages to shake up the formula, offering new mechanics and callbacks to genres seemingly light years away, especially in boss fights. The first one, for example, is an homage to Punch-Out!!!, but there are also situations where you face a JRPG-like fight against what is blatantly a card from Magic: The Gathering or disputes that seem like something out of good old Nintendo's "Rhythm Paradise".At these junctures, the Plucky Squire's most glaring flaw comes out: its excessive ease. There was no challenging moment in the game. Although the puzzles are fun and well thought out, they never prove complex."The Plucky Squire" is a Toy Story that meets your favorite book from childhood. It does so with all the love and gratitude possible for those stories that inspired us as children to become who we are today, thanks to their heroes' bravery, ingenuity, and ability to speak directly to our hearts. But it is also a fantastic video game, chock-full of ideas, aesthetic inventions, and gameplay. It knows how to make two worlds communicate excellently, merging them into one unforgettable adventure.

_childDocuments_.review: I just now completed this game. I enjoyed the multiple art styles and the way each "boss battle" offered different gameplay styles like Punch-out and Bust-a-move. The main game plays similar to top-down adventure games. All very niche to popular games from the 80s/90s.Unfortunately this game is a jack-of-all-trades and master of none. It is more like a visual novel type children's book and felt like the entire game was a tutorial with how often the action was interrupted by narrative. The controls are clunky, there is lag when swapping from 2D (book) to 3D (desk), and book manipulation and some mini-games have issues with controller responsiveness. There were even times when my attacks weren't registering in 2D and 3D arenas. There is A LOT of story and it lives up to its "plucky" title, but this is not worth $30. If you can get it for sub $20 then I'd say go for it.

_childDocuments_.review: The good+ Transferring between 2D and 3D is an incredibly fun mechanic+ Some creative puzzles involving words and turning pages+ Beautiful, adorable visual style+ Interesting story with a lot of meta elements+ Cool mini games including rhythm stealthThe mediocre~ 3D world is a bit bland~ In the 3D world, jumping into other books / objects was underused. What was there was enjoyable, but I expected more. As is, it was mainly used as means of simple traversal. Wish there was more of other books with different graphical styles or comic books or weird art pieces.~ Game is really easy. Depends what you like.The bad:- Controls for tilting the book and flipping pages are annoying. I constantly had to think about what did what.Overall:Plucky Squire is a solid title. I enjoyed it for what it was and can recommend playing it just for the visual style and fun mechanics. However, it did leave me a bit disappointed. _childDocuments_.review: The Plucky Squire blows me away. I expected a fun game, as the idea was already great, but I wasn't ready for how well the game mechanics were implemented and how much attention to detail there was. It has some missable achievements, completion takes around 10 hours.  Around 10 hours 4/10 1 Yes, I used the collectible guide mentioned in  No Yes, play on the "adventure" difficulty and maybe follow a collectible guide No No No No No Yes, you have to play on the "adventure" difficulty NoWhat an amazing game and amazing story! You play as the Plucky Squire, who is helping out the local wizard on a small task... but then there are some strange things happening and the world might be in danger! So off you go to explore what is going on... and this will be the adventure you won't expect with game mechanics that will blow you away! I love the different mini-games and just the story in general. It felt so unique and so well done. And did I already mention the details? I saw so many small details, like how the world looks but also for example the price of the book and how it changed with the story. At first, the narration felt a bit childish. I wasn't sure if I would be the targeted audience. I'm so glad I stuck with the game as this changed. and the narrator does such a good job of telling the story interestingly and encouragingly. The change of tone later on after a huge event was also amazing. That I love this game shouldn't come as a surprise, as I'm such a fan of the games Devovler publishes. I don't know where they find all those gems but man they do a great job finding/publishing crazy, unique, wonderful, and beautiful games. The Plucky Squire has a lot of collectibles. 50 Scrolls, most of them can be found in the wild but always keep money on hand to buy the one from the shop. As it will be a different one in every new shop you encounter. You can also find a Glitchbird in each chapter. And you will need a lot of bulbs (coins) for all the combat skills. So I highly recommend destroying every bush and hit every tree just to find enough money. However, the screen with the mouse and the big block of cheese is a nice scene to grind out money to make sure you will have enough money for sure, as you can find quite a bit of money close to the beginning of that area and then get killed instantly by that mouse to do it all over again. I believe you find this scene in chapter 6. I followed a collectible guide to not miss out on any of the collectibles as different guides mention different things about missables. It might be that with one of the later updates they aren't missable anymore but I didn't want to try that out and find out it would still be missable. The guide by PowerPyx will also mention the areas for some achievements and what to do, so you don't have to replay those areas to get back to that point, while it doesn't tell you how to solve everything or where to go. With just checking the next collectible in that guide, so you can keep it in mind you can still explore and enjoy the game without reading too many spoilers.  I give The Plucky Squire 4.5 out of 5 stars, and I'm looking forward to what All Possible Futures (The developer behind The Plucky Squire) will be cooking up next, as I hope they will continue making games!
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: The Zelda equivalent of bowling with bumpers. Gosh, I was so excited for this one. The storybook art direction is wonderfully whimsical and you can feel the passion that went into making this game. I think it'd be more enjoyable as a literal storybook or an animated feature. Unfortunately, it's just...not fun. I expected something a bit more "all-ages," but instead it feels infantile. I absolutely love cute characters and stories, so it's not that I wanted something mature and edgy here. It Baby's First Zelda—as if Fi from Skyward Sword is hovering over you, asking repeatedly if you need help or if you understand what you're doing when all you've been asked to do is walk up to a sign and press Y to read it. There are two separate characters that exist specifically to give hints, some of which are forced upon you before you even attempt to proceed. The game doesn't seem to trust the player to simply digest it at their own pace. It takes no time at all for it to start feeling like a chore to complete.I don't intend to refund this because I want to support the idea behind it. The creativity on display in the game's visual presentation is notably absent in its level, combat, and puzzle design. The writing is tougher to deem objectively bad; it's simply twee. I found it hard to endure, personally.It's a shame that actually playing The Plucky Squire is much less exciting than imagining the adventure it could've been.

_childDocuments_.review: I could nitpick a couple things here and there (game holds your hand too much at times, 3d sections for the most part aren’t as interesting as 2d, etc.) However this didn’t bother me at all really. _childDocuments_.review: Ok, let's start with the good stuff.The game is gorgeous. Both the 2d and 3d phases are really immersive, you really get the feeling that you're in a book version of The Legend of Zelda ambient-wise, and Sam's desk really holds so much soul it's impressive. Big shoutout to the artists, their work on this is amazing. The concept of going from 2D to 3D is really well exploited on this side, and the visuals live up to the expectations.I found the mage quite funny as well ; he looks like he's out of this world, his contrast with the world he lives in is well done and expressed (shoutout to his music taste!)Now with that being said, I have a lot of problems with this game. I had been expecting it for quite some time. I had been sold a mind blowing adventure playing between different mediums and supports, with a large variety of gameplay, some kind of It Takes Two experience.First off, the gameplay isn't very new ; as we say in French, it doesn't break the 3 legs of a duck. What I mean is for the approximately 2 hours I played, I didn't experience anything different from any other top-down adventure game. The infiltration during the 3D phase was clunky in my opinion ; I restarted 10 times the sequence where you have to walk over a bridge above the beetles, just because I couldn't see where I would land at the end of it ; in the worst case scenario the challenges aren't difficult, just annoying. The bug boss for instance wasn't hard ; the bow gameplay is the same as in the sequence from 5 minutes ago, it's as boring as before, to the exception that the whole body of the bug isn't where you must aim : you have to reach SPECIFICALLY for the eyes. I might have missed the memo ; but I had to die once with the frustration of aiming on the boss and not touching him or dealing any damage, before I understood that I had to go for the eyes. The mosquitoes that he throws are too fast and too close to each other for you to snipe them when the boss throws them ; your target has to go back and forth from the boss to your character, to try and get them before they get you (which they often did). You are encouraged to aim for the longest possible time so that you deal optimal damage, but nothing actually tells you that hey, you don't need to do that for the trash mob, any 0.1 second charged arrow will do.It's not the case for all of the challenges, thanks god, but when they aren't annoying they are just very easy.The puzzles as well are not very challenging ; the only time I got stuck was when there was a whole mechanic I did not know existed ("oooooooh so I can do that ??? but how would've I known ?"). The game is awfully linear, and it's a shame in my opinion the 2D-to-3D twist wasn't exploited for more than "go get this 2 pages ago and get it 2 pages forward"; there is no room for any type of creativity for the puzzles. I almost always immediately understood what the game wanted from me, and all I had left to do was the execution (the only exception being the broken bridge with the frogs sleeping at night ; this one got me stuck for 2 minutes. It was quite good, but imo it should be the low/standard challenge for the puzzles, instead of being the hardest one I encountered). The use of words to impact gameplay could've left so much room for creativity as well ; you could have a dozen of different words, each of which impact the game in some way, and up to you to figure out how to solve the puzzle ; but most of the time there are 2 to 3 words you can move, the solution is to intervert them, and tadaaaaa - moving on to the next page ; the average use of the words being "switch a door from Closed to Open".The narrative rythm is quite slow, which isn't in itself an issue, it's nice sometimes to take your time and enjoy a story being delivered slowly instead of just skipping through every dialogue ; but I perceived every interaction with any NPC as a waste of time. Here it's not "Show don't tell", it's Show AND Tell. "Oh you need a long range weapon" *the camera moves to show a playing card with an archer on it* > ok, I get it, I must reach the archer. I understood : it's a pretty common structure, I'm being shown the point I must reach, so obviously I'll go there. But just to be sure, let's have the worm interrupt me to tell me "Hey, you should get that bow and arrow over there, shouldn't you ?" I didn't find the dialogues to be very well written as well ; they state a lot of obvious things that were already implied (like the example just before), and use the same cliché lines you've already heard thousands of times. I found the two sidekicks to be useless as hell, they don't help, I didn't find them funny ; they just follow you around, interrupt you from times to times and desperately try to catch a smile from you.To conclude : I'd say the game is overall more of an aesthetic experience. Play it for the immersion, for the -once again- STUNNING visuals, but don't play it for the gameplay as such ; it's really been disappointing for me. In the end I think there was a lot of passion and hard work behind this project nevertheless ; making videogames is hard, especially today, and nothing comes easy ; it's also always easier to criticize than to make, and I would be far from achieving anything as impressive as this (even gameplay-wise). *I also figured out that I probably wasn't the target audience* ; I really wanted to love this game, but I think it's just not a game for me. If you have kids and want to play a relaxing, fun, immersive experience with them - go for it ! This is in any case and regardless of what I've been saying above better than a lot of kids-targeted games.I won't put a thumbs down, because I want to acknowledge the work of the devs and artists, and a lot of people seem to love the game ; good for them, good for the team !I just want to warn potential players, so that you don't get caught by marketing and overhype as I've been : this isn't the game of the decade, don't play it for some revolutionary gameplay ; but it's an above average fun little story.
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful mix of 2d top-down action-adventure, like Zelda: A Link to the Past, and 3d action-adventure. There's a good variety of fun mini-games, perhaps a dozen types, that don't overstay their welcome as most aren't repeated until the end. Can also be skipped. Environments in 3d are limited to the desk of the kid because of the game's concept, but the designers made the most out of it as the objects on it change with time creating drastically different environments. The 2d art style is simple but charming. The creature models in 3d are nice but very basic. The 3d environments and objects look very good. Combat is not as elaborate or varied as a Zelda game, but it does the job. The puzzles are fair, clever and use the 2d/3d transition mechanic very well. It's a delightful whimsical game worth playing. Not just for kids despite what you might think of the esthetics.
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: These kind of games really piss me off. It makes me feel this rollercoaster of elation to anger. It's so exciting because of its combined concepts of art and mechanics. But then I start to feel frustrated that gamers have put up with such slop like the garbage dumped out of Activision, EA, and Ubisoft for so long. Where was more of stuff like TPS before? And I know this game won't do as well as it deserves because gamers will keep glazing games like CoD.Truthfully, the gameplay is a little simple and the time spent may not be as high for the price as people would like to see, but the way the devs chose to present this art as a story game is really delightful. I personally feel like this is something I am fine paying $30 for the unique experience that sets it apart for other great games in the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: (Steam stats are wrong for me due to playing in offline on my Steam Deck; actual time is closer to 10 hours played)Most disappointing game I've played in a while. The aesthetic is cool, but it can't save the gameplay. There's no depth to the game at all, and you're constantly interrupted for obligatory comments from your allies to hold your hand, even when you've just completed something that would imply you have the observational skill to not need a 5 second camera pan combined with 5 text boxes from a friend to tell you "Woah maybe you should look for a green portal and use your special ability!" Everything in the game is really just super half-baked. The combat is incredibly simple, all the skills you can buy are pointless, buying stuff from the shop basically just mandates you to have cut down every bush you see to have money, and your minimal range of special powers rarely get combined in a meaningful way. The only mercies offered to you are that you can skip the very simplistic minigames (with no punishment), the game is short, and that they clearly realized at some point in development how obnoxiously tedious the more "clever"/involved puzzles were and slowed down on implementing them, with how solving them isn't really hard but just tedious because even once you know how to solve them, you still will often have to go through a minute or two of rote gameplay where you already know what to do but to execute it you have to run across a room to a portal, use a special power, hop in a portal, run to a thing, etc. which makes it even more painful when the game extends the process even further with its insistence on obligatory unskippable text boxes to tell you what to do, despite having a little guy in most rooms with puzzles who will give you hints who you can talk to if you actually need help. It's just... bad. The game has a promising start with some of these puzzles being a bit interesting but annoying to execute the solution to, but it never goes deeper and the interruptions just wear on and on (and honestly get worse) and you realize that that's just the game.Some will probably still enjoy the game overall because it does have some charm, and it's short enough that they'll be willing to put up with annoyances, but even the biggest Adventure Time fans  children are likely to end up frustrated to an extent by how obnoxious the hand-holding interruptions are, and the gameplay past those interruptions still fails to actually be fun at any point. I've never played a better example of "style over substance" in my life. Even other crowning offenders of excessive hand-holding that I've experienced like Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword at least have some engaging/clever gameplay to make you want to continue playing in spite of constant interruptions. The only thing that kept me playing this to the end was that I realized it was already almost over (and it still didn't end fast enough).

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fantastic and does what it aims to very well.1. Unique artwork and style2. The mix of 2D and 3D gaming inside and outside of the book3. Classic collectables4. Throw backs to retro games in the mini game eventsIt is fun, funny, and well worth your time if you love this style of game.6-10 hours of gameplay, and it is not difficult. The game will hold your hand the entire time, so also perfect for those with kids who want to play but may not get all the references.As an adult, it is the perfect game to just switch off for a bit and enjoy the whimsical theme and story.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could recommend the game. There is a lot to like about it. I really only have 2 problems with it. 1) The game will not shut up. Ever. There is so much dialogue, and it's always something that you could figure out yourself. It's just too much when the game gets interrupted constantly. You are always spoon fed information, and it gets in the way of exploring, it breaks the flow of the game, and ruins any sense of discovery for yourself. I get that it's meant for kids, but even kids will get bored of just being told what to do all the time. It's a puzzle based game, you should have to actually problem solve for yourself at some point. And you should be able to explore the world in peace, especially since it's not like it's a massive open world to get lost in. 2) There are several times (especially in chapter 6) where portals simply do not appear, or do not work when they do appear, forcing you to reset the game. Sometimes controls do not pop up, like when you need to turn the page to the book, but the game only lets you tilt the book, not turn the page entirely. I have reset the game 5 times in chapter 6 alone, and it's getting very frustrating. I think this can be fixed with an update, and I really hope they do. If they fix the game breaking bugs, and let users opt out of puzzle hints then the game is an easy recommend. The graphics and soundtrack are excellent, it's a unique twist on the old Zelda formula. It's so good that, these two issues aside, it truly could be on par with Nintendo's IPs. But as is, it needs some polish. Please, PLEASE update the game asap.
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: Although this is labeled a negative review, that doesn't mean I think the game is bad. It's charming, has a good visual style and a nice soundtrack. However, I just can't recommend it for a two main reasons; the game holds your hand too much and constantly interrupts you, and this is all the way through the game. I would understand if this was only during the prologue, but it isn't. It doesn't respect your time or intelligence. Good for a younger audience maybe, but if you've played any Zelda game, this will feel too easy by comparison. If they added a no-dialogue feature, this game would be a recommend for me, but as it stands now, it's a drag to play.
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: I've never been so torn when reviewing something. I hit credits so I must have enjoyed it but It's strangely a game of high highs and low lows. Some bits feel like they drag on a bit too long and not all mini games hit but some mini games and parts of the story were great. The 2D/3D nature of the game is awesome and unique and the devs clearly put alot of effort into making it seamless. It had a good enough story and it does make you want to get to the end to see how it plays out. For me this is a firm 7/10 I'd recommend it to others but it's not a run out and buy tomorrow kind of game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: Like a lot of people, the game really got my attention with its art style (which is absolutely delightful), but I didn't expect it to be the only thing it would have going for it.The gameplay is simple (if not primitive) to the point of dullness, the few interesting puzzles and gameplay sections that are there are often immediately spoiled by your companions, the mini-games are fun but have bizarre difficulty spikes while the rest of the game is piss-easy, there's barely any flow or pacing as the game CONSTANTLY interrupts you to explain something, and it has no respect for your time as everything takes waaay too long (the animations, the unskippable dialog and cutscenes). About a third of the way through I was so bored, I could barely bring myself to finish it, but it was too late to request a refund.Not to mention the game's awful technical state — nearly every session I ran into some kind of progression-blocking bug or glitch, where I had to either reload an earlier save or replay an entire section because an important object wouldn't spawn or I'd run into an invisible wall.This all sounds pretty harsh, but I wouldn't say the game is necessarily bad, just really really disappointing. While the visuals are undeniably charming and beautiful, the rest has barely any depth or substance to it.If you're looking for something simple you could play with a small kid, then by all means give it a shot (after another patch or two), but if a more substantial Zelda-like adventure is what you're after, then you're gonna have to look elsewhere.
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: I was really looking forward to this game.It looks great with really cool concepts but unfortunately, it's far too simple with a ton of hand holding. It's so easy that it feels like it was made for 7 year olds.  The gameplay stops you constantly to show more text and tedious story narrative.The constant page flips & slow animations make the pace of the game feel like molasses.I just wanted to play a fun action/puzzle game like Mario or Zelda.You won't find that here.They didn't explore each of the fun mini games enough. They should have been much longer and more challenging.  There was a nod to Punch Out for a few seconds, and then it was gone. There's no exploring either. The levels are extremely small and linear. This game could have been fun with a co-op mode also, but they opted out. I have more game time off of steam.It's unfortunate as I know this game was being made for many years, but they made it far too simple and slow.

_childDocuments_.review: Not sure if the people saying this is for 4 year olds were playing in Story Mode or what, but like any good book, I simply could not put it down. I, personally, wholeheartedly enjoyed and loved every minute of this game. The art style and animation are superb. The jokes and easter eggs are great. I've played games that have been in development much longer than this that do not hold a candle to this one.Don't expect a super hard, super long, impossible to figure out game. _childDocuments_.review: A first look:Honestly, from the moment the "dust-up" scene came to play, I just knew this game would rock socks throughout, and so far, it's been a joy. A little bit of hack and slash, a little bit of puzzling, some stealthy moves. It makes me super curious about what else we will get and see beyond the little time I could spend there before I had some RL stuff I had to deal with first.So, yes, this is an early thumbs-up for support, and I highly doubt that will change. I love the art/music, the collaboration between 2D and 3D worlds, and the story; I genuinely snickered aloud several times. I also love the fact that there are collectables! _childDocuments_.review: To start this review I would like to point out that the game is very charming and kind of cozy. The overall art design is cute, colorful and unique, the music is pretty good and I appreciate the idea to basically bring a children‘s book to life, to adventure in its cute little world and to switch between 2D and 3D. (Also I didn’t have any technical issues, one small bug in 9 hours)But I do have some problems with the game. First of all I had different expectations for what the game would have to offer based on trailer footage and some preview videos. For the story I won’t go into any spoilers. I will just say that the story itself is pretty basic, which is not bad but simply not what I was hoping for in advance. Same goes for characters and dialogue. A bit more interesting and thought-out characters as well as a hint of a deeper, more complex story would really benefit the game in my opinion. The humorous moments are fine, but while playing I thought that there could have been more smart or witty jokes that would still fit in a videogame for a younger audience. I also wished for more diversified mini games. The mini games are fun, the puzzles get kind of repetitive, but they‘re short and keep up a good pacing which is why the game doesn’t get boring.One more small thing is that you should be able to change language in the menu. It’s a standard nowadays. I couldn’t find a way to change it.A thumbs down here on steam doesn’t mean that this game is by any means bad. But before I played the game I had hoped for more with regard to the story, characters and gameplay. Nonetheless I genuinely hope that this game will succeed economically and resonate with a younger audience, families and people who can appreciate it a little more than I do.
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: I must give this game a positive review because I do think overall it is very charming, cute, enjoyable, interesting, and unique. However, I think the expectations I and many had for this game were too high. While it does explore the idea of interacting between a 2D and 3D world, I found the 3D art style to be more "generic" than it's incredibly stylish 2D counterpart and so is true with the gameplay. The puzzles between worlds were certainly unique but also barely scratched the surface of the possibility space before the game came to a close. Overall I still recommend this game as I think it is very good, but for me it came up a little short of my expectations.
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR --> The Plucky Squire was less of a main character than I wished.----------------------Well, this was... more underwhelming that I expected. But maybe I expected a bit too much.The Plucky Squire (TPS) is exactly as you see on screens and trailers: you take control of the main character of a fictional kid's storybook who eventually gains the ability to leave the book's reality and also progress his adventures in the "real world", in a beautiful 3D. The game features 10 chapters with a Zelda-ish system of both combat and puzzle-solving, and during them you also will do some minigames that are basically throwbacks from classic games. While the premise is very good, and the artstyle is absolutely gorgeous, this is pretty much where it ends for me. By the time this review is made, the game is worrisomely buggy (and I will update my review if this ever changes). Not only game-breaking sequence happen (at some point my characters were DUPLICATED on a screen, causing all sorts of weird stuff happening), but also full game crashes. Moreover, for whatever reason, replaying a chapter from the Chapter Replay option doesn't allow you to save, and it is like this BY DESIGN since a prompt box appears telling you that before you jump into a chapter. I honestly don't know how this felt okay to anybody. Aside from technical issues, my absolute biggest problem with the game is that it treats you like a complete idiot. Despite focusing a lot on puzzle-solving areas, the game literally prevents you from solving anything on your own. Characters will give you all the hints BEFORE you can even start trying to figure out anything at all. It brings the "let's make sure noone gets stuck" to an extreme I haven't seen before. This goes along a very childish story that will not give you many surprising or unexpected events.The game's difficulty is laughable too. I don't know why there are two sets of difficulty when the "hardest" one is completely trivial all the way through. Every single enemy and wave can be easily dealt with by simply spamming the sword attack, and in case you lose health they will start dropping hearts very, very often. Finally, the game's variety also drops down after certain progress. At the beginning you will be presented with many different things you can do and you might get excited to see how this will go on. Well... it barely does. Some new mechanics are presented later on but they are more lacking or just less interesting. The final chapters catch up a little bit, though.Overall, I can see a target audience for this game being kids, but even kids might feel discouraged about how much everything absolutely given right away here. It is not a bad game by any means and I wish Steam, once again, would allow me to give a neutral review, but right not and at a 30-euro price tag I felt this game ended up below my expectations.
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: Nothing in the game is overly challenging, not puzzles nor fights, but that’s not the point. Its more about the mechanics than the technical challenge. Being able to merge 2D and 3D worlds into a story narrative is where the game shines. Its a good 8-10 hours worth of good honest story telling fun and its nice to see that there are still devs that have an imagination and can bring abstract ideas to life.

_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: Really lovely game that definitely won me over with its story and characters a ton. The game as a whole isn't all that difficult, but there are a couple of quirks that make it much rougher an experience than I'd have liked.The main adventure and puzzle aspects work great and feel creative, but I just ran into one too many freezes, glitches or slow texture loading during my playthrough that irked me some. Also, while all the mini games are fun - the rhythm minigame in particular is awful. Even with VSync + 60FPS, it feels like you should be playing to the visual cues and not the beat in the slightest.If the game seems charming to you and you aren't looking for something to deeply challenge you, I adored this even at full price. It's even possibly that perfect "first game" to introduce a younger gamer or friend to.
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: I made one key mistake in the lead up to this game, and that was coming in with the assumption that this game was much deeper and mature of an experience than what is honestly marketed as. But that's entirely on me, because this game absolutely nails everything it sets out to achieve. It has impeccable art direction and it understands children's writing, being very pallet-able but never talking down. And it has very much the same approach to puzzles, ensuring all the pieces are clearly laid out, but never condescendingly directing.The game is however incredibly linear. If like me you had thoughts of having every page of every chapter eventually at your disposal or an overworld map to freely explore akin to its obvious zelda inspiration, you would be mistaken. Every chapter has its set pieces and designated pages to explore. And it uses those pages well, often in very interesting ways. Similarly the world outside of the book is very linear, and you will only ever have access to obstacles pertinent to the current chapter. Its yet again something that caught me off guard for reasons that would be very hard to explain without both spoiling the game and giving my interpretation of the themesThe puzzles, minigames, and combat, while all greatly competent, also are not hard. All of this leads to the obvious conclusion that the game with the very kid friendly aesthetic is very much made for kids. A design philosophy that I'm always 50/50 on. A good family game does not have to be one with a low skill ceiling. However I'm also not one to glorify the regrettable and intentionally frustrating design decisions of games of the past, and understand that not every game is going for a Link to the Past type learning curve that taught a lot of us how to play video games in the past, especially if the game is trending to be accessible for children under 7. In that case this game is absolutely fantastic. If you are a parent or a cool Uncle/Aunt with the fancy Steam Deck or Gaming PC, this is a must buy even at this price. But, while I still think this is a great game for all ages, even adults, its length and relative difficulty leaves me to say you might not get 30 dollars worth of personal value from it, and therefore might want to wait for a sale. Unless of course you just pop of for chill, wholesome, cute things, then its 8 hours of pure bliss.
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: The Plucky Squire has a charming art style and a novel concept but is too concerned with making sure the player is never stuck to give them a chance to do much of anything on their own.The art direction for this game is really strong and was a large part of what kept me playing to the end. I really appreciate the effort that went into making the characters look good both hand drawn and as 3D models, the mix of art styles to represent different genres and media, the lighting that really emphasizes the time of day on the desk, and the way the music fades in and out between the desk music and storybook music as you move to or from the book. I also really liked the narrator and having text pop up on the page further cements that you are playing out a story in a book. The mini-games also help add some variety and was the other part of the game I continued to look forward to as I played. Mechanically, the game has everything it needs to be a competent top-down Zelda style game, including tools that play into the idea of being able to pop in and out of the book, but it stumbled on the execution.There is nothing wrong with having a generous hint system, especially in a game that is clearly aimed at a younger audience, but it is a problem when one is not allowed the option to figure things out on their own. Far more often than not, when you gain a new tool or encounter something you haven't seen before, the game will take control from you, explain what you're looking at and how to deal with it, pan the camera to exactly where you need to go, and for good measure mention that there is an npc you can talk to if you get stumped. The combat is also problematic because mashing the basic attack button is almost always the best answer even in "adventure mode."
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: It's not like this is a bad game. But it's incredibly underwhelming in terms of what i had expected. From the trailers we had been shown i had though this was gonna be a zelda like adventure game the likes of link to the past/link between worlds, where the outside world was gonna be the major focus and you manipulate your own book/world by doing stuff and maybe other books and stuff were gonna be the dungeons. However that is not the case at all. Instead this is an incredibly linear and handholdy puzzle game with a relatively short amount of actual game to play. I was shocked when i was in chapter 5 out of 10 after less then 2 hours of gameplay. And while my total amount of hours ended up being a little bit over 7 hours, that was with me searching for hidden stuff, which i gave up torwards the end of the game when i realized there is no way to visit locations from previous chapters. It didnt help that it felt like i was on autopilot for half the game cause characters keep interupting you almost constantly to comment on whatever just happened. You picked up an item? "Goody let me explain" okay, fair enough. You picked up a collectable? "Goody let me explain" okay, i guess. You solved a puzzle? "Wow great going" okay thanks but please just let me play. You picked up another collectable? "Goody let me explain" Come on, i know what it is a short pick up message is enough don't halt the game again and again for this. You solved another puzzle? "Wow great going" PLEASE JUST SHUT UP AND LET ME PLAY! You screen transitioned? "Oh wow a new environment! And that looks like a puzzle up ahead" *cutscene plays showing a puzzle you haven't even gotten the chance to walk up and inspect on your own* "Gee i wonder how this will work" Can i just have break... can i just have one break? Again this feels incredibly handholdy and almost like their artificially stretching gameplay time.The Puzzle Solving itself isn't even bad, there were a few that i thought were really smart and used neat ideas. But a lot of it feels like you don't even need to use your brain, its just "you know how to do thing, so go do thing" which again constantly gets interrupted by characters commenting either before or after the puzzle or both. Imagine slightly less annoying fi from skyward sword. It also doesnt help that at the date of this review i've experience multiple bugs, like things not loading correctly after dying, environmental items suddenly not being interactable anymore, picking up box and it getting stuck in my character.TL;DR: Overall i'd say it's not worth its current asking prices of 30 bucks, its too short, too linear and doesn't deliver much in return. This is not to say it was an awful game, but more on the mediocre side. Definetly would say if you wanna grab it wait til it's atleast half off. That's the highest i'd pay for it if i could go back.
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: I wish there was a neutral option...So basically it is a game with unique visuals and interesting mechanics, but that's it.I hoped for an Adventure Time-, Gravity Falls-, Gumball-, Flapjack-like experience where tone and humor are a bit more mature and don't match the artstyle, but here you can expect what the visuals show. Too childish for my taste to be honest.The mechanics would be great and it would be good to find out for yourself how to solve the puzzles with the toolset you have, but the game just simply feeds you the solution every single time (except for maybe 1-2 occasions).The graphic is really nice both for the 2D and the 3D parts, I haven't seen more beautiful pages of a book in a game before and the music is enjoyable too, matches the tone of the chapters really well.The story is like 8-9 hours long which is not much considering that it is very easy. The enemy variaty is okay for this lenght.I wouldn't feel good if I gave a negative review for the game as it really is well made, just not my cup of tea and also I find the 30€ price tag a bit high, for this lenght and experience I would find 20€ more appropriate.

_childDocuments_.review: This game would be perfect for my 6-year-old kid (which I don't have). I have had it on my wishlist since forever and was hoping for a fun, diverse gameplay. Just when I started to feel a little impatient about the currency farming with the bushes and trees, I started to become excited again when I found out I could get out of the book.However, the story does not mostly carry on outside the book. It becomes repetitive even after 3 hours of gameplay. If I wanted, I could have just walked around and hit trees for hours just to buy skill upgrades.Now, I understand being able to change the pages of the book to travel from one page to another, though it does start to become long and tedious since I need to be at a certain spot to change the page. It's a lot of walking considering how frequently I do it. The game includes parts where you need to move the words from one page to another, which can only remind me of Baba is You. Having played that game, this just feels like an annoying task considering how often we need to do it.Although the art style is a winning point, I doubt the gameplay will ever be. Some may have purchased this game with hopes of reminiscing their experience with It Takes Two. Instead, The Plucky Squire is far too limited and redundant to attain a similar or better level of success. It might be hyped for the moment, but not for a long time. Maybe, what is missing is an 'adventurous fun' kind of touch. It does not feel the same as launching It Takes Two, Little Nightmares, Grounded, Another Crab's Treasure, Hypercharge: Unboxed, Fall Guys, Dave the Diver, etc. I found these games I named to be pretty fun (some of which following a similar 'cute', 'childish' or 'human world' style. The mechanics are pretty basic; you can dash, jump, hit, throw your sword, etc. Bosses don't require a mastery of mechanics though. I've played games that were frustratingly difficult for me, but this one was frustratingly easy. That said, I would rather use similar mechanics and launch Fall Guys to troll 12-year-old kids.I'm going to finish the game nonetheless because I'm a sucker for achievements: P---UPDATE: I am not going to finish this useless game. I have never felt so much inner rage for a game that is so full of narration EVERY second. I kid you not. I was already getting super pissed that I couldn't just go straight to the boss and finish the game. Who wrote the dialogues for this game? Trust me, none of that was necessary.I admire the artistic effort that went into this game but GOSH, just because I selected Story mode doesn't mean I bought this game for a stupid bedtime story. 50 % of my hours are from the dumb narrations, 10 % are from the bugs that forced me to reload the chapter or from the last checkpoint (7 min ago), 30 % of the game is walking back and forth like an idiot and I can't even tell if the last 10% is worth calling gaming. Enemies offer zero variety. It's always the same damn thing. You can always effortlessly kill enemies. HOWEVER, the final boss is INCREDIBLY difficult for the sole reason that it gives you a rhythmic challenge where you have to click buttons at the right time. It lasts so long before you actually do end up landing a hit! I just wanted to rip my head apart. This is such a lack of consistency, especially when it comes to the distribution of levels of difficulty.A little heads up if you are buying this game: farming currency has proven to be especially useless later because you end up with too much money and you only have scrolls to buy in the shop starting mid-game. That just means they ran out of ideas.Music can honestly be better. The game looks so "lively" but the music can just make the whole experience boring or, at best, mediocre. Even at some point, it started to feel depressing. That's one of the reasons why I feel like the atmosphere of the game is truly a weak point. Somehow, we always get shot into random environments with random quests with no real correlation to the storyline or to the objective whatsoever. I don't know what the goal is? Why are we just constantly doing quests to unlock random doors and all? Did we need all those weapon upgrades? Not at all. A waste of time.I cannot even fathom doing this game twice (story mode and adventure mode) to get both achievements. I guess my patience ran thin mid-game. DO NOT get this game!---Maybe there is a better world in some unidentified dimension where this game can be significantly improved with:- varied enemy attacks and fighting style- automatic saves every time there is a dialogue or just a save button!- FIXED BUGS FIXED BUGS FIXED BUGS FIXED BUGS- removal of unnecessary narrations/dialogues (I cannot stand one more second of the worm in the post-its talking and saying the obvious)- removal of all skills from the shop and make them into something you earn from boss kills- ability to upgrade skill level with the accumulation of XP from killed enemies- removal of health drops from enemy kills- repurposing of the shop such as to sell potions for health or boost attacks- reduced amount of time it takes to turn a page -a better mechanic for getting in and out of the book- better music in the first biome and in the area where the MC saved Violet- a better use of the cycle between day- and nightime (in real time, it does not take that long to read a book and it felt pointless. Moreover, nightime had too many shadows, I could hardly see in some corners)- better puzzles because they are simply linear and it is impossible to get something 'wrong', hence making them tentative- replacement of the sorry-of-an-excuse skills that Crash and Violet have. They were super underwhelming, especial Violet's. She said she was going to perform magic, and I expected magic. Whatever happened in the game was not it- include a skip button for dialogues and cutscenes- merge dialogues and cutscenes to reduce the intervals of said things- more involvement from the MC's friends because they are useless and just follow me around when they could have just done something to help (can't we incarnate them during the 'exploration' as well? not just during boss fights?)

_childDocuments_.review: Positives: Beautiful art direction, especially with the 2D elements. I love the unique style of the art too.Negatives: The writing is bad. Kind of reminds me of the Star War prequels type of bad writing, for example, you are introduced to your friends but not in any sort of fun or interesting way. You're just told that they are your friends and that's the end of the story. They also reuse words constantly, I hope you like the word "plucky" because you're going to hear it like 10,000 times throughout the story as if they don't know any other words or adjectives to describe anything.The gameplay is just awful and far too easy. People will tell you this game is meant for little kids and that's why it handholds so much but I've been a little kid and this would drive me absolutely insane if I was playing this as a child. No kid wants to be paused every five minutes to be told how to play basically. When they're not holding your hand, basically all you have to do is swing your sword like once and everything is dead. Even little mini-games that you hope will be fun will last like ~10 seconds and it's basically impossible for you to lose.I know I got the product for free, but if I didn't - I find it overly expensive. $30 for 8 hours of subpar gameplay is a total ripoff. It's a buggy mess too, includes gamebreaking bugs that will stop you in your tracks. I kind of expect this problem with Devolver products honestly but still - it's a problem.The game feels like some artists got together to show off their skills/display their art and they forgot to actually make a game.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to love this game so badly. It's got so much style & a unique concept. But ultimately it's very shallow. It has a very strong emphasis on story which in itself isn't a problem, but it's the main focus with little game play in between. It introduces concepts & mechanics that are hardly used & never gives you an chance to breath constantly cramming story & exposition down your throat. Also you get a couple of sword abilities that you'll rarely ever use because your basic sword attack for some reason is so much more powerful that it's not even worth wasting your time on spin attack, jump attack, or sword throw. A handful of decent puzzles, but overall underwhelming if you're over the age of 13. Clearly a children's game. The game also has a tendency to freeze on Steam Deck. I had deleted that comment from this review after changing to lower graphical settings, but still experienced freezing.Edit: It's unfortunate that Steam only has a recommend or don't recommend option. I would very much recommend this game for young kids. My 6 year old daughter is loving it. However given the Steam platform demographic is typically older people, for this platform I will keep my review as don't recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is riddled with bugs, to the point where getting softlocked happens far too often. In the first four chapters alone, I encountered so many issues that I genuinely question whether the game was properly playtested at all.On top of that, the handholding is excessive. Nearly every room has dialogue interruptions explaining the simplest, most uninspired puzzles, leaving no room for the player to figure things out on their own. It's frustratingly dull and undermines any sense of challenge or discovery.It’s especially disappointing because this was one of my most anticipated games of the year. Sadly, it turned out to be a really huge letdown and one of the most boring games I have probably ever played. The only redeeming quality of this game is its art style, which is admittedly really cute and well done. However, the gameplay is deeply flawed, making it hard to enjoy the experience.I can’t even recommend this game for children, as the excessive handholding and constant interruptions, not to mention the bugs, make it more frustrating than fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Painfully dull.Plucky Squire is visually impressive and has a strong core premise but is held back by boring gameplay, an anaemic story and very little substance.It would be easy to pin it as a 'good game for children' but its insistence on holding the player's hand by pointing out solutions and constantly interrupting the flow of play by spelling out the next objective suggests it espouses the creativity and wonder of children but doesn't trust them to apply it here. On numerous occasions control is taken away to pan over the area, have an NPC point out what to do 'oh? those two keyholes look like we need two key. i think theres a key to the east and one to the west!' and then, to really drive the boot in it has a hit system for some reason. All of this is even more confusing as the puzzles are straightforward with very few moving parts, so why so much explanation? The combat is much the same with each enemy taking only a few hits and offering no strategy so to speak in defeating them. Even when you misstep and lose life the game hides hearts EVERYWHERE meaning there is no stakes. Goes without saying that there is a death system but it immediately starts you on the same page, so why even hard it.But maybe you can move past that and want to indulge in the storybook world and 3D spaces. Well, they are fine...You spend very little time in each area with not much depth to each. It really emphasises how well games like Katamari, Pikmin and Tinykin did to create a miniaturized toy room and how much this does not.Ultimately, The Plucky Squire is incredibly underwhelming. It assumes very little of children and the player and a more cynical person might look into the constant emphasis on how GOOD the Squire is as a franchise within the text as fairly self-congratulatory for what is a forgettable title.

_childDocuments_.review: I think “style over substance” is a phrase that is frequently overused by game reviewers and video essay youtubers alike. However, it does work well in summarizing how I feel about The Plucky Squire. It’s got all the correct ingredients, but none of the seasoning and intrigue that would make it a truly excellent experience.Puzzles and GimmicksThe dynamic between switching between and interacting with the 2D and 3D worlds is a genuinely interesting gameplay twist and it’s a real shame none of the puzzles that involve you switching between the two worlds ever go beyond the surface-level. Upgrades like the stop and bomb stamps and being able to flip pages to move stuff in the environment are super technically impressive and definitely wowed me. However, I couldn’t help but see the missed potential as when I continued to progress through the game I realized the gimmicks never went beyond that initial spectacle. You can see visages of a good game bellowing under the surface, but the game is just so sanitized and so afraid of letting the player fail or get stumped that it just ends up feeling empty.Controls and BossesThe entire game is generally way too hand-holding. Even during enemy encounters, the game just showers you with so many health pick-ups that you’re probably never going to see a single death screen during your playthrough. And this isn’t a compensation for any flaws in the general game-feel. No, the game controls absolutely fine. Switching between 2D and 3D feels natural. I had no issues during my entire playthrough as your basic combat controls feel great; it is almost too great as no enemy is really going to give you any trouble. On that note, a lot of boss encounters have a unique gameplay-style where the game has you switch game-genres. Sometimes you’re playing a Punch-Out! Style boss fight and other times you’re playing a Puyo Puyo knock-off. These boss encounters are great and were a highlight during my playthrough. The only gameplay-style I didn’t care for was the stealth segments. They felt stiff and unforgiving that feels antithetical to the rest of the experience. They feel unnecessarily and are such a minor portion of the game that it feels like a waste to have them at all.Story and PresentationThe game’s story is also nothing to write home about. You have a set of two additional party members that stick with you during most of your journey. However, since the Squire is the only character that can jump between the 2D and 3D worlds, they don’t get to do much. Most of their screentime is dedicated to their characters' arcs of needing to “believe in themselves” and “need to prove themselves.” It is a super basic characterization that felt kinda hollow and didn’t move really get me invested in the game's characters at all. It doesn’t help that many of the cutscenes involve the physical book having to flip the page every single time there was a scene transition. It’s novel and quirky at first but it does eventually get old and slogs the pace down. It’s a shame too cause presentation-wise, the cutscenes are the biggest showcase of the unique art-style that defines the game. Each cutscene does a great job in selling the premise of a children’s book come to life. To add to that, the presentation is basically flawless. I love how the 2D segments look and plopping between the 2D and 3D sections is basically seamless. The 3D sections are also really well done. The desk is a fun area to explore and I kind of wish the game took place in more 3D locations so that the game could fully showcase the fun setting. It’s just a shame that the game's flaws do end up hampering my final enjoyment of the story and presentation.Most of my issues with Plucky Squire might stem from the fact this game is clearly targeting a target audience that is way younger than I am. It’s probably a great game for your kids. But even most children’s media has something for adults to latch onto. This game has so much potential with its excellent premise, gimmicks, and presentation. It just needed to plunge deeper into its puzzle design and a slightly more difficult experience for me to get the most out of it. I hope that the developers take this feedback this game is getting and put it into a sequel that expands upon this game’s strengths which may give us a truly great game experience when the potential is fully realized.
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: On the one hand, the game is a bit of a victim of the hype it has generated since its first public presentation, but it's impossible to forgive its catastrophic pace.In the 2D phases, the game constantly takes the player's hand away in favor of incessant dialogue phases on every screen. It's a pity, because there are some good ideas and varied gameplay phases that are fun in theory, but neither very deep nor very fun to play in practice.A Nintendo feel on the surface, but very dull in the end.What's left is a superb art direction, but it's no match for the systematic dialogues that break the pace and the bland gameplay phases.Not bad, just bland.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the cutest game I played in a long while. A must buy for those out there who enjoy fun and unique action adventure games.
