_childDocuments_.review: So, tough game to evaluate, a lot of very good, a lot of very bad (finished Simon pre nerfs).First thing first, yeah, even if I give a negative review the game was woth the 60 by far. If you dont want bs tracjing and delayed attacks then just run away.Now, good things:- Great level design, the game looks good and was running great at launch, unfortunately no longer expected nowadays- A lot of ideas, not all good but they did try to spice things up. I love being able to regen my healing potion when I am empty, it's not easy to get but rewarding (best thing they implemented), legion arms are surprisingly fun. Not sure about the grindstone, kind of gimmicky but overall more frustrating in some boss fights than anything- Weapons: even if there are not enough different weapons, each felt unique that was great- Story: borderline cringe but at least they did try to make something so A for affort I guess- Great first attempt at soul games for this studio, with the kind of story they went for they can easily make others and I'll wait them eagerly to see if they can do better :)Mixed feelings:- Too much fromSoftware influence. You can chose a worse reference but it was a limitation in many regards: come on, everything about Sophia was just a copy paste for example, try to get your own brand- Tried to much to be Bloodborn and Sekiro but achieved neither, pick your horse (I think BB suited them better)Negative, why I ended up frustrated enough to give a negative review:- Red attacks: you have little choice but to remember (not be good enough at the game to consistently do it through fights though) the timing for the parry, little chance you can away from it if it is a better choice most of the time. Then you can get 100% if RNG sucks.Let us chose if we want to stay in the fight or kite please, feeling like a RNG parrying street lamp atm- Every bosses/mob and their mothers and their mothers before them can attack you when you are facing their hairy backs- Insert random soul boss music- They never managed to chose what was the gameplay they wanted: they try to force you into a parry playstyle (stagger mechanics, red attacks) but the reward is ridicule compared to the risk. You lose way too much hp if you just block, if you manage to parry you still lose stamina, and at the end of the day even with great parries you don't necessarily get a counter-attack even if you parried a 7 attacks combo, so you have no reward for playing well. You then are kind of forced into a more dodge playstyle, which doesn't feel like the game was really designed for. Finally, your reward for playing well eventually is to stagger through a charged attack. You don't have any idea when the stagger bar will be full, and landing a charged attack when your stamina bar is empty, the boss ran away, you don't know if your attack is 'charged enough', it just ruins the pace a parry game could have, everything ends being kinda awkward is pretty frustrating when it is close to be very good.- Some OS mechanics, never good about any game. You miss the weird timing on the parry of a red attack, boss then combo you just when you get out of stagger trying to roll, fun- First bosses were good, and Laxasia is awsome enough to appear in any top X soul bosses (actually forces you to be better at the game + unique mechanics ), but the other were just poorly adjusted even when they had good ideas. Interminable phases 1 into much more fast-paced phase 2 (get me to phase 2 already omg), delayed attacks after delay attacks, DS2 level of tracking, amnd as said before you never know when you'll get the stagger, so eventually you learn the boss rather than the game (you learn the combo by heart rather than knowing visuallty when to land your parry). Once more, many of those were close to be great but end up frustrating.To summarise, gameplay a bit awkward, bosses not rewarding enough when you beat them because they don't make you better at the game and have too many cheap mechanics

_childDocuments_.review: The Soulslike genre is one of the only spaces in video games completely dominated by one studio. Not for a lack of trying, other studios can’t seem to match From Software’s masterful grasp of Souls game design. I’ve been playing and replaying From Software’s catalog for almost half of my life, and I’ve tried my hand at most attempts by other studios to capture that Souls magic. In every one I’ve tried, the magic is just not there. Most Soulslike games seem to buckle under the weight of expectations brought on by the original Souls trilogy.Lies of P is an enigma in the Soulslike genre for a lot of reasons. You play as a set character, there’s a direct, overt story, and there are no oddball dynamic multiplayer elements. Right from the beginning, Lies of P shrugs at some of the sacred cows of the Soulslike genre. Some might balk at these changes, but Lies of P carries itself with such grace, such precise artistic intent, that it almost leaves me speechless; Lies of P is strange for a Soulslike because it momentarily punches higher than anything From Software has made.The city of Krat, the setting of Lies of P’s apocalyptic twist on Pinocchio, is totally captivating. Krat speaks to you in every moment of gameplay, from the corpses battered in the street to the comforting whine of a violin in a nearby window. Cats meow, fires rage, broken speakers blare crooked music - it all puts you there on Elysion Boulevard. Bloodborne reached for atmosphere like this, but it seemed to drop that sense of a lived-in place after the first few areas. Different games with different design intentions, but I digress.One of the immediate differences between controlling the player character in Lies of P compared to other Soulslikes is the movement speed. Lies of P is noticeably slower, more deliberate with its movement; it actually reminds me a lot of the original Dark Souls in that regard. Make no mistake - the combat is fast, blisteringly so. Enemy attacks either fly out faster than the speed of light, or they wind up for 3-5 business days to throw off your parries. Say what you will, Lies of P at least gives you more interesting tools to handle complex attack patterns than some of FromSoft’s catalog ever did (Sorry, Dark Souls 3). The weapons you get feel distinct, and you can customize them in all the ways you’d want. The blade and hilt system is extremely robust, although it definitely takes too long to get enough options to make the customization really sing.More than anything, Lies of P just keeps surprising you. Another secret, another fun character twist, another ambush you definitely ran right into, another bombastic, meaty boss fight. It’ll clock you about 25 hours if you’re being thorough, and the pacing never breaks its confident stride all the way to the credits.The story is where my endless comparison to other Soulslikes ends. Lies of P is bold, both in its adaptation of the classic story of Pinocchio, but also in how it doesn’t needlessly pull from its source material. Here is a world distinctly colored by the classic folktale, but with that color it paints a macabre picture of identity, memory, and conspiracy. Krat has a rich history, completely original to Lies of P.Sufficed to say, Neowiz sort of pulled off a miracle here. I think the gaming community at large has gotten very used to Soulslike games not created by the esteemed From Software to land with a thud, but Lies of P proves there’s more out there. We were all pulled to Demon’s Souls because it experimented in ways that the industry had never seen before - Lies of P uses FromSoft’s catalog as a springboard, pushing to greater heights in distinctly new ways. Perhaps the most surprising thing about Lies of P is that it proves the Soulslike genre is not a walled garden; it’s not only From Software’s playground anymore.And that’s it, no notes - Lies of P rules.

_childDocuments_.review: It is a great beginning for a Souls-like, but it severely lacks when it comes to fluid gameplay and mechanics. The parry and dodge timings are entirely inconsistent and unrewarding. The left arm tools are not satisfying to use or are completely useless. And the boss encounters rely on the broken parry and dodge and making it artificially difficult by having to fight constant multiple boss fights absolutely which forces you to study the boss mechanics for hours. Or you have to rely on the hamfisted Spectre mechanic which I personally do not find interesting or satisfying to use in any game.If they would have removed one or two mechanics to simplify the design and focus on polishing the other mechanics this could have been a good game. Otherwise, it feels like a cobbled together version of From Soft souls games where the devs ripped the most popular mechanics from those games and shoddily implemented them in this game.

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing souls-like that needs to be put out there. It has unique story, style, and game play with the look and feel of a souls-game that gets better as you play it. It looks good, feels good, rewarding if you're a loot bug like me, and provides a lot more than I was looking for when I bought this (Happened to stumble onto it a lil ago, and forgot it was in my wishlist). The only gripes I have: 1. The currency in this game is "ergo" and you can either receive that through killing enemies or drops that you can sell for ergo (Ergo Fragments/Chunks). So, common enemies and common drops tend to be dim/radiant ergo frags, and drops from elite enemies are dim/radiant ergo chunks. Adding to that, bosses drop there own "special" ergo frag that sell for 10,000. The problem that arises is that boss drops don't look all that special and if you are not a big reader like me, u will skip the "someone might want this in the future" as there is no use for the first 3 boss drops. You only get to get the boss drops after you get the merchant that takes those and it is barely hinted too. On my play through I sold those boss drops thinking that 10,000 wasn't all that much (as there was no use for them at the time, thinking  bosses weren't as rewarding) and after selling there is no way of getting them back  2. The drops in this game are a little confusing with how they are spread. At the beginning you don't get much to play around with weapon-wise, legion arm wise, and advance usage wise. I never really found a use in changing legion arms after I found the one I liked and same goes for the weapons, till I got the puppet ripper. Advance is used to upgrade attribute based attacks (meaning acid, fire, and shock), I love the addition of these, but the usage of this is not really needed and its not very usable until mid to late game.3. I wish there as more to buy/do with the golden tree coin fruit as it is very cool and you get alot. I wish there were secret gold coin vendors scattered or something. Otherwise, If you love souls games or you are getting into souls games, I would definitely have to say this is a great choice as this is a somewhat upcoming company that finally made a great game (hell a great souls game) in 2023. P.S. Don't sell you frisckin boss ergos

_childDocuments_.review: The game is Phenomenal. Feels like a mix of Bloodborne and Sekiro, with a significant amount of originality from the devs. Story is Fantastic, Exploration is worth it (A lot of secrets), and it feels Great to play. Also, I don't know how its possible, but the optimization of this game is ridiculous. I had a stable 120 fps the entire time, and I barely manage 60 on most other games. This helps a lot for making combat feel smooth as butter. If you want more details, look up a YouTube review that goes into that kind of thing. Something I will mention, however, is that they implemented NG+ really well. A lot of new items to grab, golden collectible records with new music (and old music but now with vocals), and much easier to understand bosses. (Bosses have heavily garbled subtitles until you get a certain item in very late game, you get to keep that item in NG+, so all the old bosses now have clear subtitles).Also, just straight up new upgrades you don't get access to in the normal new game. To summarize: Game fun, feels good, New game+ is worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Lies of P is one of many soulslike clones that just like the others, ends up falling short in terms of gameplay. At first glance, this game both visually and gameplay-wise looks like Bloodborne. Don't be fooled. Most of the time, this game doesn't know if it wants to be Bloodborne, Sekiro or Dark Souls. This game encourages you to play with an aggressive play-style, but at the same time it punishes you for every tiny mistake you make. It wants you to perfect parry enemies, but then throws in a mix of 0.2ms attacks that you are barely even able to read, without having fought the same enemy 100 times and memorizing it. And when you think you got the attack pattern down, the enemy will delay their attacks like it was an Elden Ring boss. The game also wasn't made for big weapon builds. The windows of opportunity to attack after parrying/blocking is so small that most of the time you won't even have enough time to hit a single attack. The easiest workaround for this is ignoring the game mechanics and just bringing out your biggest weapon, roll to the side and spam through the damage in hope to stagger them. Simply put, the best way to deal with the game, is by not playing it as intended. Now the biggest flaw this game has so far, are the bosses. While their design visually are impressive, the boss fights in themselves are atrocious to say the least. Again with the insanely fast attacks and some bosses bringing out a Malenia combo from Elden Ring, it gets boring really fast. And most bosses have a second or third phase. Not to mention that compared to other souls games, these bosses have an insane amount of HP for first playthrough. The gameplay doesn't get good or any fun until you find yourself about half-way through the story and putting in 10-15 hours depending on your pace. And it's a real shame because I was excited for this game and it does have an interesting setting/story set up for it, but the gameplay leaves so much to be desired. Lies of P did do a good thing though, it made me realize that Steelrising was at least was fun to play.Oh and if you want to do yourself a favor, go buy a good souls-like game like Lords of the Fallen (2023)

_childDocuments_.review: Lies of P is far and away the best of the genre, and it's only close with the greatest ones like Bloodborne and Sekiro.Where FromSoft lost their touch with Elden Ring, Lies of P delivers greatly: every fight is amazing, intuitive and difficult, but without artificial difficulty. The setting is amazing, the enemy variety is amazing. Every area is unique and introduces new enemies.The game is more linear than most other Soulslike games; which isn't necessarily a bad thing. You explore one area after another without any forking pathway through the game; but each areas has enough alternative paths and nooks containing some drops that they are interesting.Lies of P also manages to do something else FromSoft was never quite able to: it's balanced incredibly well. The game has both quick dodges (a la Bloodborne) and parries (a la Sekiro). Both defensive styles can be used on any build, and they are both very strong for any boss. Strenght, Dexterity and Advance (basically elemental weaponry) builds are very viable.The game also has a pretty unique weaponry system: you find handles and blades, which can be combined in almost any combination. The weight, moveset and weapon abilities are determined by each part, so that there are a multitude of possible combinations to try out to find the weapon you like the most.Overall it is definitely the best game of the genre for me and I am so excited for the DLC expansion that is announced for later this year!
_childDocuments_.name: Lies of P

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR : It's a great game, I definitely recommend it!Duration (first playthrough) : My first playthrough was just under 30 hours and you can definitely take it slower than that and explore every nook and cranny of every level.Overall :The combat is fun, the art style is well defined and entertaining and the story is an interesting reimagining of Pinocchio (the writer of which is Carlo Coloddi to whom the game is dedicated to) although there is more to it as you will discover.Soulslike :In terms of "soulslikes" it's linear but (mostly) interconnected like dark souls 1 or 3 and the combat is much like Sekiro where the ultimate strategy is a well timed block. As you progress through a level you start unlocking shortcuts that lead back to the original "bonfire" (stargazer) making it really satisfying to unlock everything and explore around.Weapons and upgrading :The weapon variety is great, and the system where you can mix the handle and blade of different weapons is a great twist on the standard weapon upgrade system. The scaling of your weapon goes off of the handle and so does the moveset but the blade determines the overall damage. Both parts have their own "special move" and you can combine them as you please. The game showers you in upgrade mats late game (and they are purchasable from an NPC) so you can try multiple weapons at max rank. At the end of my playthrough I had 3 max upgraded weapons.Bosses :There were very few points of frustration, mostly one specific gank bossfight but ultimately the fighting is fun and doesn't feel unfair. All bosses have 2 phases so don't get too comfortable. You will need to refight the first part of the boss to get to the 2nd one over and over. It sounds worse than it is. Usually, after a few runs, you are able to defeat the first boss pretty easily and move on to the "real challenge". Learning the moveset of the first phase will help a lot for the 2nd part as well.Performance :The game runs very well, there are no laggy areas or anything that breaks your PC. (I have a 3080 and all my PC parts are about 1 or 2 years old at this point - your milage may vary depending on your set up, of course)Give it a try while we wait for the Elden ring DLC!

_childDocuments_.review: I have completed new game plus once to try several builds and here is my conclusions.It is easier than people say. Yes, parry (prefect guard) is quite hard to do, but blocking and donging are good enough to handle everything. Story is quite interesting. Some advices:You need to have the best body parts in any type of build. Just keep the weight below 60% and never aim for lightwigth bonus (< 30% weight) because it gives you no viable bonuses. As for weapons - I used greatswords in first playthrough and daggers in second. Swords/blunts are not very different from greatswords, just a bit faster. But in NG+ you need faster attacks to survive. So I recommend you to use daggers. I used acidic dagger - it is very good for any type of enemies and you can get it quite early (chapter 3 if I remember correctly, maybe chapter 4). Don't bother with second weapon - it will be useless. Stats - health, weight and acid damage. With daggers you don't need too much stamina so don't invest much there.Arms - Fulminis (electric damage) is the best. Shield is good too. Sometimes you will want to use long range arm. Amultes - anything you like actually. I prefer damaging amulets and life regeneration for common enemies or physical resistance for bosses. Perks (heart improvements) - focus on healing charges and defence first, then attack, and utility at last.

_childDocuments_.review: The best non FromSoftware soulslike I've played.  It's even better than some of said company's own games.  Not just a ripoff, but it's got a soul of it's own.  From customizable weapons and organs (skills) to tight gameplay.  If you've never blocked/parried in a soulslike, this game will teach you why it's important.  Really a game changer IMO.The game is not without problems though.  It needs some weapon balancing and a map.  Speaking of the map, the levels are not quite up to the level of From's games, but it does an adequate job.  Staggers could be a little longer; even with added stagger you almost never get an opportunity for a fatal attack.The story is interesting with a good cast of characters.  FairytailxSteampunkxNoir.  Neowiz has a excellent blueprint for the future.  I could see them starting some sort of Metaverse.Worth the price.  Hoping there's some QoL improvements and DLC.The soundtrack is absolutely brilliant.  I would pay just to have that.

_childDocuments_.review: For context, I've played and finished almost every single Souls game, and a few other Soulslikes. I've never played a non-Fromsoft title before that holds up so well to direct comparison to their games. Normally it's always a "it's good, but it ain't Fromsoft". Lies of P requires no softening that way, it just holds its own.Lies of P is a brilliant fusion of deeply faithful, mindfully implemented adaptations of the core mechanics of the genre, and their own ambitious touches that bring their own flavor and expertise to the final result.It plays like an unholy fusion of Bloodborne, Sekiro, and little bit of Dark Souls, but the things that make it unique bring more to Lies of P than I really expected, with how closely it emulates Fromsoft's execution in a lot of other areas.It goes without saying the combat is excellent, as it must be for a stand-out Soulslike. The weapon movesets are a little small, especially if you compare them to Bloodborne, but you easily forget about that with how much of a focus on perfect guarding there is. (A parry equivalent, and like Sekiro, you are often incentivized to perfect guard long chains of attacks that are *brutally* satisfying to guard properly.) The step-dodge you do while locked on feels great, and the dodge attacks of the game often feel extremely satisfying, which adds a sense of speed to the combat even more intense than Bloodborne sometimes. But what really elevates and makes Lies of P truly unique is the aesthetic and atmosphere. The combination of steampunk/clockwork technology, the fashion, the fallen technological utopic environments, it all almost makes it feel like some kind of Bioshock Soulslike in some areas, which is a fusion I never knew I needed. There are a few misses on enemy and boss design I feel, but not enough to meaningfully lower my score.The music is also fantastic. The ability to play music tracks in game can be just lovely.Lies of P is an easy 9 or 9.5 out of 10 for me. I'll settle on a score after I complete a few more playthroughs, and also when I've finished the DLC. Can't wait for that!

_childDocuments_.review: Unironically the best souls gameEvery single fromsoft game has strengths and weaknesses, 2 steps forward and 2 steps back. Lies of P might not reach the highs of the world of dark souls 1 or build variety of elden ring but it does:- outclass every single souls game's combat (yes including sekiro's) - provide levels that are more interesting and varied than ds2 and ds3- provide a unique contained story and atmosphere that doesn't spend its entire lifetime referencing dark souls 1 (wow remember gwyn? remember ornstein and smough? remember artorias? remember solaire?)The biggest design limitation elden ring has shown is that you can only make bosses attack so fast and complex when your only defensive option is rolling or running away, which is why the future of this genre needs parries. Lies of P has a great blend of parries and dodging while letting blocking still be a viable way of learning fights, as you can rally back the chip damage you lose bloodborne style.This is not another "souls like", this is the first true souls competitor and I cannot wait for the DLC

_childDocuments_.review: Have to be honest here, Lies of P is a very conflicting experience.First: don't be fooled by the game's advertisements of marketing itself as a mostly souls-like. If anything, I find this game plays a lot more like Sekiro, which personally I think is a good thing. Perfect Guarding (this game's version of "deflecting" from Sekiro) is imperative to learn how to do, and it feels good for the most part. Some of the windows to perfect guard are a little too tight in my opinion, but folks diving into a game like this will expect the ramped up difficulty. Second: The way the world is built is beautiful and enthralling, beckoning you to learn more about it. The art team did a kick-ass job with this game; if you showed me this game before I knew anything about it and told me Fromsoft developed it, I would believe you. It also runs very well on my system, and my rig doesn't get too hot when running it.Okay, nothing but good things to say about this game so far, so why am I conflicted? I'm conflicted primarily because of the way boss fights are handled. Don't get me wrong, boss designs are incredible and all of them in the first half of the game are a good and fun challenge. The problem lies with bosses in the second half of the game. Naturally these bosses are tougher, but it feels artificially difficult when almost every boss has multiple phases, sometimes even having multiple phases across multiple forms! That's a lot of moves to memorize! I played all of the souls games, Sekiro, and Elden Ring multiple times; those games naturally have a lot of bosses, but I never felt exhausted like I do while playing Lies of P when discovering that a new boss has a second phase/form. Additionally, if you miss Perfect Guards, bosses will almost always follow up, making it even more punishing. Perfect Guarding is *required*, by the way; a significant amount of enemies have "Fury Attacks", which are essentially attacks that can *only* be Perfect Guarded. Even though your dodge has i-frames, you cannot dodge through fury attacks (which doesn't really bother me, it's just annoying to get up after getting pancake'd and then immediately having to prepare for another perfect guard.)Overall the game is good, but Lies of P throws some pretty brutal boss fights at you later in the game. If you decide to dive in, be prepared to spend a lot of time learning fights.

_childDocuments_.review: Heavily inspired by Bloodbornes aesthetic with Sekiro combat. I'm a huge From Software guy and rarely care to 100% games outside of them. I don't ever play "Soulslikes" as they never feel right to me. Something about this one in particular caught my eye and I'm happy it did. This felt like a new release from From Software, nothing felt off. I enjoyed the experience so much I got all the achievements and went through the game 3x to get all my +2 upgrades. Now I feel comfortable in leaving a review.Combat feels refined and developed, with a very unique and interesting weapon system. I enjoyed learning the bosses with the Twin Dragons Sword in particular, and never felt the need to cheese the game in anyway. It's a very rewarding feeling when you get the bosses down and perfect guard their attacks consistently. I enjoyed the similar mechanic from Sekiro and it felt flawless in this game too.Most of the bosses were simply amazing to fight, especially The Puppet King and Laxasia for me. I'm not a fan of the optional summons that can assist you with a boss but understand their purpose to help players that are struggling. It is a tough game after all!The music, in particular the records you obtain were 10/10 and truly helped make the game a memorable experience for me. I will continue to listen to these.The atmosphere gripped me. I loved the characters and felt very attached to P. I thought he was badass the whole way through. I truly enjoyed the dark spin on a fairy tale.Awaiting the DLC and whatever new game Neowiz cooks up. They've gained a supporter and believer in me and I will continue to play whatever they make after playing Lies of P. The secret ending left me very intrigued to see what's next. A masterpiece...Strong recommendation!

_childDocuments_.review: While FromSoftware's IP has spawned a smattering of clones and inspired many others, the most successful of which never travel too close to the sun. While games like Hollow Knight have seen great success with only light inspiration to great acclaim, others that attempt to mirror the quixotic appeal of Dark Souls and Bloodborne too closely end up feeling like cheap copies, whether or not that's fair to the game. In that sense Lies of P has an immense hurdle to climb, in that it will inevitably be compared to it's contemporaries that it's not shy about drawing inspiration from. I'm pleased to say that it excels, and even surpasses in some ways, even though it fails in others. The fundamentals are where the game shines brightest. While it's easiest to compare Lies of P to Bloodborne, it's combat system is a mishmash of Elden Ring/Dark Souls, Bloodborne and Sekiro. From Bloodborne comes the "hop" dodge and the "rally" system. While the traditional dodge roll is still present, the snappier Bloodborne hop is, and has served as a new demarcation point for faster, more aggressive enemies, and this is no less true in Lies of P. The rally system, which was Bloodborne's method of rewarding aggression by allowing the player to recuperate lost health through attacking, instead applies exclusively to chip damage acquired through blocking. The chip damage and stamina attrition acquired from blocking can be avoided entirely however from the "deflection" system inherited from Sekiro, in which a block timed to be raised just before you're struck negates stamina attrition, chip damage, and damages the opponents "posture". "Deflection" in Lies of P is dramatically more challenging that in Sekiro however, this is due to the removal of an "activation" period for raising your guard which made tapping the guard button a common tactic for procuring a deflection. Simply put, when you let go of the button, you have no parry frames, and you must allow your guard to return to a neutral state before raising it again in order to procure a deflection. This effectively removes the mashing element of deflection entirely, so that the player absolutely must know when the attack is about to connect, and the luck element is gone. I suspect the timing is also more strict, but without intricate knowledge of frame data I would merely be speculating. While deflection is often the most rewarding defensive option, as it accrues posture damage, avoids damage, and doesn't penalize your stamina the way a dodge would, it is also the most challenging due to the aforementioned changes, and it isn't *always* the best option. This is in part because breaking posture doesn't automatically segue into a riposte state the way it does in Sekiro and Elden Ring. Once enough posture damage is accrued, you must strike your foe with a charged heavy attack. This is a thoughtful change as landing said move requires so much time and commitment that often necessitates the kind of lateral positioning only a dodge can provide, but setting aside from that specific use case, just like in Elden Ring, basic attacks and especially heavy attacks accrue posture damage instead of being the sole province of deflections. The reason I take so much time to illustrate the nuances of Lies of P's combat system is to explain that each mechanic has been carefully considered to take every Fromsoft game's core combat mechanics, and intertwine them in a way that creates a better overall system than any individual Fromsoft game has accomplished. This is the game's strongest suite and the sole attribute that exceeds it's contemporaries even when others pale, so it deserves a proper hearing. More can be said about the game's "fable" system, the mixing weapon components, and the innate weapon skills, but for the sake of brevity I will simply say that Lies of P has a meaningful variety of weaponry without becoming too cluttered with hundreds of weapons only superficially different from one another in the way that Elden Ring was. Lies of P's second strongest suite is it's boss design. I don't profess to be the ultimate gamer, I have plenty of experience with the Fromsoft suite of games, and nonetheless plenty of the chapter bosses required dozens of attempts for me to complete. The difficulty curve was a smooth curve rising to a maddening crescendo. Although as a heavy weapons enthusiast, the "modular" combos where it's never entirely clear if I have a safe window to attack *can* seem cheap and unfair, I understand this is a cross I chose to bear by wielding a giant hunk of steel.Up until this point I've had nothing but good things to say about Lies of P. It's combat system, it's array of tools and weaponry, it's challenging pulse racing boss fights. With all that said I'm afraid that's where the game's strengths end, and the rest ranges from middling to outright bad. While the aesthetics as it relates to combat are superb, and the bosses are great, the common enemy design never graduates past the bland array of harmless mooks that meander around in modest groupings. These enemies are fine at the start of the game, as you're only gathering your bearings by that point, but by the time I'd gotten my footing they were nothing more than a conveyor belt of zombies marching into my charged heavy attacks. Outside of boss arenas, the only real challenge exists with "elite" or "miniboss" style enemies, but even they became helpless prey to my giant sawblade around the midway point of the game as each charged heavy attack sent them reeling.If there's a single red line I could draw that differentiates the Fromsoft games from their clones, it's the level design. Fromsoft at their best are experts at crafting winding interconnected areas that're in equal parts convincing, branching, challenging and varied. The level design in Lies of P checks absolutely none of those boxes. The most you can expect from Lies of P's level design is a solitary side path that dead ends or loops around to an earlier point, perhaps with a radiant ergo fragment or a resistance ampoule waiting at it's end. Each area a rectangle populated by a smattering of chattering puppet butlers wielding candlesticks or tacky looking petrification zombies bursting with turquoise goo, occasionally punctuated by an elite enemy who is the sole possible threat of death around any corner. Each time you might expect a level to meaningfully diverge paths you're met by an indestructible, impassable stack of luggage. Regardless, the streets of neo London still look beautiful replete with gothic architecture and enough tattered furnishings to make a convincing looking area. The metro stations, exhibition hall, opera house, and lower income neighborhood all look pleasing albeit very similar, and none offer much more in terms of actual navigation than what I've already explained. Occasionally you'll walk across narrow rafters and be ambushed by hiding foes, but never enough to make you mutter more than an "oh". This is truly the red line that distinguishes Fromsoft from it's aspirants. In Lies of P, much of the game is just a freeway that leads to your ultimate destination: a boss arena. Anywhere outside of Lies of P's Neo London is totally bereft of any creative vision. The muddy rural swamps, caves and the lategame aztec temple like structure could be lifted from any JRPG in recorded history and nobody would tell the difference. Around the time you revisit Neo London ravaged by earthquakes and strange ergo infused formations, fight recycled bosses infused with petrification to augment their moveset, and navigate a remote island temple that's comprised entirely of sandstone brick rectangular rooms and ramshackle wood structures it becomes clear that the developers started to run out of steam around the latter part of the game, but thankfully they have enough to give the game a good sendoff with 3 great bossfights at the tail section. Overall, an easy recommend albeit it's flaws.

_childDocuments_.review: Quick and dirty review to show support for the devs.Completed the game once and I’m now on the way finishing NG+ for achievements. Was outstanding for me, I had no hiccups, framerate was stable all the way, no crashes.Even on the Steam Deck, the performance is great (around 60 fps, depending on the settings) and the game feels very optimized. I love the fact they used basically the fairy tale of Pinocchio and turned it into a dark fantasy world.Everything from architecture to the Belle Époque inspired props and clothing as well as weapons and lighting is spot on. You see victorian boulevards, industrial workshops, beautiful opera house, ghastly swamps and claustrophobic arcades.The story is clearly communicated   ambiguous lore as its common in most From Software games. Lies of P is more in the vein of, say Sekiro for example.You get a couple of cutscenes, plenty of background story and comprehensible quests.It’s basically the story of Pinocchio but with so much own ideas that it could be a complete original plot.I also love the fact that when you lie in the game (you get different options throughout the game) – which is a very human reaction - you more and more become a human yourself, just like in the original story.There’s also a couple of twists and NPC stories that quite hit me in the feels.Precise controls tho, I had to get used to at first.Combat is satisfying and perfect blocking or parrying is a core element of the game.Again, comparable to Sekiro where you use (perfect) parry to break the poise of enemies but with much tighter frames.If done properly, you can even break the boss’ weapons this way, reducing their damage and reach.Dodging is tight also and can be used but, better to adapt the parrying system early on as it’s the reliable way of this game.You also can get a special buff that allows perfect block for every block you do for a limited amount of time to help breaking the poise of bosses. Most of the bosses are very well designed and fit very well in the world and are fun to learn and fight.Other later bosses in late game are unfortunately a bit not-so-great () and feel straight ridiculous.Had to use the Spectre a couple of times (AI assist, similar to spirit ashes summons in Elden Ring).Other bosses are somewhat easy but I think that depends on personal preference and skill.Throwables are a viable option too.This can be a curse and a blessing at the same time. I like the linear and tight design of the game, especially after the open-world-games galore recently, but I would like a bit more exploration nonetheless. Some ppl really like it - I personally don’t. Got used to but it’s more a PITA.. like in every game I think this mechanic doesn’t contribute in any meaningful way.I recommend this game for fans of Bloodborne, Sekiro and the likes of, as it’s  influenced by these games.

_childDocuments_.review: Lies of P – 8/10World-Building and Atmosphere (8.5/10)Strength: Lies of P leans heavily into the gothic, industrial aesthetic, drawing clear inspiration from Bloodborne and Sekiro, while also nodding to its Pinocchio roots. The world of Krat feels eerie and mysterious, with its dark streets, twisted machinery, and haunting atmosphere. There’s an impressive amount of detail in the environment that sets the tone for the game.Critique: However, while the world is beautifully designed, it doesn’t have the same interconnectedness that makes Miyazaki’s worlds feel so alive. In Dark Souls or Bloodborne, every area feels organically woven into the next, creating a sense of discovery and cohesion. Lies of P feels more disjointed, with areas that, while visually stunning, don’t always feel like they belong to a larger, connected world. The level design lacks the tight-knit, maze-like brilliance that we’ve come to expect from FromSoftware titles.Combat and Mechanics (8/10)Strength: Combat in Lies of P is sharp, visceral, and undeniably influenced by the Soulsborne series. The parry system and the emphasis on timing is directly comparable to Sekiro and Bloodborne. It requires precision, forcing players to learn enemy patterns and strike when the moment is right. The weapon customization system is a neat touch, allowing players to experiment with different combinations to suit their playstyle.Critique: While the combat is engaging, it often feels like a watered-down version of Miyazaki’s best work. The parrying mechanics feel a bit clunky compared to the tight, responsive system in Sekiro. The combat, while challenging, sometimes feels like it’s trying too hard to emulate Soulsborne titles without truly innovating. The enemy variety is limited, with many encounters feeling repetitive after a while. Miyazaki’s games always manage to keep combat fresh by introducing new mechanics or enemies at the right time, whereas Lies of P struggles to maintain that balance.Boss Fights (7.5/10)Strength: The bosses in Lies of P are impressive in terms of design. Their grotesque, mechanical designs fit the game’s dark, twisted world perfectly. Some boss fights, like the King of Puppets, are visually stunning and serve as memorable, tense challenges.Critique: However, the boss fights lack the variety and depth seen in FromSoftware titles. Many of the fights boil down to memorizing patterns and perfecting parries, but without the intricate lore or emotional weight behind the battles that Miyazaki often excels at. In Dark Souls or Bloodborne, bosses often feel like living parts of the world’s lore, with their defeat carrying narrative weight. In Lies of P, while they’re visually striking, the bosses can feel soulless, as if they exist purely as gameplay challenges rather than integral parts of the story. They also fall into predictable attack patterns, which diminishes the tension after a few attempts.Story and Narrative (7/10)Strength: Lies of P introduces an interesting twist on the Pinocchio story, with a darker, more dystopian take on the classic tale. The idea of lying as a mechanic that influences the world and the character’s growth is unique and intriguing.Critique: While the story has potential, it doesn’t hit the narrative depth we’ve come to expect from Soulsborne games. In Bloodborne or Dark Souls, the lore is rich, layered, and often hidden beneath cryptic dialogue and environmental storytelling, leaving players to piece it together. Lies of P tries to replicate this, but its lore feels shallow in comparison. There’s a lack of emotional engagement with the characters, and the narrative doesn’t feel as mysterious or captivating as it could be. It’s a game that’s trying to be deep, but it ends up being surface-level in its storytelling.Innovation (7/10)Strength: The lying system is a novel mechanic that adds an interesting twist to the decision-making process. It adds layers to the protagonist’s morality and offers some variation in how the story unfolds, even if it’s somewhat underutilized. The weapon crafting system is another nice touch, offering players some customization in combat.Critique: But outside of these small innovations, Lies of P doesn’t do much to stand out from the shadow of Miyazaki’s influence. It feels like a follower rather than a game that’s breaking new ground. Where Miyazaki constantly pushes boundaries—whether it’s with the Posture system in Sekiro or the seamless open world of Elden Ring—Lies of P feels like it’s playing it safe. It mimics the surface-level elements of a Soulsborne game without truly understanding what makes those games great on a deeper level.Pacing and Progression (7.5/10)Strength: The game does a decent job of keeping players engaged with a steady flow of upgrades and new abilities. The difficulty curve, while steep, feels fair, and players are rewarded for their perseverance.Critique: However, the pacing can feel uneven at times. The game tends to drag in certain areas, with long stretches of enemy gauntlets that don’t add much to the overall experience. Where Miyazaki’s games excel at keeping the player hooked with carefully curated moments of tension and release, Lies of P lacks that ebb and flow, leading to moments of frustration rather than satisfaction. The progression feels more grindy than rewarding, with certain parts of the game dragging on longer than necessary without meaningful progression in the story or combat systems.Replayability (8/10)Strength: With multiple endings and the option to explore different choices through the lying system, there’s definitely incentive for multiple playthroughs. The various builds and weapon combinations also offer some variety in gameplay, giving players reason to experiment.Critique: Despite these options, Lies of P doesn’t have the same replayability appeal as Soulsborne games. The lack of meaningful build diversity and limited enemy variety means that, once you’ve beaten the game, there’s less incentive to dive back in for another round. In contrast, Dark Souls or Elden Ring offer near infinite replayability thanks to their rich build systems, intricate world designs, and ever-changing metas.Final Verdict: 8/10Lies of P is a solid Soulslike that offers a unique twist on the genre with its Pinocchio-inspired world and the lying mechanic, but it’s clear that the game is heavily influenced by the works of Hidetaka Miyazaki. While it captures some of the magic of Soulsborne titles, it falls short in key areas like boss variety, narrative depth, and combat precision. It’s a game that wears its influences proudly but struggles to forge its own identity.For fans of the genre, Lies of P will scratch that challenging, gothic action itch, but it never quite reaches the brilliance of its inspirations. If you’re looking for a true evolution of the Soulslike formula, you might walk away feeling like Lies of P is more of an imitation than a revolution. That said, for what it offers—a gritty, mechanically challenging experience—it’s still a fun and rewarding journey, just not a game that redefines the genre the way Miyazaki has done so many times before.

_childDocuments_.review: Picked it up because of the autumn sale, based on other reviews. This is definitely an Elden Ring-style HUD with the combat speed of something like Bloodborne. Very much a "get gud" game, and when you get combat right it feels. So. F***ing. Good. Art style is also awesome; like a marriage of Bioshock's art deco with Victorian steam punk, Lovecraftian horror. I don't know how the designers made a bunch of really disparate ideas and themes come together so fluidly with a Pinocchio story in a Souls-like game, but it's phenomenally done and absolutely scratches the twink-murder itch finishing a souls game leaves in your heart.Edit: Played about 20hr more of it and I still love it. @Devs: Major QOL improvement could be made on the P-Organ screen making the select system free-move with the joystick instead of grid/cell-based. It's really clunky and awful to navigate as it is.Edit again: I'm to end game bosses/areas and the way they managed difficulty gets cheap. It's the trap many Souls games fall into where instead of making bosses require consistent, great skills, they just let the bosses cheat. Whether that's making them meatshields, energizer stamina bunnies, impenetrable poise, or whatever, it's lame and cheap and having to constantly cheese minibosses (because you sneeze and there's a miniboss/elite at the end), it's putting a negative slant on a game that's been so incredible up until this point.

_childDocuments_.review: Here we are. We finally get a souls-like not only worthy of being called great, but arguably surpassing its inspirations in more ways that matter. The combat system is basically flawless. Whereas Jedi Survivor went more into the direction of Devil May Cry, being something in-between that, soulsborne and Sekiro. Lies of P stays much closer to the latter two, evolving upon them and ultimately surpassing them with flying colors. The combat feels visceral and brutal, just like a robot's imbued with super strength should. The parrying and deflecting feels snappy, yet more tactical than in Sekiro due to being forced to commit to attacks. I've seen people complain about that, but I think it's really a matter of overall game design and how both of those end up mutually serving one another.For the most part it succeeds in this endeavor. The puppets are simply amazing foes. They are easy to read, telegraph their attacks properly, and have a metric ton of variation in design. Sadly the same cannot be said about the carcass enemies which all blend together into a giant green blob. All of it ultimately culminating into the swamp thing boss fight which is just atrocious no matter which way you look at it... Because it really doesn't matter, as from every angle it looks like a green blot on your screen. This is where the problems with the game start to appear. For some reason only half the game is about fighting puppets. Why? Please tell me why, Mx. game developer person. Puppets are simply perfect and the game should have more of them, not less. It really tells you something that almost all good boss fights are puppets. All other bosses just suck with the sole exception of the Walker.Now, later Pinocchio gets to fight the alchemists which are okay, but nowhere near as good as the puppets. But they're at least tolerable. Which makes this fortunately to be not such a complete disaster. Otherwise I'd just implore you to quit playing past the opera house. Speaking of which, this part of the game is tiny, and the puppet enemies there are incredible, why don't we get more of them later in the game? Why not have broken versions of the opera singer puppets be in the swamp? And speaking of swamp levels, Lies of P somehow manages to pull it off even here. Just for that alone the game would get my glowing recommendation. Yes, I'm looking angrily at you, Dark Souls 3 right now.The mixing and matching hilts and blades mechanic is unfortunately more of a gimmick than anything else. But that is perhaps due to the fact that there isn't that many useful combinations, and the community has already figured out the meta, Such as the wrench head and the police baton handle being the go to for motivity (strength) builds. Nevertheless the weapons in Lies of P vary from good to great. It's just that some weapons just clearly outclass others.When it comes to meta in general: stagger damage is everything. Especially in NG+ and beyond, for a very simple reason that stagger remains constant, This means that you'll stagger an enemy in the same manner and within the same time frame regardless of how much HP buff it gets from NG+. That's why I personally didn't bother to deflect or perfect block. The rewards for doing so are just not worth it, especially for the motivity builds which I prefer. I suppose red attacks are worth deflecting because doing that incurs massive stagger damage, But even then I never bothered, I did however learn to perfect block about a third of incoming blows just by playing the game a lot. So definitely don't get discouraged by all the "this game is too difficult" cries. It's really not. Even for perfect blocks, Jedi Survivor on Grand Master difficulty has infinitely more unforgiving parry timings.Sekiro is a much more difficult game in my opinion, simply because it doesn't allow for a variety of approaches. Lies of P does in spades. Even this game's prosthetic (here legion) arms are much more useful. Wreak havoc on carcasses with flamberge and absolutely demolish bosses with the puppet string. Also the game is much more liberal with grinding than even the Souls games. Multiple stats are useful to max out, And the ergo (souls) cost for doing so evens out past level 100 or so. Also you get a ton of ergo in NG+ even without grinding. The items too are extremely useful, especially the cluster grenade and the put shot. The former because it does heavy stagger damage and the latter because it lets one put an enemy (bosses included) into a fatal attack position from a distance. I like that a lot, the items in Dark Souls 3 were nigh useless. So why even have them in the game if that's going to be the case?Graphically the game is stunning. It's unbelievable that a moderately staffed studio could produce something so beautiful and with AAA fidelity no less. Even if sometimes you do see some rough edges if you squint, but that's unsurprising. This is not EA. It's honestly a miracle what they managed to achieve here both artistically and technically. The game also runs flawlessly and hasn't crashed a single time in my 100+ hours of playing,The atmosphere is something else. As someone who can't stand most things French except for the food, I was enamored with the world (and yes, the French rendition of Someday is perfect and the best song in the game which already has a lot of great songs as it is). The city of Krat in particular. There's this incredible lyricism and humanity emanating from every corner of it and every character who really start growing on you by the mid point of the game. The last game I experienced that feeling at was in Metro Exodus. Both games are about being truly human, and not the parodies of ourselves puppeteered by the peer pressure, by the algorithm, by authority figures, by what have you. It poses the question of what makes one truly human, and answers it beautifully, putting the original tale of Pinocchio on its head. I do love a good subversion always, and there's plenty to subvert in Carlo Collodi's original, especially looking at it through the eyes of a 21st century dweller.Lies of P is a masterpiece. You can trust me on this, because I don't use it often, much less lightly. I can't wait for where the team goes next with it. If the DLC is going to be a 40k Leagues Under the Sea affair I think I'll just die from happiness on the spot. If we get a soulsborne version of the Wizard of Oz we're basically set at that point (wink to those who completed the game). And if Alice in the Wonderland finishes the trifecta, then I'll die a happy woman (again). Go buy it, what are you waiting for?

_childDocuments_.review: This is what a souls type game should strive to be, other companies that aim to make souls-clones should look at this game for reference. Not only does it actually polish the gameplay of the fights, it actually aims to tell a good story while also adding unique gameplay besides your weapon build. Not only that, but it breaks the norm of being your traditional dodge and roll attack soulsborne formula by allowing the player to parry every single move if they choose to.THAT is what makes this game stand out from others, and honestly, it's a breath of fresh air that Fromsoft themselves should take pointers at too. Sekiro was my favorite game of theirs, but it was a shame they didn't adapt that gameplay mechanic in Elden Ring, and Lies of P proves that you can have the best of both worlds and make it good too.I'm excited for the DLC that they have in store, only downside I could possibly give this game is the fact that it has Denuvo which will memory leak your game at times which is annoying.

_childDocuments_.review: Ahhhhhh YES, this was such a good game...it scratched that itch that Sekiro left behind so long ago for me. Some brutal, punishing moments for sure but an overall very satisfying experience from beginning to end.Amazing story, fantastic combat, outstanding world design...the game does hold your hand a little though unlike other souls-likes where you have to figure things out yourself or unravel a cryptic mystery...its actually harder to miss things simply because there's a marker that appears when there's something to do or someone to interact with, but that's all entirely subjective as to how you feel about that type of stuff. I didn't mind personally, just something to mention I suppose.Loved the "build your own weapon" system where you can dismantle weapons you find or buy (excluding special weapons) and mix'n'match handles and blades. The handle determines the style of attacks while the blade determines things like damage and a number of other variables...I have to admit though, having jumped into this just after the Wo Long Collab, you start off with Guan Yu's Glaive that's classed as a special weapon and feels EXTREMELY nice to use, though it isn't overpowered and you can't really upgrade it until way later in the game.There's no armour in the typical sense of like helmets, chest pieces, etc...you get parts that determine armour, weight, resistances and so forth, whilst your visual appearance is entirely cosmetic and you'll unlock a few different outfits as you go. They are unfortunately limited to full body outfit, hat and glasses so no real deep "fashion souls" thing going here if that's what you're all about.An all in all very interesting experience, not at all what I had initially expected and a great addition to anyone's souls-like collection!Now...about that post-credits scene...

_childDocuments_.review: I've played several souls-like games and have found just about all of them disappointing compared to Fromsoft. Seeing this game, I suspected it to be the same story, but Payday 3 screwed up their servers. After a quick refund, I spent my money here. And my goodness, I could hug Starbreeze for being such royal screw ups! This hit the souls itch that only Fromsoft could scratch! Make no mistake, the game is challenging. Despite having 2,000 hours in the Dark Souls/Elden Ring franchise, I still got stuck on a few bosses for an hour at a time. But they were hard in the right way. Making mistakes felt like your fault. You saw the attack, you attempted to parry or dodge it, and you screwed up the timing. The vast majority of attacks were also not one-shot, or death combos. This means a death was a result of many mistakes in a given fight. This truly has been quite a treat. From the environment, weapon selection, puppet upgrades, and minor secrets. This is a world that will leave you wanting more. Fromsoft better keep an eye on Neowiz. If they continue to produce quality products like this, they will have a serious competitor on their hands. Seriously, buy the game now. Stop reading this review. For you souls and Sekiro fans, just do it! Worth every penny

_childDocuments_.review: Updated Review: Post update to the game I find the experience way more enjoyable.  There are certainly still some things I do not personally enjoy, but overall the games functions better after the newest update.  A couple changes were made to bosses health levels and a huge change was made to multi fable bar consuming attacks - they now have hyper armor.  Long and short of it is, you can enjoy this game if you do not play it at all like other souls games.  The mash up of different systems and general resource economy leans into a very weird rhythm and a heavy reliance on consumable items.Original Review: A beautiful disaster would be the title of my review.  By all accounts there is a lot that someone could love here.  Visually and thematically the game is awesome, but the shortcomings run to deep to the core for me to consider this an engaging and balanced experience.My personal issues are very specific to the combat, the level design, and the enemy types.  The unfortunate truth is that this game is an amalgamation of every souls game into one and it is obvious that the developers wanted people to feel nostalgic when playing.  But the reason that each of the previous souls games kept their system separate and made moderate changes along the way was because these are almost always mutually exclusive and opposing ideas that do not mesh well together.  Dark souls would not be Dark souls if there was no parrying, only blocking and deflecting.  Bloodborne would not be the masterpiece that it still is today if it were an open world game with shields and 500 weapons to choose.Lies of P threw everything souls into a bucket and tweeked 1-2 things into sort of new ideas, with extremely varied results.  There are high highs, and very low lows.  My experience may differ from others, granted, by the vast majority of time I spent in the game was pretty low and uneventful.  Most of the levels are a drab and dull trudge through typical souls nonsense implemented in a really tropey way.  Want to walk across that super thin wooden board to your destination, well ahve fun with dodging 3-5 enemies who have no eyeballs but can somehow throw homing projectiles at you from across the room.  Want to deal with them with some cool ranged weapons...well...you have none...or you ran out of ammo for it and had to use the insanely unbalanced consumable economy to keep yourself armed.Bosses range from 2 button encounters, to...what the hell is going on I literally can't predict a single portion of their moveset because even calling it a moveset is being generous.  The camera is typically the actual boss fight, but that's nothing new, but also an area where these developers seemingly have no interest in making changes to the formula.  Let's shove an enemy that takes up 300% of your FOV in a room smaller than a new york apartment and give them a charging attack...(slow clapping in the distance).I personally cannot recommend this as a game for anyone who wants to enjoy a souls like game.  Most of the systems here are derivative and unbalanced, you are shoehorned into a playstyle rather than having any freedom, and you will ultimately spend most of your playthrough sprinting through bogus levels to find the next stargazer just to move the story along because somehow that is the part that is intriguing and worthwhile?!

_childDocuments_.review: After trying Demon Souls, Dark Souls and Bloodbourne and loving them all but struggling to get to even 1/3 of those games finally a game that just clicks difficulty and progression wise. It has the best of Souls and Bloodbourne, neither being as aggressive and fast as Bloodbourne nor as methodical and stiff as either Demon or Dark Souls. Amazing art direction, sound design, pitch perfect soundtrack and level design that matches From Software's genius whilst being less cryptic and open ended (a plus on the first playthrough for me at least).Story is pretty good with lore granted the same attention to detail and love as From Software games, despite not reaching the same heights. It is hard as nails and according to most people harder than most From Software gams but so far I have found it easier and with quicker progression than either Dark Souls or Bloodbourne.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is beautiful and has nice emotional story but you risk getting your first impression killed by horrible last segment of the game that is nothing but boring maze crowded with unnecessary encounters at every turn, after the main plot twist had already been revealed. It's like if a good movie kept going for another 2 hours after where it should have ended and all your emotion would have died out by the time you see the titles.I don't know why some people say this game is like Bloodborne, when it's actually a Sekiro that happens to look like Bloodborne, as the game prioritizes parrying over dodging, doesn't have guns as dedicated parrying tools, and has straightforward storytelling. But, unlike Sekiro, it has a normal character and gear progression so at least you have motivation to explore the game world for the new gear. There are a few good bosses here, but there was no reason at all to give every single one of them two health bars.With that being said, it's a very nice game, but it shouldn't have pushed some things to the limits in an attempt to stand out from other souls-likes, which outweighed the impression of the game's main assets, its world and its story.

_childDocuments_.review: Most definitely the best 3D Soulslike game made thus far. The level of polish this game has is incredible. Not one crash and barely any stuttering throughout my entire experience; something that should be the norm, but is so rare to see nowadays. Gotta congratulate the dev team for releasing such an incredible game this year. Definitely worthy of accolades.On my first playthrough, got the true ending for the game and it is definitely amazing, and giving us a glimpse at what is to come in the sequel which I am so stoked about. Now about the game.The basic synopsis of Lies of P: You play as a puppet that was just awakened to fight back against the Puppet Frenzy while discovering the dark truth hidden within this city, and learning what it means to be human. The game play, is simply put, a mixture of Bloodborne and Sekiro. From Bloodborne comparison, It has a trick weapon like system that has you mix and match weapon heads with handles however you like to figure out your move set preference. Personally, I did not use the system that much since most of the weapons I used later on were already fine as is, especially some of the boss weapons you get that are very fun to use. As for the Sekiro part, it is the guard parry system, which is also the core combat mechanic in this game that you have to master in order to beat the game effectively. Dodging is there and useful, but the parry system is really a must use, especially when you can break enemy weapons, including bosses to make them deal reduced damage, which is a really freaking cool expansion on the mechanic, adding even more reason to train yourself to get good at it.The general gameplay is very smooth soulslike combat you come to expect in a game that takes obvious inspiration from Dark Souls/ Bloodborne, where you have your wide variety of weapons, status effects, and special moves that use up a Fable Art gauge that each weapon have their own type of move set. The combat feels really polished, with barely any bugs to see.The story is pretty straightforward and clear to understand, especially when this game has a more up front storyline, unlike the From Soft games having it hidden. There are some nice twists and turns in the story kept me engaged from start to finish, especially with the solid voice acting throughout. Sophia being my favorite female character and the other being a particular character you get to meet later if you do things right that really stole the show for me with how devious they are.The level design is quite amazing with plenty of shortcuts leading back to the Stargazer, this game's form of Bonfire resting station. The time it takes get from Stargazer to the shortcut back to it feels really good. I do not recall having situations where I felt desperately needing the Stargazer, I would always get it to available at a comfortable pace throughout the game, which is really impressively done. This game is not a fully interconnected world, but mini areas that all do connect nicely with one another at times. There are going to be obvious comparisons between this and Lords of the Fallen since they released really close to each other. By far, Lies of P is the better game overall. I got immensely frustrated with LOF so much that I just wanted to finish the game to be done with it; have no interest in ever playing Lords again, but Lies of P I am getting very tempted to do another playthrough to collect the stuff I missed, which says a lot to the quality and fun factor Lies has over LOF.Speaking of playing again, when you first beat the game, do not start NG+ right away or you will miss quite a few things in the post game.Absolutely recommend Lies of P if you are itching for a new very good Soulslike to play or want a taste of what a Soulslike game is like.

_childDocuments_.review: From the moment I plunged into the enigmatic world of Lies of P, I was utterly swept away. Over the course of this riveting journey, I found myself captivated by its meticulously designed gameplay, the narrative, the intricate details accompanying it, and its highly intuitive controls. However, what really accentuated the experience was its sublime artistry and aesthetics, creating an immersive atmosphere that kept me glued to the screen.The gameplay of Lies of P is an inventive tour de force that streamlined my interaction with the game. It seamlessly blends shortcuts into a cohesive and addictive whole. As someone who often struggles navigating twists and turns even with maps, I never found myself lost in Krat.  Every battle was charged with an undeniable tension that had my heart racing as I maneuvered through the darkened and bloody/oily streets of Krat. I never once got tired of any of the mobs.  Boss fights were hard but not impossible.  A lot of souls-likes think difficulty should be added in such an obtuse and annoying way, but Lies of P was a breath of fresh air giving the mobs and bosses unique move sets.  None of my builds were all of a sudden obsolete because someone was "immune" to something.The story — oh, what a story! Exquisitely narrated and artistically nuanced, the tale of the protagonist, puppet C, in a dystopian setting is breathtaking. Lies of P masterfully intertwines its story with the gameplay, cohesively connecting each development and discovery in a distinct and profoundly emotional manner. It's a compelling narrative that does more than tell a tale; it questions the essence of humanity and lures you into a spiderweb of lies and truths that are sure to keep you riveted.The myriad of minute, yet impactful details enthralled me. Whether it was the haunting tune of a distant phonograph, the etched anguish on the faces of the city's tormented residents, or the gradual transformation of C; all these elements converged into an astounding demonstration of meticulous craftsmanship that truly distinguished Lies of P.The cherry on top was the ease of controls. Intuitive and comfortable, the game’s interface makes handling the puppet protagonist effortless. The controls are well-suited to the game’s design, cleverly simplifying complex actions and making the gaming experience a satisfying one. Both experienced players and novices will find navigating this dystopian universe highly enjoyable.However, the real feast comes from the aesthetic aspect of the game. Lies of P excels in creating a captivating atmosphere, that while could be overly dark and grim was still awe inspiring. Each environment is a beautifully illustrated portrait of despair and decay that manages to captivate despite its inherent sadness. Paired with a hauntingly melodic soundtrack echoing the dread and hope of our puppet protagonist, the game reaches sublime heights.In conclusion, Lies of P is a must-play title for any gaming enthusiast. Its unique amalgamation of horror, action and RPG elements, coupled with an artistically melancholic aesthetic and an engaging narrative, is nothing short of the highest performance in the orchestra of gaming today. As you venture into Krat, be ready to immerse yourself in a deeply immersive and stimulating experience that is Lies of P. I guarantee, you won't be able to tear yourself away.

_childDocuments_.review: Finally finished the game, took me 50+ hours for some reason - this included doing everything that's possible, messing around with different weapons, and most bosses solo. Amazing game and brilliant effort for a first-try Soulslike from a new studio.The list of things done well will be probably very long, but here we go:+ great atmosphere+ fun combat: fast, responsive, with proper feedback and no strange hitboxes+ very good weapon variety keeping things fresh, with each weapon being unique in some way+ good enemy variety, new enemies introduced even 1h before you're done with the game+ very cool idea with weapon altering mechanism (handle + blade separated), allowing for interesting combinations+ consistent difficulty, game is kicking your ass even at the end, elite enemies are no joke+ great boss fights: memorable, difficult, but not being cheap at the same time+ no 'Lost Izalith' areas: attention to detail was kept until the end+ fantastic optimization, 4K & 100fps++ nice music+ surprisingly interesting story+ good writing+ interesting characters+ side quests are not as cryptic as in From games and actually doable without a guide+ some serious C&C that influences the ending+ decent character development with different amulets / P-Organs / Legion Arms+ very good level design at times (not consistent though)+ very polished product, both in terms of overall attention to detail, no bugs and optimization+ tons of references to Bloodborne / Dark Souls / Sekiro; the guys clearly played all those and knew what makes the game goodHard to point out anything bad to be honest, maybe some minor stuff:- game is pretty linear, you need to progress chapter by chapter- 3 of the Legion Arms seem to have limited usability- some of the fights will require you to 'git gud'- game may be too difficult for people with poor reflexes (at times)9/10, definite GotY for me. The game is leagues above your typical Souls clone, the only non-From game that can stand the comparison is Nioh 2. I had more fun playing this than Dark Souls 2 to be honest. Must play for anyone who liked Bloodborne / Sekiro / Dark Souls.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall: Good game, but overpriced at $60-70. Worth closer to $30-40 bucks, so wait for a price drop/sale. It's much shorter than Elden Ring, which often goes on sale for cheaper than this game.Combat: it's a mixture of Bloodborne and Sekiro, mostly Sekiro. Proper combat in this game will see you learning attack patterns and blocking accordingly, but unlike Sekiro you can dodge most attacks (with some exceptions). You can get by with dodging for the most part, but it's better to learn to parry as you'll encounter plenty of enemies that chain attacks to punish dodge spam.As for enemy design, it's mixed. Some bosses have clean, consistent and easy to read movesets that make for fun parrying. Others have inconsistent or poorly telegraphed patterns. On average, most if not all bosses have at least 1 or 2 attacks that are poorly telegraphed, which leads to a lot of frustration. Sekiro remains the gold standard for boss design.As an aside, I felt there was an issue with the hitboxes several of the bosses, most notably Laxasasia and Simon. When they preform large swing attacks while the player is close up, their arms are included as part of the hit box. This means that on the swing, the boss will hit you with their arm first, then their weapon. It's very weird and doesn't feel good to parry.Level design: aesthetics aside, level design is fairly basic. You'll encounter the usual shortcuts to earlier areas here and there, but there wasn't anything particulalry standout in terms of how levels are laid out. One thing to note is that the level designers seemed very fond of baiting the player. Typically, when you go down a long-narrow passageway, there will be an enemy or item at the end of it. If you rush to kill the enemy/grab the item, you'll usually be ambushed by an enemy waiting out of sight. This isn't a bad thing in itself, but it happened enough times throughout the game to become noticeable.Art design/ Aesthetics: very good. The artists went to work creating a city from the Belle-Epoque era of Europe. There are several interior areas that perfectly resemble the irl interiors of French palaces. There were times where set design became redundant or dull, most noticeably in the leadup to the final boss area. Not awful per say, but I feel more could've been done to make those areas stand out.Music: it's good. Not much to add beyond that.

_childDocuments_.review: Feel exactly like a Fromsoft game (controls, level design). Well optimized, no major bugs. (Can zip, used by speedrunners).Gameplay Mechanics:* Weapon building. Take a blade from one weapon, handle from another - PPAP. Moveset comes from handles, so you can stab stuff with a gigantic axe as if it's a rapier if you want* Blades and handles have unique special abilities each* Has a gadget arm like Sekiro offering different additional offensive/defensive abilities with limited use.* Parry (perfect guard) mitigates all damage, faster recovery and inflicts damage to enemy posture bar* Block with partial damage mitigation (amount depends on weapon)* Lost health from blocking can be recovered by attacking (amount can be increased through a talent tree)* Enemies can be broken through attacking and perfect guarding, opening them up for finisher attacks* Player character has no poise, every attack staggers/interrupts.* Talent tree allowing to customize character to fit your playstyle/boss encounter (respec becomes available)* Leveling through use of ergo (souls) with stat increase of your choice* Challenging boss encounters requiring study of their abilities. Not a lot of cheese options, getting gud requiredp.s. above and below opinions/"jokes" suck :)

_childDocuments_.review: This is a review that I thought would have been 100% positive but it is more a mixed review unfortunately and that will be explained in length in this review.To start with though the first 8 chapters or about 75% of the game is fantastic! I loved every second playing this games.The level design is amazing! The developers did an amazing job with this game when it came to level design as everything flowed smoothly with great interconnecting corridors.The bosses are also top notch! (with some exception, see further on) The arena design and the design of the bosses themselves visually were stunning.And overall the combat in this game is snappy, rapid and feels awesome! Honestly this is my favourite (for the most part) souls-like that isn't made by From-Software.Honestly if the game was just these first 8 chapters, I would 100% recommend this game and I would be replaying it over and over again... But unfortunately this is not the case and so we get onto what I hated, the last 25% of the game!The story as well is fantastic! The main story is very well paced, each character is unique and has their own personality. Also the side quests are great as well as they play directly into the "Humanity" system at play in this game.As you play the game decisions you make, the side quests you complete and the music you listen to will increase your "Humanity" and this is how you get the different endings. I loved this system as it was mostly hidden but it felt like a good incentive to go a do a lot of the side stuff in the game.Here we go...Near to the end of Chapter 9 is where I would say the game just went off the rails and ultimately became really bad!Chapter 9's second to last boss () is one of the worst bosses in the entire game! With a move set that gives zero room to manoeuvre and also next to no way of dodging.Then Chapter 10 which is so short that I don't understand why it is even in the game at all!And now Chapter 11. This entire chapter is full of recycled enemies from other chapters in the game, it introduces nothing new and the entire chapter feels like a time waste simply to pad out the playtime.On top of that, we now have the camera breaking throughout Chapter 11. Below is how many times I had the camera break for :	- 26 --> Total Times	- 3 --> Boss Fight ()	- 1 --> Boss Fight ()	- Infinite --> Completely Broken Going Down Elevator After Boss Fight ()	- 2 --> Boss Fight ()Honestly from the end of Chapter 9 all the way through to the end of the Chapter 11, felt like it was designed and built by a completely different team who had absolutely no idea what they were doing and had zero imagination.Now initially this review was going to be a "Not Recommend" but having thought about it more and more, this is more a mixed/neutral review and overall it does lean just enough into "Recommend" but I am disappointed into the game overall thanks to the last 25%.
