_childDocuments_.review: For a short game (I beat it in 1 hour) the game is beautiful and has beautiful music. The story of two people in love is told here, in a very different way than I have seen before! The puzzles are simple yet creative, and I was engrossed in the whole thing and didn't notice how I finished it.I highly recommend playing it yourself!
_childDocuments_.name: Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery

_childDocuments_.review: This was a beautiful gaming experience, the music and relaxing atmosphere really soothed my mood and set a tone for my day. So, developers, thank you for that. Only note that I may leave is a very obvious one, I wish we could have had more say in the storytelling, as the player, but nothing that soured my play-through. The ending was unexpected but still nice. I would say definitely get the DLC for an interesting prospective, that sort of "finishes the scene off."  If the developers were to add more DLC to this game, I believe I would get those, as well. I am not so interested in just the music for DLC, but I am glad it is offered for anyone who may want it. The music really does set the tone for the game. Really? the audio period. Is an important element of the cozy feel to this particular experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery

_childDocuments_.review: Holy heck, this game gave me all the feels in such a beautiful and amazing way. Completely worth getting. I had seen this at the E3/Gameshow and knew I would want this game. If you love Studio Ghibli or Studio Ghibli inspired works/games, please play this. Absolutely worth every penny and then some. This game is short and sweet. There are a couple puzzles, but even if you aren't someone who enjoys puzzle games, I still recommend this game for the story and art alone.
_childDocuments_.name: Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery

_childDocuments_.review: I will become the two thousand and fiftieth review, maybe, no idea how quickly stats update, which is also my first review on Steam so that's fun. Ignoring that and talking about the game itself it's very much more akin to a playable movie or art piece as you try to piece together the story as it evolves. The visuals are beautiful and the soundtrack compliments it with The Color You Love The Most being a very dazzling song while capturing the emotions of the game perfectly. It's a heartwarming experience with a bit of a bittersweet feel. Certainly something I feel is worth experiencing as the price is quite fair too. Though admittedly it's a short game roughly an hour maybe some more if you struggle with the light puzzle elements. You can wait for a slight sale, but also when you compare it to the price of a movie, which this is more a visual delight than a mechanic heavy game, I'd say it's not overly expensive.
_childDocuments_.name: Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game, especially if you are a fan of things done in the style of studio Ghibli's works.  It's a reasonably simple puzzle game that you will likely be able to progress through without needing to look up solutions.  The story, music, and artwork are all wonderful.It took me approximately 90 minutes to full clear the game and achievements moving at a relaxed pace.
_childDocuments_.name: Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery

_childDocuments_.review: An absolutely beautiful game. I was looking for a comfy game to play and came across this gem. It's not normally my type of game but I gave it ago since it only takes just over an hour to finish and it was amazing. Beautiful art style, similar to Studio Ghibli. The animation was gorgeous.This game needs to be more recognised!Definitely pick it up and finish it. I had a bunch of theories on what was happening the more I played but the ending was, as with everything else in the game, beautiful.
_childDocuments_.name: Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery

_childDocuments_.review: Behind the frame is a fantastic game. The story is the game's star as it slowly unravels and you try to figure out what is happening. Despite the repetitiveness in certain spots, they somehow made those tasks like making breakfast fun. I shed a few tears at the end because it reminded me of my fiance and myself. While obviously not the same, there are many parallels. The moral of the story is never give up on someone you love, as Jack did. It's one of the few games I'm looking forward to playing again after fully understanding the story. Definitely a game everyone should play.
_childDocuments_.name: Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery

_childDocuments_.review: Narrative storytelling at it's absolute best! This is a stunning visual novel.  It's casual, simple, succinct, engaging, has fantastic music and spectacular art direction/animation. I downloaded this out of curiosity and to take a break from my heavier RPG oriented adventure gaming and was pleasantly surprised. While the puzzles are simple, what really grabs you is the story. No spoilers here, but suffice to say the desire for discovery drew me in to keep playing. The payoff on this is pure gold. Tightly written, meaningful and fun.  It will hit you in the feels. It is short and sweet in the best way. I recommend this to everyone. 10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery

_childDocuments_.review: This is the only game to date that I have ever went back to 100% the achievements, partially because I loved the game so much I wanted to reach 2 hours so I could buy items from the point shop. The mechanics were easy to understand and straight forward. If you're a veteran to point and click games you'll understand it immediately, but bit of a learning curve that lasts ten seconds if you're new. The puzzles were at just a high enough difficulty that it makes you think but just easy enough to allow yourself to be engrossed into the visuals and metaphors laid ahead of you. Although a shorter game, I don't mind especially since they used that to polish the mechanics and coding to near perfection, runs beautifully and the transition to different sections of the game are smoother than waxed ceramic.Oh the art, oh my god THE ART! from the animated cutscenes to the backgrounds and interact-ables this game shows a type of perfection I like to call replicated nature. The rooms are messy and unkempt, the nature messy and wild, but you could clearly tell that it was all on purpose, the purpose being to represent life, people and mother earth. The details of rust on the sink, the color shift of the dried paint blended beautifully with digitally illustrated cell shaded characters. Everything goes together well and feels like a spiritual successor to ghibli's Howl's moving Castle. Which of course, showed the same methods of oil painted surroundings and cell shaded animation and color theory. I went out of my way to buy and download both of the art books' pdfs and the absolute GENIUS to make the background on a panorama! I'm unaware of current game develop technology and how it would work but I imagine that it was difficult to make such detailed work warp. Another comment about the art books is the how both   As a freelance artist myself this game hit hard. The mc is the type of person I aspire to be, in personality, life style and hope, this game may even inspire my next vtuber model design. I don't share her medium due to being a digital artist, and how oil painting is such an expensive endeavor it is if you don't make much and it isn't your true aspiration. When I played this and the dlc on my live stream it left such a mark in me I was utterly speechless. My brain stopped working and for a moment I was nor longer an entertainer. I had to stop my stream soon after to process my thoughts, never has a video game hit me like this. I MISSED small meaningful passion games that don't require 100 endings or tons of chores to keep track of. I miss how... humble...games could feel. If I had anyone in my life that cared about this type of media I would talk their ear off about this game. After I'm done writing this review I'm going to go check out what other games and media silver lining studios have in store. I know there won't be a sequel, the story is done and this doesn't feel like the type of game to need one. But I desperately want to find merch on this, I beg!art and creative direction 10/10Story 9.5/10   -0.5 premise was a llliiitttttlllleeee predictableMusic and Sound 9/10 -1 had to go back and edit my audio settings a few too many times due to how loud everything was.(i'm just a little salty dw dw)mechanics and game play- 9.5/10 -0.5 wish I could alter my audio settings mid game, and the painting had to be a little too exact for my taste.
_childDocuments_.name: Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery

_childDocuments_.review: What looks like a simple phone game hits you right in the gut with its beautiful story. With a beautiful soundtrack and graphics, grab a cup of tea and get cozy. And bring a box of tissues. The puzzles are a perfect balance (at least for me) of difficulty, where they weren't too easy, but weren't so challenging that I was struggling too bad. While not a very long game, you'll enjoy every second of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so underrated! Very well thought out and the art style is super pretty, not to mention the soundtrack is one of the best I've heard and I'm in love with the ending song. It's a short game with a simple story but told in a way that tugs your heartstrings and makes you wonder what will and could have happened. Highly recommend!!
_childDocuments_.name: Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery

_childDocuments_.review: While this game is short, it effectively packs an emotional experience within its 1.5-hour length. The animation and scenery are beautifully done. The music fits every scene nicely. Lastly, the gameplay elements are charming, and none of the puzzles were annoying to solve.I highly recommend buying this game at full price. I am very excited to see more games from this developer. They are showing a lot of potential with this first title!
_childDocuments_.name: Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery

_childDocuments_.review: A love letter to art, story, and atmosphere. I put on my headphones and just felt my anxieties melt away as my eyes and ears feasted on this beautiful, peaceful and inspired game. After years of botching stickpeople drawings, it was very satisfying to "create" beautiful art in this game. It's a short story with few achievements, but honestly the immersion was so well done that I have replayed it twice through already and will probably go for a third run in due course. In my opinion, if you enjoy peaceful, story-driven games with light puzzle elements, and like to replay games, this is worth the modest price tag, especially to support the team that brought us this game. I hope to see more in the future.Some tips for playing: I thought I was solving some puzzles incorrectly, but it turns out I had the right solution, I am just terrible at 'drawing' with a mouse and the game didn't properly register my terribly uneven lines. I recommend playing on a touchscreen device with your finger or a stylus to avoid any solution confusion. Definitely take your time with this game, it's best enjoyed when you allow yourself to soak in everything it has to offer.
_childDocuments_.name: Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful storytelling and illustrations albeit somewhat of short play through. The atmospheric music suited each chapter as the story progressed. I thoroughly enjoyed it and wanted more, but the Jack DLC (which is free) at the end of the main story was a very nice surprise. A slow-paced casual puzzle game - perfect for a lazy Sunday.
_childDocuments_.name: Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting little story focused adventure game about some painters. The story is much more important and fleshed out than the gameplay which is really simple. The story is actually really nice as you try to figure out who the characters are and why the world around you changes. It takes a simple narrative and twists it into a scenario where you really feel for the characters. The way the game messes with the environment also really helps a lot. The first half really has some ambiguity and interpretation of how you see the characters while the second half rounds the characters off. Overall, an actual good story in a decent game. Get it on sale since it's like 90 mins.
_childDocuments_.name: Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery

_childDocuments_.review: I did not enjoy this game.It was too short (at least you're quickly done with it, not sure if it's a bad point) and the 'story' (if there was even one ?) relies on a single 'twist' that you can easily guess in the very first minutes you play the game.And that's pretty much all.. The 'gameplay' is tedious, the puzzles can barely be named as suchThe dialog is pointless and almost non-existent.At least there is something like 4 different tracks of music which are a bit cozy.
_childDocuments_.name: Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery

_childDocuments_.review: Even considering this is an "artistic game", the gameplay is just boring. The puzzles are toddler level and the painting parts are just a glorified version of A Little to the Left's hints. It's also extremely slow, as they force you to wait between each line before you can click to continue. If you're a fast reader, get ready to spam click impatiently.There's also a few bugs, it stopped playing cutscenes completely at some point and I had to restart.The story is cute I guess but very predictable yet doesn't make sense. You can see they tried to go into the supernatural but there is no explanation whatsoever. It ends up feeling like they're trying to trick you into believing it's more than just the most boring and cliché story, but they couldn't come up with anything original.The achievements make no sense at all, to the point where there is no way you could get them without a guide (why would you click 11 times on something that gives the same flavour text every time and have you wait a couple seconds between each click?)I finished it out of spite, but even if you have it because it was in a bundle or something, it's not even worth playing in my opinion. That's 2 hours I had to waste and I regret wasting it on this.

_childDocuments_.review: That was... extremely underwhelming. The story was rather boring and didn't actually bring any answers? _childDocuments_.review: Regret is the sweet dream of things that were and could've been. Sometimes bitter, sometimes sour, sometimes salty, but always sweet until it isn't. Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery is an unexpectedly mature game. Not mature in the 'let's discuss dark topics' sense but mature in the wizened 'I intimately understand this topic' sense. I had my suspicions midway into the game but the free Jack DLC more or less confirmed it. Jack and Amber  Very brief game but well worth the time spent. Heartily recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery

_childDocuments_.review: Very unimaginative and underwhelming. An interactive movie at best. The story pretends to be deep but it's nothing more than an uninspired cliché with flat characters. For a painting-inspired game it feels like a cheap escape room with repetitive, boring mechanics and no room for creativity. The achievements are illogical and designed to extend the length of the game. On top of that, it's full of text bugs that cause the screen to freeze too often, turning a supposedly relaxing experience into a frustrating one.
_childDocuments_.name: Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery

_childDocuments_.review: If you're into point and click adventure games from a mechanical point of view primarily, this might not be the game for you. The puzzles are not complex, the game is not long. However, the story is what makes this game and the technical work done to put the player into a Ghibli style animation/illustration story well worth the play through.I recommend play through this twice, play through it the first time, focus on just completing the game and finding out the story. Once you know the story, take a break, play again and take time to really look around. The enviroment is very impressive from a technical standpoint of seeing parts of the background move like you're living in that animation. There's also some enivromental storytelling you may miss because of lack of context to first time around.The story is really good, again it's not complex, but it's a story that I think a lot of people can relate with. A story about what-ifs and missed chances.
_childDocuments_.name: Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery

_childDocuments_.review: Behind the Frame is a very charming little game, not what I would usually consider my cup of coffee, but definitely worth the price (especially since the price is so ridiculously low). It is short, yes, but the experience you get is one of a kind, and considering the effort that had to be put into creating the visuals, I wouldn't blame the devs for asking more than that. And they don't.Admittedly, the story is rather predictible ("I got the twist before the game even started hinting at it and it's not because I'm so smart" kind of predictible) but it can squeeze some real emotions out of you.Lastly, if you buy it, finish it, and then refund it because it's so short - yes, you do not, in fact, have a soul :DBetter spend your days as best as you can, because when this is over, not even hell awaits you :D
_childDocuments_.name: Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery

_childDocuments_.review: This is just like the Nancy Drew mystery PC games I used to grow up playing, but with a romantic storyline filled with gorgeous artwork and design. _childDocuments_.review: Behind the Frame is a bittersweet and cute little game. The art style is lovely and the puzzles are straightforward and easy to complete. At first, I thought our protagonist was a slightly creepy voyeur who liked to peer into her elderly neighbor's window and draw him while watching him live his life, but really this story is about life, loss, and perhaps missed opportunities.
_childDocuments_.name: Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely beautiful,. A powerful story told by gorgeous art and cutscenes and a wonderful soundtrack! _childDocuments_.name: Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery

_childDocuments_.review: A decent try, but poor execution.Playing this game, I was motivated by the mystery of what would happen between the two neighbors and what had happened in their past. It took me about 40 minutes to finish the game (I accidentally left it on in the background - you will NOT get 20+ hrs of gameplay out of this lol!)I really liked the animation in the little cutscenes, the cozy vibe was strong, and I was interested to understand the backstory. However, the gameplay and puzzles were way too simple for the storyline to ALSO fall flat.Fun fact: I played this game on January 23rd and thought it was cute that the in-game calendar sets to whatever date it is for you in real life. Apparently, that is not the case - I just happened to play on Manet's birthday, which is the day the story is "stuck" on.

_childDocuments_.review: In 2020, during the heartache of the pandemic, I found myself contemplating the fleeting nature of memory more deeply than ever before. Days stretched long and lonely, filled with a sadness that seemed to permeate everything. In those moments, it was my books, my dear younger sister and mommy and the comforting presence of my former boyfriend who held me close. There lingered an anxious fear within me, a fear that the moments shared with loved ones might slip away into the ether of forgetfulness. The uncertainty of life weighed heavily on me, whispering doubts about my own worthiness, that I wasn't good enough, never capable enough, always falling short.From the days of my childhood to this very day, I've always kept a diary close at hand. Its pages became a sanctuary where I poured out my heart's troubles and joys, albeit I don't see myself writing as often as I used to. Though my artistic talents may be humble, I found solace in sketching alongside my written thoughts. These creations, both words and drawings, became etched into my heart. Nowadays, in quiet evenings, I find myself drawn back to those cherished pages, reliving moments through scents, sights, and the faded photographs I've collected over the years. It's easy to get caught up in the rush of life, but these memories anchor us, reminding us of who we are and where we've come from.Discovering "Behind the Frame" felt like stumbling upon a kindred spirit. Its gentle narrative, exploring the lives of two artists, resonated deeply with me. Despite its brief duration, the game left an indelible mark on my heart, a reminder of the beauty found in creation and connection. As I played, tears welled in my eyes. Yes, there was sadness in Amber's story, but it served as a poignant reminder. Our memories are treasures to be nurtured, for those we love remain with us always, guiding us from the unseen realms of heaven. Though they may be gone from our sight, their presence is felt in every beat of our hearts. So let us cherish each moment, for our memories are the threads that bind us to those we hold dear, now and forevermore.

_childDocuments_.review: I was really sceptical when starting the game. The art was very good, and the environments were beautiful, and cutscenes were high quality. But first three chapters really felt a bit too pretentious. I managed to figure out what is happening during that time too. But once chapter 4 starts the pace of the game improves, the puzzles get a bit more involved, and the story, while predicable, gets to the feelings just enough to be good.It takes about 1 hour to beat, another 15-20 minutes for the free DLC chapter. I'd say give the full game a try even if you didn't like the demo. It gets better. Worst case scenario you can always refund it. But please don't, if you like the game. This game left me fully satisfied, and within such a short timespan managed to touch my feelings. Some games I play for 100 hours and they do nothing.There is one issue with the game - all the story is told trough subtitles. But they appear while you're doing stuff, and during anime cutscenes. They really feel like they should have been voiced. I think it would have enchanted the game to a higher level. As it is it's great, but it could have been the best.The rooms you're in are in 3D, but they so good looking I was initially fooled into thinking those were 2D.The game also plays great on Steam Deck, where you can interact with touchscreen. The game is very nice to play that way.

_childDocuments_.review: - I like that the game creates a cozy atmosphere with its laid-back music and hand-painted backgrounds (not a big surprise, considering that painting is the main theme here). It was also interesting to watch the story unfold, since even though it seems very simple, some unexpected things happen around the middle of the game.- It was rather short. It has six chapters but it can be finished in less than 90 minutes. Not a big issue however, if you look at the price of slightly above 8€.- The gameplay elements are REALLY basic. There are some tasks you do around the apartment like making coffee or writing up a CV, which you do multiple times over the first few chapters. Thankfully the game occasionally switches it up with painting-based puzzles, but then those are also rather easy. There is definitely more focus on the story than the gameplay and even that seems to only have a symbolic purpose- The ending felt a bit underwhelming. I'm not heartless enough to claim that it didn't make me feel happy for the main characted, but again it was a basic feeling, maybe summarized by saying "Oh, is that where this was going? Ok, good for you."Overall, if you are looking for a "game" game, you probably won't get much out of this, as it's basically a visual novel with some basic puzzles. However, if you have a free evening during which you want to relax and experience a short story that leaves you with a warm feeling inside, I'd say check it out, especially for this price.

_childDocuments_.review: Disappointing Puzzle ExperienceAs a puzzle game, this title has left me quite disappointed. Here are the main issues I encountered during my playthrough:1. Too Short for Its PriceFor a game priced like this, the gameplay is far too short. I was expecting a more substantial puzzle-solving experience, but I finished the game very quickly, making it feel not worth the cost.2. Clunky Screen Transitions and Hard-to-Reach CluesWhen searching for clues, the screen transitions are often not smooth, and some clues are extremely difficult to reach. This lack of smooth operation severely affects the game's immersion, making it seem like the game design lacks finesse and attention to detail.3. Unengaging StorylineWhile I can understand that the game attempts to convey a sense of regret and leaves some things to the imagination, the current execution is far from satisfactory. There is not enough buildup for the regrets of the main characters, making the story feel very disjointed. Players are left feeling confused and unable to empathize with the characters. This emotional disconnect makes the story bland and unengaging.4. Lack of Colorful VisualsConsidering that one of the game's selling points is its art, the use of color is insufficient. The color palette in the game did not meet my expectations; it felt very monotonous and lacked visual impact. I hope the development team will put more effort into this aspect and improve the game's visual quality.Overall, this game falls short in several areas and does not meet expectations. I hope the developers will take player feedback seriously and make improvements.

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay itself is easy--- using your mouse to color in paintings and do sketches with very little mechanical precision required, and finding obvious clues around the apartment. It's meant to accompany the story and the charming, leisurely feel of a day in the life of an artist. You would especially resonate with it if your idea of a good time is waking up with no plans for the day except to indulge in a creative pursuit while sipping the simple pleasures of life, all in a cozy, rustic apartment with a big window. However, if you'd like a little bit more action then you'd probably prefer this game less. Storywise, there's no denying it's a romantic boy-meets-girl cliche, ostensibly drawn from similar stories in the Studio Ghibli movies that the creators cite as their primary inspiration. You can even say it has some similarities to 5cm Per Second. And yet, I found myself liking this execution of the cliche a lot more than the sources of inspiration, which I'm lukewarm about. Perhaps it's the fact that the video game medium naturally allows the player to be more directly immersed in the lives of the lovers, especially since the game is told from a first person POV. In addition, I think the art theme greatly enhanced the story in several ways. First, the more stylized paintings in the game compared to regular animation backgrounds allowed for a more poignant expression of the character's experiences. Secondly, it enhanced the romance by having the characters connect through their shared love of art, as opposed to just nice girl meets nice guy. At least, I personally found it be more relatable. Third, without getting into spoilers, they used the art theme to great effect by demonstrating what a work can mean to an individual artist and the power of art to preserve and communicate a precious memory. It's a short game with moderately enjoyable gameplay, but it left me with a pleasant aftertaste that I can continue to savor long after I've played it.

_childDocuments_.review: I was really disappointed by this game. It only has about an hour of gameplay, which would be an issue even if the story was incredible, and this one isn’t. A lot of other reviewers were moved by it, but I found it extremely simple and typical. The gameplay is similarly too easy. None of the puzzles required more than a minute’s thought. Honestly, it was so simple, I might suggest it as a good game for early readers, although I suspect a child would find the ambiguous ending confusing and frustrating. Typically, I love a bittersweet and unresolved story. The mix of a story that does not hold your hand and leaves a lot up to interpretation, plus gameplay that can hardly be called puzzling made for a really unfulfilling combination.

_childDocuments_.review: "Behind the Frame" is an exquisite gem that delivers an enchanting experience. _childDocuments_.review: Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery is a story rich puzzle game. where you'll be involved in solving puzzles to continue the story. usually involving adding something that's missing to a painting on the wall. There are also puzzles involving using clues to press specific buttons on an item.In Behind the Frame the player takes the role of a young woman who spends her days painting by her window. Across the alley from her is and old man who is also a painter, as well as his rather chunky cat, and she greets him everyday but he never responds to her greetings. As she sits down to color her latest work, she realizes that she has lost her tubes of paint and must search her apartment in order to find them. What follows is a slightly fantastical journey through memory lane, and a peek into the woman's goals and aspirations.The game is simple and incredible short experience, however Behind the Frames makes up for its lack of length with its gorgeous art and animation. Pair that with relaxing in game sounds and a touching story it makes the game a memorable experience. Rating: 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: Keeping things wholesome, we have Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery. This one’s a point and click adventure with a strong focus on narrative, and seems heavily inspired by Studio Ghibli and the work of Myazaki, with its gorgeous hand-drawn artstyle.  Developed by Akupara Games, Behind the Frame tells the tale from the perspective of a painter working on her final piece of art for her new exhibition. Events primarily take place in the artisit’s apartment. The walls are adorned with paintings of two lovers, and these become central to the narrative – which is fragmentary, and not always chronological, making the story a puzzle in itself.  To complete your masterpiece, you need a full palette of colours, and only yellow is available at the start. As you work through the chapters and solve puzzles, more colours become available.  Gameplay involves typical point and click mechanics, with the player moving a cursor around the apartment investigating objects and searching for clues. Many of the puzzles include adding specific colours to sections of paintings based on notes you’ve made in your journal. It won’t take long to complete Behind the Frame; it’s another game that can be completed in a single sitting. But it is one of the most memorable games I’ve played this year, with the story building to a wonderful denouement, and reveal at the end.  It’s an indie work of art, about art, and one that is an experience not to be missed.

_childDocuments_.review: Art sits alone in its creative outpouring of expression.  Mediums from centuries past tell tales to this day of men and women lost to the passage of time.  Many mediums can bring that sense of life to not only the eyes of society, but their ears and hearts as well.  Poetry, music, film, drawings, paintings: all subject themselves to the emotions of the creator, to express feelings felt within in the hopes the few who view it can share those same emotions whether in person or across the world.For this aspiring artist, she guides her emotions through paint and canvas.  Scattered pieces of personal memories to award winning details hold steady across the walls of her studio apartment.  For now, colors of green and yellow and red comfort each other closely as they reveal the scenery of a vivid town’s summer day.  Often taking a break for coffee and toast, she’ll pique her curiosity for her older neighbor, an artist himself, and his like-age cat.  Taking refuge in her notebook and sketches of a life she’s curiously watched over, she reminisces about the past, the mysteries of the present next door, and the curiosity of her future as the emptiness of her canvas becomes enveloped with each selected color.Gently mixing together Point & Click with Hidden Object and Puzzle-Mystery combines the foundation for Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery.  Detailing small tasks like making breakfast and typing out requests for inclusions to art exhibits carry over to putting final touches on past paintings to unlock various memories that have since been forgotten.  With each painting finished and memory re-awakened, more paints become available to finish her current project alongside little happenings to fill the days.While her current painting leans more towards impressionism, Behind the Frame’s art direction plants itself firmly in the magical.  Rivaling some AAA animated titles of recent years, scenery is packed with love and care as the studio apartment is lifelike yet cluttered, messy yet organized: where someone with fleeting ideas and sky high fixations would most certainly settle.  Cutscenes are short but sweet, each one striking and vivid in its color design and direction and just begs for a short film to be made alongside this game because, I mean.  Wow.  I can’t say enough about it.The musical score pulls its weight just as well.  Cassette tapes of soft jazz and tight upbeat piano fill the room with delight and creativity, while the somber bass tones amidst rainstorms and fuller orchestral pieces imbue each emotional checkpoint with a kind of grace and comfort that really shows the developers took every angle to pack as much volume into each scene.There’s not much that hasn’t been meticulously fine tuned and crafted masterfully to draw a perfect circle around this 75 minute experience.  The puzzles are not easy enough to insult the player, but intriguing enough to elicit a pleasant response to completing.  While the game may feel short, Behind the Frame doesn’t waste any time nor does it overstay its welcome.  The only issue I had was the camera pans in the room in a way that really triggered a bit of motion sickness that caused me to take a break about 45 minutes in, but this could be solely on me and shouldn’t deter anyone from trying the game.With the past year or two being a somber reminder of how fragile the world can be, it begs the mind to recollect, reflect, and rejoice the memories of good times that were had and the better times that could lay ahead.  Behind the Frame takes these emotions and paints a commandingly emotional yet poignantly human tale of what was, what now is, and what we do with what could be.

_childDocuments_.review: "Behind The Frame'' is a story of two lives. Two human beings so near yet so far away...a love born from coincidence, immortalised in memory and in art forever. During my first play-through I was initially confused: it started as a cosy art story, then it started hinting at a tragedy and the ending was somehow haunting at first. When the story resolves itself everything becomes clear and the only things I could feel were love, sorrow and gratitude.I think I should stop talking about the story now though, the game is really short but intense and any more writing could give away the feelings that the game wants to transmit at the end of the player's journey. Let's move to the technical aspect instead.Graphics are gorgeous, the game is an interactive anime with a great direction and such a great art style that for a moment I forgot I was playing entirely. Every character is well designed, places feel true and genuine and the choice of colours, camera angles and "acting" is simply spot on. This is one of the games which proves that art doesn't need realism to feel authentic and give an experience to its consumers.Music is simple, original, outstanding and really broke some tears in the end. I am a musical person, I play instruments and I always love exploring games music and even buy the soundtrack when I feel it; this game gave me excitement, worry, sadness, loss, healing, memories, happiness...all thanks to its music. It truly is a work of art, I would love to buy the vinyl as soon as I can, but at the moment it is only available from iam8bit-US, so it is a bit pricey to get plus the risk it gets damaged during shipping, I just hope some stock in Europe will be available again because it is that worth it.In conclusion, I opened my mind, ears and heart for two hours and I came back with a sad smile on my face, grateful to have experienced someone's love, someone's loss and someone's craft. I will always cherish this experience and it might be that is because I'm getting older but these little gems are really starting to leave a trace that I thought it was only possible with music and reading but I never thought it was possible to feel like that after a game. I just wanna say thank you to the devs, you just made my Christmas 2023 more special. <3

_childDocuments_.review: "Behind The Frame: The Finest Scenery" is a great point-and-click game, but very short game, and although it's a story-rich adventure, its ending is how you interpret it... It's not emotional by any means, but I'd say it's very wholesome.You take on the role of Amber, a painter, who at first seems to be absorbing inspiration from the old man living next door by peeking at him through a window. He is also a painter... The thing is, the more she does, the more she grows attached to the old man, and she can't shake the feeling that she knows him from somewhere. A few chapters in and Amber realises that she is just the MEMORY of the old man, that has become sentient in order for it to recount her story with Jack. Jack and Amber have been lovers, friends and best friends and the story depicts how some men act and react to certain things... Although Amber has moved on, and made Jack into this "penpal" after she had left for New York to pursue a career in painting, Jack, who is by far the BETTER painter, could not move on; Amber was his muse, his source of inspiration, and her leaving made him think that maybe he's not cut out to be a painter, and maybe his skills were not enoug (Talk about toxic femininity, right? lol). Anyways, dozens of years past and Amber hears of Jack's death, and honors him by opening a museum in his name where she showcased all the paintings he inspired her to do... Of course, she is married and has two kids, while he lived his entire life waiting for her occasional letters... I do not want to delve deeper into men's psychology but this game seems to have no problem proving that while some have the common sense to move on, others are super clingy and will live an entire imagined life with a partner they never had and never will have. Jack's paintings seem to build on that, painting him and amber in cafés, in landscapes... some of it did happen at some point, some of it was pure fiction. Even the memory of Amber seems to have forgotten Jack, but Jack, being the teenage 70 year old that he was before his death, seems to continue to live a fictional life, until his very last breath.Other than that, the game gets , what I loved most about it is the art... Whoever drew these sprites should probably get a salary raise lol

_childDocuments_.review: He was a painter, young Jack was his name,The colors he craved, a special kind of fame,A curious sight he saw one day,A white dressed lady, who caught his eye right away.Amber, the lass, a painter was she,On a rainy day a café, the place they'd meet,A friendship was born, a routine they share,A bond so strong, it’d carve its own air.Ideas and inspiration they'd bring to one another,Open fields and meadows, ready to paint and discover,Tho Jack's heart toward Amber had feelings swell,He'd brush them away and wish her “farewell”.For Amber received an opportunity divine,For her art was accepted, in a place called "The Big Apple" shine,Tho for Jack’s heart, a wound was cut that deep,He smiles as he reads her letters about things she's seen.In a cold winter night, Jack accepts his regrets,Tho all he can do is give Amber his due best,For she'd taught him a thing or two,When he had lost the courage to feel anew.Jack was an old painter with a full and adventurous lifeWhen one day he looked upon his frame, free of strifeHe knew Amber was his friend, his muse, his loveNow behind the frame – like the stars up above

_childDocuments_.review: I went in this game totally blind. I just saw few screenshots of the game and instantly fell in love with the artstyle, so I think that is the thing I should talk about first.This games artstyle is heavily, and when I say that I mean HEAVILY inspired by the works of Studio Ghibli. I personally love the artstyle, as I've grown up with movies like Spirited Away, My Neighbor Totoro and Laputa. Those movies have been a big part of my childhood, and seeing their artstyle being adapted into a game is wonderful. The art during the gameplay is beautiful, and the art in the cutscenes feel like something straight from a Ghibli movie.I am not sure if there is multiple endings available, as of right now I've only played the game once. The gameplay is typical Point & Click adventure, with quite interesting gameplay mechanics, which I haven't at least seen in a game before. The gameplay mechanics are interesting, even though they sometimes guide the hand of the player a bit too much.The story is surprisingly rich, I love how the developers managed to put in such a deep and interesting story into a fairly short game (just about the length of a short film).Then, let's talk about the music, which is absolutely beautiful. The OST is such a nice cherry on top of a beautiful story and a beautiful visual presentation.This game is less of a game, and more of a movie, with beautiful visuals, beautiful music and a nice story. And I feel like thinking of Behind the Frame as a movie/cinematic experience, instead of viewing it as a game, is the right way to view it.Overall, a beautifully crafted, beautifully written story. Even though the game is fairly short, it's still easily worth the price tag.

This experience feels more like a short movie than a game.As someone who enjoys art, sketching, and drawing, the way sketching is implemented in this game doesn't resonate with me. In the game, you simply drag the cursor across the screen, and a fully sketched version is automatically revealed where you have touched. However, in real-life sketching, you start by forming the general shape and then gradually add details. Initially, the game only provides yellow paint, followed by green paint. I wanted to mix yellow and green to create a different color, like lime green, but it's impossible to do so. Considering that paint is central to the story and the two main characters are painters, it's baffling that you can't even mix colors. Moreover, you're restricted from choosing colors in different areas when you paint , as you're forced to use the exact color dictated by the game.This lack of customization extends to other parts of the game as well. For instance, when making breakfast, I waited a long time for the egg to fry and earned an achievement for not liking over-easy eggs. However, even after waiting longer, the egg never overcooked. When I finally put toast and egg on the plate, it inexplicably turned into an egg and grilled cheese sandwich. I couldn’t add the egg between the toast slices to make a sandwich. It’s also frustrating you are always cooking the same dish.Although the art is stunning, the game lacks soul. You're forced to follow each step precisely, clicking for puzzle-solving and dragging the mouse for painting. Everything is pre-defined, leaving no room for creativity. I'll probably just watch the storyline play out through others, rather than waste my time playing it myself.Update after watching the entire gameplay: The storyline moved me to tears, and I was captivated by the breathtaking scenery, but I still believe there's significant room for improvement in this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Amber, an aspiring artist, is preparing her art piece for a gallery exhibition. Right across the street lives yet another artist, an old man with an old cat, and every morning she watches him working on his canvas. The daily routine of her life gets twisted and old memories becomes to resurface. The truth is hidden deep below the dried paint.I think I am slightly torn apart on this one, but gosh, I simply LOVE the visuals! It's like playing through some of  movies! The music is beautiful and creates a fitting atmosphere. I also liked the gameplay, you are not being rushed anywhere and can just enjoy your surroundings, but you are just a passive watcher and you can't influence a thing in the story (which is a little bit disappointing). Painting and sketching are done in a simple way, but it's fun. Puzzles are nice, varied and some even challenging.The story is bittersweet, with DLC's story being more bitter than sweet. If I understand it right, the game is inspired by the lives of two real artists… which sadly doesn't make the whole story any less sad (for me). is a relaxing and visually beautiful game. The message of the story missed its point with me, but that's just because I value and search for different things in my life... I have still enjoyed my time with it. _childDocuments_.review: It's a fantastic game, a very deep and mature story inferred from the hints provided at every step of the game. There's enough time to sink in what each means with the puzzles to break up the pacing. Did this game win any awards the year it was released? I'm not sure, but I feel it definitely deserved one for the story-telling.Spoiler warning for those who haven't played the game below:I can't begin to explain how this game makes me feel.On one hand, you have Amber, brought up in a not-so-perfect family, seeing her role models find happiness only after parting ways. She becomes inspired by them, she takes after them and seeks her own happiness without the interruption of others, a desirable solitude that's seen too often how relationships sour. She sought to maximise her own pleasure, and lives as a free spirit, unbound and untethered to anything, and that's why even at her age she understood how to use a laptop while Jack still relied on letters (but even his revised correspondent letters show hesitation like he's holding back some terrible secret - that he loves her). Eventually, her age catches up to her. She didn't remember that the paints she put in each painting were precious reminders / memories of the time she spent with Jack, until they've all been used up in her artworks. Even then, to Amber the paints were more meaningful on the canvas than they were bottled within their tubes. When her senile dementia goes in full force, her memories were to the happiest times in her life, that being the finest scenery, the time where she painted and pursued art with Jack in the purest form without the turmoils of favouritism, office politics and messy human affairs. Or perhaps, to admire each other as muses from afar is her own idea of love.On the other hand, you have Jack, the hopeless romantic who's already had commitments. He has cats to care for, bills to pay, too much baggage to let go and pursue a life with Amber. He admires her, thinks of her fondly to the extent that he remembers Amber's face, in her prime, perhaps to immortalise the version of her he cherishes the most, the version as his companion in drawing. To choose between the cats or the free-spirited Amber, he chose to minimise the pain he would cause by caring for the cats - even if he were to live in poverty, the cats must luxuriate on delicious canned food. Deep down, Jack yearns for a shared life, a family, a deeper connection with Amber, a life that was not to be, for none can tame the wind. In doing so, however, he bottles up his feelings and deprioritises his own humanity, putting himself in pain, preserving the paint in his tubes and going without bringing his palette when drawing the snowy scene. For if you truly love something, you would set it free... yet all too common we forget the survivorship bias behind the quote. Too easily do we overlook the pain of loneliness that, though imagined, is just as powerful as real pain. At least Biscuit's with him, and at the very least he can put down that baggage and finally face art honestly by Amber's side by the end of the story like a cathartic graduation from pain and trauma.Artworks are often burdened with untold pain, untold stories too difficult to capture in words. Amber sought to maximise pleasure, Jack sought to minimise pain, and though their paths crossed for a while it's not likely they'll meet ever again. It's a shame because I think they could have developed as pretty decent lovers, with them sharing a kiss in Fluge and all.One can only hope for a happier fate, one in which their love for each other becomes realised, an alternate reality where they can find joy and inspiration springing from each other on a daily basis.I guess it's time for me to hope for Taiwanese fan-fiction coupling the two of them together.

_childDocuments_.review: Behind The Frame The Finest Scenery is a short point-and-click puzzle adventure with painting elements. It’s sweet, beautiful and original, but is it a masterpiece?When the game starts you’ll immediately be painting a few strokes on your canvas with the help of your mouse. Except you only have the color yellow at your disposal at the moment; the rest of the needed colors are, somehow, lost at the moment. So time to look around your apartment where pretty much the entire games also takes place.In your apartment there are lots of items; some that can be clicked on for a little background story and others that can be interacted with for some seemingly casual fun at first, but these usually turn out to be part of a puzzle later on. The rest is basically just decoration. The apartment can be looked through in 360 degrees by using your mouse.There are six more colors you need to find in order to finish your painting - purple being the most wanted and needed color - and these are usually related to solving puzzles. Easy in the beginning, and they can get mildly difficult later on, but never truly difficult. The solutions are usually only a few feet away since it almost all takes place in the apartment anyhow, or you can find help and solutions in your notebook/sketchbook that automatically keeps track of everything you see and do. This includes your neighbor and cat from a different apartment building next door that will tie in to the story in unexpected ways. But usually the puzzles consist of finding notes (or similar items) and finishing paintings hanging around in your apartment.Solving puzzles and doing simple tasks is sometimes rewarded with a nice and simple, but beautifully animated cutscene. These feel cozy, even if they’re not always there to advance the story. Think of something like drinking a cup of coffee and looking out of the window after you’ve just made one. It’s such a simple thing, but little touches like this give the game its own personality. It would’ve stood out way less without them; it just would’ve been another puzzle game to many of us. Including me. Even though painting is the most important aspect of the game here; it’s a fun mechanic. The puzzles are just there for entertainment and for the story.You’ve probably noticed by now that I haven’t really talked about the story and that’s intentional. This is yet another one of those short games where the less is said about it the better. If you ever decide to give this a try I’m sure you’ll agree with me. Some of the last few minutes are absolutely gorgeous and beautiful.The game has six chapters in total, lasting about 60-90 minutes.Visually the game is gorgeous with lots of colors while still making it feel like a natural environment. It feels a bit like something taken out of an anime scene. So lots of detailed objects and all in 2D (or made to look like 2D).With the exception of a few simple catchphrases there’s no voice acting. Everything is told with subtitles and by reading from your notebook/sketchbook. The sound effects are limited and the music is relaxing with every day having a new instrumental song (I think?). The end credits contain a song with vocals. It's quite nice.I had one game breaking issue happen to me twice where I couldn’t move the mouse when looking from SPOILER! the inside-the-painting perspective, locking the ability to progress. Opening up the menu by pressing Escape and then returning fixed the issue.In the end I think Behind The Frame The Finest Scenery is a mighty fine game with an original way to tell a story. To be honest I haven't really seen anything like it before. At least, not in this way. I wouldn't go as far as to call it a Mona Lisa, but it comes close. It’s definitely one of the higher quality paintings out there, metaphorically speaking of course, and that’s absolutely nothing to be ashamed of. Considering the asking price this is an easy recommendation for sure. Beautiful!

_childDocuments_.review: Before anything else I have to say this game is BEAUTIFUL! No matter what I say about this game, good or bad, its absolutely gorgeous. To start, I will list a few things you should know about this game before you buy it.1. It has a start and an end so it's not like you can play it endlessly. It took me about 1-2 hours to complete.2. It's very structured in the sense that you don't just do whatever you want, it gives you hints and clues as to what you're supposed to do.3. You can replay the game but it will be exactly the same every time, so once you play it, that's how it'll go every time you replay it.4. Its not just about painting. It's a mix of painting and using clues to solve a kind of story/mystery.5. If you haven't already, I highly recommend playing the demo (I did) first to give you a feel of how the game is going to be. However, keep in mind that the demo is only chapter 1 so it has more painting and less clues/mystery than the later chapters.6. Lastly, as I'm writing this the game is $12.99 USD( plus 82 cents tax for me) and there are 6 chapters which means each chapter ends up being about $2.30 each, so make sure it's worth it to you.On to what I like about this game.1. The story. not only is it beautifully illustrated but it has some twists and surprises towards the end that leave you, in a way, trying to figure out what just happened. I think I understand the ending but I could be totally wrong.2. The "mystery". I say "mystery" because I'm not quite sure how to describe it but it was fun deciphering each clue and having it lead you to the next one.3. The music. The music is generally enjoyable with a mix of classical and elevator jazz, not distracting yet nice to fill the silence.Here's what I didn't really like about it.1. Choice is very limited. Throughout the entire game you have to just do what it's hinting at which I didn't love but I suppose that's just personal preference.2. The length of the game. I did know going in that it wasn't going to be very long but I do wish that it didn't go by so fast, and it's definitely the kind of game you start and finish in a day. It's quite nice for a cozy day at home. All that being said, I realize that it takes a lot of time and effort to make games and they did a very good job. Finally, I'll end this by saying this game was fun to play and well made, and all things considered I would recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly moving and beautiful! A perfect rainy day game. Minor critique is that I felt the game held my hand a bit too much. For example - one puzzle has you painting on your easel to make things appear in your real apartment. The second or third time this happened, the main character went "I just heard a noise! I wonder if something appeared in my apartment again". Probably could've worked that one out on my own. I do understand that the game is meant to be simple and relaxing and cozy, but I enjoyed working my way through the puzzles and it broke my immersion a bit to have the game so blatantly instruct me. Speaking of the puzzles; the puzzles! They were so sweet! The game really rewards paying attention in a way that I was impressed by for such a short game. I felt very proud of myself when I remembered a code from an early chapter in the game that helped me in a tiny puzzle in the DLC. The story was really sweet, any complaints I could have about pacing or structure were ultimately washed away by how emotionally evocative I found the plot. I do wish we could do more things though! _childDocuments_.review: A visually stunning hand drawn game. The game is short, really my only disappointment as it was so beautiful, especially the live animation scenes that I wanted more to engage with! The audio is also well done with little sounds such as brush strokes, the morning breeze and the coffee brewing. The soundtrack is low key and helps set the tone of the game. I won't spoil anything of the story as it is best to play through the narrative and experience it for yourself. This game brought back some nostalgia for me as I am an artist myself. Long ago I used to paint with traditional mediums (going more digital the last 20 years). This game brought back those memories of painting & sketching, especially during rainy or stormy days (which I still love but painting with a tablet vs a pencil or paintbrush).  This game may be short but it will resonate with you long after the credits are done. Leaving you wanting more. It is sad and happy and beautiful all at the same time. I truly found it a treat to play.  Hoping to see more beautiful games in the future from Silver Lining Studio! ❤️

_childDocuments_.review: This review is a little spoiler-ish, but it's the kind of spoilers that save lives.=======================================Man, this ends up really underwhelmingThis game starts as a really charming and gorgeous little slice of life tale. Then, something weird happens right in chapter one, I shrugged and wrote it of as a videogamey shenanigans. Then, weird things continue to happen little by little and I began the bargaining stage. They can't. They can't dissolve the whole thing into this tired-аss hackery? Right?!But they could. And they did.This game has Indie_Developer_Profound_Psychological_Narrative syndrome if you know what I mean. It becomes Layers of Fear-y. Thank god it's not quite Bloober team groanworthy but it's getting there. So, then the emotional ending happens, beautiful music plays and I feel none of it. I'm mostly just annoyed.This could've be something special. Instead you can just throw it into the pile. What a shame.Still pretty tho.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't say I really got the story but I did enjoy pretending I was a great artist for a short time. I didn't find any parts of this game to be complicated so it made for a fairy relaxing and enjoyable experience especially as there is no actual artistic skill required to create the sketches and paintings in this game. The painting portions of the game are basically memory based paint by number except instead of numbers you have to remember where to put each color based on a sketch you have to look at. If you have as bad of a memory as I do you will find yourself looking back at the sketches often. When I started on the first paining in the game I tried to be careful and stay in the lines, but I quickly came to realize that the game pretty much prevents you from painting too much accidentally outside the lines so I had nothing to worry about. Most of the time I enjoyed the painting and sketching in this game, however there was one moment near the end that I really hated. It was when I was trying to paint a letter that was required, but the game wouldn't accept it each time I did. It took me several tries before the game finally accepted it. This was the only time I felt frustrated at any point in the game so this game makes for a good experience for a player looking for a game that is short and relaxed with a good soundtrack and art style.

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful story, nostalgic Studio Ghibli art style, and cheerful music makes this a must play in my opinion.  It was short and sweet, but still gets me every single time. _childDocuments_.review: Be Warned: Spoilers Contained Below...This game strikes a unique chord with me when I play it, and as such I have gone back and forth quite a bit when considering my rating.  Were it possible on Steam, I would simply leave a written review without a recommendation one way or another.On the one hand, the game itself plays well.  It is visually striking, and both the art style and the narrative of the piece may resonate with any fans of late-era Studio Ghibli.  Similarly the puzzles, which all seem to be memory based, are well done, even if they are painfully simple.That said, the narrative seems to romanticize what I refer to as "the artist's sacrifice", namely the protagonist's sacrifice of her relationship with the deuteragonist, which, as can be seen in the epilogue/hidden chapter, haunts him for the rest of his life.  Even Amber, towards the end, seems to lament (or at least still be pained by) this decision as she sheds a tear before the portrait of her that Jack painted.  I am not saying that the decision to sacrifice something, even romance, for your art is wrong, but I am hesitant to romanticize such decisions.  A choice such as that carries tremendous weight, and, in my opinion, should be considered carefully.  Romanticizing such a thing can provide a convenient escape for people who do not want to confront such a difficult decision directly.  This avoidance can be particularly problematic, even irresponsible, when the hearts of others are involved.Of course, this is just my interpretation of the piece.  Perhaps the story is not meant to romanticize sacrifice at all.  Perhaps the intention is to draw attention to just how broadly the strokes of one's decisions can impact another person.  Perhaps it is simply a reflection on the nature of life in which every decision leaves unanswered questions, and how we can all be haunted by our own "what-ifs".  Whatever the case, there is no doubt that the story contained within this game is a tragic one, and it succeeds in stirring up heartache and frustration within those with whom the story resonates.  The narrative is incomplete without it's epilogue, so be sure to play both the main game, as well as Jack's chapter once unlocked.Visually striking, emotionally evocative, and heartrending to the core.   is the best game I will never play again.

_childDocuments_.review: A prime definition of "style over substance" that shows that the game designers have the knowledge of portraying emotional imagery through painting but failing at applying game mechanics to truly makes those emotions come through. Clearly inspired by Hayao Miyazaki and traditional East-Asian animation, Behind the Frame tells the tale of a young painter and her life through paintings. It features absolutely gorgeous animated surroundings and interactive animations with a peaceful score in the background. The problem lies in the main theme that also is meant to be the main mechanic: painting. The freedom of painting is constricted to extremely simplified puzzles that doesn't allow for any creativity or experimentation of any kind, but rather merely paint according to instructions (which barely allows you to even paint at all). The puzzles don't exist to widen the theme but merely are obstacles to progress the story. While the individual paintings are nice, the mechanics are so bare-bone that any required interactivity becomes a bore, making the Player endlessly await the next gorgeous cutscene. The game also suffers from exposition overload by including the characters thought-process at the bottom of the scene, taking every emotional moment and overexplaining it and not letting the images flow on their own (the opposite of the styles of Miyazaki for example). In short, it's a beautiful tale hindered by a flawed concept that makes the magic of painting dull.

_childDocuments_.review: I open my eyes. A canvas is in front of me. Sweet, I can draw some stuff.Nope, there is a pre-drawn draft to follow and no matter what you draw, the final painting ends up the same.I stand up, realizing I run out of paints. Should I go get some new paints?Nope, there is a to-do list, and buying new paints is not on that list.I walk around and make myself a breakfast. I want double side eggs.No can do. A single sunny side up is all you get.I put some elevator music tape in some old ass cassette player. It starts playing and becomes annoying real fast. Please stop.No, no no no. You don't get it. Once the music is on, it stays ON.I look down. I have this seemingly highly important resume to finish. Let's work on...NO. ON. NOON. Forget about it. It's not your concern anyway.------------------So. In a mere 10 minute time span, I have been constantly reminded that this is not my embodiment, not my home, and not my story to be in. I better head out, and I did.------------------Point & click games can easily be a hit or miss experience. I think what makes the genre popular back in the days is making clicking on the screen a genuinely enjoyable experience. Think  series, where every object on the screen is interactable and every scene fun to watch. Or what keeps the genre still alive today, the dialogues, monologues or even puzzles should be thought provoking for a mind to dwell with, while clicking from one object to the next. The in between such as this game leaves too much to be desired for me to care about the story behind the scene. It is to the point that I have to raise this question: What story telling purposes does making a player make breakfast and coffee in a game serve, other than training them to click on shiny objects on the screen?

_childDocuments_.review: I installed this game expecting relaxing gameplay and I was not disappointed; rather, it exceeded my expectations in this short interactive point-and-click story. Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery tells a beautiful and compelling story despite taking less than two hours to fully complete the game with all the achievements. You take upon the role of a young lady who is an aspiring artist, aiming to have her piece shown in an exhibition. The game tells her story, along with her interest in the skilful painter in the building opposite her split into multiple short chapters. The game includes an added DLC, which will show up in the main menu underneath the title upon completion of the base game. The base game came to a bittersweet conclusion which I enjoyed greatly, and in combination with the ending of the DLC it brought me to a feeling of wholesomeness, and contentment. For a game with less than 2 hours of content, there was nothing more I could ask for. The story did not seem forced, it did not appear to be abruptly brought to an end, and it was not dragged out. It was phenomenal, and enjoyable the whole way through before coming to a touching close.  Being a mobile game ported to PC, the controls were very simple and easy to get a hold of. This made it very accessible and relaxing. Having not really had any prior knowledge about the game (I hadn't read the synopsis or the tags, I simply just saw the title and quickly clicked through the images on the store page), I found out that it was a puzzle game.  The puzzles are quite simple, not requiring too much thought into it, and is quite instinctive.  I did struggle at one point to figure out what to do next in one point, and could not find the answer to one puzzle, so I ended up brute forcing it, so it may lack some clarity at times (or it could just be at the fault of the player). One thing though, is that I would have liked to have been able to access the settings of the game while in a chapter, rather than only in the main menu. However, overall the gameplay was very calming and pleasant (you can also pet the cat).  Graphically, Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery is phenomenal. The art is incredible, very reminiscent of Studio Ghibli type art for the cutscenes and it was lovely to look at. While sketching during the game, the artwork was also beautiful and intricate. For the artworks that you paint during the game, it is relatively simple, I would have liked more fleshed out pieces to paint, however, everything else was fantastic.  The soundtrack for this game is remarkable. The music was very soothing and gentle, I loved it. I originally had my own music playing over the game, but once I heard the music kick in, I turned my music off and enjoyed the experience to its fullest. I did not enjoy the voice acting so much, as it seemed minimal and there were only minor comments made by the protagonist. I would rather the voice acting be done throughout the whole game, or not at all. I was, however, very fond of the soundtrack and the sound design of the game.  Due to the game being very linear, with not much freedom with different endings or actions, I don't believe the game to be very replayable, I only did so to attain all of the achievements. Potentially once in a while if you'd like to revisit the experience, however in itself, it does not have much replayability. I loved Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery. It was a short game, but it had beautiful graphics, accompanied with a delightful soundtrack and sound design. Behind the Frame is a very chill game to play to wind down, with a short yet sweet story, as well as an included DLC from the perspective of a different character to make it all the more interesting. For those interested in a wholesome, casual one to two hour gaming session, I would most definitely recommend this. Make yourself a coffee, sit down and enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: Bought this little gem on sale a few months ago and only got around to playing it a few days ago. It's a short and bittersweet game, can be easily finished in a few hours even when going at your own pace, about a young woman, a painter, living in her apartment. An old man, also a painter, lives in the apartment across from her but never looks at her. Soon enough the game has you solving puzzles, unlocking new colours for the woman's painting and slowly giving you more and more information about your elderly neighbour. It's a very short game, as mentioned before, but one that is well worth its price. The art-style will melt your heart, everything looks so damn good and the Ghibli-esque animations will capture your heart if the rest of the game's aesthetic has not already. If this game had just been an interactive film with these same animations, I would've still bought it. Some of the scenery in Behind the Frame also heavily reminded of me Howl's Moving Castle.The gameplay is very much point-and-click, but it fits the vibe. The puzzles are really not too hard, some take a few tries to get right but there's enough of a problem-solving element to make it fun and captivating. The game really shines with its lovely, touching story though, which will be sure to at least make you choke up a tiny bit. I know it did that for me.At an extremely reasonable price of £7.19, this game is very much worth buying. Look forward to what else this studio has in store!

_childDocuments_.review: 1.9h (100% achievement, finished the game) 1.5h No. Yes (~13 achievements). No. is an interactive fiction with puzzle elements in it. You'll watch a story, displayed in anime-like visuals while trying to solve puzzles in point-and-click style in between. It has 6+1 chapters in total, all of which can be completed in a short time.- Smooth animation- Clever puzzles that utilize the use of paintings- Story that you experience with emotions rather than dialogues- Unable to speed up the game for the second playthrough- The letter detection system in the last chapter is off- Some parts in the earlier chapter can feel repetitiveIntel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650 makes you feel as if you are watching an anime while playing. Animations look smooth, although in the point-and-click sections, some objects can be differentiated easily from the backgrounds. Not that I'm complaining since I like to see all interactable objects on the screen, which the game doesn't have, though.You'll play as a woman who is trying to figure out someone else's past. This means that the story won't be spoonfed to you; instead, you'll have to figure it out based on pieces of facts that are scattered throughout the chapters. The story becomes open to interpretation, which for me, hits me more emotionally than if it was told in full. I like how the storytelling was done, to be honest. It feels as if you are the main character since you have to deduce what happened on your own, bit by bit. There are some fantasy elements in the story, but I don't really mind with it.  is played similarly to point-and-click games. You'll have to figure out what to do to progress the story, which can be done by interacting with other objects in the area. The puzzles are mostly related to painting and are easy to figure out, although there are also some in the latter part of the story that can be confusing unless you know what to do. Sadly, there is no hint system or whatsoever to help you in case you are stuck.Most of the time, you'll be doing sketches. You'll either have to color your painting or do a sketch with your pencil, all of which require you to drag your mouse around in a select area. I like how easy it is to paint and/or sketch everything, although the one part where you have to draw letters in the last chapter gave me trouble since it hardly detects what I wrote.There is no backtracking. Well, it's kinda understandable given how the game works, but it's still a bummer for achievement hunters. I had to replay a chapter once because I missed some achievements midway and had to restart the chapter from the beginning. Luckily, there is a chapter select, but you can't speed up the cutscenes or the dialogues. I finished the game in 1.5h. I then replayed the last, bonus chapter again to get the missing achievements. Some puzzles can leave you stuck for some minutes, but it's nothing difficult as long as you pay attention to the story.To be honest, there isn't much to say about this game. It's a short, beautiful game that makes you feel as if you are watching an anime. I couldn't stop saying how beautiful it is because that's the fact. The puzzles themselves are easy, and those who like to play games for the emotional aspect will enjoy it more. However, the asking price might be way too much compared to the playtime it offers (less than 2h), so I suggest buying it at a sale instead.

_childDocuments_.review: Behind the Frame is a game with beautiful graphics and a story worthy of an animated film. However, I have mixed feelings about it because I believe that presenting it as a PC game was not the most suitable choice.Graphics and Story:The graphics are stunning, creating a truly visual experience. The story is captivating and could easily be adapted into an animated film. The artistic qualities of the game are undeniable.Gameplay Experience:Unfortunately, Behind the Frame offers a limited gameplay experience. Interactions with objects are minimal, and the puzzles are simplistic. Moreover, the game is extremely short. I was able to complete it in less than 1 hour and 30 minutes. This very short playtime is disappointing.Replayability and Value:In my humble opinion, this game would have been better suited for a mobile platform or could have been transformed into an exciting animated film. As a PC game, it lacks replayability. The absence of additional content or elements that encourage replaying the game is regrettable. The initial price of $11 that I paid for the game felt too high for the limited content it offers, leading me to request a refund.Overall, I give it a negative rating. While the game boasts stunning graphics and a captivating story, it suffers from a lack of content, limited interactivity, and an extremely short playtime. I believe the game would have benefited from a different approach. If you are looking for a game with high replayability and more substantial content, I suggest looking elsewhere.
