_childDocuments_.review: Wow. What a phenomenal game. If you were to take The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past and mix it with a relatively casual (but enjoyable) twin-stick shooter/shmup, Minishoot Adventures is exactly what you'd end up with. To find out that this game is the product of a two-person development team is astounding, especially considering the game is super polished and launching in a state that some AAA titles struggle to reach.First off, the GREAT:- Exploration is fun and intuitive; as the devs claim, it's a compelling mix of top-down action-adventure and Metroidvania. Map is huge and split into distinct biomes, each with their own unique enemy types and environmental hazards to overcome.- Progression feels smooth and is incredibly rewarding. You gain red gems that contribute toward an EXP total represented by a crystal, leveling up at specific intervals and then spending those level-up crystals on the game's various abilities. in addition, there are larger red gems that can be collected to spend on various upgrade items and "charms" that each have unique effects (revealing incomplete dungeons, bullets that stun enemies, etc.). There's almost always something worthwhile to work toward that makes character progression a consistently satisfying power creep.- The game's combat mixes some classic twin-stick shooting with careful maneuvering of the player's ship, and the boss enemies have distinct movement and bullet patterns to decipher that make these encounters one of the game's highlights.- Minishoot Adventures doesn't overstay its welcome, clocking in at about 6-8 hours depending on how much of a completionist you are. It's a perfectly paced and satisfying experience that never drags or loses steam.- The music. Was not expecting the soundtrack to this game to blow me away like it has. Very reminiscent of some of the best work of Disasterpiece. Expect to get similar vibes as both Fez and Hyper Light Drifter.The Not-So-Great:- The map fragments that you can collect really facilitate one of the game's strong points (exploitation and backtracking for upgrades), but the game gives no indication of where they're to be found or how to find them. Almost every biome has a different place where its map fragment is found, with some being purchasable and others being hidden/secret items you need to dig for. I get that it's part of the game's Zelda-like charm, and it's a small annoyance but one of the only missteps the game commits.Minishoot Adventures runs phenomenally on the Steam Deck, I experienced zero crashes or bugs my entire playthrough (again, kudos to the two-person dev team), and I loved every second of it. As someone who loves Metroidvanias, Zelda games, and shmups, this title was a unique genre hodgepodge I wasn't expecting. Arguably one of my favorite games of 2024 so far.

_childDocuments_.review: Minishoot' Adventures is great, and if you're considering it even a little bit, you should really just buy it.It's a charming, Zelda-like, shmup with bouts of bullet hell and a bigger emphasis on exploration than might be initially obvious. There are secrets everywhere. XP is plentiful. As are upgrades to the ship and the map. After the first 30 minutes to an hour, it really starts to open up, and there always seems to be somewhere to look around and to push forward. Dungeons offer fun challenges and don't overstay their welcome. Great job of showing players things they can't do or get just yet all over the overworld, so it's all the more satisfying to get a new power and immediately leap back out into the world to try to recall where you could have used it previously and see where you might not have even noticed you can go now.Always be on the lookout for walls with a jagged edge, as these indicate a passage of some kind, and there's bound to be something good in there.

_childDocuments_.review: Minishoot Adventures is a straightforward story. Your little spaceship was woken up to save the land from a past calamity. This calamity saw your other spaceship pals imprisoned in crystal-like structures. During the journey you learn more about the world and who exactly put this state. Understanding history is key to not repeating it. Even though the story is straightforward, it is told subtly. Collectibles will be found around the world to fill the player in on that history (gameplay tools will assure that). In the end the story doesn’t hinder the rest of the game and is fine if you care to learn about it. For a ~10hr game, it is quick to pick up and understand  Minishoot Adventures is a straightforward story. Your little spaceship was woken up to save the land from a past calamity. This calamity saw your other spaceship pals imprisoned in crystal-like structures. During the journey you learn more about the world and who exactly put this state. Understanding history is key to not repeating it. Even though the story is straightforward, it is told subtly. Collectibles will be found around the world to fill the player in on that history (gameplay tools will assure that). In the end the story doesn’t hinder the rest of the game and is fine if you care to learn about it. For a ~10hr game, it is quick to pick up and understand   As stated above. Minishoot Adventure will always try to point you in the right direction. There are plenty of tools to make sure you explore every nook and cranny of the world. It’s very possible to 100% this game the first time around if you play on the top difficulty from the beginning. The various supplemental activities to do in the world further expand your spaceship’s kit and arsenal. Finding these supplemental activities starts with finding a map of the area. From there as long as you do some exploration, you’ll get tools that let you know where some secrets are and if you’ve fully completed them. Towards the end of the game, you’ll be introduced to challenge stages which are tough, but far from impossible. I recommend doing these, as they unlock the “True” ending to the game.  Minishoot Adventure is a beautiful game to play on the Steam Deck and should be lauded as a “must have” on it. It runs very well considering it pre-loads the whole world in the beginning for seamless transitions. Outside of it graphical crispiness, I didn’t pay much attention to music in the game outside of some solid boss music (final boss in particular). The art style is bubbly and colorful but knows how to instill the dread of the calamity by instituting  darkness. Enemy design was constantly changing, and environments were uniquely varied. I don’t know if the variation in the world design necessarily told a story non-verbally, but at least it was good looking

_childDocuments_.review: AVOID | LACKING | MAYBE | WORTHWHILE | COMPELLING | Minishoot' Adventure is a bullet hell metroidvania game with a heavy focus on exploration.In this game, you start as a little spaceship trying to save your friends and the world from corruption. Pretty early on, you can tell this game is going to be a delight; it has all the things you want you in a game like this - well-paced upgrades, distinct environments, lots of good quality of life aspects (nice map, you can buy an upgrade that tells you when you've completed a dungeon making for easy backtracking, you can downgrade abilities you have upgraded to fit various situations, easy to understand UI, etc), unique enemies, tough but fair boss fights (and lots of accessibility options to make it insanely difficult to literally being invincible), lots of secrets to discover, and the art is great to look at.The game took me ~9.5 hours to beat the "final" boss, at which point I had 100% in-game completion. It took another hour to beat the actual final boss, and then I took some time finishing the battle arenas to get the proper ending. By playing in advanced mode, finishing the battle arenas with at least 5 hears remaining, and getting 100% in-game completion, you will get all achievements.All in all, this game lit up my brain like Christmas tree - it hit every note I want in a game like this and delivered handsomely. It was pretty addicting to play, which isn't something I find is true with many games unless they're complete bangers. It's so easy to recommend. Like, do you enjoy having fun? Then you should buy this game lol. That's literally the only criterion I would use to base a recommendation of this game off of because it has so much going for it.

_childDocuments_.review: I find it strange I liked Minishoot so much. It's a very competent SHMUP being pushed through the filter of a simple Zelda-esque adventure game. You visit dungeons, find upgrades, and fight bosses. Standard stuff. Yet, thematically, the game doesn't work even a little. The story (whatever it might be) is completely out of place for a game about a spaceship doing pew pews, and it feels like the developers, ARGL and KUHO, had the skills to make a different game but a passion to make this one.The graphics are fine, and the sound is appropriate. It's easy to play and controls well. It feels simple, but moving around and shooting are engaging, so maybe it's not important that it doesn't make any sense. It's also the right length for its parts. That last part is a bit of a fib. The game has an ending, a true ending, and a more true ending. This annoys me a little because none of the endings are narratively interesting or satisfying; they are basically just more challenging fights to let you really put your skills to the test, and that's what the game does well, so... I guess I'm just annoyed that there isn't actually an ending that is worthwhile. You could stop when the credits roll, and it would be as narratively satisfying as doing the optional post-game boss fights.It also, importantly, has the right level of challenge. It's not easy, but it's also not frustratingly hard. It has secrets you might miss, but they aren't hard to find if you go looking for them. There are plenty of upgrades spread over your playtime, but not so many that it becomes a chore. The boss fights make you start over if you die, but they aren't long enough for it to feel like a punishment. It really just nails that sweet spot of being engaging without being tedious. Challenging but not infuriating. Recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Undoubtedly the most fun I've had with a game this year. And by that I mean the pure joy of sitting down for a session - a big grin on my face as I swoosh around, exploring a charming cartoon world that's one part 2D Zelda and one part twin-stick shooter bliss. Minishoot's controls are responsive, which is a must when the screen is dense with the firepower of your enemies. Being precise is better than just being quick. A whole slew of secondary quests and areas to explore entice beyond the main thrust of the game. Not quite powered up enough to face a certain arena or boss? No problem, there are a dozen other things to do that typically branch off into another set of fun adventures that'll loop back around to the main quest in ways that surprise and delight. There are a few obvious challenge bumps near the end that are a bit eye-rolling, and the final boss is the least interesting of the lot, but it's breezy enough, with plenty of post game potential to keep that keen sense of fun intact. All in all, my proverbial hat off to the two devs. They've done an incredible job on what could be one of the best of the year!

_childDocuments_.review: Clever and convenient in many ways:Projectiles show their lifespan, letting the player know how far they'll reach without memorization. Some bits, both important for navigation and not, are teased so the player knows where they are before reaching them. Not just hidden, but guaranteed things too serve as power progression catchups to decrease how much behind the power curve players are if they don't do side stuff/backtrack. Enemies have consistent and intuitive tells for how they're aiming and if they're aiming at all. The most immediate kind of power progression can be freely respecced, replacing regret with adaptation. This, having more than 1 way to go for most of the game and optional sources of power, combined with difficulty settings(which alone wouldn't achieve as much), allow players to always keep progressing or enlarge obstacles. Many collectible location spoilers require an intentional interaction to kick in, maybe too much for some, but most can have the best of both spoiled and not. Combat encounters tend to drop health pickups at the end, so getting hit little enough is the same for pacing as not at all. Overlookable things without indicators ever(except 1) are extras, not a permanent loss if overlooked. Some things are invisibly tutorialled, achieving knowledge without explicit anything. Some places have fun gimmecks that keep sameness down.I wouldn't be surprised if there's more clever/convenient stuff I don't see than I doA deliberate, but harder to agree with, decision is commiting a flowfire and making trees a lot bigger visually than they are for the purposes of collision detection, obstructing everything one needs to see to fight(stuff visible through them is everything except geometry, the player, enemies and all projectiles). Also, playing as if it was a gameplay-only game is not a valid pace to play the game at. Despite claims that everyone can play at their own pace, ~5 people can't due to forced downtime. Finite deceleration speed is frustrating in obstacle courses with instakill projectiles.Short flashes can be turned off, but longer walls of light can't. There are sound cues without visual equivalents. Don't play it without sound.

_childDocuments_.review: Usually my other reviews are nonsense, but I gave the other game by this developer a negative review. I feel obligated to make a serious review about this entry because I thoroughly enjoyed it.The movement of the main character is crisp, responsive, and natural. I played with keyboard - which is not recommended - but it still felt fine enough to maneuver through. The visuals are lovely, the animations and presentation are adorable, and the lore is intriguing while a little vague. The gameplay is also blazingly fun for what is a joystick bullet-hell shooter, and the metroidvania type of twist on it makes it very fun to go through and collect upgrades as you blast at stronger and stronger foes. If you are not too good at these types of games, it comes with a wide variety of difficulty and accessibility options - no one is left out.That said, I have a few gripes. Some of the arenas feel a bit overwhelming compared to the boss fights of the game, with spikes of difficulty feeling somewhat random or unpredictable at times. There is also a lack of variety within your weaponry; that is, you only get the basic gun attack you have at the beginning of the game and nothing else. You do get upgrades to that gun attack and some activated abilities, but I would have liked to see ways of modifying the gun into different weapons with different effects, including turning it into a bomb, making it a minigun, a laser, and more. Criticisms aside, I had a blast with the game, even if the longer section of my gripes with the game contrast with the short accolades I had given it. I feel like everything presented to you by the beginning of this review and the store page is all you need - go try it!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a surprisingly delightful little blend of oldschool Zelda and the shoot-em-up genre, and I say that as someone who's never much enjoyed either class of game. I'd been looking for a game to tide over my Hollow Knight itch, and this fit the bill well: explore, find new upgrades that both apply in combat while unlocking new areas, and fight some challenging bosses. The secret sauce is how the game manages to constantly introduce new abilities and areas and enemies at such a steady pace that it never for a second loses your attention; I wouldn't be surprised if some people get sucked into this game and marathon it 'till they've finished every part of it.The most enjoyable content for me was after the true ending, where the game offers a hall of arena fights, re-mixing enemy encounters and bosses with your entire endgame skillset in mind. It was back-to-back high-octane encounters, and after clearing the first one I didn't want to take a break until I finished them all. As one point of constructive criticism, I do think this game is lacking a true 'mega endgame final challenge' that the likes of Hollow Knight had; the arenas and remixed bosses are difficult and enjoyable, but not a single one took me more than two tries... it would've been neat to really sink my teeth into a few fights (likely by making the enemies more aggressive/proactive and making it harder to simply back out of their range to mentally reset or get some free hits in), but then again I was only playing on 'normal' mode.I've completed the game entirely, and as you can see by my playtime it's rather short. It really is a no-fluff game; no padded downtime, 'boring parts', etc. Because of that, I think it's reasonably-priced. If you've been looking for a game to scratch that challenging/exploratory/charming itch, this may be the one for you.

_childDocuments_.review: 1 / 2Minishoot Adventures reviewPlaytime – 18 hours, 100% save file and an additional playthrough on hardFor fans of – shmups, twin-stick shooters, light exploration & Puzzle solving  Straight off the top, I have to say I can’t help but recommend Minishoot Adventures, the Zelda-like Shmup developed by Soulgame Studio.  Controlling a nondescript ship, you are awoken by not-Navi and informed that the Unchosen has returned, destroying your village and imprisoning your friends & family.  With that, you are sent off into the map and very much left on your own to explore, save your friends and defeat the Unchosen.  If you go all the way to the true ending, there is a bit more plot & exposition but outside of that, the introductory context is all there is in way of plot.  Whilst virtually non-existent, the small amount of lore that there is plays with ‘The Chosen One’ narrative in an admittedly insignificant way, but one that still made me smile when all was said and done.I found the gameplay and exploration compelling, with XP and upgrades doled out to the player at a solid clip alongside stumbling across new caves & areas of the map at a consistently fast pace. The best way to describe it really is the original NES Zelda crossbred with Galaga, and some modern day quality of life improvements & accessibility on top.  Coming in with three difficulty options (which effectively dictate the speed of enemies and bullets) and a couple of additional settings pertaining to auto-aim and other assists mean that this game is approachable for people of all skill levels, without ever sacrificing the things that make it such a joy to play.  In terms of art design, Minishoot keeps it clean, simple, and incredibly readable even in the thick of the action.  Enemy ships all have simple, blocky designs which meant that no matter how intense the action gets I could still make out what was shooting at me and where from pretty much all the time.  This carries over to the light environmental puzzling, where it was always clear what could be interacted with and what couldn’t, and what walls may or may not conceal hidden paths.  Whilst I personally found myself stumped once or twice, thanks to the readability of the map it never devolved into just shooting and running into anything & everything looking for any tiny detail I may have missed.  I haven’t touched on sound design too much and admittedly don’t have much to add, as it was played without volume for the vast majority, which was an oversight.  I will go back and check out the audio design, but I don’t think it would impact my feelings towards this game even if there was no sound design at all!I did encounter one or two minor issues with my playthrough, those being some slowdown in the latter stages of the game when things get really hectic (I did play exclusively on deck so can’t really speak to how well the game runs on a proper pc) and also the game’s in-game map.  It is perfectly usable, and the QoL improvements in terms of the ways the game provides upgrades to the mapping system to show you what locations are unfinished/where hidden items are appreciated, but there are some spots of the map that just don’t do a good job of helping you understand some of the areas.  In places, it will imply there is no way forward when in fact there will be a path, and this led to one or two frustrations where the answer I wanted was somewhere I hadn’t looked because of what the in-game map led me to believe.As I said up top, I strongly recommend this one. Fairly short and sweet, Minishoot Adventures is a highly enjoyable adventure, with fun exploration and compelling combat scenarios.  It’s here for a good time and not for a long time, but boy was it a good time!  8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: This is an excellent indy developed game.  The game is advertised as a blend of of the Original Legend of Zelda with elements of shooter games such as Geometry Wars.  The game is incredibly engaging upon your initial play with excellent controls and a great atmospheric soundtrack.  My impression is that the game would be more appealing to fans of the classic Zelda games than it would be to a person who enjoys Geometry Wars or other bullet hell games, as there are portions of the game where things can drag on a bit, and it can take some real hunting to figure out how to get into certain areas.  In particular I would note the Dungeons that can really do need some sort of mapping system.   The overworld map and items that are designed to help you find the items for your adventure could use some polish too.  I mention these short comings only in hopes that they can be addressed or to service anyone who might want to improve on this excellent idea.  This an A+ game worth playing if you like classic Zelda.

_childDocuments_.review: Here it goes,Exploration: What MINISHOOT does that I have not seen in most Metroidvania games, is how open the world is. How easy it is to navigate. I don't feel the claustrophobic sensation of reaching an end point at the end of a long corridor. But instead everything is open and if you find a blocked  access to a new area you can easily keep exploring the one you are already in. You just don't feel the frustration of backtracking. In addition, the level expansion is extremely well balanced: the bigger the world gets, the faster you can go and you get more items to orient yourself. Finally my favourite part: This game is full of hidden areas and secrets, everywhere !!! Combat: you start being a cuty little warrior and you end up being a cuty killer machine. The feeling of well deserved progression is always there. Never too easy, never too hard, just in the right fun spot. There are a ton of different enemies, patterns and combinations. And there are, of course, the boss fights. Which have a crazy soundtrack and crazy bullet patterns. I found myself screaming with excitement most of the time.    Sound: Most of the music and the sound effects of the game are simply over the top! Super evocative and magic. They really put me in a magic trance state. The game's environmental effects also add a lot to create that special atmosphere. And your character sound effects are just super cute <3Verdict: MINISHOOT has become one of my favourite games of all times for two reasons. One: because I simply love that feeling of freedom during the exploration and finding hidden secrets. Two: because all the combats and the evolution of your little buddy are so unique and crafted with detail and love.

_childDocuments_.review: What could have been a great game was hampered from being able to ever reach its full potential thanks to its prevalence of horrendous euroshmup design mechanics, the most glaring and affecting of which is the heavy and painful inertia built into your ship's movement that poisons every facet of the game's mechanics design.  What am I referring to when I write about euroshmup design? What even is a "euroshmup" to begin with?  The term--a portmanteau of "European" and "shoot-em-up"--describes the design ethos for shoot-em-up/shmup games made (of the kind typically made by European developers) with experimental design goals completely at odds with classic shmup design (of the kind typically made by Japanese developers). Whereas classic shmups focus on responsive, arcadey, challenging, compact ("all killer, no filler", as they say), score-based game design, euroshmups try to blend classic shmup design recipes with foreign ingredients like RPG mechanics and simulator genre elements. This euroshmup design generally manifests in the following ways:  Considering that Minishoot' Adventure aimed to be a game in the same spirit as a Zelda title, you might think I'm being unfair to it by criticizing its euroshmup elements. After all, if your goal is to make an adventure game, you will need some kind of a progression system (like health upgrades), an emphasis on exploration with slower moments of soaking in the atmosphere of the environments you explore, and a somewhat longer game, won't you? All of this is true.  However, what I am criticizing is not the goal but rather the execution. Poor shmup mechanics implementation made the game suffer tremendously. It didn't need to suffer in the ways I am about to describe. You could have had a great adventure game without the unnecessary euroshmup mechanics problems that plague this game.  This game, most of all things, didn't need inertia. You can still play as a ship adventuring a vast world without having your ship feel like a hovercraft. Why is inertia a bad thing? Inertia doesn't just simply make your movement feel slippery. By its very nature, inertia negatively affects other aspects of game mechanics:  The game also didn't need to make your ship's default bullet speed, rate of fire and bullet reach to be so pitiful. Upgrade points could have been used for actually meaningful upgrades, like choices of different bullet shot patterns (just like how different playable ships in classic shmups had different shot patterns, like concentrated, spread and homing shots for use in different scenarios). The game also didn't need to make the player's secondary power shot take so long to regenerate and share the same resource as the player's boost ability (very euroshmuppy).  As you can see, euroshmup mechanics always end up coming at a price that negatively affects other gameplay elements. _childDocuments_.review: Is this even a finished product?I mean, it would've been fine if this was a demo. In fact, it would be a great demo but a full-fledged game? I don't think so. This game is very shallow in every aspect. Story, Upgrades/Progression, Explorations, Enemy designs, Combat.There is no choices to make in this game in terms of progression. You buy this then upgrade that in, and only in, a predetermined order. On top of that, upgrades are pretty lame and lazily designed. You shoot one bullet then two then three etc.etc. No variations to choose from. It's just that.Fighting enemies in this game feels very strange in a bad way. It's like you not only control yourself but you also control enemies too, not in a metaphorically way. For example, if you strafe left, the enemies turn accordingly in a synchronize fashion with you. If you wiggle, they wiggle as if you were controlling them. It's super weird, at least for me. Because of this, the trajectory of their projectiles is very predictable, well, you are the one who controlling them after all.I know that story isn't of concern for this kind of game but if you were to provide garbage narrative, you might as well not provide any at all. Just a world with a premise is enough, leave the rest for players. They know what to do.All in all, I regret buying this game and I'm sure that you will too. A big disappointment, considering all the positive reviews. A very big disappointment.1/5

_childDocuments_.review: Game is super cute. The artstyle is really incredible. And the "top down twin stick shooter" seems a fresh approach to metroidvania, where the genrne is overwhelmed by 10000s of sidescroller/platformers. So that's nice! But...Not having map being recorded as you explore new regions was a terrible design decision. Game has 5 map collectables that are apparently very hard to find, as after playing for ~3 hours I have found only the starting one that is given to you at the start of the game. Now I have to somehow memorize every location.I simply don't have the time for that.Maybe the devs can take a page out of the newly released "Prince of Persia: Lost Crown". Map is autorecorded and the "maps" you find on your own unlock the regions you haven't explored yet and/or highlight unlocables you missed.There is also little variability in battle. You have one weapon, while you could instead be having so many different types of weapons. Your ship also has one fixed shape. While there is battle variability in terms of the bullet-hell enemy situation, I would like to have more agency as a player over how my ship looks like and fights in battle.  See Nova Drift for a counter example. Same space ship twin stick shooter battle setting, but with 8 or so hull designs and 100s of different type of weapons.So, while I could live with the little variability in ship shape and weapon type, I just can't afford to invest 10 extra hours to memorize the map. This game is simply not worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Positives:- Exploration is fun AND engaging. The game never enters this awkward late game state where you don't even look at enemies you come across while doing objectives. Here, you have to always be aware of bullets that might be coming from enemies off screen.- The upgrades to both the offensive and defensive combat powers feel great.- Bosses are challenging because of their unique phases with lots and lots of bullets to dodge.- I really liked that they went with spaceships as characters. They do beeps and boops and have a game meachnic, which is easy to understand (e.g. a shop or a heal). And the boost mechanic makes getting from A to B pretty fast.Neutral:- The dungeons are well designed and have a nice structure and progression. They often feature smaller arenas with waves of enemies and other challenges. For the game's mechanics, this is perfect, but the dungeons are missing a unique mechanic that makes them memorable.- Secrets or buttons are mostly just hidden in walls or under rocks. It's not that exciting to find one when the last dozen were in similar places.Negatives:- Single digit player health just doesn't work. If any bullet deals 1 damage, no matter if it's a random small enemy or the big boss charge up attack, then it also doesn't really matter what you pay attention to and taking a hit is sometimes the easy way to go.

_childDocuments_.review: A hybrid of TwinStick Shooter and Bullet Hell turns out to work pretty well.This is a very charming game. Your little craft has a few individual sprites for turning so it leans over more when making tight turns. It's also very expressive so when something surprises it, little squeals and sweat beads emanate from the cockpit, it'll spin happily when achieving something, and it generally conveys that quality of being alive well.The game has an open world with the interconnectedness of a metroidvania with gated-off areas opened by abilities, but is in essence a linear game with a lot of optional paths, unlike Metroid and more like Zelda I suppose.I'm still wrestling with the accuracy of an endorsement used in the trailer, that states the game is "A really neat fusion of Zelda and Metroidvania with Bullet Hell."I'm no expert at marketing copy, but I presume getting an quote that includes Zelda and metroidvania whilst mentioning Bullet Hell, all in one pithy statement, is gold because the Bullet Hell part is kinda-true, and people love metroidvanias and are desperate for Zelda-likes.The Steam tags are much more faithful to what the game actually is. You explore, you shoot with your sticks, there are some bullet hell encounters, there are some light RPG mechanics. They could have added 'female protagonist' if they wanted some more SEO. You'll note that metroidvania is missing from those tags - cos it really isn't one.To demonstrate the point that this isn't a metroidvania - a mild spoiler... (like, really mild)You have 4 abilities that open gates in the world. You cannot get ability 2 without ability 1. You can't get ability 3 without 2, and you can't get 4 without 3. In other words, you always get your abilities in the same order. I tried to sequence break; it can't be done.Additionally, if I mention Zelda, what comes to mind? Is your first thought puzzles? Challenges? Fishing? Unskippable dialog with annoying developer-insert Owl characters? If it was grid-based world design, congrats on being so special, and hey, you might enjoy how this game honours that super special appreciation you both have for grid-based dungeons (not the overworld though, that scrolls, and most of the dungeons too for that matter.)There are no puzzles in Minishoot' Adventures. At no point does the game throw down a room with a locked door and a bunch of switches, or have you rebounding light rays, moving blocks, shooting targets, or diverting the flow of water, or whatever else you could think up.There are a number of challenges, all of which are exploration or racing challenges. For instance, a lot of routes are locked until you find a switch to open the way, and a number of dungeons need you to navigate a trapped gauntlet.The Bullet Hell shooter-ness of the game is more generous, with tons of encounters throughout. These tend to be for bosses, minibosses and large ambushes, and they're great. It's very much babbies first bullet hell, and I don't mind saying I'm no veteran. The encounters are mostly fair and can be learnt and mastered. On slower difficulties, they can be reacted to. And they're fun too - I really enjoyed dancing from gap to gap between fields of projectiles (see the trailer/pics for the cruiser, bush-boss, and squid-boss for examples.)If you're wondering how a bullet-hell works in an open world setting - it kinda doesn't. The game likes to ambush you with spawns. These tend to work better if you are locked into a room as well, but they do tend to devolve into a melee with you trying to herd a group of mobs rather than a precise encounter. In the world at large, these spawn-in encounters are made much easier for your ability find a decent choke point or burst through weaker enemies so you can get to 1:1 against a bigger mob. I think the issue is, the world doesn't scroll automatically, so there's never a time when an enemy emerges on the horizon, holds position and throws out a field of projectiles leaving a specific gap at co-ordinates x,y, then after a brief interlude throws out a different attack leaving a different gap closeby. In the boss encounters, the enemies move slowly and deliberately to allow the bullet hell to take place. In the open world, the enemies tend to move erratically, shifting their position and staying within their desired ranges. Were they also to have complicated projectile field attacks it'd be nearly impossible to avoid attacks with them moving seemingly at random, not to mention attacking en masse. There is no swarm AI here, so there's no kinda rougelike synergy between enemy attack patterns. In essence, in the open world portions, and in most dungeons outside of fixed encounters, it's not fair to say this is a bullet hell, it's just a really good fun twin stick shooter.Going back to that marketing in the trailer, I do feel that IndieArk misled everyone with the Wanderbots' quote. This game is not a metroidvania, it's a linear game in an open world with a lot of backtracking for secrets; it's got more in common with Hob than Metroid or Castlevania: Symphony. It has even less in common with the Zelda series which has always had puzzle solving, skilful and tactical combat, and experimentation at it's core. It happens that a handful of games in the Zelda series have a top-down grid based dungeon layout that this game borrows from time to time. There's this really nice single screen directly south of your starting hub for instance. Otherwise it has about as much in common with Zelda as Skyrim's lockpicking does with Oblivion's.How did we get here? I'm going to speculate it was like this - two graduate computer science BAs looking to start their career in game development teamed up and respond to an online advert for "New Game Studio Talent Needed - Work from home - Good Yuan, err, I mean Euros to be earned!!!" They proceeded to make their first game and got setup as SoulGame Studios, subsidiary of IndieArk in all but name, both entities property of some nice Chinese fellas across the globe.The first game was a success, so they made another one. This time, they poured their hearts and souls into making it the best openworld action game they could conceive of, putting in a well fleshed out world, cool boss mechanics, and tons of charm. They took this masterpiece to their European-esque Mandarins and said "hey, here's our next game", to which the publishers said "you leave to us, we sell, you wait." PR set to work handing out keys to influencers and reviewers until one came back with the most perfect, the most sublimely misinformed quotation they could hope for; what was it? "oh, something about Zelda, Metriodvania, Bullet Hell, Fusion..." and, Who said it? "it doesn't matter, I scanned their YouTube channel - seems legit" came the assurance from PR, who added through a wall of toffee and nutmeg flavoured macchiato foam, "it was a good quote."Such was the fate of Minishoot' Adventures, which has an apostrophe in the title that doesn't do anything for no good reason. The trailer guy got the call to include the confusingly misinformed endorsement from Wanderbots, shrugged a shrug that can only be shrugged when you don't care who's paying the social credit bribes, and stuck it in the trailer alongside footage of the game doing it's wonderful thing.And here we are, some 8-9 months later, and some random guy on Steam (that's me) points it all out in a Steam review that's far too long and does the developers of this amazing game no service whatsoever because he gets hung up on poor marketing.9/10 btw, really good game.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game that I highly recommend. Calls back to the old platformers like Banjo Kazooie, Mario, and Zelda (the top-down put me in mind of Link to the Past). Steam indicated that it was similar to Hyper Light Drifter, though, which I kind of get, but the art design couldn't be more different. Pros: -Fluid controls that make playing the game an absolute joy-Cutesy but affecting design of the levels-Very little hand-holding (which can be frustrating at first, but it's usually just a matter of checking your map and retracing your steps)-Great sound design-Satisfying combat that reminds me more of Enter the Gungeon -Great leveling concepts and attainable collector goals -Exceptional level design-My experience was bug-freeCons: -As I indicated above, the lack of direction at first can be frustrating, and will see you kind of aimlessly wandering when you start. -It's a tad short; it took me about 9 hours to beat. The price and the potential to 100% it without spending 100 hours kind of offsets that, though.

_childDocuments_.review: Runs phenomenally, with no stutters and a constant 144 FPS on the RTX 3090 in Linux. I didn't try this on my Steam Deck since I just played this over the weekend and finished it rather quickly.It harkens back to SNES Zelda: A Link to the Past in terms of game play and progression. There's a set number of dungeons that open up a final dungeon. There are unlockable abilities that slowly open up the map for exploration and there's an EXP system that makes your craft better in different ways. I did like that the upgrade points could be reassigned at any time. You can be strategic as to what to prioritize in different situations, whether it be movement or damage. It plays very similar to Zelda but mixed with a twin-stick bullet hell style of gameplay. You'll be dodging streams of bullets while firing back at the enemies. It's very fast-paced.The sound track isn't very memorable, but it does have a cool toccata track for one of the bosses. The secret unlocked sound effect sounds very similar to the Zelda sound effect.It's like if Zelda and Geometry Wars were smashed together. It doesn't overstay its welcome and can be run through over a weekend. The story isn't great, but the gameplay is perfect for what it is. The different abilities you unlock really make you feel stronger and able to take on armies of enemies. 2 thumb sticks up.

_childDocuments_.review: Great combination of bullet hell that adds interesting combat to typical metroidvania formula that is executed well. There’s basically no boring backtracking to find that last upgrade and traversing map is fun. New moves you unlock aren’t the most original ones but they are done right and add a lot of joy. Passive upgrades are again typical for twin stick shooter bullet hell but because you can at any point reassign points it leaves a lot of room for experimentation or adjusting to your current needs. There’s not many puzzles and those that are there aren’t hard. It’s more about agility and perceptivity than figuring out something. Game presentation has a little bit of cartoon for small children but it’s pleasant with nice attention to details so no real complaints here. If I would need to point out something that is the weakest is probably the world setting that has a very childish approach. Cute ships living in houses that fight with frog robots and bush monsters and collect keys and magic artifacts. And I’m not against less serious presentation. I would just expect to have it more coherent - swap houses with hangars, keys with nav data and artifacts with ship parts or something in that manner. Still a great game that I highly recommend.4/5Things good to know (no spoilers):- Works great on steam deck although sometimes camera can zoom out making your ship small but still playable- You can finish collecting stuff after reaching the ending- It took me to reach 100% 11h on Advanced difficulty and around extra 2h for additional stuff- Advanced difficulty isn’t super hard. Some bosses will require a few attempts to learn the patterns and rest shouldn’t be a problem for semi advanced player

_childDocuments_.review: What if top down Zelda, but also a twin stick shooter? That's Minishoot' Adventures in its simplest form, but there's a lot more to it than simply that.The world of this game is bright and expansive, with tons to find if you want to put in the time to 100% it. On its normal difficulty, it's not super challenging and I didn't have to nearly fully upgrade or find everything to be able to best the final boss. The combat uses well established twin stick shooter methods and strikes a good balance of being challenging when it needs to, but without feeling chaotic. The world is fairly large and you aren't led by the nose between objectives, but the game's very good about organically leading you in the direction you need. I only had one part where I could say I wasn't sure where to go next, but after only about a half hour of wandering, I came across what I needed, and picked up some upgrades along the way.My only gripe is that the game does have some bugs that will creep up sometimes. I had a crash that caused it to save without a quest item having spawned in a dungeon and I had to roll back to a backup save that lost about two hours of progress. There is a Bug Report button in the menu, but it just takes you to a forum the devs are completely ignoring. Not sure why they bothered. By and large though, it's polished and runs very well.If you like exploring and twin stick combat, with a simple story that's largely told without words, this is a good time, and will go on for much longer if you want to 100% it.

_childDocuments_.review: Minishoot' Adventures is a top-down adventure/exploration game combined with a twin stick shooter. There are 3 difficulties, 3 targeting modes and a slider than can slow down the speed of the game in the accessibility menu. All of this means the game can be basically played and enjoyed by anyone. The game is quite forgiving if you are defeated, simply reloading at what I'll call your "camp" or at a save point in many dungeons. Without mentioning any names it brings back awesome vibes of a super specific Japanese console entertainment system and one of their main IP's top-down games. I had a blast playing it and recommend it to anyone interested in top-down adventure/exploration games. Overall my first run on the middle difficulty took 8-9 hours. I will play it again some day but overall its replayability isn't great, it'll be something you want to play again every handful of years(maybe), especially after you earn all of the achievements.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a near-perfect indie game from a small dev team, well worth your money and time especially if you enjoy twin-stick shooters and Zelda-like exploration. I played the game on normal difficulty and found it to be challenging without being punishing. The shooting feels tight and the exploration is fun -- only a couple of times was I unsure where to go. It's cool to dig for secrets between dungeons, and I was sure to collect everything before fighting the final boss. The game oozes polish, with nice UI/menus and bold/charming graphics. Pacing is also well done. Upgrades and leveling come at a steady clip up until the very end of the game. Average players will get 8-10 hours out of the main adventure depending on how many side objectives you want to complete. But there is also some post-game content, as well as the harder difficulty if your first playthrough is on normal. Sometimes you don't need an epic open world $70+ game with 100s of hours of content. In fact, I prefer smaller games with hand-crafted experiences, especially when they are polished to a shine like this one. Don't skip out on this delightful game! (Better chances for a sequel LOL.)

_childDocuments_.review: Played to true completion, normal difficulty entirely on Steam Deck. If you can believe it I did in the official dock at native 4K initially just to test but I don't think it ever dropped below 30fps except for one minor technical issue I will describe below.This is such a great idea for a Zelda-like. Taking the top down exploration and item collection of a Zelda game and merging it with a twin-stick (light) bullet hell. And it plays great with tight controls, good collectable powerups, and a flexible skill tree. As you fight you will level up which gives you points to invest in the tree and you are free to reallocate at any time which can be very useful in some scenarios, i.e. dumping points temporarily in speed for the race challenges.The art is simple but effective and the friendly ships are all charmingly animated. There is a very good visual design of all the elements making picking out enemies and their types easy and bullet trajectories, hit boxes and fade out very easy to read.The music is most ambient stuff that fits the mood but here and there it just hits you with this awesome stanky synth (in a good way) and I really liked it.As noted the experience was mostly smooth but I did encounter 3 instances where, after the game had been running for an hour or so, it appeared to freeze up even though the music was still playing. Turns out if I held a button long enough it would eventually respond like it was advancing one frame every 10 seconds or so. Even weirder if I managed to get it back to the main menu it would immediately fix itself without quitting the game. It's like there's some edge case where the game logic gets in a loop and it's weird. Either way, no progress was lost so for me this was a very minor point but I'm mostly noting it here so the devs might see it as a report.If you like Zelda and especially if you like twin-stick shooters then this one is a no brainer. And even if you're not a huge fan of the latter or not great at them then do know that not only is there an easy difficulty setting, there are also toggles for invincibility and infinite stamina if you get really stuck and need to get through a jam. This game was clearly a labor of love an oozes soul, and it's amazing it was made by just two people. Two thumbs up.

_childDocuments_.review: I adored this game thoroughly. I was immediately sold from the demo, and bought it as something to play on my Steam Deck when I saw it got verified, but I got so engrossed in it that I never even booted it on the Deck.It somehow scratched the itch for a classic Zelda game and a bullet hell at the same time, and the amount of polish on this little game blew me away. The movement and combat feel extremely fluid, and that combined with the ability to upgrade and downgrade your abilities at any time made it exciting to explore different builds, even mid-combat. The visuals and UI are so dang smooth and appealing. The world has plenty of secrets to discover if you want to explore a little extra, even giving an item to help find everything for completionists. The main game took me just over 5 hours to 100%, and then there was a little bit of extra post-game content that was a fun little challenge.I never thought I'd be saying this, but Minishoot' Adventures has been one of my favorite games of the year, and I highly recommend checking it out. Looking forward to going back to replay it on the harder difficulty one day on my Deck. And looking forward to future games from these devs.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my personal GOTY. I enjoy it so much. A shoot'em up bullet hell combined with a Zelda adventure, I love it. It is so polished from the stylized graphics to the sound design. Shooting and destroying enemies and items in the levels feels so satisfying. There is exploration, puzzles, time based racing challenges, boss fights…What I highly appreciate in this game is what a lot of shoot'em ups do wrong: the auto collection of upgrade crystal. So when you destroy enemies, they leave behind crystal shards that you collect to upgrade your ship. You can fly over them to collect them or after a short time, they auto collect. Here comes what this game does right: they don't fly to your ship, they fly to your ruby shaped level up UI. In other shoot'em ups they fly to your ship, and when you are in the middle of a bullet hell battle it can get so confusing because bullets and collectibles fly towards your ship and you don’t know which one you need to avoid. But not in this game and I am so grateful for that design decision. Up to now there is not a single thing that bothers me. Thank you developers for this awesome game!

_childDocuments_.review: Graphics: Simple but good 2D art. 7.9 out of 10Music: Good music with some memorable tracks. 8.5 out of 10Controls: Works well but since it's a twinstick shooter, having a controller with buttons on the back will help for easier access to some skills. Unfortunately since I don't have one of these controllers (played on a dualshock 4), using some skills during battles was a bit awkward, because I had to remove my thumb from the right analog stick to press some of the face buttons, which makes it impossible to aim. 8 out of 10.Gameplay: Really good most of the time, the player ship's movements are smooth and makes both exploration and combat fun. Not much to complain here except for two things:When you fall into the water or a pit, your ship respawns in some random place near where you fell off without any invincibility frames, and so falling off during combat usually means getting hit by some enemy or bullet as soon as you respawn.Another problem is that enemies shatter in pieces when they're destroyed, and they also leave some red crystal fragments on the floor. During chaotic fights against many enemies, it becomes difficult to quickly know exactly what is destroyed enemies' pieces, crystal fragments or enemies bullets.8.5 out of 10Story: Interesting story about ancient spaceships and holy scarabs. 7 out of 10Conclusion:Excellent game that combines twinstick shooter controls with metroidvania progression.Final rate: 8.2 out of 10

_childDocuments_.review: The game is a top-down bullet-hell game, with a map and screen layout which is reminiscent of OG Zelda.  It's even got some dungeons to explore, each with its own ability to unlock and use to then explore more of the map.  I enjoyed it a lot.  There are different levels of difficulty to help players (or make them hurt).  In about 8.5 hours, I'd completed the game on 'medium' difficulty and very nearly gotten everything.  Graphics are solid, game mechanics are good, the boss fights are generally well thought out, and overall it is a fun experience.If I had to complain about anything, I was troubled more than a couple times by screen transitions pulling back the view until your ship/character is about 60% of its regular size and that throws me every time.  One section in particular I very nearly always lose track of my ship amongst a sea of enemy fire, and that enemy fire is a one-shot.  I wish I had control over the zoom in/out, because in a bullet hell that inconsistency hasn't been very fun.  Thankfully, these transitions are very limited.

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend Minishoot' Adventures because it is a very finely tuned experience; it knows what it has to offer, executes it incredibly well, and doesn't overstay its welcome.Minishoot' Adventure is a 2D Zelda-style adventure where you play as a little ship. You move with the left stick and shoot with the right stick. You explore the not-too-large world, level up, defeat dungeon bosses, and gain new abilities. The controls and gameplay are very simple. What's unique is the blend of this type of adventure game with twin-stick shooting and how well they work together in this game.The strengths of this game are exploration and combat, both of which are very simple and satisfying. I really enjoyed exploring the world and finding all of the items. Every path has some kind of reward, and the reward felt appropriate for the effort. Movement in combat is tight. Enemy bullets rarely feel unavoidable. As you progress in the game, the enemies become more difficult to deal with and you gain more ability to work with. The pacing of the game was perfect for me. The world opens up as you progress but never reveals too much at once. The game expected me to get better but I never hit a wall that tested my skill and patience.Some features that I appreciated:What to expect:

_childDocuments_.review: A great adventure game with an unfortunate name XDAfter 10 minutes in the demo, I jumped out and bought it. I really enjoyed this game and recently finished it on normal difficulty. There's a nice progression with various upgrades, and the controls are sharp and responsive. The boss fights were fun, with some great 'bullet hell' moments.It's not story-heavy at all, but you'll slowly be given visual hints as to who you are and what you're doing.It's a great game that I'm looking forward to playing through again on hard. Minishoot Adventures has a great foundation/design that could be used for DLC and/or a sequel, which I'd happily pay for.Pros:- A unique mix of 2D Zelda and twin-stick/multidirectional shoot 'em ups- Polished game and interface, with cohesive art design and thoughtful settings/options- Well-balanced difficultyCons:A couple minor cons that come to mind, though nothing major..- The name is too generic. Sorry but "Minishoot' Adventure" sounds like the name of a crappy old 80s LCD game XDWhen I first saw the poster for the game on Steam, I almost dismissed it instantly. The apostrophe ' makes it even more weird.- I would've liked a little more variety with enemies. The bush enemies, for example, were great. - The south forest section of the map has very few enemies. I thought maybe it would fill up with enemies later in the game, but it didn't happen. Seemed a bit strange.Try the demo, see if you like it :)

_childDocuments_.review: Couldn't put this one down. It oozes charm, is extremely well polished, and is an absolute blast to play. The main content is enough to justify the price and your time, but there's also a really nice endgame with additional challenges. It's one of only a few games I've played in the past few years that felt like the 100% experience was worth it. Congrats to the team; thanks for the amazing game, and I hope we get a sequel once you're proper rested!
_childDocuments_.name: Minishoot' Adventures

_childDocuments_.review: As others have said, this is a twinstick shooter combined with Zelda-like exploration. And it works really well! The sense of exploration is excellent, and the world is dense with secrets. You have to collect map pieces to fill in the world map, and since these are well hidden, you will often be forced to explore huge areas with no map. I really like this! It makes the world feel immense!The shooting and RPG elements also work well. I turned the difficulty up to its highest setting, and the so far it isn't too bad. I have to pay attention to the bullets, and sometimes I die, but it never seems impossible.The cute graphics, alien landscapes, and anthropomorphic ships remind me of Fantasy Zone, and I expect that is intentional on the part of the developers.
_childDocuments_.name: Minishoot' Adventures

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic compact experience. All my playtime was on the Steam Deck and it played wonderfully. Boss fights were challenging, elite enemies were plentiful and also provided enough challenge of their own. My only gripe is I kept getting lost and going in circles and not completely sure where to go to next. I think the map could use a badge system to leave notes. Other than that when it clicks, exploring feels pretty good and finding how they scatter secrets around felt satisfying to find out.
_childDocuments_.name: Minishoot' Adventures

_childDocuments_.review: Waited till I 100% this game before writing - it's an absolute brilliance of a game and one of my favorites to come out in years.The world design, bullet hell pattern complexity, and overall leveling mechanics and abilities are like nothing I've played before. The only negative thing I can say about this game is the bullet noise sfx - it's incredibly irritating and I wish they would have used another sound. Thankfully you can mute this in the settings, but just wish I didn't have to. Review time doesn't display correctly, but I put about 25-30 hours on this game for 100% on a single advanced difficulty playthrough. If you want all achievements just start from advanced and max out on your first play - there is no NG+; in the end game you wipe your save file as part of the story. Pick this one up, it's an absolute steal for $15.
_childDocuments_.name: Minishoot' Adventures

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful, 12 hour Zelda/bullet hell mashup. Minishoot Adventures' tight design propelled me ever forward, compelling me to keep playing to find one more secret before bed. There are so many fun upgrades and new ways to explore as you help rebuild a small, central HUB, with each rescued inhabitant adding some new way to spend currency, unlock lore, etc. With multiple endings, a post-game arena, and a story that is more heartfelt than I thought a purely ship-based cast of characters had any right to be, Minishoot Adventures is an absolute hidden gem and delight.
_childDocuments_.name: Minishoot' Adventures

_childDocuments_.review: A very fun game that combines twin-stick shooters and old-school Zelda-esque exploration. This game was a genre combination I honestly had never even considered, and the execution was essentially flawless. I spent just under 12 hours to 100% complete it, which normally falls under my general 2 hours per dollar spent metric, but it was so charming and well crafted that I am happy I was able to experience it. I recommend this to anyone who enjoys twinstick shooters or old-school exploration.Note: The game is relatively easy if you are a veteran of the genre, even on the hardest difficulty. And for exploration focused people, it is not super in depth, though there are some secrets to be found.Overall though, I give this a solid 10/10 on a good day, and a 8/10 if I am feeling more critical. Very much worth the price if you enjoy this type of game and can afford the cost, and 100% worth it on sale. Keep an eye on these devs, I think they will produce further gold for a long time to come.
_childDocuments_.name: Minishoot' Adventures

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a very pleasant surprise.First of all, it's a perfect Steam Deck game. Except at the very end, in the arena, where the performance is not as smooth. I also faced 2 freezes that forced me to shut down the game during my 9 hour journey. Fortunately I didn't lose much progress.Bit of a personal preference, but I also recommend turning off the lens filter.This game strikes a great balance between arcade and progression with its unique mix of genres. Creating something that feels this way, that is so easy to pick up and play but at the same time sets you on an adventure with such a progression is not easy to accomplish, so kudos to the devs.The biggest compliment I can give this game is that, even though I have a huge backlog, this game grabbed in such a way that I pretty much exclusively played it from start to end.
_childDocuments_.name: Minishoot' Adventures

_childDocuments_.review: I can't remember the last time I locked in on a game with zero distractions for 7+ hours in one sitting. _childDocuments_.name: Minishoot' Adventures

_childDocuments_.name: Minishoot' Adventures

_childDocuments_.review: A Refreshing Blend of Genres Done Well     This game is in many ways like the original Legend of Zelda except Link is now a spaceship and you get into fights with other ships that result in something closer to Galaga, Centipede, or some other '80's arcade top-down shooter game.  In essence, you are introduced to the world, and you head off in whatever direction you want (although some areas are gated by powers you gain along the way) not knowing what you may find in any given cave.  It does provide a slight bit of guidance by indicating the location of the next dungeon and its means of opening it on your map, but otherwise, you are on your own.The Good:-Controls are excellent, the twin-stick movement/aim works really well and you have firm control over your ships movement everywhere (except where you're not supposed to of course)-Visuals are nicely animated and even in the heaviest bullet storms you can still see yourself clearly enough without losing track of the fight-Audio is alright with decent music and sound fx-Doesn't overstay its welcome; I completed everything in the game (including the post-game) on the middle difficulty in about 11 hours and had a great time for about all of it.  I'd like more, but that's where you should be left at the end.The Bad:-Really just a technical issue.  The game crashed on me a few times when I entered a newly opened cave, and sometimes glitched if I tried to call up the map too quickly after exiting a cave, but everything worked fine again upon reloading it.The Bottomline:     This is a fantastic effort and result of a game by essentially 2 persons that is well-worth the time and efforts of the player.  Lots of optional upgrades and 'objects' to find, several cleverly designed dungeons, temples, and caves, and incredibly fun gameplay.  The game respects the player's time with minimal backtracking, and provides sufficient upgrade resources for you to proceed at your own pace without grinding.  I had a great time with it and compliment the developers on their results.  If you like Legend of Zelda and top-down shooter type games, odds are you'll have a good time here.  Be sure to check out the free demo if you are uncertain.  Good gaming to you all!
_childDocuments_.name: Minishoot' Adventures

_childDocuments_.review: This is an easy recommendation from me. The moment to moment gameplay is fun and engaging as is exploring this little world and finding secrets. _childDocuments_.review: I LOVE THIS GAME (despite being absolute ♥♥♥♥ with twin-stick shooters).This is a twin-stick shooter action-adventure game: you are a little spaceship who has to save their friends and kill the bad spaceships. Big bad bosses, smaller bad bosses and little bad enemies to annihilate.Even though I'm a disaster and died over and over again, I still had a blast. _childDocuments_.name: Minishoot' Adventures

_childDocuments_.review: Very good game. I had a lot of fun with it. It does lean more zelda like than twin stick shooter, and the shooter sections that are here are pretty easy.If you've played stuff like nuclear throne or enter the gungeon, try playing advanced mode first. The biggest con for me is the game has inertia in the water areas. Now this is only an issue when fighting enemies, as a lot of times it more has to due with puzzle solving or platforming. But when fighting enemies on the water it becomes a real pain.The game is also quite short. My playtime is for 100% all achievements. Plus a 3 heart playthrough for advanced mode.Although if you are a newcomer to twin stick shooters, you will get your moneys worth. Otherwise wait for a saleOverall good game 7/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Minishoot' Adventures

_childDocuments_.review: Minishoot Adventures is a really good game. Pretty basic, but absolutely polished where it needs to be.The game-play is pretty much perfect, at least in the Normal/Original difficulty. Hard, but manageable. No dodging, but the movement can always get you out of a situation, and if you get hit, it will be your fault. Never used the automatic shooting option, but hey, I can't complain about an accessibility option.The movement is probably the best aspect of the game. I found it so good to just roam through areas I've already been through because it really feels like gliding. Some areas are more slippery, but the game isn't too punishing, unless it's an area that uses one-shot bullets, but those only appear like 6 times max.This game is a Metroidvania, and about half of the power-ups completely change how the game is played. The others are pretty much only used to open up something, but are still incredibly useful in combatThere are a lot of extra power-ups that you don't have to obtain, but are incredibly satisfying. Some of them are default powers in other games, but going through most of the game without them makes it feel so rewarding. I will not go into detail, but the way you obtain one of them is such a video-game thing to do and also probably the most memorable part of the game. The power-up you get is also the most powerful one.The only issue I had was on my way to the second boss: The game lasted me for about 11 hours. I 100% the map, but still haven't done the post-game stuff. Maybe I'll even try to do the higher difficulty to get all of the achievements.8 or 9/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Minishoot' Adventures

_childDocuments_.review: Bullet hell games are not usually my strength, but  is so damn accessible that it makes it an absolute joy to play from start to finish, including the secret endboss and the subsequent arena. I generally don't play arenas in games, but I did play it in this game, because the movement, shooting and difficulty level was just about right. The Zelda-/Metroidvania-esque progression through the world with puzzles, items and upgrades to find, secret locations to explore and, again, a very satisfying difficulty curve is just about perfect. This is one of the best "pick up and play" games I have played in quite a while (and I play a lot of games, maybe too many...). Also one of the rare games I (nearly) 100% completed (only things missing are some upgrades tied to experience, but I didn't want to needlessly grind enemies for that; speaking of which, grinding is not necessary in this game). I wholeheartedly recommend  and hope to see more games of this quality from the developer.
_childDocuments_.name: Minishoot' Adventures

_childDocuments_.review: This game is one one of the best Zelda-likes since Death's Door. While seemingly simple, Minishoot' Adventures is creative and filled with interesting secrets. _childDocuments_.review: HESITANT recommend. Too many reviews here are ignoring some really big problems this game has. I ultimately recommend it because there's plenty here to love, and I won't drone on about that since that's what every other review here does (and I agree with much of it) So for anyone looking for a slightly more critical review, here ya go:Color: there are only a couple types of projectiles, but they are all shades of orange and red. This is frankly unacceptable for even people without colorblindness, let alone anyone else. Even on explorer difficulty it becomes very very hard to track a lot of the action.Difficultly scaling: not sure I've ever played a wonkier game when it comes to this. I found myself playing the first half of the game on Advanced (I'm a geometry wars vet), but then I hit a completely inexplicable difficulty spike in the 3rd dungeon and popped back down to Original. No biggie there. Except now the game throws a ton of instakill projectiles (that are kinda pink?) and double damage projectiles. Not too crazy until they become overused in the last third of the game and suddenly it's more of a "ship dodger" than a shop shooter. Additionally, the difficulty levels are great QoL, except that they only control projectile and enemy speed. Please tell me why it takes an agonizingly long time to kill every darker tinted enemy even with max damage, rate, bullet speed, and supershot? The last monster closets of the game are just about as fun as a root canal. It's just locked section after section with instakill projectiles on narrow walkways. You don't die if you fall off, unless you respawn on the platform that's covered in instakill balls.This makes even the explorer difficultly level incredibly tedious to play. Additionally there are some big time low effort sections that were very disappointing. All 3 (not 4) of the dungeons look identical and could really be the same dungeon. All of the mini dungeon areas are visually distinct but the main dungeons are functionally identical. Very weird choice.Equally weird is the choice to crib one of the lamest Zelda game structures. So we get to the 4th dungeon and it's not a dungeon, we just get the unlock and move on. This is lazy as ♥♥♥♥ when Nintendo does it and was downright bizarre in a game like this. So I can recommend it because there's enough stuff to like (please see other reviews for the good stuff), but definitely know what to expect if any of the above sounds dicey to you.  I sincerely hope the dev team makes a sequel or spiritual successor and makes better UI and balance decisions.
_childDocuments_.name: Minishoot' Adventures

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those games that seems so obvious when you see it that you'll be asking yourself why you didn't think of it first. It plays a lot like you'd expect based on the description of a Zelda-like twin stick shooter and it's well made and challenging. If you have any interest in the top down style Zelda games or twin stick shooters I say it's worth trying.EDIT after beating: Beat the game and it took me a little under 12 hours. I wish it was longer but the 12 hours really flew by and it felt like a lot less.I'd also say the game is challenging but not quite challenging enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Minishoot' Adventures

_childDocuments_.review: It's very easy to compare this to an old school Zelda and Metroid, but its so unique in it's own right that it stands apart from them. Sure the adventuring is very Link to the Past and discovering upgrades is very similar to Metroid, but this game has so much character. The combat is addicting (if you are an Enter the Gungeon fan, you will enjoy the combat), the world is charming, the non-linear aspect was so cool. I never had to look anything up secret wise because while it may be difficult to search sometimes, its seamless when exploring the world. Bosses were engaging, the dungeons were exciting to explore, seeking out all upgrades and power-ups were just so much fun to keep playing. Even the end-game content was very fun. _childDocuments_.name: Minishoot' Adventures

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful little adventure twin stick shooter. Definite recommend at the full 15€ price, and a no-brainer pick up if it goes on sale for 10€ or lower.The game is pretty simple, but the level of execution and polish is really nice. It looks and feels great to play the whole way through. Nice very simple "story" and characters that add just a touch of personality. The game offers some challenge but isn't punishing, so overall it's pretty easy to progress and you never really feel frustrated. I imagine the hard mode will satisfy those looking for a harder experience.I would have liked a bit more customization (maybe picking different weapon loadouts so you can change your playstyle), but the game is short enough that it wasn't a big deal.In normal difficulty, it took me 7 hours to reach the credits at 100% completion, and 10 hours to finish everything (all achievements except hard mode). Finishing the game is "easy" enough for most people to reach, and the post-game is a nice level of challenge if you still want more.I liked the little meta "easter egg" at the very, very end, putting a nice bow on this tight experience.Looking forward to this studio's next game. (Also, is it weird that I guessed it was a french game as I was playing it? lol)
_childDocuments_.name: Minishoot' Adventures

_childDocuments_.review: I just want to say after randomly coming across this game in my discovery queue, it's a really fantastic game among so many other indie games and deserves any recognition it gets. It was short but so sweet, and you guys did everything very well.The sound design is amazing, you really know how to reward people with great audio and visuals, puzzles are intuitive and encourage exploration, and having grown up with those old retro titles, this really feels like a spiritual successor to the sort of gaming that emerged from the late 80's and 90's and takes us back to a time where games weren't afraid to explore new ideas and game styles. It doesn't matter that it follows in the footsteps of a tried and true formula for a particular genre of gaming because it meshes unique gameplay with a fun story that's easy to digest for new and old players.If a Minishoot Adventures 2 ever comes out, I'll be there to get it because of how impressive this game was.This game features:- Gradual Power Ramp through XP earned by killing enemies. Spend on talents and re-talent as you see fit anytime.- Permanent Treasures which provide passive boosts to various aspects of gameplay found all over the map and in dungeons.- Fast Travel on the Overworld Map (Once you find a certain something which lets you do it.)- Mini Races! (Completely Optional, but worth doing. Trust me, I'm a Moose.)- Variable Difficulty, (I recommend Normal first and then trying it on Advanced, but there is an Easy Mode as well.)- A killer soundtrack, you will love it instantly.- Checkpoints at all areas of interest so you can try over and over should you fall in combat.- Intuitive and smooth controls, never felt janky or counterintuitive. The game does recommend a controller but keyboard and mouse works just fine, did not encounter any difficulty due to the setup.- Short and Sweet, to the point. The game can be completed very quickly if you only focus on the main story, but even with exploration and a little intuition I was able to complete the main story in 9 hours, with plenty still left to do. Great for someone who doesn't have a lot of time or a person who wants something new to plow through in a day. Won't elaborate so no spoilers. :)If you enjoy bullet hell type games, metroidvania style exploration and acquisition, and a classic story about being the hero, this is the game for you. Couldn't recommend it enough!
_childDocuments_.name: Minishoot' Adventures

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing little twin-stick metroidvania. Reminiscent of early Zelda games with snappy modern bullet hell combat. The 8bit-esque soundtrack and CRT monitor perspective effect revive the 80's nostalgia. The dialogue-free characters are cute and the difficulty strikes a nice balance of fun & challenge. Feels good, plays good. Game is on the short side, but well worth the money. These 2 devs are putting the big studios to shame with a game as good as this. Just play it.
_childDocuments_.name: Minishoot' Adventures

_childDocuments_.review: Great game. I have neurological problems making it very hard for me to play any games. I didn't think I'd ever be able to play a twin stick shooter but this game has accessibility options! I choose normal difficulty and lowered the game speed to 80% (I think) and I'm managing pretty well plus you can change the difficulty and accessibility options at anytime! I know you think it was a dead-end but when you found the key you got so excited that you remembered where it goes that you forgot to check the other path...
_childDocuments_.name: Minishoot' Adventures

_childDocuments_.review: This game was really, really lovely! I loved all the side content I found on the way. An easy recommend from me!
